exp.14:5:
Genesis 15:6 says that Abram believed what God promised him, and God counted him righteous because of that. "Believed in the Lord" means that he trusted God and his word. "Counted it to him for righteousness" means that God reckoned it to his account, as if he were a person living uprightly before Him.

God had just brought Abram out of his tent and told him to look at the stars, because his descendants would be just as numerous. Abram still had no children and was already old. Even so, he believed. After this verse, he himself asks how he will know that he will inherit the land, which shows that his faith was real, but also human.

Today, this invites us to trust God even when we do not see how his promise will be fulfilled. We can speak to him honestly, even with doubts, and still rely on his word.
exp.20:28:
Abimelech asks Abraham why he has set apart seven ewe lambs from the flock. In this older wording, "and" appears where modern English would use it normally, and "ewe lambs" are young female sheep. Abimelech does not understand the gesture and asks for an explanation.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, speaks. He and Abraham have just made a covenant, and Abraham had earlier had a dispute with the king's servants over a well. By setting apart the seven ewe lambs, Abraham prepares a visible sign. He then explains that, by receiving them, Abimelech would acknowledge that Abraham dug that well. This is where the name Beersheba comes from, which is commonly understood to mean "well of the oath" or "well of the seven."

For today: when there is a misunderstanding, it is better to clear things up honestly and peacefully, leaving agreements clear, rather than letting tension grow from assumptions.
exp.31:12:
The explanation says that Jacob spent the night in that place and that, from what was within his reach, he set aside a gift for his brother Esau. "Within his reach" means "available," what he had at his disposal. A "present" is a gift, and "slept" tells us that, despite his fear, he rested that night.

Jacob was returning to his own land after many years, and he learned that Esau was coming to meet him. Years earlier he had deceived him, and now he feared his reaction. So he prayed to God, reminding him of his promise, and then prepared this gift to soften the meeting. The texts do not say exactly what Esau expected, so Jacob prepares himself with prayer and with action.

For today: when you face a broken relationship, pray with sincerity and also take concrete steps toward reconciliation, such as asking forgiveness or making a generous gesture. Trust God, but do not sit with your arms folded.
exp.30:39:
Here Jacob describes how hard his work as a shepherd was. During the day the heat wore him out, and at night the intense cold, the "frost," struck him. Also, "sleep departed from my eyes" means that he could hardly sleep, because he had to look after the flock.

The speaker is Jacob, and he is addressing his father-in-law Laban. After twenty years of service, Laban pursued him and accused him. Jacob defends himself and reminds Laban of his faithfulness: he took good care of the sheep, took responsibility for the losses, and worked without rest. Then he says that God saw his effort.

For today: God sees the quiet, sacrificial work that no one recognizes. Do your work with integrity, even when it costs you or no one thanks you, and trust that God knows what you go through.
exp.37:15:
Judah sees a woman by the road and turns aside to speak with her. He says, "Come now, let me come in unto thee," which is a way of saying, "Come, then," and proposes to lie with her. The text makes clear that he did not know she was his daughter-in-law. She asks him what he will give her in return.

Judah is the son of Jacob. Tamar, widow of his sons, had covered herself with a veil because Judah had not given his son Shelah to her as a husband, as was the custom of that time. Judah, who had just lost his wife, took her for a prostitute. Many see here a Tamar who seeks justice, and a Judah who failed in his duty.

For today: when a decision is made on impulse, we tend to see only what we want to see. Before acting, stop, pray, and ask yourself whether your decision honors God and the people who depend on you.
exp.29:8:
Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, so she took Zilpah, her servant, and gave her to Jacob as a wife. "Bearing" means giving birth, and "gave her" is the plain meaning of the verse.

The narrator tells this in the middle of the rivalry between Leah and her sister Rachel. Rachel had just celebrated that her servant Bilhah had a second son. Leah responded in the same way: she used her servant to add children to the family. In that culture, having children brought honor and security. The Bible records the event, but it does not present it as an example to imitate.

When we compare ourselves with others, it is easy to make hasty decisions so that we do not fall behind. Before acting, stop to pray and ask whether you are trusting God or only competing.
exp.39:9:
This verse describes part of the dream of Pharaoh's cupbearer. In the vine there were three branches, or "shoots." The plant seemed to bud, its blossoms shot forth, and its clusters ripened into grapes quickly. It is an image of life, growth, and fruit reaching its full ripeness.

The cupbearer is in prison with Joseph, together with the baker. Both are troubled by their dreams, and no one explains them. Joseph tells them that interpretations belong to God and invites them to tell their dreams. Here the cupbearer speaks and recounts what he dreamed. Afterward Joseph will explain that the three branches are three days.

For today: Joseph does not boast of having wisdom of his own, but recognizes that God is the one who gives understanding. When you have doubts or worries, bring them to God first, and seek his guidance with humility before relying only on your own judgment.
exp.28:16:
This verse compares the two daughters of Laban. It says that Leah's eyes were "tender," a word that can mean delicate, soft, or weak, and scholars do not agree on its exact sense. Of Rachel it says that she was "beautiful and well favoured," with the sense of a pleasing face and a good figure.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob has been living with his uncle Laban and working for him for some time. Laban offers him wages, and the text introduces the two daughters to explain why Jacob will ask for Rachel as payment. Right away it becomes clear that he loved her.

For today: it is easy to judge people by their appearance, and that can hurt others and cause envy. Let us ask God to teach us to value each person as He sees them, with respect and affection.
exp.6:2:
God commands Noah to take birds into the ark as well, seven pairs of each, male and female. The word "kind" here means species or offspring. The purpose is to "keep seed alive," that is, so that the birds would not disappear from the earth after the flood.

The one speaking is the LORD, addressing Noah, whom he sees as righteous in his generation. He had already instructed Noah to take clean animals by sevens and the unclean ones by twos. Some think the greater number could have served for sacrifices or food after the flood; the text does not fully explain this. What is clear is that God wanted to preserve life.

For today: God attends to the details of what he does, and he invites us to obey him even when we do not understand everything. Today you can trust him and faithfully carry out a specific task he has given you, as Noah did.
exp.30:14:
Here Rachel and Leah ask whether their father Laban is not already treating them as foreigners. They say he has "sold" them, since he received Jacob's work in exchange for giving them in marriage, and that he has also "quite devoured" their money, that is, he has used up completely what should have been theirs. The King James wording "strangers" means outsiders, people who do not belong to the family.

Jacob has told them that God commanded him to return to his land. They answer that they no longer have any portion or inheritance in their father's house. Some scholars think they are referring to customs of the time concerning the dowry, but the text does not give all the details. What is clear is that they feel mistreated and they side with Jacob.

For today: when God calls you to a difficult change, seek the counsel and unity of your family. And if there are wounds from injustices, ask God for wisdom to obey him without bitterness.
exp.3:3:
Abel also brought an offering to God: the best of his flock, the firstborn lambs and their choicest part. The word "fat" in the King James text refers to the fat, the most valuable part of the animal.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Cain and Abel, the sons of Adam and Eve, bring offerings to God. The text does not clearly explain why God accepted one and not the other. Some think the attitude of the heart mattered; others, the quality of the offering. Hebrews 11:4 says that Abel offered "by faith."

God deserves the best of us, not the leftovers. Before giving time, money or service, ask yourself honestly: am I doing it with gratitude and trust in God, or only to fulfill an obligation?
exp.25:18:
This verse tells that Isaac's servants dug in the valley of Gerar and found a well of "living water." That expression means water that springs or flows from a source, not stagnant water or water kept in a cistern. In a dry land, that was a great treasure.

The one telling the story is the author of the book of Genesis, who recounts the life of Isaac. He lived as a foreigner among the Philistines. He had reopened the wells that his father Abraham had dug and that the Philistines had stopped up. The wells were vital for the livestock and the family. That is why disputes over water come right after this.

For today: God can provide for us in the midst of difficult places, but sometimes we must keep working with patience. Isaac did not give up or respond with violence. He keeps digging, trusts God, and receives with gratitude what He gives you.
exp.46:6:
Joseph brought his father Jacob before Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, and presented him. Then Jacob blessed Pharaoh. "Brought in" means that he caused him to enter, and "presented" means "set him before" the king. To bless here can be understood as wishing him well and asking that God would favor him.

This is the account of the meeting between Jacob, already an old man, and the most powerful ruler of his time. The family had come to Egypt because of the famine, and Joseph, who held authority in the kingdom, accompanied them. Pharaoh had already offered them the land of Goshen. Some think Jacob blessed as a man who knew that God was caring for his family, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: we can honor those in authority and wish them well, without ceasing to trust in God. Praying for those who govern is a practical way of blessing them.
exp.0:26:
This verse says that God created human beings in his own image. The word for "created" is "created," and "male and female" means man and woman. The phrase "in the image of God" is repeated to stress that this is the most important point: every human being has a very special value.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who tells of the creation. Just before, God makes a decision: "Let us make man in our image." After creating the animals, God creates humankind and blesses them, giving them the task of caring for the earth. Scholars explain in several ways what "image" means: it can mean dignity, the capacity to relate to others, or the responsibility to care for creation.

For today: treat each person, even someone you find difficult, as someone created by God and of great worth. That changes how you speak, how you listen, and how you help.
exp.10:8:
This verse explains why the city was called Babel. There the Lord "confounded" the language of everyone, that is, he caused them to stop understanding one another. From that place he scattered them across the whole earth.

The narrator closes the story of the tower. The people wanted to build a city and a tower to make a name for themselves and to avoid being scattered (Genesis 11:4). God intervened and halted that project. Some see here a judgment against human pride; others emphasize that God was directing humanity to fill the earth. Many see both. The name "Babel" is often connected with the Hebrew verb meaning "to confuse," although the name is also linked with "Babylon."

For today: do not seek to make your name great without taking God into account. Place your plans in his hands and work with humility, seeking the unity that is built under his guidance.
exp.30:16:
The explanation says that Jacob got moving and put his sons and his wives up on the camels. This is the moment when the journey back begins. "Put up" here means that he mounted them or arranged them for the road.

The narrator tells what Jacob does after hearing Rachel and Leah. They told him that their father Laban treated them as strangers, and that Jacob should do what God had commanded him. Earlier, God had told him to return to the land of his fathers. Jacob acts quickly, while Laban was away shearing sheep.

For today: when you know what God is asking of you, understanding it is not enough; you have to take the step. And it is good to do it while caring for your family, with order and attention to each person, trusting that God goes with you.
exp.3:25:
Genesis 4:26 says that Seth had a son and named him Enos, which means "man" or "mortal." At that time people began to call upon the name of the Lord. The phrase "call upon the name of the Lord" can be understood as praying to God and worshipping him. Some think this was the beginning of public worship; others think it was a time of deeper prayer.

The speaker is the narrator of Genesis. Earlier, the story told of Cain's violence and Lamech's arrogance. Now the account turns to the family of Seth, born after the death of Abel, where faith in God is still alive. It is a contrast with pride and revenge.

For today: even when the world around you seems harsh or violent, you can choose to call upon the name of God. Begin with a simple prayer each day, and perhaps invite your family to pray with you.
exp.42:19:
Here the brothers of Joseph say to the steward: "Oh, sir, truly we came down the first time only to buy food." The phrase "in very truth" means "with complete sincerity." The word "came down" refers to their going down into Egypt from Canaan. "Food" means the grain they would eat.

The brothers are frightened because they are being taken to Joseph's house. They remember that on the previous trip they found their money inside their sacks, and they fear they will be accused of theft. That is why they speak first with the steward, before going in, and explain their intentions. They do not know that the governor is their brother Joseph.

For today: when we feel guilty or misunderstood, it is good to speak with clarity and honesty, hiding nothing. And even when we do not understand what God is doing, we can trust that He works even behind what frightens us.
exp.43:0:
It says that Joseph gave an order to the person in charge of his house, the steward. He was to fill his brothers' sacks with food, "as much as they can carry," that is, as much as they were able to bear. He was also to put each man's money back in the mouth of his sack, that is, in the opening at the top. "These men" in the older wording is simply "these men."

Joseph speaks here as governor of Egypt. His brothers had come a second time to buy grain, and he had not yet told them who he was. The verse that follows shows that he was preparing a test: he put his silver cup in the sack of the youngest. The Bible does not explain this here, but many think he wanted to know whether they had changed and whether they would protect Benjamin.

For today: Joseph's generosity invites us to bless others even when they have been unfair to us. And when the truth is tested in difficult moments, it is good to ask God for a sincere and faithful heart.
exp.17:11:
Sarah laughs inwardly, without anyone hearing her, and wonders whether at her age she can still have "pleasure," that is, joy or delight, when her husband is also already old. "Within herself" means in her inner being, and "my lord" is how she refers to Abraham.

Three visitors, one of them the Lord, have arrived at Abraham's tent. One of them promises that Sarah will have a son. She listens from the entrance of the tent. Since she is now very old and has been unable to conceive for years, the promise seems impossible to her. Her laughter sounds like doubt, although some think it also mixes wonder and pain over a long-held hope.

Today we can be honest with God about our doubts. He knows them, and still asks us: "Is anything too hard for the Lord?" You can entrust to him whatever seems impossible.
exp.20:25:
Abimelech answers that he does not know who took Abraham's well. He says that Abraham had never told him and that he himself had only just heard of it that very day. "Reproved" (from the previous verse) means that Abraham rebuked him or complained to him.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, speaks alongside Abraham. The king's servants had taken a well, something very valuable in a dry land. Abraham complains, and Abimelech defends himself by saying he was not aware of it. Afterward they make a covenant. The Bible does not say whether Abimelech was telling the whole truth or only distancing himself from responsibility; the text does not make this clear.

For today: when something bothers us, let us speak face to face and calmly, without holding on to resentment. Often the other person does not even know the problem, and a sincere conversation can lead to peace and a fair agreement.
exp.44:15:
The explanation says that the news reached the palace of the king of Egypt: Joseph's brothers had arrived. The phrase "it pleased Pharaoh well" is an old way of saying that something was pleasing or welcome. Pharaoh and his servants were glad to hear it.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joseph has just revealed himself to his brothers, who had sold him years earlier, and he has wept with them. Pharaoh had already seen Joseph's wisdom and owed him a great deal, since Egypt had been saved from famine through his work. That is why he rejoices with Joseph's family and, right away, invites them to live in Egypt.

For today: when God restores a broken relationship, the joy does not stay private but reaches others. Let us seek to be reconciled and to rejoice in the reconciliations of others, without envy or distrust.
exp.44:7:
Here Joseph tells his brothers that it was not they who sent him to Egypt, but God. He made him a "father to Pharaoh," that is, a very close and respected counselor to the king. He also made him lord of his house and ruler over all the land of Egypt.

Joseph is speaking to the brothers who had sold him as a slave years earlier. Now there is famine, and they have come without knowing that he is the ruler. When he reveals himself, Joseph reassures them: he does not deny their guilt, but he sees that God used even the evil to save many lives.

For today: when someone has hurt you, trusting that God can work even through painful things helps you let go of resentment. That does not excuse the wrong, but it allows you to forgive and to seek reconciliation with hope.
exp.13:12:
The verse says that someone who had escaped from the battle came to Abram with the news. "Told" here simply means that he reported what had happened. "The Hebrew" is the first time Abram is given that name. "Confederate" means that they had an alliance or a pact of friendship with him. Mamre, Eshcol, and Aner were Amorites, allies of Abram.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Invading kings had just defeated Sodom and Gomorrah and carried off Lot as a prisoner. The text does not say who the fugitive was or why he went to Abram, but thanks to his warning Abram was able to act to rescue his nephew.

For today: when you learn that someone in your family is in trouble, do not stay silent or indifferent. Let others know, pray, and help however you can. Also take care of your friendships, because good allies are valuable in hard times.
exp.17:5:
The explanation says that Abraham went quickly into the tent and asked Sarah to prepare bread right away. The words "hastened" and "quickly" convey speed. Three measures of fine meal were a generous amount of flour, of the best quality. The bread was baked "upon the hearth," that is, among hot embers and ashes.

Abraham speaks with Sarah. Three visitors had arrived at his tent, and he offered them rest and food. They accepted, and he hurried to prepare everything. The text later reveals that one of them is the Lord. Abraham did not know this at first, since he treated them as travelers. Some interpreters see in this a foreshadowing of the Trinity, and others do not; the question is debated.

Today we can practice hospitality with generosity and a good spirit. Abraham did not give what was left over, but the best. Perhaps today you can invite someone to your table, without overcomplicating things, and do it with joy.
exp.20:16:
God heard the voice of the boy, who is Ishmael. Then the angel of God spoke to Hagar from heaven. He asked her what was wrong, told her not to be afraid, and assured her that God had heard the boy right where he was.

Two words in the explanation need a comment: a "waterskin" is a leather bag for carrying water, and to "take hold" of something is to grip it firmly. (These two words are not in the verse as the reader sees it, so they are explained here as glosses on the passage's imagery.)

Hagar and her son had been sent away from Abraham's house and were lost in the wilderness of Beersheba. Their water ran out, and she, in despair, moved away so she would not have to watch him die. The account says that God heard the boy's voice, and then opened Hagar's eyes to see a well.

When you feel you have no resources and no way out, do not think that God does not see you. Cry out to Him sincerely. He hears the pain, and often He helps us discover the provision that was already close by.
exp.6:3:
God tells Noah that in seven more days he will make it rain for forty days and forty nights. "Blot out" means "remove completely" or "wipe out." "Substance" refers to every living thing that God had created on the earth.

God (Jehovah) speaks to Noah, just after giving him instructions to enter the ark with the animals. Humanity had filled the earth with wickedness and violence, and God decided to judge the earth. At the same time, he gave a week of waiting so that Noah could finish preparing. Scholars debate how far-reaching the flood was, but the text emphasizes God's judgment and care.

For today: God keeps what he says, and he also gives us time to obey. Noah did everything "as the LORD had commanded him." Today we can ask ourselves: is there something God has already asked of me that I am putting off? Let us obey with confidence, today.
exp.16:13:
The explanation says that any male who is not circumcised, that is, who has not had the foreskin (the skin covering the tip of the member) cut away, will be "cut off from his people." That means he would be separated from the community of the covenant. God gives the reason: that person "has broken my covenant," that is, he has rejected or disregarded it.

God is speaking to Abraham when He confirms His covenant with him. Circumcision was the visible sign of that covenant, and it was applied to sons and to the servants of the household. Interpreters debate whether "cut off" refers to death, to exile, or to exclusion from the people. The text does not specify.

For today: God desires a faith that shows in one's life, not only in words. We can ask ourselves what concrete signs show that we belong to Him.
exp.18:12:
The angels tell Lot that they are going to destroy Sodom. The "cry" refers to the complaints raised over so much wickedness and injustice, which has "waxen great", meaning it has grown to a very serious level. God sent them to carry out the judgment. The KJV's "waxen great" is an older way of saying "has grown great".

The two angels speak; they had the appearance of men and visited Lot. They had just struck the violent men of the city with blindness. Now they urge Lot to bring his family out. Earlier, in chapter 18, God had said he would see whether the cry was true. The passage shows a just judgment, and at the same time a warning that gives an opportunity to be saved.

For today: God sees injustice and hears it. If He warns us, let us not take it lightly as Lot's sons-in-law did. Let us heed His voice with humility and act quickly.
exp.24:7:
This verse tells of the death of Abraham. "Gave up the ghost" means that he stopped breathing and died. It says he died "in a good old age," that is, as an old man and at peace, and "full of years," meaning after a long and full life. "Was gathered to his people" is an old way of speaking of being joined with his own people who had already died. Some believe it points to a hope beyond the grave, although the text does not explain this.

The narrator of Genesis closes the story of Abraham here. Before he died, he gave gifts to the sons of his concubines and sent them away, so that Isaac would remain the heir of God's promise. Abraham lived 175 years. Afterward, his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him beside Sarah.

For today: a life well lived is not measured only by its length, but by faithfulness to God. We can prepare our family with order, generosity, and trust, and leave the future in God's hands.
exp.21:1:
God speaks to Abraham and asks him to take his son Isaac, the only one he has with Sarah, whom he loves, and to go to the land of Moriah. There he is to offer him as a burnt offering, that is, a sacrifice that was burned up completely, on a mountain that God would show him.

God speaks after years in which Abraham waited for this promised son. The text says it was a test. Abraham answers "Here I am," that is, "I am here." That is why he obeys without argument, although the text does not say what he felt. Many see here a foreshadowing of Christ, though this is a Christian interpretation.

Today, this story invites us to ask ourselves what we love most and whether God holds first place. We can surrender to God our possessions, plans and relationships, trusting that he is faithful, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.46:21:
This verse says that, in the middle of the famine, there was one group whose land did not pass into the hands of Pharaoh: the priests of Egypt. The reason is that they already received a fixed portion from Pharaoh, that is, a regular provision of food. Since they had something to eat, they did not need to sell their lands. The word "portion" here means the daily or assigned share of food.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. He tells how Joseph, who held authority in Egypt, managed the crisis of the famine, and how the Egyptians went on selling their lands in order to survive. The priests stood apart as the exception, because they had that official sustenance.

For today: having a steady provision protects us from making desperate decisions. We can take care of our finances with order and saving, and above all trust that God is the one who sustains our life in difficult times.
exp.36:24:
They sat down to eat after throwing Joseph into the empty pit, and the narrator says that when they looked up they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were loaded with spices, balm, and myrrh, valuable goods they were taking down to Egypt. "Spices" here refers to fragrant spices or resins.

The narrator tells what happened after his brothers, full of envy, stripped Joseph and threw him into an empty pit. What is shocking is that they eat calmly while their brother suffers. The arrival of the caravan opens the way to Judah's idea of selling Joseph instead of killing him. In the Bible, the Ishmaelites are sometimes also called Midianites, and scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: do not get used to eating in peace while someone close to you suffers because of your fault or your indifference. God can work even through evil, but that does not excuse our wrongdoing.
exp.31:4:
Jacob sends a message to his brother Esau. He tells him that he has oxen, donkeys, flocks, menservants, and maidservants. The King James Version uses "asses" for donkeys, and "servants" for workers or attendants. He says he is sending this word to "my lord," that is, to Esau, hoping to "find grace in thy sight," in other words, to be well received and treated with kindness.

Jacob speaks after twenty years away from home, where he lived with Laban. Years earlier he had deceived Esau and fled out of fear. Now he returns and wants to be reconciled. He presents himself with humility, calling himself "thy servant" and Esau "my lord." He reports his possessions to show that he does not come to ask for anything, but in peace. His fear appears right away.

For today: when a relationship is broken, taking the first step with humility and without pride can open the door to reconciliation.
exp.49:6:
Here the account tells us that Joseph went to bury his father Jacob, and that he did not go alone. He was accompanied by Pharaoh's servants, that is, his officials or officers, the elders or leaders of Pharaoh's house, and the elders or authorities of all Egypt. "Went up" is used because Canaan lies higher up, toward the north, and "bury" means to lay in the grave.

The narrator tells what happened after Pharaoh gave permission. Jacob had asked Joseph, under an oath, to bury him in Canaan, in the family tomb. Joseph kept his promise. That so many important Egyptians went with him shows the respect Joseph had earned, and that Pharaoh supported his duty as a son.

For today: keeping what we promise our loved ones, even when it costs time and effort, is a way of honoring them. And whoever lives with integrity, as Joseph did, gains respect and support from those around them.
exp.12:10:
Lot chose for himself the whole plain of the Jordan, a well-watered and fertile area. He went toward the east, and so uncle and nephew parted ways. "Went" means "set out," and "parted" means "separated."

Abram had offered Lot the first choice, because their herdsmen were quarreling over the pasture and the two of them had many flocks. Lot looked over the landscape and picked what seemed best. The text says he "chose for himself," and right after that it notes that the cities of that plain, such as Sodom, had very wicked people. It does not say Lot sinned in choosing, but it shows that he decided by looking only at what could be seen.

Before deciding, it is not enough to ask what suits me. It is also wise to ask what effect this decision will have on my faith, my family, and my friendships. Let us ask God for wisdom to choose well.
exp.29:1:
This verse says that Jacob became angry with Rachel. She had urgently asked him for children, and he answered with a question: "Am I in God's place?" By this he meant that he was not the one who had closed her womb. The phrase "fruit of the womb" refers to children. "Withheld" means that something was denied to her or held back from her.

Jacob, Rachel's husband, is the one speaking. She was suffering because she had no children, while her sister Leah did, and she felt envy. In that culture, having children was seen as a blessing and gave a woman security and worth. Jacob acknowledges that only God gives life, although his answer sounds harsh and shows little tenderness toward her pain.

For today: when someone we love is suffering, being right is not enough. Let us stand beside them with patience and pray together, trusting God, rather than responding with anger.
exp.34:19:
Jacob set up a monument over Rachel's grave. The word "pillar" here refers to a stone marker or column, something raised to remember an important place. The text says that this marker was still there "unto this day," that is, up to the time when the account was written.

It is the narrator who tells us what Jacob did. Rachel died while giving birth to Benjamin, on the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Jacob, in the midst of his grief, did not want her grave to go unmarked. The text gives no further details about what the marker was like, so we should not imagine more than it says.

For today: grief is real, and remembering with affection those we love is healthy. You can honor their memory with a simple gesture, such as visiting a place, writing a few words, or telling their story. And as you remember, keep walking, as Jacob did, trusting that God sustains those who suffer.
exp.44:10:
Here Joseph asks his brothers to tell Jacob to come down to Egypt. There Joseph will provide for him, because there are still five years of famine left. In this way Jacob, his family, and all that belongs to them will not be lost to poverty. The phrase "come to poverty" means to be ruined or to perish, and "to poverty" indicates that it would be from lack of resources.

Joseph speaks to the brothers who sold him years earlier. He has already made himself known to them, and he holds no grudge against them. As ruler of Egypt, he wants to care for his family in the middle of the famine. Goshen was a fertile region where they could live together. The text shows that God used Joseph's story to preserve that family.

For today: when someone has harmed you, ask God for a heart like Joseph's. You can help that person in a wise and concrete way, if it is possible and prudent, instead of seeking revenge.
exp.31:0:
This verse tells us that Jacob went on his way, and that angels of God met him. The phrase "went on his way" means that he continued his journey. "Met him" means that the angels appeared to him along the road.

It is part of the account in Genesis. Jacob had just taken leave of his father-in-law Laban and was returning to the land of Canaan. Later he would have to face his brother Esau, with whom he had had a serious conflict. So this encounter with the angels comes before a moment of great fear. The text does not explain in detail how he saw them or what they did; it only says that Jacob recognized that place as "God's camp."

For today: when you face an uncertain road or a situation that frightens you, remember that God accompanies you even when you cannot see Him. Ask Him to give you peace and confidence before taking the next step.
exp.0:29:
God says that to all the animals of the earth, to the birds of the air, and to every creature that moves and has life, he gives the green plants as food. "Beast" here means animal, and "it was so" means that it happened just as God said.

God is speaking on the sixth day of creation. He has just given human beings the plants with seed and the fruit of the trees. Now he also provides for the animals. Some understand this to show a world without violence at the beginning; others see it as a general description of God's provision. The text does not explain this further. Right after this, God looks at everything and says it is "very good."

For today: God cares for every creature. We can imitate him by being thankful for what we eat and by treating animals and the earth that he has entrusted to us with respect and care.
exp.29:41:
He says that Jacob used his method only with the strong sheep, the "early" ones, which are the ones that mate in the first season. When the "late" ones came, the weaker ones, he did not place the rods before them. So the feebler ones were left for Laban and the strong ones for Jacob.

The narrator is Moses, as the traditional author of Genesis. Jacob had been working for years for his father-in-law Laban, who had cheated him several times. Now they agreed that Jacob would keep the animals that were speckled and dark. The method of the rods is hard to explain; the text does not say it worked by itself. Later, Jacob says that God saw Laban's mistreatment (31:9-12).

For today: do your work with diligence and wisdom, but trust that God is the one who prospers and cares for you, even when others treat you unjustly.
exp.29:37:
Jacob set peeled rods, with their white stripes, in the gutters and watering troughs. That was where the flocks came to drink, and it was there that the animals would conceive, that is, become sexually excited while drinking.

The text is a narrative; Moses tells the story, and there is no speech. Jacob has worked for years for his father-in-law Laban and seeks to prosper, since Laban had cheated him before. Many think the method of the rods was a belief of the time and not a science. Later, Jacob will say that God saw Laban's mistreatment and blessed him (Genesis 31:9-12).

For today: do your part with diligence and wisdom, but do not put your trust in your tricks. Recognize that true provision comes from God, who cares for you even in the midst of injustice.
exp.9:5:
This verse is part of the list of Noah's descendants after the flood. It names the four sons of Ham (called "Cam" in this version): Cush, Mizraim, Put, and Canaan. Mizraim is the Hebrew name commonly associated with Egypt, and many scholars think Cush points to a region south of Egypt, though this is interpreted in several ways.

The text is narrative, and Christian and Jewish tradition attribute the book of Genesis to Moses. This list, known as the "table of nations," shows how peoples developed from Noah's family. It explains the common origin of humanity and prepares the way for what follows, such as the story of Nimrod and later the story of Abraham.

For today: God knows each people and each family by name. We can remember that every person shares the same origin and the same worth before God, and treat others with respect, regardless of their culture or country.
exp.45:4:
This verse tells that Jacob left Beersheba for Egypt. His sons lifted him into the wagons, along with the little ones and the wives. Those wagons had been sent by Pharaoh to carry him. The words "rose up" and "to" in the older wording are forms that mean "got up" and "to" in modern English, but the King James wording here reads "rose up," which keeps the same sense.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jacob was already an old man, and he had learned that his son Joseph was alive in Egypt. Before the journey, at Beersheba, God spoke to him and promised to go with him, to make him into a great nation, and to bring him back. That is why Jacob dared to take this step, so difficult.

For today: when God asks us to move toward the unknown, we can take the step relying on his promise to be with us. We do not know everything that is coming, but we do know who walks beside us.
exp.36:23:
The explanation says that Joseph's brothers seized him and threw him into a cistern, a large pit dug in the ground to store water. But that pit was dry, without water. "They took him" and "cast him" are the old forms of saying "they took him" and "they threw him."

The narrator tells what happened after the brothers, filled with envy, stripped Joseph and took away his coat of many colors. Reuben had proposed not killing him, and the Bible says his intention was to rescue him later and return him to his father. That the pit was empty kept Joseph from dying by drowning, and some readers see in this a discreet care of God, although the text does not say so directly.

Today, when you find yourself in a "dry pit," wounded or abandoned, remember that God may be at work even in what you do not understand. Pray and trust that He has not lost sight of you.
exp.42:14:
The brothers of Joseph obeyed their father. They took the gift, the double amount of money, and Benjamin. Then they traveled to Egypt and presented themselves before Joseph. "Present" means gift, and "double money" means twice the amount.

Jacob had spoken before. He did not want to send Benjamin, but the famine forced them to return for food. In addition, they had to return the money that they had found in their sacks. Jacob asked God for mercy for his sons and accepted the risk with sorrow. The brothers did not yet know that this ruler was Joseph.

For today: sometimes God asks us to move forward even when we are afraid and do not understand everything. We can do what is ours to do with responsibility and prayer, entrusting the outcome to God, as Jacob did.
exp.17:27:
Abraham asks God what would happen if the fifty righteous people were short by five. He asks whether God would destroy the entire city over such a small difference. God answers that he would not destroy it if he found forty-five. The word "peradventure" means "perhaps," and "righteous" refers to people who live uprightly before God.

Abraham speaks with the LORD while Sodom faces judgment for its great wickedness. His nephew Lot lived there. Abraham approaches with humility, recognizing himself as "dust and ashes," and lowers the number little by little. God listens with patience and shows that he does not want to punish without need.

For today: we can pray with confidence and humility for other people, for our family, our city, and our country. God is not troubled by someone who speaks to him with respect and compassion.
exp.18:3:
It says that, before Lot and his guests went to sleep, all the men of Sodom surrounded the house. "Compassed" means surrounded. "Men" here are the males. The text stresses that it was everyone, both old and young, without exception.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. The two visitors were angels in the form of men, and Lot had received them with hospitality. What follows shows that the crowd wanted to abuse them. By saying "all the people from every quarter," the account presents a wickedness spread through the whole city. Later, the Bible also mentions their pride, their indifference toward the poor, and their violence (Ezekiel 16:49).

For today: when evil seems to be the common practice around us, let us not treat it as normal. Let us ask God for the courage to keep doing good, to care for the vulnerable, and to practice hospitality, even when no one else does.
exp.40:4:
The verse tells that Pharaoh fell asleep again and had a second dream. In it he saw seven ears of grain, full and good, growing from a single stalk. The word "stalk" here refers to the stem of the plant. The ears that are "rank" are the ones full of good grain.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Pharaoh had just dreamed of thin cows eating fat cows. Now he receives a second dream that is similar. Later Joseph will explain that both dreams carry one message, and that the repetition shows God had decided it and would soon bring it about (Genesis 41:32).

For today: God can speak and give warning in advance. If you have abundance today, do not spend it without thought. Save, plan, and share, trusting that God gives you wisdom to care for what he gives you.
exp.44:22:
It says that Joseph sent gifts to his father Jacob: ten donkeys loaded with the best things of Egypt, and ten female donkeys loaded with grain, bread and food for the journey. The word "donkeys" refers to the male animals, and the female ones are the "she donkeys" of the King James wording. "Food" is what is meant by the word rendered here as "corn."

Here the narrator speaks, telling what Joseph did, now that he was ruler of Egypt. His brothers had just learned who he was, and Pharaoh wanted the whole family to come to Egypt because of the famine. Joseph not only forgave them, but also took care of his father, whom he had believed dead from grief for so many years.

For today: true forgiveness is shown through concrete acts of kindness. Let us think of someone who has hurt us, or someone we should care for, and make a practical gesture of generosity toward that person today.
exp.20:9:
She says that Sarah asks Abraham to drive out Hagar, the servant, and her son Ishmael. She does not want the son of the servant to share the inheritance with Isaac. Some old words: "cast out" means "send away" or "throw out," "bondwoman" is a woman who serves as a slave, and "heir" is someone who receives the father's possessions.

Sarah is the one speaking. Isaac had just been weaned, and at the feast she saw Ishmael mocking. Sarah reacts with harshness and jealousy, and asks Abraham for something that grieves him deeply. Then God tells Abraham to listen to Sarah, because the promise would pass through Isaac. Even so, God would also care for Ishmael.

For today: when family conflicts wound us, we can ask God for wisdom before we react. He can guide even painful situations and care for those who are left hurt.
exp.41:32:
Joseph's brothers, back in Canaan, tell their father Jacob what the ruler of Egypt said to them. He asked them for proof that they were honest: leave one brother behind as a prisoner, take grain for their families' hunger, and go on their way. "True men" means sincere and honest people. "Be gone" means "go."

Simeon and his brothers speak, reporting to Jacob. They do not know that this "lord of the country" is Joseph, whom they sold years earlier. He was testing them, and the Bible does not say here everything he felt; the text shows that his brothers were already beginning to face their past.

For today: sometimes God uses difficult situations to bring to light what we have kept silent. Instead of running away, we can acknowledge our faults with humility, ask for forgiveness, and seek reconciliation.
exp.22:0:
This verse says that Sarah lived one hundred and twenty-seven years. The phrase is repeated to emphasize the total of her life. The old-fashioned spelling "an hundred" in the King James wording is an archaic form of "a hundred." She is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is given.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He opens the account of Sarah's death, the wife of Abraham, which took place in Hebron, in Canaan. Right after, it is told that Abraham mourned for her and looked for a place to bury her. The text does not explain why it repeats the figure; many think it wants to honor her whole life.

For today: God counts and values every life, and we can do the same. Honor those you love while they are with you, and when loss comes, allow yourself to weep, as Abraham did, without haste or shame.
exp.31:18:
Jacob gives the same instruction to the second servant, the third, and all who followed the droves. Each of them was to say the same thing to Esau when they came upon him.

Jacob returns to Canaan after many years away. Years earlier he had deceived Esau and fled out of fear of his anger. Now he learns that Esau is coming with four hundred men, and he is afraid. Before meeting him, he prays to God, and then he sends gifts in waves to soften his brother's heart. The text does not say here how Esau will react; we see that later.

For today: when a broken relationship needs repair, it is wise to combine prayer with concrete and humble actions. Asking forgiveness or making a kind gesture does not guarantee the outcome, but it shows a sincere heart, and we can leave the result in God's hands.
exp.6:20:
This verse says that the flood destroyed every living thing that lived on the dry land: birds, domestic animals, wild animals, creeping creatures, and human beings as well. "Flesh" refers to living creatures. "Cattle" are the domestic animals, "beasts" are the wild animals, and "creeping thing" refers to any creature that crawls along the ground.

The account is told by the narrator of Genesis. God had seen that human wickedness was very great and the earth was filled with violence (Genesis 6). For this reason he sent the flood, but he cared for Noah, a righteous man, and his family in the ark. Scholars debate whether the flood was worldwide or regional, but the text stresses that the destruction was total for everything living on that land.

For today: this passage reminds us that God takes evil seriously, but he also saves those who trust in him. Today we can respond to his mercy with an obedient faith, like Noah's.
exp.30:10:
Verse 11 tells that Jacob, while he was sleeping, heard the angel of God calling him by name. Jacob answered, "Here am I," which in today's English would simply be "Here I am." It is the reply of someone who is attentive and ready to listen.

Jacob speaks to his wives, Rachel and Leah, to explain why he wants to leave Laban's house. He tells them that God guided him in a dream and that he had seen how Laban treated him. After this call, the angel reminds him of the promise of Bethel and tells him to return to his land.

For today: God still speaks to those who are willing to listen. We can set aside a moment each day to pray and read the Bible, saying simply, "Here I am, Lord." Listening with humility helps us make decisions with peace.
exp.19:8:
Abimelech called Abraham and confronted him with anger and astonishment. He asked what Abraham had done to him and how he had offended him, so that he would bring such a great sin upon him and his kingdom. "Brought" here means that Abraham caused this problem. He ends by saying that Abraham did to him things that ought not to be done.

Abimelech was king of Gerar. Abraham had said that Sarah was only his sister, and the king had taken her for himself. God warned him in a dream that he would die if he did not return her. Now, already fearful, the king confronts Abraham. It is striking that a pagan king shows more uprightness here than the patriarch.

For today: when fear leads us to hide the truth, we can harm others without meaning to. Trusting God is better than protecting ourselves with lies. And if someone rightly rebukes us, even though they do not share our faith, it is wise to listen to them with humility.
exp.4:21:
The explanation says that Enoch "walked with God" for three hundred years after he had his son Methuselah, and that he also had other sons and daughters. To "beget" means "to have as a son." To "walk with God" is a way of saying that he lived in closeness, trust, and obedience to Him.

The author of Genesis is a narrator who tells the story of humanity through a list of generations. Almost everyone in the list ends with "and he died," but Enoch stands out for his relationship with God. The verse that follows says that God "took him," and gives no further explanation; the Bible does not give details of how it happened.

For today: faith is lived in everyday life. Enoch walked with God while raising his family. We can do the same if, in the midst of work and home, we seek God each day with prayer and simple obedience.
exp.3:0:
Genesis 4:1 says that Adam "knew" his wife Eve, an old and respectful way of speaking about marital intimacy. She became pregnant and bore Cain. Then she exclaimed: "I have gotten a man from the Lord," meaning that with the Lord's help she had had a son. "Bare" means "gave birth to."

The speaker is Eve. This is the first birth recorded in the Bible, after Adam and Eve had left the garden of Eden. Her words show gratitude to God. Some think she may have hoped that this son would be the fulfillment of the promise of a descendant who would defeat evil, but the text does not state this clearly. The name Cain sounds like the Hebrew word for "to acquire."

For today: recognize that children and every good thing are a gift from God. Thank Him simply, and pray that those He has entrusted to you will learn to follow Him.
exp.46:16:
The Egyptians, with no money and hungry, brought their animals to Joseph. He gave them bread in exchange for horses, sheep, cattle and donkeys. In this way he kept them alive through that year. "Donkeys" are asses, and the old word "fed" in this verse means "provided for" or "kept alive."

The account describes the great famine that affected both Egypt and Canaan. The Egyptians come to Joseph, who managed the grain under the authority of Pharaoh. They no longer had money, so Joseph proposed receiving their livestock as payment. The text tells what happened, but it does not say whether Joseph acted with generosity or with harshness; readers have interpreted it in different ways.

For today: when someone is in need, the power and resources we have are a great responsibility. Let us ask God for wisdom to help with justice and compassion, without taking advantage of those who suffer.
exp.35:38:
The explanation says that King Baal-hanan, son of Achbor, died and that Hadar took his place. It also mentions that his city was called Pau and that his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred and granddaughter of Mezahab. Here "duke" refers to a clan chief.

This passage is part of the list of the kings and chiefs of Edom, the descendants of Esau. The narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, though some dispute this, records these names to show that God's promises about Esau's descendants were also fulfilled. Some scholars think this list was expanded later, but that is not certain.

For today: God notices people the world forgets. Although these kings are hardly mentioned anywhere else, they appear in Scripture. We can live with humility, trusting that our work and our lives matter to God, even when no one else remembers them.
exp.36:0:
Jacob settled down to live in the land of Canaan, the same land where his father Isaac, and before him Abraham, lived as a stranger. "Wherein his father was a stranger" means that they lived there as foreigners, without owning the land. The word "dwelt" shows that Jacob has now settled down.

This is the beginning of the story of Joseph. Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, tells it as a narrative, not as a speech. After years of running away and of conflict with Esau and Laban, Jacob finally lives in the land God promised to his family. It seems like a moment of calm before the storm, because soon tensions among the sons appear.

For today: even when you live in a peaceful season, remember that you are still a "pilgrim" who depends on God's promises. Be thankful for the peace you have, but stay alert and seek God's wisdom to care for your home.
exp.36:17:
This verse says that Joseph's brothers saw him coming from a distance, before he got close to them. While he was still walking toward them, they had already made an evil plan to kill him. "Planned" means they thought about and arranged something on purpose.

Here the narrator of the story is speaking. Joseph, sent by his father Jacob, went to look for his brothers to find out how they were doing. They envied him and held a grudge against him because of his father's special affection for him and because of his dreams. That buried resentment now turns into a violent plan.

For today: resentment that is never faced grows quietly and can lead us to do harm. If you feel envy or anger toward someone, bring it to God in prayer and speak honestly before your heart becomes hard.
exp.41:5:
It says that Joseph had authority in Egypt and was the one who sold grain to the people. When his brothers arrived, they bowed before him with their faces to the ground. Some older words: "governor" means ruler, and "bowed down themselves" is the old way of saying they bowed themselves down.

The narrator tells us there was famine in Canaan, and Jacob's sons traveled to Egypt to buy food. Years earlier, they had sold Joseph as a slave. Now they do not recognize him, but their bowing recalls the dreams Joseph had as a young man (Genesis 37:5-10). Many see here the fulfillment of God's promise in the midst of pain.

God can be at work even when we do not see how. If today you are waiting for an answer or a healing, trust that his timing and his purpose are greater than your pain. And if someone has hurt you, ask God for a wise heart and freedom from the desire for revenge.
exp.43:20:
This verse recalls what Joseph, the governor of Egypt, asked of his brothers. "Bring him down" means "bring him to me," and it refers to Benjamin, the youngest brother. "That I may set mine eyes upon him" means "I want to see him with my own eyes." It may sound like a kind request, although in the account it also functioned as a demand.

The one speaking is Judah, who explains to Joseph (without knowing who he really is) why Benjamin cannot stay in Egypt. Judah recounts the facts to show how much his father Jacob would suffer if he lost this son. It is the beginning of a sincere plea, in which Judah ends by offering himself in Benjamin's place.

For today: when we have to ask for something difficult, let us do so with truth and humility, thinking of the pain of others. Judah teaches us that truly loving someone sometimes means bearing another's burden.
exp.32:9:
Jacob insists that Esau accept the gift he offers. He says that, if he has truly found favor in Esau's sight, then Esau should receive the present. He explains that seeing Esau's face, now calm and kind, has been to him like seeing the face of God. "Present" means gift, and "thou wast pleased with me" is like saying "you have shown me favor."

Jacob speaks with his brother Esau after many years apart. Years earlier, Jacob had deceived him and fled, fearing his revenge. Now he returns in fear, but Esau welcomes him warmly. Esau says he already has plenty, and Jacob insists as a gesture of gratitude and reconciliation. Some think his words express relief at having been forgiven; others see them as also a courtesy typical of the time.

When someone forgives you or shows you kindness you did not expect, acknowledge it with sincere gratitude. If you have failed, seek to repair the harm with humility. And if you are the one who must forgive, remember that your grace can reflect something of the face of God.
exp.10:1:
The passage says that a group of people traveled from the east and found a wide plain in the land of Shinar, which is the region of Mesopotamia, and there they stayed to live. The word "plain" refers to a fertile, low-lying flatland. "Settled" means that they established themselves, that they stopped moving from place to place. Some scholars translate "from the east" as "from the east," while others think it could mean "toward the east"; the Hebrew allows both readings.

Here no person speaks; it is the narrator of Genesis. He tells how humanity, which still spoke a single language, began to gather in one place. This step prepares the story of Babel: what seems like a simple settlement soon becomes a plan of pride and of unity without God.

For today: settling down and making plans is good, but it is worth asking ourselves whether, in our projects, we rely on God or only on our own strength.
exp.43:16:
Here Joseph says that he will not do such a thing: only the man in whose hand the cup was found will become his servant. To the other brothers he says that they may go home peacefully, "in peace," to their father. The words "God forbid that I should do so" mean "far be it from me to do that." "Was" and "found" are the same as in modern English.

Joseph speaks to his brothers, to whom he has not yet revealed himself. He had ordered his cup to be hidden in Benjamin's sack in order to test them. By offering to let them go free, he sees whether they will abandon Benjamin as they once did with him. Many understand this to be the test of their change of heart.

Today, this scene invites us to take responsibility for those we love and not to abandon them when things are hard. God can heal old family wounds and transform the heart.
exp.10:16:
The explanation says that Eber lived 430 years after he became the father of Peleg, and that he had other sons and daughters. The words "begat" and "unto" are old forms: "begat" means that he became a father, and "unto" today is written as "to."

These words are part of the genealogy that runs from Shem to Abram. The narrator, traditionally Moses, does not speak of great deeds but follows the family line through which the people of Israel would come. Some believe the ages are literal; others think they have a symbolic meaning or are shaped by the writer's style. The Bible does not fully make this clear.

For today: God cares for every generation, including people who barely appear in the accounts. Your everyday life, your family, and your faithfulness also matter to Him and can be part of something greater than you can see.
exp.7:7:
This verse tells that Noah released a dove from the ark to check whether the water had already gone down from the surface of the earth. "Also he sent forth a dove from him" means that he sent it out from his side, and the word "from" in the King James reading corresponds to the idea of sending it away from himself.

Noah had already sent out the raven, which went back and forth without giving a clear answer. Now he tries the dove. Inside the ark he could not see the ground, so he used the means he had to know when it was safe to leave. The text does not say why he chose these birds; that is only one possible conclusion.

For today: Noah did not rush or guess. He waited and went step by step. When you face an important decision, trust God, pray, and move forward with patience, without losing heart if the first answer is not the one you hoped for.
exp.11:9:
This verse tells that a great famine came upon the land of Canaan. Because of it, Abram went down to Egypt to stay there for a while. "Sojourn" here means to live as a foreigner, without settling there permanently. The King James Version uses "went down into Egypt to sojourn there," and the word "sojourn" carries this same sense of temporary residence as a stranger.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Genesis. Abram had just arrived in the land God had promised him, and there he worshiped the LORD. Now he faces a crisis. The Bible does not say that God commanded him to go to Egypt, and so some see it as a human decision made out of fear, while others see it as a prudent way out. What follows shows that this decision brought problems.

For today: when hard times come, before acting out of fear, stop to pray and seek God's guidance. He can care for you even in scarcity.
exp.35:18:
This verse closes the list of the chiefs who descended from the sons of Esau. The word "dukes" sounds old-fashioned; here it means chiefs or clan leaders, that is, the heads of large families. It then makes clear that "who is Edom": Esau and Edom are the same person, since Edom was another name for Esau, and later it also named his people and his land.

Genesis 36 has no character who speaks; it is the narrator, traditionally attributed to Moses, who gathers family records. It shows that God fulfilled his promise to make Esau a nation, even though the main promise continued through Jacob. It also helps Israel know its neighbors, the Edomites.

For today: God notices people whom we may see as nothing more than names in a list. You can thank him for caring for every family, and pray for those who seem to be "on the margins" of history.
exp.28:1:
This verse describes what Jacob sees as he arrives at his destination: a well in the middle of the field, with three flocks of sheep lying down nearby. "Watered" means gave them drink, and "lying" means they were resting on the ground. The well was covered with a large stone.

It is the narrator who speaks. Jacob is fleeing from his brother Esau and heading to the land of his mother's family, seeking refuge and, according to the account, a wife. Without knowing it, he is about to meet Rachel. Some see here the hand of God guiding him, as he had promised him at Bethel, although the text leaves this suggested rather than stating it directly.

For today: when your path is uncertain, keep going with faith and attentiveness. God often works in simple, everyday places, like a well in the field, and it is wise to be alert to what He places before us.
exp.18:21:
The explanation says that the angel urges Lot to hurry and escape to the small city he himself chose. The phrase "Haste thee" means "hurry up." The angel states that he cannot do anything, that is, he cannot destroy Sodom, until Lot arrives there. That is why the city was called Zoar, a name that sounds like the Hebrew word for "small."

The angel speaks as one sent by God, answering Lot. Lot was afraid to flee to the mountains and asked to take refuge in that nearby city. God accepted his request and asked for haste, because the judgment on Sodom and Gomorrah was about to fall.

For today: when God opens a way out, do not leave it for later. Act with promptness and confidence, and give thanks that He listens even to your fears and your simplest requests.
exp.49:24:
It says that Joseph made the Israelites swear an oath. To take an oath means to make a solemn promise. Joseph assures them that God will "visit" them, meaning that God will remember them and come to help them. And he asks that, when they leave Egypt, they carry his bones with them.

Joseph speaks shortly before he dies, to his brothers and to their descendants. They were living in Egypt, but God had promised Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob that he would give them another land. Although Joseph held a high position in Egypt, he did not want to stay there forever. He wanted to be buried in the land of the promise. This shows that he trusted God to keep his word. Later, the book of Exodus tells how Moses took his bones with him.

For today: we can trust God's promises even when we cannot see how they will be fulfilled. Joseph did not live to see the departure from Egypt, but he waited for it in faith. That same hope helps us stand firm in hard times.
exp.21:20:
This verse continues a list of the children that Milcah had with Nahor, Abraham's brother. Three are named here: Huz, the firstborn (the eldest son); Buz, his brother; and Kemuel, who is called "the father of Aram." The phrase "the father of" may indicate that he was the ancestor of a people or family, though it is not known with certainty which one.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, right after Abraham was about to offer Isaac. News reaches him that his family in the land of his origin had grown. This list prepares the way for Rebekah, daughter of Bethuel, who will later become Isaac's wife.

For today: God works even in details that look like simple lists of names. What we do not understand about our own story, He is already preparing for the future. Trust that your life also has a purpose in His hands.
exp.34:28:
It says that Isaac died at the age of 180. "Gave up the ghost" means that he breathed his last breath. "Was gathered unto his people" is an old expression meaning that he joined his ancestors in death. "Being old and full of days" means that he lived a long and full life. His sons Esau and Jacob buried him together.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, closing the story of Isaac. Jacob had returned to Hebron, where his father lived. It is remarkable that Esau and Jacob, who had been estranged, appear united to bury him. The text does not explain more about how that reconciliation came about.

For today: life and death are moments that can bring a family together. If there is division with someone in your family, do not wait for a funeral to seek peace. Take a simple step today, such as a phone call or an apology.
exp.3:23:
Lamech says that if Cain was promised vengeance sevenfold, then he will receive vengeance seventy-sevenfold. In other words, he boasts that he will take revenge far more fiercely. "Shall be avenged" means that there will be punishment for whoever harms them. "Seventy and sevenfold" is a way of speaking of an enormous vengeance.

Lamech, a descendant of Cain, is speaking to his two wives, Adah and Zillah. He has just said that he would kill anyone who wounds him. In Genesis 4:15 God had protected Cain with a promise of vengeance; Lamech uses that promise to justify his own violence. Many see here how sin grows: from one killing we move to the boasting of killing.

For today: when we are hurt, let us not be carried away by pride or by the desire to return even greater harm. Jesus, in Matthew 18:22, spoke of forgiving "seventy times seven," turning Lamech's words around. Let us ask God for a heart that forgives.
exp.41:3:
This verse tells us that Jacob did not let Benjamin, Joseph's younger brother, go with the other ten sons to Egypt. Jacob was afraid that some "mischief", that is, some harm or misfortune, might befall him.

Here the narrator speaks, and shows us what Jacob was thinking. There was famine throughout the land, and Jacob sent his sons to buy grain. But Benjamin was now the only son left to him from his beloved Rachel, since Jacob believed Joseph was dead. That is why he did not want to risk him. He still carried that grief.

For today: fear of losing what we love is natural, but it can make us very controlling. We can bring our fears to God in prayer, and trust that he cares for ours better than we do. God continues to work, even when we cannot see the way ahead.
exp.26:13:
This verse tells that Jacob obeyed his mother Rebekah. He went to the flock, took the two young goats, and brought them to her. She prepared the savoury meat, that is, the food, seasoned the way Isaac, her husband, liked it. The word "fetched" means "went and got" them.

Rebekah wanted Jacob to receive his father's blessing, since his father was old and nearly blind. Jacob feared being discovered and receiving a curse. She told him that the blame would fall on her. Although the Bible recounts the deception, it does not approve of it; its painful consequences appear later in the family.

For today: even when people we care about pressure us, we must not take part in anything deceitful. Before obeying, it is wise to ask ourselves whether what we are being asked to do pleases God. Trusting his promise does not need tricks.
exp.20:21:
This verse tells that Abimelech, king of Gerar, and Phichol, the commander of his army, approached Abraham. They said to him that God was with him in everything he did. The word "prince" here means a commander or military chief. In the King James wording, "chief captain of his host" conveys the same idea: Phichol was the head of Abimelech's army.

Abimelech and Phichol speak because they have seen Abraham's life up close. Shortly before, God protected Sarah and blessed Abraham in Abimelech's land, and Isaac had just been born. For this reason, Abimelech wants to secure peace with a covenant. That a foreign king would recognize this is remarkable, although the Bible does not say how much he actually knew about God.

Today, the way we live can speak of God more than many words. Try to be honest and fair at work and in your family, so that others notice that God is real in your life.
exp.39:6:
It says that Joseph, while in prison, asked two officials of Pharaoh why they looked so sad that day. The word "officers" here is used for officials of the court; it does not always mean the same thing today, and some translate it as "attendants" or "servants." The phrase "look so sadly" refers to their faces, and it means that their discouragement was visible.

The one speaking is Joseph, who was imprisoned although he was innocent. The king's cupbearer and baker had had dreams they could not understand, and in the morning Joseph noticed their sadness. He was in charge of looking after them in the prison, and his question comes from genuine concern, which then opens the door to speaking about God.

For today: even if you have your own sorrows, notice the people around you. A simple sincere question, such as "How are you really doing?", can be the beginning of real comfort.
exp.17:10:
This verse says that Abraham and Sarah were already old, "well stricken in age," that is, advanced in years. Moreover, Sarah had already stopped "after the manner of women," an old way of referring to menstruation. For that reason, humanly speaking, she could no longer have children.

The narrator explains this just after one of the three visitors, whom the text calls the LORD, promises Abraham that Sarah will have a son. Sarah listens from the entrance of the tent. The detail emphasizes how impossible the promise seems and prepares her laughter of disbelief in the verses that follow.

For today: when your situation seems closed and without a way out, do not measure God's promise by your limits. You can bring Him your doubts with sincerity, trusting that He can act where you no longer see a path.
exp.21:5:
Here the account tells us that Abraham laid the wood for the sacrifice on his son Isaac. He himself carried the fire and the knife. A "burnt offering" was an offering that was burned whole for God. "Laid it upon" means he placed it on him. The fire was probably an ember or torch to light the wood. The two of them walked together.

God had asked Abraham to offer Isaac, the son of the promise, as a test of his faith. The narrator describes the scene in few words, and this makes the weight of the moment felt. Isaac carries the wood without yet knowing what will happen. Abraham had already told his servants that they would return, and later he answers that God will provide the lamb.

For today: when God asks us for something difficult, we can take the next step with confidence, even if we do not understand everything, remembering that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.28:9:
This verse tells how Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban, who was the brother of his mother Rebekah. When he saw her with her uncle's sheep, Jacob went over, rolled away the stone that covered the mouth of the well, and watered the flock.

Where the explanation mentions the word "abrevó," it means to give water to the animals. The earlier spelling of "saw" in the original text is not reflected in the King James wording, so no note is needed there.

Here the narrator speaks. Jacob had made a long journey searching for his mother's family. The shepherds had told him they waited until all the flocks were gathered before moving the stone. Jacob did not wait. Some think the stone was very heavy and that his strength draws attention, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: when you see a need near you, take a concrete step to help. Sometimes serving others gladly, without waiting for someone else to act first, opens doors you did not expect.
exp.48:17:
He says that Jacob confidently waits for God's "health." Today "health" is not understood as physical well-being, but as "salvation" or "deliverance." The Hebrew word (yeshuá) speaks of liberation. "Jehovah" is the name of God. It is a brief prayer in the middle of a long blessing.

Jacob speaks, now elderly, on his deathbed, as he blesses and foretells the future of his twelve sons. He has just spoken about Dan, with images of danger and struggle. Many think that, thinking about those struggles, Jacob turns to God and places his hope in Him. The text does not explain exactly why he says it here, so it is interpreted in several ways.

For today: when you see conflicts or an uncertain future, pause and pray. Place your hope in God, not only in your own strength.
exp.23:43:
This verse is part of the prayer that Abraham's servant makes. He asks that the young woman he asks for water would answer him kindly: "Drink, and I will draw water for your camels too." That would be the sign that she is the woman whom the Lord had chosen and prepared for Isaac, the son of his master.

The servant of Abraham speaks, and he tells Laban and Bethuel what happened by the well. Abraham sent him to find a wife for Isaac among his own family. The servant did not want to make a mistake, so he asked God for a clear sign. Drawing water for ten camels was a big job, so the sign asked for an unusual kindness.

For today: when you face an important decision, pray with humility and seek God's guidance. In the meantime, pay attention to people's character, since kindness and generous service say a lot about a heart.
exp.30:12:
Here the angel of God speaks in God's name and presents himself as "the God of Beth-el." He reminds Jacob of two things: that there he anointed a stone as a sign (the "title" is that pillar or memorial stone), and that he made a vow. Then he gives him a clear command: get up, leave Laban, and return to the land where he was born ("of thy kindred").

Jacob tells Rachel and Leah about it. About twenty years of work with Laban have passed, during which Laban deceived him several times. God says he has seen all of that. Beth-el was the place where, fleeing from his brother Esau, Jacob had dreamed of the ladder and God promised to be with him (Genesis 28).

For today: God sees what we suffer and remembers his promises and ours. If we have promised something to God, it is worth reviewing it with sincerity. And when God points us to a step, we can trust and obey.
exp.3:2:
It says that, after some time, Cain brought to God an offering of what the ground produced. "In process of time" means that days or years passed; the text does not specify how long. "Lord" is the name of God, and "offering" is a gift given to him as a sign of gratitude or worship.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Cain was a farmer and Abel a shepherd, so each brought something from his own work. The passage sets up what follows: God looked with favor on Abel and his offering, but not on Cain and his. The text does not fully explain why, and it has been interpreted in different ways. Some point to the attitude of the heart, others to the quality of what was offered.

For today: when you give something to God, whether time, service or money, do it with a sincere and grateful heart, not just to fulfill an obligation.
exp.24:0:
This verse tells us that Abraham married again, and that his new wife was named Keturah. The word "took" was a common way of saying he married her. Some scholars think Abraham married her after Sarah died; others believe it may have been earlier, because 1 Chronicles 1:32 calls her a "concubine." The text does not fully settle the question.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking, not a character in the story. He introduces Abraham's descendants, who will form several peoples, many of them in lands near Canaan. In this way the account shows how God's promise to give Abraham a great family was being fulfilled. Afterward, the story will return its focus to Isaac, the child of promise.

For today: God keeps working in our lives at every stage. Abraham was already very old, and yet his story was not over. Never think it is too late for God to use you.
exp.16:23:
The explanation says Abraham was ninety-nine years old when he was circumcised. "Foreskin" is the skin that covers the tip of the male organ, and "circumcise" means to cut it away. The text stresses his age to show that he obeyed even while already an old man.

God had established a covenant with Abraham and asked for circumcision as the sign of that covenant (Genesis 17:10-14). The narrator tells us that Abraham obeyed the very same day, together with Ishmael and all the males of his household. God had just promised him that Sarah would give him a son, Isaac.

Obeying God has no expiration date and no age limit. Abraham did not wait or make excuses, even though the command was uncomfortable and difficult. Today we can ask ourselves: what is something I know God is asking of me that I am putting off for later? Today is a good day to take that step with confidence.
exp.5:13:
God tells Noah to build an ark, that is, a large boat shaped like a box. It was to be made of "gopher wood," a Hebrew word that appears only here, so we do not know for certain what kind of tree it was; some think of cypress or pine. It would have "rooms," that is, chambers or compartments. Coating it "within and without with pitch" means covering it with a sticky substance so that water would not get in.
