The servant asks what to do if the woman is not willing to come. Abraham answers firmly, because God had promised to give this land to his descendants. Isaac was to remain where God had led him. Abraham trusts that God will guide the way.

For today: when God has led us to a place or to a calling, let us not allow the comfort of the past to draw us back. We may seek counsel and plan wisely, but trusting that God continues to guide.
exp.35:33:
It says that Jobab, king of Edom, died, and that Husam, who came from the land of Teman, began to reign in his place. It is part of a list of Edomite kings. The phrase "reigned in his stead" simply means that he succeeded him on the throne. Teman was a region associated with Edom, although its exact location is not known.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, recording the descendants of Esau, also called Edom. This list shows that Edom had kings before Israel had one. It is noticeable that the throne did not pass from father to son, since each king comes from a different place. Scholars explain this in various ways: perhaps they were elected chiefs or rulers of different cities.

For today: all human power is passing. Kings die and others take their place. For this reason it is wise to place our trust in God, who endures, and not in leaders or positions.
exp.9:28:
And Ophir, and Havilah, and Jobab: all these were the sons of Joktan. Here the list of the thirteen sons of this descendant of Shem comes to an end. Jobab is the name in question, and in older spellings it appears as "Jobad," though the form in your verse is Jobab.

This belongs to what is traditionally called the "table of nations" in Genesis 10. The narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, lists the families that arose after the flood. His purpose is to show how humanity spread out from the sons of Noah. Scholars do not know with certainty where each of these peoples lived; many place them in Arabia, but that is an interpretation.

For today: God knows the names of people whom history has almost forgotten. You too are known to Him. Live today with the assurance that your life matters to Him.
exp.40:42:
This verse tells us that Pharaoh had Joseph ride in his second chariot, meaning the chariot that came right after his own in rank. As he passed, the people shouted "Bow the knee," which means "kneel" or "give honor." In this way, Joseph was set in authority over all of Egypt.

Pharaoh speaks here after Joseph interpreted his dreams and advised him to store up grain for seven years of famine. Earlier, Joseph had been sold by his brothers and unjustly imprisoned. Now Pharaoh gives him his ring, fine clothing, and a gold chain as public signs of his authority. The phrase "they cried before him" refers to a loud public proclamation. Some scholars debate the exact meaning of the original word translated "Bow the knee."

For today: God can work in the midst of injustice and seasons of waiting. Remain faithful and upright wherever you are; He knows when and how to lift you up.
exp.9:22:
This verse lists the four sons of Aram: Uz, Hul, Gether, and Mash. Aram was a son of Shem, and Shem was a son of Noah. The word "begot" simply indicates family descent.

It is part of the so-called "Table of Nations" in Genesis 10. The narrator, traditionally Moses, notes how the peoples were formed after the flood. Here the account follows the line of Shem. Many believe the descendants of Aram are related to the region of Syria, but scholars are not entirely certain where each of these sons lived.

For today: God knows every name and every family, even though to us they may seem like just a list. If He cares for the names of ancient generations, He also knows you and values you. Give thanks today for your family and pray for them.
exp.26:2:
Isaac asks his son Esau to take his hunting equipment: the quiver (the bag where the arrows are kept) and the bow. He is to go out into the field and hunt an animal for him. The phrase "take me some venison" means "bring me game meat."

Isaac speaks as an old man, nearly blind. He feels his life is nearing its end and wants to give his blessing to Esau, the firstborn, after eating his favorite dish. Rebekah listens, and this leads to what happens next. The text does not explain all of Isaac's reasons, but it shows that he wants to carry out this important step before he dies.

For today: let us not put off saying important words to our family. Blessing, advising and praying for our children must be done with clarity, with uprightness and with faith, not in secret or out of favoritism.
exp.0:18:
This verse closes the fourth day of creation. The phrase "the evening and the morning" is the way Genesis marks each day: evening comes first and then morning, and so a day is completed.

In this chapter, the narrator tells how God orders the world step by step. On the fourth day he set the sun, the moon, and the stars to give light, to mark day and night, and to signal the seasons. People have understood the "days" in various ways: as days of twenty-four hours or as longer stages. The text itself does not settle that discussion, and believers have approached it in different ways.

For today: God works with order and patience. If you feel rushed today, remember that each day has its evening and its morning, and you can rest in the confidence that God is still sustaining all things.
exp.8:13:
This verse says that when God brings clouds over the earth, the rainbow will appear in them. "It shall come to pass" means "it will happen," and "I bring" means "I will bring" or "I will cause to appear." The bow is the rainbow, which God chose as a sign.

God speaks, after the flood, addressing Noah, his sons, and all living creatures. He promises that he will never again destroy the earth with water. The bow is the visible reminder of that covenant, and God himself says he will see it and remember. Some understand this as a human way of speaking about God's faithfulness.

For today: when cloudy times come into your life, remember that God keeps his promises. Pause, look calmly, and give thanks for his faithfulness.
exp.43:9:
Here the steward of Joseph answers the brothers. He says he will accept their proposal, but changes it a little: whoever has the cup will be his servant (slave), and the rest will be free of blame. "Found" in the King James wording means "discovered," and "blameless" means innocent.

Joseph's brothers have just been accused of stealing the silver cup. Without knowing it, they promise the death of the guilty one and the slavery of all. The steward speaks following Joseph's plan, which is to test whether his brothers have changed and whether they would abandon Benjamin as they once abandoned him. This is understood from the complete account.

For today: before speaking with great certainty, it is wise to weigh our words. The brothers promised too much without knowing the whole truth. Let us be humble, prudent, and compassionate when we judge.
exp.16:8:
God speaks to Abraham again and tells him that he too has a part in the covenant: to keep it. This includes his descendants, generation after generation. The King James wording "therefore" carries the sense of "then" or "in response to what I have promised," and "seed" means descendants or offspring.

God has just promised Abraham that he will be his God, that he will give him the land of Canaan, and that his family will be numerous. Now he makes clear that the covenant is not only a promise received, but a relationship that calls for faithfulness. In the verses that follow, God identifies circumcision as the sign of that covenant.

For today: God offers us his friendship by grace, but he expects us to respond with a faithful life. We can think of one concrete step of obedience this week, and also of how to pass on the faith to our children or to those who come after us.
exp.16:14:
In this verse God tells Abraham that he should no longer call his wife "Sarai", but "Sarah". It is a change of name. The archaic words are "á" (to) and "mas" (but). The two names are related to the idea of princess; scholars do not agree on the exact difference in meaning.

God speaks with Abraham just after establishing circumcision as the sign of his covenant. Abraham is already ninety-nine years old, and God affirms that his wife will also have a part in the promise. She will not be a mere companion: God will bless her, and the promised son will be born from her.

For today: God knows us by name and can give us a new identity and a new purpose, even when it seems late or impossible to us. Trust in his promise, even though, like Abraham, sometimes it is hard for you to believe it.
exp.28:26:
Laban tells Jacob to finish the wedding week with Leah, and after that he will also give him Rachel. In exchange, Jacob would have to work for him another seven years. "Fulfil her week" refers to the week of wedding celebration. "This one" is Leah, and "the other" is Rachel.

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, is the one speaking. Jacob had worked seven years to marry Rachel, but Laban gave him Leah, his older daughter. When Jacob complained, Laban justified himself by local custom. His proposal guaranteed himself another seven years of work. The Bible does not explain all the details of the custom, but it shows that Laban acted with cunning.

For today: when we are deceived or things do not turn out as we expected, it is wise to act with patience and honesty, without repaying deceit with deceit. God can work even in unjust and difficult situations.
exp.13:18:
Melchizedek blesses Abram. The explanation's quoted wording, which is in another language, is not something to preserve here, so the verse's own words carry the meaning: he blessed him, and said that Abram is blessed by God Most High, the possessor of heaven and earth. Melchizedek says that Abram is blessed by the God who owns heaven and earth.

Melchizedek speaks, as king of Salem and priest of God. Abram was returning from rescuing his nephew Lot and from defeating the enemy kings. Melchizedek comes out to meet him with bread and wine and acknowledges that the victory came from God. Afterward Abram gives him a tenth of everything. The Bible says very little more about him, and so there are different ways of understanding who he was.

For today: when something goes well for you, don't keep the credit to yourself alone. Stop to give thanks to God, who owns everything and sustains you. You can also encourage others by reminding them that God is with them.
exp.48:16:
It says that the tribe of Dan will be like a serpent hiding beside the road. The adder is a poisonous snake. This serpent bites the horse's heels, and the rider falls backward. It is a picture of a small group that defeats stronger ones through cunning and surprise.

Jacob, now very old, is speaking. He blesses his twelve sons and announces what will come upon their tribes. Earlier he said that Dan would judge his people. Some think this image speaks of cleverness and courage. Others see it as a warning, because later Dan fell into idolatry (Judges 18). Jacob immediately responds: "I have waited for your salvation, O Lord."

For today: cleverness without God can turn into deceit. Ask the Lord for wisdom and use it honestly. Remember that true salvation comes from God, not from our own schemes.
exp.18:25:
It says that Lot's wife looked back as they fled from Sodom, and she was turned into a pillar of salt. "From behind him" means she was following behind Lot. "Pillar" here is understood as a figure or column of salt.

This is the narrator of the book of Genesis speaking. God was judging Sodom and Gomorrah, and earlier he had sent angels to bring Lot and his family out, with the command not to look back (Genesis 19:17). Looking back seems to show a heart still attached to what was being left behind. The text does not explain in detail how the transformation happened, so it is best not to invent more. Jesus recalled this in Luke 17:32.

Today we can ask ourselves what things from the past hold us back when God calls us to move forward. Trusting his word means letting go, in faith, of what he asks us to leave behind.
exp.20:17:
God tells Hagar to get up, to lift her son and take hold of him firmly by the hand. "Lift him up" is an old way of saying "take hold of him" or "support him." "Lad" refers to Ishmael, and "great nation" means a large nation. God promises that from this young man a numerous people will come.

The speaker is the angel of God, who calls to Hagar from heaven. She and her son had been sent away from Abraham's house and were lost in the desert, without water. Hagar, in despair, moved away so as not to see her son die. God heard the boy's crying and responded with comfort and a promise.

For today: when you feel there is no way out, remember that God hears you even when you do not know what to say. He asks you to get up and take the next step, and often He opens your eyes so you can see the help that was already close by.
exp.37:16:
Judah promises Tamar that he will send her a young goat from his flock as payment. She asks him for a pledge, that is, a guarantee or something of value that he leaves in her hands until he keeps his promise. The word "pledge" is the one the verse uses, so it stays as is.

Judah speaks without knowing she is his daughter-in-law, since she had covered her face. Tamar had been left a widow, and Judah had not given her his youngest son as a husband, as was expected. She acts with deception, and the Bible neither approves nor condemns every step she takes here. Her pledge would later serve as proof of the truth.

Today we can learn that promises made lightly, and decisions taken on impulse, leave traces that later come to light. Let us live with integrity, keeping what we have promised and not expecting that anyone will see us.
exp.24:9:
This verse says that the field where Abraham was buried was the same one he had bought from the sons of Heth. There he was laid to rest beside his wife Sarah. "Field" here means a piece of land held as property, and "was buried" means that they placed his body in the ground.

The account is traditionally credited to Moses. It comes right after the record of Abraham's death, and Isaac and Ishmael bury him together. In Genesis 23, Abraham bought that land in order to bury Sarah. Although God had promised him the whole land, the only part he owned was this burial place. This shows that his hope remained fixed on the promise.

For today: we can live with our eyes fixed on God's promises, even though we do not see everything fulfilled in this life. And we can leave our children, more than possessions, an example of faith and of family unity.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that God named the firmament, the open space that separated the waters above from the waters below. He called it Heaven. The phrase "the evening and the morning were the second day" marks the close of the second day of creation.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking, telling how God puts the world in order step by step. God separates and sets boundaries to prepare a place where life can exist. Interestingly, on this second day the phrase "God saw that it was good" does not appear. Some think this is because the work of separating the waters continues into the third day, but the Bible does not explain it.

For today: God works with order and patience. If your life feels confusing, you can ask him to bring order little by little, step by step, and trust that he is still at work even though you cannot yet see the complete result.
exp.5:7:
This verse says that Noah found favor with God. The word "but" at the start marks a strong contrast with what came before. "Found grace in the eyes of the Lord" means that God looked on him with approval and kindness. "Lord" is the name for God used here.

The narrator of the book tells us that God was deeply grieved by human wickedness and had decided to judge the earth. Against that dark backdrop, Noah stands out as the exception. The following verse describes him as righteous and as someone who walked with God. The grace was not something he earned; it was God's favor, which the story presents alongside Noah's faith and faithful life.

For today: even when the atmosphere around you seems far from God, you can live close to Him. His grace is available, and walking with Him each day, with humility and obedience, is a simple and real response to that favor.
exp.45:25:
This verse counts how many direct descendants of Jacob went down to Egypt with him: sixty-six people. "Loins" is an old way of speaking of the children born from his own body. The wives of his sons are not counted. The word "souls" can also be understood as "persons," that is, lives.

Here the narrator of Genesis is keeping a family record. Jacob moved to Egypt because of the famine, to be reunited with Joseph. The text then gives a total of seventy, adding Joseph, his two sons born in Egypt, and Jacob himself. The numbers vary among biblical lists, and scholars explain this in different ways.

For today: God cares for people one by one, each with a name and a place in his story. Today you can value your family and those around you, praying for them and remembering that every life counts for God.
exp.23:64:
In this verse, Rebekah, seeing a man walking across the field, asked Abraham's servant who he was. The servant told her, "It is my master," that is, Isaac. Then she took a veil and covered herself. "Servant" and "attendant" refer to the same person, and "man" means a male.

The narrator describes the end of a long journey. Abraham's servant had been sent to find a wife for Isaac, and Rebekah agreed to go with him. Now she sees her future husband for the first time. The text does not say with certainty why she covered herself; many understand it as a gesture of respect, modesty, or preparation for marriage, according to the customs of that time.

For today: the moment of meeting someone important deserves respect and humility. Rebekah did not act with haste or carelessness, but with reverence. We can learn to begin our relationships with honor, and to trust that God guides the steps of those who seek him.
exp.16:16:
Here Abraham bows down to the ground, laughs, and thinks to himself: How can a man of one hundred years have a child? And will Sarah, at ninety, give birth?

Dios has just changed Sarai's name to Sarah and promised that she will have a son and be the mother of nations. Abraham reacts with amazement. Some understand his laughter as doubt; others, as joy and surprise, since he bows down in worship. The text does not fully clarify this. What is clear is that Abraham thinks quietly and then speaks to God with sincerity.

We can bring God our doubts and questions with honesty. He already knows what we think, and He remains faithful to His promise even when we find it hard to believe.
exp.18:9:
The explanation says that the two visitors, who were angels, reached out their hands, pulled Lot inside the house, and shut the door. The word "men" here means men, and "put forth their hand" means they stretched out their hands to reach him.

Lot was outside, facing a violent crowd that wanted to harm his guests. He had made a terrible and wrong offer involving his daughters, and the people threatened him even more. Then the visitors step in. The one who rescues is not Lot but them. The text calls them "men," but the context shows they were messengers of God.

There are times when we make mistakes and do not know how to get out of the trouble. This passage reminds us that God can act with mercy even when we fail. That does not excuse the error, but it invites us to ask for help and to trust in his care.
exp.30:46:
Verse 47 tells us that Laban and Jacob each gave the heap of stones a name, in their own language. Laban called it "Jegar Sahadutha," which is Aramaic, and Jacob called it "Galeed," which is Hebrew. Both names mean something like "heap of witness."

Jacob and Laban had a tense relationship. Jacob had left secretly with his family, and Laban caught up with him. In the end they decided to make a peace covenant, and the heap of stones would serve as a witness to that agreement. That each one used his own language suggests that they came from different cultures.

Today we can learn that important agreements are worth more when they are made with clarity and honesty. If there is a conflict, let us seek peace, put our promises in plain view, and remember that God is witness to what we say.
exp.33:23:
The explanation says that all the men who went out of the city gate listened to Hamor and his son Shechem. Then all the males of the city were circumcised. "Hearkened" here means that they listened to and accepted their proposal. "Those who went out of the gate" refers to the men who were part of the community and took part in the city's decisions.

Hamor and Shechem spoke at the city gate, which was the place of meetings and decisions. They had persuaded the men with a promise of gain: the goods of Jacob and his household would become theirs. Earlier, Shechem had dishonored Dinah, and Jacob's sons demanded circumcision with deceit. The text does not approve of the violence that follows.

For today: before following the majority or a leader, examine their motives. When selfish interest is involved, ask God for wisdom so that you are not carried away.
exp.18:10:
This verse tells that the men who were outside Lot's house were struck with blindness, from the youngest to the oldest. Even though they could no longer see, they kept struggling and wearing themselves out trying to find the door.

Lot's visitors, who according to the account are sent by God, had brought him into the house and shut the door. Outside, the crowd wanted to abuse them violently and even attacked Lot. This punishment stops the assault and protects Lot and his guests. Right after, the visitors tell him that the city will be destroyed.

For today: when we insist on evil, we can become blind to what is plain. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that recognizes its error in time and repents.
exp.20:5:
Sarah says that God gave her cause to laugh for joy. "Laugh" here speaks of gladness, and it also echoes the name Isaac, which sounds like "he laughs." She adds that whoever hears of her story will rejoice along with her. The phrase "all that hear" means "everyone who hears it."

Sarah, now an old woman, is speaking after giving birth to Isaac. Earlier she had laughed in doubt when God promised a son (Genesis 18:12). Now her laughter is different: it is the joy of seeing the promise fulfilled. Her next remark shows her amazement at nursing a child in her old age.

For today: when God fulfills something you were hoping for, do not keep it to yourself. Tell what He has done and rejoice with others. And if you are still waiting today, remember that God can turn doubt into joy.
exp.36:3:
This verse says that Joseph's brothers realized their father loved him more than all of them. Because of this they hated him, and they could no longer speak to him peaceably, that is, with kind and calm treatment. The phrase "they hated him" in the King James wording renders the same idea found in the original text.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition, and he describes how the conflict began in the family of Jacob, also called Israel. Jacob loved Joseph in a special way, since he had him in his old age, and he gave him a coat of many colors. Joseph had also brought his father a bad report about his brothers. All of this fed their jealousy, which later grew along with his dreams.

Today we can learn that favoritism and jealousy damage relationships. If we are parents or leaders, we should treat everyone with fairness. If we feel envy, it is wise to bring it to God before it hardens our hearts.
exp.40:11:
This verse says that in the prison there was a young Hebrew man, who served the captain of the guard. The two prisoners told him their dreams, and he explained the meaning of each one, according to the dream each had had. The words "young man" and "explained" are the ones to note here: in the King James wording, "young man" appears as "young man" and the explanation is given as "he interpreted to us our dreams," which means he explained or interpreted them.

The one speaking is the chief cupbearer of Pharaoh. Years earlier he had been imprisoned with the baker, and there he met Joseph. Now Pharaoh has dreams that no one can interpret, and the cupbearer finally remembers Joseph and tells him about him. In this way Joseph is brought from the dungeon to the palace.

For today: God can use what we do faithfully, even in difficult places and without anyone noticing. Serve with honesty where you are; God's timing may come when you least expect it.
exp.26:18:
Jacob speaks to his father Isaac, who is now old and blind. He pretends to be Esau, saying that he is the firstborn and that he has done what his father asked. He invites him to sit up and eat the game so that he may bless him.

Rebekah, the mother, planned this deception so that Jacob would receive the blessing that belonged to Esau. Here Jacob tells a direct lie. The Bible records the event without approving it, and then shows the painful consequences for the family. God had said earlier that the younger would serve the older, but that does not make the lie right.

For today: there is no need to deceive in order to obtain what God promises. Trusting Him means waiting and acting with honesty, even when it seems that the opposite would be to our advantage.
exp.6:14:
This verse says that the animals came to Noah and entered the ark two by two. They were creatures "wherein is the breath of life," that is, beings that breathed and had life. The word "went in" shows that they drew near, and "flesh" here refers to living creatures in general.

The account is narrated by Moses, according to tradition, and describes the moment when the flood begins. God had commanded Noah to build the ark to save his family and the animals. Two verses later it is said that everything happened "as God had commanded him." The text emphasizes Noah's obedience and God's care for life.

Today we can learn that God keeps what he promises and cares for his own. When he asks something of us, we can obey with confidence, even though we do not yet see the result. A simple step of faith can be to hand over a worry to him today in prayer.
exp.40:30:
This verse says that the years of plenty will no longer be noticed or remembered, because the famine that comes afterward will be very harsh. "Shall not be known" is an old way of saying "will not be noticed." "Very grievous" means very heavy, very hard.

Joseph is speaking to the Pharaoh of Egypt. He has just interpreted the king's dreams: seven years of great abundance followed by seven years of scarcity. Joseph explains that the famine will be so severe that it will erase even the memory of the plenty. For this reason, he immediately advises seeking a wise and discerning man to manage the resources well.

For today: when things are going well, it is easy to live without thinking about the future. This passage invites us to be wise and orderly in good times: to save, to share, and not to spend everything. Then, when hard days come, we can face them with more peace and trust in God.
exp.27:1:
Isaac tells Jacob to get up and go to Padan-aram, to the house of Bethuel, the father of his mother Rebekah. There he is to look for a wife among the daughters of Laban, Rebekah's brother. Padan-aram was a region of Mesopotamia, where the part of Abraham's family that had stayed behind lived.

Isaac speaks as an old man, just after blessing Jacob. He forbids him to marry Canaanite women, just as Abraham had made sure Isaac would not do. It is likely that he wanted to preserve the family faith and the promise of God, which Isaac mentions next. In addition, Jacob had to flee from Esau's anger, although the text here emphasizes the reason for the marriage.

For today: important decisions, such as choosing a spouse, are best made with God's guidance and the counsel of wise people, thinking about faith and the future of the family.
exp.31:25:
Here the "man" asks Jacob to let him go because dawn is already coming. Jacob answers firmly that he will not let go unless he first receives a blessing.

Jacob is alone at night, about to meet his brother Esau, whom he had deceived years earlier. He wrestles with a mysterious man. The text later calls him God, and some believe he was an angel or a manifestation of God himself. Although he is wounded in the thigh, Jacob does not give up and asks for a blessing.

When you are in a difficult situation, do not run from God. Come to Him with sincerity and perseverance, asking for His help, even if the process hurts or leaves you marked.
exp.35:21:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Lotan had two sons, Hori and Hemam, and that Timna was his sister.

The writer of Genesis records here the family line of the Horites, the people who lived in the region of Edom before the descendants of Esau settled there. The Bible includes these records to show that God knows all peoples and to explain how they were related to one another. Nothing more is said here about Timna; some think she is the same woman who appears in other passages connected with Esau, but this is not certain.

For today: God takes notice of every person, even those whose names almost no one remembers. If you ever feel forgotten, remember that your life matters to God.
exp.33:20:
Hamor and Siquem tell the men of their city that Jacob's sons are peaceable people. They can live and trade in the land, since there is room enough for everyone. The verse says "trade" where the older wording used "traffic," meaning doing business. They propose marrying between the two peoples, exchanging daughters.

Hamor and his son Siquem speak at the city gate, which was the place where public decisions were made. Siquem had dishonored Dina, and now he wants to marry her. Hamor presents the arrangement as a benefit for everyone, but the Bible shows that self-interest is also present: later in the chapter they mention gaining possession of Jacob's goods.

For today: when someone presents a proposal as good for everyone, it is wise to ask what their real motive is. Pleasant words do not always reveal a fair heart.
exp.28:29:
It says that Jacob also married Rachel, and that he loved her more than Leah. After that he had to work for Laban another seven years.

The older wording is easy to follow. "He went in also unto Rachel" means he had a marriage relationship with her, and "he loved also Rachel more than Leah" means exactly what it says: he loved Rachel more.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Laban had deceived Jacob by giving him Leah first, even though Jacob had worked seven years for Rachel. Then Jacob also received Rachel, and he stayed in that household another seven years. The text does not justify this situation; it only shows the pain it caused. Leah was placed at a disadvantage, and God saw her, as the next verse says.

For today: when a person feels less loved or overlooked, God sees them. And it falls to us to treat everyone with justice and kindness, without playing favorites that hurt others.
exp.20:27:
It says that Abraham took seven young female lambs from the flock and set them apart from the rest. "Ewe lambs" are small female sheep, and "by themselves" means he placed them to one side, where they could be seen, for a special purpose.

The narrator tells us that Abraham and Abimelech, king of Gerar, had just made an agreement. There was a dispute over a water well that Abimelech's servants had taken. Abraham set aside the seven ewe lambs to give to him later as proof that he was the one who had dug that well. Many scholars see here a custom of the time: a gift that served as a witness. The text does not explain why there were seven, although that number often appears in the Bible.

Today we can learn to resolve conflicts honestly and peacefully. Abraham did not fight or stay silent: he sought a clear agreement, with a concrete gesture that would prevent future misunderstandings.
exp.16:3:
God tells Abram that He makes a covenant with him, that is, a solemn and firm promise. He announces that Abram will be "a father of a multitude of nations," that is, the father of many nations. The phrase "behold" serves to draw attention: "look, this is what I promise you."

The one speaking is God, at a time when Abram was already old and still had no promised son. Abram falls facedown in a sign of respect and awe. Soon after, God changes his name to Abraham, which is connected to this promise. The change of name would always remind him of what God was going to do.

For today: God keeps His promises even when circumstances seem impossible. When you are called to wait, remember what God has said in His Word, and respond to Him with confidence and humility, as Abraham did.
exp.33:4:
This verse says that Jacob heard that Shechem had dishonored his daughter Dinah. The word "defiled," as used in the King James Version, means stained, violated, or wronged. Jacob's sons were out in the field with the flocks, and Jacob kept silent until they came back.

Here the narrator is speaking. Earlier the story tells how Shechem took Dinah and then said he loved her, asking his father to arrange her as his wife. The text does not explain why Jacob stayed silent. Some think it was prudence, others caution or weakness. His silence contrasts with the furious reaction of his sons afterward.

For today: when faced with injustice or painful news, it is wise to pause and think before acting. But silence should not become indifference. One should seek counsel, protect the one who was hurt, and act with justice and without revenge.
exp.24:11:
This verse opens the list of Ishmael's family. "Generations" means his descendants, the story of his family. Remember that Ishmael was the son of Abraham and Hagar, the Egyptian maidservant of Sarah. "Bare" is an older way of saying "gave birth to."

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, speaks. Right after recounting Abraham's death and God's blessing on Isaac, the account pauses to close the story of Ishmael before continuing with Isaac's line. This shows that God kept His promise to make Ishmael a great nation (Genesis 17:20).

For today: God does not forget anyone, even when their story began in difficult circumstances. Trust that He sees and cares for you and yours, and treat with respect those who seem to be on the margins.
exp.25:10:
Abimelech gives an order to all his people: whoever harms Isaac or Rebekah will be punished with death. "Touch" here means to do harm or abuse. "Surely" means "without doubt." "Charged" means that he gave a command.

Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar, had just discovered that Rebekah was Isaac's wife, not his sister, as Isaac had said out of fear. Although Isaac had lied, the king recognized the danger of sinning without knowing it and decided to protect the family. After this, God blessed Isaac with an abundant harvest.

For today: sometimes our mistakes and fears can cause problems, but God continues to watch over those who belong to him. Let us trust in his protection instead of resorting to half-truths, and act with honesty.
exp.26:27:
Isaac blesses Jacob and wishes that God will give him "the dew of heaven," that is, the moisture that makes crops grow in dry land. He also wishes him "the fatness of the earth," which means the best and most fertile part of the soil, and "plenty of corn and wine," that is, much bread and much new wine, freshly pressed grape juice.

Isaac speaks as an old man who is nearly blind. He believes he is blessing Esau, his firstborn son, but Jacob has disguised himself as him, deceiving his father with the help of his mother Rebekah. In that culture, a father's blessing carried great weight and was understood as a word that God stood behind. The account shows the deception without approving it, and its consequences will come later.

For today: every provision comes from the hand of God, not from our schemes. We can trust that He cares for us and wait for his promises without resorting to lies or shortcuts.
exp.18:15:
It says Lot hesitated and lingered before leaving Sodom. Then the two angels (called "men" in the text) took hold of his hand, along with his wife and his two daughters, and brought them out of the city. The phrase "laid hold upon" means "grabbed hold of." "The Lord being merciful unto him" means that God had compassion on them.

The angels had come to Sodom to warn Lot of the judgment that was coming on the city. Lot had already spoken with his sons-in-law, but they thought he was joking. At dawn, the angels urged him to hurry. The text does not explain why Lot hesitated; some think it was hard for him to leave his possessions and his life there. What is clear is that they were saved by God's compassion, not by their quickness or their merits.

When God calls us to leave something that harms us, let us not wait until we feel ready. Let us trust in his mercy and take the step today.
exp.48:4:
Jacob calls Simeon and Levi "brethren" because they were alike in temperament and acted together. He says their "weapons" were "of cruelty," that is, instruments of wickedness and injustice. Some translations read the phrase differently, because the Hebrew is difficult to render.

Jacob, now an old man, blesses and warns his sons before he dies. Here he recalls the violence of Simeon and Levi at Shechem (Genesis 34), when they killed the men of the city to avenge their sister Dinah. Jacob does not approve of that anger and distances himself from it.

For today: anger can look like justice, but if it leads us to hurt or to take revenge, it becomes wickedness. Before we react, ask God for calm and wisdom. Defending what is right must never be done with cruelty.
exp.34:11:
God repeats to Jacob the promise he had earlier made to Abraham and Isaac: the land he gave to them will now be for Jacob and his descendants. "Seed" means offspring, that is, his children and their families in future generations. "I will give" expresses a certain promise.

God himself speaks, presenting himself as God Almighty. Jacob was returning to Bethel, and God confirms his new name, Israel, and renews the covenant with him. After years of fear, struggle, and mistakes, God reminds him that his plan continues and does not depend on Jacob's perfection. Jacob responds by setting up a stone and pouring out a drink offering.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it seems late or our failures appear to stand in the way. You can rest in his faithfulness and respond as Jacob did, with gratitude and worship, confidently remembering what God has already said in his Word.
exp.25:7:
This verse tells how, after living many days in Gerar, King Abimelech looked out through a window and saw Isaac "sporting" with Rebekah. The word "sporting" here suggests an affectionate, intimate way of behaving between husband and wife, not simple childish play. That is why the king understood that she was his wife and not his sister.

The narrator tells this after Isaac, out of fear, had said that Rebekah was his sister. He feared that he would be killed on her account, since she was very beautiful. An everyday scene exposed the lie. Afterward, Abimelech confronted him.

For today: fear can lead us to half-truths that seem to protect us, but sooner or later they come to light. Trust in God and speak honestly, even when it frightens you.
exp.37:13:
She took off her widow's clothes, covered herself with a veil, and wrapped herself up well. Then she sat down in an open place, by the road to Timnath. The word "veil" here means covering her face with cloth. She did this because she saw that Shelah, Judah's youngest son, was now grown up, and she had not been given to him as a wife.

Here the narrator is speaking. Tamar had been widowed by two of Judah's sons, and Judah had promised her Shelah, but he did not keep his word. She was left without a son or protection. Her plan was deceptive and risky. The Bible tells the story without approving of everything she did, and Judah later admits his own wrongdoing (v. 26).

For today: when someone has failed us, let us not justify wrong with another wrong. It is better to keep our promises and seek justice with honesty and prayer.
exp.36:2:
It says that Israel, that is, Jacob, loved Joseph more than all his other sons, because he had him when he was already old. For this reason he made him a "coat of many colours," a special robe. Some versions say "coat of long sleeves"; the exact meaning of the Hebrew term is not entirely certain.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He tells how the tension in the family began. Joseph was seventeen years old and had reported the bad conduct of his brothers to their father. The gift showed Jacob's favoritism, and the verses that follow say this stirred up his brothers' hatred.

For today: if you have children, or people in your care, try to love them all fairly. Favoritism, even when it springs from affection, can wound and divide. Ask God for wisdom to care for each one.
exp.41:12:
Joseph's brothers explain to the Egyptian ruler who they are. They say they were twelve brothers, sons of one man in the land of Canaan. They report that the youngest had stayed with their father and that "one is not," that is, that he was gone or no longer there. "Servants" here is a respectful way of speaking before an authority.

The ten older brothers are the ones speaking. They had come to Egypt to buy grain because of the famine, and Joseph, whom they do not recognize, accuses them of being spies. They defend themselves by giving details about their family. Without knowing it, they speak of Joseph as though he were lost, and he is standing right in front of them.

For today: when we carry something unresolved, such as an old guilt, sooner or later it comes to light. It is better to be honest with God and with others, and to seek reconciliation before the past catches up with us.
exp.4:29:
It says that Lamech kept on living 595 years after his son Noah was born, and that during that time he had more sons and daughters. "Begat" means that he became a father.

The narrator of the book of Genesis goes on giving the list of Adam's descendants, noting how long each one lived. Here Lamech is not the one speaking; it is the person telling the story. Earlier, Lamech had given Noah his name in hope of relief in the midst of the hard labor of the cursed ground. Scholars understand these very long numbers in different ways, and the Bible does not explain them.

For today: Lamech raised his family for many years after that hope. We can hope in God and also be steady in everyday life, caring for and teaching our own people day after day.
exp.45:7:
This verse opens a list of the names of the children of Israel, that is, of Jacob, who came into Egypt. It begins with Reuben, Jacob's firstborn son. "Firstborn" means the eldest son, the one who was born first. "Came into" refers to their arriving there to live.

The narrator is the author of the book, traditionally identified as Moses. Jacob was already old, and he moved to Egypt because of the famine, since his son Joseph lived there. The narrator lists the family to record who they were and how many went in. In this way the beginning of the people of Israel is shown, a people who would later grow greatly in Egypt.

For today: God knows each person by name, and He also values families. We can remember and give thanks for those who went before us in the faith, and pray for our family by name, trusting that God cares for each one.
exp.11:12:
Abram asks Sarai to say that she is his sister. "That it may be well with me for thy sake" means that things will go well for him because of her, and "my soul shall live" means that they will spare his life.

Abram speaks with his wife as they enter Egypt, where he had gone because of a famine. He fears that he will be killed so that the Egyptians can take her, because she is very beautiful. Later, Sarai is in fact Abram's half-sister through their father (Genesis 20:12), so it was not a complete lie, but it was a half-truth that put her in danger. The Bible does not approve of his plan here; it shows his fear and its consequences.

For today: when we feel afraid, it is easy to look for escapes that seem clever but put others at risk. Before acting, let us pray and trust that God protects, even when we cannot see how.
exp.25:34:
This verse says that Esau's two Hittite wives were a source of "bitterness of spirit" for Isaac and Rebekah. In other words, they caused them deep sorrow, distress, and worry.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking, not a character in the story. Esau married women from a local people, the Hittites, who did not follow the God of Abraham. The text does not spell out exactly what behavior caused the pain, so it is best not to invent details. Later, Rebekah expresses her anguish over this (Genesis 27:46), and Jacob is sent to find a wife among his own family.

For today: important decisions, such as marriage, affect the whole family. Before deciding, it is wise to pray, to listen to the counsel of parents, and to think about how that decision will affect the faith and peace of those we love.
exp.31:27:
The explanation says that the man who wrestled with Jacob changes his name. He will no longer be called Jacob but Israel, because he struggled with God and with men, and came out the victor. "Prevailed" means that he wrestled, and "hast power" means that he did not give up. Many explain that "Israel" sounds like "struggles with God" or "God struggles," although its exact meaning is debated.

Jacob is alone, at night, and fears meeting his brother Esau, whom he had deceived. A mysterious man wrestles with him until dawn. Jacob holds on and asks for a blessing. Later, he himself says that he saw God face to face. The new name marks a change in his life.

For today: when you are distressed, do not run from God. Come to Him with honesty, pray with persistence, and ask for His blessing. God can transform you in the midst of the struggle.
exp.19:10:
Abraham explains why he acted as he did. He says he thought that in Gerar nobody respected God, and that for this reason they would kill him in order to take Sarah, his wife. "The fear of God" means respect and reverence toward God, which shows in how a person treats others.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, confronts Abraham because Abraham said Sarah was only his sister. Abraham answers out of fear, not from any real test. He assumed the worst about that place. The text shows that God had already protected Sarah and that Abimelech acted with integrity, so Abraham's assumption was not entirely fair.

When fear takes hold of us, we can judge others without knowing them and make foolish decisions. Before assuming the worst about someone, it is wise to pray, to trust that God cares for us, and to act with honesty.
exp.1:1:
This verse says that God finished his work of creation on the seventh day, and that on that day he rested. "Ended" means he brought the work to completion, and "rested" means he stopped working. It does not speak of a tired God, but of a finished and complete work.

The text is part of the creation account in Genesis, written as narrative. Here the narrator speaks, not a character. It is traditionally attributed to Moses, although how it was composed is debated. Its purpose is to show that God created everything with order and that rest has a special place, as the following verse confirms, where God blesses and sanctifies that day.

For today: learn to rest without guilt. If God himself set aside a time of rest, you too can set apart a moment each week to stop, give thanks, and trust that God sustains what you cannot finish.
exp.45:9:
This verse lists the six sons of Simeon, the second son of Jacob by Leah: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul. About Shaul it is made clear that his mother was a Canaanite, that is, a woman from the land of Canaan rather than from Abraham's family. "The son of a Canaanitish woman" is the way the King James Version puts it.

The narrator of the book (tradition attributes it to Moses) presents the list of those who traveled with Jacob to Egypt, when Joseph was already ruling there. He wants to record each family that formed the people of Israel. Shaul's mother is mentioned, and not the others, perhaps because it was something notable; the text does not explain the reason.

For today: God knows concrete names and families, including those that seem ordinary or imperfect to us. You are not a number to Him. You can trust that He sees you and includes you in His story.
exp.2:4:
The explanation says that the serpent tells the woman that God knows something she does not: that if she eats of the fruit, her eyes "shall be opened" and she "shall be as gods," knowing good and evil. Where the older wording reads "the day ye eat thereof," the text you are reading says "in the day ye eat thereof," and "then your eyes shall be opened" and "ye shall be as gods" are the same promises in the King James wording.

Context: The serpent speaks, and it contradicts what God said about the forbidden tree. It suggests that God is hiding something good from them and is not being sincere. What follows shows that their eyes were opened, but only so that they felt shame. Some think that "as gods" can also be understood as "as God," since the original language allows both readings.

For today: When a voice makes us doubt that God is good and that his limits are there to protect us, let us remember that a lie often mixes a half-truth with an attractive promise. Let us return to God's word and trust his character.
exp.40:52:
This verse says that the seven years of abundance in Egypt came to an end. "Plenteousness" is an old word meaning abundance, having more than enough to eat. It is a short phrase that marks the close of one period.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Joseph is already a ruler under Pharaoh and has stored up grain, as God had made known to him through the dreams. Shortly before, Joseph named his two sons with gratitude for what God had done in his life. Now the account moves forward toward the time of famine he had foretold.

For today: good times do not last forever, so it is wise to live them with gratitude and wisdom. We can save, prepare, and trust God, without letting comfort make us forget him.
exp.23:36:
Here the servant of Abraham recounts what his master commanded him under oath: not to seek a wife for Isaac among the daughters of the Canaanites, the people of the land where Abraham lived as a foreigner. To "swear" is to make a solemn promise, calling God as witness.

The speaker is Abraham's servant, who is now in Haran, beside the well, and he explains his mission to Rebekah's family. He first describes how God blessed Abraham and gave him Isaac. He then explains that Abraham wanted a wife from his own kindred. Many understand that the purpose was to preserve faith in the true God, although the text does not state this in so many words.

For today: important decisions, such as marriage or choosing with whom to walk through life, deserve prayer, counsel, and faithfulness to God. Keeping a promise and seeking his direction is wise.
exp.7:19:
It says that, upon coming out of the ark, the first thing Noah did was build an altar for God. He took some of the clean animals and birds, meaning those the biblical tradition regarded as fit for sacrifice, and offered them as a burnt offering, an offering that was burned up completely. The word "Lord" in this verse is the name of God, rendered in the King James Version as LORD.

It is part of the account of the flood. The narrator tells us that Noah and his family have just come out safe and sound. Noah does not speak here; he acts. His sacrifice expresses gratitude and worship. Right after this, God responds with a promise: he will not again destroy the earth with a flood, even though the human heart remains inclined toward evil.

For today: before making plans or rushing into what comes next, we can pause to thank God for his care. A moment of sincere prayer can be our "altar."
exp.45:32:
This verse is part of Joseph's instructions to his brothers. He tells them in advance that Pharaoh is going to call them in and ask what they do for a living. The words "call" and "say" appear here in the forms used in the King James Version, and "occupation" means work or trade.

Joseph is speaking to his brothers and to Jacob's family, who have just arrived in Egypt because of the famine. He wants to prepare them to answer honestly that they are shepherds. That way they could live apart, in the land of Goshen. The text says that the Egyptians looked down on shepherds, though it does not explain in detail the reasons for that rejection.

For today: Joseph does not ask them to pretend to be something they are not, but to speak with clarity and truth. Before an important conversation, it is good to think and pray ahead of time, and to present ourselves with honesty, trusting that God can open doors.
exp.23:59:
Her family blessed her before sending her away. They said to her, "You are our sister," and they wished that she would have a huge number of descendants ("thousands upon thousands," that is, a great many). They also asked that her children would "possess the gate of their enemies," a way of saying that they would have victory and authority over those who opposed them. In that time, the city gate was the place of defense and government.

It is her relatives who speak, probably Laban and her mother, in Haran. Abraham's servant had already explained how God directed his journey, and Rebekah agreed to go. Now they send her off with a wish for good. Their blessing resembles the promises God made to Abraham.

For today: when someone in your family or your church begins a new stage, send them off with a sincere blessing. Pray for that person and encourage them with words of faith and affection.
exp.14:8:
God tells Abram to bring him animals: a heifer (a young cow), a female goat and a ram, all three years old, along with a turtledove and a young pigeon. The word "take" here means "separate them and choose them for me."

Here God is speaking. Abram had just asked how he could be sure he would inherit the land. God does not rebuke him but answers him with a covenant ritual. In that time, cutting animals in half and setting the halves facing each other was a way of sealing a solemn commitment, although the details are explained in several ways.

For today: when you have doubts, bring them honestly to God, as Abram did. He can give you signs of his faithfulness, especially in his Word, and he invites you to trust his promises with patience.
exp.46:15:
Here José tells the Egyptians that, since they no longer have money to buy food, they should hand over their animals. In exchange, he will give them bread. The word "cattle" refers to horses, sheep, cows and donkeys. "If money fail" means that there is no money left.

Joseph, who managed Egypt's food supplies under Pharaoh, is the one speaking. There was a severe famine, and the people had already spent all their money buying grain. They had asked him for bread so that they would not die. Joseph offers them a way out: trade their animals for food. The Bible does not judge here whether all of this was fair, and people have interpreted it in different ways.

For today: when our resources run out, it is wise to ask for help in time and to think carefully about what we can offer. Also, those who hold authority should use it with compassion, caring for the lives of the most needy.
exp.46:1:
It says that Joseph chose five of his brothers from the last, that is, from the least prominent, and brought them before Pharaoh. The word "men" in the verse means men, and "presented" means "brought before."

The passage tells how Jacob and his family came to Egypt because of the famine. Joseph, who was already a ruler under Pharaoh, announced their arrival and presented some of his brothers. It is not known with certainty why there were five or why these particular ones were chosen; some think it was so as not to overwhelm the king, or that they were the most suitable to speak. The text does not explain this.

Today, Joseph teaches us to act with order and respect, caring for family while remaining prudent. If you have to help others in an important matter, do it with humility, prepare well, and trust that God can open doors.
exp.10:27:
This verse tells that Haran, son of Terah and brother of Abram, died while still young, before his father. It happened in the place where he had been born: Ur of the Chaldees. The King James phrase "the land of his nativity" means "his native land," the land of his birth.

The narrator of Genesis presents Terah's family, from which Abram will come. Here neither God nor a character speaks; it is a historical account. Haran's death is mentioned because his son Lot will later accompany Abram, and because it explains why Lot is under the care of his uncle. Scholars do not know for certain the cause of his death, and the text does not state it.

Today we can remember that life is fragile and that grief comes to families everywhere. God, however, continues to work in the midst of loss. If there is mourning in your home, you are not alone: you can draw near to God with your sorrow and tenderly care for those who have been left most vulnerable.
exp.23:38:
This verse says that Abraham's servant had a doubt. He asked his master, "What if the woman will not come with me?" The word "peradventure" shows an uncertain possibility, and "follow me" means coming along with him to a distant land.

Here the servant of Abraham is speaking. He tells Rebekah's family what happened before his journey. Abraham had made him swear that he would seek a wife for Isaac among Abraham's own kin and not among the Canaanites. The servant shares his concern honestly, and then he recalls the promise that God would send his angel and make the journey prosper.

For today: it is not wrong to ask hard questions or to admit our doubts. What matters is to bring them to God and keep moving forward, trusting that he guides our path even when we do not yet see the outcome.
exp.7:21:
God promises that, as long as the earth exists, the rhythms of nature will not stop: the time for sowing and the time for reaping, the cold and the heat, the summer and the winter, the day and the night.

Here, "seedtime" is the time of sowing, and "harvest" is the time of gathering the crop. The phrase "while the earth remaineth" means "as long as the earth lasts."

The Lord speaks "in his heart," that is, as an inner resolve. The flood has just passed, and Noah offers a burnt offering in thanksgiving. God answers with this promise: he will not again destroy life in this way, even though the human heart remains inclined to evil. It is an act of mercy, not a reward for people's goodness.

For today: every sunrise and every season reminds us that God is faithful. When you feel anxious about the future, give thanks for simple things, like the rain, the bread, or a new day, and trust that he sustains his creation.
exp.12:6:
This verse tells us there was a quarrel between the herdsmen of Abram and the herdsmen of Lot. "Strife" means a fight or a dispute. The KJV's "Perizzite" is the name of one of the peoples who lived in the region, and the verse mentions the Canaanite and the Perizzite to say that the land was already inhabited by others.

The narrator explains why the conflict arose: the flocks of the two men were so large that the land could not hold them all. Abram and Lot were uncle and nephew. The herdsmen were fighting, and that put the peace of the family at risk. Also, since other peoples lived nearby, a fight among them would look bad.

For today: when good things, such as work or money, cause tension, do not let the quarrel grow. Speak up early, with humility, and seek peace before the relationship is harmed.
exp.37:25:
Judah recognizes the items Tamar showed him: his signet ring, his cloak, and his staff. He admits that she is "more righteous", that is, that she was more in the right than he was. The reason is that he did not give her his son Shelah, as he should have. The phrase "he knew her again no more" means that he did not have relations with her again. The older words "fornicated" and "with child" in the earlier wording are now expressed simply as "she has played the harlot" and "pregnant" in the King James wording, which describe illicit relations and pregnancy.

Judah speaks before everyone, and he does so when Tamar was about to be burned. He had left Tamar a widow and without hope, without keeping his promise to give her Shelah. She acted deceptively, and the Bible does not present her as a model to imitate. Even so, Judah publicly acknowledges his own fault, and the text shows this as a moment of humility.

When we are shown a fault of our own, we can either defend ourselves or honestly admit it. Acknowledging a mistake in time, without excuses, can stop a greater harm and open the way to real change.
exp.14:17:
That same day God made a covenant, that is, a solemn promise, with Abram. He promised to give Abram's offspring ("seed" means children and descendants) a broad land, from "the river of Egypt" to the Euphrates. Some believe "the river of Egypt" is the Nile; others think it is a stream on the border of Egypt. It is not known for certain.

The Lord, Jehovah, speaks. Shortly before, Abram saw in the night a smoking furnace and a torch of fire pass between the divided animals, a sign that God himself was binding himself to fulfill the promise. God also said that the promise would take generations to come true, until the wickedness of the Amorites reached its limit.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes longer than we expect. When your waiting is long, do not despair; trust that God is faithful and keeps working, even when you cannot see it.
exp.12:2:
It says that Abram returned little by little, in stages ("journeys"), from the south of Canaan, called "the South" (the Negev), to Bethel. He arrived at the very place where he had earlier pitched his tent, between Bethel and Hai. "Journeys" are the stretches of the trip covered each day.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Abram had come from Egypt, where he had gone because of the famine, and there he made mistakes (Genesis 12). Now he returns to the place where he had built an altar and worshiped God. The text does not explain his feelings, but many understand this return as a fresh start with God.

For today: if you have drifted away or made mistakes, you can return step by step to the place where your relationship with God was simple and sincere. Take up prayer, the Word, and fellowship with other believers again. No great leap is needed; it is enough to take the next step back.
exp.0:9:
This verse tells how God gave names to what he had separated on the third day. The dry land, which this older version calls "the dry," he named Earth. The gathering together of the waters he named Seas. The English word "saw" in the King James wording is the same in modern usage, so the reader will see it as it is. At the end, God looks at what he has made and says that it is good.

The author of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, narrates how God orders the world step by step. God speaks, and things come to be. First he separated the waters and then shaped the land, preparing a place where life could exist, as the following verses show with the plants.

For today: creation is not an accident, nor something without value. If God called it good, we can care for it with respect and gratitude. Today you can give thanks for something natural you see and look after it in a concrete way.
exp.41:7:
This verse says that Joseph immediately recognized his brothers, but they were unable to recognize him. The word "knew" here means "recognized." Although the brothers were standing before him, they did not know that this Egyptian ruler was the brother they had sold.

It is part of the account in which famine brought Joseph's brothers to Egypt to buy grain. Joseph was already an important authority. About twenty years had passed, and he appeared to be an Egyptian, spoke through an interpreter, and dressed like a high official. That is why they did not identify him. The text does not explain everything Joseph was thinking; it only shows that he recognized them and remembered his dreams.

For today: at times God works in our lives without our noticing, and only afterward do we understand what He was doing. We can trust that He continues to care for the story, even when we do not yet see the whole picture.
exp.46:9:
This verse tells us that Jacob, already an old man, blessed Pharaoh and then withdrew from his presence. "Blessed" here means that he asked for God's good on him. The King James wording "went out from before Pharaoh" is simply the plain way of saying that he left, or went out, from the king's presence.

Jacob had just arrived in Egypt with his family, fleeing the famine, and Joseph presented him before the king. Pharaoh asked him his age, and Jacob spoke honestly of a hard life, which he called his "pilgrimage." After that, he blessed him. Some think that, being older and carrying God's promise, his blessing had a special weight. The text gives no further details about the exact words used.

For today: even when we have gone through pain and weariness, we can end our conversations with a word of good for others, even for those who have more power than we do.
exp.49:8:
This verse says that, in addition to the people who went to Jacob's burial, chariots and horsemen also went up with Joseph. Together they formed a very large company, a "squadron." The word "mourned" (in the following verse) means to weep with songs of sorrow, and "on horseback" refers to men riding on horses.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. Jacob had died in Egypt, but he had asked Joseph to bury him in Canaan, the land promised to his forefathers. Pharaoh allowed it, and that is why the journey included Egyptian officials. The chariots and horsemen may have served as an honor and also as protection on the road, though the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: honoring those we love, including at their farewell, is something valuable. Accompanying a family in their grief with presence, time, and concrete help is a real form of love.
exp.10:24:
This verse says that Nahor, the grandfather of Abraham, lived 119 years after he became the father of Terah. He also had other sons and daughters. The word "begat" means "fathered" or "had as a son," and the name "Terah" is the name of Abraham's father. The archaic word "an" in "an hundred" is an older form of "a," meaning "one hundred."

This is not a speech by a person; it is the account of the writer of Genesis, who lists the generations from Shem to Abram. It is a family list that connects ancient history with the calling of Abraham. It shows that God keeps the story of each generation, even of people about whom we know very little. The numbers of years are understood in several ways, and there is no complete agreement on how to interpret them.

For today: God values ordinary people, even those who pass through life without making any noise. Your daily life, your family, and your simple faith are also part of what God is doing for the generations to come.
exp.11:13:
This verse tells that, when Abram came into Egypt, the Egyptians noticed that Sarai was a very beautiful woman. The phrase "very fair" in the King James Version means extremely beautiful. "It came to pass" means "it happened."

The narrator tells what happened after Abram, out of fear, asked Sarai to say that she was his sister. There was famine in Canaan, and Abram went down to Egypt as a foreigner. He feared they would kill him in order to take her. The Bible does not approve his plan here; it only shows his fear and its consequences. Later God intervenes and protects Sarai (Genesis 12:17-20).

For today: when we feel afraid, it is tempting to look for ways out through half-truths. This passage invites us to trust that God cares for us, even when we fail, and to choose honesty even in difficult moments.
exp.20:11:
God tells Abraham not to be distressed over the boy Ishmael and over Hagar, his servant woman. He asks him to listen to Sarah in whatever she says to him. "Let it not be grievous in thy sight" means "do not let it weigh on you or hurt you so much." "Seed" and "descendants" mean the children and the generations that would come after. God makes clear that the promise would continue through Isaac.

God speaks in the middle of a family crisis. Sarah had seen Ishmael mocking Isaac, and she asked that Hagar and her son be sent away. Abraham suffered greatly because he loved Ishmael. God comforts him and confirms that the promise continues through Isaac. In addition, he promises to care for Ishmael, because he is also Abraham's son.

For today: when a difficult decision causes us pain, we can bring it to God with sincerity. He understands our suffering, guides our steps, and cares for the people we do not fully understand.
exp.46:2:
Pharaoh asks Joseph's brothers what their occupation is. They answer that they are shepherds of sheep, just as their fathers were before them. "Occupation" means work or trade, and "servants" is a respectful way of speaking before a king.

Joseph had just presented five of his brothers before Pharaoh. Jacob's family had come from Canaan because of the famine and needed a place to live with their flocks. They state honestly what their work is, and that allows them to ask for the land of Goshen. Some think this also helped keep them separate from the Egyptians, but the text does not say so clearly.

Today we can learn to speak honestly and without shame about who we are and where we come from. God can use our simple work and our family history to open doors for us and to care for us.
exp.40:19:
This verse describes part of Pharaoh's dream: the seven lean, ugly cows devoured the seven fat cows that had come up first. The word "devoured" means they swallowed them up greedily.

The one speaking is Pharaoh, who tells his dream to Joseph. No one in Egypt had been able to explain it. According to the account, God was showing him what would come: seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine. The dream seemed strange, but it carried a serious and urgent message.

For today: good seasons do not last forever, and God invites us to be wise. When things are going well, we can save, help others, and trust in Him, without living as if hard times will never come.
exp.44:4:
What it says: Joseph asks his brothers not to be distressed or blame themselves for having sold him as a slave into Egypt. "Be not grieved" means do not be filled with sorrow, and "nor angry with yourselves" means do not let remorse consume them. Joseph states that God sent him ahead of them to preserve life, that is, to save many from death.

Context: Joseph, now a ruler in Egypt, is speaking after revealing himself to the brothers who betrayed him years earlier. They are frightened and speechless. There is famine in the region, and Joseph sees that God used even that evil to save his family. This does not erase their guilt, but it shows his forgiveness.

For today: When someone has hurt you, or you have hurt others, you can seek forgiveness without letting resentment or guilt master you. Trust that God can bring good even out of painful situations.
exp.35:13:
This verse lists the three sons that Aholibamah, another wife of Esau, bore to him: Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah. She was the daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon. The word "bare" means "gave birth to," and "dukes" later on means chiefs or leaders of clans.

The narrator, whom tradition associates with Moses though the text does not say so, presents here the genealogy of Esau, father of the Edomites. After the story of Jacob, the Bible closes the account of Esau by recording that his descendants became a people with their own leaders. This shows that God kept His word to make Esau also into a nation.

For today: God pays attention to every family and every name, even to those that seem minor. Value your family history and trust that God keeps what He promises, including with those who do not follow the main path.
exp.23:45:
Rebekah quickly lowered her jar from her shoulder and offered the servant water. She also offered to give his camels a drink. The word "made haste" in the King James wording means she did it at once, without delay. The servant reports that she did exactly what he had asked.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, who tells his story to Rebekah's family. Abraham sent him to find a wife for Isaac. The servant had prayed for a sign, and now he explains how God answered. Giving water to ten camels was a large task, so her gesture showed a generous heart.

Today we can learn to pray with confidence and to watch for how God answers. We can also imitate Rebekah: serving willingly and generously, even when no one requires it of us.
exp.1:13:
The explanation says the third river of Eden was called Hiddekel, which corresponds to the Tigris, and that it flowed east of Assyria. The fourth river was the Euphrates. "Goeth toward the east of Assyria" means that it passed along the front or eastern side of that region.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, describing the place where God placed the man. He mentions real rivers that were well known to the ancient reader, although no one knows with certainty where Eden was. Interpreters understand it in several ways: as a geographical place, or as a description with symbolic meaning.

For today: Eden had abundant water, and from it life flowed. In this way, God provides what we need to live. Today you can thank Him for everyday things, such as water, food and work, and take responsible care of what He has entrusted to you.
exp.1:17:
God says it is not good for the man to be alone, and so he decides to make him a "help meet." "Help meet" means a helper suitable for him, one fitting to his needs. The word "help" in the original Hebrew is also used in the Bible for God himself as the helper of his people, so it does not imply inferiority.

God, the Creator, is the one speaking. Up to this point, everything created had been called "good"; this is the first time something is described as "not good." After the command about the trees, God shows that the man needs companionship. The animals pass before Adam, but none of them is the suitable companion. Some scholars see here a basis for marriage; others, a broader truth about community.

We were created to live in relationship with others. Today, seek out and nurture healthy friendships, in your family, your church, or your community, and do not carry your struggles alone.
exp.7:15:
God commands Noah to go out of the ark. He says it plainly: he, his wife, his sons, and his sons' wives. That makes eight people in all. The words "Go out of the ark" are an invitation to begin again, now that the danger has passed.

God himself speaks. Noah had waited inside the ark for a long time, and the earth was already dry. Noah did not go out on his own, but waited for the word of God. Afterward, God also commands that the animals be brought out so that they may multiply. Thus a new stage begins for creation.

For today: learn to wait for God's direction before taking the next step, even when everything seems ready. Trusting his timing keeps us from rushing ahead. And when he opens the door, going out in faith is also obedience.
exp.31:1:
Jacob sees the angels of God coming to meet him, and he exclaims, "This is God's host." So he calls that place Mahanaim. "Host" here means an army or camp, a company of people gathered together. Mahanaim means "two hosts" or "two camps."

Jacob has just left his father-in-law Laban and is on his way back to his own land, where his brother Esau is waiting, the brother he had deceived years before. He is afraid of that meeting. Before he sends messengers to Esau, God shows him that he is not alone. The Bible does not explain in detail what exactly he saw, and it is not certain which "two camps" the name refers to. It may have been Jacob's camp and the camp of the angels.

When you face something that frightens you, remember that God is with you even when you cannot see him. Ask him to open your eyes so you can trust in his care.
exp.40:35:
This verse says that the grain gathered during the good years would be kept in reserve as a supply for the land. So when the seven years of famine came in Egypt, the people would not die. The explanation of the word "quintar," which means taking a fifth part, and "hartura," meaning abundance, and "alleguen," meaning to gather together, have been left out because those words do not appear in the English text.

Joseph is speaking before Pharaoh. He has just interpreted his dreams, which announced seven years of plenty followed by seven years of scarcity. Now he advises him on a plan: to appoint officials, collect a portion of the harvest, and store it. Pharaoh and his servants thought the plan was good, and they recognized in Joseph a man with the Spirit of God.

For today: in good times it is wise to be prudent. Saving, planning, and not spending everything we have is a wise way to care for our family, and also to be able to help others when difficult times arrive.
exp.48:25:
Here Jacob says that the blessings he gives to Joseph are greater than those received by his ancestors, and that they will last as far as the "everlasting hills," that is, the ancient hills that seem never to end. That blessing will rest upon the "head" and the "crown" of Joseph's head (the highest part of the head). The "separated one from his brothers" means the set apart, the one who was distinguished among them. Some understand this as the prince or the consecrated one among his brothers.

Jacob is already old, near death, and he gathers his twelve sons to declare what will come upon each one. He speaks to Joseph with great tenderness, remembering that God sustained and cared for him, even when his brothers had sold him.

For today: God can bless his people across the generations. We can give thanks for what we have received from those who went before us in the faith, and we can pray for and bless our children and the younger ones with our words.
exp.44:20:
This verse says that the sons of Jacob, who was also called Israel, did what they were told. Joseph gave them wagons, just as Pharaoh had commanded, and he gave them provision for the way, meaning food for the journey.

Joseph had already made himself known to his brothers, the same men who years earlier had sold him. Pharaoh was pleased and wanted the whole family to move to Egypt, where there was food in the midst of the famine. The narrator tells how Joseph carried out that invitation with generosity and care, holding no grudge.

We can learn to respond with concrete kindness, not just words of forgiveness. Joseph did not merely forgive: he helped, provided, and made the way easier. Think of someone with whom you have had an offense, and ask yourself what practical gesture of generosity you could offer them this week.
exp.23:58:
