This verse tells that Rebekah's family let her go. Along with her went her nurse, the woman who had raised and cared for her since she was small, Abraham's servant, and the men who accompanied him. "Sent away" means they gave her permission to leave.

The narrator recounts what happened after Abraham's servant arrived in Haran to seek a wife for Isaac. Rebekah's family recognized that the matter came from God, and she herself accepted with a "Yes, I will go." Then her family sent her off with a blessing. The nurse is mentioned here, and later it is said that her name was Deborah (Genesis 35:8).

For today: when God opens a path, moving forward in faith can be an act of courage. It is also good to say farewell with a blessing rather than resistance, supporting those who take important steps.
exp.33:0:
This verse tells us that Dinah, the daughter Leah bore to Jacob, went out to get to know the young women of the region. The word "bare" in the King James Version means "gave birth to," so it refers to Dinah as Leah's child. "The land" refers to the land of Canaan, where the local inhabitants lived. It is a simple detail, but it opens a very painful story.

The narrator of the book of Genesis introduces Dinah here as the only daughter of Jacob who is mentioned. The family lived near Shechem. The text does not explain why she went out, nor does it say that she did anything wrong. What follows shows that she was the victim of a serious injustice. Some scholars see in this a contrast between God's people and the customs of their surroundings, although the text does not state this clearly.

For today: Let us care for the most vulnerable and never blame the victims. If someone suffers abuse, they deserve protection, a listening ear, and justice, and the church should be a safe place.
exp.21:6:
Isaac speaks to his father Abraham and calls him "My father." Abraham answers tenderly, "Here am I," which means "Here I am." Isaac notices that they are carrying the fire and the wood, but there is no lamb for the burnt offering, an offering that was burned up completely in honor of God.

God had asked Abraham to offer his son Isaac. The two walk together toward the mountain. Isaac asks a sincere question, not knowing what is coming. Abraham answers with faith: "God will provide himself a lamb." Some see here a sign of total trust; others see an answer that does not reveal everything.

There are moments when we do not understand the path. Like Abraham, we can keep moving forward with honesty and trust that God will take care of what we cannot see.
exp.32:19:
Jacob built an altar on the piece of land he had just bought and gave it a name: "The God of Israel." "Erected" means he raised or built it. "Called" means he gave it a name. Israel is the new name God had given Jacob. In the Hebrew, some understand the name as "El-Elohe-Israel," that is, "God, the God of Israel."

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob was returning from Paddan-aram after many years away and after his difficult reunion with Esau. He arrived safe and sound in Canaan, bought a plot of land near Shechem, and settled there. His first act in the land was to worship. By calling the altar "the God of Israel," Jacob acknowledges that this God is now his own too, not only the God of his father and his grandfather.

For today: when God brings us safely to a new place or stage, let us begin by giving thanks and acknowledging him. May our faith be personal, not merely inherited.
exp.35:16:
These are the sons of Reuel, Esau's son: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. They are the dukes who came from Reuel in the land of Edom. Their mother was Bashemath, Esau's wife.

The word "duke" here does not refer to European nobility, but to a chief or leader of a tribe. Edom is another name for Esau, and also the name of the land where his descendants lived.

No one is speaking in a discourse here; it is the narrator of Genesis who records the genealogy of Esau. This list shows that God kept his promise to make Esau into a nation, even though the line of the promise passed through Jacob. Scholars believe these records were preserved to document the origin of Edom, Israel's neighbor.

For today: God remembers families and people, including those who seem less important in history. Your life and your family have value to Him, even when no one mentions them.
exp.32:3:
This verse tells how Esau ran to meet his brother Jacob. He embraced him, threw his arms around his neck, kissed him, and the two of them wept. "Ran to meet him" means he went out to receive him, and "kissed him" was a sign of affection in that culture.

The narrator recounts the reunion after many years. Jacob had deceived Esau and had fled out of fear of his revenge. Now he returns with his family, and he approaches with humility, bowing down seven times. Esau responds with tenderness, not anger. Some believe it was a sincere reconciliation; others see a certain caution on Jacob's part. The text says nothing more.

For today: we do not know how the person we have wronged will respond, but we can take the first step with humility. And if someone seeks us out to be reconciled, we can receive them with grace, as Esau did.
exp.33:21:
Here it is stated that the men of Shechem would agree to let Jacob's family live among them and form one people, but with one condition: that every male in the city be circumcised, just as Jacob's sons were. The wording "will the men consent" means "will agree" or "will accept" the arrangement, and the verse's phrasing "for to dwell with us" reflects an older English construction meaning simply "to live among us."

Hamor and his son Shechem speak to the men of their city at the gate, which was the place where public decisions were made. Shechem had dishonored Dinah, Jacob's daughter, and now wanted to marry her. Dinah's brothers had set circumcision as the condition. Hamor presents the arrangement as something peaceful, but he also lets it be seen that he is interested in the wealth of Jacob's household.

For today: before accepting an agreement, it is wise to ask what motives lie behind it, both in others and in ourselves. Kind words can hide selfish interests, and God calls us to act with truth and justice.
exp.25:8:
Abimelech calls Isaac in and confronts him: when he saw how they were treating each other, he realized that Rebekah was his wife and not his sister. He asks him why he said otherwise. Isaac answers honestly: he did it out of fear that he would die because of her.

The speaker is Abimelech, king of the Philistines in Gerar. Isaac had settled there during a time of famine. Out of fear, and because Rebekah was beautiful, he said she was his sister. It was a half-truth, since it hid the fact that she was his wife. His father Abraham had done something similar before. Abimelech is concerned because someone might have sinned without knowing it.

Today, fear can lead us to hide the truth and to trust our own plans more than God. When we feel afraid, let us ask him for courage to be honest and to rest in his care.
exp.15:4:
Sarai complains to Abram about what is happening. She says, "My wrong be upon thee," meaning that the injury should fall on him. She says she put her servant "into thy bosom," that is, gave her to him as a secondary wife. Now Hagar, having conceived, looks on Sarai with contempt. Sarai ends by asking that the Lord be the judge between the two of them.

Sarai speaks with pain and anger. She could not have children, and after ten years in Canaan she sought a human solution to God's promise. It was an accepted custom in her time, but the plan brought rivalry and jealousy. Now she blames Abram, even though the idea was hers.

When our plans become complicated, it is easy to accuse others. It is better to stop, acknowledge our own part, and bring the situation before God with humility, trusting that He works better than our shortcuts.
exp.44:3:
Here Joseph asks his brothers to come near. The word "come near" in the verse is the direct invitation, and "I pray you" makes it a gentle request. They draw close, and then Joseph tells them plainly who he is: the brother they sold into Egypt. He does not hide what they did.

Joseph speaks after weeping loudly in front of everyone. His brothers had come to Egypt for food, and they did not recognize him. Now they are frightened and speechless. By bringing them close and naming the truth, Joseph opens the way to reconciliation. In the verses that follow he tells them not to be distressed, because God sent him ahead to preserve life during the famine.

For today: the healing of a broken relationship often begins by speaking the truth calmly and without revenge. If there is an open wound, ask God for courage and kindness to speak about it with love.
exp.6:10:
This verse states with great precision when the flood began: when Noah was six hundred years old, on the seventeenth day of the second month. "Fountains of the great deep" refers to deep waters that burst forth from the earth, and "windows of heaven" are the openings of the sky through which much water fell.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, recounting how God fulfilled what he had announced. Noah had already entered the ark, just as God commanded him. The exact date shows that this is an event remembered with seriousness. Scholars debate how the calendar should be understood, but the text emphasizes that the judgment came at the appointed time.

For today: God keeps his word, both his warnings and his promises. If you feel today that God is asking you to obey even though others do not understand, remember that Noah trusted before he saw the rain. Take one concrete step of obedience today.
exp.46:7:
In this verse, Pharaoh asks Jacob a simple question: how old are you? The King James wording "How old art thou?" is an older way of asking how many years a person has lived, and Pharaoh can see that Jacob is very old.

Pharaoh is the ruler of Egypt, and Jacob has just arrived with his family thanks to Joseph. Jacob had blessed Pharaoh, and this probably stirred respect and curiosity in the king. Jacob's answer shows that he saw his life as a "pilgrimage," a path of passing through, with joys and also much sorrow.

For today: when someone asks you about your life, answer with honesty and faith. You can acknowledge difficulties without ceasing to bless others, trusting that God has sustained you on the way.
exp.30:33:
Here Rachel takes the household idols of her father Laban and hides them in the camel's saddle, which is the pack or basket in which a load is carried on the animal. Then she sits on top of them. Laban searches the whole tent and does not find them. "Searched" here means he felt around by touch with his hands.

Laban caught up with Jacob because he accused him of stealing his gods. Jacob, not knowing that Rachel had taken them, said that whoever had them would not live. Rachel, without saying anything, hid the idols and deceived her father. The Bible recounts the event without approving or explaining it; we do not know with certainty why she took them.

For today: a secret or a small deception can put at risk those we love. It is better to live with sincerity, and to ask God to free us from clinging to any hidden "idol" in the heart.
exp.48:23:
It says that Joseph, although he was attacked by the "archers" (archeros), kept his bow firm, that is, his strength. His arms were strengthened ("made strong") by the hand of God, called "the Mighty One of Jacob." From that same God come the "shepherd" who cares and the "stone of Israel," an image of firmness and refuge.

Jacob, already old and near death, blesses his sons and speaks about the future of each one. When speaking of Joseph, he recalls his brothers' hatred, the sale into slavery, and the trials in Egypt. The "archers" can be understood as those people who wounded him, though some also see them as a general image of hostility. Jacob attributes Joseph's endurance to God, not to his own ability.

When someone hurts you or pressures you, do not depend only on your own strength. Ask God to sustain your hands and your heart, and trust that He can care for you as a shepherd and be your firm refuge.
exp.3:20:
This verse says that Jubal was the brother of Jabal, and that he was the ancestor of all who play musical instruments. "Harp" is a stringed instrument, and "organ" probably refers to a flute or wind instrument, not to the church organ we know today. "Was the father" means that he started that craft.

Here no character is speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis, who presents the sons of Lamech, a descendant of Cain. Each son begins an activity: herding, music, and metalwork. It shows how human culture advanced. Then Lamech boasts of violence, and that shows that progress does not always go together with a just heart.

For today: music and talents are gifts that can be used well. Let us put ours at the service of God and of our neighbor, and not of pride.
exp.16:11:
It says that every male had to be circumcised when he was eight days old. This included Abraham's sons, the servants born in his household, and those bought from foreigners. "Seed" means descendants, and "generations" refers to his descendants in the future.

God speaks to Abraham when he confirms his covenant, that is, his promise to be their God and to give him a great descendance. Circumcision would be a visible sign of belonging to that covenant. Including the servants shows that the blessing reached the whole household. Today it is understood that this was typical of that time, and most Christians see that Jesus fulfills the covenant and that faith is central (Romans 4:11).

God wants his people to live with clear signs of his faithfulness. Today we can ask ourselves: does my life show, through simple deeds, that I belong to God?
exp.23:42:
Here the servant of Abraham recounts that he stopped by the well and asked God for a specific sign: that the young woman who came out to draw water, when he asked her for a little from her jar, would answer him kindly. "Maiden" refers to an unmarried young woman, and "pitcher" is a vessel for carrying water.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, and he is telling his story to Laban and Bethuel, Rebekah's family. Abraham sent him to find a wife for his son Isaac among his relatives. He explains how God guided his way, so that the family understands what happened.

For today: before making an important decision, we can pray simply and ask God for direction, and then stay attentive and act with faith, humility and good character, like that of this helpful young woman.
exp.30:3:
Jacob sends for his two wives, Rachel and Leah, asking them to meet him in the field where he is tending his flock. The words "sent" and "called" show that he wants to speak with them privately. "To the field" means the meeting takes place far from Laban's house.

The narrator tells us what Jacob is doing. He notices that Laban, his father-in-law, no longer treats him as he did before, and God has told him to return to the land of his fathers. Before deciding something so important, Jacob wants to talk it over with his family. He chooses a secluded place, probably so that Laban will not overhear, although the text does not state this clearly.

When we face an important change, it is wise to speak with the people closest to us, in a quiet place and with honesty. Seeking God's direction does not remove the need to listen to and respect our family, because great decisions affect all of us.
exp.23:54:
Here the family of Rebekah, her brother Laban and her mother, asks that she stay with them "at the least ten days" before she departs. "Damsel" means a young woman, and "at the least" means "at least." It is a request for more time to say goodbye.

Abraham's servant had come to seek a wife for Isaac. He had already given gifts, and the family had accepted the proposal. But at dawn, he wants to leave at once. Her brother and her mother respond with this request, probably because it was hard for them to part with her so soon. The text does not explain their reasons in detail; it could be affection, custom, or a wish to prepare.

Acting with haste or with delay can both be reasonable, but it is wise to recognize when God is already opening a path. We can say goodbye with love without holding back what God is doing.
exp.18:27:
This verse says that Abraham, from the same place where he had earlier spoken with God, looked toward Sodom, Gomorrah, and the whole plain. He saw smoke rising from the land, like the smoke of a great furnace, a sign that the cities had been destroyed.

The narrator tells us what Abraham saw the next morning. He had pleaded with God for the people of those cities, thinking of the righteous who might be found there (Genesis 18). Now he sees the result of the judgment. The following text makes clear that God remembered Abraham and brought Lot out of the destruction. Some think this shows the value of a believer's prayer, although the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: sin has serious consequences, but God is just and also merciful. We can pray with confidence for family and friends, remembering that God hears and remembers his own.
exp.29:5:
Here Rachel says that God has "judged" her, meaning that he has done her justice and ruled in her favor. She also says that God has "heard my voice" and given her a son. The name Dan comes from a Hebrew word related to judging or doing justice.

The speaker is Rachel, Jacob's wife. She could not have children, and her sister Leah already had several. Rachel suffered because of that rivalry and because of her pain. So she gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob, a custom of that time, and Bilhah had a son. Rachel sees this as God's answer to her cry. The Bible tells this story without approving of every method they used.

For today: when you feel pain or injustice, bring it to God honestly. He listens. But be careful not to take shortcuts or compare your life with the lives of others.
exp.39:14:
Here Joseph says that he was "stolen away", that is, kidnapped and taken by force, out of the land of the Hebrews. He also states that in Egypt he did nothing wrong to deserve the dungeon. The word "that" here means "for the reason that" or "because".

Joseph speaks with Pharaoh's cupbearer, to whom he has just explained his dream with good news. He asks him to remember him and speak to Pharaoh. Joseph mentions his history because his brothers sold him and he was later imprisoned unjustly (Genesis 39). He tells the truth simply, without insulting anyone, and seeks help to get out of that situation.

For today: when you suffer an injustice, you can tell the truth calmly and ask for help without bitterness. Do what is within your reach, but trust that God works in his time, even when people forget you.
exp.40:44:
This verse tells how Pharaoh gave Joseph a new Egyptian name, Zaphnath-paaneah, and married him to Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. The phrase "he gave him to wife" means "he gave him as a wife" in the sense of a wife for him. Afterward, Joseph went out to travel through all the land of Egypt. The meaning of the Egyptian name is not certain; scholars have put forward several proposals.

The narrator describes how Pharaoh honored Joseph after he interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and proposed a plan for the years of famine. Pharaoh placed him in charge of the country and welcomed him into Egyptian society with a name and a family. Then Joseph travels across the land to prepare the store of food.

For today: God can raise up and use a faithful person even in a foreign place and after years of hardship. Serve with integrity wherever you are, without losing your faith, and trust that God can prepare the way for the good of others.
exp.20:4:
This verse says that Abraham was one hundred years old when his son Isaac was born. The Bible records it plainly, as an important fact: God fulfilled what he had promised, even though it seemed impossible because of the ages of Abraham and Sarah.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. From chapter 12 onward, God had promised Abraham a descendant, and many years of waiting had passed. Now, at last, Isaac is born. Abraham gives him the name God had indicated and circumcises him on the eighth day, as a sign of obedience to the covenant. Afterward Sarah rejoices and laughs for joy.

For today: God does not forget his promises, even when they take longer than we expect. While you wait, keep obeying him in faith, and trust that he fulfills them in his time.
exp.27:7:
This verse says that Esau realized his father Isaac did not approve of the Canaanite women. The phrase "pleased not" means that Isaac did not like them or did not approve of them. In the King James wording, the older English form "seeing" is the equivalent of the modern "seeing" in the sense of "noticing," and "pleased not" is the older way of saying "did not please."

Here the narrator is speaking, not a character in the story. Esau already had Hittite wives, who had made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah (Genesis 26:34-35). When he saw that Jacob had been blessed and sent to find a wife among their relatives, Esau understood his parents' displeasure. So he took another wife, a daughter of Ishmael. Some think this was an attempt to please his father, although the Bible does not state this clearly, and he did not put away the other women.

For today: it is not enough to recognize what pleases God and our parents; we must truly change. A superficial arrangement does not replace an obedient heart.
exp.25:28:
Here Abimelech and his companions ask Isaac to promise that he will do them no harm. They say that they did not "touch" him, meaning they did not mistreat him, and that they only did him good and sent him away in peace. They end by recognizing that Isaac is "the blessed of the Lord," that is, someone whom God favors.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, speaks together with his adviser and his captain. Earlier they had driven Isaac out of their territory, but now they see that God is with him. That is why they seek a covenant of peace. Their account of what happened is somewhat generous, since Isaac had indeed suffered rejection. Isaac, however, does not take revenge: he offers them a feast.

For today: when someone who has wronged us seeks peace, we can respond with grace, without bitterness. Reconciliation does not always erase the pain, but it reflects the goodness of God.
exp.49:10:
The verse tells that the Canaanites, the inhabitants of that land, saw the great mourning that was held at the threshing floor of Atad (a threshing floor is a flat piece of ground where grain was beaten out). They said, "This is a grievous mourning to the Egyptians." For this reason the place was called Abel-mizraim, which sounds like "mourning of Egypt." The word "mourning" here refers to lamenting with songs or cries of grief.

Jacob had just died in Egypt, and Joseph was taking him to be buried in Canaan, as his father had asked. A large Egyptian company accompanied him. The ones speaking are the Canaanites, outside observers who did not know the family. It is not known with certainty where Atad was; "beyond Jordan" can be understood in different ways depending on where one looks from.

For today: grief is part of life, and honoring those we love is something good. When someone suffers a loss, accompany them with your presence, without rushing them or offering empty words.
exp.35:6:
The explanation says that Esau and Jacob had so much wealth, especially livestock, that they could no longer live together. The land where they were living as foreigners could not support so many animals. The KJV's word "substance" means possessions and property.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator of Genesis, who explains why Esau moved to the mountain country of Seir, where the people of Edom came from. The situation is similar to that of Abraham and Lot in Genesis 13, when they also separated for lack of pasture. The text does not mention any quarrel between Esau and Jacob, so the separation seems practical and peaceful.

For today: sometimes parting in peace is better than forcing a living arrangement that no longer works. If there is tension over money, space, or work, look for an orderly and respectful way forward, without resentment.
exp.23:49:
Laban and Bethuel answer and say that this matter comes from the Lord, that is, from God. They say they cannot speak to Abraham's servant "bad or good," meaning they have nothing to object to or to add. In today's language: "This is God's doing, and we cannot oppose it or offer an opinion."

The speakers are Rebekah's family, in Mesopotamia. Abraham's servant has just told them how God led him to them to find a wife for Isaac. Hearing the account, they recognize that God was directing events. Some note that Laban is named before his father, though the text does not explain why.

For today: when you see God opening a clear path, and it agrees with his Word, do not resist it out of self-interest or custom. Listen, recognize his hand, and respond with humility and obedience, as this family did.
exp.26:43:
Rebekah tells Jacob to stay with her brother Laban for "a few days," meaning only a short time. The phrase "turn away" means that Esau's fury would go away, so his anger would slowly die down.

The speaker is Rebekah, Jacob's mother. She learned that Esau, furious that Jacob had received their father's blessing, planned to kill him. She wants to protect her son's life, so she proposes that he flee to Haran. She believed it would be only a short time, but the Bible shows that Jacob was away for many years.

For today: when there is a serious conflict, giving it time and distance can sometimes help emotions settle. But this is no substitute for honesty or reconciliation. Ask God for wisdom to repair what you have damaged.
exp.38:21:
The explanation says that the keeper of the prison placed Joseph in charge of all the prisoners. In addition, Joseph directed everything that was done there. "The chief keeper of the prison" is the head or principal jailer, and the phrase "committed to Joseph's hand" means that he gave him the responsibility and control.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. Joseph had been falsely accused by Potiphar's wife and was unjustly imprisoned. But the text stresses that the LORD was with him and gave him favor in the sight of the keeper of the prison. For this reason the man trusted Joseph and gave him authority. The following verse explains that the success came from God.

Even in unjust or difficult places, God can be with you. You can keep serving with honesty and responsibility, trusting that He does not abandon you and can give you favor where you least expect it.
exp.47:0:
This verse tells that someone brought word to Joseph that his father Jacob was ill. Then Joseph took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and went with them to see him. The phrase "after these things" only indicates that some time had passed since the events before it. "Sick" here suggests that Jacob was already very weak because of his old age.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. The scene takes place in Egypt, toward the end of Jacob's life. Joseph, who was a ruler, sets aside his duties to visit his father. Bringing his sons is no accident: the following account shows that Jacob will bless them. The text does not say who gave the warning.

For today: when someone dear to you is weak or ill, make time to visit them, even if you are very busy. And if you can, bring the younger ones with you, so that they may receive their blessing and their words of faith.
exp.8:9:
God says that his covenant is not only with Noah and his family, but also with all the living creatures that were with them: birds, livestock, and the animals of the earth, that is, all those who came out of the ark. "Living creature" means a creature that has life. "Seed" means descendants. "Perish" means come to an end or be destroyed.

God speaks to Noah and his sons after the flood. He had judged the wickedness of humanity, but now he promises that he will never again destroy the earth with a flood of waters. He includes the animals because they too had been saved and are part of his creation. The rainbow appears afterward as a sign of that promise.

For today: if God cares for every living creature, we too can treat animals and nature with respect and responsibility, while trusting in the faithfulness of his promises.
exp.0:3:
God looked at the light he had just created and saw that it was good. Then he "divided" it from the darkness, that is, he separated them and set a boundary between the two.

This is the account of creation, written in the third person; the narrator tells what God does. Before this, there was an earth "without form and void," and darkness. God speaks and brings order, step by step. Separating is part of that order: later will come the day and the night, and then other separations. Some read this literally and others as poetic language about God's order; Christians have understood it in several ways.

For today: God looks at what he does and calls it good. We can learn to recognize the good in our lives and give thanks for it. We can also ask him to bring order where there is confusion, separating what harms us from what does us good.
exp.28:32:
Leah became pregnant again and gave birth to a son. She says that God heard that she was "hated," that is, loved less than her sister, and so he gave her this son too. She names him Simeon, a name that sounds similar to the Hebrew word for "hear." The King James wording "bare" means "gave birth to," and "womb" refers to the belly.

Leah, Jacob's wife, speaks here. Jacob received her through a deception by her father Laban, since Jacob loved Rachel. Leah lives in pain and seeks her husband's affection. Here she sees that God attends to her suffering, although at this moment she still does not speak of receiving Jacob's love.

For today: when you feel ignored or undervalued, bring that pain to God with sincerity. He hears the one who suffers and can give you comfort and hope, even if people do not respond as you would wish.
exp.23:60:
Genesis 24:61 says that Rebekah got up with her maids, meaning her female servants or young women who accompanied her. All of them mounted the camels and followed Abraham's servant. "The servant" is Abraham's trusted attendant, and "followed" means they went after him on the road.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Rebekah's family had just blessed her and let her go. The servant had been sent to find a wife for Isaac from among Abraham's relatives. Rebekah had agreed to go, and now her journey begins toward an unfamiliar land, to join a man she had not yet met.

For today: when God opens a clear path, sometimes the right response is courage and taking the step, even without seeing the whole future. Taking that step is trusting Him, and it is also good to do so with the blessing and counsel of those who love us.
exp.18:28:
This verse sums up what happened to Sodom and Gomorrah. When God destroyed the cities of the plain, he remembered Abraham and brought Lot out from the middle of the ruin. "Overthrow" means complete destruction, and "sent out" means he led Lot out safely.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After describing the smoke Abraham saw from a distance, the text explains why Lot was saved. It does not say this was because of Lot's merits, but because God remembered Abraham, who had interceded for those cities (Genesis 18). In the Bible, to "remember" someone means to act on their behalf.

For today: our prayers for others matter. Pray for your family and friends, trusting that God cares for them with mercy, even when you cannot see how.
exp.34:17:
She says that Rachel, giving birth with great pain, was dying. While "her soul was in departing," that is, while she was breathing her last, she named her son Ben-oni, which means "son of my sorrow" (some render it "son of my affliction"). But Jacob, his father, named him Benjamin, which is commonly understood as "son of the right hand," a sign of honor and favor.

This is the account of the birth of Jacob's last son, on the way near Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife, names the child out of her pain. Jacob, in the midst of his own grief, chooses to give him a name that looks forward.

Today we can learn that pain is real and deserves to be acknowledged, but it does not have to define the future. We can weep and still bless, with hope, those who come after us.
exp.19:17:
This verse explains why the women in the household of Abimelech were unable to have children. It says that the Lord had "fast closed up" every womb, meaning that he had caused every woman in his house to be unable to conceive. The reason was Sarah, Abraham's wife. "Womb" is the place in the body where a baby is formed.

The narrator is the author of Genesis, who clarifies what happened earlier. Abraham had said that Sarah was his sister, and Abimelech, king of Gerar, took her for himself. God warned him in a dream, and he never came near her. Here we understand that God protected Sarah and his promise. When Abraham prayed, God healed that household.

For today: God cares for those who love him, even when we make mistakes. And our prayer can be an instrument of healing and reconciliation, even for those who have wronged us.
exp.49:17:
The brothers of Joseph come in person, kneel with their faces to the ground, and say: "Here we are, we are your servants." "Bowed down" means they bent low until they touched the earth. "Here we are" means "we are here."

After Jacob's death, the brothers fear that Joseph will finally take revenge on them. They send him a message that they say comes from their father, asking for forgiveness. We do not know whether Jacob really said that or whether they added it out of fear; the text does not make this clear. Now they present themselves, and so Joseph's dream from Genesis 37 comes true, when his brothers bowed down before him.

When we have wronged someone, fear can lead us to hide or to beg without trusting. Joseph's response, which follows, invites us to ask for forgiveness with humility and to trust in the grace of God and of others.
exp.31:2:
Jacob sent messengers ahead to his brother Esau, who lived in the land of Seir, also called the country of Edom. "Before him" means that he sends them ahead before he himself arrives. "Country" here means region or territory.

The account tells us what happens after many years of absence. Jacob is returning from living with Laban, and the last time he saw Esau, Esau wanted to kill him for having received the father's blessing. Just before this, Jacob saw angels of God at Mahanaim. Even so, he does not simply do nothing: he seeks reconciliation and approaches with humility.

For today: trusting God does not remove our responsibility to take steps. If there is a broken relationship, we can pray and also take the first step with humility, without knowing how the other person will respond, but leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.23:66:
He says that Isaac brought Rebekah into the tent that had belonged to his mother Sarah. There he took her as his wife, and he loved her. Through her, Isaac found comfort over the death of his mother.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, closing the story of Abraham's servant, who went to look for a wife for Isaac. After the servant told Isaac everything, the marriage is finalized. Sarah had died about three years earlier, as can be worked out from the ages the text gives, although the account does not say so in those words. The mention of Sarah's tent seems to show that Rebekah holds an important place in the family.

For today: God often comforts us through the people he places beside us. If you are grieving, you do not have to carry it alone; let others walk with you, and be a source of comfort to someone else too.
exp.42:13:
Jacob prays that God Almighty will move that man of Egypt to show compassion toward his sons. He asks that they be given back Simeon, "the other brother," and Benjamin. Then he says that if he must lose his children, so be it. "Man" here means a man, and "mercies" refers to compassionate treatment.

Jacob speaks as an old man. There is famine in the land, and his sons must return to Egypt for food. Simeon was kept there, and the governor demanded to see Benjamin. Jacob does not know that this man is Joseph. After resisting, he gives in and sends Benjamin, along with double money and a gift.

For today: when you cannot control the outcome, do what is prudent, entrust the matter to God in prayer, and rest in the knowledge that he cares for those you love, even when it hurts.
exp.31:26:
Here the man Jacob is wrestling with asks him a simple question: "What is thy name?" Jacob answers: "Jacob." It is a short answer, but a very important one.

Jacob is wrestling through the night with a mysterious man, whom the text later connects with God. The next day he will meet his brother Esau, whom he had deceived years earlier. In Hebrew, the name "Jacob" is linked to "the one who supplants" or "the one who grasps the heel." By saying his name, Jacob acknowledges who he has been. Then he receives the name Israel.

For today: before asking for a blessing, we can come before God honestly, without hiding our failings. He can change our story when we tell him the truth.
exp.4:24:
The explanation says that Methuselah lived 187 years and then had his son Lamech. The verb "begat" is an old word meaning "had a son." "Lived" here marks the moment the next descendant in the family list was born. The names Mathusalam and Lamech are written today as Methuselah and Lamech.

No character speaks here; it is the narrator of Genesis, who records generations from Adam onward. Methuselah was the son of Enoch, the man who "walked with God." Later the text says Methuselah lived 969 years, the longest life recorded in the Bible. Scholars interpret these ages in different ways: some take them literally and others as numbers with symbolic meaning. There is no certainty.

For today: God cares for each generation, even when it seems that only names and dates are being recorded. Your faith can influence your children and grandchildren. Live with God each day, as Enoch did, and leave a quiet but real mark on your family.
exp.42:16:
This verse tells us that the steward did what Joseph had ordered. He brought Joseph's brothers into his house. "Brought in" means "made them come in." "The man" is the manager of the house, and "the men" are the brothers who had come from Canaan.

Here the narrator is speaking. Without his brothers recognizing him, Joseph had seen Benjamin with them and ordered that a meal be prepared for them. The brothers did not understand anything, and the next verse says they were afraid, because they thought they would be accused over the money they had found in their sacks. In reality, Joseph was preparing a moment of reconciliation.

For today: sometimes God leads us along paths that frighten us, even though His intentions are good. We can trust that He works with purpose, even when we do not yet understand it.
exp.29:9:
This verse tells that Zilpah, Leah's servant, gave birth to a son for Jacob. The word "bare" is an old way of saying "gave birth to." It is a brief detail, but it opens the account of the birth of Gad.

Here the narrator speaks. The scene takes place amid an intense rivalry between Leah and Rachel, both wives of Jacob. Leah had stopped having children, and following the custom of her time, she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob. The Bible only reports this event; it does not present it as an example to imitate, and it shows how much pain there was in that competition.

For today: when we feel we are in competition with someone, it is good to stop and ask God for peace and trust. Comparisons can lead us to decisions that bring more wounds. God continues to work even in imperfect families.
exp.31:17:
Jacob tells the servant who leads the first drove what to answer if Esau asks him. He must say that the animals are a gift from Jacob, whom he calls "your servant," sent to Esau, whom he calls "my lord." He must also let Esau know that Jacob himself is coming behind. "Present" means gift, and "servant" here is a gesture of humility.

Jacob speaks after years of fleeing from his brother, whom he had deceived to obtain the blessing. Now he knows that Esau is approaching with four hundred men and fears for his life. For that reason he sends gifts in stages, seeking to calm his anger before the meeting. The text shows his fear, and it does not say how Esau would have reacted without them.

For today: when there is an unresolved offense, taking the first step with humility and concrete actions can open the door to reconciliation, without ceasing to pray and to trust in God.
exp.13:7:
This verse tells that five kings from the region of the Jordan valley went out to fight: those of Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela, which was also called Zoar. "Ordered battle" means they drew up their armies in line to fight. The place was the vale of Siddim.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks, recounting events without commenting on them. For years these kings had been subject to Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, and had rebelled. Now he and his allies were coming to punish them. This war is the background for Lot, Abram's nephew, being taken captive afterward.

For today: our decisions affect others. Lot lived near Sodom, and when this war broke out, he suffered the consequences. It is wise to think prayerfully about where we stand and who surrounds us, and to trust that God cares for us even in the middle of our troubles.
exp.6:13:
This verse continues the list of those who entered the ark. First Noah and his family are named, and then the animals: the wild ones, the tame ones (the domestic animals), the creeping things that crawl, and the birds of every sort. "Every bird of every sort" is the King James wording for the birds, so the phrase "every fowl" points to the same group. The phrase "after his kind" shows that there was variety among the creatures, each one with its own type.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book, who tells how what God had commanded Noah was carried out. The text dwells on the details to show that everything was done in an orderly way, just as God had directed. After this, the account says that God shut the door.

For today: God cares for even the smallest details and takes an interest in every creature. We can trust that he also cares for our lives. And like Noah, we can obey him step by step, even when we do not understand everything that lies ahead.
exp.49:19:
It says that Joseph's brothers planned to harm him when they sold him, but God used that same evil for a good end. "Ye thought" means "you planned" or "you intended," and "ye" is the old form of "you." "Meant it unto good" means that God directed it toward something good. That good was saving the lives of many people.

Joseph speaks to his brothers after the death of their father Jacob. They feared that he would now take revenge for what they had done to him. Joseph, who was a ruler in Egypt and had stored up food in the time of famine, does not put himself in God's place to judge them. He answers them with forgiveness and comfort.

Today, this invites us not to live bitter because of the harm we have received. God does not approve of evil, but he can work even in the midst of it. We can hand over our wounds to him, forgive, and trust that he is still at work, even when we do not yet understand everything.
exp.28:6:
Jacob tells the shepherds that it is still broad daylight and not yet time to gather the flocks. He suggests they water the sheep and then take them back out to graze. "Water" means giving them something to drink, and "feed" means taking them to eat grass.

Jacob speaks shortly after arriving in Haran, near a well. He has already learned that Laban, his relative, is well, and that Rachel is coming. His advice may show that, as a man experienced in shepherding, he noticed that useful time was being wasted. The shepherds answer that they are waiting for all the flocks to gather and for the stone to be rolled away. The Bible does not say whether Jacob had another motive, such as wanting to be alone with Rachel; that would only be a guess.

For today: value the time God gives you. Do not waste it waiting without need; use it wisely, and if there is a good reason to wait, respect it.
exp.14:13:
God tells Abram that He Himself will judge the nation that is going to enslave his descendants. "Judge" means that God will do justice and punish that oppression. After that, the people will come out free and "with great substance," that is, with many possessions. "Nation" in this verse refers to a people or nation.

God speaks with Abram in a vision at night, while a dread and a great darkness come over him. He has just made a covenant with Abram and promised him descendants. Before that, He warns him that they will spend a long time suffering in a foreign land. Almost everyone understands this to refer to Egypt, although the text here does not name it. God wants Abram to know that his plan will not fail.

For today: when you suffer injustice or a long wait, remember that God sees, has a time for everything, and will do justice. You can trust Him without taking revenge on your own.
exp.18:17:
Lot answers the angels, saying, "No, please, my lords." It is a respectful way of saying that he does not want to do what they have just commanded. The word "please" means "I beg you," and "my lords" is a form of respectful address.

The two messengers had just brought Lot and his family out of Sodom, and they had told them to flee to the mountain to save their lives. Lot is the one speaking, and he raises an objection: he is afraid he will not make it to the mountain. It is striking that, even after God's mercy, he still hesitates and bargains. Afterward he will ask to take refuge in the small city of Zoar. The Bible does not fully explain his reasons; it only shows his fear.

For today: when God shows us a path of salvation or care, let us trust Him even when it seems difficult. We may speak to Him honestly about our fears, but let us also ask for a heart willing to obey.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that Reu lived two hundred and seven years after he became the father of his son Serug. During that time he had more sons and daughters.

The explanation is not speaking through a character; it is the narrator of Genesis, who presents the genealogy from Shem to Abram. These lists show how humanity continued after the flood and connect to the promise made to Abraham. Some scholars think the list may summarize generations, and the ages are understood in several ways.

For today: God cares for every generation, even the one that hardly appears in the story. Your daily life, your family, and your simple faithfulness matter, even when no one remembers them. Pray today for your family and for those who will come after you.
exp.26:6:
Rebekah tells Jacob what Isaac said to Esau: that he should bring him game and prepare a savoury dish, or tasty food, so that he may eat and bless him "before the LORD," that is, as a solemn blessing, in God's presence, before he dies.

Here Rebekah repeats Isaac's words, since she had been listening. Isaac, now old, wanted to give the family blessing to Esau, his firstborn son. Rebekah, for her part, will use these words to push Jacob into acting. The Bible recounts what happens without approving the deception that follows. Some see here a lack of trust in the promise God had already given about Jacob (Genesis 25:23).

For today: when we believe God has promised something, we do not need to manipulate or lie to bring it about. Trusting Him means waiting and acting with honesty.
exp.19:4:
Abimelech defends himself before God. He reminds God that Abraham said Sarah was his sister, and that she herself confirmed it. For this reason he claims he acted with "integrity of heart," that is, with good intentions and without deceit, and with "innocency of hands," meaning that he had committed no wrong.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, speaks with God in a dream. He had taken Sarah into his household because he believed she was unmarried. God warns him that he is in danger, and he answers that he acted without knowing the truth. In the following verse, God acknowledges his sincerity, but orders him to return Sarah.

For today: Having good intentions is valuable, but it is not always enough. It is wise to seek the truth before acting. And if we discover that we were mistaken, we should correct the error promptly, with humility and obedience.
exp.7:17:
This verse tells us that Noah came out of the ark together with his wife, his three sons, and their wives. In all there were eight people. They had spent a long time shut inside while the flood covered the earth. Now, at last, they were standing on dry ground again.

God himself had given Noah the command to come out. He waited for God's word and obeyed, just as he had done when he went in. The author recounts that the family came out together, and right after them the animals come out too. Then Noah builds an altar to God to give him thanks.

For today: before rushing into what is new, let us learn to wait for God's direction. When he brings us out of a difficult season, the first thing we can do is give him thanks, and also care for and accompany our family along the way.
exp.4:23:
It says that Enoch lived in constant friendship with God. "Walking with God" means living close to Him, in obedience and trust. "He was not" means that he was no longer found on the earth, and "God took him" indicates that God Himself took him. The text does not explain how it happened.

The narrator of Genesis is going through the list of descendants from Adam. In that list the phrase "and he died" is repeated, but with Enoch the account changes: it does not mention his death. Hebrews 11:5 says that Enoch was taken up so that he would not see death. The details of that event are not clarified further, so it is better not to speculate.

For today: walking with God is something for every day, not only for special moments. You can begin with a simple habit: talk with God when you wake up and listen to His Word, even in the middle of family and work responsibilities.
exp.31:10:
Jacob asks God to rescue him from the power of his brother Esau. He frankly says that he is afraid. He fears that Esau will come and attack him, and strike down the mother along with the children. The King James wording "lest he will come and smite me" uses "smite," which here means to strike or kill, and "lest" means "so that not" or "in case." The word "peradventure" is not used in this verse, so no comment applies to it.

Jacob returns to Canaan at God's command. Years earlier he had deceived Esau to take away the blessing, and he fled. Now he knows that Esau is coming with four hundred men. Jacob prays, recalling God's promises, acknowledges that he is unworthy of God's faithfulness, and asks for protection for his family.

For today: when you feel fear, do not hide it. Tell God honestly, as Jacob did, and lean on what He has promised. Prayer does not replace doing what is yours to do, for Jacob also prepared a gift for his brother, but it gives you peace to act with confidence.
exp.0:30:
The explanation says that God looked at everything he had created and considered it "very good," meaning very good, in abundance. The notes about the words "saw" and "was" being old spellings do not apply to the King James wording, so they are dropped. "Evening and morning" is the Hebrew way of counting a day, and here it marks the close of the sixth day of creation.

The one telling this is the author of Genesis, who describes how God made the world. Just before, God had given humans and animals the plants as food. This verse works like a closing note: God reviews his whole work and approves it. Christians understand the "day" in different ways, and that does not change the central message that creation is good.

For today: care with gratitude for what God made, including your body, your family and nature. Today, give thanks for some created thing you enjoy.
exp.1:15:
This verse says that God gave the man an order in the garden of Eden. First he tells him that he may eat from all the trees of the garden. "Commanded" means he gave a clear instruction, and "freely eat" here works as a generous permission: he had freedom to enjoy everything.

It is the Lord God, the Creator, who has just placed the man in the garden to care for it. Before the prohibition that comes in the next verse, God begins with abundance and provision. The text does not say how many trees there were, but it emphasizes that the freedom was very wide. Its limits had a purpose, and they were given within a relationship of care.

For today: before we focus on what God forbids us, let us remember everything he has given us. Giving thanks for his blessings helps us trust that his limits are also for our good.
exp.20:3:
This verse tells us that Abraham circumcised his son Isaac when the boy was eight days old. He did it because God had commanded him. "Circumcise" means to cut away the skin that covers the tip of the male organ. The phrase "being eight days old" tells us the child's exact age at the time.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character in the story. He reports that God kept his promise by giving Abraham and Sarah a son in their old age. In Genesis 17 God had established circumcision as the sign of his covenant with Abraham and his descendants, and in that passage he also indicated that it should be done on the eighth day. Abraham simply obeys what God had already told him.

For today: God kept his promise, and Abraham responded with simple and punctual obedience. When God shows you something clearly in his Word, do not put it off for later. Obeying with joy is a beautiful way to thank him for what he has done in your life.
exp.29:7:
Rachel says she has had "wrestlings of God" with her sister Leah, and that she has prevailed. That is why she names her son Naphtali, a name connected with the idea of wrestling or struggling. "Contended" means that she has fought or competed. The phrase "wrestlings of God" can be understood in several ways: a very intense struggle, or a struggle in which she felt God was intervening.

The speaker is Rachel, the wife of Jacob. She could not have children, while Leah could. So she gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob, and Bilhah bore this second son. It was a painful rivalry between sisters, and Rachel interprets the birth as a victory. The Bible recounts this without approving every decision the family made.

For today: when you feel pain or comparison with others, take care that your identity does not depend on "winning." Bring your pain to God with honesty, and ask him for healing and peace in your relationships.
exp.38:9:
This verse says that Potiphar's wife kept speaking to Joseph every day, insisting that he lie with her. But Joseph would not give in to her. The word "hearkened" here means "obeyed" or "yielded to," not merely hearing her.

The narrator tells us what happened after Joseph had already said no clearly. He was a slave in Egypt, and his master had placed the whole household in his care. Joseph explained that accepting would mean betraying his master and sinning against God. Even so, she did not give up and kept pressing him, day after day.

Today, temptation sometimes does not come just once, but as constant pressure. Joseph teaches us to keep our decision firm, not to negotiate with what we know is wrong, and to remember that our faithfulness is first owed to God.
exp.38:7:
Here it is said that Joseph refused what she was asking of him. The word "Á" is the old spelling of "a," and "my master wotteth not what is with me in the house" means that Potiphar does not concern himself with checking what is in his house while Joseph is in charge. Joseph reminds her that his master has entrusted him with everything he has.

Joseph, a slave in Egypt, speaks to the wife of Potiphar, his master. She had proposed that he lie with her. Joseph does not answer with excuses but appeals to the trust Potiphar placed in him. Shortly afterward, in verse 9, he will say that it would be a sin against God.

For today: integrity is protected by remembering to whom we owe faithfulness. When someone tempts us to betray a trust, it helps to say a clear no, without going around the issue, and to think of the people who trust us and of God.
exp.25:2:
It says that God asks Isaac to stay and live in the land of Canaan, and promises to be with him and to bless him. It also promises to give these lands to him and to his descendants. "Seed" means offspring, and "oath" is a solemn promise that God had already made to Abraham, Isaac's father.

It is Jehovah who speaks, appearing to Isaac in the middle of a famine. Isaac had gone to Gerar, and it was natural to think of going down to Egypt for food. But God tells him not to go and to remain where he is. In this way he confirms that the promise given to Abraham now continues with him.

For today: when difficult times come, the most logical way out is not always the one God wants. Before deciding out of fear, seek God in prayer and in his Word. If he asks you to wait, trust that his presence and his faithfulness will sustain you.
exp.10:6:
God says he will go down and confuse the language of the people building the tower, so that they can no longer understand one another. "Let us go down" means "let us go down," and "confound" means "mix up or throw into disorder." "Speak to one another" refers to the speech of their neighbor.

God speaks. The people of Babel wanted to make a name for themselves and stay together in one place, but God had commanded them to fill the earth (Genesis 9:1). The plural "let us go down" has been understood in different ways: as the heavenly court or as a reference to the Trinity. The text does not settle the question. The result was that they were scattered.

For today: when you make plans, ask yourself whether they seek the glory of God or only your own name. Projects done in pride end in confusion, but those done in humility can bring honor to God.
exp.20:10:
This verse says that Sara's words caused Abraham great distress. "Said" here refers to what she asked for, and "grievous" means painful or hard to bear. "Because of his son" refers to Ishmael, whom Abraham loved as a son.

Sara saw that Ishmael, the son of Hagar, was mocking, and she asked that Hagar and her son be sent away from the house to protect the inheritance meant for Isaac. Abraham suffered because he had to be separated from a son of his own. Then God comforted him: Isaac would carry on the promise, and Ishmael too would become a nation, because he was a descendant of Abraham.

For today: when a difficult decision hurts us, we can bring it to God in prayer. He understands our pain, guides us with wisdom, and cares for those we love, even when we cannot see how.
exp.8:19:
It says that Noah began to work the land as a farmer and planted a vineyard, that is, grape plants. The word "began" may mean that he resumed the work of the field after the flood. To "till" means to cultivate or plow the soil.

The narrator tells how humanity began again after the flood. The three sons of Noah, from whom the earth was filled, have just been named. This verse sets up the account that follows: Noah drinks wine and becomes drunk. The Bible does not say that planting the vineyard was wrong; the problem comes afterward. Some think Noah did not foresee the effects of the wine, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: Working and enjoying the fruits of our effort is good, but even good things require care. Let us ask God for wisdom and self-control so that we do not fall into excess.
exp.8:6:
God tells Noah and his sons to have children, to be many, and to fill the earth. "Be fruitful" means to bear fruit, and "multiply" means to have children.

God speaks after the flood, when humanity begins again with Noah's family. Just before this, God has said that human life is very valuable, because man was made in his image. So this verse contrasts with what comes before it: against the violence that takes life, God commands giving life. It is a blessing that repeats what was said at creation, and after it comes his covenant with Noah.

For today: value and care for every person's life. You can do this with your family, your children, or your neighbors, using your words and your time to encourage and protect, not to harm.
exp.9:1:
This verse gives the names of the seven sons of Japheth, one of Noah's three sons. They are Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras. The spelling "Meshech" is the same in the King James Version, so no change is needed there.

The passage belongs to the "table of nations," a list of the families that came to be after the flood. Moses, traditionally recognized as the author of the book, presents it to show how humanity spread out from Noah.

Many scholars connect these names with peoples who lived north and west of Israel, but not all of these identifications are certain, and they remain debated.

For today: God knows the names and stories of all peoples, and all of humanity comes from one common origin. This invites us to look at each person, regardless of culture or country, with respect and as someone whom God values and loves.
exp.42:12:
The explanation says that Jacob finally allows Benjamin to go with his brothers to Egypt. He tells them, "Take," "arise," and "go again." These are simple commands. "Man" here means "a man," and it refers to Joseph, although they do not yet know who he is. "Brother" is Benjamin, the youngest son.

Jacob speaks, also called Israel. There is hunger in the land, and the food from Egypt has run out. The Egyptian ruler, who is Joseph without their knowing it, asked to see Benjamin. Jacob resisted out of fear of losing another son, but Judah offered to answer for the boy. Then Jacob gives in, though with pain.

For today: sometimes we must let go of what we fear losing most and trust God. Jacob did the prudent thing, preparing gifts and money, and then asked God for mercy. We can plan wisely and then entrust the outcome to Him.
exp.11:8:
This verse tells how Abram broke camp and kept traveling, little by little, toward the south. In that region the south refers to the Negev, a drier area. The word "journeyed" means that he set out.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Abram had already received God's promise about the land and had built altars where he worshiped. Now he keeps traveling as a nomad, without settling down. A famine will soon come, and Abram will go down to Egypt. The text does not say that God directed him on this course, so some readers see here the beginning of a decision made without consulting God, while others see it simply as part of the journey.

For today: even when we have received a promise from God, life brings seasons of waiting and uncertainty. In those moments, it is good to stop and pray before moving, so that we do not decide only under the pressure of circumstances.
exp.8:3:
The explanation says that God allows eating the meat of animals, but with one condition: the meat must not be eaten with its blood. The word "but" in the verse, in the King James Version, is the word that introduces the exception; the verse reads "But flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat." The Bible explains that life is in the blood, which is why blood is treated as something special.

God speaks to Noah and his sons after the flood, when life on the earth begins again. He gives them permission to eat animals, but teaches them to respect life. The verses that follow connect this with the value of human life, made in the image of God. Some see here a lesson of respect for all life; the text does not explain further details.

For today: we can receive with gratitude what God gives us and live with respect for life, caring for people and handling responsibly what God has created.
exp.20:33:
This verse says that Abraham lived as a foreigner in the land of the Philistines for a long time. The word "sojourned" means "lived" or "dwelt" for a while. "Many days" indicates a long period, but it does not say how many years there were.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. He has just told of the peace agreement between Abraham and Abimelech at Beersheba. Abraham had planted a tree (the King James Version says "tamarisk tree") and had called on the name of the LORD, the everlasting God. This verse sums up that Abraham kept living there, still as a stranger, waiting for God's promises.

For today: sometimes God places us in situations where we spend long seasons of waiting. Like Abraham, we can live at peace with others, worship God every day, and trust that He fulfills His promises in His own time.
exp.47:2:
Jacob tells Joseph that God Almighty (in Hebrew, El Shaddai) appeared to him at Luz, in the land of Canaan, and blessed him. "Appeared to me" means that God made himself present in a visible or clear way. Luz is the old name of the place that Jacob called Bethel.

Jacob speaks in Egypt, now old and ill. He makes an effort to sit up in bed because Joseph arrives with his sons Manasseh and Ephraim. Before blessing them, Jacob recalls the promise God made to him, since everything he is about to say rests on it.

For today: when you face moments of weakness or uncertainty, remember the times God has been faithful to you. Telling those stories to your children or to others strengthens faith and gives them a firm foundation for trusting God.
exp.47:10:
Israel, that is, Jacob, tells his son Joseph that he never expected to see him again. Now God has not only granted this to him, but has also allowed him to know his grandchildren. "Seed" means descendants, and "face" means the countenance or the person.

Jacob is an old man, nearly blind. Years earlier he believed Joseph had died, and he mourned him for a long time. Now he is living in Egypt, and Joseph presents to him his sons Ephraim and Manasseh. Before blessing them, Jacob acknowledges with wonder that God has done more than he had hoped.

For today: sometimes we give up on certain things as lost, and God surprises us with more than we asked for. Let us learn to recognize his goodness and to thank him out loud, as Jacob did, especially when we see blessing in our family.
exp.23:21:
It says that, when the camels had finished drinking, Abraham's servant gave Rebekah a gold earring of half a shekel and two bracelets (bangles) of ten shekels. The King James wording "as the camels had done drinking" corresponds to this. "Earring" here is usually understood as a ring worn in the nose, though some translate it as a stud or hoop worn in the ear. A shekel was a unit of weight, roughly eleven grams by common estimates.

The one acting is Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac. He had asked God for a sign: that the young woman would offer water to his camels as well. Rebekah did so with generosity. He watched her in silence, wanting to know whether God had given success to his journey. He did not yet ask about her family; first he gave the gifts.

For today: when we seek God's guidance, we can pray, observe calmly, and act with gratitude. And simple kindness, like Rebekah's, has value in the eyes of God.
exp.36:11:
The explanation says that Joseph's brothers went to take care of their father Jacob's flocks at Shechem. To "feed" means to lead the sheep to graze and look after them. Shechem is a region with good pasture, quite far from the family home in Hebron.

The narrator of Genesis tells this. It comes right after Joseph's dreams, which caused envy in his brothers. This detail seems simple, but it prepares the scene in which Jacob will send Joseph to look for them. This is how the journey begins that will lead him to Egypt. The text does not say what the brothers were thinking as they left; it only reports where they were.

God can work in the everyday. A grazing trip, something very common, becomes part of a greater plan. Today, trust that God can also use your ordinary days, even when you do not understand what is coming.
exp.2:9:
Adam answers God that he heard his voice in the garden, and he was afraid, because he was naked, and for that reason he hid himself. "I hid myself" is the form used in the King James Version, rendered here as "I hid myself"; the older wording of the source text is "Escondíme."

Adam speaks after eating the forbidden fruit. God calls to him with the question "Where art thou?" not because he did not know, but to give him the chance to speak honestly. Before this, Adam and Eve felt no shame; now they feel guilt and fear. His answer does not confess the sin directly, and shortly afterward he blames his wife.

For today: when we fail, our first impulse is often to hide or make excuses. God seeks us out with love and invites us to be honest. Today, in prayer, tell him honestly about what you have wanted to keep hidden.
exp.29:13:
Genesis 30:14 tells how Reuben, Leah's eldest son, went out into the field at the time of the wheat harvest and found mandrakes. In that period these plants were associated with fertility. He brought them to his mother.

Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife, could not have children and lived in pain. Leah already had several children, but she suffered from feeling less loved. The two women were competing for Jacob's affection. That is why Rachel asks for the mandrakes, hoping for a solution. The text does not say that the plants worked.

Today, when something hurts us, it is easy to look for quick fixes or to compete with others. The story invites us to bring our longings to God, who is the giver of life, and not to depend on human remedies.
exp.21:0:
This verse says that, after the events that came before, God tested Abraham. The word "tempt" here means "test" or "try," not that God wanted to make him fall into sin. God called him by name, and Abraham answered, "Here I am," meaning he was ready to listen.

The one speaking is God, and he addresses Abraham, to whom he had already promised numerous descendants through Isaac. The following verses show that the test was to ask him to offer Isaac as a sacrifice. The text does not explain everything Abraham was thinking, but it does show that he rose early and obeyed. Later in the account, the story reveals that God did not allow the sacrifice to take place.

For today: when God calls you, you can answer with a willing heart, saying "Here I am." Trials are not always understood right away, but we can trust that God is faithful and good.
exp.38:1:
The explanation says God was with Joseph, even though he was a slave in a foreign land. "He was a prosperous man" means that things went well for him in what he did. The explanation glosses the wording of the verse, with "was" standing for "was" and "master" for his owner. Joseph lived in the house of Potiphar, an Egyptian.

The narrator of Genesis tells this after Joseph's brothers sold him and Ishmaelite merchants took him to Egypt. The author wants to highlight that, even in an unjust and painful situation, God had not abandoned Joseph. His prosperity did not come from his circumstances but from the presence of God. Even his master noticed.

For today: Even if you go through a difficult or unjust time, God may be with you. Do your work faithfully wherever you are, trusting that his presence matters more than your situation.
exp.40:18:
This verse describes the second part of Pharaoh's dream. After the seven fat cows, seven other cows come up out of the river, very thin and of a dreadful appearance. "Poor" means their condition was wretched, and "very ill favoured and leanfleshed" means they were extremely unsightly and had almost no flesh on their bodies. Pharaoh says he had never seen cows so ugly in all the land of Egypt.

Here Pharaoh speaks. He tells Joseph his dream in detail, because none of Egypt's wise men could explain it. Joseph was in prison, but he was called to interpret it. Later, Joseph explains that God was showing Pharaoh what was going to happen: years of plenty followed by years of famine.

For today: God can use warnings to help us prepare. We can be wise in good times, saving, sharing and trusting God, so that hard times do not catch us by surprise.
exp.23:0:
It says that Abraham was already elderly, with many years behind him ("well stricken in age" means of very advanced age). It also affirms that God, here called "the Lord," had blessed Abraham in all things: in family, possessions, and protection.

The narrator of the book of Genesis presents this scene before telling how Abraham takes care of the future of his son Isaac. Sarah had already died (chapter 23), and Abraham, aware of his age, wants to settle an important matter: that Isaac marry within the faith and the family, not among the Canaanite women. For that reason he calls his oldest servant.

For today: God remains faithful to the end of life. Looking back with gratitude at how He has cared for us helps us trust Him and, with wisdom and prayer, prepare the spiritual future of those who come after us.
exp.16:18:
God answers Abraham's laughter and doubt with a clear promise: Sarah, his wife, will have a son. Abraham is to name him Isaac. God says he will confirm his covenant with that son as an everlasting covenant, that is, one that has no end, and that it will extend to his "seed," an old word meaning descendants.

God is the one speaking. Abraham is ninety-nine years old and Sarah is ninety, and to him it seems impossible. For that reason he asks that Ishmael, his son already born, may live before God. God does not reject Ishmael, since he later promises to bless him, but he makes clear that the covenant will be fulfilled through Isaac. The name Isaac is usually connected with laughter.

Today we too can bring our doubts honestly to God. He is not angry with someone who speaks to him from the heart, and he can fulfill what he has said even when it seems impossible to us. Trusting means waiting for his timing and not relying only on our own plans.
exp.30:42:
Laban answers Jacob that everything he sees belongs to him: the daughters, the grandchildren, and the flocks. Then he asks what he could do today to his own daughters and to the children they have borne. "Borne" means "given birth to."

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, speaks after he has pursued him and caught up with him. Jacob had just reproached him for twenty years of work and changed wages. Laban admits no guilt and keeps speaking as if he owns everything. Yet he recognizes that he cannot harm his family, and for that reason he proposes making a covenant. Probably God, who spoke to him the night before, influenced this change (Gen 31:24).

For today: when we believe we have a right over everything, we tend to harden ourselves. Acknowledging limits and seeking peace, rather than imposing ourselves, protects the family and honors God.
exp.41:19:
Here Joseph, who is governor of Egypt, asks his brothers to bring him Benjamin, the youngest brother. In this way he will confirm that they are telling the truth, and he will not put them to death. The King James wording "verified" means confirmed or proven, and "unto" is the old form of "to." The brothers accept the condition.

Joseph speaks with ten brothers who came to Egypt to buy food because of the famine. They do not recognize him, since years earlier they had sold him as a slave. Joseph accuses them of being spies and tests them. It is not known for certain what he felt at that moment, but what follows shows that his brothers begin to remember their guilt.

For today: sometimes God uses trials to awaken our conscience. Instead of hardening ourselves, we can humbly acknowledge what we did wrong, ask forgiveness, and seek reconciliation.
exp.48:11:
It says that Judah's eyes will be red with wine and his teeth white with milk. It is a poetic picture of abundance: so much wine and so much milk that the body itself shows it. Some understand the eyes as dark and deep, others as reddened; the Hebrew allows both readings.

Jacob is speaking. He is old, and he is blessing his sons and announcing what will come upon each tribe. Here he speaks of Judah, from whom the king would come, and many Christians see in this blessing a sign of Christ. The wine and the milk portray a prosperous reign, full of blessing.

For today: instead of living in fear of scarcity, trust that God knows how to give abundantly. Give thanks today for one specific blessing and share it with someone.
exp.46:28:
Jacob, also called Israel, senses that his death is drawing near. He calls his son Joseph and asks him for a very serious oath: to place his hand under his thigh, an ancient gesture of solemn promise. He asks Joseph to show him "kindness and truth," that is, goodness and faithfulness, and not to bury him in Egypt.

Jacob speaks as an old man, after living seventeen years in Egypt. God had promised his family the land of Canaan, and there Abraham and Isaac were buried. Many understand that Jacob wanted to rest in the promised land, as a sign of his trust in God. Joseph had power in Egypt, which is why Jacob makes this request of him.

For today: think about God's promises more than the comfort of the moment. Also, when someone close to us asks us for something important before they depart, let us fulfill it faithfully and with affection.
exp.24:29:
Esau comes in tired from the field and asks Jacob to give him something to eat from that reddish stew. "Red" means red or reddish, and "I pray thee" means "I ask you, please." The text says that because of this, Esau was given the name Edom, which sounds like the Hebrew word for "red."

Esau, the older brother, speaks with his twin brother Jacob. He was exhausted, and Jacob had prepared a pot of lentil stew. The verses that follow show that Jacob takes advantage of that moment to ask him for the birthright, that is, the rights and blessing of the firstborn son. Esau, at that moment, thinks only of his hunger.

For today: when we are in great need or weariness, it is easy to decide poorly and trade something valuable for quick relief. Before deciding, it is good to stop, pray, and ask ourselves what we are giving up in exchange for what is immediate.
exp.3:4:
What it says: God did not look upon Cain and his offering with favor. "Did not look with favor" means that he did not accept it kindly. Cain was "very wroth," that is, filled with anger, and "his countenance fell," meaning his face became downcast and dark. His anger showed on the outside.

Context: The narrator of Genesis describes what happened when Cain and Abel presented offerings to the LORD. The text does not clearly explain why God accepted one and not the other. Some think it was because of the attitude of the heart; others, because of the quality of what was offered. Soon after, God speaks with Cain and warns him, with care, about the sin that lies in wait.

For today: When something hurts you or seems unfair, do not let anger grow in silence. Bring it honestly to God, listen to his correction, and choose to do what is good before the resentment becomes something worse.
exp.38:17:
