Here the wife of Potiphar gives her version to her husband. She says that she cried out and that Joseph, frightened, left his garment with her and ran away. The phrase "left his garment with me" means he left it in her hands, and "fled out" means he ran out of the house.

It is Potiphar's wife who speaks; she had tried to seduce Joseph, but he refused her. She uses the garment he left behind as "evidence" to falsely accuse him and protect her own reputation. So Joseph, who was innocent, ended up in prison.

Doing what is right does not always spare us from being unjustly accused. Even so, we can remain firm in our integrity, trusting that God sees the truth. And when we are wrong, it is better to admit it than to blame others.
exp.43:31:
Judah says to Joseph, without knowing it is him, that he became a "surety" for the lad, that is, a guarantor or someone responsible for his safety. He had promised his father that if he did not bring Benjamin back to him, he would bear the blame "for ever," that is, forever. "Lad" means a young man or boy.

Judah speaks before the governor of Egypt, who is Joseph, whom his brothers still do not recognize. Joseph had kept Benjamin back, accusing him of stealing his cup. Judah pleads for him and recalls how much Jacob would suffer if he lost this son, the other son of Rachel, after believing Joseph was dead. His offer to remain as a servant shows a change in him, since years earlier he had taken part in selling Joseph.

Keeping what we promise can cost us, but it shows character. Today we can take a commitment to someone vulnerable seriously, without excuses or running away, and rely on God's help to fulfill it.
exp.28:31:
Leah became pregnant and had a son. She named him Reuben, which sounds like "look, a son" in Hebrew. She says that the Lord has seen her affliction, that is, her pain and her sorrow. She also hopes that now her husband Jacob will love her.

It is Leah speaking, the wife whom Jacob did not prefer. Jacob loved his sister Rachel more, and the text says Leah was "unloved," a way of saying she was less loved. The Lord saw her pain and gave her children. Leah acknowledges God, though she still longs for her husband's love.

God sees those who feel rejected or undervalued. We can bring our pain to him with confidence. We can also learn that God's love sustains the heart, even when some people do not value us as they should.
exp.40:14:
Pharaoh tells Joseph that he has had a dream and that no one has been able to explain it to him. He also tells him that he has heard that Joseph can interpret dreams.

The words "thou canst understand a dream to interpret it" mean "you can understand a dream so as to explain it." The word "and" in "I have dreamed a dream, and there is none" is used here to link the two statements.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is troubled because his wise men gave him no answer. Joseph has just come out of prison; he has been shaved and given clean clothes so that he can appear before the king. The cupbearer, who had been imprisoned with Joseph, told Pharaoh about his gift. Joseph answers at once, however, that the interpretation does not come from him but from God.

For today: when others recognize a gift or talent in you, learn from Joseph. Serve with willingness, but give the credit to God and not to yourself. Humility reminds us that everything good we can offer comes from Him.
exp.6:4:
He says that Noah obeyed completely everything God had commanded him. The phrase "according unto all" means that he did not carry out only part of the instructions or change them, but fulfilled each one just as it was given. "Jehovah" is God's name in the Old Testament.

God had just told Noah that in seven days he would send rain for forty days and forty nights. He also indicated how many animals Noah was to bring into the ark to preserve life. The verse is a brief conclusion to the account: faced with so great and difficult a command, Noah responded with obedience. The text does not record his words or his feelings, only his actions.

Obeying God sometimes means trusting without seeing the whole picture. Today we might ask ourselves: what specific thing do I know God is asking of me, and am I still putting it off? A simple step of obedience, taken in faith, is worth more than many good intentions.
exp.18:35:
This verse says that Lot's two daughters became pregnant by their own father. The word "conceived" in the original sense means that they became pregnant. It is a sad event, told briefly and without praising it.

Context: It is the narrator who speaks. Sodom had been destroyed, and Lot was living with his daughters in a cave, isolated. They feared being left without descendants, so they made their father drunk and acted on their own, without consulting God. The text does not approve of what happened. From this came the peoples of Moab and Ammon, who later became rivals of Israel.

For today: Fear and desperation can lead us to make crooked decisions, even when we have come out of a situation of rescue. When we feel there is no way out, let us seek God and wise counsel before acting, instead of forcing solutions that leave long-lasting wounds.
exp.23:1:
Abraham calls his oldest servant, the one in charge of all his possessions, and asks him to put his hand under his thigh. "Servant" is the word used for the one who serves, and the old spelling "unto" is simply the way "to" was once written. It was a solemn gesture for making an oath.

Abraham is now an old man, and God has blessed him in everything. He wants to make sure that his son Isaac marries someone who does not worship the gods of Canaan. So he asks his trusted servant for a serious promise. Scholars believe the gesture is connected with descendants and with the importance of the promise, but the text does not explain it with certainty.

For today: the important decisions of life, such as marriage, deserve prayer, wise counsel, and trustworthy people. Abraham did not act carelessly, but with faith and responsibility.
exp.46:4:
Pharaoh speaks to Joseph and tells him that his father and his brothers have already arrived where he is. It is a short sentence that serves as a bridge: Pharaoh confirms that Joseph's family is present in Egypt. The word "unto" is an older form of "to," and the phrasing "are come" is an older way of saying "have come."

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is the speaker. Joseph's brothers have just told him that they are shepherds and that they came because of the famine in Canaan. Pharaoh addresses Joseph because he is the one who has authority before the king and who had arranged the arrival of his family. Right after this, Pharaoh grants them the land of Goshen.

For today: God can use open doors, and sometimes unexpected people, to care for his family in difficult times. We can ask him for help with confidence and thank those who extend a hand to us, as Pharaoh did for this needy family.
exp.13:5:
This verse continues the list of peoples who were defeated by Chedorlaomer and his allies. Here the Horites are mentioned. They lived in their mount Seir (the region later called Edom), and the campaign reached as far as El-paran, which is by the wilderness.

Context: the narrator of Genesis tells of a war between kings. The kings of the east come to punish a rebellion by the cities of the Vale of Siddim. The route is described in detail to show how powerful this alliance was. Later, Lot, Abram's nephew, will be captured in this war, and that is why the account matters.

For today: the decisions of the powerful can affect innocent people, like Lot. We can pray for those who suffer from conflicts they did not choose, and trust that God cares for his people even in troubled times.
exp.20:26:
It says that Abraham took sheep and oxen and gave them to Abimelech. Afterward, the two of them made a covenant, that is, a formal pact or agreement of peace.

The account tells that Abraham had complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized. Abimelech said he knew nothing about the matter. Then Abraham, instead of continuing to argue, gave him animals and sealed an agreement. In that time, water in the desert was vital, and a pact protected both sides. The animals were a gift and also a sign of goodwill.

When there is a conflict, it is good to speak clearly and directly, but also to seek peace with generosity. A humble gesture can settle what an argument fails to resolve.
exp.37:4:
The explanation says that Judah's wife became pregnant again and had a third son, whom she named Shelah. It also notes that Judah was in Chezib when the child was born.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He tells how Judah's family grew after he separated from his brothers and went to live near Canaanite people. His wife was the daughter of Shua. Chezib is mentioned as the place of birth, but it is not known for certain where it was; it could be the same as Achzib in the region of Judah. This detail prepares the story that follows, in which Shelah will be important for Tamar.

For today: God watches the small details of our families. Even when a story has dark moments, He keeps working in it. Entrust your home to Him, including what you do not understand.
exp.28:5:
Jacob asks the shepherds whether Laban is well, and they answer that he is, that he has peace. Here "peace" means health and well-being, much as when today we ask "how is he doing?" And just at that moment, they say, Rachel, Laban's daughter, comes up with the flock.

Jacob has just arrived in Haran, fleeing his brother Esau and seeking his mother's family. He speaks with some shepherds beside a well. They confirm that they know Laban and point him to Rachel. The Bible does not explain the detail, but the account shows how God guided Jacob to the right place at the right time.

For today: when you feel lost or are on the way toward something uncertain, keep taking simple steps, such as asking questions and speaking with respect. God can meet you in the middle of everyday life and guide you with more care than you imagine.
exp.21:11:
Here the angel of the LORD stops Abraham just as he was about to sacrifice his son. He tells him not to harm the boy, because it is now clear that Abraham fears God: he has not held back his son, his only son. "Fearing God" means reverencing Him and trusting Him, and "withheld" means refusing to give or keeping for oneself.

God had tested Abraham by asking for Isaac, the son of the promise. The angel speaks from heaven on God's behalf and calls Abraham's name twice. God did not want Isaac's death; He wanted to see whether Abraham trusted Him above all. Then He provides a ram in his place.

For today: examine what you find hard to surrender to God, such as your plans, your children, or your future. Trust that He cares for what you hand over to Him and knows how to provide at just the right moment.
exp.46:8:
Jacob answers Pharaoh that he is 130 years old, which he describes as the days of his "pilgrimage," that is, of living as a traveler or stranger. He says his days have been "few and evil": short compared with those of his fathers, Abraham and Isaac, and full of hardship.

Jacob is already an old man and is in Egypt, where Joseph presents him before Pharaoh. His life was marked by flight, family conflicts, hard work, and the loss of Joseph, whom he believed dead. Even so, both before and after he speaks, he blesses Pharaoh. He sees himself as a pilgrim who waits for the promises of God.

For today: even if your life has had sorrows and has not turned out as you hoped, you can be honest about your pain and still live with gratitude and bless others. God continues to guide your path.
exp.20:1:
It says that Sarah became pregnant and gave Abraham a son when she was already old. It happened right at the time God had announced. The archaic words are "conceived" (became pregnant), "bare" (gave birth) and "old age" (advanced years).

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. God had promised Abraham and Sarah a son many years before, even though it seemed impossible because of their age. The previous verse says that God "visited" Sarah, that is, he acted on her behalf. Then Abraham named the child Isaac and circumcised him at eight days old, as God had commanded.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it seems to us that it is already too late. We can keep trusting and obeying while we wait, knowing that his timing is not ours, but he is faithful.
exp.36:20:
Reuben heard the plan of his brothers to kill Joseph. So he rescued him from their hands and said, "Let us not kill him." The phrase "delivered him" means "rescued him" or "saved him." At this moment Reuben does not save him completely, but he stops the murder.

Joseph's brothers were filled with envy because of his dreams and because their father Jacob showed him favoritism. Reuben, the eldest son, speaks here. The text that follows explains that he wanted to return Joseph to his father. His plan was not perfect, but it did stop the worst at that moment.

When everyone is going after evil, sometimes one voice is needed to say "no." Ask God for courage to halt an injustice, even though you cannot fix everything at once. One step in favor of good can open the way to something greater.
exp.29:24:
It says that after Joseph, Rachel's son, was born, Jacob asked Laban to let him go. The old words are "born" (given birth to) and "Send me away" (let me depart). Jacob wanted to go back "unto mine own place, and to my country", that is, to Canaan, where his family lived.

Jacob is speaking. He had been working for his father-in-law Laban for about fourteen years in exchange for Leah and Rachel. With the birth of Joseph, Rachel finally had a son, and Jacob felt it was time to return home. Laban did not want him to leave, because he recognized that God had blessed him on account of Jacob.

For today: God leads us in stages. When one stage is complete, it is good to pray, to speak clearly and with respect, and to take the step toward what God has placed on our heart, even when others would prefer that we stay.
exp.25:20:
It says that Isaac's servants dug a second well, and once again the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled over it. "Strove" means that they argued or fought. Isaac gave it the name Sitnah, which in Hebrew is related to "accusation" or "enmity," that is, a place of opposition.

This is part of the story of Isaac in the land of the Philistines of Gerar, in a time of famine. God had blessed him, and his neighbors envied him. Isaac does not respond with violence: he moves away and keeps digging. The narrator (Moses, according to tradition) tells how the names of the wells reflect what he went through: first Esek (contention), then Sitnah (enmity), and then Rehoboth (wide space).

For today: when you face a conflict that keeps coming back, you do not always have to win the argument. Sometimes wisdom is yielding with peace, moving on, and trusting that God will open a wide place for you.
exp.1:18:
It says that God formed out of the ground every beast of the field and every bird of the air, and brought them to Adam to see what he would call them. The name Adam gave to each living creature became its name. "Brought" is the English rendering of the old form "trájolas," and "call" here means "to give a name."

The narrator recalls that God had said, "It is not good that the man should be alone." Before forming the woman, God presents the animals to Adam. Many understand that in this way Adam saw that none of them was a suitable help for him, and also that he was given responsibility over creation. The text does not explain the whole purpose, so it is interpreted in several ways.

God entrusts us with real tasks. We can care responsibly for what He has created, whether a pet, a garden, or the environment where we live, and also value human relationships, because we were made to live in companionship.
exp.10:13:
It says that Salah lived thirty years and then had his son Eber. The phrase "begat" means that he was the father of someone. It is a brief detail within a list of families that moves from generation to generation.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book of Genesis, which is traditionally attributed to Moses. This list of Shem's descendants connects the story of Noah with that of Abraham. It shows how God was preserving the family line from which the people of Israel would come. Scholars debate whether the list has gaps or whether the ages should be understood literally, so it is wise to be humble about that.

For today: God notices quiet, ordinary lives, like that of Salah. Your daily faithfulness, though no one notices it, can be part of what God is doing in time.
exp.30:51:
The verse says that this heap and this pillar will be witnesses that neither will cross over this heap to the other to do harm. A "heap" is a pile of stones, and the "pillar" is a standing stone set up as a sign. Laban and Jacob agree not to cross that line to harm one another.

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, is the one speaking. Jacob had left in secret with his wives, Laban's daughters, and his possessions, and Laban caught up with him. After the tension, both make a covenant of peace. The markers serve as a reminder, and Laban also asks that God be witness and judge between them.

For today: when there is a conflict, it is worth setting clear boundaries and honest agreements. Putting things in writing or speaking them plainly, and placing them before God, helps protect the peace and keep the harm from happening again.
exp.7:14:
God spoke to Noah. It is a short sentence that serves as a bridge: it introduces the words that come after. Almost the whole verse is simple, and the word "saying" announces what God is about to say next.

The one who speaks is God, and He speaks to Noah. Noah had been inside the ark for more than a year. He had already seen that the earth was dry, but he did not go out on his own. He waited for God's word. After this verse, God commands him to leave the ark with his family and the animals, so that they may begin again and multiply upon the earth.

For today: when you are waiting for a change, do not rush ahead just because things seem ready. Seek God in prayer and in His Word, and trust that He will tell you when and how to take the next step.
exp.30:36:
Jacob tells Laban that he has already searched all of his belongings and found nothing that belongs to Laban. The words "stuff" and "goods" here mean the household goods and furnishings, not jewels. Jacob challenges Laban to put forward whatever he has found in front of their relatives, so that they may judge between the two of them.

Jacob speaks in anger. Laban pursued him because his household gods had been taken, and Rachel had taken them in secret, although Jacob did not know it. After a search that turned up nothing, Jacob defends his honesty. He will later recall twenty years of faithful work.

For today: when you are accused, defend yourself calmly and with facts, not rumors. Living with integrity day by day gives you the freedom to say, "Let everything be examined." And if there is something hidden in your life, now is a good time to put it right.
exp.44:8:
Here Joseph asks his brothers to hurry and go to their father Jacob. He tells them to say that God has made him lord of all Egypt, and to come down to him without delay. "Haste ye" means "hurry up," and "tarry not" means "do not wait long."

Joseph is speaking to the brothers who sold him years earlier. He has already revealed himself to them, and he reassures them by saying that God sent him ahead of them to save lives. There were still five years of famine to come, so he wants to bring the whole family close to him, in Goshen, to care for them.

For today: Joseph does not let the pain of the past hold back his generosity. We can ask ourselves whether there is someone to whom we should extend a hand, even after a wound. Trusting that God works even in difficult circumstances helps us act with kindness and without delay.
exp.29:32:
Jacob tells Laban that his honesty will be the proof of his wages. When Laban comes to inspect the flock, every animal that is not speckled or spotted among the goats, or brown among the sheep, must be considered stolen. "Shall be counted stolen with me" means he would be accused of being a thief.

Jacob speaks with his father-in-law Laban after years of serving him. Now he wants to form his own flock and proposes a simple payment: the animals of an uncommon color. These were few, so the agreement seemed very favorable to Laban. Jacob offers that any mistake could be easily checked.

For today: try to live with such transparency in your work and your agreements that your conduct speaks for you. Integrity does not need to hide anything, and it makes trust easier.
exp.23:4:
Here the servant of Abraham asks a sincere question. He says that perhaps the woman will not be willing to leave her land to follow him, and he asks whether, in that case, he must bring Isaac back to the land from which Abraham came. "Peradventure" means "perhaps", and "unto me" in "follow me" means that she would have to come after him, behind him.

The servant is the eldest servant of Abraham's household, and the text does not give his name here. Abraham has just made him swear that he will seek a wife for Isaac among Abraham's own kin and not among the Canaanites. The servant raises the possible problem, and Abraham answers that Isaac must not go back there, since God promised him that land.

For today: it is wise to think through difficulties before acting, but without losing sight of what God has already promised. We can ask honest questions and plan with care, and at the same time trust that God guides the way.
exp.49:20:
The explanation opens with a stray slip ("Josué... no,"), which I'll omit as it's a self-correction in the source, not content. Translating the rest:

Here Joseph tells his brothers not to be afraid any longer. He will provide food for them and for their children. The Bible adds that he comforted them and spoke kindly to them, that is, with tender and sincere words. "Nourish" means to provide food and care. The old English "fear ye not" is a more formal way of saying "do not be afraid."

After Jacob died, the brothers feared that Joseph would take revenge for having sold him years earlier. Joseph, already a ruler in Egypt, answers them that he is not in the place of God to judge them. He acknowledges that they acted wrongly, but that God used that story to save many lives.

Today we can learn to respond to those who have hurt us with kindness and not with revenge. If someone asks us for forgiveness, we can comfort them with sincere words, trusting that God can bring good even out of painful situations.
exp.13:8:
This verse closes the list of the kings who fought in the Valley of Siddim. On one side stood four kings: Chedorlaomer of Elam, Tidal "king of nations," Amraphel of Shinar, and Arioch of Ellasar. On the other side stood the five kings of the cities of the valley, mentioned earlier. The phrase "four kings with five" sums up the battle.

Context: Moses, as the traditional author, narrates a war between kings. The five kings had rebelled against Chedorlaomer, whom they had served before. This war sets up the story of Lot, who lived in Sodom and was taken captive, and Abram's intervention to rescue him. The exact location of some of the kingdoms is debated.

For today: even when the great powers seem to be in charge, God guides the story. Trust in Him, and care for your family as Abram cared for Lot.
exp.41:25:
The passage says that Joseph's brothers loaded the grain they had bought onto their donkeys and left Egypt. The word "asses" refers to donkeys, and the verb "departed" simply means they went away.

It is the narrator who speaks. The brothers had gone down to Egypt for food during a famine, not knowing that the governor was Joseph, the brother they had sold years earlier. Joseph tested them, kept Simeon imprisoned, and ordered that their money be put back into their sacks. They leave without knowing it, and they will soon discover it with fear. We also see that Joseph wept in private, which suggests that his heart was not filled with revenge.

Today we can remember that God sometimes works in silence, even when we do not understand what is happening. Trust that He may be guiding your situation with a purpose.
exp.30:18:
This verse tells that Laban went off to shear his sheep, that is, to cut the wool from his flock, a job that could take several days and kept him away from home. While he was gone, Rachel stole her father's images. These were small religious figures kept in the household.

Here the book's narrator speaks. Jacob takes advantage of Laban's absence to return to Canaan with his family and his possessions. The Bible does not explain why Rachel took the images. Some think she was seeking protection or that they gave her some family right, but the text does not make this clear. What is certain is that her faith was still mixed with pagan customs.

For today: check whether there are "hidden idols" in your heart, things you trust more than God. Lay them before Him with sincerity.
exp.39:3:
The captain of the guard assigned Joseph to take charge of the two new prisoners, the king's cupbearer and the baker, and Joseph waited on them. "Charged" means "put in charge" or "appointed." "Served them" means he attended to what they needed. "Continued a season" indicates that some time passed, without saying how long.

The narrator tells us that the pharaoh became angry with his two high officials and had them locked up in the same prison where Joseph was held. Although Joseph was an unjustly imprisoned man, the captain trusted him. This sets up the next scene, when the two men have dreams that Joseph will interpret.

For today: even in difficult or unjust places, we can serve faithfully and care for those nearby. Joseph did not wait for a better situation before being useful. God can use that simple, daily service to prepare opportunities we cannot imagine today.
exp.39:0:
It says that, after the events before, two important officials of the king of Egypt, the cupbearer (who served the king's wine) and the baker (who prepared his bread and food), "offended", that is, committed a fault against their lord, the Pharaoh. The Bible does not say what that offense exactly was.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He introduces these two men because they will end up in the same prison where Joseph was, unjustly held. Their dreams, which Joseph will interpret, will be an important step for Joseph to later come before Pharaoh.

For today: God can use even difficult and unexpected moments, including the mistakes of others, to carry out his plans. If today you are waiting in an unjust situation, remain faithful and serve with love. Your waiting does not go unnoticed by God.
exp.31:15:
Jacob hands the animals over to his servants, one herd for each group. He orders them to go on ahead of him and to leave a space between one herd and the next. A herd is a group of animals.

Jacob is returning to his homeland and fears meeting his brother Esau, whom he had earlier deceived. He knows Esau is coming with four hundred men. So he prepares a large gift. By separating the herds, the gift arrives in waves and, according to many interpreters, seeks to gradually soften Esau's anger. The Bible does not state exactly what Jacob was thinking, but the context points to that purpose.

For today: when you have to repair a broken relationship, you do not need to wait until you feel ready. You can take concrete, humble, and patient steps, and at the same time place everything in God's hands in prayer, as Jacob did before this.
exp.12:14:
God tells Abram that all the land he can see will be given to him and to his descendants (his "seed") forever. The phrase "forever" can be understood in several ways, and believers have interpreted it in different ways.

The one speaking is the LORD. Lot has just separated from Abram and has gone toward Sodom, an area full of very wicked people. Abram had generously given the better land to his nephew. Then God confirms his promise and invites him to look out toward the four points of the compass.

For today: when you do what is right and let go of what others want, God does not forget you. Trust that he keeps his promises in his own time, and do not cling to what you see now as the only thing you have.
exp.23:14:
This verse tells us that Rebekah appeared just before Abraham's servant had finished praying. It explains who she is: the daughter of Bethuel, who was the son of Milcah and of Nahor, Abraham's brother. She was going out to the well with her pitcher (a water jar) on her shoulder. "It came to pass" means "it happened."

The narrator recounts what took place after the servant's prayer. Abraham had sent him to find a wife for his son Isaac among his relatives. The servant asked God for a sign, and Rebekah arrived before he had finished speaking. Her kinship with Abraham was exactly what was being sought.

For today: we can pray with confidence about our important decisions, knowing that God listens. He may answer in his own time and his own way, sometimes sooner than we expect. In the meantime, it is good to stay attentive and faithful.
exp.34:10:
God presents himself as "God Almighty," that is, the All-powerful. He tells Jacob, "be fruitful and multiply," and promises him that from him will come a nation and also a company of nations. He adds that kings will come out of his loins, an old expression meaning from his descendants.

God speaks with Jacob after his return from Padan-aram, and just after renaming him Israel. He repeats to Jacob the blessing he had earlier given to Abraham and Isaac. It is a promise of descendants and of land, which God would fulfill in time.

For today: when you feel small or carry an imperfect past, remember that God keeps his promises by his power, not yours. Trust that he can do something great in your life.
exp.0:0:
At the beginning of all things, God made the heavens and the earth. The word "created," as used in the King James Version, is the older-sounding form of the verb meaning to make something from nothing. "The heavens and the earth" is a way of saying "the whole universe," both what we see above and the ground we walk on below.

The book of Genesis does not name who wrote it, although tradition attributes it to Moses. Here the narrator presents God as the origin of everything, before describing how he brought order to the earth. The verses that follow describe an earth "without form, and void" and God speaking to bring forth light. Christians understand this passage in different ways, but all agree that God is the Creator.

For today: if God is the origin of everything, your life is not an accident. You can entrust your worries to him, because the One who made the universe also cares for you.
exp.45:12:
This verse lists the four sons of Issachar, the fifth son of Jacob by Leah: Tola, Puah, Job, and Shimron. The names appear in the older spelling (Issachar, Tola, Phuvah). In other passages, such as Numbers 26:24, the third name is written "Jashub," and some scholars think it is a variant of the same name.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally Moses, presents the list of Jacob's family who go down to Egypt to live near Joseph during the famine. Each descendant is named because from them would come the tribes of Israel.

For today: God knows each person by name, even when in the story a detail seems small. You can trust that your life and your everyday faithfulness matter to Him. And you can also value those who serve quietly.
exp.43:12:
The explanation says that, upon finding the cup in Benjamin's sack, the brothers tore their clothes, a sign of very deep grief. Then each one loaded his donkey again and they returned to the city. "Donkey" is the ass, and "sack" is the bag where they carried the grain.

It is the narrator who tells the story. Joseph, without his brothers knowing, had ordered his cup to be placed in Benjamin's sack in order to test them. They could have left Benjamin alone, but none of them left. All of them returned together, which shows that they had changed since they sold Joseph.

For today: when someone in our family suffers the consequences of a problem, we can choose to stand by them instead of abandoning them. Loyalty in difficult moments reflects a transformed heart.
exp.45:24:
This verse closes the list of the descendants of Bilhah, the servant whom Laban gave to his daughter Rachel. Bilhah had children with Jacob: Dan and Naphtali, and from them came seven people in all. "Bare" means "gave birth to," and "souls" means "persons."

Here the narrator of the book speaks, listing the family of Jacob as he goes down to Egypt with Joseph. Names and numbers are recorded because God was forming the people of Israel, and every family counted. Some scholars explain in different ways how the totals of 66 and 70 are added up, so it is not wise to force a single explanation.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those whom the story could have passed over, like Bilhah. You are not an anonymous number to Him either. Today you can thank Him that He knows you by name and value those who usually go unnoticed.
exp.36:7:
Joseph's brothers answer him with anger: "Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?" And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words. "Reign" and "have dominion" mean to rule or have authority over others; "hated" means to despise and resent him.

The older brothers of Joseph are speaking, right after he has told them his dream of the sheaves bowing down to his sheaf. They already felt jealousy, since their father Jacob loved him in a special way. They understood the dream as a promise that Joseph would rule over them. The text does not say that Joseph spoke with bad intent, but his words increased the envy.

For today: jealousy can harden the heart and make us reject the one God wants to use. Let us ask God to help us rejoice for others instead of competing with them. It is also wise to speak with humility and wisdom when we share what we believe God is showing us.
exp.25:25:
This verse tells us that Abimelech, king of Gerar, went to look for Isaac. He was accompanied by Ahuzzath, who was his friend or close adviser, and Phichol, the chief of his army. The phrase "went to him" means "went to where he was." The word "captain" means commander or military leader.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Isaac was in Beersheba, and God had just promised him that he would be with him and bless him. Earlier, these men had driven him out of their land. Now they arrive with authority, and then they explain that they saw that God was with Isaac and want to make a covenant of peace.

For today: when you live with faith and without revenge, God can change the hearts of those who rejected you. You do not have to force reconciliation; trust God and keep doing good.
exp.36:9:
This verse tells that Joseph shared his second dream with his father and his brothers. Jacob rebuked him and asked, in amazement, whether his father, his mother, and his brothers would really have to bow down to the ground before him. "Rebuke" means to correct with strong words. "Bow down to the ground" means to make a deep bow, as a sign of respect.

Jacob, Joseph's father, is the one speaking. His brothers already hated Joseph because of the first dream, and this second dream added more tension. Jacob corrects Joseph, although afterward the text says that he "kept the matter in mind," that is, he kept it stored in his thoughts and pondered it. The Bible does not explain why Jacob mentioned "your mother," since Rachel had died; some think it refers to another maternal figure, but this is not certain.

For today: even when we receive something valuable from God, it is good to share it with humility and sensitivity, thinking about how it affects others.
exp.42:21:
Joseph's brothers tell the steward that, besides the money they found in their sacks, they have brought more money to buy food. They insist that they do not know who put the earlier money there. "Sacks" are the bags of grain, and the "inn" is the lodging where they spent the night.

The brothers of Joseph speak here in fear. On the earlier trip they found their money returned, and they fear they will be accused of theft. They do not yet know that the ruler of Egypt is their brother Joseph. That is why they hurry to explain themselves honestly. The steward reassures them and tells them that God gave them that treasure.

When we have failed or fear the consequences, the best course is to act with sincerity and to make right whatever we can. Honesty opens the door to peace, and God can work even in what we do not understand.
exp.8:10:
God promises that he will never again destroy all living creatures with a flood. The words "cut off" in the verse mean to be destroyed or to come to an end. A covenant is a solemn promise that God makes and commits himself to keep.

God speaks with Noah and his sons after they leave the ark. The earth had been judged because of the great wickedness of humanity, and now God is beginning again with them. His promise includes the animals as well. As a sign, he will set the rainbow in the clouds, as the following verse says.

For today: when storms come or moments of fear arrive, remember that God is faithful to his word. You can rest in the fact that he keeps what he promises, and that his care reaches all of his creation. Trust in him and take care of what he has created too.
exp.31:16:
Jacob gives instructions to the first servant who leads a herd. If Esau, his brother, meets him, he will surely ask him three questions: Whose are you? Where are you going? And whose are all these animals in front of you? The words "meeteth" and "asketh" are old forms of "meets" and "asks."

Jacob is returning to his land after many years, and he knows that Esau is coming to meet him with four hundred men. He remembers that years earlier Esau wanted to kill him. So he prepares a large gift, sent in separate groups, to soften his brother's heart. Some see prudence here; others, fear. There is probably both.

Jacob prays to God and also acts wisely. If you have a broken relationship, ask God for help, and then take concrete and humble steps toward reconciliation, without waiting for the other person to take the first step.
exp.43:29:
This verse is part of a sentence that continues into the next one. It says that if Judah returns to his father without the young man, the old man will suffer greatly, because his life is bound up with that son's life. "Lad" means a young man or boy, "servant" is the humble way of speaking of oneself, and "bound up in" expresses a very deep attachment.

Judah, brother of Joseph, is speaking before Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize and sees as the ruler of Egypt. Benjamin, the youngest, has been accused of theft. Judah pleads that he be set free and offers to stay as a slave in his place, so as not to cause more suffering to his father Jacob, who, as he believed, had already lost Joseph.

For today: true love shows itself when we are willing to bear the cost for others. Let us think today about who needs us to protect or accompany them, and take one concrete step of help.
exp.17:16:
The explanation says that God asks himself a question out loud: "Am I going to hide from Abraham what I am about to do?" The phrase "hide" in the King James wording means to conceal or keep secret. It is a rhetorical question: God makes clear that he does not want to keep Abraham on the outside.

The Lord speaks, the one who had come to Abraham's tent with two companions in the form of men. Now they look toward Sodom, the city that is going to be judged. The verses that follow explain the reason: God chose Abraham to form a nation and bless all the peoples, and he expected him to teach his family to live in righteousness.

For today: God deals closely with those who walk with him. If you seek his company and obey, you can expect him to guide you and help you understand his heart. Cultivate that friendship through prayer and reading the Bible.
exp.9:23:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Arphaxad was the father of Salah, and that Salah was the father of Eber. "Begat" is an old word meaning "was the father of." The names appear in the old spelling of this version: today many write Arfaxad, Sala, and Éber.

We are in the "Table of Nations" in Genesis 10. The narrator, whom tradition identifies with Moses, reviews the descendants of Noah's sons after the flood. Here the text follows the line of Shem. This line leads to Eber, and later in Genesis it leads to Abraham. Scholars debate how direct each connection is, but the text shows how humanity spread out.

For today: God pays attention to every generation, even when some names seem to us to be only a list. Your life and your faith are also part of a larger story. Live with gratitude for those who came before you, and with the desire to pass on faith to those who come after.
exp.28:19:
This verse says that Jacob worked seven years in order to marry Rachel. Those years seemed to him "a few days" because he loved her. The word "served" means that he worked for Laban, and the original's "seemed" simply means that they seemed to him to be a few days.

The account is told by the narrator of Genesis. Jacob had arrived at the home of his uncle Laban and fell in love with Rachel, the younger daughter. Since he had no bride-price to offer, he proposed to work seven years in exchange for her, and Laban agreed. In that time, serving in this way was a known way of paying for a marriage.

For today: true love makes sacrifice lighter. When we serve God and people with love, the effort and the waiting weigh less. Ask God to renew your love for what He has entrusted to you.
exp.32:18:
It says that Jacob bought a plot of land in Shechem, right where he had pitched his tent. He bought it from the children of Hamor, the father of Shechem, and paid "a hundred pieces of money." The Hebrew word is "qesitah," and it is not known for certain what its value was; it may have been a weight of metal or a unit of exchange.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jacob had just returned from Paddan-aram after many years and after being reconciled with Esau. Now he settles in Canaan, the land God had promised to his family. This is the first property of Jacob's in the land that is mentioned, and he acquires it legally, without taking it by force. Then he sets up an altar to God.

For today: when God gives us a place to start over, it is good to secure it with honesty and order, and not to forget to worship him. May our affairs and our home be built on what is just and on gratitude.
exp.22:15:
This verse tells how Abraham accepted the price Ephron asked and paid him four hundred shekels of silver. He did it in the presence of the sons of Heth, that is, as witnesses. The phrase "hearkened unto" means that he agreed to what Ephron said. The phrase "current money with the merchant" means that the silver had the value and quality accepted in the trade of that time.

Sarah had died, and Abraham, who lived as a foreigner in the land, needed a place to bury her. Ephron had mentioned the price almost in passing, and Abraham did not bargain. He paid immediately and in public. In this way the cave of Machpelah became his property, with witnesses. Scholars debate how much a shekel weighed exactly in that period.

For today: be clear and honest in your dealings. Keep what you agree to, pay what is fair, and leave things in order, so that your word inspires trust and you avoid conflicts.
exp.10:12:
It says that Arphaxad, after he had his son Salah, lived 403 more years, and during that time had other sons and daughters. "Begat" means "fathered as a son," and "Arphaxad" is the old spelling of the name now written Arphaxad in modern English Bibles.

This is part of the genealogy of Shem, which runs from the flood to Abram. The narrator of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses, is not addressing any particular person here but records the family line through which God's promise continues. The very long lifespans are understood in several ways, and the Bible does not explain them.

God cares for the generations, even when no one remembers them. Every life counts in his plan. Today you can live with faith in everyday life, raising children, serving, and teaching others, trusting that God uses what is simple for something greater.
exp.7:11:
He waited another seven days and sent out the dove a third time. This time it did not come back. The phrase "toward him" is what the older wording means by "unto him." The words "waited yet" show that Noah did not rush, but kept waiting patiently.

The narrator is describing the flood, and here Noah is inside the ark, waiting for the earth to be ready. In the previous verse the dove brought back an olive leaf, a sign that there was plant life. Now, since it did not return, it is understood that the dove had found a place to rest and live. Even so, Noah did not leave right away; the verses that follow show that he waited until God told him to come out.

For today: sometimes we already see signs that things are getting better, but God calls us not to get ahead of Him. We can wait patiently, pray, and trust that He will show us the right moment to take the next step.
exp.44:1:
Here the account tells us that Joseph wept so loudly that he could not keep it hidden. "Aloud" means weeping in a very loud voice. His crying was heard throughout the house where he was, and the news reached Pharaoh's palace. "The Egyptians" were the servants and officials whom he had ordered to leave.

Joseph is the governor of Egypt, and he stands before the brothers who sold him years earlier. After testing them, he can no longer hold back and is about to tell them who he is. He had sent everyone away so he could have that moment in private, but his emotions could not remain hidden.

For today: weeping is not weakness. When there are wounds, forgiveness, or reconciliation involved, it is normal to feel a great deal. God allows us to express what we carry inside, and often tears open the door to healing.
exp.41:21:
Reuben reminds his brothers that he warned them: "Do not harm the boy." But they did not listen. Now he says "his blood is required," meaning that God is calling them to account for the life of Joseph.

Speaking is Reuben, the oldest of the brothers. They are imprisoned in Egypt and believe their distress is the result of what they did to Joseph years ago. They do not know that the ruler who treats them harshly is Joseph himself, who is listening to them in secret. The Bible does not say that Reuben was right in every detail, but it does show that guilt still weighed on them.

For today: let us not hide our wrongs over time. Let us ask God for forgiveness and, where possible, repair the harm with humility. A clear conscience begins with the truth.
exp.42:22:
Here the steward of Joseph answers the brothers, who had nervously explained the matter of the money found in their sacks (bags or sacks). He tells them to be at peace and not to be afraid. He attributes the discovery to God, whom he calls "your God and the God of your father," and says that he himself did receive their payment. Then he brings Simeon out to them, who had been held in prison.

The steward speaks on Joseph's instructions, though Joseph has not yet revealed himself. The brothers fear they will be accused of theft. We do not know whether he understood well what he said about God or whether he was only repeating kind words. Even so, his words calm the brothers.

For today: when you are afraid of something you do not understand, do not jump to hasty conclusions. Calm your heart and remember that God may be at work, even in what seems to be a problem.
exp.10:15:
It says that Eber lived thirty-four years and then had his son Peleg. "Begat" is an old word that means "had as a son."

This verse is part of the genealogy of Shem, which runs from the flood to Abram. The narrator, whom tradition identifies as Moses, does not tell every detail of their lives but follows the thread of one family. Some think these lists may have gaps, and others read them more literally. Even so, they show that God preserves the history that leads toward Abram and his promise.

For today: even if your life seems like just one more line in a list, God sees you and works through generations. Live faithfully, and pray for those who will come after you.
exp.8:1:
This verse says that the animals will feel fear and dread before human beings. "Dread" means a strong fear, and "delivered into your hand" means that they are placed under the care and dominion of humanity. This includes animals of the earth, birds of the air, and fish of the sea.

God speaks with Noah and his sons just after the flood. He blesses them and gives them a new beginning. Here he grants them authority over creation, and in the verses that follow he sets down rules, such as not eating blood. Some scholars also see in this fear a protection for people in a world changed by judgment.

For today: the authority God gives is not permission to abuse. We can care for animals and for nature responsibly, remembering that everything belongs to God and that He asks us to be good stewards.
exp.23:34:
This verse says that God has blessed Abraham, the master the servant speaks of, very greatly. He has made him prosper and has given him flocks of sheep and herds of cattle, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and donkeys. The word "asses" means donkeys, and "he is become great" means that he became a wealthy and important man.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, probably the oldest servant in his household (Genesis 24:2). He had traveled far to look for a wife for Isaac. Upon arriving at the home of Rebekah's family, before eating, he presents his message. By listing Abraham's riches, he makes clear that everything comes from God and that his master is a man who can be trusted.

For today: when you speak of what you have or what you have achieved, acknowledge God as the one who gave it to you. A grateful life, which gives Him the credit, inspires trust in others.
exp.5:8:
This verse introduces Noah as the central story that follows. "Generations" means the account of the family and what happened to it. "Just man" means a man who is upright before God. "Perfect" does not mean without sin, but whole and sincere. "Walked with God" speaks of a life of closeness and daily obedience.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Before this, God had decided to judge human wickedness, but Noah "found grace," that is, he received God's favor. This verse shows what Noah was like in the midst of a violent and corrupt society, as the following passage makes clear. Some understand "in his generations" to mean "among the people of his time"; the exact sense is debated.

For today: even when the atmosphere around you does not help, you can seek God every day through prayer, obedience, and sincerity. Walking with God is lived out in everyday life, step by step, trusting in his grace.
exp.10:3:
The explanation says the people agreed to build a city and a very tall tower, "whose top may reach unto heaven," meaning its peak would reach the clouds. They wanted "to make us a name," that is, to become famous and admired. They did it "lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth," that is, out of fear of being dispersed across the earth.

The speakers are the inhabitants of Shinar, a region of Mesopotamia. They had already learned to make bricks, and now they wanted something great. God had commanded them to fill the earth (Genesis 9:1), but they sought to stay together and secure their own glory. The text does not say the tower was wrong merely because of its height; it shows a proud and self-sufficient heart.

Today we can ask ourselves: does what I build seek to honor God and serve others, or only to give me a name and security? Let us ask him to give us humility.
exp.23:15:
This verse describes Rebekah: she was very beautiful, a virgin, meaning that no man had known her intimately. She went down to the spring, filled her pitcher, and came back up. "Damsel" means a young woman, and "known" here is an old way of speaking about sexual relations.

The narrator tells the story. Abraham's servant had prayed for a sign to find a wife for Isaac. Before he finished his prayer, Rebekah appeared. The text highlights her purity and her beauty, and presents her as a simple young woman going about her daily work when God placed her in the servant's path.

For today: God often works in the midst of everyday life. Living with integrity and serving diligently, even in common tasks, prepares us for the opportunities God places before us, though we may not see them coming.
exp.40:20:
It says that the lean cows ate up the fat ones, yet nothing could be noticed: they remained just as lean and ugly as before. Here the Pharaoh of Egypt is speaking. He is telling Joseph his dream, because no one in his court could explain it. He repeats it almost exactly as he dreamed it, and adds that the lean cows did not improve even though they devoured the fat ones. Joseph will later explain that these are seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine, and that God had warned Pharaoh of what He was going to do.

For today: abundance without planning runs out quickly and leaves no trace. We can ask ourselves how we manage what God gives us in good times: saving wisely, sharing generously, and trusting that He sustains us in difficult times too.
exp.43:14:
Here Joseph rebukes his brothers over the silver cup that was found in Benjamin's sack. He asks them what deed they have done, and adds that a man like him can surely divine, that is, he can discover hidden things. "Deed" means an action or a thing done.

Joseph speaks while still disguised as the ruler of Egypt, and his brothers do not know it is him. He had ordered the cup hidden in order to test them. He wants to see whether they will abandon Benjamin, as they once abandoned him. Whether Joseph really practiced divination or only pretended to, the Bible does not make clear; many think it was part of his act.

For today: Judah and his brothers acknowledge their past guilt before God. When something brings our mistakes to light, instead of hiding them or blaming others without hope, we can humble ourselves, be honest, and seek to change, trusting that God works even through trials.
exp.34:18:
This verse tells us that Rachel died after giving birth to Benjamin. She was buried beside the road that led to Ephrath, which is the same place later called Bethlehem.

Here the narrator of the book relates a very painful moment in few words. Jacob and his family were traveling, and Rachel had a difficult labor. Before dying, she named her son Ben-oni, "son of my sorrow," but Jacob named him Benjamin. Its meaning is interpreted in several ways, such as "son of the right hand" or "son of good fortune." Afterward, Jacob set up a marker over the grave.

For today: the Bible does not hide pain or loss. If you are going through grief, you can bring your sadness honestly before God. And like Jacob, you can lovingly honor the memory of those you loved.
exp.1:7:
The verse says that God planted a garden in a place called Eden, toward the east, and that there he put the man he had created. The word "garden" refers to an enclosed area with trees and plants. "Planted" indicates that the garden was already prepared when the man arrived.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks, traditionally attributed to Moses. After describing how God formed the man from the dust and gave him life, the account shows the place where God set him. The text does not say with certainty where Eden was, and people have interpreted it in different ways. What matters is that God provided a home full of beauty and food.

For today: God takes care of preparing what we need before we ask. We can thank him for what he has already given us and trust that he continues to care for us.
exp.30:13:
Rachel and Leah answer Jacob with a question: do we still have any portion or inheritance in our father's house? "Portion" is a share of the goods, and "inheritance" is what is received as heritage. They imply that the answer is no.

Jacob had told them that God commanded him to leave Laban's land and return to Canaan. Laban's daughters speak here and side with Jacob. Later they say that their father treated them as strangers and spent what had been paid for them. For this reason they support the departure and ask Jacob to obey God. Some scholars see in this a complaint about unfair treatment; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when God guides us into a difficult change, it helps to listen to family with honesty and to seek agreement. Obeying God can cost something, but he cares for those who obey him.
exp.43:10:
They say that Joseph's brothers acted quickly. Each one lowered his sack (his bag of grain) to the ground and opened it. "Lowering" here means setting the sack down on the ground in a hurry.

We are in the test that Joseph is setting up for them. His steward caught up with them and accused them of stealing the silver cup, which Joseph had ordered hidden in Benjamin's sack. The brothers, sure of their innocence, offered that whoever had the cup should die and the rest would become slaves. Their haste shows that they had nothing to hide. They did not know what was coming.

For today: when you are accused, acting with openness and without fear helps a great deal. But let us also watch our words, because the brothers promised too much without knowing what would happen. Let us think before we speak.
exp.15:10:
The explanation says that the angel of the Lord spoke to Hagar again and announced that she was already pregnant. She would have a son, and she was to name him Ishmael, which means "God hears." The reason is that God had heard her affliction. "Shalt bear" means "will give birth to," and "affliction" means suffering or anguish.

The speaker is the angel of the Lord, who in this passage is presented as one who represents God himself. Hagar was the servant of Sarai, and she had fled into the desert because Sarai was mistreating her. There, alone and pregnant, she receives this word of comfort and also the command to return. Some scholars see the angel as an appearance of God; others see him as God's messenger.

For today: God hears the pain of those who suffer, even of those whom no one takes into account. You can tell him your anguish with confidence, and you can also be someone who listens to those who suffer around you.
exp.36:10:
The explanation says that Joseph's brothers felt envy toward him, meaning that it bothered them that he received attention and that his dreams suggested he would become more important than they were. His father, on the other hand, "kept the matter in mind," which means he stayed thinking about the matter, holding it in his heart and wondering what it might mean.

It is the narrator who tells us this. Joseph has just recounted his second dream, in which the sun, the moon, and eleven stars bowed down before him. Jacob (Israel) rebuked him in public, but inwardly he did not dismiss it. The brothers already resented him for being the favorite, and the dreams deepened their grudge. Scholars do not agree on how much Jacob understood of the dream; the text only says that he pondered it.

For today: envy hardens the heart and pulls us away from others. When something troubles us or we do not understand it, we can follow Jacob's example: pause, reflect, and ask God for wisdom before we react.
exp.4:31:
It says that when Noah was five hundred years old, he had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The word "begat" means "had as sons," and "Ham" and "Japheth" are the names as spelled in the verse above. Some think they were not all born in the same year, but that the text names Noah as their father from that age onward.

This verse closes chapter 5, which is a list of descendants from Adam. There is no speaker; it is the narrator's account, following the family line down to Noah. It prepares the story of the flood, where Noah and his three sons will play an important role. The Bible shows that God keeps his plan across the generations.

For today: God also works in everyday life, such as raising a family. Your faith and your example can influence your children and those around you. Live faithfully today, even when it seems like a small thing.
exp.10:23:
Nahor lived twenty-nine years and then had a son named Terah. "Begat" means that he became the father of Terah. Terah is the name that appears in your verse. It is part of a list of families that follows the line of Shem down to Abram.

Genesis does not say who is speaking here; it is a narrative, a genealogy that moves from generation to generation. Its purpose is to connect the history after the flood and after Babel with the calling of Abram, which comes right after. Terah will be Abram's father. Some scholars think the ages should be understood literally, while others see a more symbolic or literary use of them; the text does not make this clear.

For today: God works through generations, even through names that almost no one remembers. Your faithfulness each day, though it may seem small, can be part of something God is building beyond what you are able to see.
exp.24:15:
This verse closes the list of the twelve sons of Ishmael. It says that they gave names to their "towns" (settled villages) and their "castles" (fortified places). Each one was a "prince," that is, the head of his family or tribe.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. God had promised Abraham that Ishmael would become a great nation (Genesis 17:20). This list shows that the promise was fulfilled: twelve leaders, similar to the twelve sons of Jacob. After this, the text returns to the story of Isaac.

For today: God keeps what He promises, even when it takes time and comes in ways we do not expect. If you are waiting for something God has told you, trust that He is faithful, and remember that He also cares for those who seem to be outside the center of the story.
exp.35:5:
It says that Esau gathered together his whole family: his wives, his sons and daughters, and everyone who lived in his household. He also took his livestock, his animals, and all the property he had acquired in Canaan. Then he went off to another land, moving away from his brother Jacob. The word "went" here carries the sense of "departed" or "set out for," and "substance" refers to his goods and possessions.

Here it is not a character speaking, but the narrator of Genesis, who is recording the descendants of Esau, also called Edom. The text that follows gives the reason: both men had so many possessions that the land could not support them together. Esau settled in the mountain country of Seir. Genesis does not describe any quarrel here; it simply notes that there was not enough room.

For today: sometimes the best decision is to part ways in peace, without disputes, when there is no room to live together. It also reminds us that wealth can complicate life if we do not handle it with wisdom and humility.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came upon the earth. The phrase "the flood of waters" refers to the great flood that covered the known world.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, recounting what happened after God had given Noah a clear command: enter the ark, because the rain was coming. The text has just said that Noah did everything the LORD commanded him. So this verse marks the moment when what was announced comes to pass. Some scholars debate how widespread the flood was, but the account highlights God's faithfulness and Noah's obedience.

For today: Noah obeyed before he saw the results. We can trust God's word and obey him today in what he has already shown us, even when we do not yet understand everything that lies ahead.
exp.15:7:
Here the angel of the LORD finds Hagar in the wilderness and addresses her by name and by her condition: Sarai's maid. He asks her two questions: where has she come from, and where is she going? She answers honestly that she is fleeing from her mistress Sarai. "I flee from the face of" means "I am running away from the presence of."

Sarai, the wife of Abram, had mistreated Hagar, and Abram did not intervene. Hagar, alone and pregnant, escaped toward the wilderness. The angel does not scold her at the start; he seeks her out and asks her questions. Some think this angel is a special appearance of God himself, though the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: God sees the one who suffers and asks with tenderness. When you are fleeing from a problem, be honest with him, because his questions are not meant to accuse you, but to help you think and find a way forward.
exp.42:0:
This verse says that the shortage of food was still very severe throughout the region. The word "famine" here refers to a true food crisis: there was not enough to eat. "Sore" means that it was severe and was not getting any better.

No person is speaking here; the narrator is describing the situation. Jacob's family in Canaan had already used up the grain that his sons brought back from Egypt. That is why Jacob tells them to go and buy more. But Judah recalls that the Egyptian ruler, whom they did not yet recognize as their brother Joseph, insisted that Benjamin go with them. So the need forces the family to face a difficult decision.

For today: sometimes our needs push us to face what we have been avoiding. Instead of running away, we can ask God for wisdom and trust that he can guide us even in hard times.
exp.23:27:
The explanation says that Rebekah, the young woman, ran off and told her mother's family everything that had happened at the well. The word "damsel" means a young girl. "Told them" means she let them know, or related it. "Her mother's house" probably refers to the home where the women of the family lived.

Abraham's servant had been sent to find a wife for Isaac. After Rebekah gave water to him and his camels, he worshiped God, giving thanks for guiding him. Now Rebekah, filled with excitement, runs to share the news. The text does not say everything she told them, but what follows shows that she spoke of the encounter and of the gifts she had received.

For today: when God shows us his goodness, it is good to tell our family about it soon. Sharing what God is doing encourages the faith of others and opens doors for them to come to know him too.
exp.36:22:
This verse tells us that as soon as Joseph reached his brothers, they forcibly stripped him of his clothing. It was the coat of many colors, the special gift from his father. The phrase "stript Joseph out of his coat" means that they took his clothing from him. The archaic wording "came to pass" is the old way of saying "happened."

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joseph's brothers envied and hated him because Jacob favored him, and because of his dreams. Reuben had intervened so that they would not kill him, seeking to return him to his father. Taking away his coat was taking away the sign of his father's favor.

For today: envy, if we let it grow, hardens the heart and leads us to hurt others. Ask God to heal your jealousy before it turns into action, and learn to rejoice in what others receive.
exp.43:4:
The explanation says that Joseph's steward is to accuse the brothers of having taken his lord's cup. "Divineth" is an old word here, meaning to consult or try to learn hidden things. It is debated whether Joseph really used the cup this way or said it only as part of his plan. The text does not make this clear.

The steward speaks, following Joseph's orders. Joseph, already governor in Egypt, had had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack. He wanted to test whether his brothers had changed, and whether they would abandon another brother as they had done to him years earlier.

Today, this reminds us that God can use difficult trials to bring to light what is in the heart. Let us ask him to give us faithfulness and love for others, especially when it is costly.
exp.44:0:
Here, Joseph can no longer hold back his emotions. In front of the servants and officials who surrounded him, he cries out that everyone should leave the room. He is left alone with his brothers and reveals who he is. Old-fashioned wording: the King James phrase "could not refrain himself" means he could no longer control himself, and "made himself known" means he revealed who he really was.

Joseph was second only to Pharaoh in Egypt. Years earlier, his brothers had sold him as a slave. Now they have come for food during a famine, not knowing that he is the ruler. Joseph had tested them, and at this moment he decides to show his identity. He asked for privacy, probably to protect both their dignity and his own.

When there are wounds from the past, it is wise to handle what is painful in private and with care, without exposing anyone. Ask God for wisdom to seek reconciliation with humility and tenderness.
exp.48:5:
Jacob says he does not want to take part in the secret plans of Simeon and Levi, nor join their gatherings. When they grew angry, they killed men, and out of willfulness they "pulled down a wall." The word "secret" speaks of their hidden counsels, and "honour" refers to his soul or his person. About "pulled down a wall," other versions say they hamstrung or mutilated bulls or oxen, so its exact meaning is uncertain.

Jacob speaks in his final blessing to his sons. He remembers the violence of Simeon and Levi against the people of Shechem, after what happened to their sister Dinah (Genesis 34). Jacob rejects that cruelty and condemns it.

For today: stay away from groups, conversations, or plans that feed revenge and anger. Ask God for self-control, and seek to resolve offenses with justice and gentleness, not with violence.
exp.42:29:
Here the account tells us that Joseph had to leave quickly because he felt a very strong emotion on seeing his brother Benjamin. "His bowels did yearn" means that he felt deep affection and compassion. "He sought where to weep" means that he looked for a private place, and "chamber" is a room.

This is the account of Joseph, already ruler in Egypt, when his brothers come to buy food. They do not recognize him. It is the first time he sees Benjamin, his brother from the same father and mother, after many years. Joseph has not yet revealed who he is, so he withdraws to weep without being seen.

God made us with emotions, and weeping is not weakness. Joseph shows that true love is felt in the depths of the heart. Today we can seek a quiet moment to weep and pray, and also let love for our family move us to forgive and to be reconciled.
exp.41:13:
Here, Joseph repeats his accusation: "That is what I said to you: you are spies." The brothers had already explained that they were twelve brothers, honest men, sons of one father. But Joseph does not change his position. The phrase "to see the nakedness of the land" means the weak points of the land, where an enemy could get in.

Joseph speaks as a ruler of Egypt, and his brothers do not recognize him. He had seen them bow down before him, but he keeps his identity hidden. Many understand that he uses this accusation to test whether they had changed, especially when he asks them to bring their youngest brother, Benjamin. The Bible does not explain all his reasons, so we do not know for certain what he felt.

For today: when God allows trials or uncomfortable situations, they sometimes bring to light what is in the heart. Let us ask for sincerity to recognize our faults, and for the humility to change.
exp.4:20:
This verse says that Enoch lived sixty-five years and then had a son named Methuselah. The King James Version uses older wording: "begat" means that he became a father, and the names appear here in their traditional English forms.

No character speaks here; the narrator of Genesis repeats the list of generations from Adam onward. It is a family record that shows how the line of descent continued. What stands out comes next: the text says that Enoch "walked with God" after Methuselah was born. Some believe his life of faith deepened when he became a father, though the text does not explain this.

For today: the major changes in life, such as having a child or taking on a new responsibility, can be a good time to draw closer to God. Today you might set aside a few minutes to pray sincerely for your family.
exp.9:14:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Ham. It says that Canaan had as his children Sidon, his firstborn, and Heth. The word "begat" means that he was their father, and "firstborn" is the eldest son. The names Sidon and Heth also appear later as peoples and places: Sidon was an important city on the coast, and the Hittites are connected with Heth, although scholars debate how much connection there is.

The narrator of Genesis, traditionally identified with Moses, presents what is called the "table of nations." He wants to show how, after the flood, humanity spread out from the sons of Noah. The Canaanites matter because their land will later be the setting for the promise to Abraham.

For today: God knows the names and families of all peoples, even those that seem to be just a list. Remember that each person has value before Him, so treat with respect those who are different from you.
exp.6:12:
This verse says that on the very day the flood began, Noah entered the ark together with his wife, his three sons (Shem, Ham and Japheth) and their wives. In all there were eight people. Ham is the name given in the King James Version, and Japheth is spelled that way too; in this older translation the names appear as they are written there.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks, recounting events. God had already warned Noah about the flood and had asked him to build the ark. This verse shows that Noah obeyed, and that his whole family went in with him. The text stresses that everything happened "in the selfsame day," just as the fountains of the great deep were broken open.

For today: obedience to God is not put off until later. Noah trusted God's word and acted on it. We can ask ourselves what God has asked of us that we are still postponing, and take one concrete step of faith today.
exp.23:2:
Abraham asks his oldest servant to make a solemn oath in the name of the Lord, the God who rules heaven and earth. He must promise that he will not seek a wife for Isaac among the Canaanite women, the people among whom Abraham was living. "Make swear" means to cause someone to take an oath. "Take a wife" means to get a wife for someone.

Abraham is already old, and God has blessed him in everything. He speaks with the servant who manages all his possessions. He wants Isaac to marry someone from his own family, who worshipped God, and not from those who followed other beliefs. Scholars agree that his concern was above all spiritual, although the text gives no further detail.

For today: important decisions, such as marriage, deserve prayer and good counsel. Think about faith and not only about feelings or convenience.
exp.23:48:
Here the servant of Abraham asks for a clear answer from Rebekah's family. He says to them: "If you will deal kindly and truly with my master, tell me; and if not, tell me also." The phrase "kindness and truth" means goodness and faithfulness. "I will turn to the right hand or to the left" means he will go to the right or to the left, that is, he will look for another way.

The servant of Abraham speaks after telling how God guided him to Rebekah. Abraham sent him to find a wife for Isaac among his relatives. Now the servant needs a decision from Laban and Bethuel, and he does not want to go around in circles or leave the matter hanging.

For today: when we believe God has guided us, it is good to act with honesty and to ask for clear answers, without pressuring others. A sincere and respectful conversation helps us make decisions with peace and trust in God.
exp.27:11:
Jacob has a dream. He sees a "ladder," which was like a large staircase or ramp, set on the earth with its top reaching up to heaven. Angels of God were going up and down on it. The King James wording "behold" is an old way of saying "look" or "see."

This is Moses' account of Jacob, who flees from his home toward Haran, alone and with a stone for a pillow. Then, in the dream, God himself speaks to him and repeats the promise made to Abraham: land, descendants, and blessing for all the families of the earth. Some scholars see in the ladder a bridge between God and people; the text does not explain it further.

For today: even if you feel alone or far from home, God is near and cares for you. You can speak to him with confidence anywhere, because he is already present.
exp.25:16:
Isaac left that place and went to live in the valley of Gerar. "Pitched his tent" means he set up his camp, since he lived as a nomad, in tents. "Dwelt there" means he settled in that place to live for a time.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Abimelech, king of the Philistines, had asked Isaac to leave, because Isaac had become very powerful and they felt fear or envy. Moreover, the Philistines had filled with earth the wells that Abraham, Isaac's father, had dug. Isaac does not fight; he simply withdraws.

For today: when someone rejects you or closes doors on you, you do not have to answer with a quarrel. You can step away calmly, trust that God takes care of you, and continue on, seeking the good that He has prepared.
exp.29:27:
Laban tells Jacob to set his own price for his work. "Appoint me thy wages" means "tell me what you want" or "name your pay," and "wages" is the payment for his services. Laban promises: "I will give it."

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, is speaking. Jacob had just asked permission to return to his own land with his family after years of service. Laban realized that God had blessed him because of Jacob, and he did not want to lose him. That is why he offers to pay whatever Jacob asks. Some readers see more self-interest than generosity here, since Laban was looking to keep his gain, though the text says nothing more about his intentions.

For today: value and pay fairly the work of others, without taking advantage of them. And if you work, do it with integrity, trusting that God sees your effort.
exp.27:14:
God tells Jacob that he is with him, that he will watch over him wherever he goes, and that he will bring him back to this land. He promises not to leave him until he has done everything he has spoken to him about. "Keep" means to protect and watch over. "In all places whither thou goest" means "wherever you go."

The LORD speaks to Jacob in a dream. Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau and leaving his home alone, heading toward Haran. God renews to him the promises made to Abraham and Isaac. Jacob had done nothing to deserve this; God took the initiative. On waking, Jacob recognizes that God was there, although he did not know it.

Today we can remember that God is not limited to one place. If you are going through a time of change, fear, or loneliness, you can trust that his presence accompanies you. Take a moment today to say to him: "Lord, help me to realize that you are with me."
exp.28:8:
