While Jacob was still speaking with the shepherds, Rachel arrived with her father's sheep, because she was a shepherd. The word "sheep" here refers to the flock. "Water" means giving the animals something to drink.

Jacob was fleeing from his home and was looking for his mother's family. He had asked some shepherds by the well whether they knew Laban, and they told him yes. While Jacob kept insisting that they water the sheep, they explained that they had to wait until all the flocks were gathered together. Just then Rachel appeared. The text does not explicitly say that God planned it, but her arrival is very timely.

For today: God often works in the middle of everyday life. As you faithfully carry on your way, you may find answers or important people when you least expect them.
exp.30:37:
Jacob tells Laban that for twenty years he served him and took good care of the flocks. The ewes and she goats did not lose their young before birth; in other words, they reproduced in good health. The King James wording "cast their young" is the phrase that matches this idea here. Jacob also states that he never ate a ram, that is, a male from the sheep of Laban's flock.

Jacob is speaking after fleeing with his family. Laban caught up with him and accused him of stealing his household gods. Jacob, unaware that Rachel had taken them, defends himself with anger. He asks that his relatives judge whether there was any fault in his work.

For today: working with honesty and diligence, even when no one is watching us, gives peace of heart and steadiness when someone accuses us. Let our conduct speak for us.
exp.27:21:
Jacob says that the stone he set up as a sign or pillar will be a place dedicated to God, "the house of God." He also promises that from all that God gives him, he will set apart a tenth for Him. "Pillar" here means a sign or monument, and "tithe" means the tenth part.

Jacob speaks after his dream at Bethel, where he saw a ladder between heaven and earth and God promised to be with him. He was fleeing from his brother Esau and leaving home with very little. His vow sounds like a thankful response, though some readers see in the "if" of his earlier words a faith still growing. The Bible does not explain this in detail.

Today we can imitate that attitude of recognizing that everything we have comes from God. One practical way is to decide ahead of time, in prayer, how much you will give to the church or to help those in need, and to do it with gratitude, not out of obligation.
exp.0:4:
God gives a name to the light: he calls it "Day." The darkness he calls "Night." Then the text says "the evening and the morning were the first day," and this is how the first day of creation ends.

Here the narrator of Genesis describes how God orders everything by his word. After creating and separating the light, God names what he has made, showing that he rules over time. Christians understand the length of these "days" in different ways, and the Bible does not require one single reading.

For today: God orders time in cycles of work and rest. You can begin and end your day by giving God your morning and your evening, trusting that he sustains your life.
exp.33:15:
Here the sons of Jacob propose a deal to Hamor and Shechem: if all the males of the city are circumcised, they may intermarry, live together, and become one people.

The brothers of Dinah, the sons of Jacob, are speaking. Shechem had dishonored their sister, and now he asked to marry her. The brothers answer with deceit: they use circumcision, the sign of the covenant with God, as a pretext. The text shows that they did not speak sincerely. Later their true intention becomes clear, which was revenge.

For today: let us take care that our words are sincere. Using sacred things to cover an evil purpose harms others and dishonors God. Let us seek justice without deceit or violence.
exp.43:28:
Judah repeats to Joseph, without knowing he is his brother, what Jacob said. If they also take Benjamin and some "disaster" (a misfortune or harm) befalls him, Jacob, already elderly, would die of sorrow. The "gray hairs" are his old age, and "the grave" is the tomb.

Judah speaks before Joseph, whom he believes to be an Egyptian ruler. He is defending Benjamin, the youngest son, so that he will not be kept as a prisoner. Jacob had already lost Joseph, whom he believed dead, and would not be able to bear losing Benjamin as well. Judah offers to stay as a slave in his place.

For today: when a decision affects others, let us consider the pain it may cause. Judah set aside his pride and took on the suffering of his family. Today we too can love this way, protecting the most vulnerable and accepting the responsibility that falls to us.
exp.43:1:
Here Joseph gives his steward one more order: besides the grain money of each brother, he must put his silver cup in the sack of the youngest, who is Benjamin. A "sack" is a bag, and "the mouth of the sack" is its opening. The steward did exactly what Joseph commanded.

Joseph is the one speaking, and he is governor of Egypt. His brothers do not know it is him. Later he will accuse the group of theft. The Bible does not explain his full purpose here, but many understand that he wants to test whether the brothers have changed and how they will treat Benjamin, whom they might abandon as they once did with him.

For today: difficult trials can reveal the heart. Let us ask God to change us within, so that when pressure comes, we choose to protect and not abandon others.
exp.24:1:
This verse says that Keturah, the other woman Abraham took, had six sons with him: Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah. The word "bare" means "gave birth to." The word "unto" at the start of the names is simply the old way of saying "to" and is not part of the names themselves.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of the book of Genesis, giving a family list. It is written after the story of Sarah and before the account of Abraham's death. Scholars debate whether Keturah came after Sarah's death or before it; the text does not make this clear. These sons gave rise to several desert peoples, among them Midian, who appears later in the Bible.

For today: God keeps his promises, even in the details. He had promised Abraham many descendants, and this list reminds us that God is faithful even in what seems small or little noticed.
exp.26:29:
This verse tells us that Isaac had only just finished blessing Jacob, and Jacob had barely left his father's presence, when Esau arrived back from hunting. The phrase "it came to pass" means "it happened," and "scarce gone out from the presence of" means "had hardly left the presence of." Everything took place within a matter of minutes.

Here the narrator is speaking. Jacob, on the advice of his mother Rebekah, had pretended to be Esau in order to receive the blessing of the firstborn. Isaac, now old and nearly blind, did not realize it. Esau arrives right afterward, unaware of what had happened. The scene sets up a very painful moment for the family.

For today: deceptions may seem to work out for a while, but sooner or later their consequences arrive. It is wise to trust God's promises without resorting to dishonest shortcuts, and to always seek to act with truthfulness.
exp.48:14:
He says that Issachar saw that rest was good and that the land was pleasant. For that reason he bent his shoulder, like someone carrying a load, and accepted working under forced labor. "Tribute" was a payment or forced labor given to a ruler. "Pleasant" means agreeable, lovely.

Jacob, now old, blesses his sons and speaks of what each tribe will become. Here he describes Issachar as a strong donkey that lies down to rest. Many understand that he preferred comfort and fertile land, though in exchange he was placed under others. Others see it in a more positive light, as diligent work. The text allows both readings.

For today: comfort is good, but it is wise to ask what price we pay for it. Let us ask God for wisdom so that we do not trade our freedom or our calling for ease, and so that we work faithfully wherever we are.
exp.15:8:
Here the angel of the Lord tells Hagar to return to Sarai, her mistress, and to submit to her authority. "Submit thyself under her hands" means accepting her authority. The comment about the old verb forms does not apply to this verse, so it is omitted.

Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarai, had fled into the wilderness because Sarai was treating her harshly. The angel finds her beside a spring and speaks to her with care. Some understand this "angel of the Lord" as speaking on God's behalf, and others see in him a divine presence. His command comes with promises: God will see her affliction and will bless her son.

For today: this text does not justify mistreatment or call us to endure abuse. It shows us that God sees the one who suffers and gives direction and hope. When running away does not solve anything, we can trust that God is with us as we face the situation with help and wisdom.
exp.31:30:
Genesis 32:31 says that as Jacob crossed over Penuel, the sun rose on him. It was a new day after the night of struggle. Jacob was limping from his hip. The explanation notes that the word for "hip" or "thigh" here refers to the upper leg, and that the phrase about the sun means it dawned or shone upon him.

The writer recounts what happened after Jacob wrestled all night with a mysterious man, whom Jacob recognized as God himself. Jacob was about to meet his brother Esau, whom he feared. He was blessed, but he was left with a wound. Some understand it as an appearance of God; others, as an angel. The text does not fully clarify this.

God sometimes blesses us and at the same time humbles our pride. A weakness or wound can teach us to depend on God, and not on our own strength.
exp.22:18:
This verse tells us that Abraham buried Sarah, his wife, in the cave of the field of Machpelah. That place was before Mamre, which is Hebron, in the land of Canaan. The word "field" in the King James wording refers to the piece of ground, or property, where the cave was located. "Buried" means that he laid her to rest there.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator who tells what happened. Sarah had died, and Abraham, who lived as a foreigner in Canaan, had no land of his own. For that reason he negotiated with the sons of Heth and bought the field and the cave. In this way he had a legitimate place to bid her farewell. Many see here a first piece of the promised land in Abraham's hands, although the text does not explain this directly.

For today: saying farewell with dignity to those we love is an act of love and faith. Abraham did not act in haste or carelessly. We can honor our loved ones with respect, and even in grief continue to trust in God's promises.
exp.2:10:
God asks Adam two things: who told him that he was naked, and whether he ate from the tree that he had forbidden him. The questions are not asked because God does not know anything, but to lead Adam to acknowledge what he did.

The LORD God speaks after Adam and Eve ate of the fruit and hid themselves. Adam had said that he was afraid because he was naked. God, like a father seeking the truth, moves from "Where are you?" to asking the cause. Right away Adam blames the woman, and she blames the serpent.

For today: when we fail, God does not ask us for excuses, but for honesty. We can stop hiding, tell the truth about what we did, and draw near to Him to ask for forgiveness and help.
exp.49:0:
Here Joseph is told that, when his father Jacob died, he fell upon his face, wept over him, and kissed him. The word "kissed" in that line is the one that matters here, and it is a simple, everyday word for a gesture of affection and farewell, very human in its warmth.

The narrator describes the scene right after Jacob's death. Jacob was also called Israel. Joseph had been separated from him for many years, and then they were reunited in Egypt. That is why his grief runs so deep. Afterward, Joseph orders the body embalmed, an Egyptian custom, and the Egyptians also mourn for seventy days.

For today: do not hide your sadness when you lose someone you love. Weeping, embracing, and saying goodbye with love is healthy and natural. God does not despise mourning; you can bring your pain to him with confidence and seek comfort from those around you.
exp.28:12:
When Laban heard the news about Jacob, his sister's son, he ran out to meet him. He embraced him, kissed him, and brought him into his house. Then Jacob told Laban everything that had happened to him.

The narrator tells this meeting after Rachel ran to tell her father. Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau and was seeking his mother's family. Laban welcomes him warmly, although later we will see that he also had interests of his own. The Bible here shows only the welcome, without explaining his motives.

A sincere welcome can bring great relief to someone who arrives tired or afraid. Today we can open the door, listen with patience, and give a place to someone who needs it. And if someone receives us this way, we can thank them with humility.
exp.47:4:
Jacob tells Joseph that his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, born in Egypt before Jacob came there, will now be considered his own sons. They will have the same place as Reuben and Simeon, his firstborn sons.

Jacob, old and ill, speaks with Joseph in Egypt. He remembers the promise God made to him in Canaan: a land and a numerous descendance. By adopting Joseph's sons, he gives them a place of their own among the tribes of Israel. Many understand that in this way Joseph receives a double portion, although the text does not say it in those words.

For today: God makes us partakers of his family and his promises by grace, not by merit. We can imitate that gesture by welcoming with love those who were not born in our home, so that they feel they are part of it.
exp.44:23:
He sent his brothers back to Canaan. Before they set out, he gave them a brief warning: "See that ye fall not out by the way," that is, "do not quarrel or argue on the journey." The words "sent away" and "departed" mean that he sent them off and they left.

Joseph is speaking to the eleven brothers who had earlier sold him. He has just revealed who he is and forgiven them, and he sends them with gifts to bring back their father Jacob. Some think he feared they would blame one another for what they had done years before, but the text does not state this clearly.

For today: when God has given us forgiveness and blessing, we should not waste it on mutual reproach. In the family or in the church, let us seek to walk in peace, remembering the grace we have received, and let the past that has been healed not divide us again.
exp.37:11:
It says that a good amount of time passed and the wife of Judah, the daughter of Shuah, died. When his mourning was over, Judah was comforted and went up to Timnath for the sheepshearing, that is, the cutting of the wool from his sheep, accompanied by his friend Hirah, from the town of Adullam. "Was comforted" means that the pain of mourning gradually passed.

Here the narrator is speaking, not a character. Earlier, Judah had promised his daughter-in-law Tamar that she could marry his son Shelah, but he did not keep his word, out of fear that Shelah would also die. This verse shows that Judah has already returned to his life and his work, while Tamar keeps waiting, forgotten. That prepares what she will do afterward.

For today: comfort after grief is healthy, but it does not free us from keeping what we have promised. Let us check whether there is someone waiting for something we owe them, and keep our word.
exp.3:19:
This verse tells that Adah, one of Lamech's wives, had a son named Jabal. He is called the "father" of those who dwell in tents and keep livestock, that is, he was the originator of a way of life: families who moved from place to place with their animals. The word "bare" means "gave birth to," and "cattle" refers to herds and flocks.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of Genesis, who lists the family of Lamech, a descendant of Cain. The text shows how humanity developed trades: herding, music, and metalwork. Some see in this human ingenuity; others also note the course away from God that continues in the story of Lamech. The text does not say this clearly.

For today: occupations and talents are capacities that God allows us to develop. We can use our work with gratitude and honesty, to serve others and honor God.
exp.11:19:
This verse says that Pharaoh ordered his men to send Abram out of Egypt. They escorted him as far as the border, together with his wife Sarai and all his possessions. The phrase "gave orders concerning him" means that he gave an instruction to his servants or soldiers.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Abram had said that Sarai was his sister out of fear that he would be killed. God sent plagues on Pharaoh's house (v. 17), and so Pharaoh discovered the truth. Although Abram failed, God took care of him and kept his promise to protect him (12:2-3). Pharaoh sent him away without taking anything from him.

For today: God remains faithful even when we fail because of fear or lack of trust. We can acknowledge our mistakes, trust in his care, and learn to act with honesty, knowing that his grace does not depend on our perfection.
exp.18:19:
Lot asks the angel to let him flee to a nearby city instead of going to the mountain. He says the city is small, almost as if offering a reason for his request, and that his life will be safe there. "Flee" means to escape, and "soul" here means his life or his very self.

Lot speaks with God's messengers while Sodom is about to be destroyed. They had already told him to escape to the mountain, but he is afraid and does not trust that he can get there. God accepts his request and spares that small city, which is later called Zoar, a name related to "little." Some see here God's patience; others see Lot's weakness.

We can bring our fears to God honestly, without pretending to strength. He is patient with our limitations. Even so, it is worth asking ourselves whether we are obeying fully or bargaining out of fear, and asking him for the courage to trust.
exp.11:14:
It says that Pharaoh's princes, that is, the officials and chiefs of his court, saw Sarai and spoke very highly of her before the king. "Commended her" means that they praised her beauty. Then the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house, that is, into his palace.

Abram had come to Egypt because of a famine. He was afraid that he would be killed on account of his wife, so he asked Sarai to say that she was his sister. It was a half-truth, and interpreters see it as an error of lack of trust. Here the narrator speaks, and shows the consequences of that plan.

When fear leads us to look for shortcuts or to tell half-truths, we can put those we love at risk. God took care of Sarai despite Abram's error. We can trust that God protects, and it is better to act with honesty than with fear.
exp.24:14:
This verse completes the list of the twelve sons of Ishmael: Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Nafis and Cedema. These are only names, but they are part of a list arranged "by their generations," that is, according to their families. The KJV form "Hadar" and "Kedemah" differs slightly from the names in the list above, and "Naphish" is the form used in the King James Version.

The narrator here is the narrator of the book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses. His purpose is to show that God kept his promise to Abraham to make Ishmael a great nation (Genesis 17:20). The following verses call these sons "twelve princes," as heads of tribes. Some of these names later appear as places or peoples, although it is not always known with certainty where they lived.

For today: God remembers people, even those whom history has nearly forgotten. If you sometimes feel small or overlooked, remember that God keeps his promises and knows your name.
exp.12:0:
The explanation says that Abram left Egypt and went toward the Negev, that is, toward the south of Canaan. He was going with his wife Sarai, with all his possessions, and with his nephew Lot. "Went up" does not only speak of height: it was the common way of saying that someone was leaving Egypt for Canaan.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Shortly before, Abram had gone down to Egypt because of a famine, and there he made mistakes out of fear (Genesis 12). Now he returns, and the text marks a new beginning. Lot still goes with him, which prepares the separation that comes later, when their riches grow and conflicts arise.

For today: after we make mistakes, God allows us to return and start again. What matters is coming back to the place where we were close to Him, and also taking care of the relationships and decisions we carry with us.
exp.45:2:
God presents himself to Jacob as "the God of your father," that is, the same God of Isaac and Abraham. He tells him not to be afraid to go down into Egypt, because there he will make him into a great nation.

Jacob, also called Israel, is already an old man. He is on his way to Egypt to be reunited with his son Joseph. He stops at Beersheba, where he offers sacrifices, and God speaks to him at night in a vision. Leaving the promised land could have frightened him, since there God had promised his family an inheritance. God reassures him and confirms that he will remain with him.

For today: when an important decision frightens you, do as Jacob did. Stop to pray, seek God before moving forward, and remember that his presence and his promises go with you, even in unfamiliar places.
exp.7:10:
This verse tells that the dove returned to Noah in the evening, carrying a fresh olive leaf in its beak. With that, Noah understood that the water had already gone down from the earth. The word "pluckt" is an old form of "plucked," meaning torn off or picked, and "abated" means lowered or subsided.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Noah had been in the ark for many months and was waiting for a sign. He had already sent the dove out once, but it came back without finding a place to land. Now it brings a small but clear sign: life was growing again. Many see here a symbol of hope, although the text does not explain it that way.

God sometimes gives us small signs, not complete answers. If you are waiting in a difficult situation, be thankful for every small step forward and keep trusting with patience.
exp.47:12:
This verse tells how Joseph took his two sons and brought them near to his father Jacob, who is here called Israel. He placed Ephraim at his right hand, which faced Israel's left hand, and Manasseh at his left hand, facing Israel's right hand. The King James wording "Ephraim in his right hand toward Israel's left hand" shows this arrangement, and "brought them near unto him" means Joseph presented them to his father to receive the blessing.

Israel, already old and nearly blind, is about to bless his grandsons. Joseph wants the elder, Manasseh, to receive the main blessing, so he positions him toward his grandfather's right hand. But Israel will cross his hands, and the text does not hide it: he did so on purpose.

We can make plans with good intentions, as Joseph did, but God sometimes works in a different way. Today we can present our family before God in prayer and trust that his ways are better than ours.
exp.24:12:
This verse begins the list of the sons of Ishmael, the son Abraham had with Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarah. The first four are named: Nebajoth, the firstborn, and then Kedar, Adbeel, and Mibsam. "Generations" means the families that descended from each one, and "firstborn" is the eldest son.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses. After recounting the death of Abraham, he records the story of Ishmael before continuing with Isaac. This shows that God kept his promise to make Ishmael into a great nation (Genesis 17:20). Kedar appears later in other passages of the Bible as a people of the desert.

For today: God remembers names and keeps his promises, even with those who seem to stand at the edge of the story. You can trust that he sees you and cares for your life and your family.
exp.27:13:
God promises Jacob a descendance too numerous to count, as the dust of the earth. He tells him that he will spread out in every direction: west, east, north and south. He adds that through Jacob and his seed, that is, his descendants, all the families of the earth would be blessed.

Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau and was sleeping on the road, alone and afraid. In a dream, the LORD himself speaks to him and renews the promise he had earlier given to Abraham and Isaac. God does not wait for Jacob to earn it; he gives it out of pure grace. Many Christians see in the blessing for "all the families" a foreshadowing of Christ, a descendant of Jacob.

God can work in your moments of loneliness and uncertainty. Your plans may be broken, but his promises still stand. Trust that he is present, even if you do not yet notice it.
exp.26:22:
This verse says that Isaac did not realize it was Jacob, because his hands were hairy, like those of his son Esau. That is why he blessed him. The words "he discerned him not" mean that he did not recognize him, and "hairy" means covered with hair.

Isaac, already old and nearly blind, wanted to bless Esau, his firstborn son. Rebekah and Jacob prepared a deception: Jacob covered his hands with goatskins to look like his brother. Isaac hesitated, because the voice was Jacob's, but he let the sense of touch guide him and blessed him.

For today: the Bible recounts this deception without approving of it, and its consequences came later within the family. It reminds us that we should not reach for what is good through lies, but trust God and act with honesty.
exp.8:8:
God tells Noah and his sons that He Himself establishes a covenant, that is, a solemn promise, with them and with their descendants. The word "seed" means offspring, the children and generations who would come after. The KJV's "I, behold, I establish" carries an old-fashioned emphasis that is roughly equivalent to saying "look, I am establishing."

God speaks after the flood, when Noah and his family come out of the ark. They have just lived through a terrible judgment and need security. God takes the initiative: He asks nothing in return, but commits Himself never again to destroy the earth with water. The promise also includes the animals.

For today: when you feel fear about the future, remember that God is faithful to what He promises. You can rest in His word, and also trust that His promises reach your family and the generations that come after you.
exp.49:1:
This verse tells us that Joseph ordered the physicians who served in his household to embalm the body of his father Jacob, who is here called Israel. Embalming was the preparation of a body with special substances to preserve it.

The one who tells the story is the narrator of Genesis. Jacob has just died in Egypt, and Joseph, who was a high ruler, takes leave of him with deep sorrow, as we saw in the weeping and the kiss. He used the Egyptian custom, and the text says nothing more about his reasons. Afterward Jacob would be buried in Canaan, the land of the promise.

For today: bidding farewell to a loved one with affection and respect is a good thing. When someone dies, we can honor them with tenderness, accompany the family, and entrust our grief to God, who comforts those who mourn.
exp.47:19:
Jacob blesses his two grandsons, the sons of Joseph, on that same day. He says that when the people of Israel want to bless someone, they will say: "God make thee as Ephraim and as Manasseh." The words "blessed them" and "set" are the English of the King James Version, where the verse reads "he blessed them that day" and "he set Ephraim before Manasseh." The verse says that Jacob places Ephraim, the younger, before Manasseh, the elder.

Jacob speaks as an old man, near death, in Egypt. Joseph had asked him to place his right hand on Manasseh, the firstborn, but Jacob refused. He understood that God would make both of them grow, though Ephraim would become greater. In the Bible, God often acts outside the expected order.

For today: do not measure your worth by your place or by your turn. God does not depend on human positions. You can bless your children or other people by asking that they grow in the grace of God, and trust that He knows what He is doing.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that God sent the man out of the garden of Eden. He could no longer live there, and now he had to work the ground, that is, cultivate it. "Till the ground" means to work the soil, and "taken" means that he was taken out of it. This recalls that the man was formed from the dust of the earth.

The one acting is the Lord God, and the account is told by Moses, according to tradition. Adam and Eva had disobeyed by eating the forbidden fruit. God covered them with garments of skins and then sent them away, so that they would not eat from the tree of life in that state. Many see here both judgment and care.

For today: our decisions have consequences, but God does not abandon us in them. Even as he sent them out, he clothed them. If you have failed, you can return to him with humility, and your daily work, though it is hard, can be done with confidence in his care.
exp.39:5:
Joseph came to them in the morning, and when he looked at them he saw that they were sad. The explanation says that Joseph arrived where the king's cupbearer and baker were, looked at them, and noticed they were sad. The King James wording "looked upon them" means he gazed at them, that is, he looked closely at them. "Came in unto them" means he arrived where they were. Joseph was not distracted; he paid attention to their faces.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Joseph was unjustly imprisoned, but he had been put in charge of attending to these two officers of Pharaoh. Both had strange dreams that night and did not know what they meant. That is why they woke up worried. Their sadness opens the way for Joseph to ask them about it and to speak to them about God.

For today: even if you have your own problems, really look at the people around you. Ask with kindness how they are doing. Sometimes a simple, sincere question opens the way to comfort and to serving someone.
exp.0:28:
God speaks to the human being and tells them that he has given them as food every plant that bears seed and every tree that bears fruit with seed.

God, the Creator, speaks on the sixth day, just after creating man and woman in his image and blessing them. Before asking them to care for and rule over creation, he assures them that they will have enough food. Afterward he also provides food for the animals. Some understand this passage to describe a world without violence; others interpret it in other ways, and the text does not explain it further.

For today: we can receive our daily food as a gift from God. Before eating, we can give thanks from the heart, and not waste what he provides for us.
exp.25:23:
He says that God appeared to Isaac that same night, in Beersheba. He presents himself as "the God of Abraham thy father" and gives him three promises: "fear not," "I am with thee," and "I will bless thee." He also promises that his offspring will be numerous. "Seed" here means descendants, and "for my servant Abraham's sake" means on account of the promise made to Abraham.

God himself speaks. Isaac came after years of tension with the Philistines: he had argued over wells and had had to move several times. After arriving in Beersheba, God reassures him and confirms the promise he had already given to his father. Afterward Isaac responds with worship, and builds an altar.

For today: when you feel fear or weariness because of conflicts, remember that God does not leave you alone. Before looking for solutions, spend time with him in prayer and thanksgiving.
exp.32:2:
The explanation says that Jacob placed himself at the front of his whole family and, as he drew near to his brother Esau, bowed himself to the ground seven times. The phrase "bowed himself to the ground" in the King James Version means that he lowered himself until he touched the ground. He did this again and again, until he came close to Esau.

The one who tells the story is Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, and he recounts what Jacob did. Years earlier, Jacob had deceived Esau and fled out of fear of his anger. Now he returns and sees Esau coming with four hundred men. Jacob does not know what intentions Esau has, so he approaches with humility, protecting his family. Bowing in this way was a sign of respect before someone in authority.

When we have hurt someone, taking the first step with humility can open the door to reconciliation. We will not always know how the other person will respond, but we can do our part with sincerity.
exp.45:33:
Here Joseph teaches his brothers what to answer if Pharaoh asks what they do for a living. They are to say that they, and their forefathers before them, have always been herdsmen, "from our youth even until now." That way they will be able to live in the land of Goshen, because the Egyptians detested every shepherd.

Joseph speaks to his father Jacob and to his brothers, who would come to Egypt because of the famine. He wants them to settle apart, in Goshen, and not mixed in with the Egyptians. The Bible says the Egyptians detested shepherds, but it does not fully explain the reason; scholars understand it in several ways.

For today: Joseph does not ask them to lie, but to speak the truth with wisdom. We can be honest about who we are and, at the same time, prudently seek what helps us care for our family and our faith.
exp.26:21:
Here Jacob draws near to his father Isaac, who is already old and blind. Isaac touches him and notices something strange: the voice is Jacob's, but the hands seem to be Esau's. "Drew near" means "came close," and "felt" means "touched with the hands."

Isaac wants to give the family blessing to Esau, his firstborn son. Rebekah and Jacob deceive Isaac: Jacob covers himself with goatskins and pretends to be Esau. Isaac hesitates, and that is why he examines him. Even so, the deception continues, and Jacob even uses the name of God to support his lie.

For today: a lie may seem like a shortcut, but it leaves wounds and consequences. The Bible does not hide the failures of its characters. Trust that God carries out his plans without needing us to help him with deceptions. Let us seek to be honest, even when it costs us.
exp.35:29:
This verse ends a list of chieftains of the Horites, a people who lived in the region of Seir. Three appear here: Dishon, Ezer, and Dishan. The word "duke" does not refer to European nobility; the King James Version uses it to translate a Hebrew term meaning clan chief or tribal leader. The "dukes" are the heads of their clans or tribes, and the phrase "in the land of Seir" places them in that region.

The narrator, traditionally Moses, records the history of Esau (Edom), who settled in Seir. The Horites lived there before, and Edom eventually mingled with them or took their place. Scholars debate the details of that relationship. The list shows that God fulfilled his promise to make Esau a nation, although the line of the covenant would continue through Jacob.

For today: God notices people whom we see only as names in a list. No life goes unnoticed by Him. Today we can value those who seem unimportant and remember that our name also matters to God.
exp.24:28:
This verse tells us that Jacob was cooking a thick stew, a "pottage," probably of lentils, as the text mentions later. At that moment Esau came back from the field, worn out after hunting or working outdoors.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He introduces two very different twin brothers: Esau, a man of the field, and Jacob, quiet and a man of the tents. Their parents had different favorites between them. This scene sets up the exchange that follows: Esau, hungry, will end up giving little value to his birthright, the special right of the firstborn son. The Bible does not justify all of Jacob's actions, but it shows how Esau acted without thinking.

For today: when we are tired or strongly longing for something, let us not make important decisions right away. Let us ask God for wisdom and value what is eternal above what is immediate.
exp.37:22:
Judah tells his friend to let the woman keep the items he gave her as a pledge. He says this way they will avoid being put to shame. He recalls that he did his part by sending the young goat, but the friend did not find her.

Judah speaks after his friend searched, without success, for the woman he believed to be a prostitute. In reality she was Tamar, his daughter-in-law, in disguise. She had in her possession Judah's seal, cord, and staff. He wants to close the matter quietly, worried about his reputation more than about the truth. Soon those items will expose him.

Today we can notice that we sometimes care more about our image than about our integrity. What is hidden sooner or later comes to light. God invites us to live with honesty and to acknowledge our mistakes in time.
exp.24:21:
It says that Rebekah, already pregnant, felt the two babies pushing or colliding inside her. It was so strong that she cried out: "If it be so, why am I thus?" Then she went to inquire of the Lord, that is, to ask God what was happening. "She went to enquire" is an older spelling of "she went to inquire."

The one speaking is Rebekah. She had waited a long time for a child, because she was barren, and God answered Isaac's prayer. Now the pregnancy brings her pain and distress. The text does not say exactly how she inquired of God; some think she prayed, others that she went to a place of worship or to a prophet. The text does not make this clear.

When something hurts us or confuses us, even after a blessing, we can bring our questions to God honestly. Rebekah did not stay in her distress; she sought an answer from God.
exp.23:8:
The explanation says that Abraham's servant made a solemn oath to his master. To do so, he placed his hand under Abraham's thigh, an ancient gesture of commitment. "Servant" is the word the King James Version uses for the servant who made the oath, and "matter" refers to the charge Abraham had given him.

Abraham, already old, asked his trusted servant to find a wife for Isaac from among his own kinsfolk, and not among the Canaanites. He reminded him that God had promised that land to his descendants. About the exact meaning of the thigh gesture there are several interpretations; many connect it with family descent, but this is not certain.

Today we can learn from this servant: he kept his word with seriousness and faithfulness. Work to make your promises, great or small, firm, and entrust your important tasks to God, as Abraham did.
exp.29:39:
The explanation says that Jacob separated the striped lambs and the dark-colored animals of Laban's flock, and placed them with his own flock. In this way he formed a separate herd and did not mix it with Laban's sheep. "Herd" means a flock of animals, and "striped" means marked with stripes, which is the sense of "ringstraked" in the King James wording you are reading.

It is part of the account in Genesis that tells how Jacob worked for his father-in-law Laban. The two had agreed that the spotted and speckled animals would be Jacob's wages. Jacob used peeled rods, but the text does not say that this had any power in itself. Later, Jacob recounts that God saw Laban's unfair dealing and took care of him (Genesis 31:9-12).

For today: when you find yourself working in an unjust environment, do your part with diligence and resourcefulness, but trust that God is the one who ultimately sustains and cares for you.
exp.45:5:
This verse tells us that Jacob and his whole family went down to Egypt, taking their livestock and all the possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan. The word "goods" here means their possessions and belongings. The phrase "Jacob, and all his seed" refers to his offspring: his children, grandchildren, and other relatives. They left nothing important behind; they moved together, complete.

The passage is narrative, and the one telling the story is the writer of Genesis. Jacob, now an old man, was traveling to be reunited with his son Joseph, who was governing in Egypt. Before setting out, at Beersheba, God had told him not to be afraid, that he would go down with him to Egypt, and that he would bring him back again. So this journey was not merely a move because of the famine, but a step guided by God's promise.

For today: when God calls you to a major change, you can move forward in peace if you rest on his promise to go with you. Before deciding, pray and seek his guidance; then take the step with your family, trusting that he goes with you.
exp.40:50:
Joseph named his firstborn son Manasseh, because God had made him forget all his hardship and his father's house. "Toil" here means troubles and pains, not a job. "Firstborn" means the first son. The name Manasseh sounds similar to the Hebrew word meaning "to make forget."

Joseph is speaking as the governor of Egypt. Years earlier his brothers had sold him, and he had suffered slavery and prison. Now he has a wife, children, and a place of authority. Naming his son this way expresses gratitude to God. Some think it was not a total forgetting, but that the pain no longer controlled him.

For today: when God gives you something good after a difficult season, give a name to that gratitude. Remembering his blessings can ease the weight of the past and help you move forward.
exp.1:14:
The explanation says that God took the man and placed him in the garden of Eden with a task: to "dress" it, that is, to cultivate and work it, and to "keep" it, meaning to take care of and protect it. "Garden" is what we would today call a garden or orchard. Before any prohibition, the man receives a place and work with a purpose.

The narrator of Genesis describes how God prepared the garden, with its rivers and its soil. Here God places the man as the one in charge of that place. Then comes the command about the trees, which shows that this responsibility is lived out in trust and obedience. Some understand "keep" also as watching over or guarding, but the text does not explain against what.

For today: see the work and care of what God entrusts to us, such as family, employment, or creation, as a task with meaning, not as a burden. Doing it with gratitude and responsibility is a way of honoring God.
exp.30:1:
Here it says that Jacob looked at Laban's face, that is, at his attitude and the way he treated him. "Countenance" means the face, the expression. And he noticed that Laban no longer treated him with the same regard as before. The phrase "as before" means: as in the past, with the same warmth.

Here the narrator speaks. Jacob had been working for Laban, his father-in-law, for years. Laban's sons were saying that Jacob had grown rich at their father's expense. That envy seems to have shaped the atmosphere, and Jacob perceived it. Soon God speaks to him and tells him to return to his homeland, promising to be with him.

For today: sometimes changes in an environment, such as a job or a relationship, make us notice that a season has ended. Instead of responding with anger or fear, we can pray and ask God for direction, for he guides our steps faithfully.
exp.18:8:
The men of Sodom push Lot away with contempt. "Stand back" means "Get out of the way!" They tell him that he is a foreigner who came to live among them and now wants to give them orders. They threaten to treat him worse than his visitors, they shove him violently, and they try to break down the door.

The crowd of Sodom, which had surrounded Lot's house, is speaking. He had just tried to protect his guests, who were angels, although his offer to hand over his daughters is very harsh, and the Bible does not present it as an example to follow. The people take offense because Lot, being a foreigner, calls them out for their wickedness.

For today: when someone corrects us, it is easy to respond with mockery or anger. Let us ask God for a humble heart to listen, and for courage to speak the truth with love, even when it costs us.
exp.29:12:
Leah says that this birth is "for my happiness," that is, for her joy or blessing. She believes the women will call her "happy," meaning glad and blessed. For this reason she names the boy Asher, a name connected with the idea of happiness or joy.

Leah, the wife of Jacob, is speaking. Her servant Zilpah has just given birth to another son, and Leah considers him hers according to the custom of that time. She lives in a painful rivalry with her sister Rachel over Jacob's love and over having children. With this name she expresses joy and a longing to be valued.

For today: We can thank God for our blessings without living in comparison with others. Leah sought to be recognized by the other women, but our true happiness comes from knowing that God sees us and cares for us.
exp.33:30:
The sons of Jacob, Simeon and Levi, answer their father with a question: "Should he deal with our sister as with a harlot?" The word "harlot" means a woman who gives herself for money. The King James Version uses this older word where modern English would more often say "prostitute."

The speakers are the brothers as a group, especially Simeon and Levi. Their sister Dinah had been dishonored by Shechem, and they took revenge by killing the men of the city and plundering it. Jacob rebuked them for the danger they had put the family in. They do not admit any wrong and only defend their anger. The text does not approve their violence; Jacob condemned it even at the end of his life (Genesis 49:5-7).

For today: feeling hurt is not enough to justify responding with violence or revenge. Before acting, let us ask God for calm and seek justice without causing further harm.
exp.8:28:
It says that Noah lived 950 years in total and then died. This closes his story. The phrase "all the days of Noah" means "the whole of Noah's life." The 950 years add up this way: 600 years when the flood came, plus 350 afterward.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, using the same style as the genealogies: he gives the age and ends with "and he died." After recounting the blessing on Shem and Japheth and the curse on Canaan, the account closes Noah's life. Scholars do not agree on how to understand these very long ages: some take them literally and others as a way of expressing things in that period.

For today: even a man of faith like Noah, who was saved from the flood, ended his life on earth. This invites us to live with humility, trusting God each day and leaving others a good example.
exp.39:4:
This verse tells us that the cupbearer and the baker of the king of Egypt, who were in prison, each had a dream on the same night. The phrase "both of them" means "the two of them." The "butler" was the one who served the king his wine. "Each man according to the interpretation of his dream" means that each dream had its own meaning.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Joseph was in prison unjustly, but the captain of the guard had put him in charge of attending to these two officials. The dreams prepare the moment when Joseph will interpret them, and later this will bring him before Pharaoh. The text does not yet explain what the dreams mean.

For today: even in times of waiting or injustice, God may be preparing doors we cannot see. Serve faithfully where you are, and trust that God is at work even in difficult places.
exp.23:30:
Laban goes out to meet Abraham's servant and invites him to come in. He calls him "blessed of the Lord", that is, someone whom God has favored. He asks why he is still standing outside and assures him that he has already prepared the house and a place for the camels. The King James wording "prepared" here means having the space made ready and in order.

The speaker is Laban, brother of Rebekah. He had seen the jewels she received and heard how the servant had found her at the well. His warm welcome shows the hospitality of the time. The Bible does not fully clarify his motives; the jewels may have influenced him, but there is also sincere courtesy.

For today: opening our home with generosity reflects the love of God. We can receive others with attention and practical care, and recognize the hand of God in those who come into our lives.
exp.20:31:
Here is what the verse says: Abraham and Abimelech made a peace agreement at Beersheba. Afterward, Abimelech and Phichol, the commander of his army, got up and returned to the land of the Philistines. "Covenant" means a solemn agreement, and "chief captain of his host" refers to the military commander.

The narrator tells of the end of a dispute over a water well. Abimelech, a king of the region, recognized that God was with Abraham and wanted to secure peace. Abraham gave him seven ewe lambs as proof that the well was his. This is where the name Beersheba comes from, which is commonly understood to mean "well of the oath" or "well of the seven."

Conflicts can be resolved through clear and honest agreements, without fighting. If you have a disagreement with someone, seek to speak with sincerity, put things in writing if needed, and pursue peace, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.26:37:
Esau asks his father whether he has only one blessing to give. He begs that his father bless him too, and he breaks into loud weeping. "Lifted up his voice" means that he wept loudly, without holding back. "Birthright" is the special right of the firstborn son.

Isaac, already old, had given the main blessing to Jacob, believing he was Esau. Jacob pretended to be his brother with the help of their mother, Rebekah. Esau grieves what he has lost, though earlier he had sold his birthright for a bowl of food. Hebrews 12:17 mentions his tears, and the Bible does not make clear everything that was in his heart.

For today: hasty decisions have consequences that cannot later be undone. Value what God has given you and take care of it with wisdom. If you fail, God remains merciful to whoever comes to Him with sincerity.
exp.30:22:
The explanation says that Laban gathered his relatives and went out to pursue Jacob. He traveled seven days' journey until he overtook him on the mount of Gilead. "Brethren" here means relatives or people of his family. "Overtook" means that he caught up with him.

This is part of the account in the book of Genesis. Jacob left secretly with his wives, his children, and his flocks, after twenty years with Laban, his father-in-law. Laban found out on the third day and set out after him, probably angry and wanting to recover what he considered his own. But the text goes on to show that God intervened that very night and protected Jacob.

For today: when someone stronger or angrier seems to be coming after us, we can trust that God sees everything and cares for his own. Even so, it is good to face conflicts honestly and not by running away in secret.
exp.47:9:
It says that Jacob, also called Israel, was already so old that he could hardly see. That is why he asked for his grandsons to come close. "Weighed down" means heavy or weakened by age. "Bring near" means to draw close. When he had them near him, he kissed them and embraced them.

The narrator describes the scene in which Jacob, near the end of his life, is in Egypt with Joseph. He is going to bless Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's sons. Although he could not see well, he wanted to have them beside him. Earlier he had believed he had lost Joseph forever, and now God allowed him to see even his descendants.

For today: even when our strength fails, we can still bless others with affection. A hug, a kind word, or a prayer for the younger generation can leave a deep mark. And whoever serves God can look back and see his faithfulness.
exp.24:10:
It says that when Abraham died, God continued to care for his family and blessed Isaac, his son. Isaac went to live near a well called "of the Living One who sees me." The words "dwelt" and "by" mean that he lived beside it.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses, speaks. He tells us that God's promise did not end with Abraham's death. That well recalls Hagar, who there found God in the wilderness (Genesis 16:14). Perhaps Isaac lived in a place where God had already shown himself as one who sees and cares.

For today: even when important people in our lives pass away, God remains faithful and present. We can trust that he sees us, sustains us, and continues his work in us.
exp.40:29:
The explanation says that after seven years of great abundance, another seven years of hunger will come. The scarcity will be so severe that people will completely forget the earlier abundance. The KJV's "plenty" means abundance, having more than enough. "Shall arise" is the verse's own phrasing for what comes next. "Consume" means the hunger will wear away the land and its resources.

Joseph, a Hebrew prisoner, speaks before Pharaoh. Pharaoh had two dreams that no one in Egypt could explain. Joseph makes clear that the interpretation does not come from his own wisdom but from God, who shows Pharaoh what he is about to do. Shortly afterward, Joseph advises him to prepare in advance.

For today: good times do not last forever, and it is wise not to live trusting only in abundance. We can learn to save, to be generous, and to depend on God, both when there is plenty and when there is want.
exp.41:8:
This verse tells us that Joseph, already ruler in Egypt, recognizes his brothers, but they do not recognize him. He remembers the dreams of his youth, in which they bowed down before him. Then he accuses them: "You are spies." The phrase "to see the nakedness of the land" means the weak or undefended places of Egypt.

Joseph is the one speaking. His brothers came from Canaan because of the famine to buy grain. Years earlier they had sold him as a slave. The commentators do not agree on the exact reason for the accusation: it may be a way of testing them, of learning news of their family, or of seeing whether they had changed. The text does not fully explain it.

For today: when someone has hurt us, God can give us time to act with wisdom and not in haste or revenge. Remembering what God has shown us helps us to seek truth and reconciliation with care.
exp.6:11:
This verse says that the rain fell on the earth without stopping for forty days and forty nights. That is, the rain was constant, both by day and by night. In the text before it, there is mention of "the fountains of the great deep" broken open and "the windows of heaven" opened, which are poetic ways of saying that the water came both from below and from above.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book of Genesis, not a character. He tells how God fulfilled what He had announced to Noah: a judgment on the wickedness of the earth, and at the same time the protection of Noah and his family inside the ark. Scholars understand the extent of the flood in different ways, but all agree on the central message.

For today: God keeps His word, both His warnings and His promises. We can trust Him and obey Him even when we do not yet see the storm, as Noah did.
exp.27:19:
Jacob makes a promise to God. He says that if God is with him, watching over him on this journey and giving him bread to eat and clothing to wear, then he will respond with commitment.

The words "will be with me" and "will keep me" carry the sense of "is with" and "watches over me," and "vowed a vow" means a solemn promise made to God.

Jacob is speaking as he flees from his brother Esau and travels toward Haran, alone and with nothing. He has just dreamed of the ladder and heard God's promise at Bethel. Some read his "if" as an expression of doubt; others see it as a way of accepting what God had already promised him. The Bible does not fully settle the question.

For today: in times of uncertainty, we can speak to God with sincerity and trust that He cares for our basic needs. And when He answers, we can return gratitude to Him with a life committed to Him.
exp.40:40:
Here Pharaoh officially declares that Joseph is put in charge of all Egypt. The phrase "I have set you" is a formula of appointment: it is not a suggestion but an order carrying authority. In the King James wording, the phrase "And Pharaoh said unto Joseph" uses the older word "unto," which simply means "to," and the verb "said" is the plain past tense of "say."

Joseph had been sold by his brothers and unjustly taken to prison. Pharaoh had dreams that no one could explain, and Joseph, recognizing that the interpretation came from God, told him what would come: seven years of abundance and seven of famine. Pharaoh saw wisdom in him and gave him command, giving him a ring, clothing, and a chariot as signs of his authority.

For today: God can use difficult years to prepare a person. Keep doing well what is yours to do, even when no one notices, and trust that God knows when and where to use you.
exp.32:6:
This verse tells how Leah came near with her children, and they all bowed down before Esau. After that, Joseph and Rachel came near, and they bowed down too.

Jacob is returning to his land after years away, and he fears meeting his brother Esau, whom he had deceived long before. So he presents his family in order: first the servants, then Leah, and last Rachel and Joseph, whom he loved most. Bowing was a sign of respect. Esau, instead of attacking, responds with kindness. Some think the order shows Jacob's favoritism; the text does not explain it.

For today: when a relationship is broken, seeking reconciliation with humility and respect is a good step. We do not know how the other person will respond, but God can soften hearts.
exp.22:14:
Here Ephron tells Abraham that the land costs four hundred shekels of silver. Then he adds, "What is that between you and me?", as if to say that this price is a small matter between them. And he tells him to bury his dead, that is, Sarah. A shekel was a unit of weight, and here it was paid in silver.

Abraham had just lost his wife and needed a place to bury her. Ephron, a Hittite, spoke in front of the people of the town. He seemed generous, but he named a very high price. Some think it was a way of bargaining with courtesy, though this cannot be stated with certainty. Abraham paid the full price.

For today: when a situation is hard, act with integrity and clarity. Abraham did not argue or seek an advantage; he paid what was fair and left everything in order and in plain sight of all.
exp.5:5:
It says that God was saddened for having created human beings. "Repented" does not mean that God made a mistake, but that he felt deep sorrow and changed his attitude toward what he saw. "It grieved him at his heart" means that it hurt him deeply, like a sorrow in the innermost place.

The narrator of Genesis tells this after describing that human wickedness was constant and that every thought leaned toward evil. God responds with pain, not with indifference. Scholars explain the language of God's "repentance" in several ways, but almost all agree that it shows how much he cares for his creation. And right after this, Noah appears, who found grace.

Today we can remember that God is not cold toward evil or toward our sin. This invites us to draw near to him with sincerity, to ask for his grace, and to live in a way that does not grieve him.
exp.23:7:
Abraham tells his servant that, if the young woman is not willing to come with him, the servant will be free from the oath. The one thing he must not do is take Isaac back to the land from which Abraham came.

Abraham, now an old man, speaks to the servant he trusts most. He wants a wife for Isaac from among his own kin, but he does not want his son to return to Mesopotamia. Abraham remembers that God brought him out from there and promised the land of Canaan to his descendants. For this reason he trusts that God will guide the way.

For today: we can do our part faithfully and leave in God's hands what we do not control. It is also wise to recognize the limits of a charge: do what is possible, without forcing anyone or the circumstances.
exp.22:5:
The sons of Heth answer Abraham with great respect. They call him "my lord" and address him as "a mighty prince," which can be understood to mean someone powerful or greatly blessed by God. They offer him the best of their tombs to bury his dead and assure him that none of them will refuse him that place.

Abraham is a foreigner in Canaan, and he has just lost his wife Sarah. He needs a place to bury her, but he has no land of his own. That is why he asks the Hittites, who are the inhabitants of the region, for a burial property. Their response shows that they respected him for his character and his faith. Some think their offer was generous and sincere; others think it was the opening of a courteous negotiation.

Today this reminds us that living with integrity and kindness earns the respect of others, even when we are "strangers" in a place. In addition, we can tenderly accompany someone who is in mourning.
exp.22:4:
This verse is a transitional sentence. It says that the children of Heth, the people living in that land, answered Abraham. The Hittites were a local people, descended from Heth, who lived in Hebron.

Sarah has just died, and Abraham, who was a foreigner, asks for a place to bury her. That is why he describes himself as a stranger and a sojourner, a foreigner with no land of his own. The Hittites respond with respect: in the following verses they call him a mighty prince and offer him their best tombs. We do not know exactly what they meant by that title; it may have been an expression of honor for his good reputation.

For today: when we go through a time of grief, we can ask for help with humility. And those of us who have the chance to help a foreigner or someone who is suffering, let us do so with respect and generosity.
exp.6:8:
This verse tells that the animals came into the ark two by two, a male and a female, just as God had commanded Noah. The words "went in" and "unto Noah" are older forms; today we would say "went into the ark with Noah" or "came to Noah."

The narrator of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses, recounts the moments before the flood. He insists that everything happened "as God had commanded." Noah had already received instructions earlier (Genesis 6:19-20), and now the account shows that they were carried out exactly. Some passages also mention seven pairs of clean animals (7:2); the text presents this in different ways, and scholars explain it in various ways.

For today: Noah obeyed God even when no rain was yet visible. We can trust God's word and do what he asks us today, without waiting to understand everything.
exp.26:9:
Rebekah tells Jacob to bring his father Isaac the food she is going to prepare. In this way Isaac will eat and bless Jacob before he dies. Some older words: "savory food" means dishes of food, and "smooth" (from the following verse) means without hair.

Rebekah speaks because she has heard that Isaac, now old, intends to bless his firstborn son, Esau. She proposes a plan of deception so that Jacob will receive that blessing. The Bible reports what happened without approving the means they used. Before they were born, God had already said that the older would serve the younger (Genesis 25:23), but that does not make the lie right.

For today: even when God has promised something, we do not need to manipulate or lie to bring it about. Trusting God means waiting and acting with honesty, without forcing things through trickery.
exp.49:25:
This verse says that Joseph died at the age of one hundred and ten. Then they embalmed him, that is, they preserved his body with spices and Egyptian techniques, and placed him in a coffin, or case for the body, in Egypt.

It is the closing verse of the book of Genesis. The narrator tells of the end of Joseph's life, a man who had become a figure of authority in Egypt. Shortly before, Joseph had told his brothers that God would bring them to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and he asked them to carry his bones with them. That coffin remained as a sign of hope: Egypt would not be the people's final home.

We can live with our eyes fixed on God's promises, even when we do not live to see them fulfilled. Joseph died trusting that God would keep his word, and that faith can encourage us to remain steadfast in times of waiting.
exp.21:3:
It says that Abraham and his household traveled for three days. On the third day, Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw the place from afar, the place to which God was sending him. The phrase "saw the place afar off" in the King James Version is written in plain modern English, so no old spelling needs comment here, and "lifted up his eyes" means that he looked up, toward the horizon.

God had asked Abraham to offer Isaac, his beloved son, on the mountain of Moriah. The account is traditionally attributed to Moses. Abraham obeyed without arguing and set out early. The three days of travel may have given him a great deal of time to think, and the text does not say what he felt. What it does show is that he kept walking.

For today: when God asks you for something difficult, you do not have to see the whole road at once. Take the next step in faith, and trust that God will show you the place in his time.
exp.41:22:
The verse says that Joseph's brothers did not know that he understood what they were saying. Because Joseph used an interpreter, they assumed he did not understand their language. The word "interpreter" refers to someone who translates from one language into another.

The brothers were talking among themselves, believing they spoke in private. They acknowledged their guilt for having mistreated Joseph years earlier, and Reuben reminded them that he had warned them. Joseph heard them, stepped away, and wept. Here the account shows that his heart was still tender, even though he was testing them.

For today: what we say when we think no one is listening reveals what is in our heart. God does know everything. We can ask him to lead us to sincere repentance and to repair the harm we have done, without waiting to be found out.
exp.34:8:
This verse says that God appeared to Jacob once more, after he came back from Padan-aram, and blessed him. Padan-aram is the region of Mesopotamia where Jacob lived with the family of his uncle Laban.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob was already in Bethel, the place where God had shown himself to him when he was fleeing from his brother Esau. Now that he was returning, God appeared to him again and then confirmed his new name, Israel, and repeated his promises. In this way he reminded Jacob that he was still at his side.

For today: God does not forget us on the long and difficult roads of life. If you are coming back today from a hard season, draw near to him in prayer and give him thanks, because he keeps seeking you out and blessing you.
exp.41:16:
This verse says that Joseph had his brothers put in prison and left them there for three days.

The King James wording, "put them all together," uses the English phrase to mean that he gathered them all into the same place, that is, he put all of them in one place together.

Joseph was governor in Egypt, but his brothers did not yet know it was him. They had come to buy food during the famine, and Joseph accused them of being spies. He wanted to test whether they were telling the truth and whether they had changed since they sold him years earlier. Some think those days also gave them time to reflect, although the text does not explain this.

For today: sometimes silences and uncomfortable waiting make us look into our hearts. Instead of running from them, we can ask God to show us what we should acknowledge and correct.
exp.14:19:
This verse continues a list of peoples who lived in the land that God promised to Abram. Here the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Rephaim are named. "Seed" means descendants. The Rephaim are remembered in the Bible as a people of great stature, although the details about them are not entirely clear.

The one speaking is the LORD, who makes a covenant with Abram. Abram still had no children, yet God promised him a land for his descendants. The list of peoples shows that the promise was real and concrete: it spoke of true places and true people. This happened long before it was fulfilled.

For today: God keeps his promises even when they take a long time and even when there are great obstacles. If you are waiting for something God has promised you, trust in his faithfulness and keep walking with patience, without ceasing to pray.
exp.42:27:
They answer that their father Jacob, whom they call "your servant," is well and still alive. Then they bow down their heads and pay him respect. "Is in good health" means "is well," and "bowed down... and made obeisance" means that they prostrated themselves as a sign of respect.

The sons of Jacob are speaking. They are in Egypt and do not yet know that this ruler is their brother Joseph. Without realizing it, they bow before him, and so what Joseph dreamed as a young man comes true. Joseph asks about his father because he loves him and misses him.

For today: genuinely asking about the well-being of others is a form of love. Today, ask with sincere interest about someone in your family and listen to their answer with attention.
exp.41:11:
Here José insists on accusing his brothers of being spies. He says they have come "to see the nakedness of the land", that is, to look at the weak or undefended parts of Egypt. The phrase "the nakedness of the land" is the wording used in the King James Version.

José speaks as the governor of Egypt. His brothers have come from Canaan to buy food because of the famine, but they do not recognize him. He does recognize them. His reasons are not fully stated here; many think he wanted to test whether they had changed and to learn about his father and Benjamin. The text does not explain it in those words.

For today: when someone presses or accuses us, it is wise to respond with truth and calm. And if we have failed others, God can use difficult moments to bring us to honesty and repentance.
exp.24:19:
This verse tells us that Isaac married Rebekah when he was forty years old. It makes clear who she was: the daughter of Bethuel, from the region of Padan-aram, and the sister of Laban. "Syrian" refers to a people from that area, in the north of Mesopotamia. The text says "he took her to wife," an older way of saying that he married her.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. He begins the story of Isaac's family, after that of Abraham. He recalls the journey of Abraham's servant, told in chapter 24, to find a wife among the relatives of the family. The verses that follow show that Rebekah could not have children, and that Isaac prayed for her.

For today: in big decisions, such as marriage, it is wise to seek God's guidance and the counsel of wise people. And when there are times of waiting or difficulty, we can pray with confidence, as Isaac did.
exp.46:29:
Jacob asks Joseph that, when he dies ("lie with my fathers" is a gentle way of saying die), Joseph carry him out of Egypt and bury him in the tomb of his ancestors. "Carry me out" means "you will carry me out." Joseph promises to do it.

Jacob, now an old man after living seventeen years in Egypt, speaks. He asks Joseph for a solemn oath, with the gesture of placing the hand under the thigh, an ancient custom of those times. Jacob wants to be buried in Canaan, the land God promised to Abraham, Isaac, and their descendants. In this way he expresses his confidence that God will fulfill that promise.

For today: Jacob thought about his end with faith, not fear. We can ask ourselves whether our decisions and words show that we trust God's promises. Also, Joseph reminds us of the importance of keeping what we promise, especially to those we love.
exp.3:9:
God asks Cain, "What have you done?" Then he tells him that the blood of Abel, his brother, cries out to God from the ground. "Cries out" means it calls out for help or justice.

God, the Lord (Jehovah), is speaking. Cain has just killed Abel, and when God asked him where his brother was, he lied and answered with defiance: "Am I my brother's keeper?" God did not need the information; he was giving Cain the opportunity to acknowledge his guilt. Then comes the punishment: the ground will no longer yield its fruit for him, and he will live as a wanderer.

For today: God sees what is done in secret, and he cares about the life of every person, especially those who suffer injustice. We can be honest with God about our failings and look out for others instead of making excuses.
exp.30:28:
Laban tells Jacob that he has enough power to do him harm. But he makes clear that he will not do it, because the God of Jacob's father spoke to him the night before. God warned him to take care not to speak to Jacob "either good or bad," that is, not with harshness, anger, or violence out of place.

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, is the one speaking. He caught up with Jacob after Jacob had secretly left with his wives, his children, and his possessions. Laban is upset and complains about the flight. His threat shows power, yet he also acknowledges that God intervened. God was protecting Jacob even though the atmosphere was tense and there was distrust between the two men.

For today: when we are angry with someone, we can stop and ask God for self-control before we speak or act. His guidance helps us not to hurt others, even when we have the "power" to do so.
exp.4:4:
This verse sums up the life of Adam: he lived a total of 930 years, and then he died. The Bible uses simple, firm words: "and he died." The older forms "Adam" and "begat," which appear in the King James wording, mean Adam and "became the father of" (or "had a son"). Here the reader sees the King James wording, where "begat" is the archaic word for "became the father of."

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of the book of Genesis, within a list of generations. This list connects creation with the stories that follow. After Genesis 2–3, where God warned that death would come from disobedience, this verse shows that death truly arrived. Some understand the ages literally; others, symbolically. The text does not make this clear.

For today: our life is brief, even the longest one. We can live with gratitude, use our time well, and trust in God, who gives hope beyond death.
exp.30:38:
He says that Jacob never brought Laban an animal that had been torn apart by wild beasts as proof of his innocence. On the contrary, he himself covered the loss out of his own means. "Torn of beasts" refers to an animal killed by wild animals. "Stolen" means taken by theft. Whether the animal was stolen by day or by night, Laban demanded that he pay for it.

Jacob speaks with Laban, his father-in-law, after fleeing with his family. Laban caught up with him and accused him of theft, even of carrying off his household gods. Jacob, not knowing that Rachel had taken them, defends himself by recalling twenty years of honest and hard work, and of unjust treatment.

For today: work with integrity even when no one sees you or gives you credit. Taking responsibility for your mistakes and fulfilling your duty, even when it is costly, builds solid character and a clear conscience.
exp.17:26:
Abraham says he has now taken it upon himself to speak to God, whom he calls "my Lord." He acknowledges that he does not deserve to do so, because he describes himself as "dust and ashes," that is, someone small and frail. The King James wording "I have taken upon me to speak" conveys this sense of venturing to speak boldly, and "dust and ashes" is the phrase used for human lowliness.

God has just said that he would spare Sodom if he found fifty righteous people there. Abraham, concerned for the people of the city, and perhaps for his nephew Lot who lived there, continues to ask with respect. That is why he humbles himself before asking whether God would spare the city for the sake of forty-five.

For today: we can pray with confidence and humility at the same time. God invites us to speak to him and to intercede for others, but not by demanding, rather by acknowledging who he is and who we are.
exp.10:29:
This verse says that Sarai, Abram's wife, was barren, meaning she could not have children, and so she had none. The word "barren" describes this condition directly, and "had no child" states the result plainly.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. After listing the family of Terah, the account pauses on a painful detail that seems to close every hope of descendants. In that time, not having children was a heavy burden. This sentence prepares the way for the promise God will make to Abram in the next chapter.

For today: there are situations that seem closed, such as a long wait or a need that is not resolved. This verse reminds us that God can begin his work exactly where we see a limit. We can pray honestly and keep trusting him, even without knowing yet how he will respond.
exp.4:7:
This verse sums up the life of Seth: he lived a total of 912 years and then died. "Seth" is Set, the son of Adam and Eve. The phrase "and he died" is repeated throughout this list in Genesis 5.

Here no character is speaking; the narrator of the book presents a genealogy, that is, a list of generations from Adam. It shows how humanity continued after Cain and Abel, and how the line advanced that would lead to Noah. The very large numbers are understood in different ways: some take them literally and others as a form of expression typical of that time. There is no complete certainty.

For today: the repetition of "and he died" reminds us that life is brief and precious. We can ask ourselves what we will leave to those who come after us: faith, example, and love for God.
exp.1:10:
This verse names the first of the four rivers that flowed out of Eden. It was called Pison, and it wound around the whole land of Havilah, a place known for its gold. "Compass" here means to surround or border. We do not know for certain where Havilah was, and scholars have placed it in various locations.

The speaker is the narrator of Genesis, who describes the creation of the garden. After mentioning the trees and the river that watered the garden, he gives geographical details so that the reader sees that Eden was a real place, abundant and full of blessings. The gold, the stones, and the rivers show the generosity of God in preparing a home for the human being.

For today: God provides with abundance and care. Before you ask Him for anything, He has already prepared what you need. Today you can give thanks for one concrete provision in your life.
exp.0:1:
This verse describes the earth at first: "without form and void," meaning without shape and without inhabitants. The phrase "face of the deep" refers to the surface of the deep waters, and the old wording "upon the face of the deep" shows that the darkness lay over those waters. The deep waters were under darkness, and the Spirit of God "moved upon the face of the waters," like someone who watches over and prepares to act.

Some think the image is that of a bird hovering over its nest, though this is understood in various ways.
