The narrator tells the beginning of all things, not a person within the scene. Tradition attributes the account to Moses, though there are different opinions. After saying that God created the heavens and the earth, the text shows how God brings order, light and life, beginning with the words: "Let there be light."

For today: when your life feels disordered, empty or dark, remember that God does not stay away from chaos. His Spirit is present, and He can bring order and hope step by step.
exp.44:11:
This verse says that Joseph's brothers, and Benjamin, can see with their own eyes that the one speaking to them is really Joseph. "My mouth speaks to you" means that he himself was talking to them, and he was doing it in his own language, without an interpreter.

Joseph has just revealed himself to his brothers, who had sold him years earlier and now did not recognize him as the ruler of Egypt. He mentions Benjamin, his full brother from the same father and mother, because Benjamin was the only one who had not taken part in that betrayal. Joseph wants them to believe him and to carry the news to their father Jacob. For that reason he offers them protection in Goshen during the five remaining years of famine.

For today: when God restores a broken relationship, sometimes it is necessary to speak clearly and to face the situation directly. If there is someone with whom you have a wound, consider approaching them with sincerity, without resentment, and with a willingness to care for that person.
exp.17:15:
The explanation says that the three visitors, who had eaten with Abraham, got up to leave and looked toward Sodom. Abraham went with them for a stretch to see them off. "Men" simply means "men," and "went with them" means that he walked alongside them, as one does with a dear guest.

The visitors appear as men, but the account shows that one of them is the LORD himself (v. 17). They have just announced that Sarah will have a son. Now the account changes subject: they look toward Sodom, the city that will be judged. God walks with Abraham and is about to entrust him with what he intends to do.

For today: hospitality and closeness to God go together. Abraham does not send his guests off in a hurry but accompanies them. When we give time to God and to people, we become more attentive to what He is doing and to what He wants to show us.
exp.32:13:
Jacob asks Esau to go on ahead, and he will travel slowly, at the pace of the livestock and the children, until he reaches him at Seir. "Servant" is a humble way of saying "I"; the King James wording "cattle" is the livestock; "pass over" is the same sense as going on ahead and crossing ahead; "lead on softly" is the pace of travel.

Jacob speaks with Esau after years of estrangement. Esau offers to accompany him, but Jacob explains that the children and the animals cannot withstand a fast march. His tone is very courteous. It is not clear whether Jacob really intended to go to Seir; the account says he then went to Succoth, and scholars interpret this in different ways.

For today: caring for the weakest in our family or community means going at their pace and not ours. We can also be kind and clear, and be honest in what we say and do.
exp.29:0:
This verse tells how Rachel, seeing that she could not bear children to Jacob, became jealous of her sister Leah, who was bearing him sons. She then made a demand of Jacob: "Give me children, or else I die." The word "envied" here refers to the pain and resentment over what another person has and one does not. "Or else I die" expresses her desperation.

Rachel and Leah were sisters and both were wives of Jacob. Leah already had several children, while Rachel, whom Jacob loved more, still had none. In that culture, having children gave a woman great value and security. Jacob responds with anger, saying that he is not in the place of God. Rachel then proposes using her servant Bilhah, a practice of the time.

For today: when you compare yourself with others and feel pain over what you lack, bring that desire to God in prayer, instead of venting it on the people you love.
exp.5:3:
It says that in those days there were "giants" (in Hebrew, nefilim), and that they continued to exist after the "sons of God" came in to the "daughters of men." From those unions were born mighty men, famous since old times. "Bare" means that they had children, and "men of renown" means men who were very well known.

The one telling the story is the author of Genesis, describing the time before the flood. Christians interpret "sons of God" in several ways: descendants of Seth, human rulers, or spiritual beings. There is no single certain answer. What is clear is that the text shows a society turning away from God, and it prepares the judgment that follows.

For today: fame and power do not make anyone righteous. Let us ask God that our decisions, even those of the heart, be guided by his will and not only by what attracts us.
exp.25:15:
Abimelech tells Isaac to leave his territory. The reason he gives is that Isaac has become "much mightier" than they are, that is, stronger and with more wealth and influence. The word "go" here means "leave" or "go away from here."

Abimelech, king of the Philistines in Gerar, is the one speaking. Isaac had settled there, and God had blessed him with crops, livestock, and many servants. The Philistines envied him; they had even stopped up the wells that Abraham had dug. It is likely that Abimelech feared losing his position before such a prosperous neighbor, though the text does not detail his exact motives.

For today: the blessing of others can stir up envy or rejection, and sometimes we will have to endure it. Isaac did not argue or take revenge; he left in peace and dug the wells open again. When someone treats you unjustly, respond with calm and keep doing good.
exp.6:6:
This verse tells that Noah went into the ark together with his wife, his three sons, and their wives, eight people in all. They entered "because of the waters of the flood," that is, because of the waters that were already coming over the earth. The word "ark" refers to a large vessel or floating box.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. God had commanded Noah to build the ark and enter it, because a flood was coming. The previous verse says that Noah did everything the LORD commanded him. Here we see that his obedience carried through to the end, when at last he went in.

For today: obeying God is not only about starting well, but about persevering until we do what He asks. Also, Noah did not enter alone; his faith also protected his family. We can live out our faith with steadiness, caring for those who are close to us.
exp.24:3:
This verse lists the five sons of Midian: Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. Midian was a son of Abraham and Keturah, so these men are Abraham's grandsons. The verse closes by stating that all of them are descendants of Keturah.

The narrator of Genesis presents a family list before recounting the death of Abraham. After Sarah, Abraham had another wife, Keturah, and many descendants. It is then made clear that the main inheritance went to Isaac, and that the other children received gifts and settled toward the east. The Midianites appear later in the Bible, but it is not always certain how they are related to these names.

For today: God keeps his promises, even in small details, and every person matters to him, even when their name appears only once. We can value others with that same care.
exp.28:14:
Laban tells Jacob that it isn't fair for him to work for nothing just because they are relatives. He asks Jacob to name what he wants to be paid. The word "for nought" means "without pay," and "wages" is the payment given for work. "Tell me" means "say to me."

Laban, Jacob's uncle, speaks after Jacob has been in his house for a month and helping with the work. Laban seems generous in offering fair pay. Some believe he was also aware of how useful Jacob was and wanted to keep him in his service. The text does not say what his intention was, so we cannot be sure.

For today: work deserves fair pay, even among family or friends. Speaking clearly about what has been agreed prevents resentment. And it is good to do this honestly, seeking the good of both parties and not only one's own.
exp.41:26:
This verse tells how, during the journey back to Canaan, one of Joseph's brothers opened his sack at the inn to give his donkey some feed. There he found his money, right in the mouth of the sack. An inn is a place where travelers spent the night, and the donkey is the animal he was feeding.

The narrator of Genesis then recounts what happened after Joseph, now ruler in Egypt, sold grain to his brothers without them recognizing him. Joseph ordered their money returned to them in secret. The Bible does not say here why he did it; some think it was an act of kindness, others that he wanted to test them. The brothers, seeing the money, became frightened and thought that God was intervening because of their past guilt.

For today: when something unexpected happens to you, do not jump to conclusions. Stop, pray, and examine your heart calmly, trusting that God works even in what you do not understand.
exp.13:4:
A year after the rebellion, Chedorlaomer came with the kings allied to him and defeated several peoples: the Rephaims at Ashteroth Karnaim, the Zuzims in Ham, and the Emims at Shaveh Kiriathaim. "Defeated" means that they beat them in battle.

Here the narrator (tradition says it is Moses) recounts an ancient war. Chedorlaomer wanted to punish the kings who had stopped paying him tribute and to show his power in the region. This account prepares the story of Lot, Abram's nephew, who will be caught up in this conflict. Scholars are not certain how to identify these kings and places precisely.

For today: the decisions of the powerful can affect innocent people. Pray for those who govern, and remember that God cares for his people even in the midst of conflicts he did not cause.
exp.33:6:
When the sons of Jacob heard what had happened, they came in from the field. They were filled with grief and great anger. The verse says they were "very wroth," meaning they were extremely angry. The verse calls what Shechem did "folly" in Israel, a deeply shameful act, and it describes it as lying with Jacob's daughter, which refers to a sexual assault. The verse states that such a thing ought not to be done.

This is part of the story of Dinah, Jacob's daughter, and Shechem. Jacob heard about it and kept silent until his sons came home. The narrator describes their outrage, while Hamor, Shechem's father, is already on his way to speak and propose a marriage. Later, the sons will respond with deceit and violence, and the Bible does not present that as an example to follow.

For today: it is right to feel indignation at injustice and abuse, and to protect the one who was harmed. But we must carry that anger with self-control, seeking justice without revenge, so that we do not cause even more harm.
exp.37:6:
This verse says that Er, Judah's oldest son, did evil things that God saw and rejected, and for that reason God took his life. "Firstborn" means the eldest son. "Was wicked in the sight of the Lord" means that his conduct was displeasing to God. The Bible does not say what his sin was, so it is better not to invent one.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He tells the story of Judah's family, who had married and had three sons. Er had married Tamar. His death left her a widow without children, and this leads to what follows: Judah asks Onan to fulfill the duty of raising up offspring for his brother.

For today: God sees beyond appearances, even what others do not know about us. Today you can ask him to show you something in your life that needs to change, and to respond to him with humility and without delay.
exp.8:27:
This verse says that Noah kept living 350 years after the flood. The word "after" marks the time from when they came out of the ark and the earth began again. "Three hundred and fifty" is the King James wording for 350.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. After recounting the blessing and the curse Noah spoke over his descendants, the story closes this man's life with a note of time. Added to his 600 years before the flood, the next verse gives the total: 950 years, and then he died. The very long ages in Genesis are understood in several ways, and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: Noah's life did not end with the flood. God gave him many more years to live with Him. Even when we go through very hard moments, God lets us keep going. With His help we can live with faith and leave a good example.
exp.31:8:
Jacob begins to pray. He addresses God as the God of Abraham and of Isaac, that is, the God of the family promise. Then he reminds God of what God himself had told him: that he should return to his land and to his family, and that God would deal well with him. "Kindred" means relatives, and "the Lord" is the name of God.

Jacob is speaking as he returns to Canaan after years with Laban. He learns that his brother Esau is coming to meet him, and he is afraid, because years earlier he had deceived him. That is why he prays: he does not begin by asking, but by resting on God's promise.

For today: when you are afraid, pray by remembering what God has already said in his Word. You can be honest about your fears and, at the same time, rest in the fact that God is faithful to what he has promised.
exp.42:8:
Judah says to his father Jacob: "I will answer for the boy. You may hold me responsible if anything happens to him. If I do not bring him back to you safe and sound, I will bear the blame forever." The word "surety" here means standing as guarantor, that is, taking responsibility for someone. "Require him of my hand" means you may demand him from me.

Jacob did not want to send Benjamin to Egypt because he had already lost Joseph, or so he believed. But the famine was severe and the Egyptian governor demanded to see Benjamin. Reuben had already offered his own sons as a pledge, and Jacob refused. Now Judah speaks, and Jacob yields. Judah shows himself as a man who takes personal responsibility.

For today: when someone depends on us, our word should be serious. Taking responsibility with humility, without excuses, builds trust and can open a path where there had been fear.
exp.10:4:
This verse says that God "came down" to look at the city and the tower that human beings were building. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "the children of men" simply means people, the people of that time.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Earlier, the people wanted to build a city and a very tall tower so they could make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. That God "came down" is a human way of speaking: the tower was enormous to them, but God sees it from his height. Some think there is a touch of irony; others think it simply shows that God examines what we do.

For today: God sees our projects and also the reasons of our heart. Before undertaking something big, ask yourself: am I doing it to honor God and serve others, or only to make a name for myself?
exp.7:2:
The verse says that the waters of the flood were gradually withdrawing from the earth. The phrase "going and returning" suggests a constant movement, like a tide slowly going out. The words that once described the water as turning back or pulling away mean the waters were receding, and "were abated" means they went down. After a hundred and fifty days, the level of the water had dropped noticeably.

The one telling the story is the author of Genesis, recounting what happened after God remembered Noah. That does not mean He had forgotten him, but that He acted on his behalf. God sent a wind, closed the fountains of the deep, and stopped the rain. The account shows that God cares for those under His protection.

Today, this text reminds us that God works with patience. Sometimes trials do not end all at once, but little by little. We can keep trusting that He has not forgotten us.
exp.31:24:
This verse tells that the man wrestling with Jacob saw that he could not overcome him. So he touched the hollow of Jacob's thigh, the part where the bone fits into the socket, and it was put out of joint while they kept wrestling. "Out of joint" means a bone has slipped out of its place, and "the hollow of the thigh" refers to the hip joint.

Jacob is alone at night, by the ford of the Jabbok, and tomorrow he must meet his brother Esau, whom he had deceived. The text calls his opponent a "man," and later Jacob says he saw God face to face. There are different interpretations of who he was exactly, but the account shows a real encounter with God. The injury leaves Jacob marked and weakened.

For today: sometimes God allows us to be left without our own strength so that we learn to depend on Him and to ask for His blessing, instead of trusting in our own strategies.
exp.46:14:
The people of Egypt and Canaan had already spent all their money buying grain. In their desperation, they came to Joseph and asked him for bread. They said they did not want to die in front of him just because their money had run out.

The people speaking here are the Egyptians. We are in the second year of a very severe famine, which had been foretold years earlier by Pharaoh's dreams. Joseph, as the administrator of Egypt, was selling the grain he had stored. Now the people no longer had anything to pay with, and that is why they cry out for help.

For today: when our resources run out, asking for help with humility and sincerity is wise, not shameful. It also reminds us that if God places us in a position to help, we can do so with compassion and justice toward those in need.
exp.42:25:
This verse tells us that Joseph arrived home at midday. His brothers handed him the gift they were carrying in their hands and bowed down to the ground before him. The word "present" here means gift, and the phrase "to the earth" means they lowered their heads until they touched the ground.

The narrator is describing the brothers' second journey to Egypt. They had come back with Benjamin and with gifts to win the governor's favor. Without knowing it, they were fulfilling the dreams Joseph had as a young man, when his brothers bowed down before him (Genesis 37). They still did not recognize him.

God can carry out His plans even when we do not understand them. If you are living through a long wait or a confusing situation today, remember that God is still at work behind what you cannot see. Trust in Him and act with humility and honesty.
exp.17:30:
Abraham continues speaking with the Lord and tells Him that he has now made bold to speak to Him. He asks what would happen if twenty righteous people were found in the city. The Lord answers that He will not destroy it for the sake of those twenty.

Abraham pleads for Sodom, where his nephew Lot lived. God had told him that He would look into the outcry against the city. Abraham lowers the number little by little, with respect and humility, and God answers with patience. This shows that God is both just and merciful.

We can pray with confidence and humility for other people, even for those who are far from God. He is not bothered by our sincere prayers. Think today of someone who needs mercy and bring them before God with respect and hope.
exp.40:0:
This verse says that two full years passed, and then Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, had a dream. In the dream he saw himself standing by the river, which here is the Nile. "It came to pass" means "it happened," and the wording of the King James Version uses the old phrase "it came to pass" where modern English would simply say "it happened."

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Before this moment, Joseph had been in prison in Egypt for years on a false accusation. He had asked the king's cupbearer to remember him, but the cupbearer forgot. These two years of waiting set the stage: Pharaoh's dream will be the means by which Joseph is called. The text does not explain why so much time passed, but it shows that God works in his own time.

For today: when you feel your waiting stretches on and no one remembers you, remember that God's timing is not stalled. Keep being faithful where you are.
exp.3:11:
God tells Cain that when he works the ground, it will no longer yield its strength to him, that is, its good crops. "Tillest" means "working" or "cultivating." Cain will also live as a "fugitive and a vagabond": without a fixed place, moving from one place to another, never feeling at home.

God speaks with Cain after Cain has killed his brother Abel. Cain was a farmer, so the punishment strikes directly at his trade and his way of life. Cain then answers that the punishment is too heavy and fears that he will be killed. Some understand that the ground "will not yield its strength" to mean a smaller harvest; others understand it as a life of great hardship.

For today: our bad decisions leave real consequences. If we have harmed someone, the best thing is to acknowledge it with humility, ask God for forgiveness, and seek to repair the damage, rather than hiding it.
exp.11:2:
God tells Abram that he will look after those who treat him well, and that he will be against those who treat him with contempt. Above all, there is the final promise: through Abram, all the families of the earth would receive a blessing. "Curse" here means to treat with contempt or to wish harm.

It is the LORD who speaks, the God who calls Abram to leave his land, his family and his father's house and go to a place he does not know. With this promise he gives Abram assurance for the journey. Abram was seventy-five years old, and he obeyed. Many Christians see in this a announcement of the blessing that would come through Jesus, a descendant of Abram.

Today we can remember that God blesses so that we may bless others. If you trust in Him, ask yourself: whom can I help, encourage or serve this week?
exp.48:7:
Judah is said to be praised and honored by his brothers. "Thy brethren shall praise" means "your brothers will praise you." "Thy hand shall be in the neck of thine enemies" is an image of victory: having your enemy defeated, turning their backs to you, or brought under your control. "Thy father's children shall bow down before thee" means that the other sons of Jacob will recognize his authority.

Jacob, now an old man, speaks here, blessing and announcing the future of each of his sons. Earlier he had rebuked Simeon and Levi for their violence. Now, with Judah, the tone shifts to honor. The verses that follow speak of a scepter and of someone called Shiloh; many Christians see in this a sign pointing to Jesus, although the term has been interpreted in several ways.

For today: character matters more than birth order. God can raise up imperfect people, and for us the task is to live with humility and faithfulness, trusting that He honors those who serve Him.
exp.48:24:
It says that Joseph will receive help from the God of his father Jacob, and that the Almighty will bless him in every way: with rain and sun "of the heavens above," with water and fertility "of the deep that lies beneath" (the underground waters), and with children and family "of the breasts and of the womb." "Almighty" means the Almighty, the one with all power.

The one speaking is Jacob, now an old man, as he blesses his sons before he dies. Joseph had been attacked by his brothers and others, but God sustained him. Jacob looks back at that suffering and looks ahead to the blessing on Joseph's descendants.

For today: when you feel wounded or unjustly treated, remember that God can sustain you and bless you in ways you do not expect. Trust in his help, and give thanks for the faith that others have passed down to you.
exp.46:5:
Pharaoh tells Joseph that the land of Egypt is at his disposal. He may settle his father and his brothers in the best of the land, in Goshen. If among them there are "men of activity," that is, men who are capable and skilled, he should appoint them as "chief herdsmen" over the king's cattle.

Pharaoh speaks out of gratitude for what Joseph had done during the years of famine. Jacob's family had come fleeing the scarcity in Canaan, and they asked to live in Goshen, an area good for pasturing flocks. Many scholars place it in the eastern part of the Nile Delta, though its exact location is not known.

God uses the faithfulness of one person to provide shelter and provision for others. We can serve with excellence wherever we are, and also give thanks and receive with humility the help God offers us through others.
exp.41:6:
This verse tells us that Joseph recognized his brothers right away when he saw them. But he pretended to be a stranger and spoke to them harshly. He asked them where they came from, and they answered that they came from Canaan, to buy food.

The narrator describes the scene. There is famine throughout the region, and Joseph, already a ruler in Egypt, is selling grain. His brothers, who years earlier had sold him as a slave, arrive and bow down before him without recognizing him. The Bible does not fully explain his reasons, but the passage that follows shows that Joseph remembers his dreams and seems to be testing his brothers. Some think he wanted to see whether they had changed.

For today: when someone has hurt us, we do not need to respond in haste or in anger. We can ask God for wisdom to seek the truth, repentance, and reconciliation with patience and care.
exp.28:4:
Jacob asks some shepherds whether they know Laban, the son of Nahor, and they answer that they do. Nahor was Abraham's brother, so Laban was a relative of Jacob's family. The word "Know ye" is the old form of "Do you know," and "We know him" means that they know who he is.

Jacob has arrived in Haran after fleeing from his home, and he is looking for his family. He speaks with shepherds who are waiting by a well. His question is direct and practical. He does not yet know that God is guiding him, but the story lets us see it: the first shepherd he meets confirms that he is in the right place, and soon Rachel will arrive.

For today: when you do not know where to go, take simple steps and ask questions with humility. God often guides through ordinary conversations and through the people we meet along the way.
exp.38:14:
This verse is part of what Potiphar's wife tells the people of her household. She claims that when she lifted up her voice and cried out, Joseph left his garment beside her, fled, and got himself outside. "Lifted up my voice" means she cried out loudly, and "got him out" means he left the house.

The one speaking is Potiphar's wife, and what she reports is false. Earlier she had insisted that Joseph lie with her, and he had refused out of faithfulness to God and to his master. Now, having been rejected, she changes the story to accuse him. She uses the garment Joseph left behind when he fled as if it were evidence against him.

For today: sometimes we will do what is right and still be misunderstood or unjustly accused. Joseph fled from temptation and kept his integrity. We can do the same and trust that God sees the truth, even when others do not.
exp.11:4:
This verse tells how Abram left Haran, taking his wife Sarai, his nephew Lot, and all his possessions. He also took "the souls that they had gotten," which most likely refers to the servants and people in his household; some understand it to include people who had joined his household. The word "substance" means goods or property. At the end, the text emphasizes that they arrived in the land of Canaan.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. God had already told Abram to leave his country and had promised him a blessing. This verse shows that Abram obeyed and that the journey was not left unfinished: he arrived at the place to which God had sent him.

For today: obeying God often means taking concrete steps without seeing the whole road ahead. If you feel that God is calling you to something, begin with one simple step and bring along those who depend on you, trusting that He will guide you.
exp.13:20:
Here the king of Sodom speaks to Abram after the victory. He asks him to return the people who were rescued, that is, the captured inhabitants, and tells him to keep the "goods," meaning the possessions, the property and the spoils. It is a generous offer at first glance.

Abram had just rescued his nephew Lot and the other captives, and had recovered everything the enemy kings had carried off. He had also just received the blessing of Melchizedek. The king of Sodom, who found himself in debt to him, tries to reward him. In what follows, Abram refuses the spoils so that no one can say his wealth came from that king, but from God.

For today: not every advantageous offer is worth accepting. Before receiving something, it is wise to ask whether it will bind us to someone or dim our trust that God provides.
exp.18:0:
The text says that two angels came to Sodom in the evening. Lot was sitting at the city gate. When he saw them, he got up, went to meet them, and bowed low with his face to the ground as a sign of respect. Some older wording: "at even" means in the evening or at nightfall, and "seeing them" is the phrase "when he saw them."

Here the narrator of the book speaks. The two angels came on the mission announced earlier, and they arrive in the form of men. The city gate was a place where people gathered and handled public business. The text does not say why Lot was there. Some think he held some official role, but the text does not state it. What is clear is that he offered hospitality to strangers, and that was very important in that culture, especially at night and in a dangerous place.

For today: let us be attentive to helping simply anyone who arrives in need. A humble gesture of welcome can matter a great deal, even in a difficult setting.
exp.14:7:
Abram answers God: "Lord GOD, how shall I know that I shall inherit it?" That is, "How can I be certain that I will receive this land as an inheritance?" The word "inherit" means to receive something as a possession that passes from God to one's descendants.

Abram speaks right after God reminded him that he brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees to give him this land. Earlier, Abram "believed in the LORD," and that was counted to him as righteousness. For this reason, the question can be understood as a request for confirmation, not necessarily a lack of faith, although some read it as doubt. God responds with a covenant: He asks for animals, and Abram cuts them in two, a ritual of that era.

For today: you can believe God and still ask Him, with humility and sincerity, to strengthen your trust. He does not get angry at your honest questions.
exp.40:37:
Pharaoh asks his servants whether they could find another man like Joseph, a man in whom is the Spirit of God. It is a question that already carries its answer: there is no one else like him.

Joseph had just interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and proposed a plan to store up food during the seven years of plenty. Pharaoh was an Egyptian king who worshiped many gods. Even so, he recognizes that there is something special in Joseph, something that comes from God. Some understand that Pharaoh was speaking according to his own idea of the divine, and not as someone who already knew the God of Israel.

Today, the wisdom and character of a person who trusts in God can speak for themselves, even before those who do not believe. Work with honesty and humility, and let God be the one who opens doors for you.
exp.21:13:
Abraham gives the place a name that marks where God intervened: "The Lord will provide." By this he remembers that God gave him the ram just in time. The phrase "will be provided" means that God himself takes charge of what is needed. "As it is said to this day" shows that this saying remained in use for a long time afterward.

This is the end of Abraham's hardest test. God had asked him to offer Isaac, and the angel stopped him. Abraham saw a ram caught in a thicket and offered it in place of his son. This verse is the voice of the narrator telling what Abraham said. Some believe the "mount" refers to Moriah, but the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: God does not always show us the way out ahead of time, but we can obey him and trust that he cares for us. Ask him today to teach you to rest in his provision.
exp.29:33:
Laban answers Jacob's proposal by saying that he agrees. "Would it might be according to thy word" is a way of saying: "Very well, so be it." It sounds kind, but the word "would" also shows that Laban accepted the deal gladly because he believed it suited him.

Jacob had just proposed his wages: he would keep only the animals that were speckled, streaked, or dark, which were few. Laban speaks here, and according to what follows, he acts quickly: he sets those animals apart and places them far off, a three days' journey away, in the care of his sons. Many understand that in this way he sought to make sure Jacob would be left with very little. The text says nothing more about his motives.

For today: when someone accepts an agreement with ease, it is good to remember that kind words do not always reveal good intentions. Let us be sincere in our agreements and trust that God sees what happens in secret.
exp.15:9:
The angel of the Lord promises Hagar that her descendants will be so numerous that no one will be able to count them. "Seed" means descendants, and "multitude" means a very large number of people.

Hagar was the servant of Sarai, and she had fled into the desert because Sarai mistreated her. There the angel of the Lord finds her, first asking her to return and then giving her this promise. It is remarkable that God speaks to a woman alone, a foreigner, in a humiliating situation. Afterward the birth of Ishmael is announced. Some believers see in this "angel" a special presence of God himself, but the Bible here does not fully explain it.

For today: when you feel ignored or without a way out, remember that God sees you and hears you. He can give you hope even before your situation changes, and he invites you to trust him step by step.
exp.16:0:
This verse tells us that Abram was ninety-nine years old when God appeared to him. God introduces himself as "the Almighty God" (in Hebrew, El Shaddai). Then he gives two commands: "walk before me," which means living always aware that God sees you, and "be perfect," which here means whole, sincere, without duplicity, not without error.

God himself is speaking. Thirteen years have passed since Ishmael was born, and the promise of a son from Sarah has still not been fulfilled. God presents himself in his power before renewing the covenant, which appears in the next verse. In this way Abram can trust that God will do what seems impossible given his age.

For today: when a promise of God is delayed or seems impossible, remember who He is. Respond with an honest and steady life, walking each day as one who knows that God is present.
exp.30:15:
Here Rachel and Leah tell Jacob that all the wealth that God took away from their father Laban now belongs to them and to their children. That is why they urge him to do everything God has told him. The word "substance" refers to goods and animals.

Rachel and Leah, Jacob's wives, are the ones speaking. Jacob had told them that God commanded him to return to his land. They feel that their father treated them as strangers, since, as they put it, he "sold" them and spent what was paid for them. Seeing this, they decide to support their husband. Some think they are referring to Jacob's years of labor for them.

Today we can learn to support, in faith, decisions we believe come from God, especially within the family. Before acting, it is wise to speak honestly, seek unity, and obey with confidence.
exp.22:12:
Abraham answers Ephron in front of the people of the city. He says: "Please listen to me; I will pay the price of the field. Accept it from me, and there I will bury my dead." Some older words in this passage: "field" here means a piece of land or property, "I pray thee" means "please," and "my dead" refers to Sarah, his wife.

Sarah had just died, and Abraham, who was a foreigner in that land, needed a place to bury her. Ephron offered to give him the field and the cave. Abraham does not refuse him rudely, but he insists on paying. He probably wanted the property to be his in a clear and public way, without debts or doubts later on. Some think it was also a custom of negotiation in that time.

For today: act with honesty and clarity in your dealings. Even when someone offers you a favor, it is sometimes better to pay what is fair to avoid misunderstandings later.
exp.45:0:
This verse tells us that Jacob, also called Israel, left his land with his whole family and everything he owned. He came to Beersheba and there offered sacrifices to God, the same God whom his father Isaac had worshiped. In the King James wording, "took his journey" means "set out" or "went on his way," and "came to" means "arrived at."

The narrator of the book describes this moment. Jacob is on his way to Egypt because his son Joseph is alive there and there is famine in Canaan. Beersheba was an important place in the story of his fathers, Abraham and Isaac. Before taking such a big step, Jacob stops to worship. Soon afterward, God speaks to him and promises to be with him.

Before making important decisions, seek God. You can pause to pray, give thanks, and ask Him for direction. In this way you move forward with greater peace, knowing that He walks with you into the unknown.
exp.22:8:
Abraham asks that they give him the cave of Machpelah, which is at the end of Ephron's field. He wants to buy it at its full worth, as a possession for burying his dead among them. In the King James wording, "possession" refers to land or property held as one's own, and "buryingplace" is a place for burying.

Abraham is the one speaking. His wife Sarah has just died, and he lives as a foreigner in Canaan, without land of his own. So he respectfully asks the sons of Heth to speak on his behalf to Ephron. He does not want a gift, but a clear and lawful purchase, made openly before everyone, so that no one can later dispute ownership of that place.

For today: when you face a difficult moment, act with humility, honesty, and order. Abraham, in the midst of grief, treated his neighbors with respect and wanted to pay what was fair. Doing things with integrity leaves a good witness and prevents future conflicts.
exp.11:6:
The explanation says that God appeared to Abram and promised to give that land to his "seed," meaning his descendants. Abram responded by building an altar to the Lord. "Jehovah" is God's name, and "appeared" indicates that God made himself present in some way; the text does not explain how.

The one speaking is God, and he does so after Abram had arrived in Canaan with his family. He had left because of an earlier call from God. The promise carries weight because the Canaanite was living in that land at the time, so Abram did not yet see its fulfillment.

For today: when God gives you a promise you do not yet see fulfilled, you can respond with gratitude and worship, as Abram did. Before there are results, you can pause, give thanks, and trust that God is faithful.
exp.48:29:
The explanation says that the cave where Jacob wants to be buried is in the field of Machpelah, in front of Mamre, in the land of Canaan. Abraham bought that field with the cave from Ephron the Hittite. "Burying place" means a property set aside for burying the family. "Before" means "in front of" or "east of."

Jacob, now an old man, is speaking just after blessing his twelve sons. He asks them to bury him with his fathers, not in Egypt, where they were living at that time. This shows his faith that God would keep the promise to give Canaan to his family. That land was the place of his hope.

For today: Jacob thought about his spiritual inheritance and about God's faithfulness to the very end. Today we can ask ourselves what we leave to those who come after us: not only possessions, but a firm faith in God's promises.
exp.49:11:
This verse says that Jacob's sons did what their father had asked of them before he died. The phrase "did so" simply means "they did it that way." The phrase "just as he had commanded them" means "exactly as he had ordered them." It refers to Jacob's wish to be buried in Canaan.

The narrator is telling the end of Jacob's story. Before he died, he asked to be buried in the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham and Sarah were laid. His sons, with Joseph at their head, travelled from Egypt to carry it out. The mourning at the threshing floor of Atad was so great that the Canaanites took notice.

Honouring the last wish of someone we love is a form of respect and gratitude. When a father, a mother, or a grandparent asks us for something good before they go, keeping that request faithfully is an act of love.
exp.2:12:
God asks the woman, "What is this that you have done?" She answers that the serpent deceived her, and that is why she ate the fruit. "Deceived" means to make someone believe something false. She admits that she ate, but points to the serpent as the cause.

God speaks after having questioned the man, who blamed the woman. God does not ask because He lacks information, but to give them the opportunity to confess honestly. Then God turns to the serpent. The Bible says the woman was deceived, and the text does not explain further how the serpent is connected with evil. Some Christians see Satan here, although the text does not say it in those words.

For today: when we fail, it is tempting to explain what happened by putting the blame on others. God invites us to tell the truth, "I was wrong," and to return to Him, who offers forgiveness.
exp.0:22:
This verse closes the fifth day of creation. The phrase "the evening and the morning" is the way Genesis marks the end of each day. In the King James wording, "were the fifth day" is the phrase that states this closing.

The narrator of the book tells us that on this day God filled the sea and the sky with living creatures, blessed them, and commanded them to multiply. The account then moves on to the sixth day. Christians understand in different ways whether these days are twenty-four hours long or longer periods, but all agree that God is the author of life.

For today: just as God works in order and rests when each stage is finished, you too can close your day by handing over to God what you have done and trusting that he continues to care for life.
exp.43:22:
Here the condition that the governor of Egypt had set is repeated: if the youngest brother does not go down with them, they will not be able to see him again. The word "go down" here means "come down," and the phrase "ye shall see my face no more" means that he would not receive them again.

The speaker is Judah, addressing Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize. He is recounting what happened on the first journey to Egypt. Judah explains why Benjamin had to come, even though his father Jacob suffered over letting him go. His account prepares the offer he will make afterward: to stay behind as a slave in Benjamin's place.

For today: when we face a difficult situation, we can speak with sincerity and take responsibility for those we love. Judah does not defend himself or hide; he puts himself at the service of his family. That humble and courageous attitude can guide our decisions.
exp.39:15:
Here the chief baker of Pharaoh hears that Joseph gave a good interpretation of the cupbearer's dream. Encouraged, he tells Joseph his own dream: he saw three white baskets on his head. The King James Version says "chief baker," and the word "chief" means the head or leader of the bakers. The phrase "white baskets" refers to small baskets, perhaps for bread; some believe "white" may refer to the kind of bread or the material, but this is not certain.

The baker speaks while he is in prison with Joseph in Egypt. He hopes for a favorable answer, like the one the cupbearer received. What follows shows that his dream had a very different meaning, and Joseph will tell him so honestly.

For today: it is natural to desire good news, but we will not always receive it. We can seek the truth with humility, listen with courage, and entrust our future to God, who remains faithful even when the outcome hurts us.
exp.9:18:
This verse describes how far the territory of the Canaanites reached. It ran from Sidon, in the north, south through Gerar to Gaza, and then eastward, toward Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboim, and Lasha. The old wording "as thou comest to" means "as you travel toward," and "border" is the word for the limit or boundary.

No one speaks in the first person here. The narrator of Genesis presents what is called the "table of nations," which lists the peoples descended from Noah. This passage concerns the descendants of Canaan, son of Ham. It places on the map the peoples who will later appear in the story of Abraham. Some of these places, such as Sodom and Gomorrah, become well known later on. The exact location of some of them is uncertain.

For today: God knows the places and the peoples by name and in detail. Your story is also within his sight, and you can trust that he knows you and cares for you.
exp.24:30:
Jacob says to his brother Esau, "Sell me this day thy birthright." The birthright was the special right of the eldest son: it usually included a double portion of the inheritance and a place of leadership in the family. Asking Esau to sell it means asking him to give it up in exchange for something, here in return for food.

It is Jacob, the younger brother, who speaks. Esau has just come in from the field, tired and hungry, and asks for some of the red stew. Jacob takes advantage of that moment of need to ask for something far more valuable. The Bible does not say that Jacob acted well; rather, it shows how Esau placed little value on what God considered important (Hebrews 12:16).

Today we can learn not to exchange what is eternal for a passing desire. Before deciding while hungry, exhausted, or under pressure, it is wise to stop and ask: what am I willing to lose for this?
exp.7:18:
This verse says that all the animals came out of the ark: the beasts, the creeping things, and the birds, each according to its kind. Whatever moves upon the earth returned to it after the flood. "Creeping thing" refers to animals that crawl or move close to the ground.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Earlier, God had commanded Noah to bring out all the animals so that they would be fruitful, multiply, and fill the earth. This verse shows that Noah and creation obeyed. Then Noah offers a sacrifice to God, and God promises never again to destroy the earth in this way.

For today: when God brings us out of a difficult time, the first step is to go out trusting and obeying, and afterward to thank him. A new beginning is best lived with a grateful heart.
exp.34:4:
The explanation says that Jacob and his family left Shechem on their way to Bethel. Along the way, God caused a great fear to fall on the neighboring cities, so no one pursued them. The word "terror" here refers to a fear sent by God, not one caused by Jacob's strength.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Shortly before, Jacob and his sons had acted violently in Shechem (chapter 34), and Jacob feared revenge from the nearby peoples. Then God told him to go up to Bethel. Jacob asked his household to put away the foreign gods and the earrings, and he buried them under an oak. After that cleansing, protection came.

For today: when God calls us to obey him, we can trust that he watches over our path. First remove whatever gets in the way of your faith, and take the next step with confidence in his protection.
exp.44:25:
Joseph's brothers arrive in Canaan and give Jacob an incredible piece of news: Joseph is still alive and rules all of Egypt. Hearing it, Jacob's heart "fainted," that is, he was left as if paralyzed, without strength from the shock. And he "believed them not," because it seemed impossible to him.

The ones speaking are Jacob's sons. For many years they had led him to believe that Joseph was dead. That is why the news costs him so much. Then they tell him everything Joseph said, and Jacob sees the wagons Joseph sent. Then his spirit revives and he decides to go and see him.

Sometimes a good piece of news seems too big to believe, especially after a long time of pain. God is not bothered by our difficulty. We can bring that doubt to Him honestly, and He often helps us believe little by little, with concrete signs of His faithfulness.
exp.46:22:
Here Joseph speaks to the Egyptian people after the famine. He tells them that they and their land now belong to Pharaoh, but he gives them seed to plant. The King James wording "seed" is the grain they will sow, and "I have bought you" means he acquired their land in exchange for the grain he gave them.

Joseph is the administrator of Egypt under Pharaoh. During the years of famine, the people had already spent their money and their livestock to buy food. Now they also hand over their land. Joseph gives them seed and sets one condition: a fifth of the harvest will go to Pharaoh. The priests were left out because they already received their allowance. The text describes what happened and does not say whether everything was fair or ideal.

For today: when someone goes through hardship, helping them is not only giving temporary relief but also giving them a way to work and support themselves again, with clear and fair arrangements.
exp.23:47:
This verse says that Abraham's servant bowed his face to the ground, worshipped the LORD, and gave thanks. He recognizes that God led him "in the right way," that is, on the correct path, to find Abraham's niece and bring her to marry Isaac. "Blessed" here means "praised" or "gave thanks." "Worshipped" means "bowed down in worship."

Here the servant speaks, although the Bible does not give his name in this passage. He is in the house of Bethuel, telling Rebekah's family how he came to them. He explains that his prayer was answered at the well. With this account he wants them to see the hand of God in everything and to give an answer about the marriage.

For today: when you see that God guides or answers you, stop to thank Him. Before moving forward, acknowledge that it was He who opened the way.
exp.14:11:
It says that, as the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram. And suddenly he felt a great dread, like an enormous, heavy darkness covering him. "Overwhelmed" means that it took him by surprise and overpowered him. "Dread" is a very great fear.

Here God is making a covenant with Abram. Abram had prepared the animals cut in two, as was done in certain ancient covenants. While he waits, he drives away the birds that came down upon the carcasses. Then this sleep comes, and God himself begins to speak to him. He announces that his descendants will suffer in a foreign land, but that God will judge that nation and bring them out with great possessions. Some see here a reference to Egypt.

For today: sometimes God lets us see that there are dark and difficult moments along the way. Even so, his promise stands. We can trust that he is present and in control, even when we feel afraid or do not understand everything.
exp.17:17:
This verse is part of a question God asks himself: "Shall I hide from Abraham the thing that I do, seeing that Abraham shall surely become a great and mighty nation, and all the nations of the earth shall be blessed in him?" The word "nations" here means peoples or nations.

The LORD speaks while the three visitors head toward Sodom. God remembers the promise he made to Abraham and decides to tell him about the judgment that is coming, because he has chosen Abraham to guide his household in the way of righteousness. Some understand that in this way God treats Abraham as a trusted friend.

For today: God invites us into a close relationship, not a distant one. When we set aside time to listen to him in his Word and in prayer, we learn to see the world as he sees it, and we are encouraged to live righteously and to lead our family in his way.
exp.36:29:
Reuben returns to his brothers and says, "The boy is not, and I, where shall I go?" The Hebrew word for "boy" refers to José, who was a young man. The King James wording "is not" carries the sense of "is gone" or "is missing," meaning he cannot be found. Reuben speaks in anguish, because he does not know how to face what has happened.

Reuben, the eldest brother, is the one speaking. Earlier he had proposed throwing José into the cistern, and the text of Genesis 37:22 says he intended to rescue him afterward and return him to his father. But while he was away, the others sold José. Reuben feels responsible before Jacob, his father.

For today: when a situation gets out of our hands, feeling pain is not enough. We must act in time, with courage and with truth. Reuben tried to do the right thing only halfway; today we can ask God for the firmness to defend what is right from the very beginning.
exp.34:9:
God tells Jacob that he will no longer be called Jacob, but Israel. The text says "told him" and "descendants" appears in the verses that follow, meaning offspring. God confirms the new name, and Jacob is called Israel.

God speaks here, appearing to Jacob again at Bethel, when he returns from Paddan-aram. Earlier, in Genesis 32, he had received that name after wrestling with a divine being. Here God affirms it and repeats his promises: a numerous nation, kings, and the land promised to Abraham and Isaac. The exact meaning of "Israel" is explained in several ways; many connect it with wrestling or persevering with God.

For today: God does not define us by our past or by our mistakes. Jacob had deceived and fled, but God gave him a new identity. We can trust that, if we walk with him, he is shaping us and calling us by what he wants to do in us.
exp.31:20:
The explanation says that the gifts Jacob prepared for his brother Esau went on ahead, passing over before him. Jacob, by contrast, stayed that night in the camp. "Present" means gift or offering, and "company" refers to the group of people with whom he was camping.

The narrator tells us that Jacob was afraid of meeting Esau, whom years earlier he had deceived. For that reason he sent animals in groups, with messengers who would say that he was coming behind them. He wanted to calm his brother's anger. Shortly afterward, that same night, he would get up, cross the river Jabbok, and wrestle with God. Some see in that quiet night only a brief moment before the great trial, although the text gives no further details.

For today: doing what is ours to do to be reconciled, such as asking forgiveness or taking a humble step, is good. But afterward we must hand the outcome over to God and rest in Him, without living ruled by fear.
exp.37:8:
It says that Onan knew the child born would not be considered his. For that reason, when he was with the wife of his dead brother, he would spill his seed on the ground so as not to give offspring to his brother. The King James wording "seed" means offspring, and "went in unto his brother's wife" means had relations with her.

The text tells what happened after the death of Er. Judah asked Onan to fulfill the custom of raising up an heir for the deceased brother, so that his name and family would continue. Onan agreed in appearance, but acted out of selfishness. The passage says that the LORD was displeased with what he did. Many understand that the sin was refusing to fulfill his duty to Tamar and his brother.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we fulfill our responsibilities to others or seek only our own benefit. God looks at the heart behind our actions.
exp.41:33:
Here, what Joseph, still without revealing himself, had asked of his brothers is repeated. They were to bring him Benjamin, the youngest brother, to prove that they were not spies but "true men", that is, honest and sincere people. The wording "so will I deliver you your brother" means he would release Simeon; and "ye shall traffick in the land" means they could trade and move freely in the land.

The one speaking is Jacob, to whom his sons recount what happened in Egypt. There was famine in Canaan, and they went to buy grain. The ruler, who was Joseph, kept Simeon as a guarantee. The brothers report to their father, but he suffers greatly, because he fears losing Benjamin as well.

For today: trust is tested by deeds, and sometimes God leads us through difficult situations to bring to light what is in the heart. When fear dominates us, we can remember that God works even where we see no way out.
exp.2:13:
God the Lord speaks to the serpent and tells it that it will be cursed above all the animals. "Cattle" and "beasts of the field" refer to both tame animals and wild ones. Going "upon your belly" means crawling, and "eating dust" is an image of humiliation and defeat. "Because" is the sense of "because" in the King James wording "Because thou hast done this."

The Lord God speaks after the man and the woman have eaten the forbidden fruit. First He questioned them, and now He pronounces judgment on the serpent, which had deceived the woman. Many understand that the serpent was an instrument of God's enemy, although the text does not say this in those words. Christians often see in the following verse a first promise of victory.

For today: evil does not have the last word. Even in the midst of the consequences of sin, God acts with justice and leaves hope open. We can trust that He takes care of us.
exp.4:10:
This verse closes the account of the life of Enos, grandson of Adam through his son Seth. It says that he lived a total of 905 years and that he died. The word "begat" in the King James Version is an older form meaning that he became a father, and "and" here is the same as in modern English.

The narrator of Genesis (tradition points to Moses, though it is not known how the text was brought together) presents a list of generations. The same pattern repeats: a man is born, has children, lives many years, and dies. This shows how humanity continues and, at the same time, how death remains present after the fall of Adam. About Enos, the text gives no further details of his life.

For today: our life is brief, even if it is very long. We should live it with purpose, teaching the faith to the next generation and trusting in God, who is the one who gives meaning to our days.
exp.27:20:
It says that if Jacob returns safe and sound to his father's house, then the Lord will be his God. The word "come again" means "return," and "in peace" means without harm, in well-being. It is the last condition of a vow that Jacob makes.

Jacob is speaking, as he flees from his brother Esau on his way to Haran. He has just dreamed of a ladder reaching to heaven, and God promised to be with him. Jacob responds with a vow. Scholars explain the phrase "then shall the Lord be my God" in different ways: some see a promise of total loyalty, others a response still weighed down with conditions.

For today: trusting God is not enough when everything goes well. We can decide to follow him from now on, sincerely and steadily, remembering that he has already cared for us along the way and that his faithfulness does not depend on how we bargain with him.
exp.43:26:
In this verse, Judah repeats what Jacob, their father, told them. Jacob reminds them that his wife Rachel bore him only two sons: Joseph and Benjamin.

The word "bare" means "gave birth to." The KJV's "Ye know" is the older form of "you know."

Judah speaks before Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize as his brother, and who is governor of Egypt. He wants to persuade him to let Benjamin go free. To do so, he explains how much their father would suffer if he lost this son, since he already believes Joseph is dead. Rachel was Jacob's most beloved wife, and for that reason their two sons were very dear to him.

For today: when we ask something on behalf of others, let us speak with humility and empathy, showing the pain a decision may cause. Thinking about the hearts of others helps us act with compassion and seek the good of the family.
exp.35:17:
This verse lists the sons of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives. Three chiefs came from her: Jeush, Jaalam and Korah. The word "duke" is an older English term, and here it means a chief or head of a clan, not a European noble title. Aholibamah was the daughter of Anah.

Moses, traditionally recognized as the author of the book, includes this list to record how the descendants of Esau, called Edomites, were formed as a people in the land of Edom. Before continuing with the story of Joseph, the account closes the line of Esau. This shows that God kept his word to make him into a nation, even though the main promise continued through Jacob.

For today: God cares for every family, even those that do not carry the central thread of the story. Value your place and trust that God sees you. Live with gratitude, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.42:5:
Israel, that is, Jacob, asks his sons: "Why did you treat me so badly by telling that man you had another brother?" The word "man" here means "man," and "declaring" means "telling" or "reporting."

There is famine across the whole land, and Jacob's sons need to go back to Egypt for food. That man, Joseph, whom they do not yet recognize, demanded that they bring Benjamin. Jacob believes he has already lost Joseph, and he fears losing Benjamin too. That is why he is distressed and looks for someone to blame. The sons explain that they only answered the questions they were asked.

When we are afraid, it is easy to complain and blame others. Before reacting, it is wise to pause, listen calmly, and entrust our fears to God, who works even in what we do not understand.
exp.45:15:
This verse lists the seven sons of Gad, one of the sons of Jacob. The names appear in the spelling used in this version, and in other Bibles some of them are written differently, such as Zephon, Haggi, Ezbon, Shuni, Eri, Arodi, and Areli. The verb "bore" that appears in the surrounding context simply means "gave birth to."

Here there is no character speaking; it is the narrator's account. Jacob and his family are preparing to go down to Egypt, where Joseph lives. The writer gives the list of those who went with him to show how the people of Israel began. Gad was a son of Zilpah, Leah's servant.

For today: God pays attention to each person and remembers their name, even when we pass over lists like this one. This encourages us to value others, even those who seem unimportant, because they are part of God's plan.
exp.25:14:
This verse tells us that the Philistines stopped up all the wells that Abraham's servants had dug years before. They "stopped them," that is, they blocked them and filled them with earth so that they could no longer be used. In that dry land, water meant life for people and for animals.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Isaac is living in Gerar, and God has blessed him greatly. The Philistines envy him, and for this reason they destroy what his father had left behind. Shortly afterward, Abimelech asks him to leave. Some think they stopped up the wells to harm him or to drive him out of the region. The text does not state this clearly.

For today: sometimes others can damage the good things we receive, out of envy or selfishness. We should not respond with violence. Isaac remained at peace and kept trusting in God.
exp.5:1:
This verse tells how the "sons of God" saw that the "daughters of men" were beautiful, and they took as wives those they chose. "They took" means they took for themselves, and "chose" means they picked as they pleased, guided by appearance.

The narrator describes how wickedness grew before the flood. It is not known for certain who the "sons of God" were. Some think they were descendants of Seth, the faithful line, who mixed with the line of Cain. Others believe they were fallen spiritual beings. Both views have been held for centuries, and the text does not fully settle the question. What is clear is that God responds with judgment in the verses that follow.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we choose a partner, or make other important decisions, only by what we see. Beauty is not wrong, but we also need to seek God's guidance and a faithful character.
exp.48:10:
He says that Judah will have so much abundance that he ties his donkey colt to a vine, without fear that it will eat it. A "colt" is a young donkey, and "choice vine" refers to the vine plant. He even washes his clothes in wine, "the blood of grapes," as if it were plentiful. It is a poetic image of great prosperity.

Jacob, already old, blesses his twelve sons before he dies. Here he speaks of Judah, from whose tribe the royal line would come. Many Christians see in the previous verse, "until Shiloh comes," a sign of the Messiah, and read this abundance as a picture of his kingdom. Others understand it only as the future wealth of the tribe. The text allows both readings.

For today: God knows how to bless generously. Acknowledge what you have received, give thanks for it, and use it simply, without clinging to it. And trust that Christ, the promised king, offers an abundance deeper than any harvest.
exp.29:30:
Laban asks Jacob what he should pay him, and Jacob replies that he does not want to receive anything up front. He only asks that Laban accept a proposal, and in return he will go on tending Laban's flocks.

Jacob has worked for his father-in-law Laban for years, and Laban has grown very prosperous. Now Jacob wants to build his own property for his family. The proposal that follows is that he ask, as his wages, the spotted and dark-colored animals, which were the minority, so that everything would be clear and fair.

For today: when you negotiate something, be clear and honest from the very start. A transparent agreement prevents misunderstandings and protects relationships. And trust that God can bless you as you work with integrity.
exp.17:25:
It says that God, here called Jehovah, accepts Abraham's request. If there were fifty righteous people within the city of Sodom, God would spare the whole place for their sake.

The verse uses the word "find" for what the Hebrew-era text conveys, and "for their sakes" means "out of consideration for them" or "because of them."

Jehovah speaks, answering Abraham. The divine visitors had warned him that they were going to examine the wickedness of Sodom. Abraham, concerned for the righteous and for his nephew Lot, who lived there, prays with reverence and asks whether the Judge of all the earth will not do what is just. God shows patience and a willingness to listen.

Today we can pray with confidence for our city, family, and country, appealing to God's justice and mercy. Our prayer matters, and the presence of faithful people can be a blessing to others.
exp.23:22:
Here the servant of Abraham asks the young woman whose daughter she is and whether there is room in her father's house for them to spend the night. The word "lodge" in the King James wording is an older way of saying "to stay overnight" or "to find lodging." Before asking, he had already given her a gold ring and two bracelets.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac among his master's relatives. He had prayed for a sign, and Rebekah fulfilled it by giving water to him and to his camels. He watches quietly to see whether God was giving success to his journey. That is why he asks about her family: he wants to confirm whether she is from Abraham's kin.

For today: when you ask God for direction, observe carefully and without rushing how he answers. Then take concrete steps, as this servant did, trusting that God also guides through the everyday.
exp.6:1:
God gives Noah instructions about how many animals he must take into the ark. Of the "clean" animals (those that were later permitted for eating and for sacrifices) he was to take seven, that is, seven pairs or, according to some, seven in total; the text can be understood in either way. Of the "unclean" animals he was to take only one pair: male and female.

The LORD speaks shortly before the flood. He had already told Noah to enter the ark because He saw him as righteous in his generation. These instructions were meant to preserve the life of the animals on the earth. The clean animals would later be used to offer sacrifices (Genesis 8:20).

For today: Noah obeyed in detail, even though the rain was still a week away. We can trust God's instructions and carry them out carefully, even when we do not yet see the result.
exp.49:12:
This verse tells us that the sons of Jacob carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah. Abraham had bought that field from Ephron the Hittite to have it as a burial place. It lay before Mamre. The phrase "a possession of a buryingplace" means a piece of property set aside for burying one's family.

The speaker here is the narrator of the book. Jacob had asked to be buried in Canaan and not in Egypt. His sons carried out that request. This shows that the family still believed in God's promise concerning that land, even though they were living in Egypt.

For today: carefully keeping what we promise to our loved ones, especially when it expresses their faith, is a way of honoring them and of trusting that God keeps his promises.
exp.1:21:
It says that God took the rib he had taken from the man and with it made a woman. Then he brought her to the man. The word "rib" can also be understood as "side," according to some Hebrew scholars.

The one telling the story is the author of Genesis. Earlier, Adam had named the animals and found none that was a suitable companion for him. So God acts. Afterward, Adam celebrates with joy: "bone of my bones." Many see here that the woman is equal to the man in dignity and nature.

For today: God created relationships so that we would keep each other company, not live alone. Today we can value the people close to us, such as a spouse, family, or friends, and treat them with respect, as equals before God.
exp.36:30:
This verse tells that Joseph's brothers took his coat, the long colored tunic that Jacob had given him, killed a young goat, and stained the garment with its blood. The word "killed" here refers to slaughtering the animal, which is the term used for killing a goat for food or for sacrifice.

The narrator recounts what Jacob's sons did after selling Joseph to some merchants. Reuben, who wanted to save him, had just discovered that the cistern was empty. The brothers prepare a deception to hide their guilt and make their father believe that a wild animal had killed Joseph.

A great sin often leads to another: unresolved envy ended in lies and deceit. Today we can learn to face our resentments in time and to ask forgiveness honestly, instead of covering our mistakes with more lies. God can forgive and heal what we hide when we bring it into the light.
exp.42:11:
The explanation says that the brothers were to take double the money in their hands. They were also to return the money that had been found in the mouths of their sacks, because perhaps it was a mistake. "Double money" means twice the amount; "oversight" means an error or mistake.

Jacob, also called Israel, is the speaker. There is famine in the land, and his sons have already bought grain in Egypt. On the first trip, the money appeared in their sacks, and that frightened them. Now Jacob, though fearful, agrees to send Benjamin and prepares everything with care and honesty. Here the text does not say whether Jacob thought it was a real error; it only says "perhaps."

For today: when you have received something that does not belong to you, return it with sincerity, even when it is frightening. Honesty opens the way and leaves the outcome in God's hands.
exp.36:26:
Judah proposes to his brothers that they sell Joseph to some Ishmaelite traders, instead of killing him. He says "let not our hand be upon him" so that they themselves would not be the ones who kill him, and he reminds them that "he is our brother and our flesh," that is, of the same blood. "Were content" means that they agreed.

Judah, one of Jacob's sons, is the speaker. The brothers were jealous of Joseph and resentful toward him, and they had thrown him into a pit. Judah sees a way out that avoids shedding blood, but it is still a cruel act: they sell their brother. The following text also mentions Midianites, and there have been several explanations of how they relate to the Ishmaelites.

For today: be careful not to justify wrongdoing by saying it is "less bad." Recognizing our bond with another person should lead us to protect them, not merely to avoid the worst. God can work even through our failures, but that does not erase our responsibility.
exp.9:25:
This verse begins the list of the sons of Joktan, brother of Peleg and a descendant of Eber. The names are Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth and Jerah. "Begat" means that he was their father. The list continues in the following verses until it reaches thirteen sons.

The narrator is the author of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses. This section, called the Table of Nations, shows how the families descended from Noah's sons spread out after the flood. Many scholars connect the sons of Joktan with peoples in the south of the Arabian Peninsula, but the exact identification of several of the names is uncertain and is debated.

God knows each person by name, even when the story may seem to us to be nothing more than a list. Today we can remember that no one is insignificant to Him. Value others and pray for them by name, including those who go unnoticed.
exp.48:30:
Here Jacob lists who is buried in the cave of Machpelah: Abraham with Sarah, Isaac with Rebekah, and Leah, his wife. "Buried" here means they were laid to rest in the tomb, and "I buried" means "I laid her to rest." Leah is mentioned, but Rachel, Jacob's other wife, is not.

Jacob is about to die in Egypt and gives his final instructions to his sons. He asks them not to leave him there, but to carry him back to Canaan, to the family tomb. That cave was the only piece of land Abraham had bought in the land God had promised him. For Jacob, being buried there expressed his trust that God would fulfill that promise.

For today: think about the faith that others have left you, and live in such a way that your trust in God also becomes a clear witness to those who come after you.
exp.4:25:
It says that Methuselah lived 782 years after he became the father of his son Lamech, and that during that time he had other sons and daughters. "Begat" means that he became a father. The older forms of the names, which the explanation notes, are Mathusalam and Lamech. Adding the 187 years before, his years total 969.

This is part of the genealogy in Genesis 5, a third-person account with no character speaking. Its purpose is to show the line of descendants from Adam toward Noah, and how life continued even under the shadow of death. Earlier, Enoch is mentioned, who walked with God. Methuselah was his son. How to understand these very long lifespans is interpreted in several ways, and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: our life is much more than a name in a list. Methuselah raised a family over many years. We can use our time to form our own children in the faith, just as Enoch left an example of walking with God.
exp.28:13:
Laban says to Jacob, "Surely you are my bone and my flesh," an old way of saying "you are of my own family, my own blood." After that, the text tells us that Jacob stayed with him a full month.

It is Laban speaking, the brother of Rebekah and the uncle of Jacob. Jacob had just arrived, fleeing from his home, and he told Laban everything that had happened. Laban received him with embraces and brought him into his house. These words show that he accepted Jacob as part of the family. What follows, with the matter of wages and the dealings between the two, shows that the relationship would soon become more complicated.

For today: welcoming others with affection is a beautiful gesture, like opening your home to a relative or to someone who arrives weary. But it is also wise to be clear and wise in agreements, so that a good relationship is cared for and lasts.
exp.16:7:
God promises Abraham that he will give to him and to his descendants all the land of Canaan as an inheritance forever. "Descendants" means offspring, and the "land where you were a stranger" refers to the places where Abraham had lived as a foreigner. God also promises: "I will be their God."

God himself is speaking, when Abraham was ninety-nine years old. God is confirming his covenant, or agreement, and shortly afterward asks for circumcision as its sign. The word "everlasting" is understood in different ways: some see it as a promise for all time, and others emphasize that its fulfillment unfolds throughout history.

The most valuable part of this promise is not only the land, but that God says: "I will be their God." Today you can trust that God keeps what he promises, even when it takes time. Take a moment to thank him for wanting a close relationship with you.
exp.16:15:
God speaks to Abraham about his wife Sarah. He says that he will bless her, and that through her Abraham will have a son. Furthermore, she will be the mother of nations, and kings of peoples will come from her.

God is renewing his covenant with Abraham, and has just changed Sarah's name (formerly Sarai). Until now Abraham had Ishmael, the son of the servant Hagar, but God makes clear that the promise will pass through Sarah. Abraham is nearly a hundred years old and Sarah ninety, so the promise seems impossible. That is why Abraham laughs, astonished, in the next verse.

For today: God keeps his promises in his own way and in his own time, even when they seem impossible to us. Today you can hand over a situation that looks hopeless and trust that he is faithful, while you continue to obey him with patience.
exp.33:13:
The sons of Jacob answer that they cannot give their sister Dinah to a man who is uncircumcised, because that would be a disgrace to them. "Foreskin" is the skin that is cut away in circumcision, and "abomination" here means something shameful or unacceptable. "Defiled" means dishonored or abused.

The sons of Jacob speak, answering Shechem and his father Hamor. Shechem had dishonored Dinah and now wanted to marry her. The text says they answered "deceitfully": they used circumcision, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham, as a pretext to hide their plan of revenge. Later we will see that they used religion to deceive.

For today: let us take care that our faith is not an excuse to justify anger or revenge. When we have been wounded, let us seek truth and justice honestly, not with deception.
exp.1:8:
It says that God caused every kind of tree to grow from the ground, trees that are beautiful and good for food. Two trees stand out in the middle of the garden: the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. "Pleasant to the sight" means pleasing to look at. "Knowledge" here means understanding.

The narrator tells how God prepared a home for the man he had just formed. The writer presents God as a generous provider: he gives beauty and food.
