The two special trees set up what comes next, when God gives a command about one of them. Scholars explain in various ways what these trees symbolize, and the text does not fully make it clear.

For today: God gives us much to enjoy and be thankful for. He also sets limits for our good. We can trust that his limits do not take our life away, but rather care for it.
exp.16:20:
God tells Abraham that his covenant, that is, his solemn promise, will be with Isaac. Sarah will give birth to this son "at this set time next year," that is, roughly in one year. The word "bear" means "give birth."

God speaks with Abraham, who was already nearly a hundred years old. Abraham had asked that Ishmael, his first son, might live before God. God promises to bless Ishmael, but makes clear that the promise of the covenant would continue through Isaac. No one could bring this about by their own strength, because Abraham and Sarah were very old. Shortly afterward, Abraham obeys and circumcises the males of his household.

For today: God keeps his promises in his own way and in his own time, even when they seem impossible to us. We can trust Him and obey Him today, without waiting to understand everything.
exp.4:1:
The explanation says that God created human beings as male and female, blessed them, and gave them the name "Adam", which in Hebrew means "human" or "person". This happened on the same day they were created. Some older wording: "created" is the word used here for "made", and the word "female" in this verse refers to a woman.

The narrator of Genesis, traditionally associated with Moses, opens a list of families with "the book of the generations of Adam". Before going on to the descendants, he recalls the origin: God made humankind in his likeness. It is then told that Adam had a son in his own likeness, named Seth. This shows a line running from God, to Adam, and to his children.

For today: if every person, man or woman, was created and blessed by God, they deserve respect and dignity. Today you can treat others, even those who think differently from you, as someone who carries the worth God gave them.
exp.4:14:
Genesis 5:15 says that Mahalaleel lived sixty-five years and became the father of Jared. Some of the wording is old: "begat" means that he was the father of someone, and the word "and" is used in its older, repeated way to link each step of the list. The verse does not say that Jared was the firstborn; it only names the son who continues the family line that is being recorded.

We are in the genealogy of Genesis 5, which runs from Adam to Noah. No character speaks here; it is the narrator, traditionally credited as Moses, who records the descent. The chapter shows how life continues from generation to generation, and that death reaches everyone, as seen in the repeated phrase "and he died."

For today: our life is brief, but it leaves a mark on those who come after us. We can ask ourselves what faith and what example we are passing on to our children, nephews, or younger friends, and begin today with something simple, such as praying with them.
exp.45:11:
This verse lists the descendants of Judah, the fourth son of Jacob. His sons were Er, Onan, Shelah, Pharez, and Zerah (in this version they appear as "Pharez" and "Zerah"). It is noted that Er and Onan died in the land of Canaan, before the family traveled to Egypt. Then the sons of Pharez are named: Hezron and Hamul.

The narrator of the book presents a list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt, during the time of the famine. The book is traditionally attributed to Moses. The list shows that God cared for this family, which would become the beginning of the people of Israel. Pharez is important because, later on, from his line would come King David and, according to the New Testament, Jesus.

For today: God pays attention to each person and each family, even with imperfect stories. Trust that He can work through your story.
exp.37:7:
Judah tells his son Onan to marry Tamar, the widow of his brother Er. "Go in unto thy brother's wife" is an old way of saying that he should have marital relations with her as her husband. "Raise up seed to thy brother" means giving descendants to his deceased brother, that is, a son who would carry on his name.

Judah, the father, is the one speaking. His eldest son, Er, died without children. In that culture there was the custom of levirate marriage: the brother was to care for the widow and secure the inheritance and the name of the deceased. Afterward, the Bible tells how Onan refused to fulfill this for his own benefit, and that displeased God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we carry out our responsibilities generously or whether we seek only our own benefit. God calls us to care for the vulnerable, even when it costs us something.
exp.33:29:
Jacob rebukes his sons Simeon and Levi. He tells them they have "troubled" him, meaning they have brought trouble upon him, because their violence has made him "stink," that is, made him hated, among the inhabitants of the land: the Canaanites and the Perizzites. Jacob fears that, since his family is small in number, these peoples will join together against him and destroy his whole household.

Jacob speaks after Simeon and Levi killed the men of Shechem and plundered the city to avenge their sister Dinah. Jacob is concerned for the safety of his household. They respond by defending their honor. The text does not approve of their revenge; later, Jacob condemns it as well (Genesis 49:5-7).

For today: even though pain and injustice may make us feel anger, let us not respond with violence or revenge. Before acting, let us think about the consequences for others, and seek justice with wisdom and self-control.
exp.29:11:
This verse says that Zilpah, Leah's servant, gave birth to a second son for Jacob. The word "bare" is an older way of saying "gave birth to." The text does not give the child's name here; it is given in the next verse: Asher.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book. Leah and Rachel, sisters and wives of Jacob, were competing to have children. Leah had stopped having children for a time and gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob, following a custom of that era. Today the Bible only recounts this event; it does not present it as a model to imitate.

For today: comparison and competition can lead us to painful decisions. God still works even in imperfect families, but we can ask Him to help us trust in Him and value what He has already given us, without measuring our lives against those of others.
exp.23:18:
Rebekah has finished giving water to Abraham's servant, and she offers on her own: "I will draw water for your camels too." She says it with determination: she will keep drawing water until the animals have finished drinking.

Rebekah is a young woman who drew water at the well. Abraham's servant was looking for a wife for Isaac and had asked God for a sign of kindness. She offers more than he asked for. Drawing water for many camels was heavy work. The servant watches her in silence, waiting to see whether God would make his journey successful.

For today: do a little more than the minimum when you can help. A generous gesture, offered without complaint, even in small things, shows a kind heart, and God often uses these everyday details.
exp.28:27:
Genesis 29:28 says that Jacob agreed to Laban's proposal. He completed the week of wedding festivities with Leah, and then Laban gave him his daughter Rachel to be his wife as well. The phrase "fulfilled her week" refers to those seven days of celebration. "Her" refers to Leah, and "gave him Rachel his daughter to wife" means that Laban gave her to him in marriage.

Jacob had worked seven years for Rachel, but Laban deceived him and gave him Leah first. When Jacob protested, Laban justified himself by appealing to a local custom: the younger daughter was not to be married before the older. He asked Jacob to wait out the week and serve seven more years. Jacob agreed, and Rachel was given to him at the end of the week, before completing those years of service. The text does not explain all the legal details of the time.

Jacob, who had deceived others, now received a deception himself. This reminds us that our actions have consequences, and invites us to respond to injustice with patience, honesty, and faithfulness to our commitments.
exp.18:23:
The explanation says that God rained down sulfur and fire on Sodom and Gomorrah from heaven. "Rained" means it fell like rain. The phrase "the Lord... from the Lord" is repeated, and some understand it as a way of stressing that the judgment comes from God himself; others see in it a distinction between divine persons. It is not certain what the exact intention is.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Earlier, the angels had brought Lot and his family out, because the cities were very wicked. God waited for Lot to arrive safely in Zoar before acting. The judgment was serious, but God also rescued those he could.

For today: God is just, but also merciful. When he warns you or opens a way out, do not delay in obeying. Listen to his voice and take the step today, without looking back with longing.
exp.35:14:
This verse begins a list of the leaders who descended from Esau, also called Edom. The word "duke" is old-fashioned; here it means a clan chief or the leader of a tribe. The sons of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau, are named: Teman, Omar, Zepho, and Kenaz.

The text of Genesis has no particular speaker; it is a genealogical record from the narrator. After recounting the separation between Jacob and Esau, the book details how Esau's family grew in the land of Edom. This shows that God kept his promise to make nations also from the descendants of Esau, although the line of the promise continues through Jacob.

For today: God pays attention to people and to families, even to those who seem to stand outside the center of the story. We can trust that He keeps his word and remembers each one, and we should treat everyone with respect, knowing that they matter to Him.
exp.27:0:
Isaac calls Jacob, blesses him, charges him, and says to him: you must not take a wife from the daughters of Canaan. The words "blessed" and "charged" in the King James wording are the equivalents of the older forms used in the source, meaning "he blessed him" and "he commanded him."

Isaac, now an old man, speaks to Jacob. The Canaanites lived in the land where Abraham's family dwelt as strangers, and they had other beliefs and customs. Isaac wanted the family to remain united to the faith of Abraham and to God's promise. For this reason, in the verses that follow, he sends Jacob to find a wife among his mother's family.

For today: when making big decisions, such as marriage or close friendships, it is good to think about what will strengthen our faith and the faith of our family. Seeking advice from people who are mature in faith also helps.
exp.42:30:
The explanation says that Joseph washed his face after weeping, went back out to the dining area, and kept himself under control. The King James word "refrained" means that he held himself back, that he mastered his emotions. Then he gave the order "Set on bread," that is, that the meal be served.

The passage from Genesis is about Joseph, who is now a ruler in Egypt. His brothers, who had sold him years earlier, have come to buy grain and still do not know who he is. When he sees Benjamin, his full brother, Joseph is deeply moved and weeps in private. Afterward he composes himself and returns to them calmly, because it is not yet the time to reveal who he is.

For today: strong feelings are not wrong, but it is wise to know when and how to express them. We can weep and pour out our hearts before God, and then return to act with calmness and wisdom.
exp.11:1:
The explanation says God makes Abram four promises: he will make him into a great nation, he will bless him, he will make his name great, and he will use him to bless others. The words "bless thee" and "make of thee a great nation" are older ways of speaking, meaning "I will bless you" and "I will make you great."

The one speaking is Jehovah, the Lord. He says this to Abram when he asks him to leave his land, his family, and his father's house to go to an unknown place. Abram was seventy-five years old and still had no children. The promises accompany the command: God asks for trust, but he also gives his word. Abram obeyed and went out.

For today: God blesses so that we may be a blessing. This week, think of something God has given you, such as time, a talent, or help, and share it with someone who needs it.
exp.18:26:
It says that Abraham got up early and went to the same place where he had earlier been speaking with God. There he had interceded for Sodom (Genesis 18:22-33). "Before the Lord" means in the presence of the Lord, where he spoke with Him.

The narrator tells us that Abraham returns, his heart surely uneasy, to the site of that conversation. From there he looks out over the destruction of the cities. The Bible does not say what he felt, so we cannot state it with certainty. What it does show is that Abraham, after praying, wanted to see what had happened, and then the text says that God remembered him and rescued Lot.

For today: after praying for someone or for a difficult situation, return to standing before God. Stay alert, trust Him, and do not let go of the prayer, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.31:19:
The explanation says that Jacob orders his servants to tell Esau that he is coming behind them. Jacob thinks: "I will appease his wrath with the present," that is, calm his anger with a gift. Then he says "I will see his face," meaning he will meet him face to face. "Peradventure he will accept of me" means: perhaps he will receive me well and forgive me.

Jacob speaks with the servants who are carrying livestock as gifts for his brother Esau. Years earlier, Jacob had deceived him and fled out of fear of his anger. Now he is returning and fears how Esau will react. The Bible shows his fear, but also that he had earlier prayed to God asking for protection (32:9-12). His plan combines prayer and human effort.

For today: if there is a broken relationship, prayer comes first, but it is also wise to take concrete steps toward reconciliation, such as asking for forgiveness with humility and repairing the harm, without demanding how the other person will respond.
exp.26:17:
Jacob goes in to his father Isaac and says, "My father." Isaac answers, "Here am I," and asks who he is.

Isaac is old and can hardly see. Rebekah and Jacob have prepared a deception so that Jacob will receive the blessing that belonged to Esau, the firstborn. That is why Jacob carries the food, and why the goatskins are on his hands and neck. Isaac's question shows that he suspects something, and what follows is Jacob's lie.

This passage shows how a lie begins with a simple question and grows bigger and bigger. The Bible tells these events without approving of them, and then shows their consequences. Today we can learn to be honest, even when we want something good, and to trust that God keeps his promises without our having to force them through deceit.
exp.34:15:
This verse tells that Jacob and his family left Bethel and were traveling toward Ephrath (another name associated with Bethlehem). They were still about half a league away, a short distance, when Rachel went into labor and had great difficulty. The word "travailed" means that she was in the pains of childbirth, and "hard labour" refers to the pain and hardship of giving birth.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator who tells the story. Jacob had just set up a stone pillar at Bethel to remember his encounter with God. The account moves from a moment of worship to a scene of pain. Afterward it is told that Benjamin was born and that Rachel died. The exact measure of the "half a league" is not certain; the text only indicates that they were near.

For today: real life mixes moments of closeness with God and moments of unexpected pain. God is not absent when sorrow comes. We can bring our burdens to him with sincerity and accompany with tenderness those who suffer a loss.
exp.47:11:
This verse tells how Joseph took his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, from between the knees of their grandfather Jacob, also called Israel. Then he bowed down with his face to the earth. "From between his knees" shows that the boys were sitting on the old man's lap, and the bowing was a sign of respect and gratitude.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob, nearly blind with age, had just embraced and kissed his grandsons. He was about to bless them. Joseph lifted them away out of respect, recognizing that what was coming was a solemn moment. Jacob had said that he never expected to see Joseph again, and now God had allowed him to see even his grandchildren.

For today: when God gives you more than you expected, respond with humility and gratitude. Bowing down, praying, and giving thanks is a good way to acknowledge his goodness.
exp.45:29:
Here Jacob, also called Israel, tells his son Joseph that he can now die in peace, because he has seen him alive. "Now let me die" is not an expression of sorrow, but of fullness. The words "since I have seen your face" show that his greatest longing has been fulfilled.

For many years Jacob had believed that Joseph was dead. Now he arrives in Goshen, in Egypt, and is reunited with him in tears. After so much pain, seeing his son alive brings deep rest to his heart. The Bible says nothing more about his feelings, but the scene conveys joy and relief.

For today: God can restore hope where we thought all was lost. When we wait for something difficult, we can keep trusting in Him. And if there is a broken relationship in your life, take steps toward reconciliation while there is still time.
exp.18:14:
At dawn, the angels urged Lot along, telling him to get up and take his wife and his two daughters who were in the house, so that he would not perish when the city was punished. "When the dawn broke" means when the first rays of the sun came up. "Urged" means they were pressing him to hurry.

The two angels who had come to Sodom are the ones speaking. They had already explained that the outcry against the wickedness of the city had reached God. Lot had warned his sons-in-law, but they thought he was joking. Now the angels insist, because the judgment was very near.

For today: when God warns us or calls us to change something, it is not wise to put it off. Obeying promptly, even when it costs us to let go of what is familiar, is an act of trust in his mercy.
exp.16:1:
God tells Abram that he will establish a covenant, that is, a solemn and firm promise between the two of them. He also assures him that he will multiply him greatly. The King James wording "and will multiply thee exceedingly" conveys the same idea as the original: "exceedingly" means "in great abundance" or "abundantly."

The LORD, God Almighty, speaks when Abram is ninety-nine years old. Years earlier God had already promised him descendants, but Sarah's son had not yet come. Now God renews and confirms his promise, and asks Abram to walk before him and be blameless. Abram responds with reverence, falling on his face.

God keeps what he promises, even when it seems to us late or impossible. Today we can trust him when the waiting stretches on, and keep walking with honesty and obedience, without depending only on what we see.
exp.31:5:
This verse tells how the messengers Jacob had sent came back with news. They tell him that they went to Esau, and that he is already on his way to meet him, accompanied by four hundred men.

Jacob was returning to his land after many years with Laban. Long before, he had deceived Esau and fled from his anger. For that reason he sent a kind message, seeking peace. The Bible does not say what Esau's intentions were. The four hundred men could be understood as a threat or as an escort, but Jacob saw them with fear.

When we face a situation that frightens us, such as an unresolved conflict, we can do what Jacob did: take steps of humility and seek reconciliation, and then bring our fear to God in prayer, as Jacob will do in the following verses.
exp.23:6:
Abraham reminds his servant who God is: the Lord, God of heaven, who took him out of his father's house and from the land of his kindred. He speaks to him of the promise that God would give this land to his "seed," that is, to his descendants. And he assures him that God will send his angel before the servant so that he may find a wife for Isaac there.

Abraham speaks with his most trusted servant, and he has him swear an oath. He is already old and wants his son to marry someone from his own family and not a Canaanite woman. But he does not want Isaac to return to Mesopotamia, because God's promise is tied to the land where they live.

For today: when you face a big decision, remember how God has guided you before. That memory gives courage to take steps of faith, doing your part with responsibility and trusting that God goes before you.
exp.27:16:
Jacob wakes from his sleep and feels afraid. "Dreadful" here does not mean "horrible," but rather it commands respect and reverent awe. Jacob understands that this place is the "house of God" and the "gate of heaven," that is, a place where God is present and heaven touches the earth.

Jacob is the one speaking. He is fleeing from his brother Esau and is alone, far from home. In the dream, God promised to be with him and to watch over him. On waking, he realizes that God was there and he did not know it. That is why he sets up the stone as a sign and names the place Bethel, "house of God."

For today: God can be with you in places and moments that seem empty or difficult. Pause to recognize his presence, and respond with reverence, gratitude, and trust.
exp.45:10:
This verse names the three sons of Levi, the third son of Jacob with Leah: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. It is part of a list of family members. The names appear in the form found in this translation, which is the King James Version's spelling. (Kohath is spelled Coath in some older texts, though the form used here is Kohath.)

Here the narrator of the book lists the descendants of Jacob who entered Egypt, when he moved there with his family because of the famine and to be reunited with Joseph. The list makes clear that the people of Israel came from a real family, with specific names. Later on, from the tribe of Levi would come the priests and those who served in the tabernacle, although this verse gives only the names.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those who seem to be only "part of a list." You can remember that your life matters to him and that he works in families, generation after generation.
exp.22:3:
Abraham says he is a "stranger and a sojourner", meaning a foreigner who lives temporarily, with no land of his own. He asks for "a possession of a buryingplace", that is, a piece of ground where he can bury his wife. "My dead" refers to Sara, and "out of my sight" means taking her away from his view so that she can have a dignified burial.

Sara has just died in Hebron. Abraham, still in grief, rises and speaks with the sons of Heth, the people of the region. He had received the promise of this land, but he did not yet own anything in it. For that reason he respectfully asks to be allowed to buy a place of burial.

For today: we can honor our loved ones with dignity and, at the same time, live with humility and hope, remembering that in this world we are all passing through. Abraham wept, but he also acted with calm and respect.
exp.33:9:
Hamor offers Jacob's sons the chance to live alongside his people. He tells them the land is open to them: they may stay, live there, trade, and take possession of property.

Hamor, the father of Shechem and the leader of the city, speaks after Shechem dishonored Dinah, Jacob's daughter (Gen 34:2). Now he seeks to settle the matter through alliances and marriages. His offer seems generous, but it also protects the interests of his son and his city. The Bible does not present this proposal as full justice, since there is no real acknowledgment of the harm done to Dinah.

For today: Be wary of kind offers that try to cover over an injustice. Before accepting any settlement, ask yourself whether the harm is acknowledged and whether the person who was hurt is being protected.
exp.34:12:
The explanation says that God finished speaking with Jacob and departed from the place where he had appeared to him. The phrase "went up from him" is an older way of saying "left him" or "withdrew." Other versions read that God "went up" from where he had spoken with him.

The narrator recounts what happened at Bethel. God had just confirmed Jacob's new name, Israel, and repeated to him the promises made to Abraham and Isaac: numerous descendants and a land. When the conversation ended, Jacob responded by raising a stone as a sign and offering a drink offering and oil.

For today: God speaks, and his promises remain, even when we no longer feel his presence in a special way. After a powerful moment of prayer or reading, do not depend on emotion. Keep what God told you, respond with gratitude and obedience, and continue trusting in his word.
exp.2:11:
Here Adam answers God's question about whether he ate from the forbidden tree. The phrase "the woman whom thou gavest to be with me" refers to the woman God gave him as a companion, and "thou gavest" is the older form of "you gave." Instead of simply saying "yes, I ate," Adam first points to the woman, and in doing so seems to point to God himself: "the woman whom you gave me."

God has just questioned Adam, who had hidden himself out of fear and shame after disobeying. Adam does admit that he ate, but alongside his confession he places the blame on someone else. Afterward God will ask the woman, and she will blame the serpent.

Today, when we fail, it is tempting to explain, justify, or blame others. We can learn to say simply, "I was wrong," and come before God with honesty, trusting in his mercy.
exp.45:28:
Genesis 46:29 tells how Joseph made ready his chariot and went up to Goshen to meet his father Jacob, who is also called Israel. The phrase "made ready his chariot" means that he ordered the animals to be harnessed to the chariot. "Presented himself unto him" means that he let himself be seen and came before him. Then Joseph embraced his father about the neck and wept for a long time.

This happens after many years of separation. Jacob believed that Joseph had died, but now he was arriving in Egypt with his whole family, and Judah had gone ahead to give notice. The account shows Joseph's emotion: he was already a figure of authority in Egypt, yet before his father he weeps like a son.

For today: do not hide your emotions or your affection for your family. If there is someone you miss or with whom you have not spoken in a long time, take the first step and seek the reunion. God can restore what seemed lost.
exp.5:12:
God tells Noah that the end of all human beings has come. The reason is that the earth has been filled with violence because of them. For this reason God announces that he will destroy them together with the earth.

God speaks, addressing Noah. Earlier, the text says that all the people had corrupted their way and that the earth was full of wickedness. God sees this situation and decides to act. He then immediately gives Noah instructions to build an ark, which shows that alongside the judgment there is also a plan to save Noah and his family.

For today: God takes violence and injustice seriously. We can examine how we treat others, reject all abuse, and seek peace. And, like Noah, we can trust God and obey him even when the world around us turns away.
exp.26:42:
Rebekah tells Jacob to listen to her and to get up and flee to her brother Laban, who lives in Haran. "Obey my voice" means "pay attention to what I say." "Flee thee" means "escape" or "run away." It is an urgent command from a mother who wants to protect her son.

Rebekah is the speaker. She has learned that Esau, furious because Jacob received Isaac's blessing, plans to kill him once their father dies. For that reason she decides to send Jacob far away, to her brother Laban. Here the Bible shows a family wounded by deception and resentment, although God continues to work in the midst of all of it.

When a conflict is very heated, sometimes the wisest thing is to give it room and keep it from growing. Stepping away for a time does not resolve everything, but it can stop a greater harm. Afterward, it is necessary to seek reconciliation, asking God for wisdom and humility.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that here begins the account of the "origins" of the heavens and the earth. "Origins" can also be understood as "history" or "generations." "When they were created" means "when they were brought into being." In addition, the name "Lord God" appears here for the first time, which in this translation corresponds to God's personal name together with the title "God."

The narrator, whom tradition attributes to Moses, closes the first account of creation and opens another, which focuses more on human beings and the garden. Many see here two complementary perspectives on the same event; others explain the transition in other ways. What is certain is that the text presents God as the personal Creator.

For today: if God is the origin of all things, your life is not an accident. Today you can thank him for something simple around you and calmly entrust to him what concerns you.
exp.27:2:
Isaac asks that God Almighty bless Jacob. He asks that God make him fruitful and multiply his family, until he becomes a multitude of peoples, that is, a gathering of many nations or tribes.

Isaac speaks to his son Jacob before sending him to Padan-aram. He wants Jacob to find a wife among his relatives and not among the Canaanite women. This blessing recalls the promise God made to Abraham about a numerous descendance. Readers often see here the continuation of that promise in Jacob.

For today: we can bless and pray for those we love, trusting that God keeps his promises in his own time. A father or a mother can pray for their children before they set out on a journey or enter a new stage of life.
exp.40:23:
Pharaoh recounts the last part of his dream: the thin, dried-up ears were swallowing the seven good, full ears. "Magicians" refers to the wise men or diviners of Egypt. "Declare" means to explain. Pharaoh says he has already consulted all of them, but none could give him the interpretation.

Here Pharaoh speaks, troubled because his dreams disturb him. This is the moment when the cupbearer remembers Joseph, who was in prison. Egypt's experts fail, and then God uses Joseph to give the answer, as seen in what follows.

For today: there are questions and problems that no human wisdom can solve. When you find yourself with no way out, come to God with humility, asking Him for light, and trust that He can use unexpected people and circumstances to give you direction.
exp.44:5:
Here Joseph explains to his brothers that the famine is only halfway over. Two years have already passed without good harvests, and five more remain in which the land cannot be plowed or harvested. The KJV's "earing" is an old word for plowing, that is, preparing the field for sowing, and "harvest" is the gathering of the crop.

Joseph is speaking to his brothers, the same men who sold him into slavery years earlier. He has just revealed who he is. He gives them this detail so they will understand the urgency and see that God placed him in Egypt to save their lives and the lives of their family during the crisis.

Today we can learn that God can work even in the midst of painful situations, even when we do not understand why. Joseph also encourages us to forgive and to look to the future with confidence, using what God gives us to care for others.
exp.40:43:
Pharaoh tells Joseph that he remains the king, but that no one in all of Egypt will do anything without Joseph's authority. "Lift up his hand or foot" means to move or act. In other words, Joseph stands as the highest authority after the king.

Pharaoh speaks after Joseph interpreted his dreams and advised him to prepare for seven years of plenty and seven years of famine. Impressed, Pharaoh appoints him ruler and gives him a ring, fine clothes, and a gold chain, signs of authority. Joseph was thirty years old and coming out of years of slavery and prison. The Bible presents this moment as a promotion that God made possible.

For today: God can use hard times to prepare a person. Be faithful and honest where you are, even when no one notices. And when you receive responsibility, use it to serve and protect others, as Joseph did.
exp.49:2:
This verse tells us that the process of embalming Jacob took forty days, which the text presents as normal in Egypt. The Egyptians also mourned him for seventy days. The King James wording "were fulfilled" means that those days were completed, and "mourned for him" means they grieved over him.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob (Israel) had just died in Egypt, and his son Joseph ordered him embalmed, probably so that he could be carried to Canaan, as his father had asked. That the Egyptians mourned for so long shows the respect people had for Joseph and his family. The exact details of Egyptian customs are not explained further in the text.

Today we can learn to give grief its time. Saying goodbye to someone we love is not done in a hurry. Walking patiently alongside someone who is grieving is a simple way to show care.
exp.29:36:
Jacob takes fresh rods from three trees: poplar, hazel, and chestnut. He strips off strips of bark so that white streaks are exposed. "Pilled," in the King James wording, means stripped of the bark, and the "white strakes" are those stripped strips or streaks.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jacob has been working for years for his father-in-law Laban, and they had agreed that he would keep the animals that were speckled and dark. Laban had already set those animals apart and moved them away. Jacob now tries to increase his flock by this method. The Bible tells it this way, but it does not say the rods had any real power. Later, Jacob acknowledges that God was the one who looked after him and made him prosper (Genesis 31:9-12).

Today we can make our effort and use our ingenuity, but without forgetting that true provision comes from God. Work diligently, and trust that He cares for you.
exp.26:19:
Isaac is surprised that his son has found the game so quickly. Jacob answers that the Lord God brought it to him.

Isaac, now old and almost blind, wants to bless Esau, his firstborn. Rebekah and Jacob have planned to deceive him so that Jacob will receive the blessing. Here Jacob lies and, even worse, uses God's name to lend strength to his lie. The Bible tells this without approving it; it shows the facts in all their harshness.

Today it reminds us that we must not use God's name to cover our lies or our own interests. God wants us to seek his promises with honesty and trust, not with deceit that harms others.
exp.2:6:
After eating the forbidden fruit, Adam and Eve realized that they were naked. Their eyes were opened, but they did not see what the serpent had promised them. They saw their shame. So they sewed fig leaves together and made themselves "aprons," that is, belts or loincloths to cover themselves. The word "both" in the verse means the two of them.

Here the narrator of the story speaks. Earlier, the serpent had told them they would be like gods. That promise led them to disobey. After eating, they did come to know evil by their own experience, but with guilt and fear. Soon they will hide from God.

For today: when we fail, we often cover up or hide what we did. But our own remedies do not remove guilt. We can approach God with sincerity, confess our wrongdoing, and trust in his forgiveness.
exp.12:16:
The explanation says that God asks Abram to rise up and walk through the land from one end to the other, along its length and across its breadth. The words "to you I will give it" mean "I am going to give it to you." It is an invitation to walk the land and a promise that it will be his.

God speaks after Abram and Lot have separated. Lot chose the best land within sight, and Abram was left with what seemed to be less. Then God confirms his promise to him: land and a descendant too numerous to count. Afterward, Abram moves, settles in Hebron, and builds an altar to the LORD, as a sign of trust and gratitude.

For today: when you feel that others have taken the best, remember that God sees and keeps his promises in his own time. Take a step of faith, trust in him, and thank him with a simple prayer.
exp.44:24:
This verse tells how Joseph's brothers left Egypt and came to the land of Canaan, where their father Jacob lived. It is simply the end of the journey home.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Joseph had already made himself known to his brothers, forgiven them, and sent them off with gifts and provisions for Jacob. Now they return with unbelievable news: the son Jacob thought was dead was alive. The text does not say how they felt on the way, but it does show that they had to tell him the truth.

For today: there is good news we cannot keep to ourselves. After receiving forgiveness and grace, we are called to share it with those who are suffering, even if it is hard to believe at first. Let us do it with honesty and patience.
exp.30:17:
This verse tells us that Jacob set out with all his livestock and all his possessions, everything he had acquired during his years in Padan-aram, to return with his father Isaac to the land of Canaan.

The explanation is given by the narrator. Before this, Jacob had listened to Rachel and Leah, who told him to do what God had commanded him. After twenty years with Laban, God directed him to go back to his own land. Jacob left without telling Laban, and the text says that he kept his plans hidden from him. Some readers see prudence in this, others fear.

For today: when God calls us to change, obeying requires decision and order. We can take concrete steps, trusting that God cares for what he has placed in our hands, even when the road is hard.
exp.2:7:
They heard the sound of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day, that is, at the time of the evening breeze, probably the evening (some understand it this way; the Hebrew allows other readings). Hearing him, they hid among the trees. "The Lord God" is the name of God; "walking" means that he was moving about through the garden.

The narrator tells what happened after they ate the forbidden fruit. They noticed they were naked and covered themselves with leaves. Before, God's presence had been a joy; now they are afraid because of their own guilt. God does not abandon them: in the next verse he seeks them out and calls to them.

For today: when we fail, we sometimes want to hide from God, from others, or from ourselves. This passage reminds us that God seeks us out with a question, not only with punishment. Today we can come out of our hiding place and speak to him honestly, trusting in his mercy.
exp.33:24:
This verse tells that on the third day after the circumcision, when the men of Shechem were most sore and weak, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, each took his sword. They entered the city without anyone stopping them and slew all the males. The King James wording "sore" means in pain or suffering, and "came upon the city boldly" means they went in with confidence and without fear.

It is part of the story of Dinah, who was defiled by Shechem. Jacob's sons proposed circumcision as a condition for an agreement, but they did so with deceit. The text relates the event without approving of it. Later, Jacob rebukes them for it (Genesis 49:5-7). Real harm was done, but the response was out of all proportion.

For today: when we are wronged, or those we love are wronged, anger is understandable, but we must not use deceit or revenge. Let us seek justice honestly and ask God for self-control.
exp.37:17:
Judah asks Tamar what pledge he should leave with her until he pays her. She asks for three things: his signet ring, his cord (or outer garment, depending on how it is understood), and his staff, that is, his walking stick. Judah gives them to her, has relations with her, and she becomes pregnant. "Pledge" means security or guarantee, and "went in unto her" means that he lay with her.

Judah did not know she was his daughter-in-law, because she had covered her face with a veil. Tamar had been widowed, and Judah had not given her his youngest son as a husband, as was the custom. She asks for these objects so she can identify him later. Later on, these proofs will expose Judah's injustice.

For today: what is hidden sooner or later comes to light. It is better to live with integrity and keep what has been promised, rather than act carelessly and hope no one finds out.
exp.38:22:
The explanation says that the keeper of the prison no longer worried about anything that had been placed under José's care. The reason is that the Lord was with José, and whatever José did, God made it prosper. "Keeper" means the chief or the one in charge. "Was with him" means "stood with him" or "was present with him." "Made it to prosper" means that it turned out well.

This is part of the account of José in Egypt. He had been sold as a slave and then falsely accused, and for that reason he ended up in prison. Here the narrator, that is, the one who writes the story, explains that his situation was not abandonment: God remained with him. Even so, the text does not say that José was set free; the prosperity happens within the prison.

For today: even in unjust or difficult places, we can work with honesty and diligence, trusting that God is present. His help does not always change our circumstances right away, but it can give us fruit, direction, and peace.
exp.9:6:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Cush, son of Ham, had five sons: Seba, Havilah, Sabtah, Raamah, and Sabtecha. Then it mentions that Raamah had two sons: Sheba and Dedan. These are names of people who later come to be associated with peoples or regions. Some scholars place them toward Arabia and Africa, but it is not known with certainty where each group lived.

The narrator of the book, traditionally identified with Moses, is writing what is called the "table of nations." Its purpose is to show how, after the flood, humanity multiplied from Noah's family and spread across the earth. These names connect the peoples with a common origin.

For today: God knows people by name and does not see families as mere numbers. If you feel small or overlooked today, remember that your story matters to Him. We can also treat all people with respect, knowing that we come from one common origin.
exp.26:5:
Here Rebekah speaks to her son Jacob and tells him what she has just overheard: the conversation between Isaac and Esau. The wording "spake unto Jacob" and "I heard thy father speak unto Esau" is an older form of saying "spoke to Jacob" and "I heard your father speak to Esau." The verse is an introduction; what she heard continues in the next verse.

Isaac, now an old man, had asked Esau to prepare his favorite meal so that he might bless him. Rebekah was listening and decided to act. The Bible does not say here that she doubted God, but her plan, which follows afterward, uses deception. Some believe she wanted to fulfill what God had said about Jacob (Genesis 25:23), although the text does not clearly state this.

When we think we know God's plans, we should not rush ahead with tricks or crooked means. It is wise to pray, to wait, and to trust that God fulfills his promises in right ways.
exp.31:14:
This verse continues the list of the gift that Jacob prepared for his brother Esau. Here it mentions thirty female camels with their young, forty cows, ten young bulls, twenty she-donkeys, and ten young donkeys. The King James wording "milch camels with their colts" refers to camels that were giving milk, that is, nursing females, and "colts" here means their young. "Kine" is an old English word for cattle, and "she asses" is an older term for female donkeys.

Jacob is returning to his land with fear, because years earlier he deceived Esau and took away the blessing. Now he knows that Esau is coming to meet him, and he is not sure how he will be received. For that reason he sets apart valuable animals in groups, to send ahead as a gift that will soften the encounter.

For today: when a relationship has been broken through our own fault, it is not enough to wish it could be repaired. Jacob prayed and also acted with humility and generosity. We can look for concrete gestures of reconciliation, trusting that God works in hearts.
exp.40:46:
The explanation says that during the seven years of plenty the earth produced enormous harvests, "in heaps," that is, in great quantity, by handfuls. The English rendering "by handfuls" is the phrase quoted here. The word "plenteous" means abundant, having more than enough to be fully satisfied.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He tells that Joseph, already placed in authority over Egypt, traveled through the land while the good years that God had announced through Pharaoh's dream were arriving. The abundance was no accident: it was the time of preparation before seven years of famine. The verses that follow show that Joseph stored the grain with order and wisdom.

For today: good times are an opportunity to be prudent and thankful. If today you have more than you need, give thanks to God, save wisely, and share generously, thinking of the difficult days that others or you yourself may face.
exp.24:31:
Esau arrives tired and very hungry, and he says he is about to die. Then he asks what good the birthright does him, that is, the special right of the firstborn son, which included honor, leadership in the family, and a double portion of the inheritance. "I am at the point to die" sounds exaggerated, and many read it as a way of expressing his desperation in that moment.

Esau speaks, the elder brother of Jacob. Jacob had prepared a reddish stew of lentils, and he takes advantage of his brother's hunger to ask him for the birthright. Esau agrees and even swears to it. The text concludes that in this way he "despised" that right, that is, he treated it as something of little value.

For today: when we face an urgent need, let us ask God for calm before deciding. A quick satisfaction can cost us something valuable and lasting, such as faith, family, or integrity.
exp.36:32:
Jacob recognizes the bloodstained robe and draws a terrible conclusion. "He knew it" means he recognized it. "Evil beast" refers to a wild and dangerous animal, and "rent in pieces" means torn apart. Jacob believes Joseph died, attacked by a savage beast.

Jacob, Joseph's father, speaks here. His sons, jealous of Joseph, had sold him, and now they present the garment stained with goat's blood to deceive him. They do not directly say that Joseph died; Jacob reaches that conclusion on his own. Afterward, his grief is so deep that he refuses all comfort.

Today, this verse reminds us that appearances can deceive and that a lie can cause great pain. Before drawing conclusions, it is wise to ask questions and seek the truth. And if we are mourning, God invites us not to carry sorrow alone, but to let ourselves be accompanied.
exp.27:17:
Jacob got up early in the morning, took the stone he had used as a pillow, and set it up as a sign, or pillar. Then he poured oil over it. "Pillar" here means a monument or marker set up to remember something. "Pillow" refers to the stone he had rested his head on.

The narrator tells what Jacob did after his dream at Bethel. He was fleeing from his brother Esau and traveling alone, far from home. God had promised him his presence and his blessing. On waking, Jacob felt awe and reverence, and he marked the place. Pouring oil over a stone was a way of setting it apart for God; scholars understand this gesture as a consecration, though the Bible does not explain all the details.

When God meets us, it is good to respond and not to forget. We can create a simple reminder: write in a notebook what God has done today, and read it again in difficult days.
exp.15:11:
He says that Ishmael will be a wild man, literally like a "wild donkey" in the Hebrew. He will be independent and strong-willed. His hand will be against everyone, and everyone's hand against him, meaning there will be conflict. And "he shall dwell in the presence of all his brethren" may mean that he will live near his relatives, or that he will live without submitting to them. Scholars understand it in different ways.

The angel of the LORD speaks with Hagar, Sarai's servant, who fled into the desert because of mistreatment. She is pregnant by Abram. The angel comforts her, promises her numerous descendants, and announces what her son will be like. The name Ishmael means "God hears."

God sees and hears those who suffer, even when no one else notices. If today you feel forgotten or mistreated, speak to him with confidence in prayer. He sees you and hears you.
exp.5:0:
This verse says that, when people began to grow in number across the earth, daughters were also born to them. "It came to pass" means "it happened," and the old wording here is simply the English of the King James Version, which is what your reader sees. This is a transitional phrase that prepares what comes next.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, a book traditionally attributed to Moses. It tells how humanity was growing and how the time of the flood was drawing near. The verses that follow speak of the "sons of God" and the "daughters of men." It is not known with certainty who the "sons of God" were: some think they were descendants of Seth, others that they were spiritual beings. Christians have interpreted this in several ways.

For today: growth and blessings can become a temptation if we forget God. Let us ask him to help us live wisely and to choose with a heart that is faithful to him.
exp.38:8:
He says that Joseph is in charge of all of Potiphar's house. No one has more authority than he does, and his master has held nothing back from him except his wife. That is why Joseph asks: "How then can I do this great wickedness?" The word "how" here matches the King James wording, and "sin against God" means that it would be a direct offense against God.

Joseph, a slave in Egypt, speaks here, rejecting the proposal of Potiphar's wife. His main reason is the trust his master placed in him, and also his reverence for God. Notice that he sees sin not only as harm done to people, but as something against God himself. Then she insists day after day, and he remains firm.

For today: when someone trusts you, guard that trust, even when no one is watching. Decide beforehand which things you will not do, because remembering that God sees you and loves you helps you stand firm in temptation.
exp.49:13:
This verse says that Joseph returned to Egypt after burying his father Jacob. He came back with his brothers and with everyone who had gone up with him for the burial. The King James wording "went up" fits here, because Canaan lay to the north in higher country, so the journey there was spoken of as going up.

The narrator tells us that Joseph kept the promise he had made to Jacob to bury him in Canaan, in the cave of Machpelah. With the burial finished, the family goes back to its life in Egypt. But the next verse shows that the brothers were afraid, thinking that Joseph would now take revenge on them.

For today: keeping what we have promised to others, even when it costs us, is a way of honoring them. And if there are unresolved wrongs between us, let us not wait until fear grows; let us seek reconciliation with humility and trust in the grace of God.
exp.2:17:
This verse says that the ground, which before gave its fruit easily, will now produce "thorns and thistles," that is, harmful and troublesome plants. "The herb of the field" refers to the plants that grow in the ground to be used as food. Man's work will become harder.

God speaks after Adam and Eve ate from the tree He had forbidden them. God speaks to Adam and explains the consequences of disobedience: the ground is placed under a curse, and work becomes wearisome. Even so, God does not abandon them, and in the following context He continues to care for them.

For today: when your work is hard or things do not come easily, remember that we live in a world marked by sin. Work with honesty and hope, trusting that God sustains you day by day.
exp.18:16:
Here is the translated explanation, adapted to the King James wording.

It says that, once the angels had brought Lot and his family out of the city, one of them gave him an urgent command: "Escape for thy life," that is, flee to save yourself. "Look not behind thee" means do not turn to look back at the city. "Neither stay thou in all the plain" means do not stop anywhere in the low country. "Lest thou be consumed" means lest you be destroyed.

It is one of God's messengers who speaks. Sodom was going to be destroyed because of its wickedness, and Lot had hesitated to leave. The angels had taken him by the hand out of the mercy of the LORD. Now they ask him to obey without delay and without being distracted, and they point to the mountain as the place of safety.

For today: when God rescues you from something that is harming you, do not keep looking back or searching for excuses. Take the next step of obedience, trusting that his help is real and that he is caring for you.
exp.6:23:
It says that the floodwaters held dominion over the earth for a hundred and fifty days, that is, about five months. "Prevailed" means they grew strong, rose up, and stayed over everything. It is not speaking of a passing rain, but of a long stretch of time in which the water covered the earth.

Here the speaker is the narrator of the book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses. He has just recounted that every living thing outside the ark died, and now he marks how long the dominion of the water lasted. Noah and his family remained inside, waiting. The account presents the flood as God's judgment on human wickedness, but also as His care for those who trusted in Him.

For today: there are long seasons of waiting, when it seems nothing is changing. Noah did not control the water, but he stayed within the shelter God had given him. When you go through a difficult time, seek refuge in God, trust that He has not forgotten you, and wait with patience.
exp.23:33:
The explanation says that the man who arrived at Laban's house introduces himself right away. "Servant" here means a servant or trusted employee. He does not give his own name but identifies himself by the person he serves: Abraham.

The one speaking is Abraham's chief servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac. Although they offer him food, he puts his errand first: "I will not eat until I have told my message." By introducing himself this way, he makes clear who he is speaking for and whom he represents. The text does not give his name in this passage, and it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: we can learn to be clear about whom we serve. This servant was faithful, humble, and focused on his task. May people in our work, family, and church notice that we live for God with integrity, without seeking the spotlight.
exp.21:9:
The explanation says that Abraham raised his hand and took the knife to kill his son Isaac. "Slay" means to cut the throat, which was the way an animal was sacrificed. He had already built the altar, laid the wood, and bound Isaac. It was the last step before the sacrifice.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. God had asked Abraham to offer Isaac as a test of his faith. Abraham had already said, "God will provide himself a lamb." This shows his trust. The text does not explain what he was thinking at that moment. The New Testament (Hebrews 11:19) suggests that he believed God could raise Isaac from the dead. Then the angel stopped his hand.

For today: trusting God does not always mean understanding what He is doing. Sometimes He asks us to give Him what we love most, such as our plans, our family, or our future. We can do this with the hope that God is faithful and knows how to provide at the right moment.
exp.23:41:
This verse tells what Abraham's servant did when he arrived at the well. He says that on that day he came to the well and prayed to the LORD, "the God of my master Abraham." He asked that the journey he was undertaking be made to prosper, that is, that it would turn out well. The phrase "if now thou do prosper my way" sounds like "if it is your will to give me success."

The servant of Abraham is speaking, retelling his story before Rebekah's family in Mesopotamia. Abraham had sent him to find a wife for Isaac among his relatives. Here the servant explains how he prayed before meeting Rebekah, and in this way he shows that everything was directed by God.

For today: before making an important decision, pray simply and ask God for direction. Then stay attentive to how He guides you in everyday life.
exp.16:10:
God tells Abraham that all the males in his household must be circumcised. The "foreskin" is the skin that covers the tip of the male organ, and "seed" means offspring. This mark on the body would be a visible sign of the covenant, that is, of the promise and commitment between God and the people of Abraham.

God speaks with Abraham, who was already elderly, when he renews his promise to give him a great offspring and a land. Before asking anything of him, God had already promised. Circumcision was Abraham's and his family's response: a sign of belonging to God and of trusting his word. Christians understand that what matters most is faith and a surrendered heart, as Paul teaches in Romans 4.

For today: outward signs of faith are not enough. Ask yourself whether your daily life truly shows that you belong to God and trust his promises.
exp.45:27:
Verse 28 tells us that Jacob sent his son Judah ahead to let Joseph know they were coming, and to have Joseph guide them or receive them in Goshen. Afterward the whole family arrived in that region. The phrase "to direct his face unto Goshen" indicates that Judah was going to meet Joseph and prepare the reunion. Some scholars understand that Judah was also to show the way; the text does not make this entirely clear.

This is the account of Jacob's arrival in Egypt, after many years of believing Joseph was dead. The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. Judah appears as a son with leadership within the family. Goshen would have been a fertile area where the family could live and care for their livestock.

For today: when God leads us into a new stage, it is wise to move forward with order and good preparation, trusting that He is already guiding the way, even when we cannot yet see how the story will end.
exp.26:35:
Esau speaks with pain and anger. He says that the name "Jacob" fits him well, because that name sounds like "the one who grabs the heel" and was also understood to mean "the one who deceives." The phrase "he took away my birthright" means that Jacob took for himself the rights of the firstborn son. Then Esau asks his father whether he has not kept a blessing for him.

Esau has just discovered that Isaac blessed Jacob, who had pretended to be him. Earlier, Esau had sold his birthright for a bowl of food (Genesis 25). Even so, he now cries out bitterly. The Bible does not approve of Jacob's deception, but it also does not overlook the fact that Esau despised what was worth something.

For today: value what is sacred before you lose it. And if you fail, avoid blaming everyone else; come to God with humility and sincerity.
exp.2:23:
He says that God drove the man out of the garden of Eden. Then he placed at the east of the garden some cherubims, which are heavenly beings, and a flaming sword that turned in every direction. Its purpose was to guard the way that led to the tree of life. Old words: the King James uses "east" for the direction, and "cherubims" is an older plural form, along with "flaming sword which turned every way," where "turned every way" means turned in all directions.

The narrator of the account tells what happened after Adam and Eve disobeyed. God had already said that it was not fitting for the man to eat from the tree of life in that state of sin. Scholars explain the meaning of the cherubim and the sword in several ways, but all agree that they show that access was closed off.

For today: sin brings real consequences, yet even in sending them out, God acted with care and did not abandon them. We can approach God with honesty, trusting that he continues to open paths of restoration.
exp.36:19:
Joseph's brothers see him coming from afar and, filled with resentment, they decide to kill him. They propose throwing him into a cistern, which was a dry pit used to store water, and making up a story that a wild beast devoured him. The word "Come" in the King James Version is the same invitation as "let us," so the line reads "Come now therefore, and let us slay him," and with "we shall see what will become of his dreams" they mock him, since they want to find out whether his dreams will come true.

The speakers are Jacob's sons, at Dothan, far from home. They were jealous because their father loved Joseph more, and because he had dreamed that they would bow down before him. Reuben, the eldest, will soon step in to try to save his life.

For today: jealousy that is not confronted can grow until it becomes violence. If we feel envy or anger toward someone, it is better to bring that to God in prayer and seek an honest conversation before the heart hardens. God can carry out his purposes even when others try to hinder them.
exp.21:2:
Genesis 22:3 says that Abraham got up early in the morning, saddled his donkey, and took two of his young men with him, along with his son Isaac. He also split the wood for the burnt offering, which was an offering burned up completely, and set out for the place God had told him about.

This is part of the account where God tests Abraham. God asked him to offer Isaac, the son of the promise. The narrator only tells us what Abraham did and does not explain his feelings. So we do not know in detail what he was thinking, but we do see his obedience.

For today: when you know what God is asking of you, do not put it off. Abraham obeyed early and with purpose. Even with doubts or pain, you can take the next step of obedience and trust that God is faithful.
exp.1:16:
God tells the man that he must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. The word "knowledge" here means knowing. In this translation the word "but" is the one that begins the verse. God warns that on the day the man eats from that tree, "you shall surely die." Some understand this to mean an immediate death in the spiritual sense, that is, being separated from God; others understand it to mean that physical death would begin that same day.

God himself is speaking, the Creator. He has just placed the man in the garden of Eden to care for it, and he gives him freedom: he may eat from every tree, except one. The prohibition is clear and comes with a warning, not a whim.

For today: God gives us great freedom, but he also gives us limits that protect us. When one of his instructions seems hard to us, we can trust that he sees farther than we do and seeks our good.
exp.3:17:
This verse lists five generations of Cain's family: Enoch, son of Cain, had Irad; Irad fathered Mehujael; Mehujael fathered Methusael; and Methusael fathered Lamech. The archaic forms of the verse are not relevant here, so no comment on spelling is needed. "Begat" means that he was the father of someone.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of Genesis, presenting a genealogy. It follows the story of Cain after he left the presence of God and prepares the account of Lamech, with his two wives and his children. The names are not explained, and scholars debate their exact meaning.

For today: God sees and records the life of families, even those that are not remembered. We can ask what inheritance we leave to the next generation, and pray that God will make our decisions inspire faith, care and good example in those who come after us.
exp.45:3:
God makes Jacob three promises: that he will go down with him into Egypt, that he will also bring him back up, and that Joseph will be with him at his death. "To put the hand upon the eyes" meant to close the eyes of the one who had died, that is, Joseph would be present at his death. Old-fashioned wording: in the King James Version, "go down" is the phrase used here, and "surely bring thee up again" is the older wording for "bring you back."

God speaks at night, in a vision in Beersheba. Jacob is old and is going to Egypt to be reunited with Joseph, but he is afraid to leave the promised land. God reminds him that he does not go alone. On "bring up," many understand it to refer to his descendants, since Jacob died in Egypt and his body was carried to Canaan.

God does not ask us to walk alone toward the unknown. When you face a change that frightens you, pray and remember that He goes with you.
exp.45:30:
Here Joseph tells his brothers and all of his father's household that he will go up and speak with Pharaoh. He announces that he will say to him: "My brethren, and my father's house, which were in the land of Canaan, are come unto me." The words "go up," "shew," and "say" in the King James wording correspond to "I will go," "I will inform," and "I will tell him" in the original.

Joseph, already ruler of Egypt, speaks just after being reunited with his father Jacob (also called Israel) in Goshen. He wants to present his family before Pharaoh with order and respect, and to prepare them for what the king might ask them. In this way he makes sure they can remain in that land.

For today: Joseph used his position to care for his family with prudence and not with carelessness. We can learn to prepare things well and to use with humility the influence that God has given us to bless and protect those we love.
exp.41:20:
The brothers of Joseph say to one another that they were indeed guilty for what they did to him. They remember that they saw his anguish when he pleaded with them, and they would not listen. Now they think that their own distress is a consequence of that. "The anguish of his soul" is Joseph's pain and deep despair.

The sons of Jacob speak in Egypt, when the governor, who is Joseph but they do not know it, treats them as spies and keeps one of them in prison. Years ago they sold Joseph, and now, in difficulty, their conscience awakens. They believe no one understands them, but Joseph does.

For today: let us not ignore the pain of others or silence it. If our conscience reminds us of a wrong, let us no longer hide it. Acknowledging it before God and seeking reconciliation is the path to healing.
exp.39:11:
Here Joseph begins to explain the cupbearer's dream. The word "interpretation" in the KJV rendering "This is the interpretation of it" corresponds to the meaning or significance of the dream. The "branches" are the shoots of the vine. Joseph says that the three branches represent three days.

Joseph is in Pharaoh's prison, where the cupbearer and the baker had dreams that no one could explain to them. Before interpreting, Joseph had said that interpretations belong to God (Genesis 40:8). For this reason he does not present himself as a diviner, but as someone who depends on God. His message to the cupbearer is one of hope: he will be restored to his position.

For today: even in times of injustice or waiting, we can be useful and faithful people. Joseph did not wait until he got out of prison to serve and honor God. Today we can do the same in our work, family, or difficulty, trusting that God sees our situation.
exp.43:33:
Judah ends his speech with a question full of anguish: how can I go back to my father if the boy is not with me? He says he could not bear it, because he would see the grief that would fall upon Jacob. "Lad" means a young man or boy; here it refers to Benjamin. "Lest peradventure" means lest perhaps, or lest by chance, and "shall come on" means it would come suddenly upon him.

Judah speaks in front of Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize, since he sees him as the governor of Egypt. Joseph had placed his cup in Benjamin's sack and wanted to keep him as a servant. Judah had given his word to his father to answer for Benjamin, and so he offers to remain a prisoner in his place. His attitude contrasts with what he had done years earlier to Joseph.

For today: when you have failed at something, seek to do what is right with humility and love, even when it costs you. Keeping your word and caring for the pain of others shows a heart that has truly changed.
exp.14:18:
This verse begins a list of peoples who lived in the land that God promised to Abram. The Kenites, the Kenizzites, and the Kadmonites were tribes who inhabited the region of Canaan and its surroundings. The Bible says little about some of them, and we do not know all the details with certainty.

God speaks to Abram just after making a covenant with him. The burning torch that passes between the divided animals was a solemn sign that God himself was committing to fulfill his promise. By naming the peoples, God makes the promise concrete and real: it is not a vague idea, but a land with actual peoples and places.

For today: God pays attention to the details of what he promises. You can trust that his word is firm and concrete. When you doubt, remember that he keeps what he says, even when it takes a while to be seen.
exp.27:18:
This verse tells how Jacob gave the name "Beth-el" to that place. Beth-el means "house of God." Before that, the city was called Luz.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau, and on the way he dreamed of a ladder reaching up to heaven, and God promised to be with him. When he awoke, he was afraid and recognized that God was there. For this reason he changed the name of the place, to remember what he had experienced. Some scholars think that Luz and Beth-el were nearby places, but the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: God can meet us in difficult places and moments. When you feel his help, do not forget it; write it down, thank him for it, and remember it. In this way your faith is strengthened in future trials.
exp.19:9:
Abimelech asks Abraham another question: "What sawest thou, that thou hast done this thing?" That is, "What were you thinking? What reason did you have for acting this way?" The word "sawest" here means something like "what did you see in us" or "what led you to do it."

Abimelech, king of Gerar, speaks after God warned him in a dream that Sarah was a married woman. Abraham had said that Sarah was his sister, and the king had taken her. Now Abimelech confronts him with astonishment and anger, because he nearly sinned without knowing it. Abraham answers right away by explaining his fear.

For today: when fear leads us to lie or to tell half-truths, we can hurt others. Before acting out of fear, it is wise to stop, pray, and trust that God cares for us without the need for deception.
exp.44:17:
Pharaoh speaks to Joseph's brothers and tells them to bring their father Jacob and their families to Egypt. He promises them "the good of the land," that is, the best that it has to offer. "The fat of the land" is an old expression meaning the richest and most abundant things, like the finest foods. "Pleased" means "pleased" in the sense of "agreed with" or "was good in his eyes."

The one speaking is Pharaoh, glad that Joseph's brothers have arrived. Canaan was suffering a famine, and Pharaoh, because of the esteem he had for Joseph, wants to welcome his whole family and care for them. It is a gesture of generosity toward them.

For today: God often blesses others through people He has placed in positions of influence. Just as Joseph served faithfully and his family was welcomed, we can use what we have to help and give shelter to those in need, and receive with humility the help that is offered to us.
exp.10:7:
This verse tells what happened after God confused the languages. "Scattered" means that he dispersed them, spread them out to different places. Since they could no longer understand one another, the people separated and spread across the whole earth, and they stopped building the city.

Here the narrator reports what the LORD did. Earlier, the inhabitants of the land of Shinar wanted to build a city and a tower to make a name for themselves and so as not to be scattered (v. 4). God responded by confusing their language. Afterward, the city was called Babel, a name that sounds like the word for "confuse" in Hebrew.

For today: human plans built with pride and without taking God into account do not endure. We can ask ourselves whether what we do seeks our own fame or honors God and serves others.
exp.42:6:
Joseph's brothers explain to their father Jacob (Israel) why they told the governor of Egypt that they had another brother. They say that the man questioned them directly about their family: whether their father was still alive and whether they had another brother. They simply answered truthfully. The "straitly" in the King James wording means closely or strictly, and "the man" is Joseph, whom they still do not recognize. And they defend themselves: how could they have known that he would ask them to bring Benjamin down?

Context: There is famine in the land, and they need to return to Egypt for food. Jacob grieves because he fears losing Benjamin, the son left to him by Rachel, after believing Joseph was dead. The brothers try to justify themselves in the face of his pain and his reproach.

For today: When something goes wrong, it is easy to defend ourselves or blame circumstances. It is better to listen with humility to the one who is suffering, acknowledge their pain, and seek a solution together, as Judah will do later.
exp.41:2:
This verse says that ten of Jacob's sons, Joseph's brothers, traveled to Egypt to buy grain. "Went down" is used because Egypt lay to the south, and people spoke of "going down" to it. The archaic "á" is the old way of writing "a".

Careful: the KJV verse uses "went down" and "corn," and the explanation's comment about the old spelling "á" does not match the KJV wording, so that comment is dropped.

Here is the corrected translation, keeping the explanation's own structure:

This verse says that ten of Jacob's sons, Joseph's brothers, traveled to Egypt to buy grain. "Went down" is used because Egypt lay to the south, and people spoke of "going down" to it.

The narrator tells what happened after Jacob, their father, noticed that his sons were sitting idle. There was famine in Canaan, and Jacob ordered them to go buy food so that they would not die. The brothers had no idea they would meet Joseph, whom they had sold years earlier. Benjamin stayed home because Jacob feared losing him too.

For today: when a need arises, do not simply stand "looking on." Take a concrete and sensible step, and at the same time trust that God may be at work in what you cannot yet see.
exp.4:19:
It says that Jared lived a total of 962 years, and then he died. This is the close of his story within the list of Adam's descendants. The word "begat" means that he was a father; in this list it can refer to a direct son or, according to some scholars, to a descendant. "Died" appears at the end of each life, except that of Enoch.

Context: No one speaks here in particular; this is the account in the book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses. It is a genealogy that connects Adam with Noah and shows that death, announced after the fall, continues its course. The very long numbers are understood in different ways: some take them literally and others as an ancient form of expression. The text does not make this clear.

For today: Our life also has an end. This invites us to live with purpose, like Enoch, who "walked with God" in the following verse, and not to leave our relationship with Him for later.
exp.42:3:
What it says: Judah is speaking to his father Jacob. He tells him that if he lets Benjamin, the youngest brother, go with them, they will go down to Egypt and buy food. The word "wilt send" in the King James means "send" or "let go," and "go down" means "travel down" to Egypt.

Context: The family is going hungry because the grain they brought back earlier has run out. Jacob wants them to return to Egypt, but the ruler, who is Joseph without them knowing it, demanded that they bring Benjamin. Judah speaks with firmness and respect, and explains that without Benjamin the journey will be of no use.

For today: When a difficult decision has to be made, speaking clearly and honestly helps a great deal. Judah does not hide the problem or demand anything harshly; he presents the truth and proposes a solution. In this way we can face the fears of others: with calm, sincerity, and a willingness to take responsibility.
exp.2:0:
This verse presents the serpent as the most subtle animal, that is, the most skillful and clever, of all the creatures of the field that God made. It speaks to the woman and asks her: "Yea, hath God said...?", which today we would say as "So, did God really say...?". It asks in a way that exaggerates God's command, as if he had forbidden every tree.

The narrator is the one who introduces the serpent, and it is the serpent who speaks with Eve. Earlier, God had allowed eating from every tree except one. The serpent twists those words to sow doubt about God's goodness. The text does not say here that this is Satan; many Christians see it that way because of other passages in the Bible, but this verse speaks only of a serpent.

Today, be careful of voices that question what God said and present it as exaggerated or unjust. It is wise to return to his Word and remember his goodness.
exp.17:6:
Abraham ran to his herd, chose a calf that was tender and of good quality, and gave it to a young servant. The servant hurried to prepare it. In the King James wording, "fetcht" is an older spelling of "fetched," meaning brought or taken, and "hasted" means hurried or made haste, and "dress" means to prepare the meal by cooking it, while "young man" refers to a young servant.

This is part of the scene where three visitors arrive at Abraham's tent, by the oaks of Mamre. The text presents them as men, and shortly before this it speaks of the Lord. Abraham, without knowing everything that would happen, offers hospitality with generosity and speed, as was the custom of honoring travelers in that culture.

For today: we can welcome others with generosity and enthusiasm, giving our best and not what is left over. Sometimes, when we serve someone joyfully, God surprises us with a greater blessing.
exp.37:14:
This verse says that Judah saw a woman on the road and thought she was a prostitute, because she had her face covered with a veil. "Harlot" means a woman who offers sexual relations for payment. "Thought her to be" means "considered her to be."

The narrator tells us that Tamar, widow of Judah's sons, had disguised herself. Judah had not given his son Shelah to her as a husband, as was the custom for providing descendants for a family.
