She was not a prostitute, and Judah did not recognize her. Interpreters differ on her exact motives, but the text shows that she was seeking justice and a child. Later Judah acknowledges that she was "more righteous" than he was (v. 26).

Today, this passage invites us not to judge by appearances or act on impulse. It also reminds us to keep our promises to others. God can work even in very crooked human stories, but that does not justify wrongdoing.
exp.2:19:
Here Adam gives his wife a name: Eve. The reason he gives is that she would be the mother of all living, that is, of all humanity. In Hebrew, the name Eve is related to the word for "life," although some scholars debate its exact origin.

The narrator tells us what Adam does right after God announced the consequences of sin, including death: "for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return." Even so, Adam names his wife with a name that speaks of life and of the future. Many see this as a sign of faith that God would continue to care for humanity, and some connect it with the earlier promise about the woman's offspring. Others see it simply as an act of authority and of accepting reality.

For today: even in the midst of pain and difficult consequences, we can choose to speak and live with hope, trusting that God continues to work in favor of life.
exp.23:28:
This verse introduces Laban, Rebekah's brother. It says that he ran out toward the man, who was beside the well, or spring of water. The word "out" indicates that Laban came out of the family house.

The one speaking is the narrator of the account. Abraham's servant had arrived looking for a wife for Isaac, and Rebekah had already run to tell what had happened in her mother's house. Upon hearing it, Laban goes out to meet the servant. The text does not explain all of his reasons. From what follows, he saw the gifts his sister had received, and some readers think that influenced his haste. Others also see simple hospitality.

Today we can learn to welcome with promptness and kindness whoever comes to our door. But it is also wise to examine our motives: that our generosity springs from a sincere heart and not from self-interest.
exp.30:40:
Jacob says he has lived twenty years with Laban. He worked fourteen years for his two daughters, Leah and Rachel, and six years for the livestock. He also states that Laban changed his wages ten times. "Changed" is the sense of the word used in this verse, which in the King James Version is rendered "changed my wages." "Ten times" may be a way of saying "many times," though it could also be an exact number.

Jacob speaks to Laban after fleeing with his family and his flocks. Laban caught up with him and accused him. Jacob defends himself and reminds Laban of his hard and honest work, even under unfair conditions. He says God saw his labor.

For today: even when you are treated unjustly at work, remain honest and responsible. You can speak clearly when it is necessary, but trust that God sees your effort and cares for you, even when others do not acknowledge it.
exp.32:8:
Esau says to Jacob: "I have enough, my brother; keep that which is yours." The word "enough" here means "sufficient" or "more than enough" and carries no negative sense. Esau kindly declines the gift that Jacob offers him.

The two brothers are speaking at their reunion. Years earlier, Jacob had deceived Esau and fled out of fear of his revenge. Now Jacob sends him gifts and bows before him, seeking peace. Esau receives him without resentment and says he needs nothing. Jacob insists, and Esau finally accepts. Some think Esau was sincere; others think it was a courtesy typical of the time. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: reconciliation is made easier when we take humble steps, and when we learn to be content with what God has given us, without holding on to resentment or greed.
exp.4:8:
This verse says that Enos lived ninety years and then had a son named Cainan. The word "begat" means that he became a father.

The text is part of the list of Adam's descendants in Genesis 5. No one is speaking in it; the narrator simply records one generation after another. This list shows how humanity continued after Adam, passing from fathers to sons. The very long ages are understood in several ways: some take them literally, and others see them as a way of speaking in that time. We do not know for certain which explanation is right.

For today: God notices every life, even those that seem like just a name on a list. Your faith can be the thread that connects your family to the next generation. Teach your children, and those around you, to know God through your daily example.
exp.3:5:
God says to Cain directly and asks him two questions. "Wroth" means very angry, and "is thy countenance fallen" means that his face had changed; his anger and sadness showed in his expression. God does not ask because He does not know the answer, but to invite Cain to look at his own heart.

The Lord speaks. Cain and Abel had both presented offerings, and God looked with favor on Abel's but not on Cain's. The text does not explain in detail why; some think it had to do with the attitude of the heart, and the New Testament points to Abel's faith (Hebrews 11:4). God speaks before Cain acts, giving him an opportunity to correct himself.

Today, when we feel anger or envy, God invites us to stop and be honest with Him before those emotions lead us to do harm.
exp.34:26:
This verse tells us that Jacob returned to the home of his father Isaac, at Mamre, near Hebron. The text also explains that this place was once called "the city of Arba." It recalls that Abraham and Isaac had lived there. The word "sojourned" here means that they lived as strangers, passing through that land.

The narrator, traditionally Moses, continues the story of Jacob. After his years in Padan-aram and the death of Rachel, Jacob comes back to the family home. This happens just before Isaac's death. In this way, the account shows that Jacob was able to reunite with his father before he died.

For today: let us not let time pass without visiting and honoring our parents and elders. Even when life takes us far away and we are busy, returning to them in time is a gift that cannot be repeated later.
exp.8:17:
This verse presents the three sons of Noah who came out of the ark: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. In the King James Version, the name spelled "Ham" is the one the explanation discusses, and it is listed here as the father of Canaan, a detail that sets up what follows.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. God has just established his covenant with Noah and set the rainbow in the clouds as a sign. Now the story moves from God's promise to the life of the family that will repopulate the earth. Mentioning Canaan anticipates the account that follows, which involves Ham and his descendants. Interpreters explain in various ways why he is mentioned here.

For today: God keeps his promises, but life in family remains real and sometimes difficult. We can trust his faithfulness and, at the same time, care with prayer and wisdom for our relationships and the example we leave to those who come after us.
exp.40:3:
The explanation says that the lean and ill-looking cows ate up the seven fat, well-favoured cows. Then Pharaoh awoke. "Leanfleshed" means very thin, with no flesh on them. "Did eat up" means they swallowed them up completely.

Here no person is speaking; the account tells of Pharaoh of Egypt's first dream. God was showing him what would happen: seven years of plenty and seven of famine. No one at court could explain it, and so Joseph was later called to interpret it. The text itself says the dream comes from God (Genesis 41:25).

For today: good times do not last forever. We can give thanks for what we have, manage wisely what God gives us, and prepare for hard times, trusting that He cares for us.
exp.4:17:
This verse says that Jared lived 162 years and then had his son Enoch. In the old wording, "begat" means that he became the father of, and "Enoch" is the same name that we read today as Enoch.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the narrator of Genesis, who presents the family line from Adam to Noah. It is a list that passes from father to son and keeps the thread of God's promise running through the generations. There is an important detail: this Enoch is the son of Jared, and he is different from the Enoch of Cain (Genesis 4:17). About the very long lifespans, scholars have several interpretations, and the text does not explain them.

For today: God works in the lives of ordinary people, and his faithfulness passes from generation to generation. Think about what faith and what example you are leaving to those who come after you.
exp.40:21:
Pharaoh tells that in another dream he saw seven ears of grain growing on a single stalk, all full and fine. The word "dreaming" in the original means "while he was dreaming." An ear is the part of the plant where the grain forms, in this case of wheat or barley.

Here Pharaoh, king of Egypt, is telling Joseph his two dreams, because no one in his court, not even the magicians, could explain them. He was troubled, and Joseph had been brought out of prison to interpret them. Afterward, Joseph says that God was showing Pharaoh what he was about to do.

For today: when something troubles you or you do not understand what lies ahead, do not rely only on your own judgment. Pray, seek wise counsel, and ask God for direction. He can give clarity and help you prepare with responsibility.
exp.25:9:
Abimelech rebukes Isaac for having said that Rebekah was his sister. He says that someone from the people might very nearly have lain with her, and that this would have brought guilt upon all of them. "You would have brought sin upon us" means that Isaac would have made them guilty of a serious wrong without their knowing it.

Abimelech, king of the Philistines in Gerar, speaks. He has just seen Isaac caressing Rebekah and understands that they are husband and wife. Isaac had lied out of fear that he would be killed. It is striking that a king who did not know Isaac's God shows here more moral sensitivity than Isaac did. He then protects the couple with a public order.

For today: a lie, even one born of fear, can harm others and damage our witness. Trusting God and telling the truth is safer than protecting ourselves with deception. God, moreover, was faithful to Isaac despite his failure.
exp.30:54:
Laban rose early in the morning, kissed his grandchildren and his daughters, and blessed them. Then he took his leave and returned to his home. The old words are "early in the morning," which means very early, and "unto his place," which means to his land or to his home.

Jacob had fled from Laban, his father-in-law, with his wives, his children, and his possessions. Laban caught up with him, there was tension and accusations, and in the end they made a covenant of peace. This verse closes that story. Here the narrator speaks, and shows that the conflict ended without violence. The "sons" are his grandchildren, whom the Bible calls that according to the usage of the time.

For today: even when there are wounds or disagreements within the family, we can seek a peaceful farewell. Blessing others, instead of holding on to resentment, helps us close conflicts with dignity and trust that God cares for everyone.
exp.43:15:
Judah speaks on behalf of all his brothers. He asks what they can say or speak, or how they can prove their innocence, and he admits that they have no defense. He says, "God hath found out the iniquity of thy servants," that is, God has uncovered a guilt. He offers himself along with all of them as servants of Joseph, including Benjamin, in whose sack the cup was found. Here "clear ourselves" means to prove that one is innocent.

Joseph had put his cup in Benjamin's sack in order to test his brothers. Judah does not know this. Perhaps he is speaking of the guilt they had carried since they sold Joseph, although the text does not say so clearly, and some readers interpret it that way.

Today, Judah teaches us to set aside excuses and take responsibility with humility. When we acknowledge our faults before God and others, the way opens to reconciliation and change.
exp.0:10:
God commands the earth to produce plants: green grass that yields seed, and fruit trees that bear fruit. "Kind" means type or class, and "seed" is the seed of each plant. Each plant carries its seed within itself, so that it can keep multiplying. "And it was so" means it happened just as God had said.

God himself speaks, on the third day of creation. He had already separated the waters from the dry land, and now he fills it with plant life. These plants prepare a place where animals and people will later live. The text shows order and careful provision. Christians understand this account in different ways, but all agree that God is the origin of life.

For today: when you eat a piece of fruit or see a tree, thank God for his provision. Caring for the earth and not wasting food is a simple way to honor what he has made.
exp.19:5:
God speaks to Abimelech in a dream and tells him that he knows he acted with a sincere heart, without evil intent. In addition, God affirms that it was He who kept him back from sinning against Him and from touching Sarah. "Integrity" means honesty and uprightness; "touch her" means to have relations with her.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, had taken Sarah because Abraham said she was his sister. God had warned him that he would die, and he was defending his innocence. Here God responds: He acknowledges his sincerity, but also shows that He Himself protected him. Afterward He commands him to return Sarah.

God sees our intentions and also guards us from mistakes we do not even know we are going to make. We can thank Him for His hidden protection and, at the same time, humbly correct whatever we have done wrong, even if it was unintentional.
exp.35:30:
This verse presents a list of the kings who ruled in Edom, the land of the descendants of Esau. It says that they reigned "before there reigned any king over the children of Israel," that is, before Israel had a king. "Dukes" here refers to clan chiefs.

The narrator of Genesis gathers the generations of Esau, also called Edom. Many understand this phrase to look ahead, toward the monarchy of Israel. Some believe Moses wrote it as a promise of future kings (as in Genesis 17:6), and others think it was added later. It cannot be stated with certainty which explanation is correct.

For today: God keeps his promises even when centuries pass. While other peoples seem to advance faster, we can trust that God works in his own time in our lives.
exp.0:6:
This verse tells that God made the "firmament," an old word that refers to the space or expanse above the earth, which God later calls "Heaven." With it he separated the waters below from the waters above. "And it was so" means that it happened just as God said it would.

Here the one who speaks and acts is God, on the second day of creation. First he commands it with his word (v. 6) and then he carries it out. His work brings order to what was without form. Scholars understand in different ways what "the waters which were above the firmament" were, and the Bible does not explain this in detail.

For today: if God could bring order to the chaos of the beginning, he can also bring order to the confusing areas of your life. Place them in his hands in prayer and take the next step with confidence.
exp.34:3:
Here the text tells us that Jacob's household handed over all the idols they had, along with the earrings they wore in their ears. The King James Version calls the idols "strange gods," which is the same idea: gods belonging to others, not to the God of Jacob. The word "earrings" is the same thing the explanation calls pendants or hoops worn in the ears. "Oak" is a large, sturdy tree. Jacob hid all of it under that tree, near Shechem.

Jacob had just lived through a very painful episode in Shechem, and God had told him to go to Bethel. Before reaching that holy place, Jacob asks his household to put away the foreign gods and prepare themselves. The earrings may have been tied to those idols, although the text does not make this clear.

For today: before we approach God with sincerity, it is good to ask ourselves what things have taken his place in our hearts. Letting them go, with humility and resolve, allows us to walk more freely and confidently with him.
exp.7:6:
This verse tells how Noah opened the window of the ark and sent out a raven. The bird kept going out and coming back, again and again, until the earth was dry. The phrase "to and fro" describes a back-and-forth movement: it went, it returned, it went again.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. The floodwaters were going down little by little, and the tops of the mountains were already visible. Noah wanted to know whether the earth was ready. The text does not explain why the raven went back and forth. Some think it rested on the ark or on things floating in the water, but that is only a possibility.

For today: Noah did not rush to leave the ark. He waited and watched patiently, trusting that God had already kept him safe. When you are waiting for an answer or a change, do not despair. Take simple steps, keep trusting, and let God set the timing.
exp.21:12:
Abraham lifted up his eyes and saw a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He went, took the ram, and offered it up as a burnt offering, that is, a sacrifice presented to God, in place of his son. The phrase "behind him" in the King James wording means behind Abraham, that is, behind his back. "Thicket" refers to a tangle of bushes with thorns.

God had tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac. Just as he was about to do it, the angel of the Lord stopped him from heaven. Then Abraham saw the ram. The account shows that God himself provided the sacrifice. Afterward Abraham named that place "The Lord will provide." Many Christians see here a shadow of Christ, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: when you feel you see no way out, keep trusting and obeying God step by step. He knows your need and often shows his provision when you take the next step of faith.
exp.33:27:
This verse says that Jacob's sons took the animals of the Shechemites: their sheep, cattle and donkeys. They also took everything that was in the city and in the field. In the King James Version, "substance" means wealth or possessions, and the word "asses" here means donkeys.

Here the narrator of the story speaks. After Shechem dishonored Dinah, Simeon and Levi killed the men of the city, and their brothers plundered the place. The Bible recounts the event without approving of it, and Jacob later rebukes them for having brought danger upon his family.

For today: even when we have suffered injustice, revenge and greed only multiply the harm. We can seek justice with honesty, leave resentment in God's hands, and take care that our pain does not lead us to make others suffer.
exp.43:32:
Judah asks Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize, to keep him as a slave in place of Benjamin, the lad. "I pray thee" means "I ask you," "lad" is a young man, and "servant" is one who serves. Judah asks that the young man be allowed to return to his brothers.

Judah speaks before Joseph, the ruler of Egypt. His silver cup was found in Benjamin's sack, and Joseph said that Benjamin would remain as a slave. Judah recalls that he promised his father Jacob to look after the young man. Knowing that Jacob would die of grief moves him to offer himself in his place.

For today: true love sometimes shows itself by taking on the cost for others. Judah, who had once sold Joseph, now changes and offers himself for his brother. We can keep our promises and care for the vulnerable, even when it costs us.
exp.4:28:
Lamech gives his son the name Noah and explains why. He hopes this child will bring them relief from the weariness of their work and their hands, because of the ground that God cursed. "Will comfort" means will bring rest or consolation. "Lord" is the name of God. The old form "hath" is an archaic way of saying "has."

Lamech, the father, speaks within a long list of generations from Adam. His remark recalls what God said in Genesis 3:17-19, when the ground came under a curse and work became hard. Many understand that Lamech longed for hope. Some connect the name Noah with the idea of rest or comfort, though scholars debate that connection. The Bible does not say how that hope was fulfilled.

For today: when your work wears you down, do not lose hope. Put your trust in God, who continues to work and bring comfort, even in difficult times.
exp.23:40:
It says the servant would be released from his solemn promise if, upon arriving with Abraham's family, they did not hand over the young woman to him. "Kindred" means family or relatives. "If they give not thee one" means "if they do not give you one," where the KJV's wording "give not thee one" is the old form of "do not give you one."

The one speaking is Abraham's servant. He tells Laban and Bethuel what his master charged him to do: find a wife for Isaac among his relatives. He repeats Abraham's words to show that his mission has a clear limit and that he acts with honesty, not pressure.

For today: keep what we promise faithfully, but also recognize what does not depend on us. We can do our part with effort and leave the result in God's hands, trusting that He guides our path.
exp.4:16:
The explanation says that Mahalaleel lived a total of 895 years and then died. It is the summary of his life: 65 years before he became the father of Jared and 830 years after, which adds up to 895. The word "begot" means that he became a father, and "Enoch," in the King James Version, is the name that appears in the verses that follow in this list.

Here no character speaks; it is the author of the book who is recording the list of descendants from Adam. Each person appears with his age, his children, and his death. That repetition shows how the family line continues from generation to generation, but also that death reaches everyone, as a consequence of Adam's fall (Genesis 3). Scholars discuss how these very long ages should be understood, and the Bible does not explain it.

For today: our life is brief and can be summed up in a few words. It is worth living it with faith and passing that faith on to those who come after us.
exp.49:18:
Here Joseph says to his brothers: "Do not be afraid." Then he asks them a question: "Am I in the place of God?" That is, he does not consider himself the one to judge them or to take revenge.

Their father Jacob had already died. The brothers feared that Joseph, now powerful in Egypt, would punish them for having sold him years earlier. So they sent him a message asking forgiveness and bowed down before him. Joseph wept when he heard this. His answer shows humility: he recognizes that judging and giving the final punishment belong to God, not to him.

For today: when someone has wronged us, we can leave revenge in God's hands. That does not make wrong into right, but it frees us from resentment and opens the way to forgiveness and peace.
exp.44:6:
Here José tells his brothers that God sent him to Egypt before them. The purpose was that his family would be kept alive on the earth and saved through a great deliverance. The explanation of the old wording is set aside here, since the King James Version reads differently: "preserve you a posterity" means keeping a family line alive, and "deliverance" means rescue or liberation.

José speaks to his brothers, who years earlier had sold him as a slave. Now he is governor of Egypt and makes himself known to them. They are frightened and ashamed, and there is famine across the whole region. José does not deny what they did, but he sees that God used even that wrong to care for the family.

When something hurts or seems unjust, we do not always understand why. We can trust that God is still at work and can bring good out of difficult situations, without that making the wrong acceptable. We can also offer forgiveness, as José did.
exp.9:17:
This verse closes the list of the sons of Canaan, grandson of Noah. It names three more peoples: the Arvadites, the Zemarites, and the Hamathites. "Spread abroad" means that the Canaanite families gradually scattered and settled across different territories.

The author of the book (tradition attributes it to Moses) is presenting the "table of nations," which explains how the lands were resettled after the flood. The Canaanites are described in detail because Israel would live among them and enter their territory. The exact locations of each people are not always known with certainty.

For today: God knows peoples and individuals by name, even when history has forgotten them. This reminds us that no person is insignificant to Him. Today we can treat everyone with respect, knowing that each one has value before God.
exp.38:6:
After these things, Potiphar's wife looked at Joseph with desire. "Cast her eyes upon Joseph" means she looked at him with interest and lust. Then she said to him plainly, "Lie with me," that is, she proposed that they have sexual relations. It was an invitation to commit adultery.

Here the speaker is Potiphar's wife. Joseph was a young Hebrew slave, to whom his master had given authority over his entire household, and God was blessing him. The text says Joseph was handsome. She used her position of power to pressure him. Joseph then refused, because it would betray his master's trust and sin against God.

For today: temptation sometimes comes directly and in moments of trust. Decide your limits in advance, and if the test comes, say "no" firmly, thinking first of your faithfulness to God.
exp.26:1:
Isaac tells his son Esau that he is now old and does not know the day of his death. It is a way of saying that he feels the end of his life is near and does not want to let more time pass. "Behold" is like saying "look" or "pay attention."

Isaac speaks as an elderly man, nearly blind. He wants to give the family blessing to Esau, his firstborn son, before he dies. In that time, this blessing carried great weight for the son's future. What comes next in the story, with Rebekah and Jacob, shows that things did not turn out as Isaac had planned. God had said something different earlier about the children (Genesis 25:23).

For today: no one knows how much time they have left. Do not put off what is important, such as forgiving, blessing your family, or setting your affairs in order with God and with those you love.
exp.28:21:
This verse tells that Laban gathered together all the men of the place and made a feast. The words "gathered together" and "men" are the same ideas as "gathered" and "men" in the older wording. A feast was a large festive meal, normal at weddings in that time.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jacob had worked seven years for Rachel and now asked to marry her. Laban prepares the celebration, but the following text shows that this celebration became the occasion for giving Leah in place of Rachel. The text does not state clearly when Laban decided on the deception, so it is best not to assume more than what is written.

For today: a celebration or a good appearance does not guarantee sincerity. Let us strive to act with truth and keep what we have promised, and ask God for wisdom to see beyond what appears on the surface.
exp.8:5:
Whoever takes a person's life will have to answer for it with their own life. The reason is that human beings were made "in the image of God." The word "shed" here refers to taking a life by violence.

God speaks with Noah and his sons after the flood. He is beginning a new stage for humanity and establishes that human life is sacred. Christians interpret this verse in different ways: some see a foundation for civil justice, while others see above all a warning about the value of life.

For today: treat every person with respect, even when you don't like them or they think differently from you, because they carry the image of God. Watch your words and how you treat others.
exp.34:27:
This verse says that Isaac lived one hundred and eighty years. It is a brief detail that marks the end of his life. By the count in the text, he lived longer than his father Abraham, who died at 175, and in the account Isaac appears as a man who reached a very advanced age.

The narrator of Genesis closes Isaac's story here. Jacob had just returned to Hebron, where his father was living, after many years away. The text goes on to say that Isaac died "old, and full of days," that is, satisfied with a long life, and that Esau and Jacob, who had once been enemies, buried him together.

For today: our days are numbered and precious. We can live them with faith and take care of our relationships, above all with family, so that, like Isaac, we reach the end in peace and not with wounds left unhealed.
exp.7:20:
It says that God accepted Noah's sacrifice with pleasure. The phrase "sweet savour" is a way of saying that the offering pleased him. Then God decided in his heart not to curse the ground again because of man, nor to destroy every living thing as he had done with the flood. The word "imagination" in the King James means the inclination or thoughts of the heart, and "from his youth" points to how early that inclination begins.

This is the account in Genesis, where the narrator tells what God thought. Noah had just come out of the ark and offered a burnt offering in gratitude. God recognizes that the human heart leans toward evil from youth, yet still promises mercy. Some think that reality is the reason for the promise; others, that it is a warning about why grace is needed. The text allows both readings.

For today: God knows us as we are and still treats us with patience. We can approach him with gratitude and sincerity, without pretending to be perfect, trusting in his mercy.
exp.26:8:
Rebekah tells Jacob to go to the flock and bring her two good young goats. With them she will prepare "savoury meat," that is, tasty food, just the way his father Isaac likes it.

Rebekah speaks to her son Jacob. She had just heard Isaac ask Esau for a meal before blessing him. She proposes a plan so that Jacob will receive that blessing instead of Esau. The text recounts the deception without approving it; its painful consequences appear later in the family. Some recall that God had earlier announced that the older would serve the younger (Genesis 25:23), but that does not make the method good.

For today: trusting God's promises does not give us permission to take shortcuts or to tell lies. If God has promised something, we can wait and act honestly, without forcing things through deceit.
exp.31:31:
This verse explains a custom of the Israelites: they did not eat the sinew of the hip, the part where the thigh joins the hip bone. "Shrank" means that it became twisted or damaged. The explanation also notes that the KJV's "which shrank" and "in the sinew that shrank" both refer to this same injured tendon, and that "hollow of the thigh" is the place where the thigh meets the hip. The memory recalled here is the moment Jacob was touched in that place.

The one who speaks is the narrator of the book. Earlier, Jacob wrestled all night with a mysterious man, who touched him on the hip, and Jacob was left limping. Afterward he recognized that he had seen God. The text does not say where or when this custom began, only that it continued "unto this day" when it was written.

For today: sometimes God uses our struggles to leave a mark that reminds us we depend on Him. Today we can think about a past difficulty and give thanks for what it taught us, rather than being ashamed of it.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that Shem, Ham, and Japheth are the three sons of Noah, and that from them the earth was filled with people. The word "overspread" means that the earth was completely populated.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. The flood has just ended, and God has made a covenant with Noah and with every living creature. This verse summarizes how the world was repopulated and prepares the next story, where Noah plants a vineyard and a painful episode occurs in his family. Some see here a common origin for all peoples; the details of how those genealogies are to be understood are interpreted in various ways.

For today: we all come from one common origin and have equal worth before God. Today we can treat every person, from any people, with respect and humility, as part of one great family.
exp.29:22:
It says that Rachel became pregnant and had a son. Then she declared that God had taken away her "reproach." The explanation notes that the wording in the older translation was "afrenta," which means shame or humiliation; that comment doesn't apply to the King James wording here, so it's dropped. "Bare" means "gave birth."

The one speaking is Rachel, Jacob's wife. For years she could not have children, while her sister Leah, the other wife of Jacob, had many. In that culture, not having children was often experienced as a heavy burden and a great dishonor. The text says that God remembered her and heard her. She recognizes God as the one who delivered her from that shame. Afterward she names the boy Joseph, and asks for another son.

For today: when you carry a shame or a long wait, bring it to God honestly. And when he answers, don't forget to thank him, as Rachel did.
exp.13:0:
This verse introduces four kings from the region of the ancient Near East. Amraphel of Shinar, Arioch of Ellasar, Chedorlaomer of Elam, and Tidal, "king of nations," are named. "It came to pass in the days of" is an older way of saying "it happened in the time of."

The narrator of the book, whom tradition attributes to Moses, here recounts the first armed conflict in the Bible. He sets the scene for the story of Abram and his nephew Lot, who lived in Sodom. Scholars cannot identify with certainty all of these kings, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: the decisions of the powerful can affect us even when we did not make them. Even so, God cares for his people in the midst of conflicts. Pray for those who govern and trust that God works even when the world seems in disorder.
exp.27:8:
The explanation says that Esau went to the family of Ishmael, his uncle, and married Mahalath, daughter of Ishmael and sister of Nebaioth. He already had other wives, and now he adds this one. "Went" here means "he went away" and "took to wife" means "he married."

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. Esau saw that his father Isaac was not pleased with the Canaanite women, and that Jacob had been sent to find a wife among the relatives. So Esau tried to please his father by marrying a descendant of Abraham. The Bible does not explain his motives further, so we do not know whether it was a sincere gesture or only a late arrangement.

For today: Correcting a mistake is good, but God looks at the heart. Let us seek to obey sincerely, not only to look good before others.
exp.40:10:
This verse says that the king's cupbearer and baker both had a dream on the same night, while the two of them were in prison. "We dreamed a dream" means that both of them dreamed. The phrase "each man according to the interpretation of his dream" means that each dream had its own meaning, which would later be explained according to what each one had dreamed.

The one speaking is the chief cupbearer, that is, the man in charge of pouring the wine for Pharaoh. Two years have passed, and Pharaoh has dreams that no one can explain. Then the cupbearer remembers Joseph, the young Hebrew who interpreted his dream in prison, and tells the king about him. This is how Joseph's path toward the palace begins.

For today: God can use moments that seem forgotten or meaningless to prepare something greater. If you are waiting in the middle of a difficult situation today, keep being faithful and trust that God is working in his own time.
exp.33:25:
The explanation says that Simeon and Levi killed Hamor, the city's ruler, and his son Shechem with the sword. Then they took Dinah out of Shechem's house and left. "With the edge of the sword" means killing with the sharp side of the blade. "Went out" means they left that place.

Here the book's narrator speaks. Shechem had abused Dinah, and the brothers answered with deception: they asked the men of the city to be circumcised and attacked when they were in pain. The Bible reports the event without approving it. Later, Jacob condemns it (Genesis 34:30; 49:5-7).

For today: pain and injustice are real, but violent revenge and deceit only multiply the harm. Let us seek justice by honest paths and ask God for self-control before acting in anger.
exp.43:7:
Joseph's brothers defend their innocence. They say that they already returned, from the land of Canaan, the money they found in the mouths of their sacks, so it would make no sense for them to steal silver or gold from the house of the lord of Egypt. "Steal" here is the word the King James Version uses for taking what belongs to someone else.

The speaker is one of Joseph's brothers, addressing the steward who had caught up with them. Joseph had ordered his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack, though they did not know it. Their argument rests on their past conduct: they had already shown their honesty by returning the money. Their confidence leads them to make a very serious promise: whoever has the cup will die.

Today we can learn to live with integrity so that our conduct speaks for us. It also warns us not to make hasty promises, even when we are sure of our innocence.
exp.0:5:
The explanation says that God spoke and ordered that there be an "expanse" between the waters. The word "expanse" refers to an open space, like a great extent over the earth, which God then calls "Heaven." Its purpose was to separate some waters from others. The text does not explain in detail how this was; some understand it as the atmosphere and the visible sky, and others according to the picture the ancients had of the world.

The one speaking is God, and he does so on the second day of creation. After separating light from darkness, he now continues to bring order. The account shows a God who does not create at random, but with order, step by step, turning what is disordered into a place where life can be lived.

Today we can trust that God knows how to bring order into what is confused. If your life feels turned upside down, bring each area before him and ask him for wisdom to take the next step, with patience.
exp.28:0:
The explanation says that Jacob continued his journey and came to the region of "the easterners," that is, to the people who lived east of Canaan. The phrase "went on his journey" can also be understood as "lifted up his feet," like someone who resumes walking with spirit.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob was fleeing the anger of his brother Esau and was heading toward the family of his uncle Laban, in Haran. Earlier, at Bethel, God had promised to be with him and watch over him (Genesis 28). This verse shows that, after that promise, Jacob simply kept walking. Nothing more is said about his feelings.

For today: when God gives you a promise, a detailed explanation of the future does not always come with it. Sometimes it is only a matter of taking the next step with confidence. Walk today in faith, doing what is in front of you.
exp.48:22:
It says that José was attacked harshly. The phrase "they caused him bitterness" means they gave him a great deal of pain. "They shot at him" means they shot arrows at him, and "the archers" are the men who shoot with bows. "They hated him" indicates that they hated him. It is figurative language: it speaks of attacks, envy, and hostility.

Here Jacob, now an old man, is blessing each of his sons before he dies. About José he looks back: his brothers envied him and sold him, and later he lived in Egypt through injustices such as a false accusation and prison. Many understand that it also refers to the future tribes that would descend from him. This cannot be fully pinned down. What matters is that the next verse shows God sustaining him.

If envy or injustice wounds you today, you are not alone. As with José, God can sustain you and give you strength. Give Him your pain and seek His help so that you do not respond with bitterness.
exp.26:15:
Rebekah covers Jacob's hands and the smooth part of his neck with the skins of the young goats. "Neck" is the nape or back of the neck, and "smooth" refers to the hairless skin there, in contrast to the hairy skin of Esau. In this way, Jacob would feel hairy like his brother Esau.

Rebekah had heard that Isaac wanted to bless Esau. She planned for Jacob to receive that blessing and prepared a deception, because Isaac was already old and could not see well. Although God had said earlier that the older would serve the younger (Genesis 25:23), the account does not approve of the deception. It shows how a divided family falls into trickery and pain.

For today: when we believe God has promised something, we do not need to hurry it along with lies or manipulation. Trusting God includes waiting and acting with honesty, even when the path seems slow or difficult.
exp.29:31:
Jacob proposes a payment to Laban. He will pass through the flocks and set apart the animals that are spotted and speckled, and the dark-colored ones among the sheep. Those will be his wages. "Cattle" here refers to the animals of the flock, and "speckled" and "spotted" describe animals with spots or mixed markings.

Jacob is speaking to his father-in-law Laban. He had already worked for him for years, and Laban had prospered. Now Jacob wants to begin providing for his own family. He asks for a payment that seems small, because most of the animals were of a single color. The Bible does not say here that Jacob was completely innocent in what follows; the story shows both his cleverness and the faithfulness of God.

For today: it is right to speak plainly about the pay for our work and to agree on terms with honesty. And when a deal seems unequal, we can trust that God cares for us while we act with integrity.
exp.30:4:
Jacob tells Rachel and Leah that he notices Laban, their father, no longer looks on him with a friendly face, as he did before. "Countenance" means the face or attitude that a person shows. The phrase "as before" means "in the past." But Jacob adds that the God of his father has been with him.

Jacob speaks with his two wives in the field, far from Laban's house. After years of work, his relationship with his father-in-law has grown cold, and there is tension. God had already told him to return to the land of his fathers and that he would be with him. That is why Jacob wants to speak with them before leaving.

For today: when someone changes how they treat you and you feel rejected, remember that God's presence does not depend on people's attitudes. You can trust that He accompanies and guides you, and seek wise counsel and prayer before making difficult decisions.
exp.20:6:
Sarah says in amazement: "Who would have said to Abraham that Sarah would nurse children?" She adds that she has already borne him a son in his old age. "Give suck" means to nurse, and "born" means she gave birth. Although she speaks of "children," she means that she can now nurse a baby.

Sarah speaks here. She had waited for years and had laughed in doubt when God promised a son (Genesis 18:12). Now Isaac has been born, whose name is connected with laughter, and she rejoices. Her joy comes from seeing that God has fulfilled what seemed impossible. Abraham was a hundred years old.

For today: If you are waiting for something that seems impossible, do not lose hope. God can fulfill his promise in his own time, and when he does, remember to give thanks and tell others, as Sarah did.
exp.39:12:
This verse says that, within three days, the pharaoh of Egypt will restore the cupbearer to his position. "Lift up thine head" means that he will bring him out of prison and honor him again. "Restore" means to return something to its place, and "butler" is the one who served the king his cup. "Wast" is the old form of "were," so the phrase means "when you were his cupbearer."

Joseph speaks from prison. The cupbearer had told him a dream about a vine with three branches, and Joseph interprets it as three days. He says this as an interpreter, but makes clear that the interpretation comes from God (v. 8). Right after, he asks the cupbearer to remember him, because he is imprisoned unjustly.

Today we can learn to be faithful and to serve with love even in difficult places, as Joseph did. It is also healthy to ask for help with humility, while trusting that God works in his own time, even when others forget us.
exp.29:15:
Leah goes out to meet Jacob as he comes in from the field in the evening. She tells him that he must come in to her, because she has hired him, that is, engaged or paid for his company, with her son's mandrakes. Mandrakes were plants that at that time were believed to have power to promote fertility. Jacob agrees, and he spends the night with her.

The speaker is Leah, the less loved wife. Rachel, her sister, longed for children and asked for the mandrakes in exchange for a night with Jacob. It was a family marked by rivalry and by human attempts to win affection or solve problems. Afterward, the text says that God heard Leah.

For today: when you feel competition, lack, or pain, avoid manipulating others or bargaining for affection. Bring your need to God, who sees and hears, even when our decisions are clumsy.
exp.23:44:
This verse tells how, while Abraham's servant was still praying silently, Rebekah appeared with her pitcher on her shoulder. She went down to the spring, drew water, and he asked her for a drink. The phrase "before I had done speaking in mine heart" means that he was still praying inwardly, without words. The old "I pray thee" of the King James wording simply means "please," which is the same request expressed in the more familiar modern form.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant. Abraham sent him far away to find a wife for his son Isaac, and here he recounts for Rebekah's family how everything happened. He explains that his prayer was answered so precisely that he saw in it the guidance of God.

For today: we can bring God our important decisions with sincere prayer, even the prayer we make in silence. He can guide us, and it is wise to be attentive, with humility and patience, to how He responds.
exp.18:11:
The two visitors ask Lot whether he has any more family in the city: sons-in-law, sons, daughters, or any other person or possession. They tell him to bring them out of that place. The "men" are the visitors who had come to his house, and the "sons-in-law" are the husbands of his daughters.

These two messengers sent by God, who appeared as men, speak. They had just protected Lot from the violent crowd of Sodom. Now they warn him that the city is going to be destroyed, and so they give him the chance to rescue his own. Some understand "sons-in-law" to mean men already betrothed to his daughters, and others, men already married to them; the text leaves the question open.

God cares for whole families, not only for one person. If you know God's hope today, think kindly about who among your own family needs to hear it. Speak to them with humility, with love, and with patience, even when some do not take you seriously.
exp.21:10:
Verse 11 tells us that just as Abraham was about to kill his son, the angel of the LORD called to him from heaven with urgency. He spoke his name twice: "Abraham, Abraham." The phrase "called unto him" means that he called out to him loudly. "Here am I" means "I am here."

God had asked Abraham to offer Isaac as a test of his faith. Abraham obeyed right up to the last moment. The angel of the LORD speaks on behalf of God and, in this passage, the voice is God himself. He stops the sacrifice and confirms that Abraham fears God. Some scholars see here a sign that God did not want human sacrifices, and others see a foreshadowing of Christ.

For today: God calls us by our name and is attentive to our lives. We can respond as Abraham did, with a willing heart: "Here am I." Trusting God even when we do not understand everything is an act of faith.
exp.17:29:
Here Abraham keeps speaking with God and asks, with great respect, that God not be angry if he persists. He asks what would happen if thirty righteous people were found in the city, and God answers that He would not destroy it for the sake of those thirty. The word "peradventure" means "perhaps," and "let not the Lord be angry" is a courteous way of asking permission to keep speaking.

Abraham intercedes for Sodom, where his nephew Lot lived. God had told him that He was going to examine the wickedness of the city. Abraham begins with fifty righteous people and gradually lowers the number. God listens to him with patience and shows His mercy.

For today: we can pray with confidence and humility for other people, even for those who seem far from God. He is not troubled by a sincere and persistent prayer.
exp.34:5:
This verse says that Jacob arrived at a place called Luz, in the land of Canaan, which is the same place later known as Bethel. He was accompanied by all the people with him: his family and his servants. "Luz" was the city's old name, and "Bethel" means "house of God."

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. God had told Jacob to go up to Bethel. Earlier, Jacob had removed the idols from his family and hidden them. Bethel was the place where, years before, Jacob had fled from his brother Esau, and God had appeared to him in a dream.

For today: before we draw near to God, it is good to set aside whatever has taken his place in our hearts. Obeying him, even when the road is long, brings us back into his presence.
exp.26:14:
This verse tells how Rebekah took the finest clothes of Esau, her older son, which she kept in the house, and put them on Jacob, the younger. The King James wording "goodly raiment" means valuable clothing, perhaps of special use.

Here the narrator speaks. Isaac, now old and nearly blind, wanted to bless Esau. Rebekah heard the plan and decided that Jacob should receive the blessing, so she prepared a deception. She had already said that if it went wrong, the curse would fall on her. The text does not approve of the deception; it only tells what happened, and serious consequences for the family follow.

For today: even when we believe God has a purpose, we must not use lies or manipulation to achieve it. Trusting God means acting with honesty and waiting for his timing.
exp.43:2:
It says that, at dawn, Joseph let his brothers leave together with their donkeys, which were loaded with the grain. The word "sent away" here means they were allowed to go; they were sent back home. The "asses" were the pack animals they used for the journey.

The narrator tells this moment in the middle of the test Joseph is preparing for his brothers. Without their knowledge, his silver and the silver cup are hidden in the sacks. Everything seems to be going well, but it is the calm before they are overtaken. Scholars understand Joseph's purpose in different ways: many think he wanted to know whether his brothers had changed.

For today: sometimes life seems calm just before a trial. We can trust that God is at work even when we do not see the whole picture, and live with integrity, since character is revealed when trial comes.
exp.39:1:
It says that Pharaoh was filled with anger against two of his closest officials: the chief of the cupbearers, who served the king wine and drinks, and the chief of the bakers, who prepared his bread and food. The word "eunuchs" here can mean officials or court functionaries, although some also understand it in its literal sense. "Wroth" means "angry."

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Genesis. He tells that these two men had offended the king, although the text does not clearly explain what their offense was. For this reason they ended up in prison, the same jail where Joseph was, and there their paths would cross.

For today: God can use difficult, even unjust, situations to prepare what is coming. Joseph kept serving faithfully in prison. Do your work well and treat others well, even if your situation is not the one you dreamed of.
exp.0:27:
God blessed the man and the woman and gave them three charges: to have children and fill the earth, to "subdue" it (to take care of it and make it productive), and to "have dominion" (to rule) over the animals. "Replenish" means "fill," and "be fruitful" means "bear fruit."

God himself, the Creator, speaks at the end of creation. He has just made human beings in his image, as male and female. Right away he gives them food: plants and fruit. For this reason, many understand this "dominion" as a charge to manage carefully what God made, not as permission to destroy. Some debate how to understand the verb "subdue," but the context shows a world that God called good.

Today we can see our work, our family, and nature as a responsibility that God has entrusted to us. Ask yourself: today, will I care for something God has placed in my hands, such as my home, my work, or the environment, with respect and love?
exp.0:23:
This verse tells that God commanded the earth to bring forth living beings. "Kind" and "species" refer to classes or types of creatures. The "beasts" are wild animals, and the "creeping things" are those that crawl. "And it was so" means it happened just as God said.

Here God speaks on the sixth day of creation. A day earlier He had filled the sea and the sky with life. Now He fills the land. It is the step just before the creation of human beings, which comes next. Some believers understand these days as literal days, and others as longer periods; the text does not fully settle the question.

God creates with order, purpose, and variety, and what He made is good. Today we can care for nature with gratitude, treating animals and the earth with respect, because they are the work of God.
exp.6:17:
It says that the water kept rising more and more and covered the earth with great force. "Prevailed" means the waters grew stronger and overcame everything. "Increased greatly" means they rose enormously. Meanwhile, the ark did not sink but floated on the surface of the waters ("the face" is the surface).

Genesis tells this as a flood account. Here it is not a character speaking but the narrator. God had already warned Noah of the judgment because of the violence and wickedness of the earth, and had commanded him to build the ark. The previous verse says that the LORD shut him in, a sign that God was caring for Noah and his family.

For today: when problems grow like a sea, remember that God can sustain you. Obeying Him does not keep every storm away, but He keeps you safe in the midst of it.
exp.9:9:
This verse says that the kingdom of Nimrod began with four cities: Babel, Erech, Accad, and Calneh, all in the land of Shinar. "Beginning" means the start or the main center. "Shinar" is the region later associated with Babylon, that is, the area between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers.

The author of the book, according to the Mosaic tradition, is presenting the list of nations after the flood. Here he tells how Nimrod, a descendant of Cush, went from being a mighty man to ruling cities. Some see in him an admirable leader; others, a figure of pride, because Babel appears later in the story of the tower. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: power and achievements can impress, but it is wise to ask ourselves for whom we are building. Let us ask God that our work and our goals honor Him and serve others.
exp.10:31:
This verse says that Terah lived 205 years and died in Haran. The name is Terah, the father of Abram. The phrase "the days of Terah" is an old way of saying the years of his life.

Here no character is speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis, closing the story of Terah's family. Terah had left Ur with his family on the way to Canaan, but he stayed in Haran. His death there sets up God's call to Abram in chapter 12. Some think Terah never finished the journey; the Bible does not explain why he stopped.

For today: sometimes we stop halfway in what God has placed on our hearts. Ask yourself whether there is some step of obedience you have put off. God is still guiding, and there is always a next step of faith to take.
exp.21:22:
This verse says that Bethuel was the father of Rebekah. It also sums up that Milcah had eight children with Nahor, Abraham's brother. The word "begat" means he was the father, and "did bear" means she gave birth.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Genesis. Right after Abraham obeys God by offering Isaac, the text gives us news about the family of his brother Nahor. It is not a speech but a family list. It seems to serve as a bridge to what comes next: Rebekah will appear later as Isaac's wife (Genesis 24). Some see here the hand of God preparing the way, although the text does not say it in those words.

For today: God cares for the details of our lives, even those we do not yet understand. Even when it seems nothing important is happening, God may be preparing people and moments for the future. We can trust and keep obeying with patience.
exp.16:19:
God tells Abraham that he has indeed heard his request concerning Ishmael. He promises to bless him, to make him fruitful, and to multiply him greatly. He will have twelve princes, that is, twelve heads or leaders of tribes, and God will make him a great nation. "Begets" means that he will be the father of those leaders, and "nation" here means a people or a nation.

God speaks with Abraham when he announces that Sarah will have a son, Isaac. Abraham had asked that Ishmael, his firstborn son, might live before God. God does not ignore him: he blesses him, but makes clear that his special covenant will continue through Isaac. Later, Genesis 25 mentions the twelve sons of Ishmael.

For today: God hears our prayers for the people we love. Even when His answer is not exactly what we asked for, He cares for them and has a plan. We can pray with confidence and rest in His goodness.
exp.16:21:
The explanation says that God finished speaking with Abraham and left his presence. The phrase "God went up from Abraham" is old-fashioned; today we would say "God withdrew from where Abraham was." It is a way of saying the conversation was over.

God had just spoken to Abraham about the covenant and circumcision. He had also promised that Sarah would have Isaac the following year, and that Ishmael would be blessed. The text does not explain how this appearance happened; it only says God "went up." Right away, Abraham obeys that same day.

For today: when God speaks to us through his Word, there is no need to wait before obeying. Abraham did not put off obedience until later. Ask yourself what God has shown you recently, and take one concrete step today to act on it.
exp.26:36:
Isaac tells Esau that he can no longer undo what he has done. He has made Jacob Esau's "lord," that is, his master or leader over him. He also gave all of Jacob's brothers to him as "servants," meaning that the relatives would be placed under his authority. He assured him of "corn and wine," which stand for abundance and provision. At the end, he asks with sorrow what he can now give to Esau.

Isaac is speaking as an old man, nearly blind. He had meant to bless Esau, but Jacob, with the help of their mother Rebekah, deceived him and received the blessing. Esau arrives weeping and hurt. Isaac recognizes that the blessing has already been given and cannot be the same for Esau.

For today: decisions and deceptions have consequences that hurt the whole family. Let us seek honesty and trust in God, instead of taking shortcuts that wound others.
exp.24:2:
This verse is part of a family list. It says that Jokshan, son of Abraham and Keturah, had two sons: Sheba and Dedan. Then it names three descendants of Dedan: Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim, which seem to be names of groups or tribes. "Begat" means "was the father of."

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis. After Sarah, Abraham had another wife, Keturah, and from her came many peoples. This shows God keeping his promise to make him the father of many nations. Even so, the text makes clear right away that Isaac received everything Abraham had. As to the exact location of these peoples, scholars do not have complete certainty.

For today: God pays attention to families and to names that seem small to us. Remember that your life and your inheritance of faith matter to Him; live today in a way that blesses those who come after you.
exp.37:2:
The verse says that Judah's wife became pregnant and gave birth to their first son. According to the custom of the time, the mother named him Er. The words "conceived" and "bare" mean became pregnant and gave birth. The text does not explain what the name Er means.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Judah had separated from his brothers and settled near Hirah. There he married a Canaanite woman, the daughter of Shua. This account continues the story of Jacob's family and prepares the way for what will happen later with Judah's sons, which will be complicated and painful.

For today: children are a gift, but also a great responsibility. We parents can ask God for wisdom to guide our children, not only to care for them, but also to teach them to live with integrity and respect toward God.
exp.35:24:
This verse says that Anah had two children: Dishon and a daughter named Aholibamah. It is part of a list of families. The word "children" here includes a son and a daughter, which is why the daughter is named as well.

Genesis 36 is a genealogy of Esau, also called Edom. No character speaks here; it is the narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, who records the lineages of the peoples neighboring Israel. Anah belonged to the people of Seir, with whom Esau's family became connected. Some scholars debate exactly how these families fit together, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: God notices every person and every name, even those that seem unimportant. Remember that you too are precious to Him, and treat others with that same respect.
exp.23:65:
This verse says that Abraham's servant told Isaac everything he had done. "Servant" here refers to the trusted servant who went to find a wife for Isaac. In today's language: the servant told Isaac everything he had done on his journey.

Here the narrator speaks. The servant had been sent by Abraham to his homeland to find a wife for Isaac. He had prayed, and Rebekah responded with kindness and went with him. Now, on arrival, the servant reports to Isaac on the mission accomplished. Then Isaac receives Rebekah, takes her as his wife, and loves her.

For today: when we have been given a task, it is wise to be faithful, to carry it out with care, and to give an account of it honestly. We can also gratefully recount what God has done along our path, acknowledging his help in what we have achieved.
exp.34:16:
It says that Rachel was having a very difficult and painful labour. The midwife, the woman who helped mothers give birth, speaks to her to calm her. "Fear not" means "do not be afraid." She assures her that another son will be born, that is, that the baby will come safely into the world.

The midwife speaks while the family of Jacob is on the journey toward Ephrath (Bethlehem). Rachel had already longed for another son (Genesis 30:24). Her labour becomes complicated, and the midwife tries to encourage her. The verses that follow tell that Rachel died in giving birth to Benjamin.

For today: in moments of pain or fear, words of encouragement do matter. We can be like that midwife, who accompanies and comforts, and we can also bring our fear to God, who is near to those who suffer, even when things do not turn out as we hope.
exp.23:29:
This verse tells us that Laban, Rebekah's brother, saw the ring and bracelets that Abraham's servant had given her. He also heard what Rebekah was telling them: "Thus spake the man unto me." Then he ran out and found the man standing by the camels, near the well. The word "earring" refers to a ring-shaped piece of jewelry worn in the ear, and "came to pass" and "behold" are older English expressions for "happened" and "look."

The narrator of Genesis describes how Rebekah brought the news home. Abraham's servant was looking for a wife for Isaac, and Rebekah had welcomed him generously. Laban sees the jewelry and goes out to receive him. Some readers notice that his interest in the gifts foreshadows his character, but the text does not say this directly.

Today we can learn to welcome others well. Showing hospitality is valuable, but it is worth examining our motives: serving with sincerity, not only for what we might gain.
exp.46:18:
Here the Egyptians ask Joseph to help them survive. They say they do not want to die before his eyes, neither they nor their fields. They offer to sell themselves and their land to Pharaoh, to become his servants, in exchange for bread and for "seed", which is grain to plant. In this way they could live, and the land would not be left "desolate", that is, ruined and empty.

The people of Egypt are speaking during a very severe famine. They had already spent their money and handed over their livestock. All that remained to them were their bodies and their lands. Joseph was managing the grain for Pharaoh. The Bible only tells what happened; it does not say that God approved of every decision in that system.

When crises come, necessity can lead us to extreme decisions. Today we can ask God for wisdom to live prudently, to save, and to help others without taking advantage of their need.
exp.38:15:
She kept Joseph's garment beside her, the one he left behind when he fled, and held onto it until her husband came home. "Lord" here means her husband, Potiphar. The garment was the piece of clothing she had torn from him.

She had just falsely accused Joseph before the people of her household, after he refused her advances. To make her lie seem believable, she used the garment as supposed proof. In this way she prepared her version of events for when Potiphar arrived, the one to whom she would tell the story in the next verse.

For today: the truth can be twisted with "evidence" that seems convincing. That is why we should not judge anyone by appearances or by a single version of events. And if we are unjustly accused, as Joseph was, we can remain faithful and trust that God sees everything.
exp.12:3:
It tells us that Abram went back to the place where he had earlier built an altar, between Bethel and Ai. There "he called on the name of the Lord", that is, he prayed and worshiped God by calling on him by name. The word "and" in the older wording of the verse is rendered as "and" in the King James Version, and the name "Lord" here is the traditional way of rendering the name of God.

The narrator of Genesis tells us that Abram returns from Egypt and the Negev, already very rich. Before the problem with Lot arises, the account shows that Abram first goes back to the place where he had worshiped God. It does not say in detail why, but it is clear that he wanted to renew his relationship with God.

When we have drifted away or stumbled, we can return to the basics: praying and worshiping God. Before facing difficult decisions, it is wise to come back into his presence.
exp.48:12:
This verse says that the tribe of Zebulun would live near the sea, in places where ships arrive and rest. "Haven of ships" means a place where vessels take shelter. "His border" is their boundary, which would reach as far as Zidon, an ancient city on the northern coast.

Jacob, now old, blesses his sons and announces what the future will hold for each tribe. Here he speaks of Zebulun, his tenth son. Scholars debate whether the tribe's territory really touched the coast, since Joshua places it instead near the Sea of Galilee and the Mediterranean. For that reason some understand the phrase as nearness or commercial influence.

For today: God gives each person a different place and task. Ask yourself where he has placed you and how you can serve there, being a shelter and a help to those who come into your life.
exp.49:7:
This verse says that all of Joseph's family went up to bury Jacob: Joseph's household, his brothers, and his father's family. Only the little ones, the flocks, and the herds were left behind in the land of Goshen. Here "house" means family or household, and "left" means they left them behind.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob had died in Egypt, and he had asked Joseph to bury him in Canaan, the land of his fathers. Pharaoh gave permission. The text says the family went in great numbers, but they left the children and the livestock in Goshen, which shows that they intended to return. This also shows that the journey was only for burying Jacob.

For today: honoring our loved ones, even in their farewell, is worth the effort and the time. When there is grief, being present and united as a family is a simple and real way of showing love.
exp.4:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book with a kind of heading: "the book of the generations of Adam," that is, the record of his descendants. It then recalls that God created man "in the likeness of God." Here "Adam" refers both to the first man and to humanity in general.

The narrator is the author of Genesis, whom tradition holds to be Moses. Before going on with the list of descendants, he returns to the beginning: humanity was made by God. The verses that follow say that he created them male and female, and blessed them. Later Adam has a son "in his own likeness," and so the image is passed down from generation to generation. Interpreters explain in various ways what exactly that "likeness" includes.

For today: every person, regardless of origin or condition, has a worth given by God. Today you can treat others with respect, remembering that they carry that dignity.
exp.48:8:
This verse says that Judah is like a young lion who goes up after making a kill. Then he stoops down and lies down to rest like a full-grown lion, so strong and secure that no one dares to wake him. To stoop down means to crouch low, and the prey is the animal that was hunted.

The speaker is Jacob, now old, who is blessing his sons and announcing their futures before he dies. To Judah he speaks of strength, victory, and leadership among his brothers. The verses that follow speak of Judah's scepter and of a figure whose coming is foretold. Many Christians see in this a sign pointing to Jesus, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, though interpreters explain that passage in several ways.

For today: true strength is not making noise but resting in security. If we trust in Christ, we can live with courage and calm, unafraid of whatever comes.
exp.35:42:
This verse ends the list of the chiefs of Edom. The "dukes" were not court nobles as in Europe, but heads or leaders of clans. The last ones named are Magdiel and Iram, and it is made clear that they governed in their various "habitations," that is, in the places where they lived, within the land they possessed. Then it is recalled that Edom is another name for Esau, the father of the Idumeans, or Edomites.

No one speaks here in the first person; it is the narrator of Genesis, who closes the chapter devoted to the descendants of Esau. It shows that God fulfilled in Esau the promise to make him a nation, although the line of the promise continues with Jacob. Who wrote or added each detail of the list is not known with certainty.

For today: God sees and remembers each person, even those who stand at the edge of the main story. He values everyone and trusts that He fulfills what He promises.
exp.21:7:
Abraham tells his son Isaac that God himself will take care of getting the lamb for the sacrifice. "Burnt offering" is an offering that was burned whole on the altar. "God will provide himself" means "God will see to it, and will supply it." The phrase "so they went both of them together" shows that father and son kept walking side by side.

God had asked Abraham to offer Isaac, his long-awaited son. Isaac, not knowing what was happening, notices that they are carrying fire and wood, but no lamb. Abraham answers in faith, without giving more details. Some think Abraham trusted that God would resolve everything; others see in his words an answer that did not yet reveal all that he knew. The text does not make this clear.

For today: when we do not understand the way ahead or see the solution, we can keep walking in obedience and trust that God knows how to supply what is needed, even when we cannot yet see it.
exp.44:13:
This verse says that Joseph threw himself on the neck of his brother Benjamin and wept, and that Benjamin also wept while embraced around his neck. The phrase "fell upon his neck" is an old way of saying that he held him tightly. It is a gesture of deep affection.

Joseph has just revealed himself to his brothers, the ones who had sold him years earlier. Benjamin is his brother through their mother and the only one who did not take part in that betrayal. After so many years apart, Joseph cannot hold back his emotion. That is why his words about bringing his father to Egypt come with tears and embraces.

For today: do not be afraid to show your feelings to the people you love. If there is a broken relationship in your family, take the first step toward reconciliation. A sincere embrace and some tears can begin to heal wounds of many years.
exp.0:8:
God commands that the waters under the heaven be gathered together into one place, and that the dry land appear. The phrase "dry land" means solid ground, the part of the earth that is not covered by water. And "it was so" means that everything happened exactly as God commanded.

Here God himself speaks, on the third day of creation. Before this, the earth was covered with water. By his word, God brings order and prepares a place where life can exist, since in the following verses he will cause plants and trees to spring up. Some scholars read these days literally and others more symbolically, but all agree that God is the source of everything.

For today: God knows how to bring order where there is disorder. If your life feels like an aimless sea, you can ask him to help you put everything in its place, step by step, and trust that he is preparing firm ground for something good to grow.
exp.41:1:
Jacob tells his sons that he has heard there is food in Egypt. He orders them to go there and buy food so that the family will stay alive and not die of hunger. In the King James wording, "corn" means grain, and "get you down thither" means "go down there," since Egypt lay to the south and the journey there was spoken of as going down.

Jacob, already an old man, speaks in the middle of a famine that affected the whole region. His sons were looking at one another without doing anything. Jacob breaks them out of that paralysis and gives them a clear instruction. The text says nothing more about what they were feeling, so it is best not to assume.

For today: when we know a solution and still freeze, it is time to take a concrete step. Trusting God does not rule out acting wisely. Today you might ask for help, make that call, or take that first pending step, while resting in the knowledge that God cares for you.
exp.4:13:
This verse sums up the life of Cainan: in total he lived 910 years, and then he died. It is the sum of the 70 years before he became the father of Mahalalel and the 840 years after. The word "begat" means that he was a father; "died" closes his story, just as it does for the other names in this chapter.

Here it is not a character speaking: it is the narrator of Genesis, who presents a list of generations from Adam. This list shows how humanity continued and how God's promise was passed on from one generation to the next. About why these lifespans are so long, there are several interpretations, and the text does not explain it.

For today: our life also has an end, and that invites us to live with purpose. Cainan raised sons and daughters over many years. We can ask ourselves what we leave to those who come after us: faith, affection, and a good example.
exp.1:0:
The explanation says that creation was finished: the heavens, the earth, and everything that fills them. "Finished" means they were brought to completion. "Host" refers to everything that adorns and fills creation, such as the sun, the plants, the animals, and human beings. Some translate it as "all their army," that is, everything that is in them.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks, a book traditionally attributed to Moses, although how it was written is still debated. This verse closes the account of the six days of creation and sets up the next verse, where God rests on the seventh day and declares it holy. The division into chapters at this point came later than the original text.

For today: God did his work with order and called it good and complete. You too can learn to rest, without living in an endless race. Set aside time to stop, give thanks, and trust that God sustains the world.
exp.21:21:
This verse continues the list of children that Milcah, wife of Nahor, Abraham's brother, bore to Nahor. Four more are named here: Chesed, Hazo, Pildash, Jidlaph, and also Bethuel. The King James wording "And Chesed, and Hazo, and Pildash, and Jidlaph, and Bethuel" repeats the word "and" before each name, a style that simply joins the names one after another. Together with Huz, Buz and Kemuel, these make eight children of Milcah.

The one speaking is the narrator of Genesis. After Isaac's test on the mountain, someone tells Abraham that his family in Haran has grown. The list brings Bethuel to the foreground, because from him will come Rebekah, the future wife of Isaac. In this way the text prepares the story that follows.

For today: God cares about the details of our lives and our families, even those that seem unimportant. Trust that He is preparing the way, and value with gratitude the people He places near you.
exp.7:4:
This verse tells us that the floodwaters kept going down little by little, until in the tenth month, on the first day of the month, the tops of the mountains could already be seen. "Decreased" means they were continually getting lower, and "tops" are the highest parts.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Genesis, who tells what happened to Noah after the flood. The ark had already rested on the mountains of Ararat in the seventh month. More than two months passed before the mountaintops came into view. Noah had to wait without yet seeing dry land all around him.

For today: sometimes God works slowly and quietly. Even when you do not see changes right away, trust that He is still at work. Wait with patience, and give thanks for every small sign of progress.
exp.9:30:
This verse closes the list of the descendants of Shem, one of the three sons of Noah. It says that his families were identified by four things: their kinship, their language, the territory where they lived, and their organization as nations. "Tongues" means languages, and the word "habitation" in the previous verse means the place where they lived.
