It is part of the so-called "table of nations." The narrator, traditionally Moses, summarizes how humanity multiplied after the flood. Scholars discuss the exact location of several places mentioned, such as Sephar. What is clear is that the text shows all peoples come from a common origin.

For today: if all peoples share a common origin, no culture or language is superior to another before God. Today we can treat people from other countries and languages with respect and kindness, remembering that they too are part of the human family that God cares for.
exp.25:6:
This verse tells how the men of Gerar asked Isaac about Rebekah, and he said she was his sister. He was afraid to say she was his wife, because he thought they might kill him on account of her, since Rebekah was very beautiful. The word "fair" in the King James wording means beautiful, that is, good to look at.

God had just renewed to Isaac the promises he had made to Abraham, and had told him that he would be with him. Even so, Isaac was frightened. The narrator reports the events, and afterward Abimelech discovers the lie. His story resembles that of Abraham, his father. The Bible does not approve of the lie; it only shows Isaac's weakness.

When we are afraid, let us not turn to lies to protect ourselves. Instead, let us remember God's promises and trust that He cares for us, even when we feel we are in danger.
exp.23:51:
This verse says that when Abraham's servant heard the response of Rebekah's family, he bowed down to the ground before the Lord. The phrase "it came to pass" is an older way of saying "it happened that." "Bowing himself to the earth" means he prostrated himself as an act of worship and gratitude.

The servant had been sent by Abraham to find a wife for Isaac. He had prayed asking for guidance, and now Laban and Bethuel agree that Rebekah may go, acknowledging that this comes from the Lord. The account does not explain all the family background, but it shows that the servant saw the answer to his prayer.

Today we can learn to stop and thank God when we see that he answers. Before moving on with our plans, it is worth pausing, giving thanks, and recognizing that God was at work along the way.
exp.2:5:
What it says: Eve looked at the forbidden tree and saw three things in it: it was good for food, pleasant to the eyes, and desirable for making one wise. "Desirable" here means it stirred up a strong desire. Then she ate, and she also gave some to Adam, "her husband," who was with her and ate as well.

Context: The one speaking here is the narrator of Genesis. The serpent had just contradicted God, saying they would not die and would be "like gods." Eve does not stop believing in God all at once; rather, she begins to look at the fruit through the eyes of deception. Then come the shame, the fig leaves, and hiding from God.

For today: Before acting, ask yourself which voice you are listening to. What "looks good" can draw us away from what God said. Pausing to remember his word helps you decide with wisdom.
exp.29:10:
Leah says "A troop cometh", that is, "a troop has come" or "what good fortune." She names the son born to her servant Zilpah Gad, which in Hebrew is related to the idea of fortune or good luck. The words "troop" and "cometh" are archaic and speak of happiness and blessing.

The speaker is Leah, the wife of Jacob. She and her sister Rachel were competing for Jacob's affection and for children. Leah had stopped bearing children, so she gave Jacob her servant Zilpah, as was done in that culture. When the son was born, Leah sees him as a good fortune. Some think her expression reflects her desire to be valued.

Today we can rejoice in blessings, but it is good to recognize God as their source, not luck. And we do not need to compete with others to feel worthy: our worth rests in God's love.
exp.0:19:
The explanation says God commands that the waters be filled with living creatures and that birds fly across the sky. "Reptile" here does not mean only what we today call reptiles, but creatures that move in the water in great numbers. "Living soul" means a being with life. "Expanse of the heavens" is the open space above the earth, the firmament.

God speaks on the fifth day of creation, after having formed the sun, the moon and the stars. He gradually fills what he had already prepared: first the spaces and then their inhabitants. By his word, life appears in the sea and in the air, and the text presents this life as part of his good plan.

For today: when you see a bird or a river, remember that life is a gift from God. Caring for nature and giving thanks for it is a simple way to honor him.
exp.33:7:
Hamor, the leader of the city, tells Jacob's family that his son Shechem has become deeply attached to Dina. The King James wording "the soul of my son Shechem longeth for your daughter" means that his heart is set on her, and "I pray you" means "I ask you." He asks that they give her to him as his wife.

Hamor speaks before Jacob's sons, who are angry and hurt. Earlier, Shechem had abused Dina. Hamor presents the matter as a simple case of love and alliance, without really acknowledging the seriousness of the harm or the pain she has suffered. He then proposes joining the families together and sharing the land.

For today: when someone does harm, pretty words or convenient arrangements are not enough. What is needed is to recognize the offense, to listen to the one who was harmed, and to seek justice in truth, without letting self-interest or appearances cover over the pain.
exp.3:16:
The explanation says that Cain had relations with his wife, she became pregnant and gave birth to a son named Enoch. Then Cain built a city and gave it the name of his son. "Knew" means had marital intimacy. "Bare" means gave birth. "Builded" is built.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. Cain had already killed his brother Abel and had moved away from the presence of God, although God protected him with a sign. The text does not explain where his wife came from, and we do not know more details. What it does show is how a family and a society begin to take shape far from God.

For today: God continues to care for people even after their mistakes, but we should ask ourselves what we are building and on what foundation. We can build our lives and families in communion with God, not only to leave behind a name.
exp.23:61:
The explanation says that this verse tells how Isaac was coming from the well called "of the Living One who sees me" (in Hebrew, Beer-lahai-roi). That place was in the region of the Negev, the "South", that is, the southern part of Canaan, where Isaac was living at that time. The word "dwelt" means "lived".

Here the book's narrator speaks. After Abraham's servant found Rebekah and her family blessed her, the caravan arrives in the south. That well already had a history: there God had seen and comforted Hagar (Genesis 16:14). That is why the name recalls that God sees the one who suffers. We do not know for certain why Isaac was there, but the text places him in a place tied to God's presence.

For today: God sees us, even in places and seasons of waiting. Look for a quiet moment to speak with Him, trusting that He watches over you with care.
exp.17:22:
Abraham comes close to God and asks him a frank question: whether God is going to destroy the one who lives in obedience together with the one who lives in wickedness. "Drew near" means that he stepped forward with boldness and respect. "Wicked" refers to a person who lives without taking God into account.

God has just announced that he is going to investigate the outcry against Sodom. The two men set off toward the city, but Abraham remains standing before the LORD. He speaks, and he does so out of concern for the righteous, among them, probably, his nephew Lot, who was living there, although the text does not say so in this verse.

For today: you can draw near to God with sincerity and pray for others, even for cities or families in trouble. God is not put off by a humble prayer, offered with respect and with confidence in his justice.
exp.30:9:
At the time when the flocks were in heat, Jacob lifted up his eyes and had a dream. In it he saw that the males that mated with the females were "ringstraked" (streaked with rings or stripes), "speckled" (dotted with spots), and "grisled" (mixed or flecked in color). The phrase "conceived" means that the animals were in heat.

The speaker is Jacob, addressing his wives, Rachel and Leah. He explains why his livestock has grown while he worked for Laban, his father-in-law, who had changed his wages many times. Jacob attributes his prosperity to God, not to his own cleverness, and says the dream came from an angel of God.

For today: when you are treated unfairly, do not grow bitter or lose hope. Trust that God sees everything that happens and knows how to care for you, even when you do not understand how He will do it.
exp.18:20:
God, through the angel who is speaking with Lot, tells him that he grants his request. "Supplication" means a humble plea. "Accepted" here means that it was granted. The small city Lot asked for will not be destroyed, so that he can take refuge there.

The one speaking is the messenger sent by God, who is leading Lot and his family out of Sodom before the judgment. Lot was afraid to flee to the mountain and asked to stay in a nearby city, later called Zoar, which means "little." Some think Lot's fear shows a lack of trust, but the text simply says that God was patient with him.

For today: you can speak to God honestly, even with your fears and limits. He is compassionate and listens. Still, it is good to also ask him for courage and confidence to continue on his path.
exp.40:54:
When the famine had spread over all the land of Egypt, the people cried out to Pharaoh for food. He did not solve the problem on his own, but sent everyone to Joseph and told them to do whatever Joseph told them. "Cried" means asking for help urgently. The King James wording "Go unto Joseph" conveys the same instruction: go to Joseph.

Here the narrator speaks, and then Pharaoh. Years earlier, Joseph had interpreted the king's dreams and proposed storing grain during the good years. Now the years of scarcity had come, just as Joseph had announced, and Pharaoh trusts him to distribute what had been stored.

For today: when hard times come, seek help from someone who has been faithful and wise, and prepare before the crisis arrives. Many Christians see in Joseph a picture of Christ, to whom we turn for the bread of life, though the text does not say this directly.
exp.1:11:
This verse describes the gold of the land of Havilah as being of good quality. In addition, there was bdellium there, which was probably a fragrant resin, and the onyx stone, which some understand as onyx or another precious stone. Scholars are not entirely sure what kind of stone is meant.

The one who narrates is Moses, according to tradition, and he does so as part of the account of creation. In describing the rivers that flowed out of Eden, the text shows that God filled the world with riches and beauty. The text does not say exactly where Havilah was, and it is interpreted in various ways.

Today we can learn to recognize God's gifts in creation and to thank Him for them. Valuable things, such as gold or stones, come from His generosity. Let us use with gratitude and wisdom what He gives us, without forgetting the Giver.
exp.30:0:
This verse tells us that Jacob learned what Laban's sons were saying about him. They accused him of taking everything that belonged to their father and of building his wealth at their father's expense. "Heard" here means that he listened to them, and "glory" refers to his possessions and his prosperity.

Jacob had been serving Laban for about twenty years, and his flocks had grown greatly. Laban's sons were envious and believed that all of it belonged to them. Genesis tells us that God had blessed Jacob, though they saw it as theft. This made the atmosphere tense, and shortly afterward God told him to return to his homeland.

For today: envy distorts the way we see others and can damage relationships. If someone judges us unfairly, it is wise to listen calmly, examine our hearts, and seek God's guidance before we react.
exp.41:9:
The brothers of Joseph answer his accusation with a firm denial: "No, my lord." They say they are not spies but servants who came only to buy food.

There is a famine throughout the region, and the sons of Jacob went down to Egypt for grain. Without knowing it, they speak before Joseph, whom they sold years earlier. He recognizes them, remembers his dreams, and accuses them of being spies. It is not clear everything he is seeking; many think he wants to test their character and learn how his family and his brother Benjamin are doing.

Today, when someone judges us wrongly, we can answer with simplicity and truth. Let us also remember that God works even when we do not see the whole picture, and that what is hidden comes to light in its time.
exp.29:2:
Rachel tells Jacob that she is giving him her servant Bilhah so that he may have relations with her. If Bilhah bears a child "upon my knees," Rachel will be able to have children through her. "Go in unto her" is an old expression for having intimate relations. "She shall bear upon my knees" suggests that Rachel would receive the child as her own.

It is Rachel who speaks. She could not have children and felt envy toward her sister Leah, who already had several. Jacob had been angered by her desperation. Rachel looks for a solution according to the customs of her time. The Bible recounts this event without expressly approving or condemning it, and we see that it brought tension into the family.

For today: when something hurts us and we are slow to receive an answer, it is tempting to force solutions on our own. It is better to bring our anguish to God in prayer, trust in his timing, and not compare ourselves with others.
exp.29:14:
Leah says to her sister Rachel with sorrow: "Is it a small matter that you have taken my husband, and now you want my son's mandrakes too?" Rachel proposes a deal: Jacob will sleep with Leah that night in exchange for the mandrakes. Mandrakes were a plant that in that time was associated with fertility, though it is not known for certain whether they actually worked.

Leah and Rachel were sisters, both wives of Jacob, and they lived in a painful rivalry. Rachel was loved but had no children; Leah had children but felt less loved. That is why the two of them argue and bargain, trying to resolve their pain by their own means.

For today: when we compare ourselves with others, envy leads us to haggle and to wound those closest to us. Better to bring our lacks to God, who, as we see later, listened to Leah.
exp.36:12:
This verse shows Jacob, also called Israel, speaking with his son Joseph. He tells him that his brothers are tending the sheep in Shechem, and he proposes sending him to them. "Feed" here means to take the flock out to graze. Joseph answers, "Here am I," which means, "I am here, ready."

Jacob is the father, and he speaks with Joseph, the son he loved most. The brothers already envied him, but Jacob wants to know how they and the flock are doing. We do not know whether he imagined any danger. What follows in the story shows that this sending will be the beginning of great suffering for Joseph.

For today: Joseph does not argue or make excuses, but says, "Here am I." At times God places us in tasks we do not fully understand. We can respond with willingness and trust, believing that He cares for us even on difficult paths.
exp.20:7:
It says that Isaac grew and stopped taking his mother's milk. "Weaned" means that he no longer fed at his mother's breast. That same day Abraham made a great feast, that is, a big celebration with food to mark the occasion.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Sarah had just rejoiced because God gave her a son in her old age. In that time, weaning usually happened when the child was several years old, and it was a reason for celebration because it showed that the child had survived the dangers of infancy. Shortly afterward, at that same celebration, conflict arises with Hagar and Ishmael, although the text does not explain everything that happened.

God keeps his promises, and it is worth pausing to celebrate with gratitude each stage of growth, whether in our children or in our own faith. Give thanks today for something God has sustained in your life.
exp.42:28:
He lifts up his eyes and sees Benjamin, his mother's son. He asks his brothers whether this is the younger brother they spoke of to him. Then he says to Benjamin, "God be gracious unto thee, my son." The word "gracious" here works like a loving blessing: may God care for you and show you favor.

Joseph is the one speaking. He is a ruler in Egypt, but his brothers do not yet know that he is the same man they sold years earlier. Benjamin is the only one who did not take part in that betrayal. Joseph sees him after a long time, and that is why the next verse says he was so moved that he went out to weep in private.

For today: when you feel strong emotions, such as gratitude or affection, do not hold them back out of pride. You can express them with a blessing or a prayer for the person you love, as Joseph did.
exp.17:13:
It says that nothing is too hard for God. "At the appointed time" is the date God had already set, and "according to the time of life" probably means "within a year," when life returns to bloom, although some interpret it differently. The phrase "I will return to you" simply means "I will return to you." The promise is clear: Sarah will have a son.

The Lord speaks, visiting Abraham along with two companions. Sarah was listening from behind the tent and laughed in doubt, since she and Abraham were old. God does not humiliate her but answers her with a question meant to awaken her faith and reaffirm the promise he had already made.

For today: when a situation seems impossible to you, do not measure it by your own strength but by the power of God. Bring him your doubts honestly, as Sarah did, and ask him to strengthen your trust while you wait for his timing.
exp.17:23:
Abraham asks God whether he would destroy the city even if there were fifty righteous people in it. He asks that, for the sake of those righteous, God would spare the whole place. The word "peradventure" means "perhaps," and "righteous" refers to people who live uprightly before God.

Abraham is the one speaking. Two of the visitors were already on their way to Sodom, but he remained standing before the LORD. God had told him about the judgment coming on the city. Abraham pleads, perhaps thinking also of his nephew Lot, who lived there, although the text does not mention him at this point. His concern is that God not treat the righteous and the wicked alike.

Today we can pray with confidence for our city, our family, and others, appealing to God's justice and mercy. Abraham teaches us to come near to God with reverence, yet with sincerity.
exp.44:16:
Here the pharaoh speaks to Joseph and asks him to give an order to his brothers. He tells them to load their beasts of burden, and the word "beasts" here means donkeys or animals used to carry things, and to return to the land of Canaan. The words "unto" and "ye" in the King James wording are simply older ways of saying "to" and "you," and they are not a difference in meaning.

Joseph had just made himself known to his brothers and had been reconciled with them, with tears. The news reached the palace, and the pharaoh and his servants rejoiced. The pharaoh, grateful for what Joseph had done for Egypt, wants to bless his family. For that reason he sends them to bring Jacob, their father, to live there.

For today: when God restores a broken relationship, joy should move us to act. If there is reconciliation in your family, take concrete steps to care for and gather your loved ones.
exp.45:23:
This verse names the four sons of Naphtali, one of Jacob's sons: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, and Shillem. In this older version the names are written in the style of their time; today many write Jahziel, Juni, Jezer, and Silem. Naphtali was a son of Bilhah, Rachel's servant.

The narrator of Genesis gives a list of Jacob's family who go down to Egypt during the time of the famine. The verses that follow say that Bilhah's descendants add up to seven. This list shows how the people who would later become Israel grew. The total of "sixty-six" is counted in different ways, and scholars explain it in several ways.

God cares for people one by one, even those who seem less important in the story. Today you can remember that your name and your family's name are precious to Him. Thank Him for your family and pray for each person close to you.
exp.37:19:
This verse tells us that Judah sent the young goat he had promised as payment. He sent it with his friend, the Adullamite, to recover the "pledges," that is, the items he had left as security: his signet, his cord, and his staff. But the friend did not find the woman.

The one speaking is the narrator of the account. Judah, son of Jacob, did not know that this woman was Tamar, his daughter-in-law, who had covered herself with a veil. She had been left a widow, and Judah had not fulfilled what he promised. He wants to pay quickly to avoid looking bad, and also to protect his reputation, since he sends someone else to do it.

For today: keep our word and live with integrity from the start, because what we do in secret sooner or later comes to light. God can work even in broken stories, but that does not mean we should take our decisions lightly.
exp.40:27:
It says that Joseph answers Pharaoh: what God is about to do, he has already shown to him. Some older wording: the phrase "he has shown" is the same as "has shown," and "is about to do" means "is going to do." Joseph sums up his interpretation by saying that the dream is no coincidence but a warning from God.

Here Joseph speaks. He is in prison, but he is summoned before Pharaoh because no one in Egypt could explain his dreams. Before giving the interpretation, Joseph makes it clear that the answer comes from God, not from his own wisdom. In this way Pharaoh knows the warning is serious and that there is time to prepare.

For today: God often gives us light to prepare us, not to frighten us. We can learn from Joseph to act with humility, giving God the credit, and to use good times wisely, saving and caring for what we have for the difficult seasons.
exp.16:4:
God changes Abram's name, which means something like "exalted father," to Abraham, which is connected with "father of a multitude." The phrase "a multitude of nations" means a crowd of peoples or nations. God says that the former name will no longer be used.

God himself speaks with Abram, who is lying prostrate with his face to the ground as a sign of respect. This is the moment when God confirms his covenant with him, even though Abram and Sarah still did not have the promised son. The new name serves as a constant reminder of the promise.

For today: God knows how to call us by what He promises, not only by what we see now. When your situation seems barren or without a way out, you can hold fast to the word of God and live with confidence, taking steps of faith even when the fulfillment is delayed.
exp.17:8:
The three visitors, who have just eaten with Abraham, ask him about his wife: "Where is Sarah?" Abraham answers that she is "in the tent," that is, in the place where they lived, close by. "Prepare" here means getting the meal ready.

The visitors are three men who came to Abraham under the tree; the text shows that one of them speaks with divine authority, and many believers see in him the Lord himself. They ask about Sarah on purpose: the promise of a son is for her too, and she listens from the entrance of the tent. That they already ask for her shows that God has her present in mind.

For today: God notices the people who stay "behind," in silence and in the background. Remember that He sees you and cares for you. He also values those who go unnoticed around you, and make room for them.
exp.20:8:
This verse tells us that Sarah saw Hagar's son, the Egyptian servant, mocking. The King James wording "which she had born unto Abraham" simply means the child she had given birth to by Abraham. The word "mocking" can be understood as laughing at someone, playing, or making fun; in the Hebrew, the word is related to the name Isaac ("laughter"), which is why it is interpreted in several ways. Paul, in Galatians 4:29, speaks of Ishmael as the one who "persecuted" Isaac.

The narrator describes what happens at the feast held when Isaac was weaned. Sarah watches Ishmael and reacts with concern for her own son and for the inheritance. Her request to Abraham in the following verse causes him great distress, because he also loves Ishmael.

For today: when tensions arise in the family, let us avoid acting only out of fear or jealousy. Let us ask God for wisdom to care for everyone with justice and compassion, remembering that He also sees and cares for those who are rejected.
exp.39:20:
This verse tells that the pharaoh restored the chief cupbearer to his former post, that is, the official in charge of serving him wine. The words "he restored him to his office" mean that he gave him back his job. Thus, the cupbearer once again placed the cup in the pharaoh's hand, just as before.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joseph was in prison with two of the pharaoh's officials, and he had interpreted their dreams. He had announced that the cupbearer would be restored and that the baker would die. The pharaoh's birthday was the moment when everything came to pass, just as Joseph had said.

For today: God keeps his word in his own time, even when we must wait. But we also learn not to be like the cupbearer, who forgot Joseph. When we receive a kindness, let us remember to give thanks and to help the one who helped us.
exp.46:25:
This verse says that Joseph made it a law, still in force "unto this day" (that is, when the text was written), that the Egyptians would give Pharaoh a fifth of their harvests. Only the priests' land was left free, because it had not passed into Pharaoh's hands.

The narrator is the one speaking here. During the famine, the Egyptians sold Pharaoh their livestock and their land in order to get bread. Joseph then set up the new order: they would give one fifth and keep four parts for themselves. Meanwhile, Jacob's family lived safely in Goshen.

For today: wisdom and good management help us care for others in hard times. Planning ahead and sharing what we have can protect many people.
exp.22:19:
The explanation says that the field and the cave in it passed into Abraham's ownership. They were a possession for a burial place, bought from the sons of Heth, a people who lived in Canaan. "Made sure" means the field or property was legally confirmed, and "by the sons of Heth" means it was transferred to Abraham.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Sarah had died, and Abraham, who lived as a foreigner, needed a place to bury her. He negotiated openly with the sons of Heth and paid for the land. In this way the property was legally secured before everyone. It is the first portion of the promised land that Abraham possesses, though it was a tomb.

For today: Abraham acted with honesty, respect and order, even in the midst of grief. We can learn to face difficult moments with integrity, doing things with clarity and without taking advantage of anyone, trusting that God keeps his promises with patience.
exp.1:24:
It says that Adam and his wife were naked and felt no shame. The word translated as "felt shame" means feeling embarrassment or disgrace about showing oneself as one really is. Here there was no fear, no hiding, and no guilt between them. Some older wording that you may see in other versions is simply rendered today as a plain word for the man and his name.

It is a sentence from the narrator of Genesis, not from a character. It closes the scene of marriage, where the man rejoices that the woman is bone of his bones, and speaks of becoming one flesh. It shows a complete unity and trust, before sin enters the story in chapter 3. Some see here only physical nakedness; others also see a complete openness and innocence.

Today we can seek relationships, especially in marriage, where there is sincerity and trust. That is cultivated by speaking truthfully, asking forgiveness, and caring for the other person without mocking their weaknesses.
exp.9:8:
The explanation says that Nimrod was a strong and famous hunter, so much so that he became a popular saying: "You are like Nimrod." The expression "before the Lord" can mean that God saw him, or that he was a very remarkable man. "Mighty" means strong and brave.

Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, lists the nations that descended from Noah. Nimrod, son of Cush, appears as a powerful leader, and his kingdom began in Babel. Some understand "before the Lord" in a positive sense, and others as a challenge to God, because of the connection with Babel. The text does not fully clarify this, so it is wise to be cautious.

Strength and fame can be a gift, but what matters is how we use them. Let us ask God that our talents serve for good and not for pride.
exp.30:43:
Laban proposes to Jacob: "Come, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between us." The word "covenant" means a solemn agreement, and "witness" is something that serves as evidence or a reminder of what was promised.

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, speaks here after pursuing him. Jacob had left secretly with his wives, his children, and his flocks. Laban admits that he can no longer do them harm, especially because God spoke to him the night before. So he seeks an agreement of peace. Jacob accepts and raises a stone and a heap of stones as a sign of the covenant.

For today: when there are conflicts in the family, it is wise to seek clear and honest agreements that protect the peace. Speaking frankly, setting boundaries, and keeping what has been promised helps prevent the wounds of the past from continuing to grow.
exp.4:27:
This verse says that Lamech lived 182 years and then had a son. It is part of the list of descendants from Adam. "Begat" means that he became a father. The text does not yet give the son's name; the next verse reveals it.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, noting generation after generation. This list links Adam with Noah. After the verse, Lamech names his son Noah and expresses his hope for relief from the weariness of labor on a cursed ground (Genesis 3:17). Many see here a hope that God would act, although the text does not explain in detail what Lamech was thinking.

For today: God works through generations, including in lives that seem ordinary. Your faithfulness, your prayer, and your example at home can sow hope in those who come after you, even if you do not see all the results.
exp.36:5:
Here Joseph speaks to his brothers and asks them to listen to a dream he had. The word "Hear" is an older way of saying "listen," and "dreamed" refers to what he saw while he was asleep. This is only the opening phrase, before he tells the dream itself.

The one speaking is Joseph, a young man whom his father Jacob loved more than the others. His brothers already hated him and could barely speak to him peacefully. Even so, Joseph tells them his dream. The Bible does not say why he did this: some think it was naivety, others that it was a lack of prudence. Whatever the reason, the account shows that this increased their hatred.

For today: not everything God shows us must be said right away or to just anyone. Before speaking, let us ask for wisdom to know when, how, and to whom to share it, always taking care of our relationships.
exp.1:4:
It says that, at the beginning, there were still no shrubs or plants of the field on the earth. That was so because God had not yet sent rain, and there was no human being to till the ground. "Till" means to work or cultivate the earth, and "spring up" means to sprout or grow.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking, not a character. It begins a second account of creation, which focuses on the relationship between God, the earth, and the man. Some see it as a more detailed look at the sixth day; others see it as a complementary account. The following verses show that God provides water and then forms the man from the dust.

For today: life depends on God, and human work is also part of his plan. We can cultivate, study, and serve with effort, while recognizing that God is the one who gives the rain, the growth, and the breath. Work with diligence and give thanks with humility.
exp.31:23:
This verse tells that Jacob was left alone, and that a man wrestled with him all night, until the day began to dawn. "The first light of day was breaking" means the first rays of morning were already appearing. "Man" is the word used for the one who wrestled with him.

The narrator describes this moment just before Jacob meets his brother Esau, whom he had deceived years earlier. Jacob was afraid, and for that reason he sent his family across the stream of Jabbok. Later in the text, the figure is called God or an angel (Hosea 12:4), and it is understood as an encounter with the divine, although some details are interpreted in different ways.

For today: when you are alone and afraid, do not run from God. You can draw near to Him sincerely, even in the middle of the struggle, and keep praying until you receive His blessing.
exp.35:0:
This verse opens a new section of the book with the list of Esau's descendants. The word "generations" means the family history, the sons and grandsons who came from him. It also makes clear that Esau "who is Edom," that is, his name is also linked to the people of Edom, who came from him.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking, not a character. This phrase appears several times in the book to mark the shifts between sections. After telling the story of Jacob, the account pauses to turn to Esau, Jacob's brother. This shows that he too received a line of descendants, and that God's promise to Isaac continues through the line of Jacob.

For today: God takes into account each person and each family, even those who do not carry the main thread of the story. We can treat everyone with respect and trust that God carries out his plans faithfully.
exp.29:23:
Rachel says that when her son was born, she named him Joseph. The name sounds like the Hebrew word for "add," which is why she says: "The Lord shall add to me another son." In other words, she gives thanks for this child and asks God to give her one more.

It is Rachel who speaks. She was the beloved wife of Jacob, but she had been barren for years and bore that situation as a shame. Now God hears her and gives her a son. His name expresses both gratitude and hope. Afterward, Jacob decides to return to his land, and so a new chapter of his life begins.

For today: when God answers a prayer of yours, thank Him sincerely and keep trusting Him for what is ahead. Giving thanks and continuing to hope do not oppose each other; they go together in a simple faith.
exp.38:11:
She grabbed Joseph by his garment and told him, "Lie with me." Joseph pulled away and left his garment in her hand, and he ran out of the house. The phrase "caught him" means she took hold of him, and "left his garment in her hand" means he left his clothing in her grasp.

The narrator describes this moment after many days of persistent pressure. Joseph was a servant in Potiphar's house, he was alone in the house, and he had no witnesses. Even so, he had earlier said that this would be a sin against God (verse 9). His escape cost him dearly, because she used the garment to falsely accuse him.

For today: when a temptation is strong, do not stay to argue with it; get away quickly. Fleeing can be a wise and courageous decision, even when no one sees you and even when obeying costs you something.
exp.23:35:
The explanation says that Sarah, Abraham's wife, bore a son in her old age, and that Abraham gave that son everything he owned. The word "bore" means gave birth. "My master" here means Abraham, the servant's employer. "Old age" refers to advanced years.

The speaker is Abraham's servant, whom the text does not name here. He had come to the family of Rebekah, in Mesopotamia, to seek a wife for Isaac. He tells his story in an orderly way so that they will trust him. First he shows that God blessed Abraham, and then he explains that Isaac is the heir of everything.

For today: God keeps his promises even when it seems late. If you wait for something with patience, keep trusting in him. And like this servant, we can speak with sincerity and gratitude about what God has done in the lives of others.
exp.16:9:
God tells Abraham that the covenant will have a sign: every male among them must be circumcised. "Seed" means descendants, and "keep" means they are to honor it faithfully. Circumcision is the removal of the foreskin, the skin that covers the tip of the male organ.

God speaks with Abraham when he is ninety-nine years old. He has just promised him a land, a great number of descendants, and that he will be his God. Now he gives him a visible sign in the body, one that would mark his whole family, including the servants of his household, as a people who belong to God.

Today Christians do not practice circumcision as a requirement of the covenant, and the New Testament speaks of a change of the heart (Romans 2:29). Even so, we can ask ourselves: does my life show that I belong to God? Ask him that your faith may be seen in your daily decisions.
exp.24:20:
This verse tells that Isaac prayed to the Lord (the name of God) on behalf of his wife Rebekah, because she could not have children. "Barren" means that she could not become pregnant. "Intreated" means that God heard his prayer and answered it. Then Rebekah conceived.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator of Genesis. Isaac was forty years old when he married, and the text suggests that he waited a long time. God had promised Abraham a numerous descendants, and that promise depended on children being born. For this reason Isaac prayed. Rebekah's pregnancies will later bring tension and questions.

For today: when a promise of God seems held up by a difficult situation, there is no need to stay silent or to solve everything alone. We can pray with confidence, even for years, believing that God hears us and acts in his way and in his time.
exp.14:14:
God tells Abram that he will go to his fathers "in peace." This is an old way of speaking about death: Abram would be reunited with his ancestors. He is also promised that he will be buried "in a good old age," that is, after a long and full life. The word "buried" means laid in the grave.

God speaks in the middle of the covenant he makes with Abram. He has just announced that Abram's descendants will suffer in a foreign land for four hundred years. Before that heavy news, he gives Abram a personal promise of comfort. Some understand that "going to his fathers" suggests life after death; others see it only as an expression about his burial. The text does not fully settle the question.

For today: God does not hide that there are hard times, but he sustains us with his promise. We can entrust our future to him and rest, knowing that he cares for every stage of our lives.
exp.5:20:
It says that Noah was to gather every kind of food that can be eaten and store it close to him. That food would serve to feed both his family and the animals inside the ark. The word "food" here means nourishment or sustenance, and "gather" means to bring together or collect.

God speaks to Noah before the flood. He had already commanded him to build the ark and had explained that he would save his family and the animals. Now he gives him a very practical instruction: prepare provisions. Afterward, the text says that Noah obeyed everything God commanded him, without adding or taking away anything.

For today: trusting God does not remove our responsibility to prepare. Noah believed God's promise and also did the concrete work of storing food. We can ask God for help and, at the same time, plan wisely for what is in our hands.
exp.40:1:
Here Pharaoh tells what he sees in his dream: seven cows come up out of the river, and they look beautiful and very fat, that is, healthy and well fed. They stay there eating in the meadow, which is a place of grass. The phrase "well favoured" simply means that they looked good.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Genesis. He recounts the dream of the king of Egypt, two years after Joseph had been left in prison. This dream troubles Pharaoh, and later God will use Joseph to explain it. The river is probably the Nile, although the text only says "the river."

For today: God can speak and act in the midst of times of plenty as well as times of scarcity. It is worth being wise when things are going well, thinking about the future, and trusting that God knows how to guide us.
exp.41:35:
Jacob complains to his sons and tells them that they have left him without children. Joseph no longer appears, Simeon is gone too, and now they want to take Benjamin away. The phrase "is not" means he does not appear, that no one knows where he is. He ends by saying, "all these things are against me," meaning he feels that everything is working against him.

Jacob speaks as an old man, after his sons have returned from Egypt. They tell him that the governor has kept Simeon in prison and demands to see Benjamin. Jacob believes Joseph has died and fears losing the last son of Rachel as well. He does not know that God is working behind all of this, and that Joseph is alive.

When everything seems to be against us, it is easy to draw conclusions from the little information we have. We can tell God our pain honestly, but we can also remember that He may be working where we do not see it. Trusting does not take away sadness, but it gives us hope.
exp.36:16:
A man whom Joseph met in the field tells him that his brothers have already left that place. He heard them say they were going to Dothan, so Joseph followed after them and found them there.

The speaker is an unknown man; the text does not say who he was. Jacob had sent Joseph to see how his brothers and the flocks were doing. Joseph looked for them in Shechem, but they were no longer there. This man, without knowing it, guides him toward them. What follows shows that the brothers, filled with envy, were planning to harm him.

For today: Joseph obeyed his father and kept searching even though the path changed. Many times God guides us through ordinary people and small details. We can remain faithful in what is ours to do, trusting that God works even when we cannot see the whole picture.
exp.24:13:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Ishmael: Mishma, Dumah, and Massa. They are only names, but each one was a real person within a family. The word "begat" is an old way of saying "fathered."

The narrator of Genesis closes the story of Ishmael here, the son of Abraham and Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarah. At the end of the list, twelve princes are mentioned, which recalls God's promise to Abraham to bless Ishmael too and make him into a great nation. About the exact origin of these peoples, scholars know little, and they do not all agree.

For today: God remembers each person by name, even when the world does not take them into account. Today you can thank him for knowing you personally, and also treat with courage and respect those who seem "minor" around you.
exp.46:24:
The Egyptians say to Joseph that he has saved their lives during the famine. They ask to "find grace" in Joseph's sight, that is, to be well received and treated with kindness. And they agree to be "servants of Pharaoh," that is, to work for him in exchange for staying alive.

The people of Egypt are speaking. After several years of hunger, they had already handed over their money, their livestock, and their lands in order to get grain. Joseph gives them seed and sets one condition: they must give a fifth of the harvest to Pharaoh. The Bible does not say that Joseph did this out of malice. Some see here wisdom and provision; others, a very harsh system.

Today we can be thankful to those who have helped us in difficult times, and be generous and fair when we have power or resources, treating those in need with dignity and compassion.
exp.48:26:
It says that the tribe of Benjamin would be like a fierce and strong wolf. In the morning it devours what it has hunted, and in the evening it divides what it has gained. "Ravin" means that it seizes with force, and "spoil" refers to the goods taken when an enemy is defeated.

Jacob, now an old man, speaks as he blesses his twelve sons before he dies and foretells what their tribes would be like. This image describes Benjamin as a brave and warlike people. Later, in the book of Judges, the Benjamites appear as skilled fighters. Some think it also points to figures such as King Saul, although the text does not say so directly.

God can use the strength and character he gave us for service. Energy and courage are good when they are used with justice and respect, and not to harm others. Today we can ask ourselves: how do I use my talents for the good of others?
exp.44:12:
The explanation says that the brothers should tell Jacob, their father, how important Joseph has become in Egypt, and everything they themselves have seen. Then he urges them on: "hurry" means "make haste," and "bring my father here" means to bring him to Egypt. Here "glory" refers to his honor and authority.

Joseph speaks to his brothers after revealing who he is. They had sold him years earlier, but now he forgives them and takes care of them. He wants to see his father soon and to protect him and the whole family during the five remaining years of famine. His desire is to gather the family together, not to boast.

For today: when God has raised you up or blessed you, use it to serve and restore relationships, not to take revenge. And if there is a reconciliation pending, do not put it off; take the step with humility and promptness.
exp.42:32:
They sat before him in order of their ages, from the oldest to the youngest. The words "firstborn" and "youngest" in the verse refer to birth order and standing within the family. The brothers were astonished, that is, very amazed, and they looked at one another without understanding what was happening.

This is part of the account in Genesis where the narrator describes the meal in the house of Joseph, the ruler of Egypt. The brothers did not know it was Joseph. They were surprised that he knew their order of birth. The Bible does not explain how he knew it; it may be that he simply seated them according to what he already knew about them, although the text does not make this clear.

For today: sometimes God works in ways we do not understand at the moment and leaves us bewildered. In those moments we can trust that he continues to guide the story, even when we cannot yet see the whole picture.
exp.6:15:
This verse says that the animals, male and female of every kind, entered the ark just as God had commanded Noah. Then it says that "the Lord shut him in." "Flesh" here means living creatures, and "Lord" is the name of God.

It is part of the account of the flood. The narrator tells how Noah obeyed and how the animals came to the ark. That God himself shuts the door shows that he is the one who protects Noah and his family, and that the moment of judgment had arrived. Some also see here the door of grace being closed; the text does not explain this further.

For today: God faithfully cares for those who trust in him and obey him. We can do what he asks, even when we do not understand everything, and rest in the knowledge that he keeps our lives safe.
exp.46:17:
What it says: A year passed, and the Egyptians came back to Joseph in the second year. They told him frankly that they no longer had money, that their livestock already belonged to Pharaoh, and that all they had left were their bodies and their lands. "Hide it" means to conceal. "My lord" is Joseph, who was managing the grain.

Context: The Egyptians speak, pushed by a very long famine. First they had handed over their money, then their livestock. Now, with nothing more, they offer their land and their freedom in exchange for bread and seed. The text tells what happened; it does not say whether all of this was just, and some readers see it as relief while others see it as harsh dependence.

For today: When a crisis comes, speak clearly and in time about your needs. And take care of your finances in good times, so that you do not end up with nothing.
exp.39:17:
Here Joseph begins to give Pharaoh's baker the meaning of his dream. He says that the three baskets represent three days. "Baskets" are small wicker containers, and "declaration" is the interpretation. This is the start of an answer, and what follows in verse 19 is not encouraging.

Joseph is in prison, alongside two of Pharaoh's officials who had troubling dreams. He had given the cupbearer good news, and now the baker hopes for the same. Joseph speaks with honesty, for he had already made clear that interpretations belong to God (Genesis 40:8). He does not soften the message to please.

For today: telling the truth with respect, even when it is hard, is a form of integrity. We can be kind and compassionate without disguising reality. And when we must deliver a hard word, we can do so with humility, remembering that God is the one who holds control.
exp.27:15:
Jacob wakes from his sleep and realizes something he did not expect: God was present in that place. The verse uses "the Lord" for God here. Jacob admits that he had not realized God was there.

Jacob was running from his brother Esau and sleeping out in the open, with a stone for a pillow. In the dream, God repeated to him the promises made to Abraham: land, descendants, and blessing for all peoples. He promised to be with him and watch over him. When he wakes, Jacob speaks with awe and reverence.

For today: God can be near even in moments of fear, loneliness, or uncertainty, even when we do not notice. Today you can pause for a moment and pray: "Lord, help me see your presence here, in my everyday life."
exp.18:22:
This verse says that the day was already dawning when Lot entered Zoar, the small city he had asked for as a refuge. The phrase about the sun is the one the explanation discusses: the text says the sun had risen on the earth, which means the day was just beginning.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. The angels had brought Lot and his family out of Sodom. God granted Lot's plea to flee to Zoar instead of going to the mountains, and he waited for Lot to arrive before acting. The next verse shows that once Lot was safe, judgment came upon Sodom and Gomorrah.

For today: God cares for his own with patience and keeps what he promises. If you are going through a difficult time, you can come to him with confidence, ask him for help with sincerity, and obey his guidance without delay.
exp.42:33:
The explanation says that Joseph had portions from his own table sent to his brothers. Benjamin received a portion five times larger than the others. "Messes" are dishes of food, and "were merry with him" means they enjoyed themselves and were happy in Joseph's company. They still did not know he was their brother.

This is a scene from the account of Joseph in Egypt. The narrator tells how Joseph, now a ruler, receives his brothers, who had come for food during the famine. Joseph has been testing them without revealing who he is. Giving more to Benjamin, Jacob's youngest and favored son, may have been a way of seeing whether they would feel envy, as they once felt it toward him. The text does not explain this, so it is one possible interpretation.

Today we can learn to rejoice when others receive blessing, without envy or comparison. Let us ask God for a heart that celebrates the good of others, just as God gradually healed this family.
exp.4:9:
Enos, after he became the father of Cainan, lived 815 more years and had other sons and daughters. "Begat" means that he was the father, and the source's old spellings "á" and "é" correspond to nothing in this wording, so no comment on them is needed.

This verse belongs to the genealogy of Genesis 5, a record that follows the line from Adam toward Noah. No character speaks here; the narrator notes, generation after generation, how long each man lived. That list shows that God's promise continued and that, even with death present, life kept passing from parents to children. The very long lifespans are understood in different ways: some take them literally and others as symbolic language.

For today: most of Enos's life came after he became a father. We can live each stage with purpose, raising and caring for those who come after us, and leaving a legacy of faith.
exp.8:22:
This verse tells how Shem and Japheth took a cloak or robe, laid it across their shoulders, and walked backward until they reached their father Noah. In this way they covered him without looking at him. "Nakedness" here refers to his uncovered body, and "their faces were backward" means they were looking the other way.

It is part of the account after the flood. Noah became drunk and was left uncovered in his tent. Ham saw him and went to tell his brothers. The narrator shows a contrast: while Ham spread the news, Shem and Japheth acted with respect. The Bible does not explain in detail what else happened, and some interpreters have discussed this, so it is best not to add anything to the text.

For today: when we see someone's failure or shame, we can choose to cover it with respect instead of commenting on it. This is not approving the wrong, but caring for the person's dignity.
exp.14:10:
The explanation says that while the divided animals lay there, birds of prey came down onto the dead bodies, and Abram drove them away so they would not eat them. The word used for "drove them away" in the older text means chasing off or shooing them away.

God had asked Abram to prepare these animals to make a covenant with him, confirming his promise to give him descendants and a land. It was an ancient way of sealing a solemn agreement. Some understand that the birds represent threats or enemies who might try to hinder the promise, although the text does not explain this directly. Shortly afterward, God speaks to him about the difficult future of his people.

For today: Abram did not just stand and watch; he patiently looked after what God had placed before him. When we wait for a promise of God, we can keep praying, obeying, and protecting what is sacred, trusting that he will fulfill his word.
exp.9:4:
These verses say that the descendants of Japheth, mentioned earlier (Gomer, Javan and others), spread out over "the isles of the Gentiles," that is, the coasts and distant lands where the peoples settled. Each group lived in its own territory, with its own language, its own family and its own nation. "After his tongue" means according to their language.

This is part of the so-called "Table of Nations" in Genesis 10. The narrator, traditionally Moses, summarizes how humanity spread after the flood, starting from the sons of Noah. Here he closes the list of Japheth and then moves on to the list of Ham. Scholars debate where exactly some of these peoples should be located.

For today: God sees each people, family and language as part of his work. Today we can treat people from other cultures with respect and appreciation, remembering that we all come from one common origin.
exp.7:0:
This verse says that God remembered Noah and every living thing and all the cattle that were with him in the ark. "Remembered" here does not mean that God had forgotten them, but that he acted on their behalf. Then he made a wind pass over the earth, and the waters of the flood began to go down.

This is part of the flood story in Genesis. The narrator is speaking here, not a character. After many days of water, the text marks a turning point: God steps in to begin renewing the earth and to care for those who were safe in the ark. Some see an echo of creation, when the Spirit or wind of God moved over the waters.

For today: when you feel that your situation is dragging on, remember that God does not lose sight of you. Keep trusting and obeying, even if you cannot yet see the change. His timing is wise.
exp.35:9:
This verse lists the first two sons of Esau mentioned in this passage. Eliphaz was born to Adah, and Reuel was born to Bashemath, both wives of Esau. The names are spelled in the form used by the King James Version, with the spellings "Eliphaz" and "Bashemath."

The author of the book (tradition attributes it to Moses) follows the family record of Esau, also called Edom. After telling the story of Jacob, the account shows how God fulfilled his promise to make Esau a nation. This lineage gave rise to the Edomites, neighbors of Israel.

God takes notice of families and of names, even of those who do not continue the main line of the promise. Today we can remember that every person matters to God. Pray for your family, including relatives who seem distant, and trust that God knows them by name.
exp.37:29:
After Pharez, his twin brother was born, the one who had a scarlet thread tied on his hand. They named him Zarah. The word "scarlet" here refers to a bright red dye, and "came out" means that he was born.

This is the end of the story of Judah and Tamar. Tamar had been widowed and left without children, and Judah had not fulfilled his duty toward her. In the end she becomes pregnant by Judah. The narrator (Moses, according to tradition) recounts the birth of the twins. The thread marked the first to come out, but Pharez got ahead. Pharez later appears in the line of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:3).

For today: God does not always follow the order we expect. Our first human plans sometimes fall apart, but God can work even in messy stories and carry forward his purposes with grace.
exp.17:3:
Abraham offers his visitors a little water to wash their feet and invites them to rest under a tree.

Abraham is the one speaking. He is standing near his tent in the heat of the day. He sees three men passing by and hurries to welcome them with great respect. Washing feet was a normal custom on those dusty roads, and offering shade and food was part of hospitality. The text later reveals that one of them is the Lord (Genesis 18:1). Abraham perhaps did not yet know this, and that is why he treats him as an important guest.

For today: let us practice hospitality through simple gestures, such as offering a glass of water, a place to sit, or time to listen. God often meets us in everyday life.
exp.31:13:
This verse lists part of the gift Jacob prepared for his brother Esau: two hundred female goats, twenty male goats, two hundred ewes, and twenty rams. A male goat is the male of the goats, and a ram is the male of the sheep. These are valuable animals, chosen with care.

Jacob is returning to his homeland and fears the meeting with Esau, whom he deceived years earlier. He has just prayed, remembering God's promise to bless him. Then, from what he owned, he sets aside a present for his brother. The text does not tell us everything that was in his heart, but it shows that he wanted to seek peace and soften the encounter.

For today: trusting God does not remove the responsibility to act. If there is a broken relationship, we can pray and also take concrete steps of humility, such as asking for forgiveness or making a generous gesture.
exp.9:20:
This verse introduces Shem, one of Noah's sons. It says that children were also born to him and that he was the "father of all the children of Eber." Here "father" means ancestor or founder of a people. It also calls him "the brother of Japheth the elder." Some understand that Shem was the oldest of the three brothers, and others that the phrase speaks of Japheth as the elder. The original allows both readings, so it is not certain.

The speaker is the narrator of Genesis, who orders the families after the flood, the so-called "table of nations." He has already described the sons of Japheth and Ham, and now he turns to Shem. Naming Eber prepares the way toward Abraham, who comes from this line. Many connect the name Eber with the word "Hebrew," though this is understood in different ways.

For today: God cares for families and for generations. Today you can give thanks to those who passed on their faith to you, and pray for those who come after you.
exp.8:11:
God announces that he is going to give a visible sign of the promise he has just made. "Covenant" means a solemn commitment. "Living creature" refers to every being with life, people and animals alike. "Perpetual generations" means forever, or for all generations to come. This promise is not only for Noah, but for every creature.

God speaks with Noah and his sons after the flood, when they come out of the ark. They had seen the destruction and could fear that it would happen again. So God promises that there will never again be a flood that destroys the earth, and he gives them a sign, the bow in the clouds, to remind them of it.

For today: when you are afraid or doubt that God will keep his word, look back at the memories of his faithfulness. It may be a verse, a testimony, or a moment when he helped you. God is faithful, and remembering this renews trust.
exp.3:15:
He says that Cain went away from the presence of God, that is, he moved away from the place where God dealt with his family, and settled in a land called Nod, to the east of Eden. "Nod" sounds like the Hebrew word for "wandering," and many understand it as a symbolic place. It is not known for certain where it was.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Cain had just killed his brother Abel. God punished him, but also protected him with a sign. Now Cain goes out to live far away, bearing the consequences of his sin, and later he will start a family and build a city.

For today: when we fail, the temptation is to pull away from God. But He invites us to return with sincerity, to acknowledge the wrong, and to receive His forgiveness and His help.
exp.49:5:
Pharaoh gives Joseph permission to go and bury his father Jacob. The verse says Jacob made Joseph swear, which means Joseph was bound by a very serious promise. Pharaoh tells him to keep the promise he made to Jacob.

Pharaoh is speaking in response to the request Joseph made through Pharaoh's household. Jacob had died, and he had made Joseph swear that he would bury him in Canaan, in the family tomb. Even though Joseph was a high ruler, he still asked for permission. Pharaoh respects the oath and gives his approval.

For today: keeping what we promise, especially to loved ones, is an act of honor and faithfulness. It also shows us the value of asking permission respectfully, even when we have authority or influence.
exp.39:22:
It says that the chief butler, the one in charge of serving the king's wine, did not remember Joseph after he was set free. He forgot him completely. The words "did not remember... but forgat him" stress that this was not a small oversight but a total forgetting. Here "chief" means the head of the butlers, and "butler" is the one who carried the cup to the king.

Context: the narrator is Moses, the traditional author of the book. Joseph was unjustly imprisoned in Egypt. He had interpreted the butler's dream and had asked him to remember him before Pharaoh. The butler was restored, but Joseph remained in prison. The text does not explain why he forgot him; it only shows that Joseph had to wait longer.

For today: sometimes people forget us, even after we have helped them. Do not be discouraged. Keep doing good faithfully and trust that God does not forget you, even when his answer takes time.
exp.2:18:
The explanation says that the man will have to work hard, with effort and weariness, to obtain his food, until the day of his death. "You will eat bread" means earning your food by the sweat of your face. "Return to the ground" means that you will die, and "taken" means that you were taken out of it. The body came from the dust and to the dust it will return.

God speaks to Adam after he and Eve have eaten from the forbidden tree. This is part of the consequences of that disobedience: the ground will no longer yield its fruit easily, and death enters human experience. Even so, the passage that follows shows care: God clothes them with garments of skin. Many see here a promise of hope, though the text does not explain it.

For today: accept your work and your limits with humility. Do your labor with honesty, without believing that everything depends on you, and remember that your life is a gift from God, who continues to care for you.
exp.23:20:
The explanation says that Abraham's servant was looking at Rebekah with wonder and in silence. He wanted to know whether God had made his journey successful or not. "Wondering" means admiring, being surprised. "Prospered" means that God made the journey turn out well.

Here the narrator speaks and shows us Abraham's servant. He had been sent to find a wife for Isaac. Earlier he had asked God for a sign: that the young woman would offer water to him and to his camels. Rebekah had just done exactly that, and with great generosity. The servant did not rush to declare victory but waited quietly.

For today: when you ask God for direction, watch calmly how he responds. Do not rush or force things; trust and wait attentively, and then give thanks.
exp.49:15:
Joseph's brothers send a message to Joseph. They say that their father Jacob, before he died, left an instruction. "They sent word" means they sent someone with the message, instead of coming themselves. The verse is left open, and what Jacob supposedly commanded is stated in the following verse.

The brothers speak out of fear. Jacob had just died, and they thought Joseph might take revenge for having sold him years earlier. The Bible does not say that Jacob really gave that command, and it is not known whether it is true or whether they made it up out of fear. The text does not make this clear.

When we have done harm, fear can make us doubt that forgiveness is real, even when it has already been offered. It is better to approach with sincerity and humility, without hiding our guilt, and to trust in the grace that God and others want to give us.
exp.22:10:
Ephron the Hittite tells Abraham that there is no need to pay anything: he gives him the field and the cave that is in it. He says this in front of his people, as witnesses. "Possession" means a piece of land or property. "Bury thy dead" means: bury your dead, that is, Sarah.

Abraham, a foreigner in that land, had just lost his wife and asked for a place to bury her. Ephron answers at the city gate, where public dealings were made. His offer may be sincere generosity or a courtesy typical of negotiation; the Bible does not make this clear, and Abraham insists on paying the fair price.

For today: accepting help with gratitude is good, but it is also wise to act with clarity and honesty in agreements, to avoid debts or misunderstandings later.
exp.35:8:
This verse introduces a new list of families. "Generations" here means the descendants of Esau. He is called "father of the Edomites" because the Edomite people came from him, and Edom is another name for Esau. His family lived in the mount of Seir, a mountainous region south of the Dead Sea.

No one speaks here directly. It is the narrator of Genesis, who uses the formula "these are the generations" to organize his account. Earlier he explained that Esau and Jacob had so much wealth that they could not live together in the same land, so Esau moved away. Now the text follows his story and recalls that God also kept his promises to him.

For today: God cares for people even when they are not the center of the story. Let us ask him to help us separate ourselves peacefully from conflicts, without bitterness, trusting that he continues to guide every life.
exp.45:22:
This verse says that Dan, son of Jacob, had only one son mentioned in this list: Hushim. In other passages of the Bible, this name appears as "Hushim" or "Shuham" (Numbers 26:42), but it is not known with certainty why the form changes. Some think it is a variation in spelling.

The narrator of the book records the list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. Here the descendants of Bilhah, Rachel's servant, are being named. It is a record showing how the people of Israel began: a small family that would later become a great nation.

For today: God pays attention to names, even those that seem unimportant. Although Hushim barely appears in the Bible, he was recorded. This reminds us that no person goes unnoticed by God, even when our role seems small or hidden.
exp.17:1:
Abraham lifts up his eyes and sees three men standing near him. As soon as he sees them, he runs from the entrance of his tent to meet them and bows down to the ground. "Men" means men, "by him" means near him, and "bowed himself toward the ground" describes a deep bow as a sign of respect.

The passage begins by saying that the LORD appeared to Abraham at Mamre, while he sat in the tent door in the heat of the day. The text does not explain right away who the three visitors are. Some believers see in them the Lord with two angels, and others think of messengers sent by God. Abraham treats them with the hospitality typical of his culture, and then speaks to them with great respect.

Today we can learn to welcome others with promptness and humility. If we are attentive, a simple gesture of hospitality can become an occasion to serve, and perhaps an encounter with God.
exp.42:24:
The brothers of Joseph got the gift they had brought for him ready, while they waited for him to arrive at noon. They had heard that they would eat there. "Present" means gift, and "bread" here means a full meal.

The brothers are in Egypt for a second time, now with Benjamin, because of the famine. Joseph's steward has just calmed their fear and returned Simeon to them. They do not yet know that the ruler is their brother. They prepare the gift to win his favor, since they fear being accused over the money they found in their sacks.

When we are afraid or feel guilty, we may try to set things right with gifts or our own efforts. But God is often already working with kindness, even when we cannot see it. We can prepare ourselves with humility and obedience, trusting that He guides the outcome.
exp.17:7:
Abraham serves his visitors butter, milk, and the calf already prepared. He sets it before them and stands beside them under the tree while they eat.

This takes place in the scene by the oaks of Mamre, where Abraham welcomes three men. The text calls them men, but the account then makes clear that the Lord reveals himself in this visit. Abraham acts with haste and generosity, serving as the hospitality of his time required. Soon the promise of a son for Sarah will follow.

For today: practice hospitality with joy and without making excuses. You do not need much; simply open your table and your time with generosity. Sometimes God uses such simple moments to bless others and you as well.
exp.9:27:
The explanation says that among the sons of Joktan were Obal, Abimael and Sheba. It is part of a list of names. The accent mark on "á" is the old way of writing "a"; here it simply links the names in the list: "and Obal, and Abimael, and Sheba."

It is part of the "Table of the Nations" in Genesis 10. The narrator, traditionally Moses, summarizes how the peoples developed after the flood, starting from the sons of Noah. Joktan is a descendant of Shem. The verses that follow say that his descendants settled toward the east, in Arabia according to many scholars, although the exact location of several places is uncertain.

For today: God knows people by name, even those who barely appear in the Bible. You are not a number to Him. Today you can remember that your life, though simple and little seen, is valuable before God.
exp.35:31:
This verse says that Bela, son of Beor, was the first king of Edom mentioned in this list, and that his city was called Dinhabah. The King James wording gives the city name as Dinhabah, so the note about the spelling of the name no longer applies here.

The narrator of the book of Genesis speaks here, reviewing the descendants of Esau, also called Edom. The list shows that Edom already had kings before Israel had one. It is not known with certainty where Dinhabah was. It is also unclear whether this Bela is the same person as others with similar names; it is better not to assert it. What is clear is that God was keeping his promise to make Esau a nation (Genesis 25:23; 27:39-40).

For today: God keeps his promises even in things that look like simple lists of names. Trust that He works faithfully in history, and also in your life, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.30:7:
This verse tells how Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, kept changing the terms of his pay. If he said the wages would be the animals that were "speckled" (with spots), then all the flock bore spotted young. If he said the wages would be the "ringstraked" (with stripes), then all the flock bore striped young. "Bare" is an older English word meaning "gave birth to."

Jacob speaks to his wives, Rachel and Leah. He wants to convince them to leave their father's house. He explains that he worked with all his strength, that Laban cheated him and changed his pay ten times, and that God did not allow Laban to harm him. Jacob sees in this the hand of God working in his favor.

For today: even when someone treats you unfairly or changes the rules, you do not have to answer with revenge. Keep working honestly, and trust that God sees your situation and knows how to take care of you.
exp.9:3:
This verse lists the four sons of Javan, a grandson of Noah through Japheth: Elishah, Tarshish, Kittim, and Dodanim. These are names of people who were later associated with peoples.

The reading "Dodanim" appears in other manuscripts as "Rodanim," and not everyone is sure which reading is original. (Since the reader sees the King James wording, this note matches the spelling "Dodanim" in that text.)

The author of Genesis, traditionally Moses, presents here what is called the "Table of Nations." Its purpose is to show how, after the flood, humanity multiplied and spread out. Many connect the sons of Javan with regions of the Mediterranean, such as Cyprus or Greece, but these identifications are debated and not entirely certain.

For today: God knows the names and stories of all peoples, even when we overlook them. This invites us to see every person, from any culture, as someone important to God and worthy of respect and love.
exp.44:19:
They are told not to worry about leaving their belongings behind. "Stuff" here means the household goods, furnishings and possessions, not jewelry. "Regard not" means "do not be anxious or cling to them." The reason given is that the best of Egypt would be at their disposal.

The king speaks, and Joseph passes his command on to his brothers. There is famine in the region, and the pharaoh wants Jacob and his whole family to settle in Egypt. In this way, the king shows generosity toward Joseph's family, and they can move without fear of losing what they leave behind.

For today: sometimes God asks us to let go of what is familiar in order to receive something better that He has prepared. We do not always know what it will be like, but we can trust in His care. Today, think about what thing is hard for you to let go of, and bring it to God in prayer.
exp.43:19:
Judah reminds Joseph (whom they do not yet recognize) of what they had already told him before. They had an aged father and a younger son, born when the father was old. The word "little one" refers to a young lad or boy. It says that this boy's brother had died and that he alone was left of that mother. And the father loved him very much.

Judah speaks before Joseph, the governor of Egypt, to plead for compassion. He wants to save Benjamin from being taken as a slave, because Joseph's cup was found in his sack. Judah speaks with humility and mentions the grief of Jacob. When he says that a brother "is dead," he is referring to Joseph, although the brothers knew this was not true, since they had sold him.

For today: when we must ask for help or intercede for someone, let us do so with humility and sincerity, thinking of the pain of others and not only of ourselves.
exp.31:9:
Jacob tells God that he does not deserve any of the good he has received. "Least" means "I am very small, I am not worth so much." "Mercies" are acts of kindness, and "truth" here is God's faithfulness to his promises. The "staff" was a traveling stick. "Bands" were groups; today we would say "camps." Jacob remembers that he crossed the Jordan alone, with a staff, and now he has two large groups.

Jacob returns to his land by God's command and learns that Esau, his brother, is coming to meet him with four hundred men. Years earlier, Jacob had deceived him, and now he feels fear. For this reason he divides his people and prays with humility, relying on God's promises.

When you are afraid or face a problem, begin by praying with gratitude and humility. Remember what God has already done for you and trust in his promises, without ceasing to do what is your responsibility.
exp.19:16:
This verse tells us that Abraham prayed to God on behalf of Abimelech, and God healed him, his wife, and his female servants, and they were able to have children. "Bare" means that they gave birth. "Maidservants" were the women who worked in the household.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, had taken Sarah, thinking she was unmarried, because Abraham had said she was his sister. God intervened and warned the king in a dream. After returning her, Abimelech made amends for the wrong. The next verse explains that God had closed the wombs of his household. Here Abraham acts as a prophet and intercessor, although earlier he had failed out of fear.

For today: God can use an imperfect person to bless others. Pray also for those who have caused you trouble, even if they did not mean harm. Prayer can open the way to healing and reconciliation.
exp.9:31:
This verse closes the so-called "Table of Nations." It says that the peoples of the earth come from the descendants of Noah, organized into families and nations. After the flood, humanity spread out and was divided across the earth. The word "nations" in the King James wording refers to peoples or groups of people. The phrase "were divided" speaks of people scattering and forming distinct groups.

The one who narrates is the author of Genesis, traditionally identified with Moses. He presents Shem, Ham, and Japheth as the origin of the known peoples. He does this to show that all of humanity shares a common origin. Afterward, chapter 11 tells of the tower of Babel, which many scholars see as a more detailed account of that dispersion, although the exact order of events is debated.

Today we can remember that all people, from any country or culture, share a common origin and have value before God. Let us ask God for help to treat with respect and kindness those who are different from us.
exp.26:41:
