Rebekah learns what Esau plans to do. She calls Jacob and warns him that his brother "doth comfort himself" with the thought of killing him. That is, Esau soothes his pain and anger by imagining revenge. The King James wording "doth comfort himself" is an older form of "comforts himself," with "doth" as the archaic third-person verb ending, and "elder" and "younger" are the old English words for the older and younger sons.

Esau was furious because Jacob received Isaac's blessing, obtained through deceit, in which Rebekah had taken part. Esau was waiting for their father's death before he acted. Rebekah, who somehow learned of his words (the text does not say how), acts to protect Jacob and prepares him to flee to the home of his brother Laban.

For today: holding on to resentment and fantasizing about revenge can grow until it becomes dangerous. If someone has hurt you, seek help and forgiveness before anger makes the decisions for you. And if you see a conflict that is escalating, act wisely to prevent harm.
exp.42:10:
Jacob, also called Israel, finally agrees to send Benjamin to Egypt. He tells his sons that, since there is no other way out, they should do it, and that they should take a gift for "the man" made up of the best produce of the land: balm, honey, spices, myrrh, nuts, and almonds. Here "vessels" means containers or sacks. "Present" means gift.

Jacob speaks to his sons during the famine in Canaan. Judah has just offered himself as surety for Benjamin. Jacob does not know that the man in Egypt is Joseph, his son. He fears losing Benjamin, but the famine forces him to act. He prepares a gift as a gesture of respect and a hope for a good reception.

For today: when fear paralyzes us, we can take sensible and generous steps, and at the same time trust in God. Preparing well, acting with humility, and handing over what we most fear losing is a form of faith.
exp.17:31:
Here Abraham makes his final request to God on behalf of Sodom. He asks that the city not be destroyed if ten righteous people are found there. With "I will speak yet but this once," he means that he will speak for the last time. "Let not the Lord be angry" means that God should not be displeased with him. God responds that, for the sake of those ten, he will not destroy the city.

Abraham speaks with God, whom he addresses as "my Lord," because God had announced that he would judge Sodom. His nephew Lot lived there. Abraham begins with fifty righteous people and gradually lowers the number, with respect and humility. The Bible does not explain why he stops at ten; some think he no longer dared to ask for more.

For today: we can pray with confidence and persistence for other people, but with humility. God hears us and cares about our cities and families.
exp.45:1:
This verse says that God spoke to Israel, that is, to Jacob, at night, in visions. He called him twice by name: "Jacob, Jacob." He answered: "Here am I," which means "here I am, I am listening."

Jacob was on his way to Egypt to be reunited with his son Joseph. He stopped at Beersheba and offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. He probably had doubts or fear about leaving the promised land. Then God spoke to him to reassure him, and in the verses that follow he promises to be with him and to bring him back.

For today: before taking a big or uncertain step, stop to pray and worship God. He knows your name, sees your fears, and can speak to you with peace. Respond as Jacob did: "Here I am, Lord."
exp.10:28:
This verse tells us that Abram and his brother Nahor got married. Abram's wife was named Sarai, and Nahor's wife was Milcah. Milcah was the daughter of Haran, which means she was Nahor's niece. The phrase "took them wives" simply means that they married.

The narrator of Genesis speaks here, within the list of Terah's family. After mentioning Haran's death, the text introduces the wives, and right away it says that Sarai could not have children. In this way the passage sets the stage for the promise God will make to Abram. Marrying within the family was common in that time.

God often begins his great works in ordinary families, with real limits and real pain. If today you feel limited, remember that God can work right there, in your simple story.
exp.40:47:
This verse says that Joseph gathered all the food of the seven good years that there were in Egypt. He stored it in the cities, and in each city he put the grain that was harvested in the fields around it. Here "food" means provision or supplies, above all grain.

This is the account of the narrator of Genesis. Pharaoh had dreamed of seven years of plenty and seven of famine, and Joseph, already in charge of the plan, put it into action. Keeping the food close to where it was produced was an orderly way of preparing. The text gives no further details of how it was stored.

For today: times of plenty are a good time to be wise, not careless. We can keep some of what God gives us, with order and steadiness, for hard times, and share it generously when the need arises.
exp.18:1:
Lot invites the two visitors to stay in his house. He offers them water to wash their feet, a place to rest, and a chance to continue on their way at dawn. "I beg you" means "I ask you earnestly," and "servant" is a humble way for him to refer to himself. They reply that they prefer to spend the night in the square, that is, outdoors in the public space of the city.

It is Lot who speaks, and he was sitting at the city gate. The visitors appear to be ordinary travelers, although the text already says they are angels. Lot insists because sleeping in the square was dangerous, and the account that follows shows the wickedness of the city. Some think they refuse at first to test Lot, but the text does not explain this.

Today we can imitate Lot's hospitality: opening our homes or generously helping someone who is passing through or needs shelter, without expecting anything in return.
exp.28:2:
This verse describes the custom of that place. All the flocks would gather there beside the well. The shepherds would roll the large stone off the mouth of the well, water the sheep (to "water" means giving them water to drink), and then put the stone back in its place.

The one speaking is the narrator, who explains how that well worked. Jacob is fleeing from his brother Esau and seeks his mother's family in Haran. This detail sets up the next scene: Jacob will speak with the shepherds, and Rachel will soon arrive. The text does not say why the flocks were expected to gather together; some think it was to look after the water or to move the heavy stone together.

For today: there are blessings that are received best in community and with order. Let us learn to wait and to cooperate, trusting that God is also at work in everyday life.
exp.17:9:
One of Abraham's three visitors here promises him that he will return "according to the time of life," a phrase usually understood to mean "at this same season next year," though some interpret it differently. He announces that Sarah will have a son. Sarah was listening from the entrance of the tent, behind the visitor.

The one speaking is one of the visitors, and the text presents him as the Lord himself (Genesis 18:1, 13). Abraham and Sarah were already old and had no children. God repeats to them the promise he had made to Abraham earlier, now stated concretely and with Sarah as a central figure. She hears the promise and, as what follows shows, laughs in disbelief.

For today: when a promise of God seems impossible, do not dismiss it with laughter or doubt. God sees our limitations and still fulfills what he says in his own time. Speak with him honestly and wait with patience.
exp.38:5:
This verse says that Potiphar, the Egyptian who owned Joseph, left everything he had in Joseph's charge. He no longer worried about anything except what he ate. "He knew not ought he had" means that he did not check or meddle in the accounts of his household. "Goodly person" refers to his appearance and form: Joseph was a very handsome young man.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joseph had arrived in Egypt as a slave, but God blessed him and his master noticed. The detail about his appearance prepares what comes next: Potiphar's wife will pursue him, and Joseph will resist.

For today: faithfulness in everyday matters builds trust. Do your work well even when no one is watching, and remember that trust once earned must also be guarded with integrity.
exp.32:7:
Esau asks Jacob what he means by all the groups of animals he met along the way. "Droves" means herds or groups. Jacob answers that he sent them to find grace, that is, favor and a warm welcome, in the eyes of Esau, whom he calls "my lord" as a sign of respect.

Jacob and Esau meet again after years of hostility, since Jacob had obtained their father's blessing through deceit. Jacob fears his brother's reaction, and that is why he sent gifts ahead. Esau comes with four hundred men, but the meeting ends in an embrace. Some see here sincere humility; others also see a prudent strategy.

For today: when a relationship is broken, seeking peace with humility is worth the effort. A sincere gesture, an apology, or a concrete action can open the door to reconciliation, even though we cannot control how the other person will respond.
exp.5:21:
This verse says that Noah obeyed completely. He did everything exactly as God commanded him. He did not do only part of it or change the instructions: he carried out all that God told him to do.

God had spoken to Noah about the flood that was coming. He gave him instructions to build the ark, bring in the animals, and store up food for everyone. This verse closes that section and sums up Noah's response: he trusted God and obeyed. The text does not say how long it took or how Noah felt, but only stresses that he did what was asked of him.

For today: obedience to God shows itself in concrete actions, not just good intentions. Think of something you know God is asking of you, however small, and do it today with confidence, step by step, as Noah did.
exp.10:2:
The explanation says that the people of Shinar encouraged one another to make bricks and fire them. Thus the brick served them as stone, and the bitumen (a sticky substance similar to asphalt) served them as mortar to stick them together. Words like "Go to" mean "come on," and "throughly" means "thoroughly" or "completely."

The people speaking had at that time one language. In Shinar, a plain of Mesopotamia, there was no stone close at hand, so they used what they had. This technical step is the beginning of a larger project: the city and the tower. The text does not say the bricks were bad; what God examines afterward is their purpose: to make a name for themselves.

For today: ability and ingenuity are good gifts, but it is wise to ask what we use them for. Before starting a project, ask yourself whether you seek to honor God and serve others, or only to exalt yourself.
exp.40:39:
He says that Pharaoh places Joseph in charge of his house, that is, of the whole palace and its administration. In addition, all the people will be governed "according to your word," that is, according to what Joseph commands. Pharaoh reserves only the throne for himself: in that he will remain greater.

The one speaking is Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Joseph has just interpreted his dreams and has advised him to prepare for seven years of plenty and seven of famine. Pharaoh recognizes that God has given Joseph wisdom and a special spirit, and for that reason entrusts him with enormous authority. Until then, Joseph had been in prison.

For today: God can raise up and use a person at the least expected moment. When we receive responsibility, it is good to exercise it with wisdom, honesty and a spirit of service, remembering that what we have comes from God and is meant for the good of others.
exp.43:21:
Here Judah repeats what the brothers had told the governor of Egypt. "Lad" means a young man, and it refers to Benjamin, the youngest. Judah explains that the boy cannot leave his father, because if he did, the elderly Jacob would die of grief.

Judah speaks before Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize. Joseph asked that Benjamin be brought to him and is holding him on a charge of theft. Judah intercedes with a moving speech to keep his father from suffering another loss. He himself had taken part in selling Joseph; now he offers to remain as a slave in Benjamin's place.

For today: when there is conflict, let us think about the pain of others and not only our own. Judah teaches us to take responsibility and to care for those who depend on us, even at personal cost.
exp.28:15:
This verse introduces the two daughters of Laban: Leah, the older, and Rachel, the younger. It is a simple detail, but it prepares what comes after. The word "older" means the one who is of greater age, and "younger" the one who is newer in age.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob has already arrived at the house of his uncle Laban, fleeing from his brother Esau, and he has been living there for a month. Laban asks him how much he wants to earn for his work. Before the account of Jacob's answer, the story introduces the two daughters, because what follows will depend on them. The Bible does not explain here all the reasons behind each person's actions.

For today: God works within complicated family stories and with imperfect people. If your family or your situation is not ideal, trust that God can work in the midst of them.
exp.11:15:
Pharaoh treated Abram well for Sarai's sake. As payment or a gift, Abram received many animals, and also menservants and maidservants. "Asses" are donkeys, and "she asses" are female donkeys. "Entreated well" here means he treated him with generosity.

The narrator tells what happened when Abram went down to Egypt because of the famine. He had said that Sarai was his sister, out of fear that they would kill him. So Pharaoh took her into his house and, believing her to be unmarried, enriched Abram. But that wealth came through deception, and soon God intervened with plagues to protect Sarai.

For today: what we receive is not always a sign that we did everything right. God can care for us even when we fail, but lying is never a good path. Today we can trust God and be honest, even when we are afraid.
exp.11:7:
The explanation says that Abram continued on his way and went to a mountain east of Bethel. There he pitched his tent, with Bethel to the west and Ai to the east. In that place he built an altar to the Lord and called upon the name of the Lord, that is, he prayed and cried out to God. The phrase "pitched his tent" means that he camped.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking, not a character. Abram had just received the promise that God would give that land to his descendants, although the Canaanites lived there. He was a traveler without a fixed home. At each stop he built an altar, a sign that he acknowledged God in the middle of an uncertain journey. Later will come the famine and his journey to Egypt.

For today: wherever you are, even in a temporary or unsafe place, set aside time to pray and remember who God is. Let prayer be your first home, before the trials arrive.
exp.14:16:
When the sun went down and it was dark, Abram saw a smoking furnace and a burning torch pass between the animal pieces that had been cut in half. "Dark" here means it was already night. The words "seed" and "Amorite" do not appear in this verse, but the context speaks of Abram's descendants and of a people in Canaan.

God had just promised Abram a descendant and a land, and had told him that years of slavery would come before he received it. Abram had prepared the animals according to a custom of covenants of that time. Here only God's sign passes, and many understand that in this way He was committing Himself to keep His promise. The smoke and the fire are interpreted in various ways, but they point to His presence.

For today: when the wait is long and dark, remember that your hope rests on the faithfulness of God, not on your own ability. Rest in Him.
exp.5:18:
God commands Noah to bring into the ark two animals of every kind, a male and a female, of every living creature. The phrase "of all flesh" means every being with a body and life. "Shalt bring" means "cause to enter." The purpose is that the animals "may be kept alive with you," that is, that they would be preserved alive together with Noah.

God is speaking. He has just announced that he will send a flood because of the wickedness on the earth, but he also promises a covenant with Noah and his family. This command shows that God wants not only to save Noah but also to preserve the animals. How many animals entered exactly, and how this is to be understood, is something scholars interpret in various ways.

God takes care even with the details of what he entrusts to us. Just as Noah was responsible for caring for the animals, we can diligently care for the people, the animals, and the resources that God places under our responsibility.
exp.33:11:
Here Shechem speaks to Jacob and his sons. He tells them they may ask for as much as they want as the "dowry" (the payment given to the bride's family) and the "gifts." He will pay whatever they demand, provided they give him the young woman as a wife. The word "damsel" means a young woman, and "to wife" means as his wife.

Shechem, son of Hamor, speaks after having dishonored Dinah, the daughter of Jacob. Now he wants to marry her and offers to pay any price. The text does not hide that what happened was a grave offense, and her brothers will answer with deceit and violence. Some readers see here an arrangement settled with money; others, a sincere attempt at repair.

For today: money or fine words do not erase the harm done to another person. When we fail, we need to acknowledge it with humility, listen to the one we have hurt, and seek justice, not only quick arrangements.
exp.17:28:
Abraham continues speaking with God and asks what would happen if only forty righteous people were found in the city. God answers that he would not destroy it for the sake of those forty. The words "spake unto him yet again" mean that Abraham presses his request once more, and "peradventure" means "perhaps". "For the sake of" means "because of".

Here Abraham speaks with the Lord, shortly before Sodom is judged. Abraham knows that his nephew Lot lives there. With humility and respect, he gradually lowers the number of righteous people, and God answers him patiently each time. The passage shows that God is not impatient or harsh when someone brings him a sincere plea.

For today: pray with confidence for people and places that concern you, even if you feel your request is small or bold. Do so with humility, knowing that God hears you and is just and compassionate.
exp.9:16:
This verse continues the list of Canaan's descendants. It names three peoples: the Hivites, the Arkites, and the Sinites. The phrase "the Hivite" means "the Hivites," that is, the ancestors of that people. The Hivites are mentioned in other passages of the Bible, but about the Arkites and the Sinites we know very little, and there is no certainty about their exact location.

It is part of the so-called "Table of Nations" in Genesis 10. The narrator, traditionally Moses, lays out how the peoples spread out after the flood. Here the line of Canaan is detailed, since these peoples would live in the land that God later promised to Israel.

For today: God knows every people and every person, even those whom history hardly remembers. If at times you feel overlooked, remember that God sees you and knows you by name.
exp.30:48:
This verse explains why the place was also called Mizpah, which means "watchtower" or "lookout post." Laban asks that the Lord watch over the two of them when they are no longer together. In the King James wording, "watch" carries the sense of keeping guard or observing from a distance. A "heap" here is a pile of stones.

Laban speaks after years of tension with Jacob, his son-in-law. Jacob had left without warning, and Laban caught up with him in the mountains of Gilead. They make a covenant and raise a heap of stones as a witness. This phrase is not a warm blessing but a request that God keep watch so that neither one breaks the agreement, since they do not fully trust each other.

For today: when you make a commitment, live it as if God were present, because He is. Be honest in your words and your promises, even when no one sees you.
exp.29:3:
Genesis 30:4 says that Rachel gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob as a wife, and that Jacob went in to her. The phrase "went in to her" is an old and discreet way of speaking about the intimate relationship. The word "wife" in this verse reflects the older English wording of the King James Version, and the verse's language is more formal than modern speech.

Rachel could not have children and suffered greatly because of it. Her complaint had touched Jacob, who became angry. In that culture, a servant could bear children who were considered her mistress's. The Bible reports the event without approving or praising it; later, that household will live through rivalries and pain.

When waiting hurts, it is easy to want to solve things our own way and in a hurry. Before acting, it is wise to pray, seek wise counsel, and think about how it will affect others. God can work even amid our imperfect decisions, but that does not make shortcuts good.
exp.10:10:
This verse says that Shem lived five hundred years more after he became the father of his son Arphaxad (today it is written Arfaxad). During that time he had other sons and daughters. The King James wording "begat" means that he was the father of those children.

It is part of Shem's genealogy, which continues after the tower of Babel. The account is not a speech but a recorded narrative that connects the flood with Abraham. It shows that, although God scattered the peoples, the history of his promise continued through one particular family. The very long lifespans are understood in several ways, and the text does not explain them.

For today: God works in ordinary lives, even in those that appear only as a single line in the Bible. Your daily faithfulness, your family, and your influence on those who come after you also matter to God, even when no one notices them.
exp.25:26:
Isaac asks Abimelech and his companions why they have come to him, since they earlier treated him with hostility. "Hate" means that they rejected him or held ill will toward him, and "sent me away" means that they expelled him from their land.

Isaac speaks in Beersheba, after having left Gerar. Earlier, Abimelech had asked him to leave because Isaac had become very powerful (Genesis 26:16), and the herdsmen of Gerar had quarreled with his servants over the wells. Now the king arrives with his friend and his army commander. Isaac speaks frankly and lets it be seen that the wound is still there.

We can be honest about the pain others have caused us, without repaying evil with evil. Isaac asks plainly, and then listens and accepts peace. With humility, God can open doors to reconcile us.
exp.4:22:
This verse says that Enoch lived 365 years in all. It is a summary of his life, as is done with other figures in this chapter.

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Genesis, who lists the generations one by one from Adam. With all the others the account repeats that each one died, but with Enoch the account changes: it says that he walked with God and that God took him. His life is shorter than the others, and the text does not explain in detail what it means that he was taken. Some understand it as being taken to heaven without passing through death; others interpret it in other ways.

What matters in a life is not how long it lasts, but with whom one walks. Today we can seek God each day in simple things: praying, reading his Word, and obeying him in everyday matters, such as family and work.
exp.38:12:
This verse says that Potiphar's wife realized that Joseph had run out and left his clothing in her hands. "It came to pass" means "it happened." "Saw" and "fled" are the forms that appear in the King James Version, so the wording here is the same in modern usage. The garment left in her hands was an article of clothing, probably a cloak or tunic.

The one who narrates is Moses, the traditional author of Genesis. Joseph was a young Hebrew slave, in charge of Potiphar's house. The woman had pressed him several times, and he had refused out of loyalty to God and to his master. When she saw that he had fled, she felt humiliated and soon invented a false accusation against him.

For today: when temptation is strong, there is no need to hesitate or argue at length; sometimes the wisest thing is to get away quickly. Joseph chose to lose his clothing rather than lose his integrity, although that brought him injustice for a time.
exp.48:28:
Jacob, now elderly, gives his sons a command: they are to bury him in the cave in the field of Ephron the Hittite. "I am to be gathered unto my people" is an old way of saying that he is about to die and join his ancestors. The verse's wording is plain: "he charged them" means he gave them an order, and "bury me" is a direct request.

Jacob has just blessed his twelve sons, the future tribes of Israel. Now he gives them his final wish. That cave, at Machpelah, had been bought by Abraham as a family tomb. Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah and Leah were already buried there. Jacob was living in Egypt, but he wanted to be buried in Canaan, the land promised by God.

For today: Jacob thought about his end calmly and with faith in God's promises. We can imitate him by putting our affairs in order and telling our loved ones what we value most, trusting that God keeps what he promises.
exp.33:28:
This verse says that Jacob's sons carried off all the wealth of the city of Shechem. They also took the children and the women as captives, and plundered everything that was in the houses. In the wording the reader sees, "wealth" means possessions and goods, and "captive" means taken as prisoners.

The one who tells this is the narrator of the book. Earlier, Shechem had dishonored Dinah, their sister. Simeon and Levi killed the men by deception, and then the other brothers plundered the city. Afterward, Jacob rebukes them, because their violence put the whole family in danger. The text recounts what happened, but it does not approve of it.

For today: even though injustice hurts us deeply, revenge almost always creates more harm and reaches innocent people. We can ask God for self-control, seek justice honestly, and let Him guide us before we react in anger.
exp.13:15:
He recovered everything the enemy kings had taken: the possessions, his nephew Lot with his belongings, and also the women and the rest of the people who had been captured. Nothing was left behind. The words "goods" and "possessions" refer to what belonged to Abram, and "people" refers to the other captives. Although the verse says "brother," it refers to Lot, who was Abram's nephew; in that time the word could be used for a close relative.

This is part of the account told in Genesis. Invading kings had defeated Sodom and Gomorrah and had taken Lot prisoner. When Abram heard this, he gathered 318 men from his household, pursued them, and attacked them at night.

For today: when someone in your family is in trouble, do not just stand by and watch from a distance. Pray, plan wisely, and take the first step to help them, trusting that God works through people who are willing.
exp.39:18:
It says that, after three days, Pharaoh will have the baker's head cut off. Then he will hang his body on a timber or tree, and the birds will eat his flesh. "Lift up thy head from off thee" means beheading him. "Hang" here is not necessarily what we know today, but a post or tree on which the body was displayed. Some scholars think they hanged him after killing him.

Joseph speaks in the prison. Pharaoh's baker and cupbearer had dreams, and Joseph interprets the baker's, the one about the three baskets. He does this by saying that God gives the interpretations (Gen 40:8). The fulfillment came on Pharaoh's birthday, just as Joseph had said.

For today: Joseph told the truth with respect, though it was hard. We can learn to speak with honesty and compassion, neither softening nor hardening what we must say, trusting that God sustains what we are called to live through.
exp.24:26:
This verse tells how the twins grew up and how they differed. Esau became "skillful in hunting," that is, a skilled hunter, a man of the field who lived outdoors. Jacob was "a plain man," which some understand as quiet, simple, or peaceable in character, and he "dwelt in tents," meaning he stayed near the camp and the work of the household.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He presents the two sons of Isaac and Rebekah, who had already been described at birth. This difference sets up what follows: each parent will have a favorite, and that will bring conflict into the family.

For today: God made each person with distinct traits. Value who each member of your family is and avoid favoritism, because it divides hearts and can cause wounds that last for years.
exp.33:12:
The sons of Jacob answered Shechem and his father Hamor with deceit, and they spoke in this way because Shechem had defiled Dinah, that is, he had dishonored her and abused her. The word "deceitfully" means that they answered with lies and trickery.

Shechem had asked to marry Dinah and offered to pay whatever bride price they demanded. Dinah's brothers, especially Simeon and Levi, were filled with anger over what had happened. They hid their true intention behind words of negotiation. The text clearly states that there was deceit, and what follows shows a plan of revenge, which the Bible does not present as an example to imitate.

For today: pain and injustice are real, but answering with lies and revenge only adds more harm. When someone wounds you, seek justice honestly, ask for counsel, and surrender your anger to God before you act.
exp.48:31:
The explanation says that the field and the cave of Machpelah were not a gift or a questionable property: they were bought from the children of Heth, that is, from the Hittites, ancient inhabitants of Canaan. The word "Heth" is the old spelling of "Het"; in the verse above the name appears as "children of Heth," which matches the King James wording.

The speaker is Jacob, now old and close to death. He gives instructions to his sons to bury him in the cave where Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah and Leah rest. By recalling that it was a legitimate purchase, he makes clear that this place belongs to his family. He also shows his confidence that God will fulfill the promise to give that land to his descendants, even though he will not see it fully realized.

For today: live with your eyes fixed on God's promises, and do so with integrity in practical matters. Be honest in your affairs and leave a good example for your family.
exp.36:18:
The brothers of Joseph see him coming from afar and say to one another: "Behold, this dreamer cometh." The phrase, in the original Hebrew, sounds stronger: something like "the master of dreams." The wording "cometh" is an old form of "comes," which reads as archaic English. They say it with mockery and contempt.

The speakers are the sons of Jacob, brothers of Joseph. He had told of dreams in which they bowed down before him, and he was also the father's favorite son. This caused them envy and resentment. Now, far from their father, the resentment leads them to think of killing him.

For today: when we hold on to envy or resentment, we end up seeing the other person only as a threat, with a nickname, and not as a brother. Let us ask God to heal those feelings before they grow, and seek to speak with sincerity and be reconciled in time.
exp.29:20:
This verse tells that Leah had a daughter and named her Dinah. It is the first time the Bible mentions a daughter of Jacob. The word "bare" means "gave birth to." Here there is no explanation of the name, unlike the earlier children.

The one speaking in the story is the narrator. Leah had had six sons and hoped in this way to win Jacob's love, since he preferred Rachel. This time no words of Leah are recorded, and the Bible does not say why. Some think it is only a brief note about the family, but that is not certain. Right after, it mentions that God remembered Rachel.

For today: God sees and remembers each person, even when the Bible gives only a few words to their story. If you feel little noticed, remember that your life matters to God. And look at those who go unnoticed around you, so that you can value them.
exp.42:15:
Here Joseph sees that his brothers have returned and that they have brought Benjamin, his youngest brother, with them. So he orders the steward of his house to bring the men inside, to slaughter an animal and prepare it, because they will dine with him at noon.

Joseph is the one speaking, and he speaks as governor of Egypt. His brothers had come earlier for food, and he had asked them to bring Benjamin. Now they are doing as he asked. They do not know that he is their brother, and for that reason they are frightened by the invitation. The Bible does not fully explain Joseph's motives at this moment, but his gesture shows kindness and joy at seeing Benjamin.

For today: sometimes God works in kindness, and we, out of guilt or fear, see only a threat. Let us learn to trust and to receive his grace with calm.
exp.30:27:
Laban accuses Jacob of leaving without letting him say goodbye with a kiss to his sons and daughters, that is, to his grandchildren and to his daughters Leah and Rachel. Then he says, "thou hast now done foolishly in so doing," which means "you have acted like a fool, without thinking."

Laban speaks after catching up with Jacob on the mountain of Gilead. Jacob had left secretly with his family and his possessions. Laban shows himself hurt and offended, though his desire to control also shows. Even so, God had warned him the night before not to speak harshly to Jacob. The story does not make everything clear: Laban had some reason on his side, but he had also deceived Jacob before.

For today: when a farewell is difficult, it is better to speak with clarity and honesty than to slip away in silence. This avoids wounds and misunderstandings, and it better protects the relationship.
exp.4:11:
It says that Cainan lived seventy years and then had his son Mahalaleel. "Begat" is an old word that means "was the father of." In this list, "begat" can refer to a direct son or, according to some scholars, to a more distant descendant, but the text does not make it clear.

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of Genesis, who presents the genealogy from Seth to Noah. Each name shows that life continued from generation to generation, and that God's promise kept its course. Then come Cainan's remaining years and his death, as a repeated pattern.

For today: God notices lives that seem like "just a name on a list." Your daily faithfulness, even if it is simple, matters. Live today so that your family and those who follow you see your trust in God.
exp.1:6:
The explanation says that God, here called Jehovah, made the human being from the dust of the earth. Then he breathed the breath of life into his nostrils, and so the man became a "living soul," that is, a living being. The phrase "breathed into" means that he blew or gave breath.

The narrator of the book describes how humanity began. Moses is the traditional author, though this is debated. Before this verse there was no rain and no one to cultivate the ground. Afterward, God places the man in the garden of Eden. The text shows that the human being is bound to the earth, but also depends on the breath of God.

Your life is not an accident but a gift from God. Today, each breath can remind you that you depend on Him. Give thanks for life and treat others with the respect due to someone to whom God gave breath.
exp.23:17:
The explanation says that Rebekah answered kindly: "Drink, my lord". She then quickly lowered her pitcher to her hand so the man could take water, and gave him a drink. The phrase "she hasted" means she hurried. A "pitcher" is a vessel for carrying water. A "maiden" is a young woman.

Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac, had prayed asking for a sign. He arrived at the well, saw Rebekah, and asked her for water. She responds with respect and generosity. She will then offer to draw water for the camels as well, which was heavy work. Many understand that this shows her character, and that the account presents this scene as the answer to the servant's prayer.

Today we can imitate her attitude: to help quickly and kindly anyone who has a need, even a stranger. A simple gesture, done willingly and without complaint, can show a great deal of our heart.
exp.25:4:
God says he will bless Isaac because of the obedience of his father Abraham. Abraham "heard" God's voice, that is, he paid attention to it and did what he was told. He kept God's commandments, statutes, and laws, meaning what God indicated and asked of him.

God speaks to Isaac during a time of famine, when he was in Gerar and was considering whether to go down to Egypt. God promises to be with him and to fulfill the covenant made with Abraham. It is not known with precision what laws Abraham had, since the law of Moses came later. For this reason some think it refers to the instructions God gave him directly. Soon we see that Isaac also became afraid and failed.

Our obedience can influence those who come after us. Even so, God remains faithful when we fail. Today we can obey him with simplicity, trusting in his promise.
exp.47:1:
Here the reader is told that Jacob's son Joseph is coming to visit him. Hearing this, Jacob gathers his strength and sits up in bed. The phrase "strengthened himself" means that he made an effort to encourage himself and rise, even though he was weak and sick. "Israel" is Jacob's other name.

Jacob is now very old and near the end of his life. Joseph arrives with his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. The text does not say who told Jacob, only that someone did. Jacob wants to bless his grandsons and to recall the promises God made to him.

When there is something important to do for God or for others, it is worth giving the best we have, even when our strength is small. We can make the most of time with grandparents or elders, listen to their faith, and ask them to pray for us.
exp.14:20:
This verse closes the list of ten peoples whose land God promises to the descendants of Abram. Here appear the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites. These are ancient names of groups who lived in the region called Canaan.

God speaks in the middle of a covenant with Abram. He had already promised him children, and now He confirms that his descendants will receive this land. Earlier in this same chapter, God says it will take generations, because the iniquity of the Amorites "is not yet full." Scholars discuss the details of the list and its boundaries, but the central meaning is clear: God fulfills what He promises.

For today: when a promise from God seems slow or impossible, remember that He works on a different timeline. Trust, pray, and obey, knowing that God is faithful even when you do not yet see the result.
exp.40:31:
The explanation says that Pharaoh dreamed the same thing twice (the cows and the ears of grain) and that this repetition is a sign. "Established" means certain and settled. "Will shortly bring it to pass" means that God will fulfill it soon.

Joseph, a prisoner in Egypt, speaks before Pharaoh. He makes clear that he does not interpret by his own wisdom, but that God is the one who reveals the future. After explaining the dreams of seven years of plenty and seven years of famine, Joseph shows that the warning is serious and that action must be taken without delay, and for this reason he advises appointing a wise man.

For today: when God warns us or guides us, it is not wise to postpone our response. We can pray, listen with humility, and prepare with wisdom, trusting that God cares for us even in difficult times.
exp.39:16:
It says that in the upper basket there were all kinds of food and pastries for Pharaoh, made by a baker. But the birds were eating them from the basket that was on the dreamer's head. "Victuals" means food, and "baker's work" refers to baked goods, such as breads and cakes.

The one speaking is the chief baker, imprisoned together with the chief cupbearer. Seeing that Joseph had given a good interpretation to the cupbearer, he tells his own dream with hope. But Joseph, who interprets with God's help, will give him hard news: the dream announces his death.

For today: we will not always hear what we wish to hear, but truth spoken with respect is worth more than false comfort. Let us ask God for wisdom to speak with sincerity and love, and trust in Him when reality is difficult.
exp.18:31:
Here the elder daughter of Lot proposes to her sister that they make their father drink until he is drunk and lie with him. The word "generation" means offspring, that is, children. "Á" is the old spelling of "a", and "let us lie with him" means to have sexual relations.

The elder daughter speaks. After the destruction of Sodom, she and her sister live with Lot in a cave, isolated and afraid. They think there are no men left and fear that their family will disappear. The Bible recounts the event without approving of it; it is a deceitful and sinful plan, born of desperation and of a mindset shaped by Sodom.

For today: when we feel fear or scarcity, it is easy to justify crooked decisions with "good reasons." Before acting, let us stop to pray and trust God, who can care for us without our having to do what is wrong.
exp.6:18:
The waters rose so much that they covered all the high mountains under heaven. "Prevailed" means they became stronger and took control over the earth. "Were covered" means that they were hidden under the water.

The narrator of the book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses, tells this. It describes the most intense moment of God's judgment on a humanity full of violence. Noah and his family were inside the ark, which floated above the waters. Christians see here both judgment and God's care for those who trust in him. Some understand "all the earth" as global and others as a broad region; this is debated.

For today: when problems feel like an endless sea covering you, remember that God kept the ark floating above the waters. Trust his care and obey him step by step, as Noah did.
exp.47:13:
Jacob, also called Israel, crosses his arms as he blesses the two sons of Joseph. He places his right hand, the hand of greater honor, on Ephraim, the younger, and his left hand on Manasseh, the firstborn. He does this "wittingly," that is, on purpose, not by mistake. In the King James wording, "right hand" is the hand of greater honor, and "left hand" is the other one.

Jacob is already old and nearly blind. Joseph brings his two sons so that Jacob may bless them before his death. Joseph had arranged Manasseh in front of his father's right hand, according to the custom for the firstborn. Jacob decides otherwise, and later Joseph tries to correct him, but Jacob stands firm. The Bible shows that God often does not follow human order.

For today: God is not limited to our customs or our expectations. We can trust that his decisions have purpose, even when we do not understand them at first.
exp.34:13:
It says that Jacob set up a stone as a sign or memorial in the place where God spoke to him. "Title" is an old word that here means a pillar or memorial stone. "Libation" is a liquid, usually wine, that was poured out as an offering. Then Jacob poured oil over the stone, as a sign that this place was set apart for God.

God had just renewed His promise to Jacob: the land He promised to Abraham and Isaac would belong to him and his descendants. Jacob had already set up a stone at Bethel years earlier, when he was fleeing from his brother Esau. Now, on his return, he again responds with worship and thanksgiving. The text does not explain every detail of the rite; it only tells it.

For today: when God speaks to you or helps you, do not let it pass. Write down what He has done, give thanks, and find a simple way to remember it and worship Him.
exp.18:29:
Genesis 19:30 says that Lot went up out of Zoar, a small town where he had fled, and went to live in the mountains with his two daughters. The King James Version reads "dwelt in the mountain," and the word "dwelt" means "lived" or "made his home." He feared to stay in Zoar, so he ended up living in a cave.

The narrator is telling what happened after the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. God remembered Abraham and brought Lot out alive. Earlier, Lot had asked to stay in Zoar (19:20), but now fear drives him to leave. The text does not explain in detail what he was afraid of. What follows shows a family cut off, wounded, and confused.

For today: fear can lead us to hasty decisions. When we go through a crisis, it helps to ask God for direction, seek wise counsel, and not let fear make the decisions for us.
exp.37:28:
The explanation says that the baby who had first put out his hand drew it back in, and then his brother was born. The midwife exclaimed, "How have you broken through for yourself?", that is, "How you forced your way out!" That is why they named him Pharez, which sounds like "breaking forth" or "breach." The word "but" here is "however," and "drew back" means "turning back."

Tamar gave birth to twins, sons of Judah. The midwife had tied a red thread on the hand of the first one to appear, but the other was born first. The one speaking is the midwife, surprised by the unexpected turn of events. Pharez appears later in the line of David and in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3). The Bible does not explain more; not everything is made clear here.

For today: God does not depend on our plans or on the orders that seem fixed. He can act in unexpected ways, and even in complicated stories he continues to fulfill his purpose. Trust him when everything seems disordered.
exp.9:7:
The explanation says that Cush, son of Ham, had a son named Nimrod. Of him it is stated that "he began to be a mighty one in the earth," that is, he began to stand out as a strong man, with great power and influence. The word "begat" means that Cush was his father.

This passage belongs to the so-called "Table of Nations," a list of the families that came out of Noah's sons after the flood. Moses, according to tradition, is the one who wrote it, to explain where the peoples came from. Nimrod appears with special details, and the following verses connect him with Babel. Some see him as an admirable leader, and others as a symbol of human pride; the text does not fully clarify this.

For today: having power or success is not wrong in itself, but we must ask ourselves how we use it. Let us ask God for humility to serve others and not only to make ourselves great.
exp.37:26:
This verse tells us that, when the time came for Tamar to give birth, it was discovered that she was carrying twins. "In the time of her travail" means "when the hour of delivery had come," and "in her womb" refers to her pregnancy. The word "behold" serves to emphasize the surprise.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Shortly before, Judah had acknowledged that Tamar had been more righteous than he was, since he had not given his son Shelah to her as was due. Now the account shows the outcome: two sons are born, Perez and Zerah. Through Perez the line of Judah continues, and later his name appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Matthew 1.

For today: God can work and give hope even in stories full of mistakes and loss. He does not justify sin, but He invites us to trust that He continues writing good things, and to acknowledge our failings with humility, as Judah did.
exp.7:5:
This verse tells us that forty days passed after the tops of the mountains had become visible. Then Noah opened the window of the ark, the one he had built himself following God's instructions. "At the end of" means "when the forty days were finished" or "when they had been completed."

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of Genesis who relates the events. The ark had already rested on the mountains of Ararat (the King James Version calls the region by that name). Noah does not go out on his own: he waits, observes, and calmly tests whether there is dry land yet. That gesture prepares the sending of the raven and the dove.

For today: when God has kept us safe through a storm, there is no need to hurry. We can wait with patience, take small steps, and trust that He will show us the right moment to come out.
exp.10:0:
It says that, at that time, all the inhabitants of the earth spoke one language and used the same words. There were no differences of language among the peoples. This describes a world united in the way it communicated.

No character speaks here; it is the narrator of the book of Genesis who presents the scene. It comes after the story of Noah and his descendants. This verse prepares the account of the tower of Babel, where human beings gather in Shinar to build. The verses that follow show how they used that unity for their own plans. The text does not say when this happened, so it is best not to invent dates.

For today: unity is a valuable gift, but it depends on what we use it for. Ask yourself whether what you do together with others, in your family, work, or church, seeks to honor God and serve others, or only to make your own name great.
exp.38:4:
This verse tells us that from the time Potiphar put Joseph in charge of his whole household and everything he owned, the Lord blessed the Egyptian's house for Joseph's sake. The blessing reached everything he had, both inside the house and out in the field.

The explanation of the words here: "it came to pass" means "it happened," and "overseer" means a steward or manager placed in charge of everything.

This is not a character speaking, but the narrator of the book of Genesis. Joseph had been sold as a slave by his brothers and taken to Egypt. His master, Potiphar, saw that the Lord was with Joseph and that everything went well for him, so he entrusted his household to him. The text wants to show that God cared for Joseph even in an unjust and difficult situation. A new trial will come later.

For today: do your work well where God has placed you, even if it is not the place you dreamed of. Your faithfulness and your trust in God can be a blessing to others.
exp.46:10:
This verse tells that Joseph settled his father Jacob and his brothers in Egypt. He gave them a holding in "the best of the land," called the land of Rameses, just as Pharaoh had commanded. "Placed" means he settled them there to live, and "possession" means a piece of land of their own.

The narrator of the book recounts how Pharaoh's promise was fulfilled. Canaan was suffering a severe famine, and Jacob's family came to Egypt looking for food. Joseph, who was already a ruler, took care of them. As for "Rameses," some scholars connect it with the region of the Nile delta, but its exact location is debated.

For today: Joseph used his position to care for his family with generosity, without resentment over the past. We can ask ourselves whom God has placed near us so that we might help them with what we have.
exp.40:45:
This verse says that Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. After leaving his presence, he traveled throughout all the land of Egypt. "Was presented" means that they brought him before the king, and "went throughout" means that he journeyed across the whole land.

The narrator shows how Joseph went from being a slave and a prisoner to becoming the second most powerful man in Egypt. Pharaoh had just put him in charge of the country because Joseph interpreted his dreams and proposed a plan for the years of plenty and the years of famine. His journey allowed him to prepare the kingdom for what was coming, as the following text shows.

For today: God can use years of waiting and difficulty to prepare a person. If you feel forgotten or stuck today, keep being faithful in what is in front of you, because God works even when we do not see it.
exp.45:13:
This verse names the three sons of Zebulun, one of the sons Leah bore to Jacob: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel. They are family names, part of a longer list. Here "sons" may also include the men of the next generation, not only direct sons.

The narrator of the book records who traveled to Egypt with Jacob (Israel) when Joseph sent for him during the famine. This list appears just before the reunion of father and son. It shows that the family, which was fulfilling God's promise to form a great nation, entered Egypt together. The names of Zebulun's sons are not explained further, and how many there were by the time they arrived is not detailed.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those whom the story barely mentions. Today you can value those who go unnoticed, remembering that for God no one is insignificant.
exp.18:24:
He overthrew completely the cities of the plain: Sodom, Gomorrah and the nearby places. Their inhabitants died, and everything that grew on the land was also ruined. "Inhabitants" are the people who lived there, and "that which grew upon the ground" refers to the plants and crops.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, recounting what happened after Lot arrived safely at Zoar. Earlier, God's messengers had warned Lot to leave. The Bible presents this judgment as a response to the great wickedness of those cities, and Abraham had interceded for them. Scholars debate exactly how it happened, but the text attributes it to God.

For today: God takes injustice seriously, but He also offers a way out. If He warns you or calls you to change, do not put it off. Listen to His voice today and find your safety in His mercy.
exp.40:5:
This verse describes the second part of Pharaoh's dream. After seven full and good ears of grain, seven others appear, thin and "blasted by the east wind," meaning withered and dried out by the hot east wind that scorched the crops.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is telling what Pharaoh dreamed. The dreams left him troubled, but neither the magicians nor the wise men of Egypt could explain them. This sets up the moment when Joseph will be called to interpret them, as God reveals the meaning to him.

For today: good times do not always last, and God invites us to be prudent and to prepare ourselves with wisdom. We can also trust that, even when we do not understand what is coming, God does know it and can guide us.
exp.16:2:
This verse says that Abram bowed down to the ground, with his forehead toward the earth, and that God then went on speaking to him. "Fell on his face" does not describe an accident, but a gesture of deep respect and humility before God. The name "Jehovah" is God's proper name in this translation.

Abram was ninety-nine years old. God had just revealed himself as the Almighty and promised him a covenant, that is, a solemn commitment. Faced with something so great, Abram responded with reverence and listened. Afterward, God announced that he would be the father of many nations and changed his name to Abraham.

For today: when we pray or read the Bible, we can approach God with humility and be quiet for a moment to listen. Recognizing who God is prepares us to receive what he wants to tell us.
exp.42:31:
The explanation says that in Joseph's house three separate tables were set: one for Joseph, another for his Hebrew brothers, and another for the Egyptians who ate with him. The reason the text gives is that the Egyptians could not eat with the Hebrews, because they regarded it as an "abomination," that is, something despicable or unclean to them.

The narrator is Moses, the traditional author of Genesis. Joseph has not yet revealed who he is, and his brothers are in Egypt buying grain. He has just wept in private on seeing Benjamin. He remains the Egyptian governor, which is why he eats apart. The explanation does not fully account for the reason behind that Egyptian custom; the text only mentions it.

Today we can notice how cultural barriers divide people, even at the table. As followers of Christ, who broke down the wall of separation, we can take the first step: invite to a meal someone different from us and receive them with respect and warmth.
exp.40:51:
Here Joseph gives his second son his name: Ephraim. That name sounds like a Hebrew word connected with "being fruitful" or "bearing fruit." Joseph says that God made him fruitful in the land where he suffered. "Affliction" means prolonged pain or suffering.

Joseph speaks as a grateful father. He was sold by his brothers, made a slave, and unjustly imprisoned in Egypt. Now he is a man of authority, with a wife and children. In naming Manasseh he spoke of forgetting his pain, and with Ephraim he acknowledges that God blessed him right in the place of his suffering. He attributes everything to God, not to his own merit.

For today: God can bring fruit even in the places where we have suffered most. We can recognize with gratitude the good He has done in the midst of difficulties, without denying the past pain, and give thanks for those blessings.
exp.33:5:
This verse says that Hamor, the father of Shechem, went to see Jacob in order to talk with him. "Went out" means that he went toward the place where Jacob was. It is a simple step, but it opens a negotiation after what happened with Dina.

Earlier, Shechem had defiled Dina, that is, he had dishonored her, and now he wanted to marry her. Jacob heard about it and kept silent until his sons came back from the field. Hamor, as a father, speaks on behalf of his son. The text does not explain why Jacob was silent; it may have been prudence, grief, or caution.

For today: when there is a serious offense, it is not enough to fix things with kind words. It is wise to seek justice, to listen to those who were affected, and to wait to act with a clear head, asking God for wisdom.
exp.1:2:
The explanation says that God blessed the seventh day and declared it holy, that is, set apart for a special purpose. The reason is that on that day God rested from all the work he had created and made. "Sanctified" here means "made holy," that is, set apart. "Rested" does not mean that he was tired, but that he stopped creating because his work was finished.

It is part of the account of creation, written in the third person. Jewish and Christian tradition attributes the book to Moses, although some scholars think it had a longer process of composition. The text closes the first great narrative of creation and shows that rest is part of the order God established from the beginning, before any law.

For today: setting aside a regular time to rest and remember God is a gift, not a burden. You can choose a moment of the week to disconnect from work, give thanks for what God has done, and trust that the world does not depend on your effort.
exp.25:24:
Isaac built an altar in Beersheba and there prayed to God, calling upon him by name. Then he pitched his tent, that is, he decided to settle down and live in that place. His servants began to dig a well. "Calling upon the name of the Lord" means praying and worshiping God. "Seed" refers to his descendants.

The narrator tells what Isaac did after God appeared to him that same night. God had told him not to be afraid, that he was with him, and that he would bless him for the promise made to Abraham. Isaac was coming out of a time of conflict over wells and of being rejected in Gerar. A well was vital for life in that dry region.

When God gives us reassurance, the first thing is to respond to him with worship. Before taking care of his needs, Isaac set himself to pray. If you are in a new or difficult place, begin by seeking God and then work with confidence.
exp.23:31:
The explanation says that Abraham's servant entered the house of Bethuel, and that Laban took charge of the camels: he unloaded them, gave them straw (dry stalks) and fodder (food for animals). He also brought water so that the servant and his companions could wash their feet, something common in that era because of the dusty roads and the use of sandals.

This is part of the account in which Abraham's servant looks for a wife for Isaac. Rebekah has already run to tell what happened at the well, and her brother Laban goes out to receive the visitor. Some note that Laban is also excited at the sight of the jewels, but the text does not say this directly. Here, in any case, he fulfills the customs of hospitality.

For today: hospitality shows itself in practical details. Attending to the concrete needs of others, such as food, rest, or a clean place, is a simple and real way of loving our neighbor.
exp.3:24:
It says that Adam came to know his wife again, and she gave birth to another son. She named him Seth, a name that sounds like the word for "appointed" or "substituted." Eve explains that God had given her another child in place of Abel, whom Cain killed. "Seed" means offspring, and "bare" means gave birth.

We are talking about Eve. Before this, the story showed violence growing: Cain killed Abel, and Lamech boasted of revenge. This verse changes the tone. Eve has suffered an enormous loss, yet she recognizes that God did not abandon her. With Seth, the family of the promise continues, and afterward it is said that people began to call upon the name of the Lord.

For today: when a loss leaves you in pain, you do not have to pretend it is already past. But you can look for the signs of God's faithfulness, even small ones, and thank Him for them while you continue to trust Him.
exp.20:14:
The explanation says that the water Hagar had in the skin, a leather bag for carrying liquids, was used up. Faced with that need, she left the boy, her son Ishmael, under one of the bushes or trees, seeking some shade and relief for him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Abraham had sent Hagar and Ishmael away, as God had directed, and they were wandering without direction in the wilderness of Beersheba. With little provision, they ran out of water. The text shows the pain and despair of a mother, but it also prepares the answer of God, who hears the boy's cry.

For today: when you feel you have nothing left, do not think that God does not see you. Even in dry places of anguish, He listens. You can pray sincerely and ask Him for help, even when your strength has run out.
exp.30:26:
Here Laban rebukes Jacob for having left in secret. He asks why Jacob fled without telling him, since then he could have sent him off with celebration, with songs and music. The phrase "didst steal away" means that Jacob deceived him or left without his knowing. The "tabret" is a small drum, and the "harp" is a stringed instrument, similar to an ancient lyre.

Laban speaks; he is Jacob's father-in-law. He caught up with Jacob in the mountains of Gilead after Jacob had departed with his wives, his children and his possessions without notice. Some think Laban speaks sincerely, and others that he only defends his pride, since he had earlier treated Jacob harshly. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: when there is tension, honest and timely communication prevents wounds. Even when it is difficult, speaking with clarity and respect helps more than remaining silent or running away.
exp.17:21:
The verse tells us that the three visitors, called "men", left the place where they were and walked toward Sodom. The word "turned their faces" means that they set out, or went on their way, in that direction. Abraham, by contrast, "stood yet" (still) before the Lord.

God had just said that he would go down to see whether the outcry against Sodom and Gomorrah was true. Two of the visitors continue on their way, and the text presents the one who remains as the Lord himself. Some scholars see here a special appearance of God, although the Bible does not explain this in detail. Abraham does not leave: he stays to speak with God, and soon he will begin his intercession for the righteous of the city.

For today: when you see injustice or people in danger, do not limit yourself to giving an opinion or stepping away. Remain before God and pray for them with humility and trust. Prayer is also a way of loving others.
exp.5:17:
God tells Noah that he will make a covenant with him. Noah will enter the ark together with his wife, his three sons, and their wives. "But" in this verse is the KJV's "but," and "covenant" refers to a solemn, binding promise between God and a person.

It is God who speaks. He has just announced that he will send a flood to destroy everything that has the breath of life, because of the wickedness on the earth. In the middle of that judgment, God promises to preserve Noah and his family. This is the first time the Bible mentions the word "covenant," and it is clear that the initiative belongs to God.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when the outlook seems grim. We can trust his word and obey him step by step, as Noah did, even when we do not understand everything. Moreover, caring for our family in faith is a valuable task.
exp.18:33:
On the next day, the firstborn daughter spoke to the younger one. She told her that she had already lain with their father Lot, and she proposed repeating the plan that night: giving him wine again so that the younger sister would also lie with him. The phrase "that we may preserve seed of our father" means to have offspring.

The speaker is Lot's firstborn daughter. After the destruction of Sodom, they were living in a cave, and she thought there was no one left for them to marry. The text recounts the plan without approving it. It is a sad story, marked by fear, desperation, and deception. From these events came Moab and Ammon, peoples who later appear in the Bible.

For today: when we feel fear or hopelessness, it is easy to look for ways out on our own, even when they harm others. It is better to pause, pray, and seek wise counsel, trusting that God can open paths that are just.
exp.18:30:
Here the older daughter speaks to the younger. She says that their father, Lot, is already old, and that there is no man on the earth who would come in to them "after the manner of all the earth," that is, in the ordinary way of the whole world. The phrase "come in unto us" refers to marital relations.

After the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah, Lot and his daughters live in fear, isolated in a cave. The older daughter sees their situation as a dead end and proposes a plan to have offspring. The Bible only records what they did; it does not approve of it. Some think they believed no one else was left in the world, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: when fear and desperation make us see only one way out, we can make harmful decisions. Instead of rushing, it is wise to stop, pray, and seek God's counsel.
exp.26:25:
Isaac, now an old man, asks his son to come near and kiss him. A kiss was a normal gesture of affection in the family.

Isaac is the one speaking. He is blind and wants to bless Esau, his older son. But the one standing in front of him is Jacob, disguised on the advice of his mother Rebekah. Isaac is suspicious and uses touch, taste, and smell to check who it is. Here a gesture of affection becomes part of the deception.

For today: lies can hide behind gestures that seem loving. This scene invites us to be honest with those we love and to seek God's blessings without shortcuts or deceit.
exp.41:34:
The explanation says that Jacob's sons, on their return from Egypt, opened their sacks of grain and discovered that each one had his bag of money inside. Seeing it, they and their father were frightened. "Bundle" refers to a wrapping or small bag, and "were afraid" means they felt fear.

The account continues after the brothers told Jacob what had happened with the ruler of Egypt, who was Joseph, though they did not know it. Simeon had been left behind as a prisoner, and they were being asked to bring Benjamin. The returned money seemed a dangerous sign, perhaps an accusation of theft. The text does not explain everything they were thinking.

When we do not understand something, fear makes us imagine the worst. We can stop, pray, and remember that God may be at work even in what is confusing, as will later be seen in this story.
exp.41:37:
Jacob refuses to let Benjamin travel to Egypt with his brothers. He says that his brother Joseph is dead and that only Benjamin is left. If some harm came to him on the road, Jacob would die of grief. "Gray hairs" refers to his old age, and "grave" is the tomb. "Mischief" means harm or calamity.

Jacob speaks as an elderly man. He believes he has lost Joseph, and Simeon remains imprisoned in Egypt. His sons need to return for more food, but the governor has demanded to see Benjamin. Reuben offered his own sons as a guarantee, but Jacob does not accept. His fear comes from pain and from seeing everything as turned "against him." He does not know that God is at work, nor that Joseph is alive.

When pain has wounded us, we may cling in fear to what remains. Today, instead of seeing only what is missing, we can hand our fears over to God and trust that He cares for what we do not understand.
exp.28:34:
It says that Leah became pregnant again and had a fourth son. This time she declared that she would praise the Lord, that is, that she would give thanks and honor him. That is why she named him Judah, a name connected with the word "praise." After him, she stopped having children for a time. "Bearing" means giving birth.

Leah speaks here, the less loved wife of Jacob. In her earlier sons she expressed her pain and her desire to win her husband's affection. Now, however, her outlook changes: she no longer places her hope in Jacob valuing her, but looks to God with gratitude. Later, from Judah would come the line of King David, and, according to Christian faith, Jesus.

For today: when you feel you lack the recognition of others, do not wait for everything to improve before giving thanks. Stop and praise God for what He has already given you. Gratitude can restore your peace.
exp.41:10:
Here the brothers of Joseph defend themselves against a serious accusation. They say that they are all sons of the same father, that they are honest men (the KJV phrase "true men" means sincere, upright), and that their servants have never been spies. "Servants" is the respectful way they speak of themselves before an authority.

The ten brothers came to Egypt to buy grain because of the famine. Without knowing it, they speak with Joseph, whom they had sold years earlier. He accuses them of being spies, and they answer with fear, trying to prove their innocence. Joseph remembers his dreams, in which they bowed down before him.

When someone accuses us, it is wise to answer with truth and humility. But it is also healthy to examine the heart: these men spoke of their honesty, although they carried a hidden sin against Joseph. God invites us to live with sincerity before Him.
exp.40:24:
Here Joseph tells Pharaoh that his two dreams, the one of the cows and the one of the ears of grain, are really one single message. The words "The dream of Pharaoh is one" state this directly. Joseph adds that God has shown Pharaoh what He Himself is about to do, meaning that the event comes from God and not from chance.

Joseph speaks at the court of Egypt, a Hebrew prisoner who has just been called before the king. Pharaoh's magicians had not been able to explain the dreams. Joseph does not claim the credit for himself but points to God as the one who reveals and the one who acts. He will go on to explain that seven years of plenty and seven years of famine are coming.

For today: when you have the chance to help others with your ability or knowledge, acknowledge with humility that everything comes from God. And if God warns you of something difficult that is coming, use it to prepare yourself with wisdom, not with fear.
exp.27:10:
It says that Jacob came to a certain place and spent the night there, because the sun had already set. He took some of the stones from that spot, put them under his head as a pillow, and lay down to sleep. Some older words are used here: "place" means the spot, and "pillows" are the stones he rested his head on while sleeping.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Jacob is fleeing from his home on the way to Haran, after the conflicts with his brother Esau. He travels alone and without comforts, with a stone for a pillow. What follows is very important: in that simple place, God speaks to him in a dream and renews the promises made to Abraham and Isaac.

There are moments when we feel alone, tired, or uncertain. This verse reminds us that God can meet us right there, even when we do not have everything figured out. You can speak to him honestly tonight, just as you are.
exp.15:15:
This verse says that Abram was eighty-six years old when Hagar gave birth to Ishmael. "Bare" is an older way of saying "gave birth to" in English. It is a detail of time that closes the account of Ishmael's birth.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. God had promised Abram a son, but the years passed, and Sarai, his wife, proposed that he have a child through her servant Hagar. Abram agreed. Hagar later fled because of mistreatment, and God found her by the spring. According to the text, Abram was eighty-six years old, and later God would renew the promise to him when he was ninety-nine (Genesis 17).

For today: when God seems slow, it is tempting to look for shortcuts. We can wait patiently and trust that God keeps his promises in his own time. And if we make mistakes, he still cares for us, as he cared for Hagar and Ishmael.
exp.2:2:
Here the woman answers the serpent and explains God's rule about the tree that stood in the middle of the garden. She says that God forbade them to eat its fruit and even to touch it, "lest ye die," that is, "so that you will not die." The words "But" and "lest" carry the sense of "but" and "so that not."

Eve is speaking, and she does so in front of the serpent, which has just cast doubt on God's word. In God's account to Adam (Genesis 2:16-17) the phrase "neither shall ye touch it" is not mentioned. Some think Eve added something; others think she only explained it with greater emphasis. This cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: when someone questions what God said, it is good to remember his word exactly, without adding to it or taking anything away from it. Reading it often helps us not to be confused.
exp.43:13:
It says that Judah and his brothers returned to Joseph's house. He was still there, waiting for them. On seeing him, they threw themselves to the ground before him as a sign of humility and despair. "Fell" here means they bowed down until they touched the earth, and "was yet there" means he was still there.

The narrator tells us that Joseph had had his silver cup hidden in Benjamin's sack, as a test of the brothers' loyalty. When they found it, they tore their clothes, a sign of deep grief, and went back. Judah is mentioned first because he had guaranteed Benjamin's safety before their father Jacob. Now he steps forward for all of them.

For today: when we fail or are accused, returning and facing the situation with humility is better than running away. Judah does not hide, but presents himself and takes responsibility with courage.
exp.1:19:
The explanation says that Adam gave names to all the cattle, to the birds of the air, and to every beast of the field. But among all of them he did not find a suitable helper, that is, someone fitting and similar to him, with whom he could share life. The words "found" and "there was not found" are the wording of the King James Version.

The one speaking is the narrator of Genesis. God had said that it is not good for the man to be alone, and so he presented the animals to him. By naming them, Adam exercised the care that God had entrusted to him, and it also became clear that none of them could be his companion. This prepares the creation of the woman.

For today: God made us to live in relationship with others. Value and care for the people God places beside you, and if you feel lonely, seek community, for God understands that need.
exp.42:7:
Here Judah asks his father Jacob (also called Israel) to let Benjamin, "the lad," go with them. The word "lad" means the young one. Judah says "let us arise and go," that is, let us set out for Egypt. The reason is so that all of them can live and not die of hunger: they, their father, and the little ones.

There is a severe famine. The ruler of Egypt, who is Joseph although they do not yet know it, told them they would not see his face again without their youngest brother. Jacob resists because he has already lost Joseph and fears losing Benjamin. Judah speaks up with firmness and, in the verses that follow, offers himself as the personal guarantor of Benjamin.

For today: when there is fear and deadlock, God often calls us to take steps of responsibility. Judah does not only speak, but commits himself. We can ask ourselves what concrete step, with humility and care for others, we need to take today.
exp.20:24:
Abraham "reproved" Abimelech, that is, he took him to task or called his attention to the matter frankly. The reason was a well of water that Abimelech's servants had taken from him by force. "Because of" here means "on account of" or "for the reason of."

Abimelech was a king of the region, and he was asking Abraham for an oath of friendship. Abraham agrees, but first he raises this problem. In that dry land, a well was vital for living and for keeping the flocks. Abimelech replies that he knew nothing about it, and then they make a covenant. The text does not say who the servants were or exactly how it happened.

Before sealing a peace, it is good to speak plainly about what has hurt us. Abraham does not stay silent nor take revenge: he says it with respect and gives the other person the chance to answer. In this way relationships can heal on a sincere foundation.
exp.42:26:
Here Joseph, who has not yet made himself known to his brothers, greets them and asks how they are. Right away he wants to know about his father: whether the old man they spoke of is well and whether he is still alive. The phrase "is he well" means "is he well in health and in spirit?"

Joseph speaks as governor in Egypt. His brothers have returned with Benjamin and with a gift, and they treat him with reverence without knowing who he is. His question concerns Jacob, his own father. Some think Joseph shows sincere affection, even though he hides his identity; the text does not explain everything he was feeling.

For today: power and success should not dull interest in family. Asking sincerely about someone, especially the elderly, is a simple way of showing love. Today you could call an older relative and listen patiently.
exp.12:15:
God tells Abram that his descendants will be as numerous as the dust of the earth. Just as no one can count all the dust, no one will be able to count his descendants. The word "seed" means offspring, that is, children, grandchildren, and the generations that will come after.
