It is the LORD who speaks, and he does so right after Lot separated from Abram. Abram had given the best land to Lot and was left with less. Then God encourages him and renews the promise of the land and of a great family. Abram still had no children, so it was a promise that called for great faith.

For today: when you feel you have lost something or that you have been left with little, remember that God sees your situation and keeps what he promises. Trust in him, and respond as Abram did, with gratitude and worship.
exp.45:26:
This verse says that Joseph had two sons in Egypt, Manasseh and Ephraim, and that when all the members of Jacob's family who came to Egypt are added together, the total was seventy. The word "souls" means "persons." Note: other ancient versions, such as the Greek, give seventy-five, because they count some of Joseph's grandchildren; the numbers are explained in different ways.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, closing the list of Jacob's descendants. Jacob, already old, goes down to Egypt because Joseph was alive and there was famine in Canaan. The list shows that God was keeping his promise to make this family a great nation. Right after this comes the moving reunion between Joseph and his father.

For today: God cares for each person and remembers them by name. You can trust that your life matters to Him, and that He keeps His promises even in difficult times and times of change.
exp.29:25:
Jacob asks his father-in-law Laban to let him leave with his wives and his children. He says "for whom I have served thee," meaning that he worked fourteen years for them. Jacob appeals to what Laban already knows: his faithful work.

Jacob speaks to Laban after Joseph, Rachel's son, was born. Jacob had worked for Laban for his two daughters, Leah and Rachel, and now he feels it is time to return to his own land. Laban answers that God has blessed him because of Jacob, and he proposes wages so that Jacob will stay.

For today: when the time comes to take an important step, such as changing jobs or moving to another place, do it with clarity and respect. Remember your faithful service, speak honestly, and do not let the pressure of others turn you away from what God shows you.
exp.29:42:
It says that Jacob prospered greatly. The word "increased" in this verse, as used in the King James wording, means "grew" or "became rich." "Man" here is simply "man." Jacob came to have many sheep, maidservants, menservants, camels, and asses (donkeys). It was great wealth for his time.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Jacob had spent years working for his father-in-law Laban, who had cheated him several times. Jacob used a method with rods for the livestock, and his flock grew. Scholars do not agree on how to understand that method. Later, in Genesis 31:9-12, Jacob says that God took the livestock away from Laban and gave it to him, and he attributes that prosperity to God.

For today: when something goes well for you, recognize that God is the one who blesses, not only your effort. And if you have been treated unfairly, trust that He sees your situation and can take care of you.
exp.40:22:
This verse describes the second part of Pharaoh's dream about the ears of grain. After the seven full and beautiful ears, seven others appear that were thin, dried up, and scorched by the scorching east wind, a hot, dry wind from the east that damaged the crops.

Here Pharaoh is speaking. He tells Joseph his dream, because none of the magicians of Egypt could explain it to him. He was troubled and looking for an answer. Shortly afterward, Joseph makes clear that God himself was giving warning of what was going to happen: years of plenty followed by years of famine.

For today: God can speak and give warning ahead of time, and he invites us to be wise. When we live in good times, we can learn to save, to share, and to trust in him, so that we are not caught off guard when difficulties come.
exp.20:32:
The explanation says that Abraham planted a grove in Beersheba and there prayed to the Lord, calling him "the everlasting God." The word "grove" can also be understood as a tamarisk, a tree that gives shade; translators do not fully agree. "Jehovah" is the name of God, and "called on" means that he called upon him in prayer and worship.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Abraham had just made a peace agreement with Abimelech over a well of water. After the agreement, Abraham was not only content with human peace, but worshiped God. It is the only time the Bible calls him "the everlasting God" in Genesis.

For today: when God gives you a breathing space, a solution, or peace in a conflict, do not forget to thank him. And in the midst of what changes, remember that God does not change.
exp.29:29:
Jacob tells Laban that before he came, Laban had little, but now his wealth has grown greatly. Jacob states that God blessed Laban because of Jacob's presence and work. Then he asks: "When shall I provide for my own house also?" The phrase "provide for" in the King James wording means "to do something for" or "to make provision for."

Jacob speaks after serving Laban for many years, and Laban asks him what wages he wants. Jacob already has wives and children and wishes to begin providing for his family. His request is fair, although what follows in the story has complex details.

For today: serving others faithfully is good, but caring for one's own family is also healthy and responsible. We can recognize that God is the one who blesses our work, and at the same time speak clearly and respectfully about what we need.
exp.5:6:
Here God announces that he will wipe from the earth the human beings he created, along with the animals, the creeping things, and the birds of the air. The word "destroy" in the King James Version means "to wipe out, to remove completely." "It repenteth me" expresses deep grief, not that God had made a mistake; the Bible presents it as pain at what sin had caused.

The Lord speaks. Shortly before, it is said that human wickedness was great and that every intention of their thoughts was only evil. God grieves over this, and that is why he decides to bring judgment. But soon Noah appears, who "found grace in the eyes of the Lord" and walked with God. Thus, in the midst of judgment, there is also mercy and a way out.

For today: sin is not a small thing to God; it grieves him. But we can also trust in his grace. Let us ask him to guard our hearts and our thoughts, and let us seek to walk with him each day, as Noah did.
exp.46:27:
This verse says that Jacob lived seventeen years in Egypt, and that his life in total lasted one hundred forty-seven years. It is a simple summary: how long he stayed there and how long he lived in all. "The days of Jacob" in the source wording simply means "the length of his life," and the King James phrase "the whole age of Jacob" carries the same sense.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob, also called Israel, had come to Egypt in old age, because his son Joseph ruled there and had saved him and his family from the famine. They enjoyed years of peace in Goshen, and the verse announces that his life is drawing near its end, as becomes clear shortly afterward when he asks to be buried in the land of his fathers.

For today: our days are numbered, and God can give us years of peace and rest even after very hard times. It is worth making good use of the time, caring for family, and leaving a faith that others can inherit.
exp.21:8:
The verse says that Abraham and Isaac came to the place God had told them about. There Abraham built an altar, laid the wood in order, bound his son Isaac, and laid him on the altar, on top of the wood.

God had asked Abraham to offer Isaac, the son of the promise, as a burnt offering. Shortly before this, Isaac asked where the lamb was, and Abraham answered that God himself would provide it. Here the story moves forward in silence and with great tension. Many see it as a test of faith; the next verse shows that God stops Abraham.

For today: trust God even when we do not understand his way. We can obey him step by step, believing that he watches over what we love most and will provide what is needed.
exp.49:23:
The explanation says that Joseph, now an old man, tells his brothers that he is going to die. But he assures them that God will not abandon them: God will "visit" them, that is, he will act on their behalf, and will bring them out of Egypt to take them to the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The word "sware" means that God made a solemn promise, and "this land" refers to the land God promised.

Joseph speaks at the age of 110, at the end of the book of Genesis. He has seen his grandchildren and great-grandchildren grow up in Egypt. He knows that his family is not in the land promised to them, and he wants them to keep hope alive after he is gone. Shortly afterward he asks that his bones be carried with them when God brings them out.

For today: people pass away, but God's promises remain firm. When we must say goodbye to someone, or live through uncertain times, we can trust that God keeps his word. We can also leave others, through our words and example, a faith that will sustain them.
exp.34:21:
It says that while Israel (Jacob) was living in that region, his eldest son Reuben had relations with Bilhah, one of his father's concubines, and Jacob found out. "Lay with" is an old way of speaking about sexual relations. "Concubine" refers to a wife of lower rank. Then the text begins to name the twelve sons of Israel.

It is the narrator of Genesis who recounts this, right after the death of Rachel. The account is brief and does not say how Jacob reacted at that moment. Later, in Genesis 49:3-4, Jacob mentions this offense when he blesses his sons, and Reuben loses his place of privilege. The Bible shows here, honestly, that the family chosen by God also had serious sins.

For today: God does not hide the failures of his people, and we do not need to pretend either. Acknowledging sin and seeking forgiveness and change is better than concealing it, because our decisions affect the whole family.
exp.46:23:
It says that when the harvests came in, the people were to give Pharaoh the fifth part, that is, twenty percent. The other four parts would stay with them: they would be for sowing again, and for them to eat, their households, and their little ones. "Seed" is what is sown, and "food" is the nourishment needed to live.

Joseph speaks to the Egyptians after a very harsh famine. They had already handed over their money, their livestock, and their lands in order to receive bread. Joseph gives them seed to plant again and sets this arrangement in place. The priests were left out because they already received food from Pharaoh. The people saw it as a favor that saved their lives.

For today: learn to manage what you receive with order. Set aside one part for your obligations, another for the support of your household, and another for sowing for the future. In this way you care for your own and avoid living from day to day.
exp.24:33:
The explanation says that Jacob gave Esau bread and a stew of lentils. Esau ate and drank, got up and went on his way, without giving the matter any further thought. The words "gave" and "went his way" are older forms of the English used today. "Despised" means that he placed little value on it, that he treated it as something unimportant. The "birthright" was the right of the firstborn son to receive a special place in the family.

Esau arrived tired and hungry. He said that he was going to die and that the birthright would do him no good. Jacob took advantage of the moment and asked him to sell it to him with an oath. Here the account does not present them as models to imitate, but shows Esau's contempt for what God valued in that family.

For today: when we face an urgent need, let us take care not to exchange something valuable and lasting, such as our faith, our integrity or our family, for momentary relief.
exp.18:34:
The explanation says that Lot's daughters made their father drunk again the second night. This time the younger daughter lay with him, and Lot, being drunk, was not aware of anything. The word "perceived" means to notice, and "lay with him" refers to sexual relations.

The narrator tells what happened after the destruction of Sodom. The daughters, living isolated in a cave, feared they would have no offspring and acted through deception. The Bible reports these events without approving them. From this union were born Moab and Ammon, peoples who later became neighbors of Israel.

For today: when fear pressures us, we can justify wrong decisions. Before acting, let us ask God for wisdom and seek sound counsel, instead of settling everything our own way.
exp.23:24:
Rebekah continues speaking with Abraham's servant and offers him more than he asked for. She says that in her household there is straw and plenty of provender, that is, feed for the camels, and also room to lodge, or in other words, a place to spend the night. The word "lodge" means to stay or be housed for the night.

Here Rebekah, the daughter of Bethuel, is speaking. Abraham's servant had been sent to find a wife for Isaac and had prayed for a sign. Rebekah had already given water to him and to his camels. Now she responds generously to his question about her family. Immediately afterward, the servant worships God, because he sees that the Lord has led him to Abraham's relatives.

For today: generosity and hospitality are a simple way of serving. We can offer something more than what is asked of us: time, food, a place, or a kind word. God often works through everyday gestures like these.
exp.14:0:
The explanation says that God spoke to Abram in a vision, after certain events. He asks him not to be afraid and promises him two things: to be his "shield," that is, his protector, and to be his "reward." It says that this reward is "exceedingly great," that is, enormous.

The one who speaks is God, and he speaks to Abram shortly after Abram rescued his nephew Lot and turned down the riches of the king of Sodom (Genesis 14). Abram probably felt fear and doubt, because he still had no children, and for that reason he answers worried about his heir. God assures him that He Himself will take care of him.

Today, when you feel fear or uncertainty about the future, remember that God offers Himself as your protection and your greatest treasure. Today you can pray sincerely, telling Him your fears, and trust that He cares for you.
exp.8:15:
God says that the bow will be in the clouds, and that when he sees it he will remember his everlasting covenant. That covenant is with every living creature, with "all flesh" upon the earth. "I will look upon it" means "I will see it," and "every living creature" refers to every living being.

God is speaking to Noah and his sons after the flood. He has just promised that he will never again destroy the earth with water. The bow is the visible sign of that promise, and it does not depend on the strength of men, but on the faithfulness of God. Some think God "remembers" in a human sense; others take it as a way of saying that he fulfills what he has promised.

When you see a rainbow, let it remind you that God keeps his promises. Give him thanks and trust in him in your storms.
exp.16:12:
God tells Abraham again that every male in his household must be circumcised: both the one born in his home and the servant he bought with his money. In this way, God's covenant would be marked on the body as an "everlasting" covenant, that is, one that lasts forever. "Foreskin" is the skin that is cut away in circumcision.

Here God himself speaks with Abraham, when he confirms his covenant and his promise to give him a great offspring. Circumcision was the visible sign of that covenant. It included foreign servants, which shows that the whole of Abraham's household was placed under that relationship with God.

For today: God desires a faith that shows in life, not only in words. We can ask ourselves what concrete signs, such as honesty, kindness, and faithfulness, show at home and at work that we belong to him.
exp.43:23:
It says that when the brothers returned to Canaan and came to their father Jacob, they told him what the ruler of Egypt had said to them. "My lord" is the respectful title for that man, and "thy servant" is Jacob, their father. "It came to pass" means "it happened," and "we told him" simply means they related the matter to him.

The one speaking is Judah, who explains to the Egyptian ruler, not knowing he is their brother Joseph, what took place in his house. He is defending Benjamin and pleading that they be allowed to return to their father. Judah goes over the events honestly, and in doing so shows how much Jacob would suffer if he lost his youngest son.

Today we can learn from Judah to speak the truth and with love when there is a conflict. Telling things as they happened, without manipulating them, helps others understand our heart and sometimes opens the door to reconciliation.
exp.14:2:
Abram tells God that he has no children. "Seed" in the King James wording means offspring or descendants. Since he has none, he thinks his heir will be someone born in his house, that is, a trusted servant. Earlier he had already named him: Eliezer of Damascus.

God had just promised him protection and a very great reward. Abram answers honestly: what good is a reward if there is no son to receive the inheritance? Years had already passed since the promise that he would have a great descendance, and he was still waiting. God does not rebuke him; he answers him with a clearer promise.

For today: when the waiting drags on and you have doubts, do not hide them. Bring them to God honestly, as Abram did, and listen to what He answers in His Word.
exp.12:11:
This verse tells us that Abram stayed to live in the land of Canaan, while Lot settled in the cities of the plain of the Jordan. "Dwelled" means that he settled down or made his home there. Lot "pitched his tent toward Sodom," that is, little by little he moved his camp closer to that city.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Abram and Lot could no longer stay together with their herds, and they parted ways. Lot chose what looked fertile and prosperous. The text that follows makes clear that the men of Sodom were very wicked before God, and then God renews his promise to Abram.

For today: before choosing, it is not enough to ask what looks good or convenient. It is also wise to ask where that decision is gradually leading us, and to ask God to guide us.
exp.37:23:
About three months later, Judah was told that his daughter-in-law Tamar had played the harlot, meaning she had had relations outside of marriage, and that she was even pregnant. The word "came to pass" means "happened," and "was told" means that someone informed him. Judah, without investigating, orders her brought out and burned.

The one speaking is Judah, the head of the family. Tamar had been a widow of his sons, and he had not given her his son Shelah, as was due. She still belonged to the family, which is why Judah feels entitled to condemn her. He did not know the pregnancy was his own. Some scholars note that he judges harshly, even though he himself had acted wrongly.

For today: before condemning others, let us examine our own lives and seek the truth with humility. Jesus invites us to judge with mercy, remembering that we too need forgiveness.
exp.15:3:
Abram had relations with Hagar, Sarai's servant, and she became pregnant. Once she realized she was expecting a child, Hagar began to look down on Sarai, her mistress. "Cohabited" means that he had intimate relations with her, and "looked down on" means that she treated Sarai as though she were of lesser worth.

The narrator tells what happened after ten years in Canaan without children. Sarai, hurt by her barrenness, offered Hagar to Abram, following a custom of that time for securing descendants. It was a human decision, made without clearly waiting for God's promise. The text does not directly approve or condemn it here, but it soon shows the consequences: jealousy, pride, and pain among all of them.

For today: when we try to solve a problem on our own, without trusting God, we can cause greater wounds. And if we receive a blessing, we should take care not to use it to humiliate others.
exp.21:17:
Through a descendant of Abraham, the verse says, God would bless all the peoples of the world. The word "seed" in the King James Version means descendants, and "nations" is the word used for the peoples of the earth. "Because" is the sense of the phrase in the verse: God ties this promise to Abraham's obedience.

The one speaking is the angel of the LORD, who repeats God's oath after Abraham was willing to offer Isaac and God stopped him. The promise confirms what was said earlier in Genesis 12. The New Testament, in Galatians 3:16, sees Christ in that "seed"; Jewish readers have understood it in other ways, such as referring to the people of Israel.

For today: obedience to God, even when it costs, can bring a blessing greater than we imagine, also to other people. Trust God today in a difficult decision, and think about how your faithfulness can help those around you.
exp.34:2:
Jacob invites his family to rise up and go to Bethel. There he wants to build an altar to God. He describes God as the one who answered him when he was in distress and who has been with him on every step of his journey. "Let me make an altar" means he will set up a place for worship and for offering sacrifices. "Bethel" means "house of God."

Jacob is speaking after the violent tragedy at Shechem. God had told him to return to Bethel, where years earlier God had appeared to him while he was fleeing from Esau. Before going, Jacob asks everyone to put away their idols, purify themselves, and change their clothes. He wants the journey to be one of sincere worship and not merely a formality.

For today: remember how God has answered and accompanied you in difficult moments. Give thanks through a concrete act, and set aside whatever competes with God in your heart, so that you can put him first again.
exp.15:1:
Here Sarai tells Abram that God has not allowed her to have children. She asks him to go in to her servant Hagar, hoping to have children through her. "Go in unto" means that he is to have relations with her, and "it may be" means "perhaps." Abram agreed to the proposal.

Sarai speaks after years of waiting. God had already promised Abram a descendant, but time kept passing and there was no child. In that culture, a servant could bear children in place of the wife, and the child was counted as belonging to her. Sarai sought a human solution, and Abram followed it without consulting God, according to the text. The results were painful, as Hagar's contempt shows.

When the waiting drags on, it is tempting to hurry things along in our own way. Before acting, it is wise to pray, seek wise counsel, and trust that God keeps his promises in his own time.
exp.0:25:
God says he is going to make human beings "in our image, after our likeness." He also wants the man to "have dominion," that is, to rule and to care for, over the fish, the birds, the cattle, and every creature that creeps on the earth. "Having dominion" means having authority the way a steward or manager does.

The one speaking is God, at the end of creating the animals and just before he creates people. He speaks in the plural ("let us make"), and Christians often see this as a hint of the Trinity, though others understand it as an expression of divine majesty or of divine counsel. The following passage makes clear that both man and woman receive this image and this task.

For today: if every person bears the image of God, each person deserves respect and dignity. And if we have been entrusted with caring for creation, we can do it with affection and not with abuse, for example by caring for animals and not wasting what God made.
exp.33:8:
Here Hamor proposes that the two families join together through marriage. The verse says, "make ye marriages with us," which means becoming relatives by marriage. He tells them, "give your daughters unto us, and take our daughters unto you." It is an offer of exchange to form a single community.

Hamor is speaking. He is the father of Shechem, the young man who had dishonored Dinah, Jacob's daughter. Her brothers are very angry. Hamor tries to settle everything with a friendly and convenient deal, as if the problem could be solved with an alliance. He says nothing about justice or making amends for the harm done. Moreover, that union would lead Israel to mix with the peoples of the land, something the Bible later treats with caution.

For today: when someone does harm, it is not enough to offer a comfortable settlement. First there must be an acknowledgment of the wrong, a search for justice, and care for the one who was hurt.
exp.25:21:
He moved on from that place and dug another well. This time no one fought over it. That is why he called it Rehovot, which means "wide places" or "open spaces." "Strove" means they argued or fought. "Made room" means gave him space. "Fruitful" means that they would bear fruit and prosper.

The narrator tells what Isaac experienced in the region of Gerar. The local herdsmen contested two wells with him, which were vital in a dry land. Isaac did not insist on fighting but kept moving on. Upon finding peace, he recognized that God had made room for him. Shortly afterward, at Beersheba, the Lord confirmed His promise to him.

For today: not every battle is worth fighting. Sometimes peace and gentleness open the way for God to give us room. Trust that He can give you a wide place, and give thanks to Him when He does.
exp.8:20:
It says that Noah drank wine from his vineyard, became drunk, and was left uncovered inside his tent. "Drunken" means he lost control because of the wine's effect, and "uncovered" means naked. It is a simple and honest account that does not hide the fall of a righteous man.

The narrator tells what happened after the flood, when Noah began a new life by working the land. The Bible does not explain why he got drunk or whether it was deliberate, so it is better not to assume more than the text says. What it does do is set up the next scene, where Noah's sons react in very different ways to their father.

For today: even people of faith can fail, and excess exposes us to shame. Let us be careful about what has power over us, and when someone close to us falls, let us help protect their dignity, not expose it.
exp.41:4:
This verse says that the sons of Jacob, here called "the sons of Israel," went to Egypt to buy food along with other people who were also traveling there out of the same need. The word "corn" in the King James Version refers to grain in general, and in this context it means the grain they needed to survive, and "the famine was in the land" means there was a severe shortage of food.

The account is told by the narrator of Genesis. A severe famine was affecting Canaan, and Jacob sent ten of his sons to get grain in Egypt. He did not let Benjamin go, for fear of losing him as he had lost Joseph. Without knowing it, his sons were about to meet Joseph, whom they had sold years earlier.

For today: when times of need come, God can use those same difficulties to lead us to face what we have kept silent about. If there is something unresolved that you need to put right with someone, do not ignore it; ask God for the courage to seek reconciliation.
exp.46:19:
This verse tells how Joseph bought all the land of Egypt for Pharaoh. The Egyptians sold their fields, one by one, because the famine was so severe. In this way, the land became the king's.

The account follows the years of scarcity that Joseph had announced. The people had already spent their money and handed over their livestock, and they asked Joseph for bread and seed so that they would not die. Joseph acted as Pharaoh's administrator. The Bible only reports what happened; it does not say whether this system was fair, and readers have judged it in different ways.

For today: when hard times come, it is easy to make desperate decisions. It is wise to plan carefully, save in the good times, and seek help early. And if we are in a position to help others, we should do so with justice and compassion.
exp.34:1:
Jacob tells everyone in his household to get rid of the idols they are hiding, to wash themselves, and to change their clothes. "Foreign gods" are the images of false gods belonging to other peoples. "Change" means to exchange, and "be clean" speaks of a purification to present oneself before God.

God has just told Jacob to return to Bethel, the place where he found him when he was fleeing from Esau. Jacob speaks as the head of the family. Before drawing near to God, he wants no one to have idols. Some of them probably came from Mesopotamia or from what they took in Shechem, though the Bible does not give the details. Washing and changing clothes were outward signs of a heart turning back to God.

Before seeking God with greater closeness, ask yourself what thing occupies the place that belongs to Him alone. Set it aside, ask for forgiveness, and begin again with sincerity.
exp.41:17:
This verse tells how, after three days in prison, Joseph speaks to his brothers and offers them a way out: "This do, and live." He also says: "I fear God." The old wording is "said unto them" (said to them) and "live" (and you will live, not die). With that phrase, Joseph shows that he will act with respect toward God.

Joseph is now governor of Egypt. His brothers have come to buy food because of the famine, and they do not recognize him. He accuses them of being spies and tests them. Then he softens his decision: only one will remain imprisoned, and the others will take grain home. The Bible does not give all his reasons in detail; many think he wanted to know whether his brothers had changed.

For today: the fear of God helps us use power with justice and mercy. If someone owes us or has wronged us, we can seek the truth without revenge.
exp.28:3:
Jacob meets some shepherds by a well and asks them: "My brethren, where are you from?" They answer that they are from Haran. The word "brethren" is the King James rendering of the Hebrew for "brothers," and it is used here as a general form of address to people he has just met.

Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau and was looking for his mother's family, in a distant land. By calling these strangers "brethren," he shows a kind and friendly manner. His simple question leads him, step by step, to Laban and Rachel. The Bible does not explain how, but the account suggests that God was guiding him along the way.

For today: approach people with respect and kindness, even if they are strangers. A simple conversation can open doors you did not expect. And when you do not see the way clearly, take the next step with confidence that God also guides in small things.
exp.25:17:
Isaac dug again the wells that his father Abraham had dug. The Philistines had stopped them up with earth after Abraham died. To "stop" a well means to block it or fill it in. Isaac also gave them the same names that Abraham had given them.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Isaac had just been sent away by Abimelech, because he had become very prosperous. In that dry land, water meant life for people and livestock. By reopening the wells, Isaac was also affirming the inheritance and the promises that God had given to his father.

For today: value the good that others planted in your life, such as faith, prayer, or good habits. If they have been stopped up over time or by difficulties, you can open them again with patience and trust in God.
exp.27:12:
This verse tells that Jacob, while he slept, saw the Lord standing above the ladder. God presents himself as the God of Abraham and of Isaac, and promises him the land where he was lying. "Seed" means descendants, that is, his children and the children of his children.

Jacob was fleeing from his brother Esau, after having deceived his father to receive the blessing. He was alone, at night, with a stone for a pillow. God speaks himself, and does so without first rebuking him: he confirms the promise he had already given to his family. Interpreters see here the beginning of Jacob's personal faith.

For today: God can find you in your moments of fear, loneliness or failure. You do not need to be perfect to speak to him; he is already near and fulfills what he promises.
exp.26:30:
Esau prepares a meal with the game he hunted and brings it to his father Isaac. He asks him to get up and eat, so that Isaac will bless him. "Savoury meat" refers to a prepared dish of food, and "that thy soul may bless me" means that Isaac should bless him wholeheartedly.

Esau is speaking, the elder son. He does not know that Jacob, with Rebekah's help, has already received the blessing by pretending to be him. Esau arrives only minutes late, confident that the blessing of the firstborn still belongs to him.

For today: this passage reminds us that decisions have consequences and that deception leaves wounds. It also invites us to value in time what God gives us, without neglecting it, and to trust that his plans are fulfilled, even when people fail.
exp.24:4:
The explanation says that Abraham left all his possessions to Isaac as the main inheritance. The word "gave" is the same as in modern English. Here "all that he had" refers to his goods, his flocks, and God's promise, not only to his money.

This is the account of the narrator of Genesis, not Abraham speaking. Earlier the text mentions the sons Abraham had with Keturah, and the passage makes clear who would be the heir. Isaac was the son of the promise that God had announced. The other sons received gifts and were sent toward the east, to prevent conflicts over the inheritance.

For today: we can be orderly and clear about what God has entrusted to us, setting defined priorities so that there are no divisions in the family. Let us also remember that the true inheritance is trusting in God's promises.
exp.10:17:
Genesis 11:18 says that Peleg lived thirty years and then had his son Reu. The word "begat" means that he became a father; in the Bible, it sometimes refers to a direct son and other times to a descendant.

The author of Genesis is not a character who speaks, but the narrative that follows the family line of Shem, from Noah to Abram. It is a genealogy, and it connects the story of the tower of Babel with the calling of Abraham. Genesis 10:25 says that in the days of Peleg "was the earth divided," and some relate this to Babel, although this is not certain.

God cares for the generations and for every name. Even as the centuries pass, He continues His plan step by step. Today you can trust that your life, even in its simple and little-noticed moments, is part of what God is doing in your family and across time.
exp.33:3:
Shechem asks his father Hamor to get Dinah for him as a wife. The word "damsel" means a young woman or girl. "Get me this damsel to wife" means "arrange for her to be mine so I can marry her." In those days, fathers often negotiated their children's marriages.

Shechem, the prince of the region, is the one speaking. Just before this, the Bible says he took her by force and dishonored her, meaning he sexually abused her. Then it says he fell in love and spoke tenderly to her. Now he wants to marry her, as though that would make right what he did. Meanwhile, Jacob stays silent, and his sons still know nothing.

For today: later affection or good intentions do not erase harm that has been done. Whoever has hurt another person needs to acknowledge their guilt and seek justice, not simply settle things on their own terms. This story also invites us to defend and listen to those who have been hurt.
exp.17:32:
This verse says that the Lord left as soon as he had finished speaking with Abraham, and that Abraham went back home. Some of the wording is old: "went his way" means "went on his way," "as soon as" means "immediately after" or "when," and "unto his place" means "to the place where he lived."

Abraham had just asked God, again and again, not to destroy the city of Sodom if there were fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, and even ten righteous people in it. God answered patiently each time. Here the conversation ends. The text does not say why Abraham stopped asking; that is left unexplained. It also does not yet say what will happen to the city.

For today: we can pray with confidence and sincerity, even for other people, as Abraham did. And after praying, we learn to rest, leaving the outcome in God's hands, who is just and merciful.
exp.30:20:
This verse tells us that Jacob fled with everything he had. He got up, crossed the river (almost certainly the Euphrates), and set out toward the mountains of Gilead. "Set his face" means he headed resolutely in that direction. "Fled" here means he left secretly.

No character is speaking here; it is the narrator of Genesis. Jacob had spent about twenty years serving Laban, his father-in-law, who had deceived him several times. God had already told him to return to the land of his fathers. He took advantage of the fact that Laban was away shearing sheep and left without telling him. Some see prudence in this, others see a lack of openness.

For today: when God calls you to change, act with determination, but try to do it with honesty and without leaving unnecessary wounds. Obedience does not excuse a silence that causes harm.
exp.17:18:
It says that God knows Abraham and trusts that he will teach his children and his household to keep the way of the Lord. "I know him" means that God chose him and has a close relationship with him. "Judgment" here means acting with righteousness and fairness. In this way, God will be able to fulfill what he promised to Abraham.

The one speaking is the Lord, just before he tells Abraham what he will do about Sodom and Gomorrah. God explains why he does not hide his plans from him: Abraham has an important role in his promise to bless all nations, and he is expected to pass on a life of justice to those who come after him.

For today: faith is passed on through example and daily teaching at home. We can ask ourselves what path we are showing our own family through what we say and do.
exp.13:22:
Abram tells the king of Sodom that he will not keep anything that belongs to the king, not even something as small as a thread or the strap of a sandal. The explanation notes that the sandal strap is the shoe itself. Abram does not want the king to be able to say, "I made Abram rich."

Abram has just rescued Lot and the people of Sodom, along with their possessions, after defeating some invading kings. The king of Sodom offers to let Abram keep the goods. But Abram had already made a vow before God, and he wants his prosperity to be seen as a blessing from God, not as a gift from a king tied to the wickedness of Sodom. Even so, he lets his allies take their share.

For today: before accepting money or favors, ask yourself whether they tie you to someone or something that does not honor God. Trust that God is the one who sustains you, and respect other people's freedom to decide for themselves.
exp.43:24:
Here Judah tells Joseph, without knowing it is Joseph, what their father Jacob said. "Go again, and buy us a little food" is the verse the reader sees in the King James Version. The "food" refers to the grain they needed in Egypt, because there was famine across the whole land.

Judah speaks before the ruler of Egypt, who is Joseph in disguise. He is explaining why they do not want to return without Benjamin. Jacob sent them for food, but earlier they had been warned that without their youngest brother they would not see the ruler's face. Judah tells the story to plead for compassion for their aged father.

For today: when a need forces us to return to a difficult situation, we can do so with humility and sincerity. Judah does not hide the truth or make excuses; he speaks honestly and cares for his family. Let us ask God for courage to face what we fear, lovingly caring for those who depend on us.
exp.10:30:
This verse tells how Terah, the father of Abram, took his son Abram, his grandson Lot (son of Haran, who had already died), and his daughter-in-law Sarai, and set out with them from Ur of the Chaldees. They meant to go to the land of Canaan, but when they came to a place called Haran, they stayed and settled there. "Dwelt" means that they made their home there. A "daughter-in-law" is the wife of one's son.

This is a narrative passage; the author recounts the story of Terah's family. It does not say why they set out, although later in the Bible it is shown that God called Abram. Sarai had no children, and the family had already known loss. Here the way is being prepared for the story of Abram.

For today: sometimes we begin a journey with good intentions and stop halfway. Today you can ask God to help you finish what He has placed in your heart.
exp.1:20:
This verse tells that God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam. While he slept, God took one of his ribs and closed up the flesh in its place. "Rib" can also be understood as "side"; the Hebrew term is interpreted in both ways. "Adam" is Adam, and "the Lord God" is the name of God.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Adam had just named the animals and did not find among them anyone "suitable," that is, fitting for him. God responds to that need by creating the woman. Afterward, Adam receives her with joy.

For today: God sees our real needs and acts with care. We can trust that he provides what we need in his time. We can also value the people God places beside us, as companions on the journey, with respect and gratitude.
exp.23:19:
She hurried, emptied her jar into the trough (the watering basin where the animals drank), and ran back to the well to draw more water. She kept doing this until she had watered all the camels of Abraham's servant. Drawing water for so many animals was a long and tiring job.

Abraham's servant had traveled far to find a wife for Isaac. Before this, he had prayed for a sign: that the young woman who offered him water would also offer water to his camels. Rebekah did exactly that, without knowing anything about that prayer. The servant watched her in silence, waiting to see whether God would give success to his journey.

For today: generosity shows in the details. Rebekah went beyond the minimum and served with eagerness. Today we can help with joy, without anyone asking us to, and God can use those simple acts.
exp.36:31:
The brothers of Joseph send the coat to their father Jacob, stained with the blood of a young goat. They ask him to recognize it. "Coat of many colours" is the special robe that Jacob had given to Joseph. The old spellings of the King James text, such as "colours" and "thy" and "whether," show that this is an older English version of the Bible.

The ones speaking are Joseph's brothers. Out of envy they had sold him, and now they want to hide what they did. They use the coat as false evidence. Notice that they say "thy son," not "our brother," and in this way they distance themselves from him and from all responsibility.

For today: a lie usually needs more lies to hold it up, and it also hurts the people we love. If we have done something wrong, it is better to confess it and seek forgiveness than to hide it. God, who sees all things, can heal even the stories broken by deceit.
exp.33:18:
The explanation says that Shechem, "the young man," did not delay in carrying out what Jacob's sons had asked, which was to be circumcised. "Deferred" means he did not wait or put it off. He did this because he had greatly delighted in Dinah, Jacob's daughter. Also, he was the most honored of all his father's household.

Jacob's sons had set a condition: if the men of the city were circumcised, Dinah could be given in marriage to Shechem. Earlier, Shechem had abused her, and the brothers answered with deceit (Genesis 34:13). The Bible tells this story with pain, without approving what happened. Regarding the brothers' plan, the text does not praise it.

For today: desire and prestige do not justify an action or make it good. Before you act, ask yourself whether what you want truly respects others and God.
exp.15:2:
This verse tells us that Sarai, Abram's wife, took Hagar, her Egyptian servant, and gave her to Abram as his wife. They had been living in the land of Canaan for ten years. "After Abram had dwelt ten years" simply means that a decade had passed since they settled there.

God had promised Abram a descendant, but the years went by and Sarai still had no children. Tired of waiting, she proposed this plan, which was an accepted practice at that time for securing an heir. The text reports it without approving it, and the verses that follow show the pain it caused.

For today: when waiting drags on, it is tempting to solve things with our own means. Before acting out of impatience, it is wise to pray, to trust God, and to remember that his timing does not fail.
exp.19:13:
The explanation says that King Abimelech gave Abraham sheep, cattle, male servants and female servants, and also returned his wife Sarah to him.

Abraham had said that Sarah was his sister, and Abimelech had taken her into his household. God warned him in a dream not to touch her, and now the king corrects the mistake. The gifts show his desire to repair the harm and make peace. Some understand that it was also a way of publicly acknowledging that Abraham was under God's protection.

For today: when we make a mistake or affect others, saying "I'm sorry" is not enough. Acknowledging the wrong and repairing the harm, as far as we can, is a concrete way to live with honesty and humility.
exp.5:19:
This verse tells that God asks Noah to bring into the ark animals of every kind: birds, beasts, and creeping things. They would enter two by two, "after their kind," that is, each kind with its mate. The phrase "to keep them alive" means "so that they would go on living." "Creeping thing" refers to the animals that move along the ground.

God speaks to Noah before the flood. He had already announced judgment on the earth because of the violence of the people, but he also made a covenant with Noah to save him and his family. Caring for the animals shows that God wanted to preserve creation.

For today: God cares even for the details of what he has created. We can imitate him by being responsible with what is entrusted to us: family, work, animals, and nature. And when God asks something of us, we can obey with confidence, as Noah did.
exp.47:18:
Jacob refuses to switch his hands, because he knows what he is doing. He says that Manasseh, the older, will also become a people and will grow, but that Ephraim, the younger, will be greater. "Seed" means descendants, and "a multitude of nations" refers to a great number of nations or peoples.

Jacob, already old and nearly blind, blesses José's two sons. José believes his father has made a mistake, because in that culture the firstborn usually received the principal place. But Jacob acts with conviction. In the Bible, God often chooses the younger, as with Isaac, Jacob, and David. Later, Ephraim became a very important tribe in Israel.

For today: God is not limited by our customs or our expectations. When something does not turn out as we thought, we can trust that he continues to work with wisdom. Let us learn to bless others without envy.
exp.38:3:
This verse tells us that Joseph pleased Potiphar, his Egyptian master. "Found grace in his sight" means that Potiphar liked him and won his favor. For this reason Potiphar made him overseer, that is, the one in charge of managing his house, and put into his hand everything he had.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Joseph had been sold as a slave by his brothers and taken to Egypt. The text explains that Potiphar saw something special: God was with Joseph and made him prosper. The master's trust arises from seeing that fruit, and the verses that follow say that God blessed the whole household because of him.

For today: even in unjust situations, or ones we did not choose, we can work with honesty and faithfulness, trusting that God is present. Our character, more than our circumstances, can be a witness to those around us.
exp.35:28:
This verse begins a list of the leaders of the Horites, a people who lived in the region of Seir. The word "dukes" does not refer to European nobles; it translates a Hebrew word meaning clan chiefs or leaders. Here they are named as Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, and Anah.

The author of the book (tradition attributes it to Moses) keeps a record of families. The Horites lived in Seir before the descendants of Esau, also called Edom, settled there. That is why Genesis 36 notes carefully who belonged to each people. Some scholars think this list shows how the two peoples became mixed over time, though the text does not fully explain this.

For today: God notices people whom we consider unknown. He reminds us that every life and every family matters to him. We can value those who go unnoticed and pray for them by name.
exp.45:6:
This verse says that Jacob brought his whole family into Egypt: his sons, his grandsons, his daughters, and his granddaughters. The word "seed" means descendants, that is, everyone who came from him. "Brought with him" means they went along with him on the journey.

Here the narrator of the book is summarizing Jacob's move. There was famine in the region, and Joseph, Jacob's son, was ruling in Egypt. Before leaving Beersheba, God had spoken to Jacob and encouraged him to go down to Egypt. The text goes on with a list of names, to show that each person in this family counts and that from them the people of Israel would come.

God cares for families and also for each person by name. Today you can pray for your loved ones, one by one, and trust that God walks with them through the hard changes of life.
exp.44:26:
What it says: Jacob's sons repeated to him everything Joseph had told them. When Jacob saw the wagons that Joseph had sent to carry him to Egypt, his spirit lifted again. The word "revived" does not speak of coming back from death, but of regaining strength and hope. "Wagons" were vehicles for transport, like carts.

Context: The brothers return to Canaan with an incredible piece of news: Joseph, whom Jacob had given up for dead, is alive and governing in Egypt. At first Jacob did not believe them, perhaps because of the pain of so many years and because his sons had hidden the truth from him. Words alone were not enough; the wagons were a concrete sign that convinced him. Soon after, Jacob decides to go and see his son.

For today: When a long sadness makes us doubt good news, God can give us signs that awaken hope again. Let us ask him for eyes to recognize them and courage to set out on the journey.
exp.20:15:
Hagar moves away from her son Ishmael, roughly as far as an arrow shot from a bow would travel. She sits down facing him because she thinks: "Let me not see the death of the child." Then she weeps aloud. The King James wording "she went" and "sat her down" simply mean she went off and sat down, and "lift up her voice" means she wept out loud.

The narrator describes what happens in the desert of Beersheba. Abraham had sent Hagar and her son away with bread and water, and now the water has run out. Hagar, in despair, believes her son is going to die of thirst and cannot bear to watch him.

When we feel that we can no longer do anything, God is not far away. What follows in the text shows that He hears the weeping and responds. We can bring Him our pain honestly, without pretending to be strong, and trust that He listens.
exp.45:21:
This verse closes the list of the descendants of Rachel, Jacob's beloved wife. It says that, in total, there were fourteen "souls," a word that here means "persons." The list includes Joseph, his two sons born in Egypt (Manasseh and Ephraim), and Benjamin with his sons. The number fourteen is reached by adding up the names in that list, though scholars debate exactly how some of them are counted.

The narrator of the book explains who entered Egypt with Jacob. It is a family record that shows how God's promise to Abraham, to make a great nation, was moving forward. The family was about to live in Egypt, and this list recorded their origin.

For today: God looks at each person, with a name and a place in his story. Today you can remember that your life and your family are not a matter of chance, and pray for each one by name.
exp.39:10:
Here the cupbearer describes part of his dream: he had the cup of the king of Egypt in his hand, he took the grapes from the vine, pressed them into the cup, and gave the cup into Pharaoh's hand. "Cup" is the king's drinking vessel, and the cupbearer was the one who served him his drink. "Pressed" means squeezing the fruit to get the juice out.

The speaker is the chief cupbearer of Pharaoh, imprisoned together with Joseph. The two prisoners had both had dreams that troubled them, and Joseph told them that God is the one who gives the interpretation. At this point the cupbearer relates his dream, and Joseph will explain that it means he will return to his post in three days.

For today: Joseph did not consider himself important for understanding the dream, but gave God the credit. When you have the opportunity to help others with what you know, do it with humility, and recognize God as the source of every good gift.
exp.35:11:
Timna is said to have been a concubine of Eliphaz, son of Esau, and she bore him a son named Amalek. "Concubine" meant a secondary wife, with fewer legal rights than the principal wife. The text concludes by clarifying that all these descendants belong to the household of Adah, Esau's wife.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator of Genesis, who records the genealogy of Esau, also called Edom. The author wants to show that God fulfilled his promise to make Esau into a nation. Amalek is the ancestor of the Amalekites, who would later become enemies of Israel. Some scholars debate exactly how they relate to other peoples of the region.

For today: God pays attention to families and to their stories, even imperfect ones. Our decisions leave marks on the generations that follow, so it is wise to live with wisdom and faith.
exp.23:53:
The explanation says that Abraham's servant and the men who were with him ate, drank, and spent the night there. In the morning, the servant asked to be allowed to return to his master. The phrase "send me away" in the King James wording means "let me go" or "dismiss me," and "my master" refers to Abraham.

Here speaks Abraham's servant, who had traveled far to find a wife for Isaac. He had already prayed, had seen God's answer in Rebekah, and had worshiped the LORD. Her family accepted the proposal, and he celebrated with them. But he did not want to stay any longer, because his mission was not yet finished: he still had to return with the answer.

For today: when God opens a door for us, it is good to give thanks and enjoy the moment, but without losing our direction. Let us faithfully finish what we have been entrusted with, and not let delays, however pleasant, distract us.
exp.48:19:
Here the text says that the land and labor of Asher will yield abundant and rich food. "Fat" means substantial and of good quality, not lean or scarce. "Royal dainties" are fine delicacies, fit for a king. It is a promise of generous provision.

Jacob, already elderly and near death, gathers his twelve sons and speaks about the future of each one and of their descendants. It is a blessing with a prophetic character. Many understand that Asher, whose territory lay in a fertile area of northern Canaan, near the coast, would see this word fulfilled. The details of that fulfillment are interpreted in several ways.

God knows how to care for his own with abundance. We can receive with gratitude what he gives us and use it to bless others, sharing the table, time, and resources with generosity.
exp.12:4:
This verse says that Lot, the nephew who traveled with Abram, also had many possessions. "Flocks and herds" were his livestock, and "tents" were the portable dwellings where he, his family, and his servants lived. The word "also" means "too" or "as well."

No one speaks here; it is the narrator of Genesis who explains the situation. Abram had just returned to the altar at Bethel and called on the Lord. Then the text shows that Lot, who was traveling with him, had also prospered. This prepares the problem that follows: the land could not support both of them, and their herdsmen began to quarrel.

For today: abundance can bring blessing, but also tension. If we have more, it is wise to return to God, as Abram did, and to care for relationships before possessions, speaking with humility and seeking peace.
exp.14:3:
God answers Abram right away. Because the verse is rendered in modern English, there is no need to explain older wording here. "Bowels" refers to the body itself, meaning a biological son of Abram. God says that Eliezer, the servant of the house, will not be the heir. His heir will be a son of his own.

Abram was complaining because he had no children. He thought that his steward, Eliezer of Damascus, would receive all that was his. This was a possible custom in those times, though the legal details are debated. God speaks to calm his complaint and promises him a son. Right away he takes him outside to look at the stars, and Abram believes.

For today: when you have doubts or feel that you are waiting for something, do not hide them. Abram spoke with God honestly, and God answered him with patience. Bring your honest questions to God, and then take a step of trust in what He has promised.
exp.30:25:
Laban accuses Jacob of leaving without telling him. He says that Jacob "stole away unawares" from him, that is, that he slipped away secretly, and that he carried off his daughters as if they were captives taken with the sword, that is, as if they had been seized by force. The phrase "stolen away unawares" means slipped off without his knowledge.

The speaker is Laban, Jacob's father-in-law. Jacob had fled in secret with his wives, his children, and his flocks after twenty years of work. Laban caught up with him, but God had warned him in a dream not to treat him harshly. His words sound wounded, though they also exaggerate: Rachel and Leah had left of their own will. Moreover, we already know that Laban had deceived Jacob several times.

Today, when we feel hurt, it is good to speak honestly and without exaggeration. And if there is tension in the family, it is better to talk things through in time than to flee in silence or accuse harshly.
exp.13:23:
Abram says he will take nothing from the spoils, with one exception: what the young men who helped him have already eaten. The "young men" are the servants or soldiers who went with him. He also asks that his allies, Aner, Eshcol, and Mamre, receive the portion that belongs to them.

Abram speaks with the king of Sodom after rescuing his nephew Lot and recovering the goods of the city. He had already sworn before God that he would not keep anything, so that no one could say the king of Sodom made him rich. Even so, he does not require his allies to live by his personal promise. They were free to take their share.

We can be firm in our convictions without imposing them on others. And it is good to take care that our witness shows that our trust is in God, not in the advantages others might offer us.
exp.27:9:
This verse tells that Jacob left Beersheba, in the south of Canaan, and set out on the road toward Haran, a distant city in the north. The comment about the old spelling does not apply to the wording you see, so it has been omitted. It is a transitional verse: Jacob begins a long journey.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. Jacob leaves because his brother Esau was very angry with him, and also because Isaac sent him to find a wife among the family of his mother Rebekah, and not among the Canaanite women. Soon after, on this same road, Jacob will have the dream of the ladder.

For today: sometimes we are called to leave what is familiar, because of conflict or difficult decisions, without having everything clear. Jacob did not know everything that lay ahead, but God met him on the way. Take the next step in faith, and remember that God accompanies you also on uncertain journeys.
exp.27:6:
This verse says that Esau realized that Jacob had obeyed his parents, Isaac and Rebekah, and had gone to Padan-aram. The words "á" and "fué" are old spellings of "a" and "fue." Padan-aram was a region in northern Mesopotamia, where Rebekah's family lived.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He shows us what Esau observes: Isaac had blessed Jacob and had commanded him not to marry a Canaanite woman. Jacob left with his father's blessing and with clear obedience. Afterward, Esau tries to please his father by marrying a daughter of Ishmael, although he already had other wives. The Bible does not say here what Esau felt in his heart.

For today: obedience to those whom God has placed as guides in our lives, such as parents or wise leaders, can open paths of blessing. And when we recognize a mistake, it is good to correct it with sincerity, not merely with outward gestures.
exp.11:17:
Pharaoh calls Abram and rebukes him with two questions: "What have you done to me?" and "Why didn't you tell me she was your wife?" The words "tell" and "said" are the ones that matter here: the KJV's "tell" carries the sense of "let me know" or "say clearly," which is what Pharaoh is complaining about.

The one speaking is the king of Egypt. Abram had said that Sarai was his sister, out of fear that he would be killed for her sake. Pharaoh took her into his house, and God sent plagues upon him. Once he discovers the truth, he becomes angry and confronts Abram. It is striking that a pagan king is the one who rebukes God's servant, and the text does not hide Abram's failure.

A half-truth can hurt others, even when we tell it out of fear. Today we can trust that God takes care of us, and for that reason it is wise to speak honestly, even when it frightens us.
exp.29:21:
The explanation says that God "remembered" Rachel, meaning he turned his attention toward her to act on her behalf. It also says that he "heard" her, that is, he listened to her cry. "Opened her womb" means that he allowed her to become pregnant. The word "womb" is another way of saying belly or uterus.

The one who narrates is the author of Genesis. Rachel, the beloved wife of Jacob, had gone for years without children, while her sister Leah and the servants already had several. In that culture, not having children caused great sadness and shame. The following verse shows that she saw this birth as the end of her disgrace. The text does not detail how she prayed.

For today: when your wait is long, keep coming to God with sincerity. "Remembered" does not mean that God had forgotten before, but that he acts in his own time. Trust that he hears you, even when his answer is not the one you were hoping for.
exp.25:30:
It says that at dawn Isaac and Abimelech swore an oath to each other that they would not harm one another. Then Isaac sent them away, and they went off in peace. "Betimes in the morning" means very early in the morning, and "sent them away" means he let them go with a good attitude.

Abimelech, the Philistine king of Gerar, came with his adviser and his army commander to make a covenant with Isaac. Earlier they had driven him out of their land, but now they recognized that God was blessing him. Instead of holding a grudge, Isaac offered them a feast and sealed the peace with them. That same day his servants found water, and the place was called Beersheba.

When someone has treated you badly, pursue peace rather than revenge, without giving up wisdom. Isaac forgave, and God gave him provision. Perhaps today you can take a first step toward reconciliation.
exp.0:20:
God created the great sea creatures, all the living things that move in the waters, and all the winged birds, each one "after its kind" or "after its species," that is, in their various classes. "Created" is the word used here, and "whales" can also be rendered as great sea monsters. At the end, God looks at what He has made and declares that it was good.

The narrator of Genesis tells what God did on the fifth day. God had commanded that the waters and the sky be filled with life, and here that word is fulfilled. Right away God blesses them so that they may multiply. Here we see a God who gives life with order and purpose.

For today: if God calls His creation good, we can care for it with respect and gratitude, without despising it or using it selfishly. Today you can thank God for something living that you see.
exp.5:2:
God says that his Spirit will not keep striving or contending with human beings forever, because man is "flesh," that is, frail and mortal. For that reason he sets a limit: their days will be a hundred and twenty years. The word "strive" in the King James Version means to contend with or keep pressing against someone, and "the Lord" is the name rendered in the Hebrew as Jehovah, meaning God's name.

God speaks in the middle of a land that was filling up with wickedness. Interpreters explain the "hundred and twenty years" in different ways: as a period of time before the flood, or as the limit of human life. The text does not fully clarify this. In either case, God gives time before he acts.

Today, let us not take God's patience lightly. If you sense that he is calling you to change something, respond with humility today, without putting it off for later.
exp.26:33:
Esau hears the words of his father and understands that the blessing has already been given to another. His reaction is a loud cry, full of pain. He pleads: "Bless me, even me also, O my father." The King James wording "exceeding bitter cry" conveys an intense weeping, and the phrase "great and exceeding bitter" shows how deep his grief was.

Isaac, already old, had wanted to bless Esau, his firstborn. But Jacob, following the plan of his mother Rebekah, pretended to be his brother and received the blessing. Esau arrives late and discovers what happened. His pain is real, although the Bible also shows that earlier he had placed little value on his birthright (Genesis 25:29-34).

Today this verse reminds us that hasty decisions can bring painful consequences. It also invites us to value what God gives us and not to act with deceit, because deceit wounds families.
exp.27:4:
The explanation says that Isaac sent Jacob away to Padan-aram, a region north of Canaan. There lived Laban, the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau. The word "Syrian" indicates that Bethuel and his family belonged to that people. "Seed" means descendants, and "sent away" and "went" are older forms of expression.

It is the narrator who tells this, right after Isaac blessed Jacob. Isaac forbade him to marry Canaanite women and told him to seek a wife among the relatives of his mother. According to the account, Rebekah also wanted to keep him away from the anger of Esau, who was angry over the blessing received. The blessing of Abraham thus passes to Jacob.

God often guides our steps even in difficult or confusing situations. When you have to make an important decision, seek counsel from people of faith and look for God's direction, trusting that He keeps His promises.
exp.48:27:
All these are the twelve tribes of Israel, and this is what their father said to them when he blessed them; each one he blessed with the blessing that belonged to him.

Jacob, now old and near death, gathers his sons to tell them what would come upon them. Some of his words are blessings, others are corrections, as the ones addressed to Reuben, Simeon, and Levi. Here the text calls all of it "blessing," and scholars understand this in several ways. This is the origin of the tribes of Israel.

God deals with each person personally, not in a series. Let us ask God to speak to us according to our lives, and let us learn to bless our families with sincere words that encourage and also guide with love.
exp.36:14:
This verse tells us that Joseph was wandering lost in the field, near Shechem, looking for his brothers. A man found him and asked him, "What seekest thou?" "Found him" means he came upon him, and "wandering" means he was going about aimlessly, not knowing where to go.

Jacob, also called Israel, had sent Joseph to see how his brothers and the flocks were doing. The one speaking here is an unknown man, and the Bible does not say who he was. His simple question helps Joseph continue on his way toward Dothan. Some see here the hand of God guiding events, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: when you feel lost, put into words what you are looking for and ask for guidance. God can use ordinary people to point you to the next step.
exp.8:0:
God blesses Noah and his sons after the flood. He commands them: "Be fruitful, and multiply, and replenish the earth." That is, they should have children, let their family grow, and fill the earth with people. The word "replenish" is an old word meaning "fill." The blessing comes first, and then the command follows.

God himself is speaking. Noah has just come out of the ark, and the earth is empty of people, because the flood destroyed everything. God gives humanity a new beginning and repeats the command he gave to Adam and Eve at creation. The verses that follow explain the place of human beings among the animals and what God permits them to eat.

Today we can remember that life is a gift from God and a blessing. We can care for our families, for children, and for creation with gratitude and responsibility, trusting that God knows how to begin again.
exp.24:5:
The explanation says that Abraham, before he died, gave gifts to the sons he had with his concubines (Hagar and Keturah). Then he sent them away from his son Isaac, toward the east. "Gifts" are presents, and "concubines" were secondary wives. "While he yet lived" means that he did this while he was still alive.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. He has just said that Abraham left everything to Isaac, the son of the promise. With this act, Abraham arranges his inheritance: he protects Isaac's line without leaving the other sons without provision. It is not stated exactly where "the east country" was; only the direction is given.

For today: if you have family responsibilities, arrange things in good time and with fairness. You can care for the priority God has given you without neglecting others, so as to avoid future conflicts.
exp.43:17:
Judah comes close to Joseph, whom he does not yet recognize as his brother, and asks permission to speak respectfully. He begs that Joseph not be angry with him, because he recognizes that Joseph has as much power as Pharaoh. "Let thy servant, I pray thee, speak a word" means "I ask you to let me speak", and "let not thine anger burn" means "do not be furious".

The brothers are in Egypt. Joseph had his silver cup placed in Benjamin's sack, and now he wants to keep him as a slave. Judah speaks because he made a promise to his father Jacob to look after the boy. This is the beginning of a long speech in which Judah offers to stay in Benjamin's place.

For today: when we have to face a serious problem, we can speak with humility, without arrogance or violence, and take responsibility for our actions. Sometimes loving someone truly means being willing to sacrifice ourselves for others.
exp.26:39:
He says that Esau will live by the sword, that is, by war or violence, and that he will serve his brother Jacob. But a time will come when Esau will rebel and shake off Jacob's rule. "Neck" refers to the back of the neck or the throat, and "yoke" is the heavy wooden frame placed on working animals. In this way the verse speaks of a heavy submission that will eventually be broken.

It is Isaac, the father, now old, who speaks. Jacob had received the principal blessing, though by deception, and Esau weeps, asking for something. This answer is more a harsh prediction than a full blessing. Many relate it to Esau's descendants, the Edomites, and their relationship with Israel, although the historical details are interpreted in various ways.

For today: resentment can come to dominate the heart, as happened with Esau. When something hurts us, let us ask God for help to forgive and not to seek revenge.
exp.9:2:
This verse names the three sons of Gomer, who was a son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah: Ashkenaz, Riphath, and Togarmah. It is part of a list of families.

It is a narrative text, and the narrator, traditionally attributed to Moses, explains how humanity spread out after the flood. This list, sometimes called the "Table of Nations," presents Japheth as the ancestor of peoples to the north and west. Scholars do not fully agree on locating each people precisely, so it is wise to be cautious with identifications.

For today: God knows the names and stories of families, even though to us they may seem like dull lists. If He cares for every generation, He also knows you and values you. Give thanks for your family and pray for it.
exp.7:8:
The explanation says the dove found no dry place to land. "Setting the sole of her foot" means resting her feet, that is, resting on solid ground. Because the water still covered the whole earth, the dove returned to the ark. Noah reached out his hand, took her, and drew her in to himself. The phrase "drew her in" means that he brought her into the ark.

This is part of the account of the flood. There is no dialogue here; the narrator tells what Noah does. After sending out the raven, Noah releases a dove to find out whether dry ground was yet available to live on. A little later, the dove returns with an olive leaf.

For today: sometimes we look for signs that things are getting better and they have not yet arrived. Noah did not despair or force his way out; he received the dove and kept waiting. We can trust God and take the next step with patience, caring for those who are near us.
exp.23:9:
The explanation says that Abraham's servant took ten camels from his master and set out on the journey. He could carry many gifts and goods belonging to his lord. The word "servant" means a trusted servant, and the phrase "all the goods of his master were in his hand" means that he had at hand everything he needed. He arrived in Mesopotamia, at the city of Nahor, where relatives of Abraham lived.

Here the narrator speaks. Abraham had already made his servant swear that he would seek a wife for Isaac among his own family, and not among the Canaanites. The text does not give the servant's name; some think it is Eliezer (mentioned in Genesis 15:2), but this is not certain. The ten camels show the seriousness and importance of the mission.

For today: when you receive an important task, prepare well and carry it out faithfully, but also pray, as the servant does right away. Effort and trust in God go together.
exp.19:15:
Here Abimelech speaks to Sarah. He tells her that he has given a thousand pieces of silver to "thy brother," that is, to Abraham, whom Sarah had presented as her brother. The phrase "a covering of the eyes" is old and is understood in several ways: it may be a compensation that clears her name before everyone, or a public sign that she was not dishonored. "Thus she was reproved" may mean that she was vindicated or set right before the others.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, had taken Sarah believing she was unmarried, because Abraham had said she was his sister. God warned him in a dream, and he returned her. Now he repairs the harm with gifts and with this public gesture.

For today: when we cause harm, even unintentionally, it is wise to acknowledge it and repair it with action. Honesty also prevents bigger problems.
exp.40:48:
The explanation says that Joseph stored so much grain during the years of plenty that it was like the sand of the sea. There was so much that they stopped measuring it, because it could no longer be counted. The King James wording "corn" here means grain, and "without number" means it could not be counted. "Gathered" means he collected and stored it. "Plenty" means abundance, and "food" is the provisions.

Here the speaker is not a character but the narrator of the book. He tells how Joseph carried out the plan he proposed to Pharaoh after interpreting his dreams: to store food in the seven good years against the seven years of famine that God had announced. Joseph stored the grain in every city, close to the fields it came from.

For today: when good times come, do not spend it all without thinking. Being prudent, saving, and planning wisely is a way of caring for your family and of trusting that God also works through our responsibility.
exp.10:19:
The explanation says that Reu lived thirty-two years and then had a son named Serug. The word "begat" means that he became a father. The text follows the same pattern as the other generations: the age at which the son was born, and then the years he lived afterward.

This is part of the genealogy of Shem in the Genesis account. No character is speaking; it is the narrator who lists the names to connect the story of Noah with the story of Abraham. Scholars debate whether each name indicates a direct son or sometimes a descendant, and whether the numbers should be read literally or symbolically. What is clear is that God continues to guide the story from generation to generation.

For today: God works in the simple and the hidden. Reu barely appears in the Bible, and yet he had his place in God's plan. Your daily faithfulness, even when no one notices it, also counts.
exp.12:13:
God tells Abram to lift up his eyes and look in every direction: the word "northward" means the north, "southward" is the south, and "eastward" and "westward" name the east and the west. The word "seed" means descendants.

Abram and his nephew Lot had just gone their separate ways. Lot chose the well-watered plain and began moving toward Sodom, a city of wicked people. Abram, for his part, had allowed Lot to choose first. Right after that separation, the Lord renews his promise: the land he sees will be for him and his descendants. Some believe God meant to comfort him after the parting; the text does not state this exactly.

When we let something go for the sake of peace, we can trust that God takes care of us. If today you are the one who has to give way in a situation, pray and look ahead with faith: God can give you more than you imagine.
exp.43:8:
Joseph's brothers say that if the cup is found with any one of them, that man should die, and the rest of them will become slaves. "Servants" here means slaves or attendants, and "lord" refers to Joseph, although they do not yet know who he is.

The brothers of Joseph are in Egypt. A steward accuses them of stealing Joseph's cup, which Joseph himself had secretly placed in Benjamin's sack to test them. Confident of their innocence, they make a very bold promise. They do not know that the cup is in Benjamin's sack.

For today: speaking with too much confidence can bring us trouble. Before we promise something great or judge others harshly, it is wise to think carefully, since we do not always know the whole truth of what is happening.
exp.3:18:
