This verse tells us that Lamech, a descendant of Cain in the fifth generation after him, took two wives: Adah and Zillah. In the older text, "took unto him" means that he himself chose them as his wives. The KJV's "took unto him" carries that same sense of a man taking wives for himself.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator of Genesis following the family line of Cain. This is the first time the Bible mentions a man with two wives. The text does not say whether God approved of it, but it also does not present it as the original plan, which was "one flesh" (Genesis 2:24). Afterward his children appear, with their inventions and trades, and also the violence of Lamech.

For today: advances and achievements do not guarantee a faithful heart. We can ask ourselves whether our decisions, especially within the family, follow God's design or only our own desires.
exp.32:14:
Esau offers Jacob to leave some of his men with him to accompany and help him on the way. Jacob answers, "What needeth it?", that is, there is no need. And he adds that the only thing he wants is to "find grace" (to be well received and favored) in the sight of Esau, whom he calls "my lord."

Jacob and Esau meet again after years of enmity, since Jacob had obtained their father's blessing by deceit and fled, fearing his brother's anger. Now Esau receives him in peace. Jacob turns down the escort, perhaps out of humility, or out of caution and a desire to keep his distance. The text does not make this clear, and scholars interpret it in different ways. Then each goes on his own way.

For today: when a relationship is reconciled, value the grace received and be humble, but act with wisdom and sincerity. Reconciling does not always mean living together again, but it does mean living in peace.
exp.10:14:
This verse says that Shelah lived 403 years after he became the father of Eber, and that during that time he had more sons and daughters. "Begat" means he became a father. The names "Salah" and "Eber" are also written Shelah and Heber.

We are in the genealogy of Shem, which connects the flood with Abraham. No character is speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis keeping an orderly record of the generations. The very long lifespans are understood in different ways: some take them literally, others as a figure of speech of the time. The Bible does not clarify this here.

For today: God cares for families and for generations, even when their names seem simple to us. Your daily life, your home, and what you pass on to others also matter to Him and form part of His story.
exp.1:12:
The explanation says that the second river that flowed out of Eden was called Gihon, and that it encircled the whole land of "Ethiopia." In Hebrew the word is "Cush," and the Reina-Valera translated it as Ethiopia. Today it is not known with certainty where that region was, and scholars have located it in different ways. "Compasseth" means that it ran around it.

The narrator of Genesis, traditionally associated with Moses, describes the garden of Eden as a real place, with a river that divides into four branches. He names rivers and regions so that the reader understands that God prepared a fertile and rich land for human beings, just before placing him there to work.

For today: God cares about the details of what he gives us. Give thanks for the concrete provisions of your life, such as water, food and work, and receive them as gifts from God that you should care for responsibly.
exp.30:49:
It says that if Jacob mistreats Laban's daughters, that is, Leah and Rachel, or if he takes other wives besides them, then even though no human witness is nearby, God sees everything. "Afflict" means to mistreat or make suffer. "Beside" means "apart from" or "in addition to."

Laban, Jacob's father-in-law, is the one speaking. After a long period of tension between the two men, they make a covenant and raise a heap of stones as a sign. Laban is worried about his daughters, because Jacob is taking them far away. He cannot watch over them, so he calls on God as witness and guarantor of the promise.

For today: act with integrity even when no one sees you. Treat with respect and faithfulness those whom God has placed under your care, because your promises are heard not only by people, but by God as well.
exp.41:0:
This verse tells us that Jacob realized there was food in Egypt. Then he asked his sons, "Why do you keep looking at one another?" That is, he saw them standing there, doing nothing.

Jacob, now an old man, speaks to his sons. There is a severe famine in the land of Canaan, and the family is in danger of going without. Jacob does not stay silent: he tells them to go down to Egypt to buy grain. Later on, the Bible shows that God was at work in this situation.

For today: when we face a problem, we sometimes freeze, held back by fear or by not knowing what to do. This passage encourages us to pray, seek help, and take a concrete step, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.31:7:
Jacob divides all his people into two groups, along with his sheep, cattle, and camels. He thinks that if Esau attacks one group and destroys it, the other group will be able to escape. In the King James wording, "company" means a group or camp, and "smite" means to attack or strike.

Jacob speaks after his messengers tell him that Esau is coming with four hundred men. Years earlier, Jacob had deceived Esau and fled from him. Now he is returning to his land and fears for his life. We do not know for certain what Esau intends; the text only shows Jacob's fear.

It is wise to make careful plans when facing danger. But Jacob does not stop at his strategy: right after, he prays and remembers God's promises. We can think carefully and act responsibly, but also bring our fear before God and trust in his faithfulness.
exp.10:11:
Arphaxad was thirty-five years old when his son Salah was born. The phrase "begat" means that he became the father of Salah. In this older edition the names are spelled "Arphaxad" and "Salah," which are commonly written today as Arfaxad and Selah or Sala. The verse is simple: it gives an age and names the son who continues the family line.

There is no speaking character here; it is the narrator, following the list of "the generations of Shem." It is a genealogical record that connects Noah with Abraham after the flood. The numbers of years are very long, and some scholars take them literally, while others think they have a symbolic or literary purpose. The text does not make this clear.

For today: God cares for the generations and works in the small and quiet things. Your everyday life, though it may seem ordinary, can be part of something greater. Be faithful today and trust God.
exp.40:17:
Genesis 41:18 says that Pharaoh saw in his dream seven cows coming up out of the river Nile. They were fat, "fatfleshed," that is, well fed, and they were "well favoured," meaning they looked beautiful. They were "feeding" (grazing) in the meadow by the river. The word "favoured" refers to how they looked.

Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, is speaking. He is telling his dream to Joseph, who was brought out of prison to interpret it. Earlier, Joseph had made clear that he did not have the power to interpret, but that God would give the answer. No Egyptian wise man had been able to explain the dream, and Pharaoh was troubled.

For today: Joseph did not take the credit for himself, even though he stood before the most powerful man of his time. When someone asks you for advice or recognizes your talent, learn to say with humility that every gift comes from God, and to seek his direction first.
exp.47:5:
It says that the children José has after Ephraim and Manasseh will be considered children of Joseph. They will not form separate tribes. They will be counted within the tribes of their older brothers, and there they will receive their inheritance. "Begotten" means to have had as children; "issue" means descendants; "inheritances" are the lands received as an inheritance.

Jacob speaks, now old, ill and near death, in Egypt. He has just remembered the promise God made to him, and he adopts Joseph's two sons as his own, just as he did Reuben and Simeon. In this way Joseph receives the portion of the firstborn. The Bible does not say whether Joseph had more children, so we do not know more.

For today: God knows how to make room in his family for those who arrive by another way. We can imitate him by welcoming generously those who come into our family, church or community, without making them feel they are of a second category.
exp.20:29:
Abraham answers Abimelech that he should accept seven ewe lambs from his hand. That gift would serve as proof or a sign that Abraham was the one who dug the well. "Witness" means proof or a lasting confirmation, and "ewe lambs" are young female sheep.

Abraham is speaking, having just complained to Abimelech about a well that Abimelech's servants had seized by force. Abimelech, a Philistine king, wanted a covenant of peace with him. By accepting the lambs, Abimelech publicly acknowledged that the well belonged to Abraham. That is why the place was called Beersheba, which can be understood as "well of the oath" or "well of the seven," and the text mentions both ideas.

For today: clear arrangements prevent future disputes. If there is a disagreement, try to resolve it honestly, openly and peacefully, leaving agreements that both sides recognize.
exp.20:23:
Abraham answers with few words: "I will swear." That is, he agrees to make a solemn oath before God. He commits himself not to deceive or betray Abimelech, nor his sons and grandsons, and to treat them with the same kindness he received from them.

Abimelech, king of Gerar, and Phicol, commander of his army, saw that God was blessing Abraham. So they want a peace covenant with him, since Abraham was living as a foreigner in that land. Abraham agrees, but then raises a problem: Abimelech's servants had seized a well. In this way he seeks peace without keeping silent about what is wrong.

For today: you can be a person of your word and, at the same time, speak plainly when something affects you. True peace takes care of promises and also faces problems with respect and honesty.
exp.43:27:
The explanation says that one of Rachel's two sons "went out" from Jacob's household, and that Jacob was certain a wild animal had "torn him in pieces," that is, torn him to pieces. From then on, Jacob never saw him again.

Judah is speaking to Joseph, whom he has not recognized as his brother. He is repeating what Jacob said when they asked him to bring Benjamin to Egypt. Judah wants Joseph to understand how much pain the loss of Benjamin would cause, and for that reason he offers to stay as a slave in his place.

For today: when you come to know another person's pain, do not minimize it. Listening with compassion, and even carrying part of their burden, can open the way to reconciliation and healing.
exp.36:8:
He tells of a second dream that Joseph had and that he related to his brothers. In the dream, the sun, the moon and eleven stars bowed down before him. The word "contó" (here rendered in the old spelling) means "told," and the phrase about bowing down means they prostrated themselves before him as a sign of honor.

Joseph, the young son of Jacob, speaks to his brothers, who already hated him because of their father's favoritism and because of the earlier dream of the sheaves. Jacob understands that the sun and the moon could represent his parents, and the stars his sons. The brothers feel envy, but Jacob keeps the matter in his mind. The Bible does not say that Joseph spoke with bad intent; it only shows that his words fed the conflict.

For today: even when God shows us something valuable, it is wise to speak with humility and prudence, thinking about how others will receive it.
exp.46:0:
Here the text says that Joseph went to inform Pharaoh that his family had already arrived. His father Jacob, his brothers, their sheep, their cattle, and all their possessions had come from the land of Canaan, and now they were in the land of Goshen. The word "told" in the King James wording means "reported" or "informed."

Joseph is the one speaking in this moment, and he speaks as the governor of Egypt. There had been a great famine, and his family had come by Pharaoh's invitation. Joseph reports this respectfully, because Egypt was not his native land. Goshen was a fertile region, suitable for raising livestock. The following verses show that Joseph presented his brothers so that they would live there as shepherds.

For today: Joseph cared for his family with order and respect, without taking advantage of his position. We can help those we love by acting with honesty, humility, and good communication, without running over anyone.
exp.40:13:
Pharaoh sent for Joseph, who was in prison. They brought him out of the dungeon in great haste. Before he appeared before the king, they shaved him and changed his clothes. "They changed his clothing" means they put other clothes on him. "They brought him hastily" means they rushed him.

The chief cupbearer remembered Joseph after two years and spoke to Pharaoh about him. Pharaoh was troubled by some dreams that no one could interpret. In Egypt, shaving and wearing clean clothes was expected of anyone appearing before the king. The account comes from the narrator of Genesis, and it shows that Joseph's change of circumstances was sudden.

God can change a situation from one moment to the next, even when everything seems to be at a standstill. Joseph waited a long time, but he was not forgotten by God. Today we too can remain faithful in waiting and trust that God works in his own time.
exp.16:26:
It says that all the men of Abraham's household were circumcised along with him. This included the servants born in his house and those he had bought with money from foreigners. "Men" refers to the males, and "circumcised" means the foreskin was cut away, as a sign.

God had commanded Abraham this sign as a symbol of the covenant with him and his descendants (Genesis 17:10-14). The narrator tells how Abraham obeyed that very same day, without waiting. It is striking that the covenant reached also the servants and foreigners in his house, not only his immediate family.

For today: obedience to God is not put off for later. Abraham acted at once and with everyone under his care. If you know what God is asking of you, take a concrete step today, and make sure your home also walks in faith.
exp.47:8:
This verse tells how Joseph answers his father Jacob (also called Israel) that the two young men he sees are his sons, a gift from God in Egypt. Jacob asks that they be brought near to him ("bring them, I pray thee") so that he may bless them.

Jacob is very old and nearly blind. Shortly before, he remembered Rachel, his beloved wife, who died along the way. Joseph, with his sons Manasseh and Ephraim, visits him. Jacob is about to give them a blessing that will include them among the tribes of Israel.

For today: Joseph does not say "I had them," but "God has given them to me." We can learn to see our family, children, and loved ones as gifts from God, and to ask his blessing upon them. We can also draw near to the elders of the family to receive their prayers and counsel.
exp.23:56:
The family of Rebekah decides to ask her herself whether she wants to go. "Damsel" is an old word for a young woman or girl. "We will call" would be "let us call her," and "enquire at her mouth" means "let us put the question to her."

Abraham's servant had come to seek a wife for Isaac. After the family agreed, the servant asked to leave soon, because he saw the hand of God in his journey. Her brother Laban and her mother wanted her to wait ten days. To settle the disagreement, they decide to hear from Rebekah. She answers, "Yes, I will go." The text does not explain everything they were thinking, so it is best not to claim more than it says.

For today: in important decisions, really listening to the person involved is an act of respect. We can also seek the family's counsel without forgetting that each person must answer freely before God.
exp.8:4:
God says he will require an accounting for blood, that is, for human life that is taken. "Require" here means to call to account. This applies to every animal that kills a person, and also to a human being who kills another. He says "his brother" because all men belong to one human family.

God speaks to Noah and his sons after the flood. He gives them a new beginning and permits eating meat, but with limits: life, represented by the blood, belongs to Him. The following verse gives the reason: man was made in the image of God. Some scholars debate how to apply this passage to human justice, and Christians interpret it in different ways.

For today: value every human life as sacred, including the life of someone who thinks differently from you. Guard your words, your anger, and your actions, remembering that every person bears the image of God.
exp.25:32:
Here the text says that Isaac called the well his servants had just dug "Shebah." That is why the city is called Beer-sheba "unto this day," meaning until the time the account was written. "Called it" means "named it." "Shebah" sounds like the Hebrew word for "oath" and also like the word for "seven," so the name recalls the covenant. "Beer" means "well."

The narrator tells that Isaac made peace with Abimelech, king of Gerar, after tensions over the wells. They made an oath and parted in peace. That same day the news of the water arrived. Something similar happened with Abraham in that place, and the texts tell it differently, but the name remained tied to the oath.

For today: when you seek peace with others, even after conflict, God can give you rest and provision. Name his blessings and remember them with gratitude.
exp.30:35:
Jacob becomes angry and confronts Laban. He asks what his fault or sin is, that Laban has pursued him with such fury. The word "trespass" here means a serious offense or wrong. "Chode" means that he argued with him or rebuked him forcefully. "Hotly pursued" refers to the intensity and determination with which Laban chased him.

Jacob speaks after Laban has searched the whole camp for his household gods and found nothing. Jacob did not know that Rachel had taken them. That is why he feels accused without cause. After twenty years of hard work, he defends his honesty and asks that the matter be judged in front of witnesses.

For today: when someone accuses us, we can ask that the facts be examined calmly and with witnesses. But it is wise to do so without letting anger take control, and to live in such a way that our conduct can stand up to any examination.
exp.29:18:
This verse tells us that Leah became pregnant once more and had her sixth son with Jacob. The old words "bare" and "conceived" are archaic forms: "bare" means "gave birth to," and "conceived" means "became pregnant." Here the verse only reports the event; the child's name comes in the following verse.

Leah was the wife Jacob had not chosen, and she lived in a household marked by rivalry with her sister Rachel. That competition for Jacob's affection shows up in every birth. The Bible says that God "heard" Leah, meaning that He took notice of her difficult situation. For this reason she sees her children as a gift from God, although she also hoped they would bring her the love of her husband.

For today: when you feel overlooked or compared with others, remember that God sees you and hears you. You can look to Him for your worth, without depending on the approval of others.
exp.0:14:
The explanation says that God commanded that there be lights, that is, luminaries, in the "expanse of the heavens," which is the space above the earth that we see as the sky. Their purpose was to give light to the earth. And it ends with "it was so": what God commanded, happened.

The one who speaks is God, on the fourth day of creation. In the verses before, He had already said that these lights would serve to separate day from night and to mark seasons, days and years. The text does not explain how it happened; it only shows that God commands and his word is fulfilled. Some Christians read it literally and others in a broader way, but all recognize God as Creator.

For today: each time you see the light of day or the stars, remember that God cares for and orders your life. You can thank him and trust that his plans are fulfilled.
exp.23:55:
Here the servant of Abraham asks that they not hold him back. "Hinder me not" means "do not delay me." "Seeing the Lord hath prospered my way" means that God gave success to his journey. "Send me away" means "let me go," so that he can return to his master, who is Abraham.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac. He had already prayed and saw that God was guiding him when he found Rebekah. Her family, Laban and her mother, want her to wait ten days before leaving, perhaps to say goodbye. The servant, however, does not want to lose time, because he recognizes that God opened the way and he wants to respond promptly.

Today, when we see that God has guided us or opened a door, it is good to act with gratitude and without unnecessary delay. This is not a matter of being discourteous to others, but of not letting pass what God has already set on its path.
exp.22:6:
The explanation says that Abraham stood up and bowed himself to the people of the land, the children of Heth. "Bowed himself" means that he made a bow of respect. "People of the land" refers to the original inhabitants of Canaan, among whom he lived as a foreigner.

Sarah had just died, and Abraham wanted to buy a place to bury her. The children of Heth had just offered him, with respect, one of their best tombs. Abraham did not answer with pride, even though God had promised him that land. He answered with courtesy and humility, and right away asked them to help him negotiate a fair purchase from Ephron.

We can treat with respect and gratitude those who do not share our faith, even when we have reasons to feel secure. Humility and honesty in our dealings give good witness that we trust in God.
exp.41:28:
This verse says that Jacob's sons returned to their father in the land of Canaan and told him everything that had happened to them in Egypt. The word "came" in the sense of "having arrived" is reflected in the wording "came unto," and "befell" means "happened." After this verse begins the account of what they said.

The narrator tells us that Joseph's brothers were returning from Egypt, where they had gone to buy grain because of the famine. There they dealt with Joseph, but they did not recognize him. They were frightened because the money had appeared in a sack, and they wondered what God was doing. Now they must give an account to Jacob, their father. Let us note that their report does not tell everything in detail; the Bible does not say here that they explained everything that had happened in the past with Joseph.

For today: when we go through confusing moments, it is good to tell someone we trust what we are going through, and also to bring it to God in prayer. Speaking about it honestly helps us think more clearly and keeps us from carrying the fear alone.
exp.19:14:
Abimelech tells Abraham that his land is open to him: he may live in whatever place he prefers. "Before thee" means that the land is at his disposal. "Where it pleaseth thee" means "wherever seems best to you."

Abimelech is the king of Gerar. He had taken Sarah without knowing she was Abraham's wife, because Abraham had said she was his sister. God warned him in a dream, and the king returned Sarah along with gifts. This offer shows his desire to set things right. Some think he also seeks peace with a man protected by God; the text says nothing more about his reasons.

When we recognize a wrong, saying "I'm sorry" is not enough. It also helps to repair the harm with concrete and generous actions, and to treat with respect the person who was affected.
exp.35:12:
This verse lists the four sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. Reuel was the son of Esau and of Bashemath, one of his wives. In the King James Version, the word "sons" is used for the children named here, and the phrase "these were the sons of Bashemath Esau's wife" identifies Bashemath as the mother.

The book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses, is not the speech of any one person but a narrative account. Here it presents the family of Esau, also called Edom, who became a people living next to Israel. These lists show that God fulfilled his promise that Esau would also have a large descendant line, although the covenant promise continued through the line of Jacob.

For today: God does not overlook people, even when they are not at the center of the story. Every name matters to him. Today you can remember that your life, even if it seems simple or little noticed, is known and valued by God.
exp.29:26:
Laban asks Jacob not to leave. He says, "If now I have found favour in thine eyes," which means "I ask you to do me this kindness." He also says, "I have learned by experience," which means "I have come to know it through experience," or "I have observed," that the Lord has blessed him for Jacob's sake.

Laban is Jacob's father-in-law, and he is the one speaking. Jacob has just asked his permission to return to his own land with his wives and children, after many years of service. Laban does not want to lose a worker who has brought him prosperity. Some think his statement about the blessing is sincere; others see in it an economic interest, since he soon turns to talk of wages.

For today: let us gratefully acknowledge the people whom God uses to bless us, and value their work fairly and with sincere words, not only when it suits us.
exp.26:26:
Here Jacob draws near to his father Isaac and kisses him. Isaac, whose eyesight had failed, smells Jacob's clothing and blesses him. He compares that smell to that of a field which the Lord has blessed. The words "must" and "dew" in the verses that follow speak of the juice of the grape and of abundance.

Isaac speaks as an aging father who wants to give the family blessing to his firstborn son, Esau. But Jacob, encouraged by his mother Rebekah, poses as Esau, using his clothing. Isaac lets himself be guided by his sense of smell and touch, and blesses the one he had not intended to bless. The Bible recounts the deception without approving it, and later Jacob suffers its consequences.

For today: God can accomplish His purposes despite our mistakes, but that does not justify deception. Let us seek to obtain what is good with honesty and trust in God, not with tricks that wound the family.
exp.31:28:
Jacob asks the man he wrestled with to tell him his name. The man does not give it, but answers with a question: "Why do you ask my name?" Then he blessed him right there. "Tell me" means "tell me" or "let me know," and the word for "blessed" in the older wording simply means "he blessed him."

Jacob has spent the night wrestling by the river Jabbok, before meeting his brother Esau. He has just received the name Israel. The text does not explain why the visitor does not reveal his name. Jacob later understands that he had seen God, since he calls the place Peniel. Many believe it was God himself in human form, and others see him as a divine messenger.

For today: we will not always receive all the answers we seek, but God does bless us in the middle of our struggle. We can trust in him even when some mystery is left unexplained.
exp.34:7:
The explanation says that Deborah, Rebekah's nurse or caregiver, died and was buried at the foot of Bethel, under an oak. For this reason the place was called Allon-bachuth, which means "oak of weeping." Here "nurse" refers to the woman who looked after and raised Rebekah; the phrase "was buried beneath" means that she was buried at the foot of the place.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition, recounting the story of Jacob. Jacob had just returned to Bethel to worship God. The text does not explain why Deborah was with him; the Bible does not say, although she had come with Rebekah's family. This moment of mourning appears in the middle of a time of spiritual renewal.

For today: faith does not shield us from loss. We can grieve those we love and, at the same time, continue worshiping God, who walks with us in sorrow and in hope.
exp.8:12:
This verse says that God sets his "bow" in the clouds as a sign of his promise. The word "covenant" means a pact or binding agreement. Many understand the "bow" to be the rainbow, although the Hebrew word is also used for a war bow. For this reason, some see in this the image of a weapon hung up, one that no longer points against the earth.

God speaks to Noah and his sons after the flood. He has saved them in the ark, and now he promises that he will never again destroy the earth with water. The covenant includes all living creatures, not only people. God gives a visible sign so that they will remember his word.

For today: when you see a rainbow, or when days of storm pass through your life, remember that God keeps what he promises. You can rest in his faithfulness and give him thanks, even when you do not understand everything that is happening.
exp.48:2:
Jacob speaks to Reuben, his firstborn son, and reminds him of what he represented. "Firstborn" means the first male child. "The beginning of my strength" means the first fruit of his strength as a father. "Dignity" means honor or rank, and "power" means authority. By birth, Reuben held first place in the family.

Jacob, now old and near his death, gathers his twelve sons to tell them what will come upon them. He begins with Reuben with words of acknowledgment, but soon, in the verses that follow, he rebukes him for his serious offense against his father. For this reason, Reuben would lose the privileged place that belonged to him.

For today: having a good start, talent, or a position does not guarantee a good ending. Character and daily decisions matter more. Let us ask God for self-control to care for what has been entrusted to us.
exp.17:19:
The explanation says God tells Abraham that the "outcry" against Sodom and Gomorrah keeps growing. This outcry is like a cry of protest over the injustices committed there. It says their sin has become "very grievous", that is, it has become very heavy and serious. "The Lord" is the name of God.

Here God himself speaks. He has just decided to share with Abraham what he plans to do, because Abraham is his friend and will teach his household to live in righteousness. Right away God says that he will go down to see whether the matter is truly as grave as the outcry that has reached him. This shows that God acts with justice, not lightly.

For today: God hears the cry of those who suffer injustice. We can be people who are sensitive to their pain, pray for them and, as far as we are able, help them and act justly in the matters that concern us.
exp.22:2:
The explanation says that Abraham got up from beside the body of Sara, his wife who had died, and went to speak with the sons of Heth. "His dead" means his deceased wife. "Heth" is the Hittites, the name of a people who lived in that land. "Before" means "beside" or "in view of."

Sara had just died in Hebron, and Abraham was mourning her. The narrator tells us that, after that grief, Abraham took a practical step. He was a foreigner in Canaan and owned no land of his own. So he went to ask his neighbors for a place to bury Sara with dignity.

For today: the grief is real and deserves time, but there are also moments when we must rise up and do what is necessary with love. We can weep and, at the same time, care for our loved ones responsibly. God understands both.
exp.36:4:
This verse says that Joseph dreamed a dream and told it to his brothers. They already hated him, and they hated him even more.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Joseph was about seventeen years old, and his father Jacob (also called Israel) treated him with favoritism, even making him a special coat. His brothers already felt envy and resentment. When he told them the dream, which suggested that they would bow down to him, the tension grew. The Bible does not say what Joseph intended in telling it; some see it as naivety and others as a lack of good sense.

For today: when God gives us something, whether a gift or a hope, it is wise to share it with humility and wisdom, thinking about how it will affect those who hear us. And if there is envy in the heart, we need to bring it to God before it grows.
exp.44:2:
Here Joseph finally tells his brothers who he is: "I am Joseph." He asks whether their father is still alive, even though they had already told him before. They cannot answer because they are "troubled," that is, frightened and confused. The King James wording "unto" and "doth" are old forms of speech from that era, and "his presence" is a phrase of the time, meaning his nearness or the fact of his being there.

Joseph speaks now as the governor of Egypt to the same brothers who sold him years earlier. After weeping alone with them, he reveals himself. His question about Jacob shows that the family still hurts him, not only the past. The brothers' fear is understandable: they had guilt, and he had power.

Today, when someone has hurt us, or we have hurt others, reconciliation begins with truth and tenderness. We can ask God for courage to face the past and a heart willing to forgive.
exp.32:4:
It says Esau lifted up his eyes and saw the women and the children who were coming with Jacob. He asked, "Who are these with you?" Jacob answered that they were the children God had graciously given him, his servant.

Esau speaks, and then Jacob replies. The brothers had been separated for years, and Jacob feared that Esau might want revenge. After a reunion full of tears, Esau asks about the family. Jacob calls himself "your servant" out of humility and respect. He does not boast about his family, but presents it as a gift from God.

For today: when we talk about what we have, whether family, work, or achievements, we can do so with humility and gratitude, recognizing that every good gift comes from God and not from our own merit.
exp.25:1:
This verse tells us that God appeared to Isaac and gave him a clear command: not to go down to Egypt, but to stay in the land that He would show him. The words "appeared" and "said" in the King James wording are the older forms of "appeared to him" and "told him," and "the Lord" is the name used for God here.

There was famine in the region, and Isaac was staying in Gerar, among the Philistines. It was natural to think of going down to Egypt, where food was usually available. The one speaking is God, who reminds Isaac of the promises made to his father Abraham. God asks him to stay and trust, and promises his presence and blessing.

For today: when a need arises, it is wise to look for solutions, but it is good to ask God first what He wants. His direction may differ from the most logical way out, and His promise to be with you remains sufficient.
exp.0:24:
Here the account tells how God made the animals of the earth: the wild beasts, the livestock, and the creatures that crawl, such as reptiles and insects. "Kind" means "class" or "type." In the King James wording, "creepeth" is an old form of "creeps." When it is finished, God looked at what he had made and said it was good.

This happens on the sixth day of creation. The one who speaks and acts is God; the narrator only reports. First God commanded the earth to bring forth living creatures, and so it happened. This verse shows the result. Then, in the verses that follow, God will create human beings. In this way the account prepares the place where humanity will live.

For today: if God called each creature "good," we can care for animals and nature with respect and gratitude. Caring for them is a way of honoring the Creator.
exp.37:12:
The explanation says that someone brought word to Tamar that her father-in-law Judah was on his way to Timnah to shear his sheep. "Shear" means to cut off their wool. "Brought word" means she was told the news or was given the report.

Here the narrator speaks. Tamar had been widowed from Judah's sons, and he had told her to wait in her father's house until Shelah grew up, although in reality he did not intend to give him to her, out of fear that he too would die. Time has now passed, Shelah has grown, and Tamar was still being left out. This news gives her the opportunity to act, although her plan, which continues in the following verses, is deceitful, and the Bible does not present it as an example to imitate.

For today: when someone fails us or leaves us waiting unfairly, let us seek honest ways and ask God for wisdom, instead of responding with deception.
exp.39:19:
It tells us that on the third day, which was Pharaoh's birthday, he held a feast for all his servants. During that banquet he "lifted up the head" of the chief butler and of the chief baker, meaning he brought them out before everyone to decide their fate. The King James wording "it came to pass" is an old way of saying "it happened," and "butler" refers to the one who served the drink, while "baker" refers to the one who made the bread.

The narrator then reports that what Joseph had interpreted came true. Both men had been in prison with Joseph. He had told them that God gives the interpretations, and the dreams were fulfilled within a single day: one was restored and the other was executed.

For today: God keeps his word in his own time, even when it seems he has forgotten the one who suffers. We can trust him and be faithful wherever we are, as Joseph was in prison.
exp.13:13:
He says that when Abram learned that his nephew Lot had been taken captive, he gathered his servants, men born in his household and trained for fighting, three hundred and eighteen in all, and went out to pursue the captors as far as Dan. "Brother" here means a close relative, since Lot was his nephew. "Armed" means that he equipped them for battle. "Pursued" means that he followed them.

Context: this is the account in Genesis, told in the third person. Invading kings had plundered Sodom and carried off Lot along with his possessions. A fugitive brought the news to Abram. Although Lot had separated from him earlier, Abram did not leave him abandoned. Some think that the name Dan was added later by those who copied the text; this is not known with certainty.

For today: when a relative or friend is in trouble, even if they have drifted away or made poor choices, act with courage and love. Prepare yourself, help in concrete ways, and do not just stand by and watch.
exp.43:25:
Here Judah repeats what the brothers told Jacob, their father. They say they cannot return to Egypt without Benjamin, the youngest brother. "The man" is the ruler of Egypt, and "to see his face" means to appear before him. Without Benjamin, he would not receive them.

Judah speaks to Joseph, though he does not yet know that he is his brother. Joseph had demanded that they bring Benjamin as proof that they were not spies. Judah tells the story to ask that he himself be kept as a slave in place of the young man, because the loss of Benjamin would break their father's heart with grief.

For today: Judah, who once helped sell Joseph, is now willing to sacrifice himself for his brother. God can transform our character. We can acknowledge our past mistakes and care lovingly for those who depend on us.
exp.43:3:
This verse tells how Joseph's brothers had barely left the city when Joseph sent his steward after them. He told him to overtake them and ask why they had repaid good with evil. The steward is the man in charge of the household.

Joseph is the one speaking. He ruled in Egypt and had not yet made himself known to his brothers. He had ordered his cup hidden in Benjamin's sack to test whether they had changed, and whether they would abandon their youngest brother as they once had done to him. The accusation was part of that test.

For today: before we judge someone, let us remember that God sometimes uses trials to bring to light what is in the heart. Let us ask him to give us faithfulness and love for others when our turn comes to be tested.
exp.31:11:
Jacob reminds God of what He promised him: that He would surely do him good and that his descendants would be as numerous as the sand of the sea, too many to count. The word "seed" means offspring, that is, children, grandchildren and all the generations to come.

The one speaking is Jacob, who is returning to his land after many years away. He learns that Esau, his brother, is coming to meet him, and he feels great fear because years earlier he had deceived him. So he prays, acknowledges that he is small, and relies on God's promise, not on his own merits.

For today: when you feel afraid, pray honestly and remind God of His promises, as Jacob did. Then do what is in your hands, as he did when he prepared a gift for his brother. Trusting God does not remove the responsibility to act wisely.
exp.24:22:
God tells Rebekah that she is carrying two nations in her womb. Those two sons will become two distinct peoples who will be separated from each other. One will be stronger than the other, and the elder will serve the younger. In the King James wording, "people" here means nations, and "bowels" refers to the womb.

Rebekah, who was barren for many years, is now pregnant, but she feels the children struggling inside her and becomes distressed. She goes to inquire of the Lord, and He Himself answers her. Later on, these children are Esau and Jacob, and from them come Edom and Israel. Many understand that God is showing here His free choice, not based on the order of birth.

When something in your life confuses or troubles you, do as Rebekah did: bring it to God. He can give you clarity and remind you that His plans are moving forward, even when they do not look like what you expected.
exp.27:3:
Isaac wishes Jacob that God would give him the blessing He gave to Abraham. That blessing includes his descendants ("seed" means children and offspring). It also speaks of Jacob inheriting the land where his grandfather lived as a stranger. "Sojourning" refers to the years when Abraham moved from place to place without owning the land.

Isaac speaks to his son Jacob before sending him to Padan-aram to find a wife among his mother's family. Isaac did not want him to take a Canaanite wife. With these words he passes on to him the promise God had made to Abraham. Jacob receives it as the heir of that promise.

For today: God's promises do not depend on everything being in plain sight. Abraham and Jacob lived as strangers and still trusted. We can follow God with patience, knowing that he keeps what he promises.
exp.0:21:
God blesses the fish and the birds he has just created. He gives them the command to "be fruitful and multiply," that is, to have offspring and fill the seas and the earth. The King James wording "fill the waters in the seas" and "let fowl multiply in the earth" shows the same idea: the waters would be filled with life and the birds would spread across the land.

The one who speaks is God, on the fifth day of creation. It is the first time the Bible mentions a blessing, and it is given to living creatures. God not only creates, but also cares for what he made and gives it the ability to continue life. Earlier he had said that what he created was good, and now he sustains it with his blessing.

For today: life is a gift that God blesses. We can care for nature with gratitude, since it belongs to him. We can also ask for his blessing on our work, our family, and our days, knowing that he gives the growth.
exp.30:6:
Jacob tells his wives, Rachel and Leah, that their father Laban has deceived him and changed his wages "ten times." "Changed" means altered or switched, and "wages" is the payment for his work. Even so, God did not allow Laban to harm him. "Ten times" may be an exact number or a way of saying "many times"; the text does not make this clear.

Jacob speaks with Rachel and Leah because he wants their support before returning to his father's land. He had noticed that Laban no longer treated him the same. Jacob presents his version of events and acknowledges that God had watched over him during years of hard work.

When someone treats us unjustly, we do not have to respond with revenge or bitterness. We can keep working with honesty and trust that God cares for us, even when we do not yet see justice.
exp.32:5:
It says that Jacob's servants, Bilhah and Zilpah, came near with their children and bowed before Esau. "Servants" refers to the women who served in the household; "children" refers to their sons; "bowed themselves" means they made a bow, a gesture of respect.

Jacob is reunited with his brother Esau after many years. Earlier he had taken the blessing from him and had fled, and he feared Esau's reaction. Now Esau embraces him and weeps. Jacob presents his family in groups: first the servants, then Leah, and last Rachel and Joseph. The Bible does not explain why this order; some think Jacob was thus protecting those he loved most, but that is only an interpretation.

For today: when a relationship has been broken, approach with humility and respect. Recognizing that children and blessings come from God helps us treat others without pride.
exp.32:16:
He says that Jacob went to a place called Succoth. There he built a house for himself and put up shelters or shelters for his livestock. That is why the place was called Succoth, a word that means "booths" or "shelters." In the King James wording, "journeyed" means he traveled on, and "built him an house" means he constructed a house for himself.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Jacob had just been reunited with his brother Esau, whom he had feared for years. After that peaceful meeting, Esau returned to Seir and Jacob continued on his way separately. The text says nothing about how long he stayed in Succoth. Some think it was a long pause, others that it was brief; it is not known with certainty.

For today: after a great trial or reconciliation, one does not always have to rush on to the next step. Pausing, caring for your family and for what God has entrusted to you, and giving thanks is also part of walking with Him.
exp.0:13:
God commands that there be "lights," that is, luminaries or heavenly bodies, in the "firmament of the heaven," that is, the expanse spread out above the earth. Their purpose is to divide the day from the night, to serve as "signs," to mark the "seasons" (the appointed times), and to measure the days and the years.

God himself speaks, on the fourth day of creation. He had already created light, the sea, and the plants, and now he places in the sky the heavenly bodies that govern time. Some believe the text describes the fourth day in literal sequence, and others read it in a more symbolic way; the passage does not settle that debate.

God brought order to time, and this is no accident. Today we can receive each day and each season as a gift from him, and live them with gratitude, rest, and purpose.
exp.7:1:
This verse tells how God stopped the flood. "The fountains of the deep" are the deep waters that had burst up from beneath the earth, and "the windows of heaven" are the openings from which the rain fell. Both were closed. "Was restrained" means that the rain stopped.

Here no character is speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis. The verse before says that God "remembered" Noah. That does not mean he had forgotten him, but that he acted on Noah's behalf, in keeping with his promise. In this way the water begins to go down, and the close of the judgment is set in motion.

For today: even when a trial seems endless, God knows when to set a limit to it. Trust that he remembers you and cares for you, and wait for his timing with patience.
exp.12:12:
This verse says the people of Sodom were very wicked. "Sinners before the Lord" means that their sins were against God himself, and "exceedingly" means that they were so to a very great degree. The name of God in the Old Testament is Jehovah.

The narrator of the book of Genesis pauses the story to alert us to something. Lot has just separated from his uncle Abram and chooses the fertile plain of the Jordan, looking only at what is green and productive. Little by little he moves his tents closer to Sodom. The text does not say that Lot yet took part in that wickedness, but it does show that he was drawing near to a dangerous place. Afterward, God renews his promise to Abram.

For today: when we make decisions about work, moving, or friendships, let us not look only at what is convenient or profitable. Let us also ask what influence that place will have on our faith and on our family.
exp.42:18:
The explanation says that Joseph's brothers approached the manager of his house and spoke with him at the door, before going in. "Steward" is the person in charge of managing the affairs of the house.

The brothers had been brought to Joseph's house and they were afraid. They remembered that the last time the money had appeared in their sacks, and they thought they would be accused of theft so that they would be made slaves. That is why they speak first with the steward, to explain themselves. They still did not know that Joseph was their brother, and they did not understand that he was preparing a meal for them, not a punishment.

For today: when you are afraid or carry unresolved guilt, do not wait for things to explode. Speak with clarity and honesty, and remember that God sometimes works with kindness where you suspect punishment.
exp.44:9:
Here Joseph tells his brothers that their father Jacob will be able to live in the region of Goshen, near him. There the whole family will be together: the children, the grandchildren, the flocks, and all that they possess. "Flocks" refers to the sheep and goats, and "thou shalt dwell" means "you will live."

Joseph speaks to his brothers after revealing who he is. Egypt is suffering a famine, and five more years of it remain. He no longer blames them for having sold him, but sees the hand of God in everything. Goshen is usually placed in the east of the Nile delta, although its exact location is not entirely certain. It was good land for pasture.

Today we can learn from Joseph to offer forgiveness through concrete actions. He does not merely say that he forgives, but cares, provides, and brings his family close. Let us consider who needs from us not only words, but help and closeness.
exp.23:23:
Rebekah answers the servant's question: she says she is the daughter of Bethuel, who was the son of Milcah and Nahor. The phrase "which she bare unto Nahor" means that Milcah gave birth to Nahor, so Bethuel was the son of both of them. "Bare" is an old way of saying "gave birth to."

Abraham's servant is looking for a wife for Isaac. He has already given gifts to Rebekah, but before he knew who she was, and now he asks her about her family. She answers simply and confirms that she belongs to Abraham's kin, since Nahor was Abraham's brother. Hearing this, the servant worships God, as we see right after.

God often guides us step by step, even in details that seem small, like a name or a family. When making important decisions, pray, act with diligence, and notice how God opens the way. When you see his guidance, respond as the servant did: with gratitude and worship.
exp.42:2:
Judah answers his father Jacob. He explains that the governor of Egypt had warned them with great firmness, "with a resolute spirit," that is, decided and without doubt: they would not see his face again, meaning he would not receive them, unless they brought their younger brother with them. "Protested" here means that he declared it solemnly.

The hunger was still severe and the grain had run out. Jacob wanted to send them again to buy food, but Benjamin, his youngest son, was the one he protected most. Judah speaks plainly to show him there was no other way out. The brothers did not yet know that this governor was Joseph.

For today: sometimes God brings us to a point where we can no longer keep avoiding what frightens us. Like Jacob, trust and let go of what you grip tightly out of fear, and ask for courage to speak the truth, as Judah did.
exp.7:13:
This verse says that the earth was completely dry on the twenty-seventh day of the second month. The word "á" is an old form of "a," and "se secó" means that there was no longer any moisture or mud. Earlier, in the first month, Noah saw that the surface was "enjuta," that is, without water on top. Now the ground was already firm.

The narrator of the book recounts the dates of the flood with great care. Noah had waited a long time inside the ark. Although he could already see uncovered ground, he did not leave on his own. He waited until God spoke to him and gave the order to come out, as seen in the following verse.

For today: sometimes God makes us wait even when it seems that everything is ready. We can learn from Noah not to rush ahead, but to trust in God's timing and wait for his direction before taking the next step.
exp.40:16:
Pharaoh begins to tell Joseph his dream. He says that in the dream he was standing on the bank of the river, meaning beside the Nile, although the text says only "the river." The KJV's "I stood" is the plain, modern wording of the same idea, and the "behold" that opens the sentence is an old way of saying "look" or "see," which is why it is set off by commas here.

The speaker is Pharaoh, the king of Egypt. Joseph has just come out of prison and has told him that he has no power of his own to interpret dreams, but that God will give the answer. Pharaoh, troubled because none of his wise men could explain the dream, now relates it in detail.

For today: Joseph does not boast of his gifts but gives God the credit before he speaks. We can imitate him. When someone asks us for advice or help, let us humbly acknowledge that wisdom comes from God and seek his guidance first.
exp.36:34:
It says that all of Jacob's sons and daughters came to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. It states that he will go down "in mourning" (dressed in grief, full of sorrow) into the "grave," that is, to the place of the dead. His father wept for him.

Jacob's sons had shown him Joseph's bloodied coat, and he believed a wild beast had killed him. Jacob speaks out of deep pain. He does not know that Joseph is alive, as the following verse shows. The sons who try to comfort him are the same ones who deceived him, although the text does not say this directly.

For today: when someone suffers a loss, do not rush them to feel better. Accompany them with patience, listening and presence. And if the pain is yours, remember that God can work even in what you cannot see.
exp.5:14:
God gives Noah the exact measurements of the ark: three hundred cubits in length, fifty in width, and thirty in height. A cubit was an ancient unit of measurement based on the forearm, and it is usually reckoned at about 45 to 50 centimeters, though its exact value at that time is not known with certainty. So the ark would have been roughly 135 to 150 meters long.

God speaks, and He speaks to Noah. He sees that the earth is filled with violence and announces a judgment. But before judging, He gives Noah a clear plan to save himself and his family, along with the animals.

For today: God attends to the details of what He asks of us. When He entrusts you with something, trust that He will give you the direction you need, and obey step by step, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.10:21:
Serug was thirty years old when his son Nahor was born. The word "begat" means that he was Nahor's father. The Bible tells us nothing more here about Serug, only his name and this moment in his life.

This is part of the genealogy of Shem, in the book of Genesis. The narrator is the author of the book, who follows the family line from Noah to Abraham. Nahor will be Abraham's grandfather, so each name connects the story with God's promise. Some scholars think the list may have summarized several generations, but the text does not make this clear.

For today: God remembers ordinary people, even those who barely appear in the stories. Your everyday life also matters to Him. Today you can live faithfully in what is simple, trusting that God brings everything together in His plan.
exp.36:15:
Here, Joseph answers a stranger who asks him what he is looking for. He says he is searching for his brothers and asks him to tell him where they are pasturing the flock. "I pray thee" is an old way of saying "please." "Feed their flocks" refers to sheep eating grass in the field.

Joseph is speaking, a young man whom his father Jacob had sent from Hebron to find out how his brothers and the sheep were doing. He had lost his way in the countryside near Shechem (Sichêm), and a man, whose identity the Bible does not give, offered him help. Through that man, Joseph learned that he should go to Dothan, where his brothers would later plot against him.

For today: when we are lost or confused, let us not be ashamed to humbly ask for direction. And even when the road leads us to difficult places, God may be at work in what seems like a simple conversation.
exp.10:5:
The explanation says that the Lord observes a united people: they all speak the same language and have already begun to build. According to God, nothing will stop them from achieving what they set out to do. Some older words: "restrained" means held back or kept from; "imagined" means "planned" or "devised." The phrase does not speak of fear of God, but of how far a human plan can go when nothing holds it back.

The Lord speaks after coming down to see the city and the tower. The builders wanted to make a name for themselves and not be scattered, even though God had commanded them to fill the earth. Their unity served pride and self-sufficiency. Interpreters explain the exact scope of the sin in different ways, but the text stresses that desire for their own glory.

For today: before launching into a project, let us honestly ask whether we seek to honor God and serve others, or only to make our own name great. Let us bring our plans to him in prayer.
exp.20:20:
This verse tells us that Ishmael, the son of Hagar, settled to live in the wilderness of Paran, an arid area to the south and east of Canaan. There his mother found him a wife in Egypt, which was her homeland. "Took him a wife" means she arranged a wife for him, something that fathers commonly did in that period.

The narrator is traditionally identified as Moses. After Abraham sent Hagar and Ishmael away, God took care of them: He showed them a well and was with the boy as he grew up. This verse closes his story and shows that God kept His promise to look after Ishmael and make him a great nation.

For today: God cares for people even in hard and lonely places. If today you feel you are in a "wilderness," trust that He sees you, sustains you, and has not forgotten you.
exp.42:9:
This verse says that if they had not wasted so much time hesitating, they would already have gone to Egypt and come back twice. "Lingered" means they stayed waiting, without acting. "Surely" here means "certainly."

Judah speaks to his father Jacob (also called Israel). There is famine in the land, and the food they brought from Egypt has run out. Jacob did not want to send Benjamin, his youngest son, for fear of losing him. Judah offers himself as the guarantor and reminds his father that the delay has already cost them dearly. His words are firm and respectful.

For today: when a necessary decision is delayed out of fear, time also has a cost. It is good to pray, think calmly, and then act. And if someone trusts you, as Judah was trusted, be responsible for your word.
exp.20:19:
It says that God was with the boy Ishmael, and that he grew. He lived in the desert and became an archer, that is, someone skilled at hunting with bow and arrows. The King James wording "an archer" corresponds to the original phrase, which is the word for a bowman.

This is told by the narrator of Genesis. Hagar and Ishmael had been sent away from Abraham's household and were about to die of thirst in the wilderness. God opened Hagar's eyes to see a well, and he promised to make Ishmael a great nation. This verse shows that God fulfilled his care and his promise.

For today: God can accompany those who feel rejected or who are in difficult places. If you are going through a "wilderness" today, such as a crisis or loneliness, remember that God sees, provides, and does not abandon you. Trust in him and take the next step with faith.
exp.5:9:
This verse says that Noah had three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth. The word "begat" means "had as sons," and it is an older word than the modern "had." The names are given here in the form the King James Version uses. Readers of other versions may see the same sons spelled differently, such as Cham for Ham in some older texts.

The narrator here is the voice of the book of Genesis, which is traditionally attributed to Moses. He has just presented Noah as a righteous man who walked with God. Naming his sons prepares the story that follows: a world filled with violence, and a family that God will preserve in the midst of judgment.

For today: a faithful life before God is not only personal, it also touches the family. You can walk with God in a simple and steady way, even when your surroundings do not, and so leave a good mark on those who live with you.
exp.47:20:
Jacob, also called Israel, tells Joseph that he is about to die. Even so, he assures him that God will remain with them and will bring them back to the land of their forefathers. The words "you" here refers to Joseph and his family.

Jacob is now very old and has just blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's sons, placing the younger ahead of the older. They live in Egypt, but Jacob looks toward the promise God made to Abraham and Isaac about the land of Canaan. His confidence is not in his own life, but in the faithfulness of God.

For today: even when the people we love or who guide us pass away, God remains. We can face change and loss with hope, trusting that He continues to fulfill His promises to our family.
exp.40:6:
It says that the seven thin ears swallowed up the seven full and plump ears. Then Pharaoh woke and realized that all of it had been a dream.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. Pharaoh has just had his second dream, similar to the first, which was about the cows. No one in his court is able to explain it, and that is why Joseph appears, who will say that God is showing him what is coming: seven years of plenty and seven years of famine.

For today: God can speak in ways we do not understand right away. If He warns us or shows us something, the wise thing is to prepare ourselves with humility and seek trustworthy counsel, as Pharaoh eventually did, neither ignoring it nor falling into panic.
exp.23:39:
Here Abraham's words to his servant are repeated. Abraham trusts that the LORD, before whom he has lived faithfully, will send his angel with him and make the journey succeed. "Prosper thy way" means that everything will turn out well. "Kindred" means family or relatives, and "my father's house" refers to Abraham's relatives.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, who tells the family of Rebekah about his mission. He explains why he has come: Abraham asked him to seek a wife for Isaac among his relatives, not among the Canaanites. The servant quotes Abraham's words to show that his journey has a purpose and the guidance of God.

For today: when you make an important decision, walk with God in your everyday life and ask Him for direction. Trust that He is with you, and act with responsibility and honesty.
exp.16:5:
God tells Abraham that he will have a great many descendants. "Multiplying I will multiply thee" is rendered in the verse as "I will make thee exceeding fruitful," and "I will make nations of thee" means that several nations will come from him. He also promises that kings will come from his family.

God himself is speaking. Abraham is about ninety-nine years old and still does not have the promised son with Sarah. God changes his name from Abram to Abraham, which points to "father of many," and confirms his covenant. It is a promise from God, not an achievement of Abraham, and it is fulfilled across the passing of generations.

For today: when God's promise seems impossible or very slow, do not measure his faithfulness by your circumstances. Rely on his word, pray with confidence, and wait with patience, knowing that God fulfills what he says in his own time.
exp.30:31:
Jacob tells Laban that if anyone is found holding his gods, that person must not live. He also invites Laban to search in front of all their relatives and to take back whatever belongs to him. The text makes clear that Jacob did not know Rachel had stolen them. "Gods" here refers to small images or household idols.

Jacob speaks with Laban, his father-in-law, who has caught up with him to complain about his leaving in secret and about the disappearance of his idols. Jacob, certain of his own innocence, makes a very strong statement without knowing that his wife Rachel had them. Why Rachel took them, the Bible does not explain, and several ideas have been proposed.

For today: before speaking firmly or making drastic promises, it is wise to make sure we know the facts well, because our words can affect those we love.
exp.1:22:
Here Adam says that the woman is part of his very own nature: "bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh." The word "woman" in the verse above is the ordinary word for a female human, and "man" is the ordinary word for a male human. In Hebrew there is a word play similar to this: ish (man) and ishah (woman). The verb "was taken" and "brought her" are older ways of saying "was taken out" and "brought her," and both appear in the verse above in their modern forms.

Adam, the first man, is the one speaking. Before this moment he had been alone, and no animal was a companion equal to him. When God presents the woman to him, he joyfully recognizes that she is equal to him. Some see here the first poem in the Bible.

For today: value the people close to you, especially in marriage, as equals before God. Treat them with respect, gratitude, and joy, not as someone inferior or as a possession.
exp.2:3:
Here the serpent directly contradicts what God had said. "Ye shall not surely die" is a flat denial of the divine warning.

The serpent speaks, and in the story it appears as a cunning and deceitful creature. It answers Eve, who had just repeated God's command, though she added that they could not even touch the tree. The serpent does not argue in a roundabout way: it casts doubt on God's word and on his goodness. Many Christians see here the enemy of God at work, although the text of Genesis does not say so explicitly.

Today, when a voice tells us that disobeying God will have no consequences, we do well to stop and think. We can return to his Word and ask ourselves whether that idea sounds like truth or like deception.
exp.47:16:
This verse tells how Joseph noticed that his father Jacob was placing his right hand on Ephraim, the younger son. This displeased him, so he took his father's hand to move it over to the head of Manasseh, the older son.

Jacob, already elderly, was blessing Joseph's two sons. In that culture, the right hand and the first place usually went to the firstborn. Joseph wanted that order to be respected. But Jacob, knowing what he was doing, deliberately crossed his hands and said the younger would be greater.

For today: sometimes we want to correct God because his ways do not match our customs or expectations. We can trust that he sees further than we understand, and pray with humility.
exp.25:31:
This verse tells us that on the very day Isaac made a peace agreement with Abimelech, his servants arrived with good news. They had been digging a well and had found water. The word "servants" here means the workers or attendants who served him, and the phrase "We have found water" is the servants' report to their master.

Here Isaac's servants speak, and they inform their master. In that dry land, water meant life for the family and the animals. There had been earlier conflicts over other wells (Genesis 26:15-22). Isaac chose peace, and now this provision arrives. The text does not say that the well is a reward for making peace, but it does show a contrast.

For today: when we seek peace and do not let ourselves be dragged into quarrels, God can give us rest and provision in his time. Keep doing good, even when you do not yet see the water.
exp.35:7:
This verse says that Esau settled in the mountainous region of Seir. It also clarifies that Esau is the same as Edom, the name by which his people would become known. "Dwelt" means that he lived there in a settled way.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, recording the story of Abraham's family. Esau moved away because he and his brother Jacob had so many livestock that the land could not support both of them. Genesis 25:30 connects the name Edom with "red," and the text links it to Esau. The passage continues with a list of his descendants, the Edomites.

For today: sometimes the best decision is to separate peacefully, without a fight, when there is no room to live together. We can look for calm solutions in family conflicts, trusting that God cares for each person along their own path.
exp.30:8:
It says that God was the one who took the cattle away from Laban, the father of Jacob's wives, and gave them to Jacob. The King James wording "hath taken away" and "given them to me" are older forms of "has taken" and "has given." "Your father" refers to Laban.

Jacob speaks with Rachel and Leah, his wives, and explains to them why he now has so many flocks. Laban had changed his wages many times, and Jacob wants them to understand that his prosperity did not come from cheating, but from God. He recounts a dream in which God showed him what he should do. Some scholars debate how the methods with the sheep worked, but the text insists that God was the author of the result.

For today: when someone treats you unjustly, you do not have to seek revenge or despair. Trust that God sees what is happening, cares for you, and can give you what you need, even in the midst of difficult situations.
exp.38:0:
The explanation says that Joseph was taken down to Egypt, and there Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh and captain of the guard, bought him. He was an Egyptian, and he bought him from the Ishmeelites, who were the traders who had brought him there. "Eunuch" here probably means "court official"; the Hebrew word can be understood in several ways. The verb "bought him" in the King James wording is the same action the verse describes.

It is the narrator of Genesis who speaks. He picks up the story after Joseph's brothers sold him (chapter 37) and sets things up for what follows: although Joseph is a slave in a foreign land, the next verse says that "the LORD was with Joseph."

For today: when your situation seems like a setback or an injustice, remember that God may be with you even in places you did not choose. Keep doing your work faithfully, and trust that He has not abandoned you.
exp.19:1:
It says that Abraham claimed Sarah was his sister, without making clear that she was also his wife. Then Abimelech, king of Gerar, sent for her and had Sarah brought to his house. The phrase "sent, and took" means that he gave the order for her to be brought.

The narrator tells us that Abraham was living as a foreigner in Gerar. Out of fear, he repeated what he had already done before in Egypt: presenting Sarah only as his sister. In chapter 12 and in verse 11 of this same chapter it is clear that he feared for his life. God intervened in dreams and protected Sarah and Abimelech, who had not yet come near her.

For today: fear can lead us to speak half-truths, and that hurts others. When you feel afraid, pray and be honest, trusting that God protects even when we fail.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that God spoke and light appeared. "Let there be light" is a command, and "was" is the older form, so the verse reads "there was light." There is no delay or effort: what God says, happens.

God himself speaks, and this is his first recorded word in the Bible. Before this, the earth was "without form and void," covered in darkness, and the Spirit of God moved over the waters. With the light, God begins to give shape and order to his creation. Then he sees that the light is "good" and separates it from the darkness. Scholars debate how to understand the "days" of this chapter, but they all agree that God is the one who brings everything into being.

For today: if God could bring light into an empty and dark place, he can also work in your confusing moments. Pray with confidence, asking him for his light and direction, and wait in his timing.
exp.20:22:
Abimelech asks Abraham to swear before God that he will not betray him, nor his son, nor his grandson. "Thou shalt not deal falsely with me" means not to deceive or break one's given word. Abimelech reminds Abraham that he has treated him kindly, and asks that Abraham respond with the same goodness, both toward him and toward the land where Abraham has lived as a foreigner ("sojourned").

Abimelech, a king of the region, speaks together with Phicol, the commander of his army. They have seen that God blesses Abraham in everything he does. For this reason they want to secure peace with him through a covenant. Abraham agrees, but also clarifies a pending problem: a well that Abimelech's servants had taken from him.

For today: kindness and a given word matter. We can be trustworthy people, keep what we promise, and resolve conflicts with honesty, speaking plainly and seeking peace.
exp.14:9:
He took the animals God had asked for: the heifer, the female goat, and the ram. He cut them in half and set each half across from the other, forming a kind of path between them. The birds, the turtledove and the young pigeon, he did not cut. "Divided" in this verse means "cut in two."

Abram had asked how he could know that he would inherit the promised land. God answered him by asking for these animals. It was an ancient way of making a solemn covenant, and the Bible tells it without explaining every detail. Later, God Himself commits to Abram in that covenant.

For today: when you have doubts, you can bring them honestly to God, as Abram did. God was not offended by his question, but answered him with a firm promise. Obey what God shows you, and trust that He keeps His word.
exp.37:21:
Here the friend of Judah, the Adullamite, returns and tells him that he could not find the woman. The men of the place also said that no prostitute had ever been there. "Returned" means he came back, "find" means to locate, and "harlot" refers to a woman who works in prostitution.

Judah had left his personal belongings as a guarantee of payment, not knowing that this woman was his daughter-in-law Tamar, in disguise. He had sent a young goat to fulfill his promise and recover his things. The one speaking is the friend, and then the local men. The Bible does not fully explain why they say there was no harlot there; it may mean she was not a known prostitute from that place.

Today it reminds us that what is hidden sooner or later comes to light. It is better to act with integrity from the start, because God sees beyond appearances and can correct us with mercy.
exp.41:14:
Joseph says he will test his brothers. He swears "by the life of Pharaoh," a way of affirming something emphatically, and declares that they will not leave Egypt until they bring his youngest brother, Benjamin. "Ye shall be proved" means it will be checked whether they are telling the truth. "Come hither" is an old way of saying "come here."

Joseph speaks as the ruler of Egypt, although his brothers do not recognize him. They came to buy food during the famine. Joseph accuses them of being spies and demands a proof. The Bible does not fully explain his motives, but many think he wanted to know whether they had changed and whether Benjamin was safe.

For today: truth and a change of heart are revealed over time and under pressure. We can ask God to help us live with honesty and to repair what we did wrong, without hiding it.
exp.40:41:
Here, Pharaoh takes the ring off his hand and puts it on Joseph's hand. Then he dresses Joseph in garments of fine linen, a very fine and costly cloth, and places a gold chain around his neck. These are three visible signs of honor and authority.

Joseph had been a slave and then a prisoner. Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, has just heard his interpretation of the dreams and his counsel for facing the years of famine. Convinced that God was with him, Pharaoh raises him to the highest authority after himself. The ring was used to seal documents, so it gave him power to act in the king's name.

God can lift a person up at the moment He chooses, even after years of injustice and waiting. In the meantime, we can remain faithful and do well with what is at hand.
exp.39:8:
The chief butler, who was the official in charge of serving the pharaoh his wine, now tells Joseph his dream. He says that he saw a vine before him. "Chief butler" means the head of those who served drink to the king, and "told" is the plain word for telling.

The pharaoh's cupbearer and baker were in prison together with Joseph, and both of them looked sad because of their dreams. Joseph had told them that God is the one who gives interpretations, and he invited them to tell him what they had dreamed. So the butler speaks first, and Joseph listens closely.

For today: when someone is worried, it is worth stopping to ask how they are and to listen to them. Joseph, even while in prison, noticed the sadness of others and helped them, trusting that God is the one who gives true light.
exp.7:16:
God tells Noah to bring out of the ark all the animals that were with him: birds, beasts, and creeping things, "every creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth." He commands them to spread out over the earth, to "be fruitful" (bear fruit, have offspring) and to "multiply" (increase in number).

God speaks after the floodwaters have gone down and the ground has dried. Noah and his family had been shut in for a long time, and God himself gives them the signal to come out. The command to be fruitful and multiply recalls what was said at creation (Genesis 1:22) and marks a new beginning for life on the earth.

For today: God cares for his creation and also guides us step by step. Just as Noah waited for God's word before coming out, we can wait patiently for his direction before taking the next step. And when the moment comes, let us go out with gratitude, ready to live and to care for what he has entrusted to us.
exp.45:17:
This verse closes the list of the descendants of Zilpah. She was the servant whom Laban gave to his daughter Leah, and through Leah she bore children to Jacob. The words "bare" and "gave" are older forms of the English used today, which reads "bore" and "gave." "Souls" means persons. In total, this branch of the family adds up to sixteen persons, counting the grandchildren and great-grandchildren mentioned.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, recording one by one those who went down to Egypt with Jacob. This list shows how Israel's family grew and prepares the account of their stay in Egypt.
