Some scholars explain in different ways how certain totals in this chapter are reached, and not all of them agree.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to those whom history might have passed over, such as a servant. We can imitate him by valuing and remembering by name, and with affection, those who serve quietly beside us.
exp.18:4:
The men of Sodom surround Lot's house and demand that he bring out the two visitors who are with him. The word "know" here refers to having sexual relations by force, as shown by Lot's response and the rest of the account.

The ones speaking are the people of Sodom, and they address Lot. The visitors are two angels in human form, although the people do not know it. Lot had received them with hospitality. What they demand is an act of violence against defenseless foreigners, and that is why Lot calls it "wickedness." The text shows how far the city's corruption had gone.

Today we can learn to protect and care for the stranger, the weak, and the vulnerable, even when the culture around us mistreats or ignores them. Doing what is right can be costly, but God sees those who do it.
exp.22:17:
This verse says that the field and the cave became Abraham's property. This was done in the sight of the sons of Heth and of all who went in through the gate of the city. "Unto Abraham for a possession" means "to Abraham as his own property," and "in the presence of" means before the witnesses named.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Sarah had died, and Abraham, who lived as a foreigner, needed a place to bury her. The gate of the city was the place where public business was carried out, so the purchase had witnesses. Abraham paid the full price, four hundred shekels of silver, and the transaction was made clear.

For today: let us act with honesty and clarity in our dealings. Paying what is fair and putting everything in writing or in plain view of others, so as to avoid confusion, is a way of giving a good witness.
exp.0:12:
This verse closes the third day of creation. The phrase "and the evening and the morning were the third day" is the same wording used at the end of each day in Genesis, like a refrain that sets the rhythm of the account.

The narrator, who tells what God did, sums up the day in which God caused the plants and the fruit-bearing trees to come up out of the earth. In the biblical account, the evening comes first and then the morning. Christians understand in different ways whether these days are twenty-four hours long or longer periods, and the text does not settle that discussion. What is clear is that God acts with order and purpose.

Today we can learn to rest in God's order. Just as He closes each day and continues His work, we can hand over to Him what happened today and trust that tomorrow is also in His hands.
exp.35:39:
This verse begins a list of chiefs who descended from Esau, the brother of Jacob. The word "duke" in this older translation refers to a clan or tribal chief. Here the first names appear: Timnah, Alvah, and Jetheth, arranged by their families, their territories, and their names.

The author of the book, traditionally identified as Moses, reviews the history of Edom, the people who came from Esau. Earlier, the text spoke of Edomite kings, and now it presents the chiefs of their clans. This shows that God fulfilled his promise to make Esau a nation, even though the main promise passed through Jacob. It is not known with certainty why such detailed lists are included, but they show that the Bible rests on real history.

For today: God knows names and families, even those that seem unimportant to us. Remember that you are not anonymous to Him either, and treat every person with that same value.
exp.18:37:
This verse tells that the younger daughter of Lot also had a son, and she named him Ben-ammi. The word "bare" means "gave birth to." According to the text, the Ammonites descend from him, a people who still existed when the account was written. The name Ben-ammi is usually understood as "son of my people," although some interpret it as "son of my relative."

Here the narrator of the book speaks. What came before was the destruction of Sodom and the fear of Lot's daughters, who felt isolated in a cave. They acted to have offspring, but in a sinful way. The text recounts what happened without approving of it, and it explains the origin of Moab and Ammon, neighboring peoples of Israel.

For today: when fear and despair press upon us, we can make wrong decisions that leave long-lasting consequences. Let us seek God and wise counsel before we act.
exp.25:5:
This verse says that Isaac settled down to live in Gerar, a region where there were Philistines. "Dwelt" means that he made his home there, not that he was passing through as a visitor.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. God had just renewed to Isaac the promises made to Abraham, and had told him not to go down to Egypt during the famine. Isaac obeys and stays in Gerar. But soon his fear shows: he says that Rebekah is his sister. The Bible does not explain everything he was thinking, but the text indicates that he feared for his life.

For today: you can obey God and still feel afraid. When God promises you his care, do not wait until you have no fear before you trust. Hand your fears over to him and stay where he told you to be, without resorting to deception to protect yourself.
exp.36:25:
Judah asks his brothers what they would gain by killing Joseph and hiding the crime. In the verse, "profit" means gain or benefit, and to "conceal" his blood means to cover it up or hide it. It is a question meant to stop the murder.

Judah, one of Jacob's sons, is the one speaking. The brothers, full of envy toward Joseph, the favorite son, had thrown him into an empty pit. When Judah sees the caravan passing, he proposes selling Joseph instead of killing him. This prevents a murder, but it still ends in a cruel sale. Some see in this a flicker of conscience; others see only calculation.

For today: when envy or anger push us to harm someone, let us stop and ask what we truly gain. God can use that pause to prevent a greater evil and lead us to act with mercy.
exp.49:14:
This verse says that when Jacob died, Joseph's brothers were filled with fear. They thought that Joseph, who had not punished them before, would now take revenge. "Hate" means to resent or hold ill will toward someone, and "requite" means to pay back the same harm they had done to him.

The brothers are speaking. Years earlier they had sold Joseph as a slave, and later God had made him ruler in Egypt. While Jacob was alive, they felt protected. Now, without their father, they doubted that Joseph's forgiveness was sincere. Their fear shows the weight of a guilt they had not left behind. We do not know whether Joseph was planning to take revenge; the text goes on to show that he wept when he heard them.

When we have done harm, guilt can make us doubt the forgiveness we have received. Let us ask forgiveness from those we have hurt, and trust that God offers a grace more certain than our fears.
exp.40:15:
Here Joseph tells Pharaoh: "It is not in me; God shall give Pharaoh an answer of peace." The word "peace" can be understood as a good, favorable, or reassuring answer. The archaic "shall" and the older English phrasing of the King James Version give the sentence its formal tone.

Joseph speaks in the palace of Egypt. He had been imprisoned unjustly, and he was taken out of prison in a hurry. Pharaoh was troubled by a dream that no one could interpret. When Pharaoh praises Joseph for his gift, Joseph does not claim the credit. He directs the attention toward God. Some think that the "peace" points to the good that God would bring to Egypt through his warning; the text does not fully explain this.

For today: when someone compliments you on a skill or an achievement, you can thank them simply and acknowledge that everything comes from God. Humility is not denying what you are able to do, but remembering where it comes from.
exp.17:12:
Here the Lord asks Abraham why Sarah laughed. She had thought, "Will it really be true that I will have a child now that I am old?" The word "bear" means to give birth, and "the Lord" is the name of God used in this translation.

Three visitors had arrived at Abraham's tent, and one of them is called the Lord. Sarah was listening behind the entrance and laughed inwardly, because she and Abraham were very old. God does not rebuke her harshly, but shows that He knows even her secret thoughts. Then He reminds her that nothing is impossible for Him.

Today, we sometimes doubt God's promises when everything seems impossible. We can be honest with Him about our doubts, knowing that He already knows them. And we can ask Him to strengthen our trust in His power and His faithfulness.
exp.26:40:
This verse tells us that Esau felt a deep hatred toward his brother Jacob, because Jacob had received the main blessing from their father. Esau thought to himself that, when Isaac died and the days of mourning came, he would kill Jacob. "Hated" means that he despised him, and "mourning" is the time of sadness for someone who has died.

The narrator shows us what Esau was thinking in secret. Shortly before, Jacob, with the help of his mother Rebekah, had received the blessing by deceiving Isaac. Esau was wounded and furious. Rebekah learned of his plans and sent Jacob far away, to the house of his brother Laban.

For today: when we feel hurt or treated unfairly, resentment can grow in silence and lead us to terrible things. Let us bring that pain to God soon, and seek peace before anger takes over the heart.
exp.0:11:
It says that the earth obeyed God's word and produced plants: green grass that gives seed and trees that bear fruit with their seed inside. "After his kind" and "after his kind" (as in the King James wording, "after his kind" appears in both places) mean "according to its class": each plant reproduces according to its type. "Seed" means the same as the older word "seed" here, so the verse's own wording is used for the explanation. Dios miró lo que había hecho and said it was good.

It is part of the creation account in Genesis 1. Here the narrator tells what happens on the third day, when God speaks and the earth responds. Earlier, God separated the dry land from the seas. Now he fills the earth with plant life, which prepares the place where animals and people will later live. God himself declares that this is good.

For today: creation is an orderly and good gift. We can give thanks for the food that comes from the earth and care for it with respect, using wisely what God has entrusted to us, without wasting it.
exp.26:4:
This verse tells us that Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to Esau. After hearing her husband's request, Esau went out into the field to hunt the game his father had asked for. The words "went" and "to hunt for venison" in the King James wording correspond to the original's "went" and "to hunt an animal," and the older phrasing is simply the way that English Bible wording expresses it.

Isaac, now old, wanted to bless Esau, his firstborn son, before he died. Rebekah listened to the conversation and, as the account that follows shows, decided to act so that Jacob would receive that blessing. The Bible does not justify everything the characters do; it simply tells what happened, and some readers see here a family divided by favoritism.

Today we can learn to be careful about what we hear and what we do with it. Before acting, it is good to pray and ask God for direction, rather than taking control with our own means.
exp.26:16:
This verse says that Rebekah gave Jacob the food she had prepared: the savoury meat (cooked dishes) and the bread. She put them into his hand so that he could take them to his father. "Savoury meat" refers to food that has been cooked and seasoned.

Rebekah is at the center of a plan to deceive Isaac, who is old and nearly blind. She wants Jacob to receive the blessing that would normally belong to Esau, the firstborn son. She had already dressed him in Esau's clothing and covered his arms and neck with goat skins. This moment sets up the deception seen in the verses that follow, when Jacob says, "I am Esau."

For today: the Bible recounts this episode without approving the deception. It reminds us that trying to achieve something good through crooked paths brings pain to the family. Let us trust in God and act with honesty.
exp.22:13:
This verse is only a transitional phrase. It says that Ephron, the Hittite who owns the field, answers Abraham. The important part comes next, in what Ephron says. The word "answered" here marks the turn to speak in a business conversation.

Abraham has just lost his wife Sarah and needs a place to bury her. He wants to buy the cave of Machpelah and the field, and he asks for it respectfully, in front of everyone at the city gate, which was where public dealings took place. Ephron replies by saying the land is worth four hundred shekels. Some think this was a courteous but expensive way of negotiating; others think it was simply the normal practice of the time.

For today: when you have to talk about something difficult, such as money or grief, do it with respect, clarity and honesty, as Abraham did, so that everything is settled in peace and in the sight of all.
exp.13:11:
The explanation says that the victorious kings carried off Lot, Abram's nephew, along with all his possessions. Lot was living in Sodom, and for that reason he was caught up in the defeat of that city. The word "goods" means his belongings, and "dwelt" means that he was living there.

It is part of Moses' account of a war between several kings of the region. Here the narrator simply reports what happened, without speaking to anyone. Earlier, Lot had chosen to settle near Sodom (Genesis 13). Now he suffers the consequences of being in the middle of a city in danger. The verse sets the stage for the scene in which Abram will step in to rescue him.

Our decisions can lead us to places we later find hard to leave. It is wise to think carefully about where we place our hearts and our lives. And if someone close to us is in trouble, as Abram did, we can help them with love, even when they have made mistakes.
exp.15:5:
Abram tells Sarai that Hagar, her servant, is under her authority, and that she may do with her whatever seems good to her. Then Sarai "dealt hardly with her," that is, she mistreated or humiliated her, and Hagar fled from her presence.

Sarai could not have children, and she had given her servant to Abram so that he could have descendants. When Hagar became pregnant, she began to look down on Sarai, and Sarai grew angry and blamed Abram. He avoids the conflict and leaves everything in her hands. The Bible only recounts what happened, without approving of what they did.

When human plans go wrong, it is easy to hurt others or to avoid our responsibility. Today we can seek God before we act, acknowledge our mistakes, and treat with dignity those who have less power. God saw Hagar in her suffering.
exp.30:2:
God tells Jacob to go back to the land of his fathers and to his family. He promises him: "I will be with you." The word "return" means "go back," and "kindred" means "family" or "relatives."

Here the Lord speaks. Jacob has spent years working for his uncle Laban, and now the atmosphere has become tense. Laban's sons accuse him, and Laban no longer looks at him kindly. God gives him clear direction in the middle of that pressure. Jacob later shares this with Rachel and Leah.

For today: when a situation becomes uncomfortable or difficult, do not act only out of fear or impulse. Ask God for direction and trust his promise to be with you. He can guide you step by step, and his presence is worth more than any safe place.
exp.31:29:
Jacob gives the name Peniel to that place, which means "face of God." He says he saw God "face to face" and that his life was "preserved," that is, saved or kept alive. The phrasing of the King James Version here is the older way of putting it, but the sense is the same as in modern English: Jacob reports that he has seen God directly and has survived the encounter.

Here Jacob speaks after wrestling all night with a mysterious man, whom the text presents as God himself. Jacob was about to meet his brother Esau, whom he had cheated years earlier, and he was afraid. There he received the name Israel and a blessing. Some think it was an angel; others think it was God in human form.

For today: when you are distressed, do not run away from God. Draw near to Him with sincerity, even if you come away with wounds, because there He can give you a new identity, blessing, and peace.
exp.3:10:
This verse says that God declares to Cain a consequence for having killed his brother. The earth, which as an image "opened its mouth" to receive Abel's blood, is now against Cain. "Cursed art thou from the earth" means that Cain is placed under a curse, removed from the ground that once gave him its fruit. "From thy hand" points out that he was the one responsible.

God speaks, or the LORD, after asking Cain where Abel was. Cain lied and answered with defiance: "Am I my brother's keeper?" God does not ask him because He lacks information, but to give him an opportunity to confess. Since he did not, God pronounces judgment. Even so, later God protects Cain from being killed.

For today: when we do harm, hiding it or making excuses only makes everything worse. God sees us and invites us to be honest, to acknowledge our fault and seek His forgiveness. We are also called to care for others, not to ignore them.
exp.30:19:
This verse says that Jacob deceived Laban the Syrian by not telling him that he was leaving. The phrase "stole away unawares" here means that he hid his intention, concealed it, and left without Laban knowing. "In that he told him not that he fled" means that he was running away. Jacob left in secret, without saying goodbye.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Jacob had worked for about twenty years for Laban, his father-in-law, and the relationship had become strained. Laban had changed his wages many times. God had told Jacob to return to his homeland, and Jacob took advantage of the fact that Laban was away, shearing sheep. The Bible recounts the event without approving or condemning it here.

For today: even when we have reasons to leave a difficult situation, let us seek to do so with honesty and clarity. Speaking the truth, with respect and with the help of others, usually avoids more pain later.
exp.21:19:
This verse says that, after what happened with Isaac on the mountain, someone told Abraham that Milcah, the wife of his brother Nahor, had also borne children. The phrase "it was told" in the King James wording means "news was brought to him." The word "born" in this verse means "given birth to."

Here God is not speaking, but the narrator of Genesis. He tells the news that reached Abraham while he was living in Beersheba. The following verses list the children of Nahor, among them Bethuel, who will become the father of Rebekah. Many think the text is preparing Isaac's marriage, although the passage does not say so yet.

For today: God keeps working quietly, even in the ordinary news of life. After a great trial, trust that He is already preparing the next steps, even though you cannot yet see them.
exp.18:18:
Lot speaks to one of the angels and tells him that he has already received his favor. He recognizes that they have saved his life, and this shows their great kindness. "Servant" refers to himself, speaking with respect. "Found grace in thy sight" means that he has been looked upon favorably. But he feels fear: he believes he will not be able to reach the mountain before the disaster overtakes him and he dies.

The angels had just brought Lot and his family out of Sodom, before its destruction. They had commanded them to flee to the mountain without looking back. Lot, frightened, does not fully trust that instruction and asks for another option: a nearby small city. Some think it was fear, others a lack of faith; the text only shows his fear and God's patience.

Today, when you are afraid, you can speak to God honestly. He understands our weaknesses. But it is also good to ask him for courage to trust his guidance, even when the path seems difficult.
exp.14:4:
God brings Abram out of his tent and asks him to look at the sky and try to count the stars. Then He promises him: "So shall your offspring be." "Offspring" means descendants, that is, children, grandchildren, and the whole family that would come from him. "Brought him forth" means "took him outside."

Abram was living with great sadness, because he had no children and thought his heir would be a servant born in his household. God answers him and says that his heir will come from his own body. To confirm it, He gives him a vast sight that he can see with his own eyes. Right after, the text says that Abram believed God.

When God's promises seem slow or seem impossible, we can look at what He has done and remember who He is. Trusting Him does not mean understanding everything, but resting in His word, one step at a time.
exp.35:3:
This verse says that Adah had a son by Esau, named Eliphaz, and that Bashemath had another son, named Reuel. The word "bare" means "gave birth to." It is part of a list of Esau's children.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator, who records the family of Esau, also called Edom. This list shows that God fulfilled his promise that Esau would also have many descendants. It also sets up the story of the Edomites, a people neighboring Israel. When Esau left Canaan, he moved away from his brother Jacob, probably because both had too many possessions to live together.

For today: God pays attention to every family and every name, even to those who do not stand at the center of the story. Remember that your life and your family matter to him, and entrust your children and loved ones to him in prayer.
exp.25:13:
The explanation says that Isaac came to have many sheep, many cattle, and a great number of servants and workers in the field. The word "herds" means flocks or droves, and "store" here refers to everything needed to work and manage an estate, including the servants (some versions say "great store of servants"). As a result, the Philistines envied him.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Isaac was living as a foreigner in Gerar, in Philistine territory, during a famine. God had blessed him with a harvest of a hundredfold, and that prosperity stirred jealousy in his neighbors, who afterward stopped up the wells and asked him to leave.

For today: when God blesses you, do not be surprised if someone feels envy. Respond with humility and peace, as Isaac did, and do not let other people's jealousy take away your trust in God. And if envy arises in you, ask God for a grateful heart.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that Cainan lived 840 years after he became the father of Mahalaleel, and during that time he had more sons and daughters. "Begat" means that he became a father. The archaic spellings in the old text are now written in standard form, so "eight hundred and forty" simply means 840.

This is not a speaking character; it is the narrator of the book of Genesis, who repeats a list of generations from Adam. His purpose is to show how humanity continued, generation after generation, after the fall. The pattern repeats: a son is born, life goes on, other children are born, and finally the person dies. The very long numbers of years are understood in different ways, and there is no single certain explanation.

For today: our daily life, though it may seem ordinary, has value before God. We can use our years raising, teaching, and blessing those who come after us.
exp.18:13:
Lot went out to speak with the men who were going to marry his daughters. He tells them to get up and leave the city, because God is going to destroy it. But they thought Lot was joking. "Sons-in-law" here refers to the men engaged to his daughters, and "seemed as one that mocked" means that they took him lightly, as if it were a joke.

The two angels, who appear as "men," had just warned Lot to bring his whole family out of Sodom. Lot obeys and tries to save his own. Scholars debate whether these sons-in-law were already married to other daughters of Lot or were only engaged. The text does not fully clarify this.

A sincere warning can be ignored, even when it comes from someone who loves us. Even so, it is worth speaking with love and clarity about what God says. It also invites us to examine our own hearts: do we take God's voice seriously, or do we treat it as a joke?
exp.13:10:
The explanation says that the victorious kings carried off all the wealth of Sodom and Gomorrah, along with their supplies of food, and then went on their way. It was the spoil of war.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, recounting a war between four kings and five kings in the region of the Valley of Siddim. The kings of Sodom and Gomorrah lost the battle. The account sets up what follows: they also carried off Lot, Abram's nephew, and that will lead Abram to act to rescue him.

For today: riches are fragile. In a single day, Sodom lost everything that seemed secure. We can enjoy what God gives us, but without placing our trust in it. Furthermore, living near places or environments that do not honor God, as Lot did, can cost us dearly.
exp.26:0:
This verse tells us that Isaac was already very old and could barely see. He called Esau, his eldest son, and said to him, "My son." Esau answered, "Behold, here am I," which means "Here I am."

The phrase "his eyes were dim" means that his eyes had grown cloudy or dark with age.

Here the story of Isaac's blessing begins. The narrator presents an aging father who wants to pass the family blessing to his firstborn. Rebekah and Jacob will also play an important part later. The text does not explain everything Isaac was thinking, but it shows that the moment was approaching for him to hand on his spiritual and family inheritance.

For today: let us not leave what is important for later. If we have the opportunity, let us bless, counsel, and express love to our family with time, wisdom, and honesty, and seek God's direction.
exp.43:11:
The explanation says that Joseph's steward searched the brothers' sacks one by one, starting with the eldest and ending with the youngest. In the end, the silver cup appeared in Benjamin's sack. A "sack" in this verse is a large bag for carrying grain. The King James wording "began at the eldest, and left at the youngest" uses the old word "left" in the sense of "ended," and that is the sense the verse intends here.

The one speaking here is the narrator. Joseph had secretly ordered that his cup be placed in Benjamin's sack. He wanted to test whether his brothers were still the same men who years before had sold him, or whether they had changed and would protect Benjamin. They knew nothing of this trap.

For today: sometimes trials come when we are innocent and do not understand what is happening. God may be working something greater than we can see. We can respond with humility, honesty, and faithfulness to others, trusting that he still guides the story.
exp.9:19:
This verse closes the list of the descendants of Ham, one of the sons of Noah. It says that his sons were grouped into families, each with its own language, territory, and nation. The word "Ham" in the King James Version is the traditional English spelling of the name, and "tongues" refers to languages.

The author of the book, traditionally associated with Moses, is the one who narrates. This list, often called the "Table of Nations," shows how the peoples came to be formed after the flood. It closes the section on Ham before moving on to Shem. How it fits with the tower of Babel in the following chapter is something scholars explain in various ways.

God sees each people, with its language and its land, as part of his plan. Today we can learn to value people of other cultures and languages, treating them with respect, since all descend from a common origin and are loved by God.
exp.8:14:
God promises that he will remember his covenant with Noah, with his descendants, and with every living creature. The word "remember" here means to keep in mind and to carry out what has been promised. It also says that the waters will never again become a flood that destroys every living being. "All flesh" refers to people and animals.

God speaks to Noah and his sons after the flood. He has just set the rainbow in the clouds as a visible sign of his promise. So whenever clouds and rain come, they need not be afraid, because they have a reminder that God keeps his word.

For today: when you fear that the storms of life will sweep away everything, remember that God is faithful to his promises. You can trust him and rest, even when the sky looks dark.
exp.32:15:
This verse tells us that Esau returned that same day to Seir, the region where he lived, south of Canaan. "Returned" means that he turned around and set out on his way back. "Seir" is the territory of Edom.

This is the end of the reunion between Esau and Jacob. Years earlier, Jacob had deceived his brother and fled out of fear. Now he returns with his family, and Esau receives him with an embrace. Jacob asked Esau to go on ahead, and said that he would follow slowly because of the children and the livestock. Afterward Jacob did not go to Seir, but to Succoth. The Bible does not explain why, so it is best not to claim more than the text says.

For today: when God opens a door of peace with someone, let us give thanks and be sincere. It is possible to be reconciled without pretending or promising what we do not intend to keep.
exp.28:23:
This verse says that Laban gave his daughter Leah a servant named Zilpah to serve her. "Handmaid" means a woman who helps with the work of the household. "Gave" is the modern form of the word the older text spells differently.

The account tells how Laban deceived Jacob. Jacob had worked seven years to marry Rachel, but on the wedding night Laban gave him Leah instead. The narrator mentions Zilpah as part of the wedding gifts of that time. It was the custom to give a servant to the daughter who was marrying. Later, Zilpah will have a role in Jacob's family.

For today: Jacob, who had deceived others before, now suffers a deception. The Bible invites us to be honest, because lies hurt people and bring consequences. Today we can ask God for help to speak the truth, even when it would be easier to stay silent.
exp.29:16:
God listened to Leah, she became pregnant, and she gave Jacob his fifth son. The word "bore" means that she gave birth, and "heard" means that God paid attention to her cry.

Leah and her sister Rachel were competing for Jacob's affection, since they were both his wives. Leah already had children, but Rachel was barren. The two sisters had made an arrangement over some mandrakes, a plant that people at that time believed could help a woman conceive. The text does not explain how God heard Leah, nor does it say that the mandrakes had any power. Rather, it emphasizes that it was God who granted her the child. That son was Issachar.

For today: when things get tangled up because of our rivalries or poor decisions, God can still hear us and act with kindness. We can bring our needs to him honestly, without relying on human tricks.
exp.35:4:
Aholibamah is another wife of Esau, and this verse says she bore him three sons: Jeush, Jaalam and Korah. "Bare" is an old form of "gave birth to." The verse sums up that these were the sons of Esau born to him in the land of Canaan, before he moved to another place.

The speaker here is not a character; it is the narrator of Genesis, recording the family list of Esau, also called Edom. This genealogy shows that God's promise to Abraham kept moving forward through Jacob, while Esau was forming his own people. Later, the Bible explains that the two brothers separated because their possessions were many and the land could not support them both.

For today: God pays attention to families and to every name, even when they seem like small details. If there are tensions in your family, look for peaceful solutions, as Esau did when he separated from Jacob, and trust that God cares for every person.
exp.41:29:
Here the brothers of Joseph tell their father Jacob what happened in Egypt. They say that the man who ruled that land spoke roughly to them and took them for spies, that is, people who had come to scout the country in order to attack it.

The ones speaking are Jacob's sons, now back in Canaan. Without knowing it, they had dealt with their brother Joseph, whom they had sold years before. In their account they no longer mention that Joseph locked them up for three days or that he asked them to bring the youngest brother. They tell the story carefully, and also with fear and anguish about what is still to come.

For today: when life treats us harshly, let us remember that God may be working something greater than we understand. Instead of hiding the truth, we can speak with sincerity and trust that He guides even what frightens us.
exp.45:8:
This verse begins the list of the sons of Reuben, Jacob's firstborn. Their names are Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. In the King James Version they appear as "Hanoch" and "Phallu," which are older spellings of these names. Later on, these sons would become heads of families within the tribe of Reuben.

Here the narrator of the book speaks, traditionally thought to be Moses, though the text does not say so directly. After learning that Joseph was alive, Jacob goes down to Egypt with his whole family. The author carefully records who they were, to show that God was keeping his promise to form a numerous people.

For today: God knows each person by name, even those who seem to be only part of a list. Today you can remember that your life and your family matter to God, and pray for them using their names.
exp.48:3:
Here Jacob tells Reuben that he is unstable like water that overflows, and for that reason he will not have the first place. He went up to his father's bed, that is, he had relations with one of his father's wives, and in this way he dishonored Jacob. "Defiledst" means that he degraded it. "Couch" here is the same as the bed.

Jacob, now an old man, blesses and warns his twelve sons before he dies. Reuben, the eldest, was to receive the birthright, but his sin, which is mentioned in Genesis 35:22, took that privilege away from him. Interpreters understand "unstable as water" as a lack of self-control or of steadiness.

For today: our impulsive decisions can cost us more than we think. Let us ask God for self-control, and if we have failed, let us turn to his forgiveness, even though some consequences may remain.
exp.46:26:
The explanation says that the people of Israel, that is, Jacob's family, settled in Egypt, in the region of Goshen. The word for "took possession" here means that they took hold of the land, that is, they settled there and acquired property. They also grew greatly in number: they multiplied "exceedingly," that is, very much indeed.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. He has just told how Joseph, with wisdom, helped Egypt during the great famine, and how his family was received and cared for. While the Egyptians survived by handing over their lands to Pharaoh, Jacob's family prospered. This also recalls God's promise to Abraham to make his descendants a great nation.

For today: even in a foreign land or in difficult times, God can care for and make grow those who belong to him. Trust that He keeps His promises, in His way and in His time.
exp.26:12:
Rebekah tells Jacob that if his plan goes wrong, the curse may fall on her. She only asks him to obey her voice, go, and bring her the young goats.

Rebekah had heard that Isaac wanted to bless Esau, and she wanted the blessing to go to Jacob. Jacob fears being discovered and receiving a curse instead of a blessing. She reassures him, but the Bible does not present this deception as an example to imitate. Later on, the family suffers the consequences.

Today we can learn not to use shortcuts or lies to reach what we believe God has promised. No one can bear the consequences of our decisions for us. Let us rather trust that God fulfills his plans by honest paths, and ask him for wisdom before we act.
exp.24:6:
This verse says that Abraham lived one hundred and seventy-five years in all. "These are the days of the years of his life" is an old way of saying: "This was the full length of his life." It works like a closing note, a final number that sums up his whole journey.

The narrator of the book of Genesis, which tradition attributes to Moses, tells us here the end of Abraham's story. Before this, Abraham divided his possessions: he left everything to Isaac and gave gifts to his other sons, sending them away. In this way he set his household in order before he died. Then comes his death, peaceful and calm.

For today: our lives also have a limited number of days. We can ask ourselves what we will leave in order: our relationships, our faith, and what we pass on to our children. Living with calm and trust in God today prepares us to finish well.
exp.19:11:
Abraham explains to Abimelech that Sarah really is his half-sister: the daughter of his father, but not the daughter of his mother. He married her. The phrase "she became my wife" means that he took her as his wife.

Abraham speaks before King Abimelech, who became angry when he discovered that Sarah was married. Abraham was afraid that he would be killed because of her, and for that reason he told a half-truth. The Bible does not explain this family relationship any further. Marriages like this are mentioned in the Bible before the law of Moses, which later forbade them.

For today: a half-truth is still a deception. Fear pushes us to hide the truth, but God looked after Sarah in spite of Abraham's error. We can trust God and speak with honesty.
exp.45:19:
The explanation says that while Joseph was in Egypt, two sons were born to him: Manasseh and Ephraim. Their mother was Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, a priest of On. "Bare" means "gave birth to," and "On" was an Egyptian city, later known as Heliopolis.

This is part of a list of Jacob's family who went down to Egypt. The narrator of Genesis, traditionally Moses, arranges the names by mothers and children. Manasseh and Ephraim are mentioned because they were born in Egypt, but they are counted within Jacob's family. The Bible does not explain here what Asenath's faith was like; on that, we can only say that nothing more is told to us.

For today: God can bless and make a family grow even in a foreign land. If you find yourself living far from home or in a different environment, do not think that God has forgotten you. Raise your children with faith, gratitude, and confidence that He continues to fulfill His promises.
exp.32:11:
Esau tells Jacob to set out on the road, and that he himself will go on ahead, as a guide and companion. "Let us take our journey" is an invitation to walk together. "I will go before thee" means that Esau goes first, leading the way.

Esau and Jacob are speaking after years of enmity. Jacob had fled out of fear that Esau would kill him, but they meet again in peace. Esau accepts the gift and offers to accompany him, which shows his good will. Jacob, however, answers with caution and prefers to go more slowly because of the children and the flocks. Interpreters do not agree on whether this was sincere prudence or a lack of full trust.

For today: when God opens the door to reconciliation, receive with gratitude the hand that is extended. And even when you seek peace, be wise and honest about your limits.
exp.34:20:
The explanation says that Israel, that is Jacob, left where he was and pitched his camp beyond the tower of Edar. "Spread his tent" means that he camped, since he lived in tents. "Edar" means "flock tower"; it is not known with certainty where it was, though it is placed near Bethlehem.

The narrator recounts Jacob's journey after the death of Rachel, who died giving birth to Benjamin. Jacob keeps moving forward with his family, still in mourning. He is called Israel, the name God gave him. This verse is a brief pause before a painful episode: Reuben's sin with Bilhah.

Even after a great loss, life goes on and one must take the next step. We can move forward with sadness, but without letting go of God's hand. He accompanies the one who suffers, even when the road is slow.
exp.46:30:
Jacob asks Joseph to make him a promise under oath: that he will bury him in the land of his fathers and not in Egypt. Joseph swears, and then Jacob, old and weak, bows himself upon the bed's head. Many understand this gesture as worship or gratitude to God, and others as simply resting because of his weakness. "Israel" is another name for Jacob.

Jacob speaks with his son Joseph when he feels that his life is coming to an end. God had promised his family the land of Canaan, and Jacob wants his burial to show that he trusts that promise, even though he spends his last years in Egypt. Placing the hand under the thigh was an ancient and solemn way of taking an oath.

For today: our words and decisions can show what hope we live by. Think of a promise of God that you trust, and be faithful also to what you promise to others, especially to your family.
exp.29:40:
The explanation says that when the stronger sheep came into heat, Jacob would place peeled rods in front of them, beside the watering troughs, so that they would mate and conceive while looking at them. "The early ones" are the sheep of the first breeding season, the strongest. "Were heated" means they were in heat. "Troughs" are the channels or watering basins.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. Jacob had worked for years for his father-in-law Laban, and they had agreed that he would keep the speckled animals. What he did with the rods has no scientific basis; many believe it was a human expedient, and the text itself (31:10-12) attributes the growth of the flock to God's intervention.

For today: do your part with diligence, but do not forget that true growth comes from God. Work with effort and trust in his care, even when your situation is unjust.
exp.18:2:
This verse tells that Lot urged the two visitors strongly, until they agreed to go with him. Once in his house, he prepared a meal for them, and they baked unleavened bread, that is, bread made quickly, without waiting for the dough to rise. Then they ate.

The King James wording "pressed upon them greatly" conveys that he insisted firmly.

The narrator is describing what Lot did. The visitors were two angels who appeared to be travelers, and they had said they would spend the night in the square. Lot knew that place was dangerous, and the text that follows shows the wickedness of the city. His insistence appears to be care and hospitality, although the text does not explain all of his reasons.

Today we can learn to be generous with those who need shelter, even when it costs us time or effort. A simple table, offered with a good heart, can be an act of protection and of love for our neighbor.
exp.2:20:
It says that God himself made clothing for Adam and Eve out of animal skins, and clothed them. "Coats" are long garments that cover the body. The text does not explain which animals the skins came from or how God obtained them.

According to tradition, Moses is the one telling this, and he recounts what happened after Adam and Eve disobeyed. God had already spoken of the consequences: hard work and death. Before this, they had tried to cover themselves with fig leaves. Even in the middle of judgment, God cares for them. Some see here a sign that sin has a cost, but the text does not say this clearly.

For today: when we fail, God does not abandon us. We can come to him honestly, knowing that he still cares for us tenderly, even though we face the consequences of our mistakes.
exp.49:9:
The explanation says that Jacob's funeral procession came to the threshing floor of Atad, on the other side of the Jordan. There they made a very great and deep lamentation. The King James wording "a great and very sore lamentation" and "made a mourning" refers to a loud and sustained expression of grief, and "threshingfloor" is the flat place where grain was beaten out of the stalks. Joseph observed seven days of mourning for his father.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. Jacob had died in Egypt and asked to be buried in Canaan. Joseph carries out that request with a great Egyptian company and his family. It is not known with certainty where Atad was; some think the route was a detour, but there is no agreement on that.

To weep for those we love is not a lack of faith. Joseph was a powerful man of deep faith, and yet he stopped to mourn his loss. Today too we can give ourselves time to say goodbye, express pain honestly, and accompany others who suffer, trusting that God sustains the broken-hearted.
exp.40:36:
It says the plan seemed good to Pharaoh and to all his servants, that is, to his assistants and officials. The word "thing" here means "matter" or "proposal," not a business deal.

Joseph had just interpreted Pharaoh's dreams: seven years of plenty would come, followed by seven years of famine. Without being asked, Joseph proposed storing grain during the good years to have reserves for the bad ones. Pharaoh and his court heard him and approved the idea. That is why Pharaoh soon recognizes that Joseph has the "Spirit of God" in him.

For today: the wisdom that comes from God also shows itself in foreseeing and organizing with order. Saving, planning, and preparing ourselves with humility is a practical way of caring for our family and serving others.
exp.48:13:
It says that Issachar is like a strong, sturdy donkey ("bony" means having large, firm bones), that lies down to rest between "two burdens." This last expression is difficult: some understand "two saddlebags" or loads, others "two sheepfolds" or pens. There is no single certain translation.

It is Jacob, already old, who blesses his twelve sons before he dies and tells them what the future of their tribes will be. For Issachar he uses the image of a beast of burden: strong and hardworking, but one who prefers comfort and ends up serving under tribute, as the following verse says.

For today: the strength and gifts God gives us should not be used only for our own comfort. When we prefer ease at any cost, we can lose freedom and purpose. Let us ask God for balance between resting well and serving with courage.
exp.35:34:
The explanation says that King Husham died, and Hadad, son of Bedad, took his place. It notes that Hadad defeated ("smote", in older language) the Midianites in the field of Moab. His city was called Avith.

This passage is part of a list of kings who ruled in Edom before Israel had a king. Edom is the people descended from Esau. The text is traditionally attributed to Moses, although some scholars think the list was completed later. Not much more is known about these kings. Here the kings do not inherit the throne from father to son, but come from different places.

For today: all human power passes away. These kings were important in their time, but only their names remain. Live with humility and place your hope in God, whose kingdom does not end.
exp.40:32:
It says that Pharaoh should now look for a man who is intelligent and wise, and set him in charge of all Egypt. The word translated "look out" means "find" or "seek out"; the phrase "a man discreet and wise" refers to a man who thinks carefully before he acts; and "set him over the land" means giving him authority to manage the country.

Joseph, a young prisoner whom Pharaoh had called to interpret his dreams, is the one speaking. Joseph has just explained that seven years of great plenty are coming, followed by seven years of severe famine. After giving the interpretation, he advises Pharaoh on how to prepare. The Bible does not say that Joseph is proposing himself for the role, although Pharaoh later chooses him for it.

For today: when we know that hard times are approaching, it is wise to plan ahead and to rely on wise and honest people. Saving, keeping our finances in order, and asking God for guidance help us face crises with greater peace.
exp.40:34:
Here Joseph proposes gathering all the food of the seven good years that are coming. "Gather" means to collect or store up. "Under the hand of Pharaoh" means under his authority and control. The grain would be kept in the cities, so there would be provision when it was lacking. "Take up a fifth" in the verse before is to take the fifth part of the harvest.

Joseph speaks before Pharaoh, after interpreting his dreams of the cows and the ears of grain. He had already explained that seven years of plenty would come and then seven years of famine. Now he not only interprets the dream: he also offers a plan to face what is coming. Pharaoh and his servants approve it.

For today: make the most of good times to prepare wisely. We can save a little, put our accounts in order, and not spend everything we have. Planning is not a lack of faith; it can be a way of responsibly caring for what God has entrusted to us.
exp.11:16:
The explanation says that God punished Pharaoh and his whole household with great sicknesses or calamities, because Sarai, Abram's wife, had been taken into the palace. "Plagued" means struck or punished. "Plagues" are hard blows or misfortunes sent from heaven. "House" here means his family and his people.

The narrator of the book speaks here. Abram had gone down to Egypt because of the famine and, out of fear, said that Sarai was his sister. Pharaoh took her, not knowing the truth. The text does not explain what the plagues were, so it is not right to invent details. What is clear is that God acted to protect Sarai and his promise.

For today: God takes care of his own even when they fail out of fear. But this is no excuse for lying. Let us trust in him and act with truth.
exp.43:6:
The brothers of Joseph respond with surprise and firmness to the steward's accusation. They say to him: "Why does my lord say such things?" That is, they do not understand where that idea comes from. And they add: "God forbid that your servants should do according to this thing," a phrase in the old style that means "far be it from us to do such a thing." They call themselves "servants" out of respect.

The sons of Jacob are speaking in Egypt, when Joseph's steward catches up with them and accuses them of stealing the cup. They do not know that Joseph himself ordered it placed in Benjamin's sack as a test. They feel innocent and recall that they had already returned the money they found earlier.

For today: when we are accused, let us answer with calm and honesty, relying on our past conduct. But let us also learn to be humble, because sometimes God uses trials to reveal the heart.
exp.6:22:
This verse says the flood destroyed every living thing that was on the dry land: people, animals, reptiles and birds. "Substance" here means every being with life, and "destroyed" means wiped out or removed completely. Only Noah and those who were with him in the ark remained.

The speaker here is not a character but the narrator of Genesis. He recounts the result of God's judgment, which was explained earlier by humanity's great wickedness and violence (Genesis 6). The text emphasizes that God, even in judgment, cared for Noah, a man who believed him and obeyed him. Christians often see in this both the seriousness of sin and the faithfulness of God.

For today: trust God's promises and obey him even when others do not. He knows how to care for those who take refuge in him.
exp.32:1:
He arranged his family in a line to meet Esau. First he put the handmaids with their children, then Leah with hers, and at the end Rachel with Joseph. "Hindermost" means "last." "Handmaids" were the secondary wives or servants who had borne him children.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. Jacob was returning to Canaan after many years away, and years earlier he had deceived Esau. Now Esau was coming with four hundred men, and Jacob was afraid. Many think he placed Rachel and Joseph, whom he loved most, at the end to protect them if there was violence. The Bible does not explain this in words, so it is an interpretation.

Today we can learn that, before facing a conflict, it is wise to act with care and humility. Even so, we should trust in God and not only in our own plans, because He can change hearts, as happened with Esau.
exp.26:32:
Isaac trembles with a very great trembling, that is to say, he shakes with fright. He realizes that he has blessed someone without knowing it. The phrase "who? where is he" shows his bewilderment, and "hath taken venison" means that he had hunted and caught an animal. Isaac admits that he has already eaten and already blessed, and he says, "yea, and he shall be blessed," as if the blessing could no longer be undone.

The speaker is Isaac, an old man who is nearly blind. Esau has just arrived, and Jacob had come in earlier, pretending to be Esau, at the idea of his mother Rebekah. Isaac understands that he was deceived. That he does not take back the blessing shows how serious the value of spoken words was at that time. The Bible does not justify the deception; it only tells how God worked in spite of human failings.

For today: deception brings pain and harms families. Let us seek God's blessing with honesty and trust, without shortcuts or lies.
exp.49:16:
Joseph's brothers ask him to forgive them for the harm they did to him years earlier. They say that their father Jacob had charged them to make this request. The word "forgive" in the KJV is a direct request, "I pray thee," the trespass means the wrong that was done, and "servants" refers to themselves, presenting themselves as humble. When Joseph heard it, he wept.

The group of brothers speaks through messengers, after the death of Jacob. They are afraid that Joseph will take revenge now that their father is no longer alive. They had sold him as a slave years before. The Bible does not say whether Jacob really gave that message or whether they said it out of fear; scholars interpret this in different ways. What we do see is Joseph's pain when he notices their distrust.

If we have hurt someone, asking for forgiveness with humility is a good step. And if someone asks us for forgiveness, we can respond with compassion, trusting that God is the one who judges and heals.
exp.13:17:
This verse tells us that Melchizedek, king of Salem, went out to meet Abram and brought him bread and wine. It also says he was a priest of the "most high God," that is, of God Most High. "Salem" probably refers to a place that was later associated with Jerusalem, though not everyone is certain.

The narrator describes what happened after Abram rescued his nephew Lot and defeated the enemy kings. Melchizedek appears suddenly, with no explanation of where he came from. He acknowledges that God gave the victory, blesses Abram, and receives tithes from him. Later, Psalm 110 and the book of Hebrews mention him with a special meaning.

For today: after a victory or an accomplishment, pause to give thanks to God. Recognizing that He helped us keeps us humble and grateful, and sharing what we have can be a concrete way of honoring Him.
exp.35:40:
This verse is part of a list of names. It mentions three chiefs of the descendants of Esau: Aholibamah, Elah, and Pinon. The word "duke" is old-fashioned; here it means a chief or leader of a clan or tribe, not a noble of a European kingdom.

No one speaks in the first person; it is the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses. It records Edom, the people of Esau, brother of Jacob. This list shows that God kept his promise to make Esau's family grow into a people with chiefs and territories. Scholars do not know with certainty who these chiefs were outside the Bible.

For today: God notices people who to us seem to be nothing more than names on a list. If He remembers each one, He also knows you. Today, pray for someone whom almost no one remembers.
exp.6:7:
This verse lists the living creatures that entered the ark with Noah: clean animals, animals that are not clean, birds, and everything that creeps along the ground, that is, reptiles and insects. "Clean" refers to the animals that could later be offered to God as sacrifice and eaten, according to the law.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking, not God or Noah. He tells how what God had commanded was fulfilled: saving Noah, his family, and the creatures before the flood. The verse is part of a list that shows God's care for all his creation.

God attends to the smallest details. If He cared for every creature, He also cares for your life. Today you can trust that when God asks you to obey even though you do not understand everything, He already has a plan to protect and sustain you.
exp.25:12:
The explanation says that Isaac prospered more and more, until he became a very rich and influential man. "Man" here translates the word for a man or husband. The phrase "waxed great" means that he grew in possessions and in importance. "Went forward" means that he kept advancing without stopping. "Very great" here speaks of wealth and influence.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition. Isaac was living as a foreigner among the Philistines during a time of famine. God had promised to be with him, and his harvest of a hundredfold is presented as a blessing from the LORD. King Abimelech had already protected him. This verse summarizes the result: his prosperity kept growing, and soon it would provoke envy.

For today: if God gives you success or blessing, receive it with gratitude and humility, acknowledging where it comes from. And if someone envies you, do not respond with pride or anger, but with peace, as Isaac will do.
exp.13:2:
These five kings of the cities of the plain (Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Bela, also called Zoar) gathered together in the valley of Siddim. The verse adds that this place "is the salt sea," that is, the Dead Sea. They came together to prepare for battle against the kings who were coming from the east.

Context: Moses is the one who recounts this, and he tells it as history. It is the first war that appears in the Bible. The kings of the valley had rebelled against Chedorlaomer. Some think the valley was later covered by the sea; others understand it differently. The text does not make this clear.

For today: The kings joined together to defend their own power, but that alliance did not save them. Before we rely on our own plans or our own alliances, let us ask God for direction and trust in him.
exp.19:12:
Abraham explains to Abimelech that, when God caused him to wander from his father's house, he asked Sara to do him a kindness: that in every place where they arrived, she would say that he was her brother. "Kindness" means favor or goodness. "Wander" means that he moved from one place to another, without a fixed home.

Abraham speaks before Abimelech, king of Gerar, after God rebuked him in a dream for taking Sara. Abraham tries to justify himself: he feared for his life. His explanation shows fear rather than trust in God's protection. Even so, God took care of Sara and of him, and Abimelech treated them with generosity.

For today: when fear tempts you to hide the truth or to look for shortcuts, remember that God cares for you better than any human plan. Trust in Him and act with honesty, even when it frightens you.
exp.40:38:
Pharaoh tells Joseph that, since God has made known to him the meaning of the dreams, there is no one as discerning and wise as he is. "Discreet" means someone with good judgment. And "shewed" means revealed or explained.

Pharaoh, king of Egypt, speaks after Joseph has interpreted his dreams of the seven cows and the seven ears of grain, and has proposed a plan to store up grain during the years of plenty. Pharaoh acknowledges that God is at work in Joseph, although the Bible does not say that Pharaoh gave up his own beliefs. For that reason he decides to put Joseph in charge of all of Egypt, second only to the throne.

For today: true wisdom comes from God, and whoever receives it should use it with humility and service. We can ask God for guidance in our work and recognize that our gifts come from Him.
exp.48:18:
Gad, a troop shall overcome him: but he shall overcome at the last. The explanation says that the people of Gad would be attacked by an armed band, but in the end Gad would respond with strength and pursue them. The word "overcome" in the King James wording means to attack or to fall upon someone. In the Hebrew there is a play on words with the name "Gad," which sounds like "troop" or "armed band." So the verse reads roughly like this: a troop will attack Gad, but Gad will attack their rear guard.

Jacob speaks, now an old man, gathering his sons and declaring to them what will happen in the future. Gad later settled east of the Jordan, an area exposed to attacks from neighboring peoples. For this reason, this blessing speaks of endurance and of a final victory.

For today: when you feel attacked by problems, criticism, or pressure, do not give up quickly. Stand firm, pray, and trust God, because the final outcome matters more than the first blow.
exp.25:0:
It says there was hunger in the region where Isaac lived, and that this was a different famine from the one his father Abraham had gone through years before. That is why Isaac went to Gerar, where Abimelech, king of the Philistines, ruled. "Went" is the plain word here, and "Abimelech" is the same name spelled in the usual modern way.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He presents Isaac's situation right after God confirmed his family as the heir of the promise. The next verse shows that God appears to him and tells him not to go down to Egypt, but to stay in the land. So Isaac is in a crisis and about to decide where to go. The text does not say whether he was planning to go to Egypt, only that God spoke to him.

For today: when times of scarcity come, before you decide out of fear, stop and seek God's guidance. He can give you direction and remind you that he still keeps his promises.
exp.9:29:
The explanation says that the descendants of Joktan lived in a region that stretched from a place called Mesha, in the direction of Sephar, a mountain in the east. "Their dwelling" means "their place of residence." The phrase "a mount of the east" in the King James Version is rendered in other translations as "a mountain of the east" or "toward the east." No one knows for certain where Mesha and Sephar were; many scholars place them in the Arabian Peninsula, but this is a supposition and there are other proposals.

The narrator of Genesis (tradition says it was Moses) presents the list of nations that came from the sons of Noah. This verse closes the list of the descendants of Joktan, within the line of Shem. It serves to show how the earth was populated after the flood.

For today: God knows peoples and individuals by name and place, even when history has forgotten them. You can trust that he also knows you and cares for your place in the world.
exp.35:20:
This verse closes a list of the sons of Seir the Horite. It names Dishon, Ezer and Dishan, and says they were chiefs of the Horites in the land of Edom. The word "dukes" here means heads or leaders of clans, not nobles of European kingdoms. "Horites" is the name of the people who lived there before.

No one speaks in a scene; it is Moses' account, according to tradition. It records genealogies to show who inhabited Edom, the land where Esau settled. This helps us understand where the Edomites came from and how they related to the earlier peoples. How exactly they came to mix is something the text does not detail.

For today: God notices every name, even those that seem minor. So do not think your life goes unnoticed; God knows you and takes you into account. Live today with that assurance.
exp.20:0:
This verse says that God fulfilled what he had promised Sarah. The word "visited" here does not mean a simple visit; it means that God remembered her and acted on her behalf. "As he had said" and "as he had spoken" repeat the same idea: God did exactly what he said he would do.

It is part of the account of Abraham and Sarah. Earlier, God had promised them a son, even though they were already old and Sarah had not been able to have children. Here it is not a character speaking; the narrator tells us that the promise was fulfilled. The following verses show the birth of Isaac.

Today, this text encourages us to trust that God is faithful, even when the wait is long and the situation seems impossible. We can keep praying and obeying, remembering that God keeps his promises in his own time and in his own way.
exp.26:34:
Isaac tells Esaú that his brother Jacob came with cunning and deceit, and carried off the blessing Isaac had prepared for him. The word "came" translates "llegó," and "took away" means that he took it from him.

Isaac, already old and nearly blind, had wanted to bless Esaú, his firstborn son. But Rebekah and Jacob deceived him: Jacob pretended to be Esaú. When Esaú arrives, Isaac trembles as he realizes what has happened. Even so, the blessing had already been given. It is a painful scene in which no one comes out clean: there was lying, favoritism, and much hurt within the family.

Today we can remember that deceit and favoritism wound people and damage relationships for years. God can carry out his purposes despite our failures, but that does not justify lying. Let us seek the truth and treat everyone with justice and love.
exp.23:57:
The verse tells how they called Rebekah and asked her whether she would go with that man, Abraham's servant. She answered plainly: "I will go." Where the original has old forms, the King James wording itself is archaic, and modern readers would say "unto" as "to" and "said" as "said to her" in everyday speech.

The words "said unto her" follow the older English pattern and today would simply be "said to her." The word "man" here means a man, the servant sent by Abraham.

The speakers are Rebekah's family: her brother Laban and her father Bethuel. Abraham's servant had come to seek a wife for Isaac, and he told them how God had guided his way. Before sending her off, the family wanted to hear Rebekah's own decision. Some scholars note that this shows she also had a voice in the matter.

For today: when we feel that God opens a door, it is wise to listen to counsel, to pray, and then to decide with courage. Rebekah did not stay hesitating; she trusted and took a concrete step of faith.
exp.28:7:
The shepherds tell Jacob that they cannot water the sheep yet. First all the flocks must be gathered together, and only then do they roll the stone away from the mouth of the well. "Water" here means giving the animals something to drink.

Jacob has just arrived in Haran, looking for his family. He asks some shepherds about Laban, and suggests that they water the sheep and keep grazing them, since it is still daytime. They answer with the custom of the place: wait for everyone before moving the stone. The text does not explain why, but it seems to be a rule for sharing the water in an orderly way. Right after this, Rachel arrives.

For today: before you skip over the agreements of a group, try to understand why they exist. And when you have the strength and an opportunity to serve, as Jacob did, do it with generosity.
exp.26:31:
Isaac asks the person who has just come in: "Who are you?" And the answer is: "I am your son, your firstborn Esau." The word "firstborn" means the eldest son, the one who was born first and held a special place in the family.

Here Isaac speaks, now old and with weak eyesight, and Esau answers him. Isaac had just blessed Jacob, who deceived him by pretending to be his brother. Esau arrives without knowing this, with the food prepared, expecting to receive the blessing that belonged to him as the eldest. With this question, what happened is uncovered.

For today: deceptions and hasty decisions leave wounds that are not easily healed. Before acting, it is wise to trust God and act with honesty, because He fulfills His promises without our needing to use lies.
exp.38:2:
The explanation says that Potiphar, José's master, noticed that God was with him. Everything José did, God made to prosper "in his hand," that is, in his work. "Saw" means that he noticed it clearly. In the King James wording, "the Lord" stands for God's name, and the verse does not say that José had an easy life, but that God was present.

No one speaks here; it is the narrator who tells the story. José had been sold by his brothers and taken to Egypt as a slave. Even so, the account insists that God did not abandon him. For this reason Potiphar kept giving him more trust, until he placed him in charge of his household.

Today we can work with honesty and effort, even when we are in a difficult or unjust place. God can be with us there, and the way we live can show others that he is real.
exp.24:18:
This verse opens a new section of the book. The word "generations" means "the family history," that is, what happened with Isaac and his children. "Begat" means that Abraham was the father of Isaac. The phrase repeats something we already knew, but it does so to emphasize that Isaac is the son of the promise.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Moses. He has just finished the story of Ishmael, the other son of Abraham, and now returns to the line through which God had promised to bless the world. What follows is the story of Isaac, his marriage to Rebekah, and the birth of his children.

For today: God keeps fulfilling his promises from generation to generation, even when it takes a long time. Trust that he is working in your family, and pray for your children, as Isaac prayed for his wife, knowing that God listens.
exp.12:1:
It says that Abram was very rich. "Very rich" means that he had an enormous amount of wealth. His fortune was measured in cattle (sheep, cows, camels), silver, and gold. In that time, animals were one of the main forms of wealth.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Genesis. Abram had just left Egypt, where he had gone because of a famine. There he had a moment of fear and deception with Pharaoh (Genesis 12), and he left with possessions. The text does not say everything about how he gathered that wealth, but the account presents it as part of God's blessing. Right after this, Abram returns to the altar at Bethel and calls on the name of the Lord.

Today we can remember that what we have, whether much or little, is a gift that we should manage with gratitude. Abram returned to the altar: his priority was not his money, but God. Ask yourself today: do my possessions draw me closer to God or move me away from Him?
exp.38:13:
Here the wife of Potiphar calls the men of the household and tells them a false version of what happened. She says that Joseph, whom she calls "an Hebrew," was brought in to mock them, and that he tried to lie with her, but that she cried out. "To mock us" means to abuse or humiliate; "to lie with me" means to have sexual relations.

It is the wife of Potiphar who speaks. She has just been rejected by Joseph, and to protect herself from shame she falsely accuses him. By saying "an Hebrew" she stresses that Joseph is a foreigner and a slave, so that they will believe her and not him. The garment he left in her hands serves her as supposed proof.

For today: when someone accuses us unjustly, let us remember that God sees the truth. And if we are tempted to blame others to hide our own wrongdoing, let us instead choose honesty, even when it costs us.
exp.7:9:
He says that Noah waited another full week after the dove returned without finding a place to land. When that time had passed, he sent it out from the ark again. The words "sent forth" and "out of the ark" simply mean that he let it go once more. It is understood that the seven days before were also a time of waiting, though the text says so in few words.

The one speaking is the narrator of Genesis, recounting what Noah did. The flood had already begun to subside, but Noah could not see the ground well from the ark. So he used the dove as a way to check whether there was yet a safe place to live. He did not act in haste, but with patience.

For today: when you are waiting for an answer or a change, do not despair or give up. Take one simple step, wait calmly, and try again, trusting that God is still at work even when you do not yet see results.
exp.48:21:
The verse says that Joseph is like a branch that bears much fruit, planted beside a spring. Its branches grow so much that they reach over the wall. The picture speaks of abundant life and of blessing that overflows.

It is Jacob, now old, who is speaking. Before he dies, he blesses each of his sons and tells them what will come for their families. About Joseph, the son who suffered betrayal and later prospered in Egypt, he uses this image of fruitfulness. Some understand the wall as pointing to Joseph's influence beyond his own borders; others read it in a more general way. The following verses speak of attacks that he withstood by God's help.

Whoever stays close to God, the source of life, can bear fruit even in hard times. Take care of your spiritual life today through prayer and the Word, and let your blessing reach others too.
exp.15:0:
This verse says that Sarai, Abram's wife, could not have children. She had an Egyptian maid named Hagar, that is, a servant or slave in the household.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. God had already promised Abram many descendants, but the years passed and the son did not come. This verse sets up what follows: Sarai, tired of waiting, proposes a human solution. In that time it was an accepted custom, though it brought pain and conflict to the whole family.

For today: when God's answer is slow in coming, it is tempting to take shortcuts. Before rushing ahead, it is good to pray, wait, and trust that God keeps his promises in his own time.
exp.36:21:
Reuben asks his brothers not to shed Joseph's blood. He suggests throwing him into a cistern in the wilderness, a dry pit used to store water, and that they not lay a hand on him, meaning that they not harm him directly. "Rid him out of their hands" means to rescue him, and "to deliver him to his father again" means to return him to Jacob, his father.

Reuben, the eldest brother, is the one speaking. The brothers, filled with envy over Joseph's dreams and their father's affection, were planning to kill him. Reuben tries to save his life with a gentler idea. The text says his plan was to return him to his father, although we are not told how he intended to do this. His strategy is cautious, not an open confrontation.

For today: when a group is carried away by anger or envy, someone should speak up for what is right. Reuben reminds us that defending the weak matters, but also that it is best done with clear courage, not only with half-measures.
exp.30:34:
Rachel tells her father Laban not to be angry that she cannot stand up before him, since she has her period. Laban searches for the household gods but does not find them.

Laban caught up with Jacob, who was leaving with his family without telling him, and accused him of stealing his gods. Jacob did not know that Rachel had taken them. She hid them and deceived her father. The Bible only records the event; it does not say why she took them, and interpreters give different reasons.

For today: lies and hidden things may seem to save the moment, but they put others at risk. Let us seek to live honestly before God and our family.
exp.10:22:
Serug says that after he became father of his son Nahor, he lived two hundred more years, and had other sons and daughters. The word "begat" means "became the father of," and the old-fashioned spelling "á" of the source is not relevant here. This does not say that Nahor was his only son, but rather the one who carries on the family line that follows.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis, who presents the genealogy of Shem down to Abraham. It serves as a bridge between the tower of Babel and the calling of Abraham. Some scholars debate whether these figures are literal or serve another purpose, and the Bible does not fully clarify this.

For today: God cares for each generation, even those we barely know by name. Your faithful and simple life, in your family and your home, also forms part of what God is weaving through time.
exp.41:18:
Here Joseph tells his brothers that, if they are truly honest men, one of them should stay behind in prison while the rest return home carrying grain for their families who are going hungry. "Ye be true men" means "if you are honest, as you claim." "The house of your prison" refers to the place where they were already being held. "Corn" is the grain they had come to buy.

Joseph is the governor of Egypt, but his brothers do not recognize him. They had sold him years earlier. He accused them of being spies and put them to the test. On the third day he softens his initial condition and says he fears God, that is, that he will act justly. Interpreters differ on his exact motives; the text shows that he seeks the truth and perhaps their repentance.

For today: when we go through trials, God sometimes uses those moments to awaken our conscience. Let us ask him for the courage to acknowledge our faults and to seek reconciliation.
exp.6:19:
It says that the flood waters rose fifteen cubits above the mountains, and so covered them. "Prevailed" means the waters were stronger and took control. A cubit was an ancient unit of measure, roughly 45 to 50 centimeters, so it would be about seven meters. Some think it refers to the height above the mountains; others, to the depth the water reached so that the ark could float. The text does not fully settle this.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, recounting the flood. God had decided to judge the wickedness of the earth, but he had kept Noah, his family, and the animals safe inside the ark. This verse shows that the judgment was total and that no one could escape by their own means.

For today: God does what he says, and his care for those who trust him is firm. When everything seems covered by problems, trust that he can sustain you, as he sustained the ark above the waters.
exp.16:24:
This verse says that Ishmael, the son of Abraham, was thirteen years old when he was circumcised. "Foreskin" is the skin that covers the tip of the male organ, and "circumcise" means cutting it away.

God had made a covenant with Abraham and asked that every male in his household carry this sign in his body (Genesis 17:10-14). The narrator tells us that Abraham obeyed that very same day, without waiting. Ishmael was Abraham's son by Hagar, and here he is included in the sign of the covenant. Some scholars point out that the age of thirteen is mentioned because that people was later connected with Ishmael, but the Bible does not explain it.

Today we can learn from Abraham's prompt obedience. When we know what God asks of us, it is not wise to leave it for later. Obeying today, even when it is difficult, shows trust in Him.
exp.32:10:
