Jacob asks Esau to accept his gift. "Gift" and "present" both mean a gift. "Has dealt graciously with me" means that God has treated him with kindness. Jacob says he has everything he needs, and he pressed so hard ("urged him") that Esau finally agreed to take it.

Jacob and Esau are brothers who had been apart for years. Years earlier, Jacob had obtained their father's blessing through deception, and Esau wanted to kill him. Now Jacob returns afraid, but Esau receives him warmly. Jacob insists on giving the gift as a sign of peace and gratitude. Accepting it was also a way of confirming the reconciliation.

For today: if there is a broken relationship, taking the first step with humility can open the way to peace. And when we recognize that everything we have comes from the goodness of God, it becomes easier to be generous and to repair the harm we have caused.
exp.40:9:
Here the chief cupbearer reminds Pharaoh of what happened before. He says that Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put him in prison, in the house of the captain of the guard, together with the chief baker.

The one speaking is the chief cupbearer, the man who served the king his cup. Pharaoh is troubled by his dreams, and no one in Egypt is able to explain them. Then the cupbearer remembers his own failure and tells how he came to know Joseph in prison, years earlier, when he himself was locked up.

For today: sometimes God prepares answers in places and moments that seem dark or lost. We can trust that nothing we go through is wasted, and also be grateful and remember those who helped us, just as the cupbearer was slow to remember Joseph.
exp.30:30:
Jacob answers Laban that he left secretly because he was afraid. He thought Laban would take his daughters from him by force. The phrase "take by force" means snatching them away by violence, so that he could not stop it.

Laban caught up with Jacob and accused him of leaving without telling him and of stealing his gods, that is, his household idols. Jacob first responds to the complaint about his departure. About the idols he knew nothing, because Rachel had taken them without his knowledge. That is why he later offers that whoever has them should die.

When we are afraid, it is easy to act in secret instead of speaking plainly. Jacob explains his fear, but his flight created more conflict. Today we can seek honest dialogue, ask for advice, and trust that God cares for us, even in difficult conversations.
exp.2:8:
God calls out to Adam and asks him, "Where are you?" The name "Jehovah" is God's name, and "man" here refers to Adam. God speaks with him after Adam and Eve disobeyed and hid themselves among the trees.

God speaks, the one who walks in the garden. Adam and Eve had just eaten the forbidden fruit and felt shame and fear. God knows where they are, so the question seems to be an invitation to come out, to speak, and to acknowledge what happened. Some see here a God who seeks the lost person, although the text does not explain this in more detail.

When we fail, we tend to hide from God and from others. Today you can answer his call with honesty: tell him simply where you are, what you did, and how you feel. He is looking for you in order to restore you, not only to point out your fault.
exp.17:4:
Abraham offers his three visitors "a morsel of bread" so that they may "comfort your hearts," that is, so that they may recover their strength. "Comfort" here means to strengthen or give courage. He tells them that afterward they may go on their way, since they have come by his house for a reason. They accept: "So do, as thou hast said."

Abraham is speaking while seated at the entrance of his tent, beside the oaks of Mamre. He sees three men standing before him and receives them with respect. The text says that the Lord appeared to him, and many understand that one of them represents God. Abraham says "a morsel," but then he prepares a feast: modesty in his words, generosity in his deeds.

For today: practice hospitality with simplicity and generosity. Do not wait until everything is perfect; open your home and give the best you have, because sometimes God visits us through the one who arrives at our door.
exp.26:3:
Isaac asks his son Esau to prepare a savory dish, the kind he loves. A "stew" is a dish of cooked meat, and "venison" is the meat of wild animals. Isaac wants to eat this dish and then bless Esau before he dies.

Isaac speaks as an old man, nearly blind, who thinks his death may be near. In that time, a father's blessing was something very serious, because it shaped the future of the eldest son. Rebekah hears everything, and this leads to a plan to deceive Isaac. Some see in Isaac an excessive fondness for food; others see simply a custom of the time. The text does not fully explain this.

For today: do not put off the important words of blessing, and seek to do things with clarity and honesty, not with deception. God keeps his promises, but we must trust without manipulating.
exp.41:36:
Reuben tells his father Jacob that if he does not bring Benjamin back, Jacob may put Reuben's two sons to death. He asks that Benjamin be placed in his care, and promises to bring him back. The phrase "deliver him into my hand" means "leave him in my responsibility."

Jacob is distressed: Joseph has disappeared, Simeon is held prisoner in Egypt, and the Egyptian ruler (who is Joseph, though they do not know it) demands to see Benjamin. Reuben, the eldest son, wants to calm his father with a strong promise. But Jacob does not accept it, because no offer restores his trust. Some think the proposal was not sensible, since offering the lives of his sons would not help Jacob if he lost Benjamin.

For today: before promising something, let us think about whether we can keep it. And when someone is suffering, standing with them in presence and sincerity is worth more than exaggerated words.
exp.8:7:
This verse says that God spoke to Noah and to his sons who were with him. It is a short sentence that serves as a bridge: it introduces what God is about to say next. The word "spake" is an older English form of "spoke," and "saying" signals that an important message is coming.

God is the one who speaks. He has just given Noah instructions after the flood: to value human life, because man was made in the image of God, and to fill the earth again. Now God addresses the whole family to make a covenant, that is, a solemn promise, which also includes the animals.

For today: God takes the initiative to speak to us and to promise good things. We can approach the Bible expecting to hear a God who cares for his people and his creation, and respond with trust and respect for life.
exp.25:3:
God makes three promises to Isaac: a descendant as numerous as the stars of heaven, the giving of "all these countries" to his offspring, and that all the nations of the earth will be blessed through his "seed." "Seed" means descendants, and "nations" refers to peoples or nations.

The Lord speaks, appearing to Isaac during a famine and telling him not to go down to Egypt. Stay here, he says, and I will be with you. God renews with Isaac the promise he earlier made to Abraham, and explains that he does so because of Abraham's obedience. Christians often see in this universal blessing a foreshadowing of Christ, as Galatians 3:16 interprets it.

For today: when circumstances push you to look for ways out on your own, remember that God asks for trust and obedience. Stay where he directs you, and trust that his promise still stands.
exp.4:3:
This verse says that Adam lived eight hundred years more after he had his son Seth. During that time he had other sons and daughters. Some older words: "begat" means "fathered" or "had as a son," and "Adam" and "Seth" are the older spellings of the names Adam and Seth.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book of Genesis, who is recording the list of generations from Adam onward. This list shows how humanity kept growing and how the line of Seth continued. It also shows that Adam lived a long life, though in the end he died, as the next verse says. The eight hundred years can be understood literally or as a way of expressing a very long life; interpreters read it in different ways.

For today: life passes from generation to generation. Think about what you are leaving to those who come after you, especially your family, and seek to pass on faith, love and a good example.
exp.0:16:
This verse says that God placed the sun, the moon, and the stars in the "expanse of the heavens," that is, in the open space seen above the earth. "Set" here means placed or put. "To give light" means to shine light. Its purpose here is to give light to the earth.

It is part of the account of creation, on the fourth day. The one telling the story is not a character who speaks, but the author of the book, who presents God arranging the world with purpose and care. The following verses add that these lights separate day from night and mark the time. They are stated to be creations of God, not gods.

For today: when you see the light of the sun or the stars, remember that nothing in your life is by chance. You can give thanks to God and trust that he cares for the details of your life.
exp.37:1:
Judah, one of Jacob's sons, saw there in that region the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. He married her and had relations with her. The words "saw" and "took her" in the old wording mean "saw" and "took her," that is, he took her as his wife. "Went in unto her" is an old expression for the intimate relationship of marriage.

This is the account of Genesis's narrator. Judah had separated from his brothers and went to live near Hirah of Adullam. There he married a Canaanite woman, from a people whose religious customs differed from those of Abraham's family. The text does not condemn her openly, but the sons who were born later came to a sad end, and that suggests it was a poor decision.

For today: decisions about whom we join ourselves to matter greatly. Before taking big steps, let us ask God for wisdom and seek counsel, not guided only by what we see.
exp.23:10:
The verse tells how Abraham's servant arrived with his ten camels at the outskirts of the city of Nahor. He made the camels kneel down beside a well of water, at the time of the evening, which was the hour when the young women went out to draw water.

Here the narrator speaks. Abraham sent his servant to find a wife for his son Isaac among his relatives. The servant swore to carry out that task, which was delicate and of great weight. The Bible does not give his name in this passage. He stopped at the well, a place where people met, and soon he would pray asking for God's guidance.

For today: before making an important decision, do what you were able to prepare, stop calmly, and ask God for direction. Then stay attentive to how He responds.
exp.37:27:
The explanation says that while Tamar was giving birth to twins, one of the babies put out his hand. The midwife tied a red thread around his wrist to show who was born first. "Scarlet" was an intense red dye, and "travailed" means "gave birth."

The narrator is the one speaking, and the midwife says: "This came out first." Judah had just admitted that Tamar had acted more righteously than he had, since he had not given her his son Shelah as he had promised. The thread was meant to make clear who held the right of the firstborn, which was important in that culture. Even so, the other baby was born first, and he was named Perez.

For today: sometimes our plans and titles seem secure, but God works in unexpected ways. Trust that He can fulfill His purpose even where things look confused, and do not cling to pride or to your own rights.
exp.21:23:
This verse says that Reumah, the concubine of Nahor (Abraham's brother), also had four sons: Tebah, Gaham, Thahash, and Maachah. The word "bare" means "gave birth to," and "concubine" was a secondary wife, of lower rank than the main wife. "Begat" in the previous verse means "was the father of."

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the narrator of the book. After Abraham's test with Isaac, someone tells him that Milcah, Nahor's wife, has had children. The list ends with Rebekah, who will become Isaac's wife. Reumah's sons complete Nahor's family. Scholars often see in these names peoples or tribes from northern Arabia and Syria, although this is not known with certainty.

For today: God cares for the details of the story and of every family, even for people who are rarely mentioned. We can trust that our lives, though they may seem small or hidden, do not go unnoticed by Him.
exp.19:7:
It says Abimelech, the king, rose early the next morning. He gathered all his servants and told them what God had said to him in the dream. Hearing it, the men were very afraid. "Early in the morning" means very early, and "called" means he summoned them.

God had warned Abimelech in a dream to return Sarah, Abraham's wife, because she was married. Abimelech had taken her without knowing the truth, since Abraham had said she was his sister. The king acts at once and shares the warning, which included the threat of death. That is why his servants were frightened.

When God corrects us, the best response is to answer promptly and with humility. Abimelech did not delay in obeying, and he did not hide what had happened. Today we can imitate him: if we feel that God is showing us something through his Word or through our conscience, let us act without delay.
exp.24:32:
Jacob asks Esau to swear to him, that is, to promise with a solemn oath, that he will give him his birthright. Esau does so. The birthright was the special right of the eldest son: a position of honor and a larger share of the family inheritance. "Swear it to me" means "swear it to me" in the sense of making the oath to Jacob.

Esau comes in from the field tired and hungry, and Jacob has a pot of lentil stew. Esau exaggerates, saying he is about to die, and he thinks the birthright is of no use to him now. Jacob takes advantage of the moment. The Bible does not approve of Jacob's trick, but it says that Esau "despised" his birthright, that is, he looked down on it and treated it as worthless.

Today we can ask ourselves what valuable and lasting things we are trading away for an immediate desire. Before deciding while hungry, tired, or under pressure, it is wise to stop and think about what truly matters.
exp.16:22:
Here, the account tells us that Abraham obeyed God at once. He took his son Ishmael and all the males of his household, both those born in his house and those bought with his money as servants, and circumcised them that very same day. In the King James wording, "foreskin" is the skin that is cut away in circumcision. "Servants" here refers to those who belonged to his household.

God had just spoken with Abraham and established circumcision as the sign of his covenant. After telling him that the covenant would continue through Isaac, God "went up from him," meaning the conversation was over. This verse shows Abraham's response: he did not wait or make excuses, even though he was ninety-nine years old.

For today: when we understand what God asks of us, obedience should not be put off. We can ask ourselves what step of faith we know is ours to take, and take it today, trusting that God is faithful to his promises.
exp.34:14:
This verse tells how Jacob gave the name "Bethel" to the place where God had spoken with him. Bethel means "house of God." Earlier, Jacob had set up a stone pillar there and poured wine and oil over it as a sign of worship.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Jacob returns to Bethel, the place where years before, fleeing from his brother Esau, he had the dream of the ladder. God now confirms his promise. It is a moment of renewal, just before Rachel suffers a difficult birth.

For today: Jacob marked the place where God spoke to him so that he would not forget it. We can do something similar: write in a notebook the times God has guided or comforted us, and read it again when hard days come.
exp.42:20:
Here the brothers of Joseph recount that, when they stopped at the inn (the roadside lodging) and opened their sacks, they found each man's money in the mouth of his sack, at its full weight. They say they have "brought it again in our hand," that is, they have brought it back with them.

The speakers are the group of brothers, nervous, addressing Joseph's steward. They fear they will be accused of theft, because on their first trip to Egypt the money appeared in their sacks without explanation. That is why they hasten to make clear their innocence and honesty before anyone judges them.

For today: when something makes us feel guilty or confused, the best course is to speak with clarity and honesty, without hiding anything. And if someone treats us with a kindness we do not understand, we can remember that God often works behind the scenes, as the steward suggests.
exp.45:31:
This verse says that Joseph's relatives are shepherds, because their trade has been to raise livestock. It also tells us they came to Egypt with their flocks, their herds, and everything they owned. The words "trade" and "feed cattle" refer to their work of caring for animals.

Joseph speaks to his brothers and to his father's household before presenting them to Pharaoh. He explains what they should say about their occupation. According to the text that follows, he wanted them to live in the land of Goshen, because the Egyptians looked down on shepherds. The text does not explain why the Egyptians felt that way, so it is best not to invent reasons.

Today we can learn to be honest and straightforward about who we are and what we do, without being ashamed of our work. We can also ask God for wisdom to act with prudence in settings where what we do is not always valued.
exp.16:6:
God tells Abraham that he will make a covenant with him and with his descendants, generation after generation. It is an "everlasting" covenant, meaning it has no end. The central promise is that God will be his God and the God of his "seed," an older word meaning descendants.

God Himself is speaking, when Abram is ninety-nine years old. He has just been given the new name Abraham, "father of many." God promises him children, nations, and land, even though he does not yet have the promised son. The covenant does not depend on Abraham's own strength, but on God's faithfulness.

For today: if God promises to be your God, you can rest in the fact that He keeps what He says, even when you do not yet see results. Trust Him today, and pass that trust on to your children or to those who come after you.
exp.23:13:
Here the servant of Abraham asks God for a sign. He wants the young woman he asks for water to give him a drink and also offer to give water to his camels. That way he would know she is the one chosen for Isaac. In the verse, "damsel" means a young woman, "pitcher" is a jar for carrying water, and "shewed kindness" means to show faithful goodness.

The speaker is the oldest servant in Abraham's household. His master sent him far away to find a wife for Isaac among his relatives. He is standing by a well at the hour when the women come out to draw water, and he prays for direction. Giving water to ten camels was a big job, so the sign called for a generous heart.

For today: before making important decisions, pray simply and ask God for guidance. Also pay attention to people's character, such as a willingness to serve, more than to appearances.
exp.26:20:
Isaac asks Jacob to come closer so that he can touch him. "Feel" means to test something by touching it with the hands. Isaac is unsure and wants to know whether this really is Esau, his firstborn son, or not.

Isaac is old and can hardly see anymore. Jacob pretends to be Esau, following the plan of his mother Rebekah, in order to receive the father's blessing. Isaac notices things that do not add up: how quickly the game was found and the voice. That is why he wants to check by touch. Jacob answers with a lie, even bringing God's name into it. The Bible recounts the deception without approving it, and later Jacob suffers its consequences.

For today: when something does not sit right with you, do not ignore that unease. Ask God for wisdom and seek the truth calmly. And remember that a deception, even when it seems to work, almost always brings consequences.
exp.44:18:
The explanation says that Pharaoh orders Joseph to tell his brothers to do something specific: take wagons from Egypt to carry their little ones and their wives, and also bring their father Jacob. "Take you" means "take for yourselves," and "wagons" were load-carrying vehicles with wheels, useful for a long journey.

Pharaoh is the one speaking, and he is addressing Joseph. The brothers had already been reconciled with him, and Pharaoh wanted the whole family to come to Egypt because of the famine that struck the region. His generosity shows that he viewed Joseph and his family favorably.

For today: generosity shows up in practical details. Offering concrete help, such as transportation, food, or lodging, is worth more than simply wishing someone well. Today you might ask yourself to whom you could give real, simple help.
exp.33:17:
The explanation says that Hamor and his son Shechem accepted the proposal of Jacob's sons. "And their words pleased Hamor" means that the idea seemed good to them. The proposal was that the men of the city should be circumcised so that they could join together as one people.

Jacob's sons spoke after Shechem had dishonored their sister Dinah. They made circumcision the condition, but the account shows that they spoke with deceit (v. 13). Shechem agreed right away because he wanted Dinah, and his father supported him. The text does not present anyone as an example to follow.

For today: before saying yes to a proposal, it is wise to ask what lies behind it and not to be carried along only by desire or convenience. And when we speak, let us do so with truth, without using religion as a disguise.
exp.37:0:
It says that at that time Judah, one of the sons of Jacob, separated himself from his brothers and went to live near a man from Adullam named Hirah. "It came to pass" means "it happened." "Turned in to" means "went over to" or "went to stay with." "A certain Adullamite" means a man from the town of Adullam, in the region of Canaan.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Right after the brothers sold Joseph, the story sets Joseph aside for a moment and follows Judah. It does not state clearly why he separated himself; some think it was from guilt or family tension, but the text does not explain it. What follows shows that Judah mixed with the Canaanites, and that brought trouble.

For today: the friendships and the places we choose shape us. If we move away from family and from faith, it is wise to ask where our decisions are leading us, and to return to God with humility.
exp.45:16:
This verse lists the descendants of Asher, one of the sons of Jacob. Four sons appear: Jimnah, Ishuah, Isui, and Beriah, along with a daughter, Serah, who is named, which is uncommon in these lists. Beriah had two sons: Heber and Malchiel. The word "and" appears throughout the verse, and "their sister" indicates that Serah was a daughter of the same father.

It is part of the list of those who went down to Egypt with Jacob. The narrator of Genesis records each family, and here closes the group belonging to Zilpah, the servant given to Leah. Some scholars believe the list joins those who went down at that time with others born later, but this is understood in various ways.

For today: God remembers people by name, even those whom almost no one mentions. Today you can imitate him by giving value to those who go unnoticed, greeting them by name and praying for them.
exp.21:15:
God says he makes an oath by himself. "You have done this" refers to Abraham's willingness to offer Isaac. "You have not withheld" means "you did not refuse me." "Your only son" points to Isaac as the son of the promise. The sentence is left open and is completed in the following verse with the blessing.

The one speaking is the angel of the LORD, who calls to Abraham from heaven a second time, just after stopping his hand on the mountain. Since no one can be a greater guarantor than God, he swears by himself (Hebrews 6:13 reminds us of this). He thereby confirms the promise he had already made, because Abraham showed complete trust in God.

For today: God sees the faithfulness that is lived out in secret and at cost. We can give him what we value most, trusting that he is good and keeps what he promises. His faithfulness is greater than ours.
exp.3:8:
God asks Cain where his brother Abel is. Cain answers with a lie, "I know not," and then replies with defiance: "Am I my brother's keeper?" The word "keeper" means one who cares for or protects.

Cain had just killed Abel in the field. God speaks to Cain, and He does not ask because He is ignorant of the answer, but to give him the opportunity to confess. Cain, instead, lies and acts offended. Earlier, God had already warned him that sin was "at the door," like a threat ready to dominate him, but that he could overcome it.

Today, when we fail, the temptation is to hide our guilt or avoid responsibility. God does not ask us to humiliate us, but to open the door to honesty. And yes, He expects us to care about others: to look after with love those who are near us.
exp.40:33:
Here Joseph advises Pharaoh to appoint overseers or administrators throughout the land. "Take up the fifth part" means to set aside one-fifth, that is, twenty percent of the harvests. The phrase "seven plenteous years" refers to the years of abundance. The idea is to store a portion during the seven good years.

Joseph is speaking before Pharaoh, after interpreting his dreams of the cows and the ears of grain. He had already explained that seven years of plenty would come, followed by seven years of famine. Now he not only interprets the dream but proposes a practical plan to protect the people. He says that God is hastening to bring it about.

For today: when things are going well, it is wise to prepare for difficult times. We can save a little, order our spending, and be generous, trusting in God while acting with prudence.
exp.35:32:
This verse tells us that Bela, king of Edom, died, and that Jobab, son of Zerah and a native of Bozrah, took his place as king. It is part of a list of Edomite rulers. "Reigned in his stead" means that he succeeded him on the throne.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks, a book traditionally attributed to Moses. After presenting the descendants of Esau, also called Edom, the text lists his kings. Notice that Jobab was not Bela's son, so the throne did not pass from father to son. The phrase "before there reigned any king over the children of Israel," found in the wording of the same passage, shows that Edom had kings before Israel did. Scholars debate when this list was written or completed.

For today: every ruler, however powerful, is temporary. This invites us to trust in God, whose kingdom never ends, and to live with humility.
exp.1:9:
This verse tells us that a river rose in Eden and passed through the garden to water it. After leaving there, the river divided into four branches, called "heads" (channels or streams). The word "water" here means to give water to plants.

The author of Genesis describes how God prepared a place full of life for the man. Earlier, the trees and the place God planted were mentioned. Now it is shown that the garden had abundant water. The following verses name rivers, but scholars do not agree on exactly where Eden was, and some of those names cannot be identified with certainty.

For today: God cares for what we need to live. We can trust that He provides, and give thanks for water, food, and everything that sustains our life. Also, just as the river flowed out of the garden and brought life to other places, we can share with others what God gives us.
exp.35:36:
This verse tells us that Samlah, a king of Edom, died, and that afterward Saul reigned, who came from a city called Rehoboth by the River. "By the River" probably refers to the Euphrates River, though this is not known for certain. This Saul is not the king of Israel.

The author of the book, whom tradition identifies as Moses, is recording the list of the kings of Edom, the people descended from Esau. Notice that here the kings are not sons of the kings before them, but come from different places. This list shows that Edom had rulers before Israel had a king.

For today: all human power is temporary. Kings and important names come and go, but God remains. We can live with humility, serving God and others, without placing our security in positions or achievements that do not last.
exp.31:21:
It says Jacob got up in the night and took his family across the Jabbok River: his two wives (Leah and Rachel), his two servant women, and his eleven sons. A "ford" is a shallow place in a river where one can cross on foot. The verb "rose up" simply means "he got up."

The narrator tells us that Jacob was returning to Canaan and would soon meet his brother Esau, whom he had deceived years earlier. Jacob was afraid, so he sent gifts ahead to calm Esau's anger. That night he moved his family across, and afterward he was left alone. There follows the struggle with "a man," whom many understand as a divine being, though it is interpreted in different ways.

For today: when you feel fear about an unfinished matter, do what is yours to do with wisdom, as Jacob did, but do not stop seeking God in private prayer.
exp.40:25:
Here Joseph begins to explain the two dreams of Pharaoh. The seven fine cows and the seven good ears of grain represent seven years. With the phrase "the dream is one," he says that both dreams give one single message.

Joseph speaks before Pharaoh, who is troubled because no magician of Egypt was able to interpret his dreams. Joseph makes clear that the interpretation does not come from his own cleverness, but from God, who shows Pharaoh what he is about to do. The seven good years will be followed by seven years of famine.

For today: God does not always give us everything clearly right away, but he can give us wisdom to prepare ourselves. Make use of good times with gratitude and prudence: save, serve, and take care of what you have. And when you do not understand something, ask God for light with humility, as Joseph did.
exp.15:14:
Here is told that Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarai, gave birth to a son by Abram. Abram named him Ishmael, which means "God hears." The words "bare" and "unto" are old forms; today we would say "gave birth to" and "to."

The narrator of Genesis reports this birth after Hagar had fled into the wilderness. There the angel of the Lord found her, told her to return, and announced that she would have a son. According to the text, Abram gave the name, although it was the angel who had indicated it beforehand. This shows that Abram accepted the word that Hagar had received.

God hears the people whom no one else listens to. Hagar was a foreigner and a servant, and she was suffering, but God saw her and attended to her. Today we can pray with confidence in the midst of pain, and we can also pay attention to those who usually go unnoticed.
exp.8:16:
God tells Noah again that the rainbow in the clouds is the sign of the covenant he made. That covenant is not only with Noah and his family, but with "all flesh," that is, with all the living creatures on the earth. The word "token" means a visible mark or reminder. "Covenant" is a solemn promise.

God speaks after the flood, when Noah and his family have just come out of the ark. God promises that he will never again destroy the earth with a flood of waters. The rainbow in the clouds serves as a reminder of that promise, and the text says that God himself will see it and remember.

For today: when you see a rainbow, or when you doubt, remember that God is faithful to what he promises. You can rest in his word, even when storms come, and thank him for his care of all his creation.
exp.27:5:
What it says: Esau realizes what his father Isaac had done. Isaac had blessed Jacob and sent him to Padan-aram to find a wife among his own kin. Moreover, in blessing him, Isaac had charged him not to marry a woman of the daughters of Canaan.

Context: Here the narrator of the book speaks, not a character. He tells how Esau reacts. Isaac wanted Jacob to keep the faith and the promise of Abraham, and that is why he was sending him away from the customs of Canaan. Shortly afterward Esau tries to please his father by marrying another wife (Genesis 28:8-9). The Bible does not explain all of his motives.

For today: Decisions about a spouse and about friendships shape the faith of an entire family. Before deciding, ask God for direction and listen to the wise counsel of those who love you and walk with Him.
exp.48:9:
Judah is said to have authority, symbolized by the scepter (the king's staff) and the lawgiver (the one who rules by laws), "from between his feet," that is, from among his descendants. This will last "until Shiloh comes," and then the peoples will gather to him. The word Shiloh is difficult: it has been understood as "he to whom it belongs," as a place, or as a title of the Messiah.

Here Jacob, now an old man, blesses his twelve sons before he dies. To Judah he announces a place of leadership among the tribes. From his line would come King David. Many Christians see in this verse a promise that points to Jesus.

For today: trust that God keeps his promises even when generations pass. If today you find yourself waiting, remember that God works with patience and faithfulness.
exp.47:14:
Jacob, now very old, blesses the sons of Joseph. He says that his God is the same one before whose presence Abraham and Isaac "walked," that is, lived with faith and obedience. He also calls him the God who has "fed" him, meaning that he has cared for and guided him like a shepherd all his life until this day.

Jacob, also called Israel, speaks near the end of his life in Egypt. He crossed his hands and placed his right hand on Ephraim, the younger, even though Manasseh was the firstborn. Before blessing the boys, he acknowledges who has been faithful to his family through the generations.

For today: before asking for or hoping for something in the future, remember how God has sustained you until now. Thinking about his past faithfulness strengthens trust, and you can tell your children or others how God has cared for you.
exp.23:3:
Here Abraham tells his servant not to look for a wife for Isaac among the Canaanites, but to go to the land where his family lives, in Mesopotamia. "Kindred" means relatives or family members. "Take a wife" means he is to choose and bring back a wife.

Abraham is already old, and he speaks with the oldest servant of his household, the one who managed all his possessions. He makes him swear by the LORD. Abraham does not want Isaac to marry a woman who worships the gods of Canaan. He also wants his son to remain in the land God promised him. That is why he seeks a wife within his own family.

Today, this invites us to make decisions that shape a whole life, such as marriage, with prayer and wisdom. It is good to seek the counsel of people of faith and to put God first, rather than acting only out of emotion or convenience.
exp.19:2:
God appears to King Abimelech in a dream during the night. He warns him that he is in danger of death for having taken Sarah, who already had a husband. The phrase "thou art but a dead man" is the KJV's wording for this warning, and "for she is a man's wife" means she was lawfully married.

God speaks. Abraham, living as a foreigner in Gerar, said that Sarah was his sister, and the king took her for himself. The text makes clear that Abimelech had not yet touched her. God intervenes to protect Sarah and the promise he had made to Abraham. It is also seen that Abimelech acted without knowing the truth.

For today: God cares for his plan and for people, even when our mistakes or fears complicate things. Be honest, because the truth prevents harm to others. And if we fall, God can still correct us with mercy.
exp.11:5:
This verse tells how Abram traveled through the land of Canaan until he reached Shechem, near the oak (or terebinth) of Moreh. The King James spells the name "Sichem," which is an older form of Shechem. "The Canaanite" refers to the peoples who already lived there. The phrase "was then in the land" shows that the land was not empty.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. God had already called Abram to leave his home and had promised him a blessing. This detail reminds us that Abram arrived in a land already occupied by others. That is why the next verse, where God promises that land to his descendants, shows that the promise called for trust, not for something already visible.

For today: sometimes God guides us onto a path where we still see obstacles. We can keep trusting his promise and take the next step, as Abram did, who worshiped God in the middle of waiting.
exp.41:31:
Here the brothers of Joseph tell their father Jacob what happened in Egypt. They say that they are twelve brothers, that one "is not" (that is, he no longer appears, he is no longer with them), and that the youngest, Benjamin, stayed behind with their father in Canaan.

One of Jacob's sons speaks, on his return from Egypt, where they bought grain because of the famine. Without knowing it, they had dealt with Joseph, the brother they had sold years earlier. They repeat what they said to the ruler to prove that they were not spies. It is notable that before their father they mention Joseph with a soft phrase, "is not," without confessing what they did. The Bible does not say here what they felt inside.

Today, this verse invites us to look at our half-truths. Hiding a wrong weighs on us over the years. God offers forgiveness and freedom when we acknowledge it with sincerity.
exp.38:20:
This verse says that God was with Joseph even in prison. "Mercy" here means faithful, loving kindness. The phrase "gave him favour in the sight of the keeper" means that God caused the keeper of the prison to look upon him with appreciation and trust.

It is part of the story of Joseph in Egypt. The narrator tells that, after being falsely accused by Potiphar's wife, Joseph was imprisoned. Even so, the text emphasizes that God did not abandon him. Soon the keeper entrusted to him the prisoners and everything that was done there.

For today: when you are in an unjust or difficult situation, remember that God's presence does not depend on your circumstances. Keep doing your work with honesty, and trust that God can give you favor and care for you even in unexpected places.
exp.28:20:
Jacob asks Laban to give him Rachel, his promised bride, because he has finished the seven years of work they agreed on. The phrase "go in unto her" means that he and she would live together as husband and wife, with marital intimacy. "My days are fulfilled" means that the agreed time has been completed.

Jacob had fled from his brother Esau and arrived at the house of his uncle Laban. There he fell in love with Rachel and offered to serve seven years for her. Now he asks for what was promised. What follows in the story is that Laban deceives him with Leah, which shows that Jacob, who once deceived, is now himself deceived.

Keeping our word and waiting patiently are acts of integrity. But let us also remember that God can use the injustices we suffer to shape us, and that our past actions often have consequences. Let us trust in Him even in the unexpected.
exp.48:0:
Jacob calls all of his sons and asks them to gather around him. He tells them he is going to declare to them what will happen to them "in the last days," that is, in the future, in the times that would come after. The phrase "that I may tell you" in the King James wording is a way of saying "I am about to announce to you."

Jacob speaks as an old man, near his death, in Egypt. He wants to leave his sons, who will become the tribes of Israel, words of farewell and blessing. Some scholars understand this as a prophecy; others as a portrait of the character and destiny of each tribe. What follows includes both warnings and promises.

For today: Value the time you have with your family and speak to them with honesty and love while you can. Do not wait until the end of life to leave them words that encourage them, correct them with kindness, and point them toward God.
exp.37:3:
She became pregnant again and gave birth to a second son. The text says she named him Onan. In the King James wording, "conceived" means became pregnant, and "bare" means gave birth.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is recording the history of Judah's family. Judah had separated from his brothers and had married a Canaanite woman. The text only notes the births of his sons: Er, Onan, and Shelah. These names will become important later in the story. The exact meaning of "Onan" is uncertain; some connect it with strength or vigor, but this is debated.

For today: God sees each life from its beginning, including names that may seem like mere details. Care for your family in prayer, and teach your children to walk with God, because their character is formed by what they see at home.
exp.42:17:
Joseph's brothers became frightened when they were brought into Joseph's house. They thought they had been brought in because of the money that had been returned in their sacks on the first trip. They believed that Joseph wanted to find a reason to accuse them, to fall upon them by surprise, and to take them as slaves, along with their donkeys. The phrase "that he may seek occasion against us" means looking for a pretext to attack them. "Sacks" are the bags of grain.

The ones speaking are the brothers, and they do so out of fear and guilt. They did not know that Joseph was inviting them to eat as friends. They saw the situation through their fear, not through Joseph's actual intention. Moreover, they were still carrying what they had done years earlier against him.

Today, fear and guilt can make us misread the kindness of others, and even the kindness of God. If something weighs on your conscience, bring it honestly before God and, if necessary, before the person affected. Their forgiveness frees you from fear.
exp.47:15:
Jacob (Israel) asks that the Angel who has delivered him from all evil bless his grandsons, Ephraim and Manasseh. He wants his name and the names of Abraham and Isaac to be remembered in them, and for them to grow into a great multitude in the midst of the earth. "Lads" means young boys or children, and "grow" here is understood as "increase and multiply."

Jacob is already an old man and is in Egypt, near death. He blesses the sons of Joseph and deliberately crosses his hands, placing his right hand on the younger one. Many understand "the Angel" to be God himself acting as his protector; the Bible does not explain this in detail, and it is interpreted in several ways.

Jacob looked back over his whole life and recognized that God had cared for him at every step. Today we can do the same: remember how God has kept us and, with that gratitude, bless the younger members of our family with prayers and words.
exp.9:24:
The explanation says that Eber had two sons. One was called Peleg, a name that sounds like a Hebrew word meaning "divide" or "distribute." The reason given is that in his days "the earth was divided." The other son was called Joktan.

It is part of the Table of Nations, a list of families after the flood. Moses is traditionally considered the author of the book, although here he does not speak in the first person; he simply records the genealogy. No one knows for certain what that "division" was: some think of the scattering at Babel (chapter 11), others of a division of territories among the peoples. The Bible does not make it clear.

For today: God knows who you are and what family you come from. Each name in this list reminds us that God works through generations. Take care what you teach those who come after you, because your life is also part of that story.
exp.30:5:
Jacob tells his wives, Rachel and Leah, that they know well that he worked for their father Laban with all his strength. The word "ye" in the verse means "you," and "with all my power" speaks of work given wholeheartedly and without holding back.

Jacob speaks in the field, away from Laban, where he can talk with his wives in private. He realizes that Laban no longer treats him as before and wants to leave with his family. Before explaining his decision, he reminds them of his faithfulness in the work, and they themselves are witnesses to it.

For today: work with honesty and dedication, even when others do not value you or treat you well. Integrity brings peace of mind and lets you speak clearly when you must make difficult decisions. Also, trust that God sees your effort.
exp.17:14:
Sarah says that she did not laugh, because she was afraid. But the Lord answers her calmly: "No, it is not so; you did laugh."

The words "bear" and "old" refer to giving birth while already advanced in age. "Denied" means that she said it was not true.

Three visitors arrived at Abraham's tent, and one of them is called the LORD. They promised that Sarah would have a son. She listened from the entrance of the tent and laughed inwardly, thinking it was impossible because of her age. The Lord knew even that hidden laugh, and so He corrects her firmly, but without shouting at her.

When we fail, we sometimes want to hide it out of fear. But God already knows everything, and still He treats us with patience. We can be honest with Him, confess our doubts, and ask Him to strengthen our faith.
exp.5:11:
God looked at the earth and saw that it was morally damaged. "Corrupt" means ruined, turned away from what is good. And "all flesh," that is, all human beings, had bent their "way," or in other words, their manner of living. It was not an isolated case but something widespread.

Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking. Earlier it was said that the earth was filled with violence. God does not act blindly: he "looked" and saw the reality. Next, God announces the judgment to Noah and gives him instructions for building an ark. Some understand "all flesh" to mean all of humanity; others debate how far the scope reached, but the text stresses the seriousness of the situation.

For today: God sees what we sometimes ignore. Let us ask him to examine our way and to help us live with justice and peace, even when the atmosphere around us goes astray.
exp.26:45:
Rebekah tells Isaac that she is weary and burdened with living, because of the Hittite women, the "daughters of Heth." If Jacob were to marry one of these women, just like them, she would feel that her life no longer had any meaning. "I am weary of my life" conveys "I am worn out, life weighs heavily on me."

The speaker is Rebekah, Isaac's wife. Esau had married Hittite women, and this caused them great bitterness (Genesis 26:34-35). She wants to protect Jacob from Esau's anger by sending him to their brother Laban. To persuade Isaac, she uses this reason: that Jacob should not marry a woman of Canaan. Many think she was also hiding her plan to save Jacob, but the text does not say this clearly.

Today, when something truly worries us, let us speak about it honestly and respectfully, without manipulating others. And let us ask God for wisdom to care for our family.
exp.15:12:
Hagar, Sarai's servant, gives God a name: "You are the God who sees." She wonders whether she truly saw, there in the wilderness, the One who was seeing her.

Hagar was running away from Sarai, who treated her harshly, and she was alone beside a spring in the desert. The angel of the Lord spoke to her, promised her a son, and told her to name him Ishmael, which means "God hears." Many understand that this angel represented the Lord himself, since Hagar speaks of "the Lord that spake unto her." She was a foreigner and had no power, yet God took notice of her.

For today: when you feel alone, overlooked, or hurt, remember that God sees you and hears you. You can speak to him honestly, knowing that your pain matters to him.
exp.14:15:
God tells Abram that his descendants will return to the promised land in the fourth generation. The Amorites were a people who lived in Canaan. "The iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full" means that their sin had not yet reached the point that called for judgment. Meanwhile, God waits.

God speaks on the night he makes a covenant with Abram. He announces that his family will live as foreigners and will suffer in a land not their own. Here we see that God is patient and just: he does not punish at once. Some understand the "four generations" as about four hundred years; the text gives no further detail.

For today: when it seems that God is slow to respond, trust that his timing is just and patient. Wait without bitterness, and do not take advantage of his patience, for it seeks to lead us to repentance.
exp.2:14:
God tells the serpent that there will be a lasting struggle between it and the woman, and between their descendants. The word "seed" means offspring. The word "heel" is the back part of the foot. The woman's offspring would strike the serpent's head, a deadly blow, and the serpent would strike his heel, a painful wound but a less serious one.

God speaks right after Adam and Eve disobeyed. This is the moment when He pronounces the consequences, but it also includes a promise that evil will not have the final word. Many Christians see here an early announcement of Christ, though the text does not name Him, and others read it in a more general way.

For today: even when we face struggles against evil or against our own mistakes, we can trust that God already had a plan of rescue. Rest in that hope and do not give up.
exp.40:12:
What it says: The chief cupbearer reports that everything happened just as Joseph had explained it. He was restored to his position, and the chief baker was hanged. In the King James wording, "came to pass" and "unto" and "hanged" are older English phrasing for "happened," "to," and "hung" as in executed. "Interpreted" means "explained" or "gave the meaning of."

Context: The chief cupbearer of Pharaoh speaks here. He had been in prison with Joseph two years earlier. Pharaoh had dreams that no one could explain, and at last this man remembered Joseph. He tells how Joseph accurately interpreted his dream and the baker's dream. In this way he presents Joseph as someone trustworthy before the king.

For today: God asks us to be faithful even when no one notices or thanks us. Joseph served with integrity in prison, and the moment of being recognized came later, in God's time. Do your work well today and trust that God sees what you do.
exp.37:10:
Judah tells Tamar, his daughter-in-law, to remain a widow in her father's house until his son Shelah grows up. But in truth he fears that Shelah will also die, as his brothers did. Tamar obeys and goes to live with her father.

Judah speaks as the father of Er and Onan, Tamar's two earlier husbands, who both died. According to the custom of the time, Shelah was to give Tamar a son to carry on the name of the dead man. Judah makes a promise, but he does not intend to keep it. He blames Tamar, although the text has already pointed to the wickedness of Er and Onan.

For today: when we make a promise, we should keep it or be honest about why we cannot. Avoiding the truth out of fear or convenience can hurt others, especially those who are most vulnerable.
exp.40:7:
In the morning, the text says, Pharaoh was troubled and anxious because of his dreams. He then sent for all the magicians of Egypt and all its wise men. He told them what he had dreamed, but none of them could explain it to him.

The account follows the dream of seven fat ears of grain being devoured by seven thin ones. The narrator tells us the king sought help from his most respected advisers, but they had no answer. This prepares the next scene, where the cupbearer remembers Joseph, who was in prison and who, according to the text, could interpret dreams with God's help.

There are moments when human wisdom reaches its limit and leaves us unsettled. Such moments can teach us humility and lead us to seek God in prayer, asking for his guidance, and also to listen with respect to those whom he places in our path.
exp.39:7:
The two officials of Pharaoh tell Joseph that they have had a dream and that no one can explain it to them. Joseph answers with a question: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" meaning that the interpretation of dreams belongs to God. And he asks them, "tell me them, I pray you," that is, "tell them to me now." Here, "interpretations" means explanations or the act of making a dream's meaning clear.

Joseph is a prisoner in Egypt. In the morning he notices that two of Pharaoh's officials, the cupbearer and the baker, look sad, and he asks them what is wrong. They are troubled because, in that culture, dreams were considered important messages, and they had no one to interpret them. Joseph does not present himself as an expert, but directs attention to God.

For today: when someone recognizes a talent or wisdom in you, give the glory to God. And ask for his help before giving advice to someone who is suffering.
exp.23:26:
Here the servant of Abraham praises God with gratitude. "Blessed be the Lord God" means that he recognizes God as worthy of praise. "Mercy" is his faithful love, and "truth" is his faithfulness to what he has promised. He says that God did not stop showing these two things to Abraham, and that he himself was led "in the way" to the house of his master's brethren.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac among his master's relatives. He had prayed asking for a sign, and Rebekah responded just as he had asked. She had just told him there was room to stay. He bows down and worships, seeing God's hand in what has happened.

For today: when you see that God guided or helped you, stop and give thanks to him out loud, as this servant did. Recognizing his faithfulness strengthens your confidence for the next step.
exp.5:4:
It says that God looked at the earth and saw that human wickedness had grown enormously. It was not just that people did bad things now and then: even what they thought and planned inwardly was evil, and this was the case all the time. "Wickedness" means evil; the word translated "imagination" refers to a plan or intention formed in the heart.

Here the narrator of Genesis shows us how God sees the situation before the flood. Shortly before, it speaks of powerful people and of a time limit set for humanity (the 120 years, which some understand as a period before judgment). The verses that follow say that God grieved over what was happening. This prepares the story of Noah. Some details, such as who the "sons of God" were, are interpreted in several different ways.

For today: God looks at the heart, not only at outward appearances. We can sincerely ask him to examine our thoughts and cleanse them, and to teach us to seek good from within.
exp.28:28:
This verse says that Laban, Rachel's father, gave his daughter a servant named Bilhah to serve her. "Handmaid" and "maid" are old-fashioned words for a woman who works for another person in the household. It was a common gift when a daughter married.

No character speaks here; the narrator of Genesis is reporting the event. Jacob had just married Rachel, after having been deceived into marrying Leah. Laban acts as father and head of the family. Later, Bilhah will play an important role in the history of Jacob's family. The Bible records this without approving of everything that happens.

For today: God works even in families marked by deception, jealousy, and pain. We can ask him for wisdom to act with honesty and to care for those who depend on us.
exp.6:0:
God tells Noah to go into the ark together with his whole household. The reason is that God has seen him as righteous, that is, upright and faithful, among the people of his time. The words "unto" and "house" are understood as "to" and "household" in the wording you are reading, and "generation" refers to the people who lived in that age.

The Lord, the God of Israel, is speaking. In the earlier chapters, wickedness on the earth had grown great, and God announced a flood. Noah had already built the ark, and now comes the command to enter it. God also gives him instructions about the animals he was to take along. This is a moment of judgment, but also of rescue for Noah and his family.

For today: living faithfully before God is worthwhile, even when almost no one around us does. God sees our lives, and he also cares for the family of the one who is faithful to him. Today you can choose one concrete act of obedience, even if it looks different from what most people are doing.
exp.36:33:
Jacob tears his clothes, puts sackcloth around his waist, and mourns for his son Joseph for many days. "Tearing one's clothes" was a way of showing very strong grief. "Sackcloth" is a coarse cloth used in mourning. "Loins" are the waist. "To mourn" means to live in grief.

Here the Bible story speaks. Joseph's brothers brought Jacob the blood-stained robe to make him believe that a wild animal had killed him. In reality, they had sold him. Jacob believes the lie and weeps like a father who has lost his beloved son.

For today: pain is real and does not need to be hidden. If you are suffering, allow yourself to cry and seek company, without shame. And if someone comforts you, accept that help; God often takes care of us through other people.
exp.35:37:
This verse says that King Saul of Edom died, and that Baal-hanan, son of Achbor, was the next to reign. It is part of a list of kings. Here "died" and "reigned in his stead" are repeated like a chain of successions. This Saul of Edom is not King Saul of Israel.

Context: it is not a character speaking; it is the narrator of Genesis, who records the kings of Edom, the people who descended from Esau, brother of Jacob. It seems these kings were not all from one family, and the list shows that Edom was an organized people with power. Scholars do not agree on when this list was written or completed.

For today: all leaders, even the most powerful, pass away and are replaced. This invites us not to place our hope in people or positions, but in God, who endures. We can also live with humility, serving well wherever we are.
exp.28:18:
Laban replies to Jacob that he prefers to give his daughter Rachel to him rather than to another man. Then he says, "abide with me." The King James wording "abide with me" means "stay with me," that is, to remain living and working in his household.

The speaker is Laban, Jacob's uncle. Jacob had come fleeing from his brother Esau and fell in love with Rachel. Since he had no money to pay a bride price, he offered to work seven years. Laban agrees, though his answer sounds practical and convenient for himself: he gained a worker. He says nothing clear about the plan he would later have, for he would later deceive Jacob.

For today: when you make an agreement, be clear and honest, and do not rely only on kind words. Put what is important in writing and act with integrity, even when others do not.
exp.29:4:
This verse tells the story in a simple way: Bilhah, Rachel's servant, became pregnant and gave Jacob a son. The words "conceived" and "bare" mean "became pregnant" and "gave birth."

Rachel could not have children and suffered because of it. Her sister Leah already had several. So Rachel offered Jacob her servant Bilhah, following a custom of that time that seems strange to us today. Rachel wanted to regard the child as her own. Afterward she interpreted the birth as an answer from God and named the boy Dan, which means "judge." The Bible recounts this without fully approving or condemning it.

For today: when something takes a long time to arrive, it is easy to take human shortcuts that bring complications. Before acting out of desperation, let us ask God for wisdom and wait on Him with patience.
exp.30:23:
God appears to Laban the Syrian in a dream during the night. He warns him to take care not to speak to Jacob "either good or bad," that is, not to speak to him with extremes, whether by harshness, violence or crude threats. The phrase "take heed" means "be careful" or "watch yourself."

Laban had been pursuing Jacob with his relatives, because Jacob had left secretly with his wives, his children and his possessions. Laban felt deceived and had the power to do harm. The text does not say exactly what Jacob feared would happen, but God intervenes before the meeting and protects Jacob. It is God who speaks, and he does so to Laban in a dream.

For today: God cares for his own even when they do not see him at work. When you face a conflict or a fear, pray and trust that God works in quiet ways. And when you are angry, remember that God asks you to speak with self-control.
exp.41:23:
He turned away from them and wept by himself. Then he came back, spoke to them, and chose Simeon. He ordered that he be tied up and held right there, while they watched. "Bound" means he was tied up and kept prisoner; "before their eyes" means in front of them.

Joseph, already governor of Egypt, treats his brothers harshly, and they do not recognize him. They have just been talking among themselves about what they did to him years earlier, believing he could not understand their language. Hearing them, Joseph was moved. The Bible does not explain why he chose Simeon; some think it was because Simeon had been especially cruel to him, but the text does not say so. It also does not make clear everything Joseph was thinking.

For today: truth and reconciliation can sometimes hurt. We can feel tenderness toward someone who wronged us and still seek for them to acknowledge their wrong. Let us ask God for wisdom to act with both justice and mercy.
exp.25:27:
What it says: The men of Gerar explain to Isaac why they came looking for him. They say they saw clearly that God was with him. That is why they propose an oath, that is, a solemn promise between the two parties, and a covenant, which is a formal pact of peace. The name "Lord" is the name of God, and "with thee" means that he accompanies and supports him.

Context: Speaking are Abimelech, his friend Ahuzzath, and Phicol, the commander of his army. Earlier they had sent Isaac away from their territory out of envy, since he had prospered greatly. Now they come because they recognize that God blesses him and they want to avoid trouble with him. The text does not say whether their motive was sincere or merely practical; that remains open. Isaac responds with a feast.

For today: When someone has treated us badly, we can follow Isaac's example: receive them generously and seek peace, without letting resentment make the decisions. Our way of living can also show that God is with us.
exp.22:1:
This verse tells us that Sarah died in Kiriath-arba, which is the ancient name of Hebron, in the land of Canaan. Abraham came to mourn, that is, to express his grief over her death, and to weep for her.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. Sarah had lived one hundred and twenty-seven years, and now Abraham, already an old man, faces the loss of his wife. The Bible does not hide his weeping. Soon he will look for a place to bury her, because in that land he still lived as a foreigner.

For today: mourning a loss is not a lack of faith. Abraham, a man of great faith, allowed himself to grieve openly. If you are grieving today, give yourself time to weep, and accompany with tenderness the one who suffers.
exp.30:53:
Jacob offered sacrifices on the mountain and invited his relatives to eat a meal together. The word "bread" here means sharing a meal. After they ate, they spent the night there. "Offered sacrifice" means that he sacrificed animals. "Brethren" refers to Laban and those who were with him, that is, relatives.

It is the narrator who speaks. Jacob and his father-in-law Laban had come through a long period of tension: Jacob had left without notice, and Laban caught up with him. They had just made a covenant not to harm one another, with a heap of stones as its sign. This meal sealed that agreement. In that time, eating together after a covenant was a sign of peace.

For today: when there is a conflict and a reconciliation is reached, it is worth giving it a simple closing, such as sharing a meal and praying together. Gestures like these help make peace real and not just words. Put God at the center of the reconciliation.
exp.7:12:
In the six hundred and first year of Noah's life, on the first day of the first month, the waters dried up from the earth. Noah took off the covering of the ark, looked, and saw that the surface of the ground was already dry.

This verse is part of the account of the flood, and the narrator marks the dates with care. Noah had already seen the olive leaf and had released the dove for the last time. Even so, here he confirms with his own eyes that the earth was dry. Yet he still does not leave the ark: in the next verse the ground finishes drying, and then God speaks to him.

For today: Noah did not rush ahead but waited for God's timing. When you have to wait for an answer or a change, trust that God acts in his own time, and do not grow weary of remaining faithful in the meantime.
exp.41:30:
Here the sons of Jacob tell their father what they said to the man in Egypt. They affirm that they are honest men, "true men", that is, sincere and upright, and that they have never been spies. The word "spies" refers to people who investigate a country in order to attack it.

The brothers of Joseph speak here, now back in Canaan. They went down to Egypt to buy grain because of the famine. Without knowing it, they stood before Joseph, whom they had sold years earlier. He accused them of being spies in order to test them. Now they explain to Jacob why Simeon is missing. They recount the facts, though not everything that had passed between them.

For today: when we have to explain something difficult to our family, let us speak with clarity and without dressing up the truth. Complete honesty, even when it hurts, helps trust to hold and heals what is broken.
exp.23:50:
Here Laban and Bethuel tell Abraham's servant that Rebekah is standing right in front of him. They let him take her to be the wife of his master's son, Isaac. They acknowledge that all of this comes from the Lord. The words "Behold" means "here she is" or "look at her."

The family of Rebekah speaks. Abraham's servant had traveled far to find a wife for Isaac. He told them how God had guided him to Rebekah at the well. When they heard the account, they saw the hand of God and did not want to stand in its way. Afterward, the servant bowed down to worship God.

For today: when you see that God opens a door clearly, do not resist out of fear or self-interest. Recognize his work, respond with humility, and give thanks to him before moving forward.
exp.40:49:
It says that two sons were born to Joseph before the years of famine began. Their mother was Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. The words "were born unto" and "bare" are old forms: in the King James wording they mean that she gave birth to Joseph's sons.

Here the narrator of the book speaks. Joseph was already ruler in Egypt and, while he was storing up grain in the years of plenty, he built his family. On was an Egyptian city with an important religious center. Later Joseph gives them names that express his gratitude to God: Manasseh and Ephraim. The text does not explain more about how that marriage came about.

For today: God can give us blessings and new beginnings even in difficult lands. Let us give thanks for the good He gives us today, without waiting for everything to be perfect.
exp.33:10:
Shechem spoke to Dinah's father and to her brothers. He asks them to receive him favorably ("let me find grace in your eyes") and promises to give whatever they ask. "Dowry and gifts" was the payment offered when a man sought to marry a woman.

Shechem had just dishonored Dinah, Jacob's daughter. Now, together with his father Hamor, he seeks to make things right through a marriage and an alliance. He seems ready to pay whatever is asked, but his earlier act cannot be erased with money. Jacob's sons respond with deception, and the story ends in violence. The Bible shows a deep pain here, without approving everything the characters do.

For today: when we have hurt someone, it is not enough to offer gifts or kind words. We need to acknowledge the harm, ask forgiveness with humility, and seek justice. And if we have been hurt, let us ask God for wisdom so that we do not respond with revenge.
exp.16:25:
It says that Abraham and his son Ishmael were circumcised on the same day. To circumcise means to cut off the foreskin, the skin that covers the tip of the male organ. Abraham was ninety-nine years old and Ishmael was thirteen.

God had just spoken to Abraham and established his covenant with him. Circumcision was to be the sign of that covenant (Genesis 17:10-11). The text does not tell whose voice is heard here, but it stresses how quickly Abraham acted: he obeyed "on the very same day." Afterward he did the same for all the males of his household.

For today: when you understand what God asks of you, do not put it off. Obeying quickly, even in things that are hard or uncomfortable, shows trust in him.
exp.44:27:
Here Jacob, also called Israel, says "It is enough," which means "that is sufficient, I no longer need more proof." Now he believes that his son Joseph is still alive. He decides to go to Egypt to see him before he dies. The phrase "I will go and see him" means exactly that: he will go and see him.

Jacob's sons had just returned from Egypt with an incredible piece of news. At first Jacob did not believe them, because for years he had thought that Joseph was dead. But he listened to Joseph's words and saw the wagons that Joseph had sent, and his spirit revived. His faith and his hope rose again, and he decided to act.

For today: sometimes pain makes us doubt that God can still work for good. If He gives us signs of hope, let us not reject them out of fear of getting our hopes up. Let us make room for hope and take the step of faith that God shows us.
exp.13:3:
This verse says that the kings of the cities of the valley, including those of Sodom and Gomorrah, were subject to Chedorlaomer for twelve years. In the thirteenth year they stopped obeying him and rebelled. "Served" here means being under his rule, probably paying tribute, that is, a tax paid to a more powerful king.

No one speaks in this passage; it is the narrator of Genesis who recounts the events. It explains why a war breaks out among kings of the region. The rebellion of these cities provokes the military response of the fourteenth year. This account sets the scene in which Lot, Abram's nephew, is taken captive.

For today: the decisions of others can affect us, even when we do not make them ourselves. This invites us to think carefully about where we live and with whom we align ourselves, and to pray for wisdom. God cares for his people in the midst of conflicts he did not cause.
exp.43:30:
Judah says to Joseph (whom he does not yet recognize) that if Jacob sees that Benjamin is not returning, he will die of grief. "Lad" means a young man, "gray hairs" refers to the white hair of an old man, and "grave" is the place of the dead. In this way, the brothers would cause their aged father to die of sorrow.

Judah speaks, defending Benjamin before the ruler of Egypt. Joseph had put his cup in Benjamin's sack and wanted to keep him as a servant. Jacob had already lost Joseph, as he believed, and his life was closely bound up with Benjamin's. Judah offers to stay himself as a slave in Benjamin's place.

For today: our decisions affect those who love us. Judah went from being the brother who sold Joseph to being the one who offers to suffer on behalf of another. God can transform the heart, and we can ask him for the courage to care for our family with love and responsibility.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that the sun, the moon, and the stars were placed to "rule" over the day and the night, that is, to govern them and mark their course. They also serve to "divide" the light from the darkness, that is, to separate light from darkness. At the end, God looks at what he has made and says that it "was good."

The one speaking is the narrator of Genesis, who recounts the creation on the fourth day. God had already separated light from darkness on the first day, and now he sets lights in the sky to keep that order. Many ancient peoples worshiped the heavenly bodies, but here they are creations of God, made with a purpose and called good.

When you see the dawn or a starry night, give thanks to God. The rhythms of day and night are also a gift: respect your times of work and rest, trusting that God has ordered life well.
exp.19:6:
God tells Abimelech to return Sarah to Abraham. He calls Abraham "a prophet," that is, someone close to God who speaks on His behalf. Abraham will pray for Abimelech and he will live. But if he does not return her, he will die, together with all that is his.

God speaks to Abimelech, king of Gerar, in a dream. Abraham had said that Sarah was his sister, and the king took her. God stopped him before he sinned and now gives him a clear way out. It is interesting that God uses Abraham as an intercessor, despite his mistake.

For today: when we know that something is wrong, prompt obedience protects us. We can also pray for those who have wronged us, since God often brings healing and reconciliation through prayer.
exp.23:52:
The explanation says that Abraham's servant brought out objects of silver, objects of gold, and fine clothing, and gave them to Rebekah. He also gave valuable gifts to her brother Laban and to her mother. "Servant" is the word for a household servant, "vessels" are containers or utensils, and "maiden" means a young woman.

It is the account of the search for a wife for Isaac. After Rebekah's family acknowledged that everything came from the LORD, the servant bowed down in worship. Then he gave these gifts, which were a way of honoring the family and sealing the agreement of the betrothal, according to the custom of the time.

For today: true gratitude first worships God, and then expresses itself with generosity toward people. When God opens a door for you, give thanks to Him and honor, with concrete gestures, those who took part.
exp.29:19:
Leah says that God has given her a "good dowry," that is, a valuable gift, like the kind a husband once gave for his wife. She hopes that now her husband will "dwell" with her, meaning that he will honor her and live with her as a cherished wife. For this reason she names her sixth son Zebulun, a name that sounds close to the idea of "dwelling" or "honoring" in Hebrew.

Leah speaks in the midst of a painful rivalry with her sister Rachel. Jacob loved Rachel more, and Leah longed to be valued. She sees in her children a sign of God's favor. The Bible does not say whether Jacob changed his treatment of her.

Today we can learn to see God's gifts even in the midst of pain and the desire to be loved. Even so, our worth does not depend on others recognizing us, but on God seeing us and caring for us.
exp.14:12:
God tells Abram to know this for certain: his descendants (his "seed") will live as strangers in a land that does not belong to them. There they will be enslaved and suffer mistreatment ("afflicted") for four hundred years. Some read that figure as a round number, and others as an exact amount.

God speaks in the middle of a vision and deep darkness, just after Abram had prepared the animals for a covenant. Abram had asked how he would know that he would inherit the land. God answers him honestly: the promise will be fulfilled, but first it will pass through difficult years. Later, the Bible shows this in Egypt.

For today: God does not promise a life without pain, but he does promise to be present and to keep his word. When you go through a dark or long season, remember that delay does not mean God has forgotten.
exp.49:21:
This verse says that Joseph stayed to live in Egypt together with his family, his father's house, and that he died at the age of one hundred and ten. The phrase "his father's house" refers to his brothers and their families. In that time, one hundred and ten years was seen as a long and blessed life.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Just before, Joseph had forgiven his brothers after the death of Jacob. They feared he would take revenge, but he told them that God turned the evil into good. This verse sums up his life and prepares his farewell, where he will trust that God will fulfill his promise.

For today: when someone has wronged you, you can ask God for help to forgive and to treat that person well. A life marked by forgiveness and trust in God leaves a good mark on the family.
exp.28:22:
That evening, Laban took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob. Jacob came to her as her husband. "He went in unto her" is an old, respectful way of saying that they had marital relations. Today we would say "he took her as his wife."

Jacob had worked seven years to marry Rachel, Laban's younger daughter. When the time was complete, he asked for his wife, and Laban held a feast. But that night he gave him Leah, the older one. The text does not explain how Jacob failed to notice; some think it was dark and she was veiled, but that is a guess. Jacob, who had once deceived his father and his brother, is now deceived himself.

For today: what we sow can come back to us. This invites us to act with honesty and to ask forgiveness with humility, trusting that God works even in difficult situations.
exp.32:0:
Jacob lifts up his eyes and sees Esau coming toward him with four hundred men. Then he divides his children into groups: some with Leah, some with Rachel, and some with the two maidservants. The word "divided" means that he separated them and arranged them in order. The "maidservants" were women who served in the household and who were also mothers of some of his children.

This is a narrative, not a speech. Jacob is returning to Canaan after many years away. Long before, he had fled from Esau, who wanted to kill him because Jacob had taken his blessing. Now Jacob does not know whether his brother comes in peace or in anger, and for that reason he arranges his family with care. The Bible does not state here what Esau's intention was; the account will show it as it goes on.

For today: when you face a difficult reconciliation, pray and prepare wisely, but do not let fear paralyze you. Take prudent steps and trust that God can work in the heart of the other person.
exp.24:25:
After Esau, his twin brother was born, grabbing hold of Esau's heel with his hand. The word for heel here is "heel" itself, so the name given to the baby, Jacob, is connected with the heel he grabbed and with the idea of following closely behind, or of taking another's place. It is also made clear that Isaac was sixty years old when they were born.
