Here the narrator of Genesis is speaking, recounting the birth of Isaac and Rebekah's children. Earlier, God had told Rebekah that two nations were in her womb. The name Jacob foreshadows the struggle between the brothers, which will mark their whole story.

For today: God can work through imperfect people from the very beginning of their story. If you struggle with your own flaws, do not lose heart; trust that God is shaping you with patience and grace.
exp.23:16:
This verse tells how Abraham's servant saw Rebekah and ran to meet her. He asked her politely: "Let me, I pray thee, drink a little water of thy pitcher." "I pray thee" is an old-fashioned way of saying "please," and "pitcher" is a large vessel for carrying water.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac among his master's relatives. Before he reached the well, he had prayed for a sign from God: that the right young woman would offer water to his camels as well. His simple request was a test of her character. Some scholars think he already saw in Rebekah an answer to his prayer, although the text only says that he ran toward her.

For today: ask God for guidance with humility and pay attention to everyday details. God often works through simple acts, such as a small favor, a kind word, or a service given without expecting anything in return.
exp.40:55:
This verse says that the famine spread across the whole land of Egypt and grew more severe. Then Joseph opened all the storehouses, that is, the places where grain was kept, and began to sell it to the Egyptians. The word "sold" shows that he was not giving it away freely, but offering it in exchange for payment.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. During seven years of plenty, Joseph had stored up grain, just as God had shown him through Pharaoh's dreams. Now the seven years of scarcity had arrived, the people asked Pharaoh for bread, and Pharaoh told them to go to Joseph. Thus what Joseph had announced came to pass.

For today: preparing wisely and in an orderly way helps us serve better when difficult times come. Saving, planning, and being responsible with what God gives us can become a blessing for our family and for other people.
exp.40:26:
Here José continues explaining Pharaoh's dream. The seven thin and ill-favoured cows that came up after the fat ones represent seven years. The seven empty ears blasted with the east wind are also seven years, and they will be years of famine.

José speaks before Pharaoh, who had had two dreams that no one in Egypt could interpret. José, who was in prison, is summoned and makes clear that the interpretation does not come from him but from God. He tells Pharaoh that the two dreams are really one: a warning of what God is about to do in Egypt.

For today: God sometimes warns us of difficult times so that we may prepare with wisdom, not with fear. We can learn to save, to plan, and not to waste what we have in good times, trusting that God cares for us always.
exp.24:27:
The explanation says that Isaac had a special fondness for Esau, and one of the reasons was that he ate of the game Esau brought in. Rebekah, on the other hand, preferred Jacob. The words "loved" and "loved" speak of preference and affection. "Venison" refers to the animals that are hunted in the field.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis speaks. He tells how the twins were as they grew up: Esau, a man of the field and a hunter; Jacob, quieter and a dweller in tents. The parents each leaned toward one son. This detail prepares the family tensions that come right after, such as the sale of the birthright.

For today: if you are a father, mother, or leader, take care not to show favoritism. To love truly is to value each person for who they are, not for what they give us or how they please us. Favoritism usually wounds and divides families.
exp.39:13:
Here Joseph asks the pharaoh's cupbearer not to forget him when he returns to his post. He begs him to show kindness, that is, to do him the favor of speaking about him to the pharaoh so that he can be brought out of prison. "Make mention of me" means "name me" or "speak of me." "This house" refers to the prison.

Joseph has just interpreted the cupbearer's dream and has given him good news. Since he had been sold and taken to Egypt, and he was imprisoned without having done anything wrong, he takes the opportunity to ask for help. It is a human and sincere request. The text does not say that it is wrong to ask for it.

We can trust God and, at the same time, humbly ask for help from those who can give it. And when someone does us a good turn, let us remember those who still need a friendly hand.
exp.30:32:
Laban went through the tents of Jacob's camp, searching for the household gods. He first entered Jacob's tent, then Leah's, then the tents of the two maidservants (Bilhah and Zilpah), but he found nothing. When he came out of Leah's tent, he went into Rachel's tent. The phrase "he found them not" is repeated like a suspense before the outcome.

Laban had pursued Jacob after he had secretly left with his family. He accused him of stealing his gods. Jacob, not knowing that Rachel had taken them, proposed that whoever had them should die. Without realizing it, he put at risk the person he loved most.

Today it reminds us that speaking without knowing the whole truth can bring serious consequences. Before accusing or making strong promises, it is wise to know the facts well and to know our own family. It also invites us to let go of any "idol" hidden in the heart.
exp.13:16:
This verse tells us that Abram was returning after defeating Chedorlaomer and the kings who were with him. Then the king of Sodom went out to meet him in the valley of Shaveh, called "the king's dale." The word "defeat" refers to the victory over the enemy, and "to receive him" means "to receive him" in the sense of going out to greet him.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Abram had rescued his nephew Lot and the captured people, including the people of Sodom. That is why their king goes out to meet him. Right after this, Melchizedek appears, and the contrast with the king of Sodom is striking: one comes to negotiate, the other to bless.

For today: after an achievement, we may receive offers from many people. It is wise to pause, give thanks to God, and consider from whom we receive blessing and whom we want to please.
exp.25:19:
This verse tells how the herdsmen of Gerar quarreled with Isaac's herdsmen over a well, saying the water belonged to them. "Strove" means they fought or argued, and the word points to a strong, heated dispute. Isaac named the well Esek, a name that in Hebrew is understood as "contention" or "quarrel," because they had had that conflict over it.

The narrator of Genesis recounts what happened in a time of famine and of living as a foreigner among the Philistines. In that dry land, water meant life for the flocks. Isaac reopened the wells of his father Abraham, and the well his servants found in the valley became the cause of the dispute. Isaac does not respond with violence but withdraws and keeps searching.

For today: when a conflict arises, it is not always necessary to win the argument. Sometimes it is wise to yield in peace and trust that God will open another way, as He did later with Rehoboth.
exp.22:11:
Abraham bows low, lowering himself or inclining in respect before the people of the land. "The people of the land" refers to the Hittite residents who were gathered and listening to the transaction. Bowing was a sign of courtesy and gratitude.

Sarah had just died, and Abraham, who lived as a foreigner, needed a place to bury her. Before the witnesses at the city gate, which was the place for legal matters, Ephron offers the cave and the field. Abraham thanks him with humility, but he will insist on paying. Some think Ephron's offer was a common way to begin bargaining, though the text does not make this clear.

We can treat with respect and gratitude those around us, even when they do not share our faith. Humility and honesty, such as paying what is fair, give a good witness where we live.
exp.33:19:
This verse tells us that Hamor and his son Shechem went to the gate of the city, which was the place where the leaders gathered to deal with public matters. There they spoke with the men of the city.

After Shechem dishonored Dinah, he and his father propose an agreement to Jacob and his sons. Now they must win over their own people. What they say next emphasizes the economic advantages and does not mention what Shechem did. For this reason, some see here a self-interested persuasion.

Today we can learn to be wary of speeches that sound reasonable but hide self-interest. Before deciding, it is good to ask: is the whole truth being told? Is justice being sought, or only convenience? Let us ask God for wisdom and honesty.
exp.29:35:
This verse says that Laban put a distance of three days' journey between his own flocks and Jacob. The animals Laban set apart were kept far away, in the care of his sons. Meanwhile, Jacob stayed to tend the rest of Laban's flocks. "Fed" here means that he led them to pasture and looked after them.

Jacob had worked for Laban for many years and asked as his payment for the speckled, spotted, and dark-colored animals. Laban agreed, but he set those animals apart so that Jacob would start with almost nothing. The narrator tells this carefully, showing Laban's distrust. The Bible does not say here that Laban acted with bad intent, but the distance suggests he wanted to secure his advantage.

For today: when someone acts with distrust or takes advantage of their position, keep doing your work with honesty and trust that God sees your situation.
exp.49:3:
This verse tells us that when the days of mourning for Jacob had ended, Joseph spoke to the members of Pharaoh's household. He asked them, very courteously, to speak to Pharaoh on his behalf. "If now I have found grace in your eyes" means: "if you are well disposed toward me." "I pray you" means "I ask you, please."

Joseph was a high official in Egypt. His father had died, and he had made Joseph swear that he would bury him in Canaan. Joseph does not ask Pharaoh's permission directly, but goes through his household. Some think this was because he was in mourning and did not present himself before the king, but the Bible does not make this clear.

Even with power and a good position, Joseph asks with humility and respect, and seeks to keep his promise. Today we can imitate him: keeping what we promised to our loved ones, and asking for things with courtesy and gratitude.
exp.30:41:
Jacob says that if God had not been with him, Laban would have sent him away with nothing. "The fear of Isaac" is an old way of naming God, whom Isaac respected and revered. "Empty" means empty-handed. "Rebuked thee" means that God corrected Laban, and "yesternight" refers to the dream in which God warned him not to harm Jacob.

Jacob speaks in anger, but with firmness, after Laban caught up with him as he was fleeing with his family. For twenty years he worked hard for Laban, who changed his wages many times. Jacob acknowledges that God saw his labor and protected him. Laban answers by saying that everything belongs to him, but in the end he proposes a covenant.

For today: when you feel that your work is not valued or that someone is taking advantage of you, remember that God sees what others overlook. Trust in Him, and act with honesty and peace.
exp.30:45:
Jacob asks his "brothers," that is, the relatives and companions who were with him, to gather stones. With them they make a heap of stones. Then they eat together there, on that heap. Eating together was a way of sealing a covenant.

Jacob and his father-in-law Laban had come out of a long period of tension. Jacob had left without warning, and Laban caught up with him in the hill country of Gilead. Now Jacob proposes a covenant of peace, and the heap of stones stands as a visible sign of the agreement between the two of them.

For today: when there is a conflict, it is worth making clear agreements and sealing them with a gesture of peace. Sitting at the table with someone with whom there was tension can help heal the relationship and keep the promises made in mind.
exp.35:22:
This verse lists the five children of Shobal: Alvan, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onam. Shobal was one of the sons of Seir the Horite. The word "dukes" in other verses refers to heads of clans or tribes, not to nobles as in Europe.

The narrator of the book, traditionally identified with Moses, records here the families of the Horites, the people who lived in the region of Edom before the descendants of Esau settled there. This list appears within the genealogy of Esau. Scholars do not fully agree on how the two peoples came to mix, and the text does not explain this in detail.

For today: the Bible names people that almost no one remembers, and this shows us that God knows each one by name. Today you can treat with respect the "unimportant" people around you and pray for them by name.
exp.14:6:
God reminds Abram who he is: "I am the Lord", the same one who brought him out of Ur of the Chaldees. And he tells him why he did it: to give him this land as an inheritance. "Inherit" means to receive something as a gift, not to earn it.

God speaks with Abram right after promising him descendants as numerous as the stars, and Abram believed him. Now God adds the promise of the land, grounding it in what he has already done for him. Abram responds by asking for a sign, and God answers him with a covenant, through the animals he asks Abram to prepare.

For today: when you doubt the future, remember what God has already done for you. His faithfulness in the past gives you reasons to trust his promises, and it is fine to speak honestly with him about your doubts.
exp.8:25:
Noah keeps speaking and says, "Blessed be the Lord God of Shem." That is, he acknowledges that God has a special relationship with Shem and his family. Then he repeats that Canaan will be Shem's servant. The King James wording "shall be his servant" carries the sense of "let him be his servant," and "servant" means a worker under another's authority or, in many cases, a slave.

Noah speaks after waking from his drunkenness, once he has learned what his youngest son did to him. His words are a prophetic statement about descendants. Note that the blessing is directed to God, not only to Shem. Some interpret this as referring to the Canaanites, who were later subdued by Israel, a descendant of Shem. This passage must never be used to justify slavery or racism.

For today: our decisions and attitudes can affect our children and grandchildren. Let us seek to honor God and our parents, so that our family receives blessing and not sorrow.
exp.44:21:
This verse says that Joseph gave each of his brothers a change of clothing, called a "suit of clothes" in the King James wording, which was a set of fine or festive garments. To Benjamin, his youngest brother, he gave much more: three hundred pieces of silver and five changes of clothing.

Joseph, already governor of Egypt, has just made himself known to his brothers, who years earlier had sold him into slavery. Now he sends them off with gifts and provisions so that they may bring their father Jacob. Benjamin was the only full brother of Joseph, and he had not taken part in the sale. Some think the larger gift shows Joseph's special affection for him; others also see it as a test of how the brothers would react. The text does not explain it.

Today, this passage invites us to respond with generosity and grace when someone has wronged us. Forgiving is not always easy, but God can heal broken relationships.
exp.21:4:
Here Abraham speaks to his two young servants. "Young men" here means attendants or helpers, and "saddled" refers to putting the saddle on the donkey. He asks them to wait with the donkey while he and the boy go up to worship. And he promises them: "we will come back to you."

It is the third day of the journey. God had asked Abraham to offer Isaac, his son, on the mountain. Abraham speaks of worshiping and of returning, though he knows what God commanded him. Some understand that he did not want to give explanations; others, that he trusted God would do something. The text does not make this clear, but Hebrews 11:19 says he reasoned that God was able to raise Isaac from the dead.

For today: when we do not understand what God allows, we can keep obeying with confidence, and turn a difficult moment into worship, believing that God is faithful.
exp.3:7:
This verse tells that Cain spoke with his brother Abel, and that afterward, while the two of them were in the field, Cain rose up against him and killed him. The King James wording "it came to pass" means "it happened," and "slew him" means "killed him." Some older translations add what Cain said, such as "Let us go out into the field," but the Hebrew text is not entirely clear at that point.

God had just warned Cain, who was angry because his offering had not been accepted. He told him that sin was crouching at the door, like a force ready to seize him, but that he could master it. Cain heard the warning and gave in anyway. It is the first murder the Bible records.

For today: when you feel anger or envy, do not ignore it. God warns us in time. Speak with Him, seek peace with the other person, and do not let that anger grow until it becomes harm.
exp.34:0:
God tells Jacob to get up and go up to Bethel, to settle there for a while, and to build an altar. That altar would be for worshiping the God who appeared to him when he was running away from his brother Esau. "Dwell there" means "live there," and "appeared unto thee" means "was shown to you."

God is the one speaking. Jacob had lived for years far from home, and now he was in a difficult situation, because his sons had caused trouble in Shechem (chapter 34). Bethel was the place where God spoke to him in a dream years earlier (Genesis 28). God calls him back to that place and to remember his promise.

Today, God invites us to return to Him, especially after confusing times or times of neglect. We can set aside a moment to thank Him for what He has done and to renew our commitment to Him sincerely.
exp.5:16:
God tells Noah that He Himself is going to bring a flood, a great deluge of water, upon the earth. This would destroy every living creature that breathes, "all flesh in which is the breath of life," that is, people and animals. "From under heaven" means across the whole known or inhabited earth.

God speaks in the middle of the instructions for building the ark. Before this, the text tells us that wickedness and violence had filled the earth (Genesis 6:5, 11-13). Some believe the flood was worldwide, and others that it was very extensive but regional; the text presents it as an enormous judgment. Even so, God immediately offers a covenant and a way of salvation.

Today we can see that God takes evil seriously, but He also provides a way out for those who trust in Him. Ask yourself: what is God asking you to do in faith, as Noah did, even though you cannot yet see the result?
exp.21:14:
The verse says that the angel of the Lord called to Abraham from heaven a second time. The phrase "a second time" means that the angel had already spoken to him before, when he stopped Abraham's hand on the mountain. The word "unto" in the King James Version is an older way of saying "to".

The account describes what happened right after Abraham offered the ram in place of Isaac. The angel of the Lord speaks on God's behalf; the text presents him speaking as God himself, and there are several ways to understand that figure. God calls again to confirm his promise to Abraham, since he obeyed without withholding his son.

For today: God sees our obedience, even the kind that costs tears, and often speaks again with encouragement and promises. If you are going through a trial, keep trusting; God does not forget you or stay silent forever.
exp.2:21:
God says that the man has now come to know good and evil, and this has made him "like one of us." The word "us" in the King James wording is the old way of saying "we" with a plural sense. The sentence is left open: God is thinking about what could happen if the man also ate from the tree of life and lived forever in that state. That is why the sentence ends without being completed.

God himself is speaking, after Adam and Eve disobeyed by eating the forbidden fruit. He had already given them garments of skins to cover them. Many understand that "us" shows God's majesty or his plural nature; others see it as a reference to God and his heavenly court. The texts that follow show that removing them from the garden was both a measure of protection and a consequence of sin.

For today: God acts with justice, but also with care. When we go wrong, we can trust that he continues working for our good.
exp.15:6:
This verse tells that the angel of the Lord found Hagar beside a spring of water in the wilderness, on the road that leads toward Shur. The word "found" means that he came upon her, and "fountain" here refers to a spring of water. Hagar was fleeing and was alone, tired, and without direction.

The narrator relates what happened after Sarai mistreated her servant Hagar. She fled into the wilderness, probably toward Egypt, her homeland, although the text does not say this clearly. Some understand "the angel of the Lord" to be a messenger of God, while others see God himself speaking there; the text allows both readings.

For today: when you feel hurt, lost, or without a way out, remember that God sees you and comes out to meet you, even in your own "wilderness." You can speak to him honestly, as Hagar did, and listen for his guidance.
exp.40:56:
The explanation says that people from all the neighboring countries traveled to Egypt to buy grain from Joseph. The reason was that the hunger had become very severe everywhere. The phrase "all the earth" here refers to the region known at that time, not necessarily the whole planet.

The one who tells this is the narrator of Genesis. Joseph had interpreted Pharaoh's dreams and, after seven years of abundance, was managing the stored grain. Now the time of scarcity he had foretold had arrived, and Egypt had food when others did not.

For today: preparation and wisdom can become a blessing for many. God used Joseph's faithfulness to sustain lives. We can ask ourselves what resources, time, or skills we have and how we might use them responsibly to help those who are in need.
exp.5:10:
The explanation says that the earth became morally ruined in the eyes of God, and that it was filled with violence. The word "corrupt" means that it was damaged, spoiled morally. "Before God" means that God saw everything clearly.

The narrator of Genesis describes the situation before the flood. Just before this, Noah is presented as a righteous man who walked with God, and that makes the contrast with the people of his time sharper. Then God looks at the earth, confirms what was there, and announces to Noah his decision to judge. Violence is the reason that is repeated.

For today: Noah lived faithfully in the midst of a damaged society. We can ask God to help us walk with him at home, at work, and at school, treating others with respect and not letting ourselves be carried along by violence or by the bad example around us.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that God appeared to Abraham in the plain of Mamre. Abraham was sitting at the entrance of his tent, at the hottest hour of the day. "Appeared" here means "appeared to him," and "the Lord" is the name of God in the Old Testament.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. Abraham is an older man who lives in tents as a nomad, and he waits for God's promise to give him a son. The verses that follow tell that he saw three men and welcomed them with great haste and respect. Some understand that one of them represented God himself; others interpret it in different ways.

For today: God can visit us in ordinary moments, such as a hot and quiet day. Let us live attentively, with a heart ready to receive others with generosity, as Abraham did.
exp.4:18:
He says that Jared, after having his son Enoch, lived eight hundred more years and had other sons and daughters. The old words are "begat," which means had a son, and "Enoch," which we today write as Enoch. The spelling "and daughters" simply means "and daughters" in modern usage.

Here it is not a character speaking; it is the account from the book of Genesis, which repeats the genealogy from Adam to Noah. Each life is summed up with the same pattern: born, had children, lived, and died. The very long numbers are understood in different ways: some take them literally and others as a way of expressing a very ancient era. It is not certain what the exact intention is.

For today: Jared's life is not remembered for his achievements, but for his family and his passage through the world. We can use our days with purpose, caring for our own and leaving them a living faith, trusting that God carries history forward.
exp.20:13:
Abraham got up early and gave Hagar bread and a skin of water. A skin was a leather bag for carrying water. He placed them on her shoulder, handed her the boy, Ishmael, and sent her away. The word "gave" in the King James wording expresses the same act described in the original. She left and wandered aimlessly through the wilderness of Beersheba.

This is a narrative, not a speech. Sarah had asked that Hagar and Ishmael be sent away, and Abraham was distressed by it. God told him to obey and promised that He would also make a nation of Ishmael. Abraham acts early in the morning, trusting that promise, even though the parting was painful.

For today: sometimes we have to make difficult decisions that hurt. We can take the step in obedience and entrust to God the people we love, because He cares for them even when we are unable to do so ourselves.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that Zillah, one of Lamech's two wives, had a son named Tubal-cain. He was an "instructer" of every artificer in brass and iron, that is, someone who taught and shaped every object made of metal, whether bronze or iron. His sister Naamah is also mentioned. "Bare" is an older way of saying "gave birth to."

Here no character speaks; it is the narrator of Genesis. He presents the family of Lamech, a descendant of Cain, and shows how livestock herding, music, and metalworking came about. Right after this, Lamech speaks with pride and violence. Scholars debate whether the account values these advances or warns about a culture that advances without God. The text does not make this clear.

For today: our talents and advances are gifts that can be used for good or for harm. Ask yourself how you can use your skills to serve others and honor God, not for your own pride.
exp.17:24:
Abraham tells God that it would be unjust to destroy the righteous along with the wicked. "That be far from thee" means "that you would never do this." "Wicked" refers to someone who lives without respect for God. It ends with a question: shall not the Judge of all the earth do right? Abraham trusts that God is just.

Abraham speaks after God announced judgment on Sodom, where his nephew Lot lived. Abraham intercedes with respect and courage. God does not rebuke him; he answers that he would spare the city if fifty righteous people were found there. So we see that God listens to those who pray with humility.

For today: we can pray with confidence for difficult people and places, relying on the just and merciful character of God. To pray this way is not to make demands of him, but to speak with reverence, as Abraham did, who acknowledged himself to be "dust and ashes."
exp.23:12:
The explanation says that Abraham's servant is standing beside the spring, and that the young women of the city are about to come out to draw water. The words "Behold" serve to draw attention: it is like saying "look where I am." "Well" here means a spring or well of water, and "men" are the men of the city.

The one speaking is Abraham's servant, whom the text does not name here. His master sent him to find a wife for Isaac among Abraham's relatives. He arrived in the evening, when the women customarily drew water. In this prayer he asks God for a clear sign to recognize the right woman.

For today: before deciding something important, we can pray with humility and act with good sense. The servant prayed, but he also went to the right place at the right time, and he paid attention to what God was doing.
exp.41:15:
Here Joseph, speaking as the ruler of Egypt, sets a test for his brothers. One of them must go back to Canaan and bring the younger brother, while the rest remain in prison. In this way it will be seen whether they are telling the truth. "By the life of Pharaoh" was an oath sworn by the king. If they fail the test, he declares them to be spies.

Joseph is second in rank after Pharaoh. His brothers do not recognize him; they had sold him years earlier. He accuses them of being spies and demands to see Benjamin. The Bible does not explain his full purpose here. Many think he wanted to know whether they had changed and whether his father and Benjamin were well.

For today: truth is shown by deeds, not only by words. If you have failed someone, do not wait until you are pressed; acknowledge your wrong honestly and seek to make right what you can.
exp.35:35:
This verse says that Hadad, king of Edom, died, and that Samlah, a man from Masrekah, began to reign in his place. Masrekah was probably a place or region in Edom, although it is not known with certainty where it was. The word "reigned" means that he took over the government.

Genesis 36 is a list of the descendants of Esau, also called Edom, and of the kings who ruled that land. The text tells it as a narrator, without any speech. Note that these kings were not passed down from father to son: each one comes from a different place. The list shows that God kept his promise that Esau would also form a nation.

For today: all human power passes away, and every leader dies and is replaced. We can serve with humility in whatever task falls to us, and trust in God, whose kingdom never ends.
exp.42:23:
This verse tells that Joseph's steward brought the brothers into Joseph's house. He gave them water to wash their feet, and he also gave food to their donkeys. "Man" here refers to the steward, the one in charge of the house, and "asses" are the donkeys.

The steward has just calmed the brothers, who were afraid because of the money found in their sacks. He told them not to fear and returned Simeon to them. Now he treats them with the courtesy customary in that time toward visitors. The brothers still do not know that Joseph is their brother, and the text does not explain everything the steward understood.

For today: hospitality shows itself in simple details, such as offering water, rest, and food. When you welcome someone, attend first to their basic needs. In this way you can calm fears and open the way to trust.
exp.8:2:
It says God gives Noah and his sons all living animals as food, just as he had earlier given them the plants. "Sustenance" means provision or food. "Vegetables and herbs" refers to the green plants they could already eat. "I have given you everything" shows a broad provision.

God speaks after the flood, when he blesses Noah and his family to begin again. He confirms their place over creation, but right away sets a limit: do not eat the blood, because life belongs to God. Some think that before the flood people did not eat meat, although the text does not say this clearly.

For today: receive your food as a gift from God and give him genuine thanks. And use what God entrusts to you, including creation, with respect and without abuse, remembering that every life matters to Him.
exp.33:16:
It says that, if the men of Shechem will not agree to be circumcised, Jacob's sons will take their sister Dinah and leave. "Will not hearken unto us" means "will not listen to us" or "will not do as we ask," and "our daughter" here refers to Dinah.

Jacob's sons are speaking after the dishonor that Shechem brought upon Dinah. Hamor and Shechem propose marriage and an alliance. The brothers answer with a religious condition, but the following verse (Gen. 34:13) says they spoke "deceitfully." Their plan was revenge, and the circumcision was a trap. The Bible does not present this as a good example.

For today: using sacred things as a pretext for our own purposes is serious. If something hurts us or we have been wronged, let us seek justice honestly, not with deceit or revenge.
exp.30:50:
Here Laban tells Jacob to look at the heap of stones (the "heap") and at the pillar (the "pillar," that is, an upright stone or monument) which he has set up between the two of them. They are visible signs of an agreement. The word "cast" in this verse refers to something that has been set up or built.

Laban and Jacob separate after years of tension. Jacob leaves with his wives, who are Laban's daughters, and with his possessions. Laban fears that Jacob may mistreat him or his daughters, so he proposes a covenant of peace. Because he does not fully trust Jacob, he sets up these signs and calls on God as witness. Scholars explain the exact meaning of the covenant in several ways, but the text presents it as a boundary of mutual respect.

For today: when there is distrust, it is healthy to speak with clarity and to establish honest agreements. But above all, living as if God always sees us helps us keep the word we have given, even when no one else is watching.
exp.3:1:
She again gave birth to a second child, named Abel. The verb "bare" means she gave birth, and "his brother" shows that Abel was born after Cain. Abel took up the care of sheep, and Cain worked the ground, that is, farmed it. Both were necessary and honest occupations.

The narrator of Genesis tells this briefly to introduce the two brothers before a decisive moment. It comes after Cain's birth, when Eve recognized God in her son. The verses that follow speak of the offerings each brought to God. Here there is still no conflict; only their everyday life is described.

For today: our work, whatever it is, is part of the life God gives us. But what matters most is not the occupation, but the heart with which we live and draw near to God. We can ask ourselves today: do I work and offer my life to God with sincerity?
exp.3:6:
God says to Cain that if he does well, he will be accepted and will hold up his head. If he does not, sin is "at the door," like a crouching animal waiting to attack. "Its desire" means that sin longs to dominate him, but Cain can "rule over it," that is, have authority over it and overcome it. Some understand "its desire" to refer to Abel, but most see it as referring to sin.

God himself is speaking. Cain is angry and downcast because God accepted Abel's offering and not his. God does not condemn him at once; he asks him questions and gives him a warning full of care. Soon after, Cain ignores the advice and kills his brother.

When you feel anger, envy, or resentment, do not let them grow in silence. Bring them before God, listen to his correction, and choose to do what is right before those feelings take control of you.
exp.20:12:
God tells Abraham that he will also make a nation of Ishmael, the son of Hagar. "Bondwoman" refers to Hagar, Sarah's slave. "Seed" means offspring, that is, a son of Abraham. "Make a nation" means that he will make him into a great people.

God speaks. Sarah had asked that Hagar and Ishmael be cast out, and Abraham suffered greatly over his son. God comforts him: the main promise would continue through Isaac, but Ishmael would not be forgotten. Afterward Abraham sends them away, and in the desert God would again care for them.

For today: when a situation hurts us and has no easy solution, we can trust that God cares for the people who seem to be left outside the plan. Give Him your worries about those you love, and act responsibly toward them.
exp.41:24:
This verse tells how Joseph ordered his servants to fill his brothers' sacks with corn. He also commanded that each man's money be put back into his sack, and that they be given provisions for the journey. It was done just as he said.

Joseph is the ruler of Egypt, and his brothers have come to buy grain because of the famine. They do not recognize him. He has tested them, wept in private, and kept Simeon in prison. The verse does not say why he returns the money; many think it shows his generosity and also sets up another test for them.

For today: even when someone has hurt us, we can choose kindness instead of revenge. God can use quiet, generous acts to touch the conscience and open the way to reconciliation.
exp.37:5:
This verse tells that Judah, one of Jacob's sons, sought a wife for Er, his firstborn son. The woman chosen was named Tamar. "Firstborn" means the first male child, who held a special place in the family. "Took a wife" means that he arranged his marriage, as was the custom at that time.

The narrator of Genesis introduces Tamar, who will be very important in this story. The following verses say that Er was wicked in the sight of the Lord and died, and that Judah asked Onan to fulfill his duty toward Tamar by raising up offspring for his brother. The Bible does not explain here in detail the wickedness of Er or the background of Tamar; we should not invent those details.

For today: parents have a great responsibility in guiding their children, but each person answers before God for their own life. Let us pray for our families and live with integrity, trusting that God works even in difficult stories.
exp.44:14:
This verse tells that Joseph kissed all his brothers and wept as he embraced them. Only after that gesture did they feel encouraged to talk with him. The wording itself is simple, so there is no archaic word here that needs explaining. The phrase about talking with him means that at last they could speak with him openly and with confidence.

Here the one acting is the narrator, and the main figure is Joseph. He has just made himself known to his brothers, the same men who had sold him years before. They were frightened and ashamed. Before speaking of plans, Joseph shows them his forgiveness through tears and embraces. The text does not explain everything they felt, but it does show that forgiveness opened the door to conversation.

For today: when a relationship has been broken, sincere forgiveness and a loving gesture can help dialogue begin. Ask God for the courage to take the first step, and let reconciliation speak before reproach does.
exp.28:30:
The explanation says that God noticed Leah was "hated", that is, less loved or looked down on compared with her sister. So he "opened her womb", meaning he allowed her to have children. "Barren" means that Rachel could not have children for the time being. The name "the Lord" is the name of God.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks. Jacob loved Rachel more, and Leah lived with that pain in a marriage she did not choose. Earlier, Laban had deceived Jacob into marrying her. The text shows that God sees the one who is overlooked. Afterward, Leah names her sons, expressing her desire to be loved.

For today: if you feel undervalued or overlooked, remember that God sees you. Bring your pain to him honestly, and look for your worth in his care, not only in the approval of others.
exp.9:0:
This verse opens a list of families. It says that Shem, Ham and Japheth, the sons of Noah, had sons after the flood. "Generations" means the history of a family: who was born from whom.

Context: no one is speaking here; this is the narrator's account, traditionally attributed to Moses. It comes after the flood and after God's blessing to Noah to multiply and fill the earth. This list, often called the "Table of Nations," shows how the peoples came to be formed. Scholars debate how to match each name with specific peoples, so it is wise to be cautious.

For today: God watches over history and over families, even after great crises. If you are going through a hard time, remember that God can make life grow and bear fruit again.
exp.40:8:
Here the chief cupbearer, the official in charge of serving the king his cup, speaks to Pharaoh. He says that today he remembers "my faults." The word "I do remember" in the King James Version is an older form of "I remember." He admits that he had failed and that he now recalls something he had forgotten.

Pharaoh is distressed because no one can explain his dreams. Then this man speaks up. He had been imprisoned for angering Pharaoh, and in prison he met Joseph, who interpreted a dream for him. We do not know exactly what his fault was; the text does not say. What we do see is that for two years he forgot Joseph.

For today: acknowledging our faults with sincerity, as this man did, opens the door to correcting what we left undone. Today you can think about whom you owe a word of gratitude or a help, and not wait any longer.
exp.24:16:
This verse says that Ishmael, the son of Abraham and Hagar, lived one hundred and thirty-seven years. Then he "gave up the ghost," that is, he stopped breathing, and died. The phrase "was gathered unto his people" is an old way of saying that he died and was joined to his own family. Some see here only an expression about death; others think it hints at a hope beyond the grave. The Bible does not explain this in detail.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, and he does so to close the story of Ishmael. God had promised Abraham that Ishmael would have many descendants, and this is seen in the twelve princes of the earlier list. Afterward, the account returns to the line of Isaac, through whom the promise of the covenant would continue.

For today: life passes, but God keeps what He promises. Live thankful for the time God gives you, and trust that He cares for you and your family.
exp.36:1:
This verse begins a new part of the story of Jacob's family, centered on Joseph. He was seventeen years old and was tending the flocks with his brothers, especially the sons of Bilhah and Zilpah, Jacob's wives. The King James wording "brought unto his father their evil report" is the Hebrew phrase rendered here as he brought a bad report of their conduct to his father. José's report was a bad report about their behavior, and the word "report" conveys the sense of carrying news or telling what had been seen.

The one who narrates is the author of the book, not a character. He introduces Joseph before the conflicts to come. The verses that follow show Jacob's favoritism and the brothers' hatred. The text does not say in detail what the brothers did, and some readers think Joseph acted in sincerity while others think he acted with little discretion.

For today: when we see something wrong, let us ask for wisdom to speak the truth with humility and love, seeking the good of everyone and not our own advantage.
exp.28:11:
This verse tells us that Jacob explained to Rachel who he was: a relative of her father Laban, because he was the son of Rebekah. The phrase "told Rachel" means that he gave her the news about himself. Rachel then ran to tell her father. When the verse says "her father's brother," in the language of that time it was also used to refer to a close relative in general, since Laban was in fact the brother of Rebekah, that is, Jacob's uncle.

Jacob had arrived fleeing from his home and was looking for his mother's family. He met Rachel by the well, helped her with the flocks, and, moved with emotion, wept. Now he makes himself known. The Bible does not explain why he wept, but it is understood that he felt relief and emotion on reaching his kin.

For today: when God leads us to a new place, we can introduce ourselves with simplicity and honesty. And when someone comes into our life, we can hurry to welcome them and share the good news.
exp.11:10:
This verse tells us that Abram, now close to Egypt, speaks to Sarai, his wife. He says that he now realizes she is a very beautiful woman. The phrase "fair woman to look upon" means that she appeared lovely in the eyes of others. "It came to pass" means "it happened."

Abram speaks because he was afraid. There was famine in Canaan, and he was heading to Egypt to live there as a foreigner. The following verses reveal his plan: he feared that the Egyptians would kill him in order to take Sarai. The Bible does not say here that God had asked him to do this.

For today: when we feel fear, it is easy to look for quick solutions that do not honor God. We can learn to stop, pray, and trust his promises, even when the situation seems uncertain.
exp.33:14:
Jacob's sons set a condition for Shechem and his family: if they want an agreement between the two peoples, every male among them must be circumcised. The King James phrase "we will consent unto you" means "we will agree to your request." The word "defiled," which appears in the surrounding verses, means that Dinah had been dishonored. The word "uncircumcised" refers to a man who has not been circumcised.

The speakers are the sons of Jacob, and the text says they made the offer "deceitfully." Shechem had dishonored Dinah, and they pretend to accept an arrangement while hiding another purpose. Circumcision was a sacred sign of God's covenant with Abraham, but here they use it as a pretext. The account tells what happened; it does not approve the deceit or what follows from it.

For today: even when we have a real wound, we should not use sacred things or lies to take revenge. Let us seek justice with honesty and let God guide our hearts.
exp.43:18:
Judah reminds Joseph (whom he still sees only as the ruler of Egypt) that Joseph himself had asked them a question: "Have you a father, or a brother?" The King James wording "My lord asked his servants, saying, Have ye a father, or a brother?" shows the older English form "ye" for "you." "Servants" here means attendants, a respectful way of speaking before someone in authority.

Judah is speaking in defense of his brother Benjamin, who is accused of stealing Joseph's cup. Judah begins to tell what happened from the beginning, in order to reach Joseph's heart and explain how greatly his aged father Jacob would suffer if Benjamin did not return. He does not know that he is speaking to his own brother.

For today: when you have to ask for something difficult, speak with humility and with truth, recalling the facts calmly and thinking of the pain of others. Judah does not defend himself; he cares for his father and for his brother.
exp.19:3:
What it says: Abimelech had not yet come near Sarah. So, frightened by God's warning, he asks him: "Lord, will you also destroy a nation that is righteous?" The word "but" at the start of the verse marks a contrast with what came before, and the King James phrasing "had not come near her" means that he had not had relations with her.

Context: Abraham had said that Sarah was his sister, and Abimelech, king of Gerar, took her. God warned him in a dream that he would die. Here Abimelech speaks with God to defend his innocence, since he acted while deceived. God later acknowledges that he acted with integrity and that God Himself kept him from sinning.

For today: When we are accused or corrected, we can come to God with sincerity and humility, hiding nothing. He knows our intentions and also cares for us, even when He protects us from mistakes we did not know we were about to make.
exp.38:10:
This verse tells us that one day Joseph went into the house to do his work, and at that moment none of the other servants were there. "Business" here means his labor or his daily duties. He was left alone in the house, and that set the stage for what follows.

It is part of the story of Joseph in Egypt, where he was the steward in Potiphar's house. Potiphar's wife pressed him every day, and he always refused, saying that to yield would be to sin against his master and against God. Here the narrator, that is, the one telling the story, shows us that this time the pressure comes in a moment of solitude.

For today: when temptation keeps insisting, it is not enough to say no just once. It is wise to decide ahead of time what we will do, to guard the places where we are alone, and, like Joseph, to get out quickly from whatever leads us into sin.
exp.36:28:
Reuben returned to the pit where they had thrown Joseph, but he no longer found him there. Then he tore his clothes. A "pit" was a hole used to store water, and tearing one's clothes was a way of showing very deep grief.

The speaker is the narrator of the account. Earlier, Reuben had suggested throwing Joseph into the pit, and the text implies that he meant to rescue him afterward. The Bible does not say where he was when they sold him. That is why he reacts with anguish: his plans fell apart and his brother had disappeared.

For today: good intentions are not enough. Reuben wanted to help, but he did not clearly stand against his brothers. When you must defend what is right, do it with courage and in time, without leaving it for later.
exp.8:23:
Noah woke up from the drunkenness the wine had caused and learned what his youngest son had done to him. The phrase "his wine" refers to the effects of the wine. The text does not say in detail what Ham did. Some think he only saw it and told about it, while others believe there may have been something more. This is not known for certain. It is also not certain who "his youngest son" is: it could be Ham or, in a broader sense, his descendant.

The narrator of Genesis tells what happened after the flood. Earlier, Ham saw his father uncovered and told his brothers, while Shem and Japheth covered him with respect. Now Noah reacts, and in the following verses he pronounces a curse on Canaan and a blessing on Shem.

Today we can learn to cover the weaknesses of others with respect, rather than exposing them or talking about them without need.
exp.38:18:
This verse tells how Potiphar, Joseph's master, heard what his wife told him: "After this manner did thy servant to me." When he heard it, his anger was kindled, meaning he was filled with rage. The phrase "heard the words" reminds us that he reacted to what he was told, not to what he himself saw.

Joseph was a slave in the house of Potiphar, an Egyptian official. Potiphar's wife had pursued Joseph and, when she was rejected, falsely accused him to protect herself and take revenge. Potiphar heard only one version of events. We do not know for certain whom his anger was directed at; some think it fell on Joseph, and others suggest he may have doubted the story, since the usual penalty for that offense was more severe than prison.

For today: before we grow angry or judge someone, let us take time to hear all the sides. And when we suffer an injustice, let us remember that God remains present, as He was with Joseph.
exp.35:15:
This verse continues a list of the chiefs of the families that descended from Esau. The word "duke" is an old term; here it means a chief or leader of a clan, not a royal nobleman. The three named are sons of Eliphaz, the eldest son of Esau, and of his wife Adah. They ruled their clans in the land of Edom.

The author of the book, traditionally Moses, records the descendants of Esau, also called Edom. In this way he shows that God kept his promise to make Esau a nation, although the main promise passed through Jacob. Some scholars believe that certain details were updated by later scribes, but this cannot be stated with certainty.

God cares for and remembers even people who seem to be outside the main story. Every name in this list matters to Him. Today, this encourages us to value those whom others overlook and to trust that God keeps His word faithfully.
exp.24:24:
Esau was born first. The word "red" here most likely means reddish in skin color, and "hairy" means very hairy. A "garment" was a coat made of animal skins. So the baby looked covered in hair, like a coat. They named him Esau. The exact meaning of the name is not certain; some connect it with "hairy" or with "red."

The speaker is the narrator of the book of Genesis. He tells of the birth of Isaac and Rebekah's twins. Earlier, God had told Rebekah that she would have two nations in her womb and that the older would serve the younger. This verse shows the beginning of that fulfillment.

For today: God carries out his plans even when they do not follow what we expect. The first to arrive is not always the chosen one. Trust that God works with purpose, even when you do not understand everything.
exp.13:6:
This verse tells how the eastern kings, after defeating other peoples, returned toward En-mishpat, which is Kadesh. There they destroyed and plundered all the lands and possessions of the Amalekites. They also attacked the Amorites who lived in Hazezon-tamar. The word "possessions" here means fields, goods or territories. "Smote" means that they struck down and left everything in ruin.

Moses, the traditional author of Genesis, narrates a military campaign by Chedorlaomer and his allies. It describes how they advanced, conquering region after region. This prepares the scene for the war against Sodom and its neighbors, where Lot, Abraham's nephew, was living. Some scholars note that "Amalekites" here refers to a territory that later took that name, but this is interpreted in different ways.

For today: human power can seem unstoppable, but it is always passing. This story reminds us not to place our trust in strength, money or influence, but in God, who cares for his own even in the middle of conflicts that seem bigger than we are.
exp.28:24:
In the morning Jacob discovered that the woman he had spent the night with was Leah, not Rachel. He then confronted Laban with three questions full of pain and anger. Some older wording in the source needs a note: where the explanation says "when morning came," that means "when it was morning"; "behold" is "it turns out that"; and "deceived" means "betrayed with lies."

Jacob speaks here, addressing his uncle Laban. He had worked seven years to marry Rachel, whom he loved. Laban gave him Leah, his older daughter, and Jacob did not realize it until morning. Many readers notice an irony: Jacob, who earlier deceived his father and his brother, is now deceived himself. The Bible does not explain this, so it is one possible reading, not something the text states outright.

For today: lies and deceit leave lasting wounds. Let us be honest in our dealings, and ask God to make us humble when we reap what we have sown.
exp.18:36:
Moab was born to Lot's firstborn daughter. The verse says she gave birth to a son and named him Moab. The text states that the Moabites descend from him, a people who still existed when this was written. Many understand that the name sounds like "from the father," but this is not certain.

The narrator of the book is speaking. He tells the origin of the Moabites and the Ammonites after the destruction of Sodom. Lot's daughters, afraid of being left without descendants, acted with deception and sin. The text recounts what happened, but it does not approve of it.

For today: decisions made out of fear and without trusting God leave painful consequences. Even so, God does not abandon people. Later, Ruth, a Moabite woman, became an ancestor of David and of Jesus. We can trust that God works with grace even in broken stories.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that a man will leave his father and his mother, will join himself to his wife, and the two will become one flesh. In plain modern English: the word translated "will join himself" means to draw close to someone and stick to them firmly. "One flesh" speaks of a deep union: shared body, life, and purpose.

After Adam exclaims with joy when he sees the woman, the text shifts to a comment from the narrator. It is no longer Adam speaking, but the one telling the story, and he explains why marriage has been this way from the beginning. Jesus quoted this verse when he spoke about marriage (Matthew 19:5).

For today: if you are married or plan to marry, loyalty to your spouse should come first among your human relationships. Honoring your parents remains important, but the new home needs its own center.
exp.24:17:
The verse says that the descendants of Ishmael lived in a wide region, from Havilah to Shur, a place facing Egypt, on the road toward Assyria. It also says that Ishmael died "in the presence of" his brothers. The Hebrew phrase can be understood in two ways: that he died near his relatives, or that his descendants settled beside them. Scholars do not agree.

The narrator closes the story of Ishmael before continuing with the story of Isaac. In this way he recalls that God fulfilled what he promised Abraham about Ishmael: that he would have many descendants (Genesis 17:20). It had already been said of him that he would live "in the presence of all his brethren" (Genesis 16:12).

For today: God keeps his word and forgets no one, even when a person does not have the main role in the story. Trust that he also cares for you and your family.
exp.4:15:
Here is the explanation in plain, modern English:

It says that Mahalaleel lived 830 years after he became the father of his son Jared, and that during that time he had more sons and daughters. Some of the wording is old: "begat" means that he became a father, and "and" is what the sentence uses to join its parts. Adding the 65 years before that, you reach the 895 years mentioned in the next verse.

No character speaks here. It is the narrator of Genesis, presenting the family line from Adam onward. This list connects creation with Noah and shows that life carried on from one generation to the next, even though death appears again and again. About these very long lifespans there are different interpretations: some take them literally and others as numbers with symbolic meaning. The text does not explain which is intended.

For today: God pays attention to a whole life, not only to the famous moments. We can value ordinary things, such as raising children and living faithfully, because those too are part of the story God cares for.
exp.48:20:
Naphtali is compared to a hind (here "hind" is not a servant but a female deer) that is "let loose," that is, running free and unrestrained. From him will come "goodly words," that is, pleasant and good speech. Some scholars believe the Hebrew could be read differently, as a tree that produces beautiful branches, so the exact meaning is debated.

The speaker is Jacob, now an old man, who gathers his sons to tell them what lies ahead for them and their descendants. Naphtali is the tenth son in this list, and his blessing speaks of freedom and beautiful words.

For today: the freedom God gives you also shows in how you speak. This week, try to let your words encourage, thank, or comfort someone, instead of wounding them.
exp.39:2:
The verse says that Pharaoh ordered his cupbearer and his baker to be locked up in the prison of the house of the captain of the guard, the same place where Joseph was held. The phrase rendered "captain of the guard" in the text being translated referred to the head of the king's guard; in chapter 39 he is called Potiphar. The word "eunuchs" here refers to court officials.

The one telling the story is Moses, traditionally recognized as the author of the book. The two officials had offended Pharaoh, and that is why they ended up in prison. Although the text does not detail their offense, this meeting sets the stage for Joseph to interpret their dreams, something that will later bring him before Pharaoh.

For today: God can use dark places, like Joseph's prison, to prepare what lies ahead. If you are going through an unjust or difficult season, keep serving faithfully those whom God places beside you; no one knows what door may open from there.
exp.35:1:
The verse says that Esau took wives from the daughters of Canaan. It mentions Adah, the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Aholibamah, the daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite. The words "took" and "bore" are older forms that we would today express as "married" and "gave birth to." Hittites and Hivites were peoples who lived in Canaan.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, presenting the family list of Esau, also called Edom, father of the Edomite people. The names of his wives here differ from those that appear in Genesis 26 and 28, and scholars explain this in several ways: perhaps they used more than one name, or there are other reasons that cannot be stated with certainty.

For today: our decisions, such as whom we join ourselves to, mark the generations that follow. It is wise to decide with prayer, seeking counsel and thinking about the future of the family.
exp.2:15:
He says that God speaks to the woman after the fall. He announces that the pains of pregnancy and childbirth will increase; "conception" means being pregnant. He also says that her desire will be toward her husband, and that he shall rule over her, that is, he will have authority or dominion over her. Scholars debate what that "desire" means: some see it as longing or dependence, others as a desire to control.

The LORD God speaks just after Adam and Eve ate the forbidden fruit. These words describe the consequences of sin, not an ideal that God intended from creation. Earlier, God spoke to the serpent, and afterward he will speak to the man.

For today: this verse describes a broken world, not a command to dominate others. We can seek relationships of respect and mutual service, asking God to heal pride and selfishness in our homes.
exp.21:18:
Abraham returns to his servants, that is, the young men who had waited for him at the foot of the mountain. The explanation of the old word about returning, which the reader will not see in the verse, is dropped here. Everyone gets up and walks together toward Beersheba, and there Abraham settles down to live. It is a simple, almost quiet ending, after a very intense scene.

The one who narrates is Moses, according to tradition. He has just told how God tested Abraham by asking him to offer Isaac, and how an angel stopped the sacrifice and renewed the promise. The text does not mention Isaac in this verse, and we do not know why; some see it as a narrative detail and nothing more.

For today: after great trials or moments of faith, God also calls us back to everyday life. Trusting Him does not end on the mountain; it continues at home, at work, and in our routines.
exp.30:24:
Laban finally caught up with Jacob. Jacob had set up his camp in the mountain, and Laban also pitched his own camp there with his relatives, in the region of Gilead. The sentence about "pitched" and "brethren" in the source is a word-meaning note tied to the old wording, so I've removed it.

The narrator describes the moment when two hostile families meet. Jacob had secretly fled with his wives, his children, and his flocks. Laban pursued him for seven days, but God warned him in a dream not to treat Jacob badly. That is why the meeting begins tense, though with God already watching over Jacob.

For today: when you face a difficult conflict, do not rely only on running away or on your own strength. Speak honestly, seek peace, and trust that God sees your situation and can protect you, even when someone seems to be against you.
exp.35:25:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Dishon had four sons: Hemdan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran. Dishon was a grandson of Seir, a man from the region of Edom. Do not confuse Dishon with Dishan, who appears later and is a different person with a similar name.

The text is a record of families, written in the third person. Tradition attributes it to Moses, although some scholars think others added details later. Chapter 36 details the peoples who lived in the land of Edom, where Esau, the brother of Jacob, settled. In this way, the account shows how those neighboring nations of Israel grew.

For today: God does not overlook anyone, not even people we know only by name. If He records them in His Word, He also knows you and values you. You can trust that your life matters to Him.
exp.30:11:
He says that God showed Jacob, in a dream, that the male goats that mated with the flocks were streaked, spotted, and speckled. The first of these words, which means several colors mixed together, is rewritten here as "speckled," and the verb for mating is simply translated as "mated with."

Here the angel of God speaks, and Jacob tells his wives, Rachel and Leah. Laban had changed his wages several times and dealt with him deceitfully. Jacob explains that his prosperity did not come from his own cleverness, but from God seeing and caring for him. With this he prepares his family to return to the land of their fathers.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, remember that God sees what you perhaps cannot change. Trust in Him, keep doing your work with honesty, and ask Him for direction for the next step.
exp.8:26:
Noah wishes that God would enlarge and prosper Japheth, that is, that He would give him wide territory. He says that Japheth should dwell in the tents of Shem, and that Canaan should be a servant. There is a debate about who dwells in the tents of Shem: some think it is Japheth, others think it is God Himself.

Noah speaks afterward, after he had become drunk, when his son Ham dishonored him. Noah blesses Shem and Japheth, and pronounces the curse upon Canaan, son of Ham. It is a prophecy about descendants, not a command from God to enslave anyone. This text should never have been used to justify racism or slavery.

For today: honor your parents and those who care for you, and guard your words, because they can bless or wound for generations. May your actions bring blessing to your family.
exp.30:52:
Laban asks that the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor be the judge between him and Jacob. Jacob promises to keep the covenant, and he swears by the one his father Isaac feared, a way of naming the God whom Isaac respected and worshiped.

Laban and Jacob had quarreled for years over distrust and deception. Now they make a covenant of peace, with a heap of stones as the witness. Laban calls on God as judge. Some believe Laban mixed his faith with other beliefs, but the text does not make this clear. Jacob, on the other hand, swears by the God of his father.

For today: when there are conflicts, let us seek peace with sincerity, knowing that God sees what no one else sees. Keeping our word is a way of honoring him.
exp.12:9:
Lot raised his eyes and saw the whole plain of the Jordan. It was well watered everywhere, meaning it had water in abundance. It was as fertile as the garden of the Lord, a way of recalling the garden of Eden, and as the land of Egypt, a region known for its crops. The phrase "before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah" warns us that judgment would come afterward. Zoar was a city in that region.

Abram had just proposed to Lot that they separate to avoid quarrels between their herdsmen. Being the elder, Abram gave Lot the freedom to choose first. The narrator describes what Lot saw and, with that warning about Sodom, hints that his choice would not be as good as it seemed.

For today: what looks good and brings gain is not always the best. Before deciding, it is wise to ask ourselves not only what we will gain, but also how it will affect our spiritual life and our family, and to ask God for wisdom.
exp.3:12:
Cain tells God that his sin is too great to be forgiven. The word "iniquity" means wickedness or guilt. But the Hebrew text allows another reading: "my punishment is too great to bear." Scholars debate which meaning is more likely, and the version the explanation follows chose the first.

Cain has just killed his brother Abel. God confronted him and announced that the ground would no longer yield its fruit for him and that he would become a restless wanderer. Cain responds in anguish, fearing that he will be driven away and killed. It is striking that God, even so, protects him with a sign.

For today: when we recognize our guilt, we should not stop at fear of punishment. God continues to deal with mercy toward the one who admits his failure. We can approach Him with sincerity, without thinking that there is no hope left.
exp.38:19:
The verse tells how Potiphar, Joseph's master, took him and put him in the prison, the place where the king's prisoners were held bound. The words "put him" and "into" are older forms of "put" and "into." Joseph stayed there, shut up in prison.

Potiphar had just heard a false accusation from his wife, who lied, saying that Joseph had tried to take advantage of her. Joseph had fled and left his clothing behind. When Potiphar heard this, he became angry. No one heard Joseph's side of the story. What stands out is that he put Joseph in the king's prison and did not have him put to death, and the Bible does not explain why; some read it as a sign of doubt on Potiphar's part.

Today: sometimes we suffer injustice even when we have acted rightly. This account reminds us that God does not abandon us in such a place, since the following verse says that the Lord was with Joseph.
exp.9:13:
This verse continues the list of the descendants of Mizraim, a name that in Hebrew is also used for Egypt. It mentions Pathrusim, Casluhim and Caphtorim, which are peoples or clans. It says that the Philistines came from them, although it is not clear whether they descend from Casluhim or from Caphtorim. Other biblical texts connect the Philistines with Caphtor, which many believe is Crete, but there is no certainty.

It is part of the "Table of Nations," which tradition attributes to Moses. It shows how the lands were resettled after the flood. For the people of Israel, it also explained where their neighbors, such as the Philistines, came from.

For today: God knows the origin and the name of every people. This invites us to respect every person, regardless of their country, because we all come from one common origin and have equal worth before God.
exp.21:16:
God promises Abraham a very great blessing. The phrase "in blessing I will bless" and the phrase "in multiplying I will multiply" are ways of saying that he will do it without fail and in abundance. "Seed" here means descendants. His descendants will be countless, like the stars of the heaven and the sand which is upon the sea shore. "Thy seed shall possess the gate of his enemies" speaks of victory and rule; the gates were the key place of a city.

The angel of the LORD speaks, in God's name, after Abraham was willing to give up Isaac. God does not ask for that sacrifice in order to keep him, since he stops Abraham in time. Now he confirms his promise with an oath, because Abraham trusted and obeyed.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when the path of obedience is difficult. You can trust him with what you love most, knowing that he is faithful and good.
exp.20:30:
Abraham called that place Beersheba because there he and Abimelech made an oath, that is, a solemn promise before God. "They both swore" means that the two of them bound themselves to the agreement. The name sounds like "well of the oath," and it can also be understood as "well of the seven," because of the seven ewe lambs.

Abimelech, a Philistine king, wanted to live in peace with Abraham. A dispute had arisen over a well, something vital in that dry land. Abraham gave seven ewe lambs as proof that he had dug that well. In this way a peaceful covenant was sealed, and then Abraham worshiped God in that place.

Today we can resolve conflicts with clarity and honesty, keeping fair agreements and keeping our word. And after making peace, it is good to thank God and trust in Him.
exp.10:25:
Terah was seventy years old when he began to have children: Abram, Nahor, and Haran. The verse does not say that they were born in the same year. Many think Abram was not the oldest, and that he is named first because he is the most important figure in the story.

Here the narrator of Genesis speaks, a narrator that tradition attributes to Moses. He gives the list of families that connects the story of Babel with the calling of Abram. Through it he shows from which family would come the man through whom God would bless the nations. This list also prepares what follows: the death of Haran and the birth of Lot.

God works through the ordinary, even in common families with names that almost no one remembers. Today you can trust that your daily life, your home, and your faithfulness in small things also matter in God's plan.
exp.10:9:
This verse opens the list of the descendants of Shem, son of Noah. The word "begat" means that he became the father of someone. Shem was one hundred years old when his son Arphaxad was born, two years after the flood.

This account comes from the book of Genesis, traditionally attributed to Moses. After Babel, where God scattered the peoples, the story stops speaking of humanity in general and follows one family line. That line will lead to Abraham. Some of the dates in these genealogies are understood in different ways, and not all scholars interpret them the same way.

For today: God also works in everyday life, from generation to generation. Even if your life seems ordinary, it is part of what God is doing. Be faithful today in your family and in your faith, and leave a good example for those who come after you.
exp.11:0:
God tells Abram to leave his land, his family, and his father's house, and to go to a place that God has not yet shown him. Some old words in the source: "however" means "but," "relatives" means family or kin, and "go" means "go out" or "leave."

The one speaking is the Lord. Before this moment, the Bible says that Abram's family had left Ur and settled in Haran. Now God calls him to move on. With this call begins the story of Abram, whom God would later name Abraham, and the promise of blessing that follows in the verses after.

God often calls us to take steps of faith without showing us the whole path. Today we might ask ourselves: what comfortable or familiar thing is God asking me to let go of? Obeying one step at a time, trusting in his promise, is a simple way to live that faith.
exp.49:22:
This verse says that Joseph lived long enough to see his great-grandchildren through Ephraim, that is, to the third generation. It also says that the children of Machir, son of Manasseh, "were brought up upon Joseph's knees." That old expression suggests that he received them as his own, held them, and acknowledged them as family, although some think it could also indicate a formal adoption.

The one telling the story is Moses, the traditional author of the book. He recounts the end of Joseph's life in Egypt, after he had comforted his brothers and promised to care for them. The long years and the family growing up show that God was still keeping his promise to multiply this people.

For today: value the generations of your family and give time to the youngest. Bless them, pray for them, and teach them to trust God.
exp.29:38:
The verse says that the flocks conceived while facing the peeled rods, and that their young were born ringstraked, speckled, and spotted. "Brought forth" means gave birth, and "lambs" are the young sheep.

The narrator tells what Jacob did at the end of his years working for his father-in-law Laban. They had agreed that Jacob would keep the animals that were streaked and dark. Jacob used peeled rods so that the flocks would produce offspring of that kind. Scholars do not agree on the sense of the method: some see it as an ancient custom, others as an act of cleverness. Later, in chapter 31, Jacob attributes his prosperity to God, not to the rods.

For today: work with effort and wisdom, but recognize that the fruit comes from God, who cares for you even when someone treats you unjustly.
exp.38:16:
Potiphar, the captain of the guard, had brought Joseph into his house. Now his wife tells the others that this Hebrew servant came in to mock her. The word "mock" suggests making fun of her or taking advantage of her. It is a false accusation, because Joseph had fled from her.

The one speaking is Potiphar's wife, who had tried to seduce Joseph and was rejected. To protect herself, she turns the story around. Notice that she speaks of the Hebrew servant and of the one you brought to us, as if Joseph were a dangerous foreigner and her husband were to blame.

For today: when someone accuses us unjustly, we should not respond with revenge. Joseph remained faithful to God even without being defended. We can trust that God sees the truth and keeps working, even when it takes time.
exp.36:27:
It says that some merchants passed by the place, and Joseph was pulled out of the dry pit where his brothers had thrown him. They sold him for twenty pieces of silver, which were coins or weights of silver, and the merchants took him to Egypt. A cistern is a pit dug to store water. The Midianites and the Ishmaelites appear here almost as interchangeable names, and scholars explain this in several ways.

Joseph's brothers envied and hated him, and at first they thought about killing him. Judah proposed selling him, arguing that they would gain nothing from his death and that, after all, he was their own brother. The others agreed. Reuben was not present at that moment.

Today, the envy we keep in our hearts can grow until it leads us to hurt the very people we love. If you feel jealousy or resentment toward someone close to you, do not feed it in silence: bring it to God in prayer and seek reconciliation before it becomes a decision you regret for the rest of your life.
exp.34:23:
This verse is part of the list of the twelve sons of Jacob, who is also called Israel. Here the sons of Rachel, his beloved wife, are named: Joseph and Benjamin. They are the last two sons of Rachel, and the only ones she had.

The narrator is Moses, according to tradition, and no character speaks here. The text pauses to set in order the family that will give rise to the twelve tribes of Israel. It comes right after Rachel's death in giving birth to Benjamin, and after a painful scene of sin within the family.

For today: God notices every name. Even in a family that is wounded and flawed, he keeps his promises and works with patience. If your family is not perfect, do not lose heart; God can work with real people.
exp.19:0:
Abraham left the place where he had been living and went toward the south, to the region of the Negev. He settled between Kadesh and Shur, areas of the desert, and lived as a stranger in Gerar. "Stranger" means a foreigner, someone who lives in a place without being from there or having the same rights.

It is the narrator of the book who speaks, traditionally Moses. This verse sets up what follows: Abraham, being a stranger and feeling vulnerable, says that Sarah is his sister. The Bible does not explain all his reasons here, but the account shows his insecurity. Even so, God intervenes and protects Sarah.

Today: when you find yourself living in a new or uncertain place, do not let fear carry you away. God cares for you, even when you make mistakes. Trust in Him and act with sincerity.
exp.23:32:
Food was set before the servant of Abraham, but he would not eat until he had told why he had come. The phrase "set before him" is rendered in the verse as "there was set meat before him," and "his errand" is the matter that brought him. Then they said to him, "Speak on."
