The one who speaks is Abraham's oldest servant, sent to find a wife for Isaac among his master's relatives. He had already been welcomed in the house of Laban, Rebekah's brother. At this moment he puts his mission ahead of his hunger and his tiredness after the journey. The text does not make entirely clear who tells him "Speak on," but it is someone from the family.

Today we can learn to first carry out what is important that God has entrusted to us, without letting ourselves be distracted, even by good and legitimate things.
exp.32:12:
Jacob answers Esau, who has just proposed that they continue the journey together. Jacob says that the children are tender and that his sheep and cattle have young ones with them. If they are pushed too hard, even for a single day, the whole flock could die.

It is Jacob speaking, as he meets his brother Esau again after many years apart and after fearing the old offense. Esau received him with warmth. Jacob kindly declines to travel at Esau's pace and asks to move slowly. Some think it is a sincere and prudent excuse. Others believe he also wanted to keep a cautious distance. The text does not make this clear.

For today: caring for those who are most fragile means respecting their pace, even when others want to go faster. Speaking with honesty and kindness helps sustain peace.
exp.8:24:
Noah says that Canaan, the son of Ham, will be cursed. His descendants would serve his brothers, that is, his close relatives. The phrase "a servant of servants" means the lowest of servants.

Noah speaks after waking from his drunkenness and learning what Ham, his youngest son, had done to him. The text does not explain why the curse falls on Canaan and not on Ham; several explanations have been proposed, but none is certain. This is a statement about descendants, not a command from God. This passage must never be used to justify slavery or racism, as it has unjustly been used in history.

For today: let us care for the dignity of others, especially within the family. Let us cover faults with love, as Shem and Japheth did, rather than exposing them or mocking them.
exp.35:23:
This verse names the children of Zibeon: Ajah and Anah. It says that Anah found the mules in the wilderness while he was tending the asses of his father. The Hebrew word translated "mules" is unclear. Some translate it as "hot springs," and others in other ways. Its meaning is not known with certainty.

The text is part of a long list of the families of the Horites, a people who lived in the mountains of Seir, in the land of Edom. It is understood that the narrator is Moses, who records these genealogies. Here a curious fact about Anah is recalled, so that he can be clearly identified among several people with similar names.

For today: God notices the everyday. Anah did a simple job, caring for animals, and yet he was remembered. Pay careful attention to the small things you have today, because valuable things can come from them.
exp.34:25:
The verse mentions the last two sons of Jacob on this list: Gad and Asher, sons of Zilpah, Leah's maidservant. It then summarizes that these were the sons born to Jacob in Padan-aram, the region of Mesopotamia where he lived with his uncle Laban. A maidservant was a woman who served in the household and who, in that culture, could bear children for her mistress.

The narrator is speaking. Moses, according to tradition, closes a list of Jacob's twelve sons, who would become the tribes of Israel. It is worth noting that Benjamin was born near Bethlehem, not in Padan-aram; the summary is general, and it is understood that way.

Today we can see that God works faithfully even in complicated and unequal families. If your family story is not perfect, God can keep his promises through it. Trust that he is still working in what seems disordered to you.
exp.3:13:
Cain tells God that his punishment is too heavy. He feels that he is being driven out of the land where he lived and that he will have to hide from God's presence. He will be a wanderer with no fixed home. He also fears that anyone who finds him will kill him. "Wanderer" here means someone who moves from place to place without a clear direction.

Cain speaks after having killed his brother Abel. God has just told him that the ground will no longer yield good crops for him. Cain complains about the punishment, but in the text we do not see him showing remorse for what he did. His concern is centered on what is going to happen to him.

When we fail, it is easy to lament only the consequences. This passage invites us to honestly acknowledge the harm we cause and to seek God, who, even here, cared for Cain with a sign of protection.
exp.48:6:
It says that the anger and rage of Simeon and Levi are cursed, because they were cruel and violent. Jacob announces that he will divide them and scatter them among the other tribes of Israel.

The speaker is Jacob, now an old man, blessing and warning his sons before he dies. He remembers that Simeon and Levi, full of vengeance, killed the men of Shechem (Genesis 34). Note that he curses their anger, not the men themselves. Later in the story, Levi received no territory of its own and lived scattered among the Levitical cities, and Simeon was absorbed within the territory of Judah. Some see in this the fulfillment of these words.

For today: uncontrolled anger does harm and leaves consequences that last for years. Before reacting in fury, stop, pray, and seek peace. God can transform even stories marked by wrongdoing.
exp.36:35:
The verse says that Midianite traders sold Joseph in Egypt to a man named Potiphar. He was an official of Pharaoh, and the word used for him here can also mean a court officer or official. He was also the captain of the guard, that is, the chief of the king's guards. In the account, these traders are also called Ishmaelites, and it is not known for certain how the two names are related.

The one speaking is the narrator of Genesis. He closes the chapter with a contrast: Jacob weeps for Joseph, believing him dead, but Joseph is alive, though as a slave in a foreign country. In this way the reader sees what Jacob cannot see.

For today: when a situation seems lost, remember that we do not see everything. God may be at work in what is hidden. Trust him and keep waiting with patience.
exp.35:26:
This verse is part of a list of families. It says that Ezer had three sons: Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan. There are no hard words here; they are just ancient names. Ezer was a descendant of Seir, the ancestor of the Horites, a people who lived in the region of Edom.

The narrator, whom tradition identifies with Moses, records the family lines of Esau and of the peoples who lived in his territory. In this way he shows how Edom, a neighbor of Israel, came to be. Some names in other biblical lists are spelled a little differently, and it is not always known why.

For today: God pays attention to each person, even to names that almost no one remembers. If He preserves them in His Word, you matter to Him too. Today you can treat with respect those who go unnoticed.
exp.18:7:
Lot offers his two daughters, who are virgins; the phrase about not having known a man means they had never had sexual relations. He tells the men to do with them whatever they wish, as long as they do not touch the two visitors. Where the source says they came under the protection of his roof, the sense is that the visitors are under his roof and his protection.

The men of Sodom were surrounding Lot's house with violent intentions against his guests. In that culture, protecting a guest was a sacred duty. Lot, desperate, makes a terrible offer. The Bible tells this story but does not approve of it; it shows how even Lot's judgment had been distorted by a corrupt city.

For today: fulfilling a duty does not justify sacrificing the most vulnerable. When the pressure is great, we need to ask God for wisdom to protect everyone, without harming some to save others.
exp.9:10:
From that land, Shinar, Asshur went out and built the cities of Nineveh, Rehoboth, and Calah. Some scholars translate it so that it was Nimrod who went out to Assyria and built these cities. The Hebrew text allows both readings.

The account in Genesis, which tradition attributes to Moses, presents the list of peoples who descended from the sons of Noah. Here it continues to speak of Nimrod's kingdom and of how the first cities and nations came to be formed. Nineveh would later become very important, and the Bible mentions it further on.

For today: everything we build, whether a job, a home, or a project, matters to God. We can build with effort, but also with humility, remembering that He sees our works and asks us to use them justly and for the good of others.
exp.34:6:
Jacob built an altar in that place and called it "El-Bethel," which means "the God of Bethel" (house of God). He did this because there God had appeared to him when he was fleeing from his brother Esau.

The one telling the story is the narrator of Genesis. Jacob had been afraid after the conflict at Shechem, and God told him to return to Bethel (Luz), where years earlier he had seen God in a dream (Genesis 28). Now Jacob goes back to keep what he had promised. Notice that he honors God himself, not just the place.

For today: remember the difficult moments when God sustained you. Thank him with something concrete, such as a sincere prayer, an act of obedience, or a promise fulfilled.
exp.39:21:
It says that Pharaoh had the chief baker hanged, just as Joseph had explained to him. The word "hanged" here can mean hanging the body after the execution, or putting someone to death by hanging; scholars understand it in several ways. What matters is that the dream was fulfilled exactly.

The narrator tells what happened on Pharaoh's birthday. Joseph was unjustly imprisoned and had interpreted the dreams of two officials: the chief cupbearer was restored and the chief baker was condemned. Both outcomes matched Joseph's words, which shows that God was giving him understanding. But the cupbearer forgot about him.

For today: when God gives you a word or a promise, do not depend on people remembering what you did for them. Even if they forget you, God does not forget. Remain faithful and trust in his timing.
exp.35:2:
This verse continues the list of Esau's wives. Here Basemath is named, and she was the daughter of Ishmael and the sister of Nebajoth. That is, Esau married a descendant of Ishmael, the son of Abraham. In other passages of Genesis, Esau's wives appear with somewhat different names, and scholars explain that difference in several ways; the Bible does not fully clear it up.

The text is part of the "generations of Esau," a family record that presents the ancestors of Edom, the neighboring people of Israel. The narrator does not pass judgment here; he simply records how that family and its people grew up in Canaan.

For today: God sees and remembers every family, even those that seem to stand on the edges of the main story. We can treat all people with respect and dignity, knowing that each one has an important place before God.
exp.37:20:
Judah's friend, the Adullamite, arrives at the place where Judah had been with that woman and asks the people, "Where is the harlot who was openly by the way side?" The men answer that there has never been any harlot there. Note the older words here: "harlot" means a prostitute, and the reference to "by the way side" probably points to a place near springs or wells, though the exact name of the site is not entirely clear.

Judah had left his seal, his cord, and his staff as a pledge for the payment. His friend comes to pay with a young goat and to recover those items. But Tamar, who had covered herself with a veil, had already taken off her disguise and returned to her widow's clothing. That is why no one can find her.

When we act in secret, sooner or later the consequences catch up with us. Let us take care with our decisions, because what is hidden does not stay hidden forever.
exp.41:27:
One of Joseph's brothers opens his sack on the road and finds the money he had paid for the grain. He tells the others. Then their hearts sank within them, that is, they felt a strong fright, and full of dread they ask one another what God has done to them. "Here it is" means "look, it is right here."

The brothers were returning from Egypt to Canaan with food for their families. Without knowing it, they had dealt with Joseph, whom they had sold years before. He had ordered their money returned to them in secret. They do not understand the reason, and with the guilt they carry for what they did, they read the event as a sign of divine judgment.

A guilty conscience can read every event as punishment. But God often acts with grace where we expect condemnation. If there is something unresolved in your heart, do not flee in fear: confess it to God and seek reconciliation.
exp.47:6:
Jacob recalls that, on his way back from Padan-aram (the region of Mesopotamia where he lived with Laban), Rachel died on the road, in the land of Canaan. It happened when there was still a short distance, a few kilometers, left to reach Ephrath. There he buried her, beside the road. The text clarifies that Ephrath is Bethlehem.

Jacob, now elderly and ill, speaks with Joseph in Egypt. He has just adopted Ephraim and Manasseh as his own sons. In mentioning Rachel, Joseph's mother, he perhaps expresses his pain and his love for her. Scholars do not agree on the exact reason, but the memory connects Joseph with his mother and with the promise of the land.

For today: when we remember painful losses, we can speak about them honestly and with the people we love. Sharing our grief also helps us value family and trust that God continues to care for our story.
exp.45:14:
This verse closes the list of Leah's descendants. It says that she bore these sons to Jacob in Padan-aram, the region where Jacob lived with his uncle Laban. It also includes his daughter Dinah. The word "souls" in the verse means persons, and in total they add up to thirty-three. Some scholars explain in different ways how that number is reached.

The account, which tradition attributes to Moses, lists Jacob's family who go down to Egypt. This shows that God was beginning to fulfill his promise to make this family a great nation.

For today: God does not see people as a faceless crowd. Every name matters. Today you can value the members of your family, pray for them one by one, and trust that God cares for their story.
exp.33:26:
The rest of Jacob's sons came to where the dead were and plundered the city, that is, they took everything that was in it. They did this because their sister Dina had been defiled, an old word meaning stained, dishonored and abused.

The narrator describes what happened after Simeon and Levi killed the men of Shechem. The grief over Dina was real, but the revenge went far beyond justice. The account does not approve of what they did. Later Jacob rebukes them (Genesis 34:30; 49:5-7).

For today: when someone wounds us or wounds those we love, anger can lead us to do even more harm. Let us seek justice by right paths and leave vengeance in God's hands (Romans 12:19).
exp.4:26:
It says that Methuselah lived 969 years in total, and then adds: "and he died." It is the longest life the Bible records. The name is the one we write today as Methuselah.

The one speaking is the narrator of the book, who is recording the family line from Adam to Noah. Each life ends with the same words: "and he died." In this way the text shows that death, the consequence of the fall, reached even the one who lived nearly a thousand years. According to the figures in the text, Methuselah seems to have died around the year of the flood, although scholars debate these calculations.

For today: no matter how many years we have, life is limited. Let us ask God for wisdom to use our days well, loving those around us and trusting in Him.
exp.31:22:
He took his wives, his servant women, and his eleven children and sent them across the ford of the Jabbok. Then he sent across everything else he had. The verse's wording "sent them over" is the same act of crossing that the phrase "sent over" describes here, and the stream is the Jabbok river.

The narrator tells us that Jacob was getting ready to meet his brother Esau, whom he had deceived years earlier. He had already sent gifts ahead and felt afraid. After sending his family and possessions across, he was left alone on the other side. The text does not say exactly why he stayed behind; some think he wanted to protect them or to pray alone.

For today: when you face something that frightens you, do what is wise for those you love, but then look for a quiet moment alone with God. He can meet you there, even in the hardest night.
exp.29:17:
Leah says that God gave her her reward, or her wages, because she gave her servant to Jacob as a wife. That is why she names the boy Issachar, a name that sounds like the Hebrew word for "wages" or "payment." The words "Dí" means "gave," and "á" means "to."

Leah, Jacob's wife, speaks here in the middle of a strong rivalry with her sister Rachel. Earlier she had given her servant Zilpah to Jacob so that she could have more children. The text says that God listened to her, but this explanation of the "reward" is Leah's own interpretation. The Bible does not say that God approved of that decision.

Today we can recognize God's gifts with gratitude, but without using them to compete or to win the affection of others. We can thank Him for what He gives and rest in the fact that He loves us even in the midst of messy situations.
exp.9:15:
This verse continues the list of the sons of Canaan. It names three peoples who descend from him: the Jebusites, the Amorites, and the Girgashites. The final "-ites" in words like "Jebusite" indicates that the text speaks of a whole people, not just a single person. Older spellings such as "Amorrhite" and "Girgashite" are no longer used; today we write Amorite and Girgashite.

Genesis 10 is the "Table of Nations." No one is speaking in it; the narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, sets out the origins of the peoples after the flood. Many of these peoples appear later in the history of Israel, for example the Jebusites in Jerusalem. Scholars debate some details of these identifications, but the general purpose is clear.

For today: God knows each people and each person, even when history forgets them. Today you can treat everyone with respect, remembering that they have value before God.
exp.20:18:
The explanation says that God opened Hagar's eyes, and she saw a well or spring of water that she had not noticed before. Then she went, filled the skin (a leather bag for carrying water), and gave her son a drink.

Hagar and her son Ishmael had been sent away from Abraham's camp and were wandering lost in the desert. Their water ran out, and Hagar, in despair, moved away so she would not have to watch the boy die. God heard the boy crying, and his angel comforted her and promised that Ishmael would become a great nation. The text says that God opened her eyes; it does not say that he created the well at that moment, and this has been understood in different ways.

Often God has already provided for us, but fear or exhaustion keep us from seeing it. Ask him to open your eyes, and trust that he hears you in your need.
exp.13:14:
It says that Abram attacked the kings who had carried off Lot during the night. He did this together with his servants, defeated them, and pursued them as far as Hobah, north of Damascus. The verse's wording about his action is explained by saying he came down on them, and the striking and defeating of them is what the verse describes. The phrase about the direction is explained by noting that the reference is to the north, since in ancient Hebrew a person facing east had the north on their left.

This is part of the account in Genesis 14. Moses, traditionally its author, tells how Abram learned that his nephew Lot had been taken captive in a war between kings. Abram gathered 318 men from his household, divided them, and attacked by surprise. The text shows that rescuing Lot was his goal.

For today: when someone in your family or community is in trouble, do not look the other way. Act with courage, wisdom, and prayer, even when your resources seem few.
exp.46:20:
The verse says that Joseph moved the people into the cities, from one end of Egypt to the other. The word "he removed" in the verse is the form used for "he did it," and "end" refers to the border or limit of the land.

We are in the middle of a terrible famine. The people, desperate, had already handed over their money and their livestock, and now they offer their land and their freedom in exchange for bread. Joseph, who governed Egypt under Pharaoh, buys everything for the king. Scholars do not agree on the reason for this relocation: some think he wanted to organize the distribution of food better, others that it strengthened Pharaoh's control over the people.

For today: crises make us vulnerable, and sometimes we give up too much. Before deciding in the midst of need, let us ask God for wisdom and seek counsel, remembering that our true security is in Him.
exp.45:20:
This verse gives the names of the sons of Benjamin, the youngest brother of Joseph. Ten names appear. In other lists in the Bible the names vary a little, and many scholars think some of them were grandsons or descendants, since in that time the word for sons could include later descendants.

The account tells how Jacob's family went down to Egypt to live near Joseph. The narrator, whom tradition identifies with Moses, lists each one to show the origin of the people of Israel. God had promised Jacob that a great nation would come from him.

For today: God does not see people as a faceless crowd, but knows each name. Today you can remember that your life matters to God, and also value the people in your family, praying for them by name.
exp.26:24:
Isaac asks the person he believes is Esau to bring him the game he has hunted. He wants to eat so that his soul, meaning his whole being, may bless his son. Jacob serves him the food and also wine, and Isaac eats and drinks.

Isaac, now old and nearly blind, is getting ready to give the family blessing to his firstborn son. But the one standing before him is Jacob, who is pretending to be Esau, encouraged by his mother Rebekah. The Bible tells the story of this deception without praising it, and later shows its painful consequences.

For today: God can carry out his plans even in the middle of our failures, but that does not make lying right. If you want something good, seek it honestly, and trust that God knows how to work without tricks.
exp.48:15:
The explanation says that the tribe of Dan will govern or do justice for its people, just like any other tribe of Israel. "Shall judge" here means to lead and to defend what is right. There is a wordplay, because "Dan" in Hebrew is related to the word for "judge."

Jacob, now an old man, speaks here, gathering his twelve sons to tell them what will come upon their descendants. Dan was the son of Bilhah, Rachel's servant. For that reason, the phrase "as one of the tribes" stresses that Dan will have a full place in Israel. Some think of Samson, who was a Danite, although the text does not say so.

For today: God gives each person a place and a responsibility, regardless of their origin. Try to act justly in your family and at work, and do not feel less because of your history.
exp.29:34:
That same day, the verse says, Laban separated out all the animals in his flock that were striped, spotted, or dark, which were exactly the ones Jacob had asked for as his wages. Laban placed them in the care of his own sons, far from Jacob. "Goats" are the he goats, and "beasts" refers to any animal in the flock.

Jacob had spent years working for Laban, his uncle and father-in-law, and he wanted to build a flock of his own. He proposed a deal: his pay would be the animals that were spotted or dark, which were few in number. Laban agreed, but he quickly acted with cunning, removing from Jacob's reach the very animals that would have been his payment.

When we make an agreement, it is good to keep it honestly, without looking for loopholes. And if someone treats us with deceit, God sees everything and can care for us just the same.
exp.9:11:
This verse says that Asshur, or a person from his line, also built Resen, a city located between Nineveh and Calah. The Bible adds that it was a great city. Old wording: the word "á" means "a", and "la cual es" means "and this is". It is not known with certainty where Resen was; there are several proposals, but none is certain. Some think "great city" refers to Resen, and others to the group of cities mentioned together.

Moses, traditionally recognized as the author of Genesis, is recording the list of the nations after the flood, called the Table of Nations. He wants to show how the peoples spread out and how powers such as Assyria and Babylon arose, which would later be important in the history of Israel.

For today: God sees and records the history of every people, even that of the great empires. Although human power may seem enormous, the Lord remains the one who governs all things. We can trust that our lives are also in his hands.
exp.23:62:
Isaac went out into the field toward evening. The word "pray" here is unusual in the original, and some translate it as "meditate" or "walk and think." When he lifted up his eyes, he saw that camels were coming.

The narrator tells of the moment when Isaac and Rebekah are about to meet. Abraham's servant had traveled far to find a wife for Isaac, and now he was returning with Rebekah. Isaac lived in the south, near the well where God had earlier cared for Hagar.

Today we can set aside a quiet moment of the day to speak with God and think about what we hope for. While Isaac was praying and meditating, God was already guiding what he was waiting for. Trusting and waiting in peace is also a way of praying.
exp.2:16:
God tells Adam that, because he listened to his wife and ate from the forbidden tree, the ground is now under a curse "for your sake," that is, because of you. Working the land to get food will now be with pain and toil, all the days of his life.

The phrase "you listened to the voice" means that he gave heed to her instead of to God.

God speaks after the disobedience of Adam and Eve. Notice that the evil falls on the ground, not directly on Adam. It is the consequence of breaking trust with God. Even so, in the verse before there is a promise: someone from the woman's offspring will defeat the serpent. Many Christians see in this a first sign of Jesus.

For today: our decisions have consequences, and sometimes we follow voices that pull us away from God. Ask yourself whom you are listening to most, and return to the word of God, where there is grace.
exp.9:21:
This verse lists the five sons of Shem, one of the three sons of Noah: Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, Lud, and Aram. The names are spelled in an older style, as in "Asshur" and "Arphaxad." They are names of people, and over time they also came to be associated with peoples and regions.

The narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, presents what is often called the Table of Nations. It shows how the earth was resettled after the flood. Here the list of Ham's line ends and the list of Shem's line begins. From this line will come Eber and, later, Abraham. Scholars debate how exactly each people should be placed, so it is wise not to claim more than the text itself says.

For today: God knows every name and every family. You are not a number to Him. Remember to thank Him, because He cares for your story and for your people, even when you cannot see the whole picture.
exp.47:21:
Jacob tells Joseph that he gives him one portion more than his brothers. He says he took it from the Amorites, a people who lived in Canaan, with his sword and his bow. The Hebrew word for "portion" can also mean a place name.

Jacob is about to die, and he has just blessed Ephraim and Manasseh, Joseph's sons. Through this, Joseph receives a double share of the inheritance. About the "sword and bow" there are several explanations: it may be figurative language, or it may refer to what his sons did at Shechem. It is not certain which is correct.

For today: God keeps his promises across the generations. We can leave our children an inheritance of faith and trust that God will stay with them.
exp.26:38:
Isaac tells Esau that his home will be in fertile lands and will receive the dew of heaven. "Dwelling" is the place where he will live, and "fatness" refers to rich and productive land. The dew represents the rain and care of God. Some translators understand the original text to say "away from" the fertile land, and so this phrase can be read as a blessing or as something harsher.

Isaac speaks here in his old age. Jacob had just received the main blessing, although Isaac had intended to give it to Esau. Esau weeps and asks for something for himself. Isaac answers with words that do not cancel what has already been given, but leave him a future with difficulties.

For today: when we do not receive what we hoped for, we can avoid bitterness. Esau was filled with hatred. Instead, we can ask God to help us trust in Him and to guard our hearts.
exp.33:22:
Here Hamor and his son Shechem speak to the men of their city. They tell them that, if everyone agrees to be circumcised like Jacob's family, the livestock, the possessions, and every animal belonging to those outsiders will become theirs. "Substance" means goods or wealth. "Consent" means to come to an agreement.

Shechem had dishonored Dinah, Jacob's daughter, and now he wanted to marry her. Hamor proposes an alliance and a mingling of peoples. With the neighbors of the city he no longer speaks of love, but of gain: he offers Jacob's wealth as the attraction. That self-interested presentation has something of manipulation in it, and the narrative does not approve of it.

For today: be wary of decisions justified by gain while the true motive is hidden. Before committing to something, ask yourself whether it is moved by truth or only by convenience. And remember that the revenge of Jacob's sons was not righteous either.
exp.23:46:
The servant recounts that he asked the young woman whose family she belonged to. She said she was the daughter of Bethuel, son of Nahor and Milcah. He explains that he then placed a ring on her face and bracelets on her hands, which were gold ornaments.

The servant of Abraham speaks before Rebekah's family. He explains how God led him to her. Abraham wanted a wife for Isaac from among his own relatives, and the servant tells every detail so they can see the hand of God.

For today: when you need direction, pray with sincerity, pay attention to how God answers, and tell of it with gratitude. Trust that He guides the steps of those who seek Him.
exp.9:12:
This verse lists some of the descendants of Mizraim, which is the Hebrew name for Egypt. "Begat" means he was the father of them, though in these lists the names sometimes stand for peoples or tribes. Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim and Naphtuhim are names of groups that are thought to have lived in northern Africa and nearby regions. The exact location of these groups is not known with complete certainty by scholars.

This is part of the genealogy of the nations in Genesis 10. The narrator, traditionally identified with Moses, shows how after the flood the sons of Noah populated the earth. Mizraim was a son of Ham. The list continues with other peoples, including the Philistines.

For today: God knows the names and origin of every people. No person is a number to Him. Today we can treat everyone with respect, remembering that we come from one common origin and that God values us.
exp.7:3:
It says that the ark stopped moving and settled on some mountains on the seventeenth day of the seventh month. "Rested" means it came to a halt and stayed firmly in place. "Ararat" is the name used in the verse above; the original text names a mountainous region in the north. No one knows for certain which exact mountain it was.

The narrator tells of the moment when the flood begins to recede. God had stopped the rain, and the waters were slowly going down. After months afloat, the ark finally comes to rest. The text marks dates carefully, showing that God carried everything out in order and did not forget Noah or those who were with him.

When you are waiting for an answer, remember that God works in his own time, even when it is slow. Noah still had to wait several more months before he could leave. Trust that God has not forgotten you, and take the next step today with patience.
exp.5:15:
God gives Noah instructions for the ark. He was to make a window and finish it a cubit (about 45 to 50 cm) from the top. The door would be in the side, and the ark would have three stories: lower, second, and third. The word translated "window" is unclear; some think it refers to an opening for light and air, others to an open strip just under the roof. It is not certain what the exact meaning is.

God is speaking, having already told Noah that a flood would come because of the great wickedness of the earth. He gives precise measurements so that the ark would serve its purpose: to save Noah, his family, and the animals. God also promises to establish his covenant with him.

For today: Noah obeyed the details without changing the plan. We can trust that God cares even for the small things when he guides us. Obeying him step by step, even when we do not understand everything, is a simple way to show faith.
exp.26:23:
Isaac, now old and nearly blind, asks the one standing before him whether he is truly his son Esau. Jacob answers "I am," and so he lies. In the verse before, "felt" means that Isaac touched him, and "hairy" means covered with hair.

Isaac suspects, because the voice sounds like Jacob's, but the hairy hands seem to belong to Esau. Jacob pretends to be his brother, following the plan of their mother Rebekah, in order to receive the father's main blessing. Earlier, God had said that the older would serve the younger (Genesis 25:23), but the Bible does not present this deception as the right way. Later, Jacob suffers the consequences.

Today we can learn that it is not wise to use lies or shortcuts to obtain something, even when we believe God has promised it. Speaking the truth, waiting, and trusting God shape our character and protect our relationships.
exp.20:2:
Here the verse says that Abraham named the son who was born to him, the one Sarah bore to him, Isaac. Some older words appear in the explanation: the word translated as "bore" means "gave birth to," and the phrase "was born to him" means that the child was born to him. It is a simple phrase, but it marks the moment when a long-awaited promise is fulfilled.

Here the narrator of the book of Genesis is speaking. God had already told Abraham that he would have a son with Sarah, and that he would be named Isaac (Genesis 17:19). The name is commonly understood to mean "he laughs" or "laughter," and it recalls that Abraham and Sarah laughed when they heard the promise because they were so old. Abraham obeys by giving him the name God indicated.

For today: God does what He says, even when it takes longer than we expect. While you wait for something He has promised you, keep obeying Him in small things, and trust that His timing is the best.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that a mist rose up from the earth and watered the whole surface of the ground. The word "mist" has also been rendered as "fog," "haze," or "spring," because the original Hebrew can be understood in several ways. What is clear is that the land received water before there was rain or farmers.

We are at the beginning of a second account of creation. The author, whom tradition attributes to Moses, makes clear that there was not yet any rain or any man to work the ground. God himself was setting the stage before forming Adam and planting the garden.

For today: God was already caring for the earth before we existed, and he continues to provide with patience and order. You can rest in the knowledge that he prepares what is needed before asking you to do your part, and you can thank him today for the provisions we usually take for granted, such as water.
exp.18:32:
This verse tells that Lot's two daughters made their father drink wine. The firstborn went in to his bed and had relations with him. Lot was so drunk that he did not notice when she lay down or when she got up. The phrase "lay with" in the verse means having sexual relations.

Lot and his daughters had just escaped the destruction of Sodom and were living isolated in a cave. The daughters thought that no man was left who could give them descendants, so they devised this plan. The Bible recounts what happened without approving of it; it shows the bad decisions that come from fear and despair.

For today: when we feel afraid or see everything as lost, let us not take crooked paths on our own. It is better to trust God and ask for His guidance, because He cares for us even in the darkest moments.
exp.4:30:
This verse says that Lamech lived a total of 777 years and then died. It closes his story within the list of Adam's descendants. The phrase "and he died" is repeated in this chapter for each person, except Enoch.

Here the speaker is not a character; it is the narrator of the book, who is recording generations. Lamech is the father of Noah, and in the previous verse he had placed his hope that Noah would bring relief from the curse on the earth. This list shows that human life went on, but also that death reached everyone. The ages given are very large, and scholars understand them in various ways.

For today: our life is short, even the longest. It is good to live with hope in God, to raise children in the faith, and to leave a good example, as Lamech did in longing for a better future for his son.
exp.36:13:
Here Jacob (also called Israel) asks his son Joseph to go and see how his brothers and the flocks are doing, and to come back with word. He sends him out from the vale of Hebron, and Joseph comes to Shechem.

Jacob speaks as an anxious father. His sons were far away, tending the flocks, and he wanted to know whether all was well. Joseph obeys willingly, answering his father readily. This journey will be the beginning of his separation from the family, though no one knew it yet. The story shows how God can work through events that seem ordinary.

For today: when a simple task comes to you, do it faithfully. We do not know where it may lead us, but God does, and He can use our obedience on paths we cannot yet see.

sum.14: God tells Abram not to be afraid, and promises him a son of his own and descendants as numerous as the stars. Abram believes, and God counts him as righteous. Then God confirms his promise with a covenant: he will give the land to Abram's descendants, though first they will spend four hundred years in a foreign land.
sum.7: God remembered Noah and all the living creatures and animals that were with him in the ark, and the waters gradually went down until the ground was dry. Noah sent out a dove, which came back with an olive leaf. Later he left the ark, and he built an altar and offered a sacrifice to God. God promised never again to curse the ground or destroy every living thing, and that the seasons would never cease.
sum.44: Joseph could no longer hold back. He revealed himself to his brothers and wept with them. He told them not to be distressed, because God had sent him ahead to save lives during the famine. Pharaoh invited the whole family to come to Egypt, and when Jacob saw the wagons, his spirit revived, and he decided to go and see his son.
sum.27: Isaac blesses Jacob and sends him to Paddan-aram to find a wife among his mother's family. On the way, Jacob dreams of a ladder that connects earth and heaven, and God renews the promise of land, descendants, and companionship. Jacob recognizes this, names the place Bethel, and vows to follow God.
sum.20: God keeps his promise: Sarah, already old, gives birth to Isaac, and Abraham circumcises him when he is eight days old. Later, Hagar and Ishmael are sent away, but God takes care of them, shows them water in the desert, and promises to make Ishmael into a great nation. At the end, Abraham makes a covenant with Abimelech at Beersheba and calls on God there.
sum.32: Jacob approaches Esau humbly, bowing down seven times, and Esau receives him with an embrace and tears. Jacob insists on giving him a gift, and afterward each of them goes on his own way. Jacob settles in Succoth and then in Shechem, where he buys a plot of land and sets up an altar to God.
sum.43: Joseph has his silver cup placed in Benjamin's sack, and then has his steward catch up with the brothers and accuse them of theft. When the cup is found, Judah offers to become a servant in Benjamin's place, so that he would not bring deep grief upon their father Jacob. In this we see a changed heart, willing to sacrifice itself for another.
sum.36: Joseph, Jacob's favorite son, is hated by his brothers because of his colorful robe and because of his dreams, in which he appears to be above them. They sell him to some merchants who take him to Egypt, and they make Jacob believe that a wild animal killed him, so Jacob mourns his son with great grief.
sum.8: God blesses Noah and his sons and permits them to eat meat, but without blood. He affirms the value of human life because we are made in his image. And with the rainbow he promises never again to destroy the earth with a flood. Afterward, Noah becomes drunk, Ham disrespects his father, and Noah pronounces a curse on Canaan and blessings on Shem and Japheth.
sum.17: The LORD visits Abraham along with three men, and he welcomes them generously. They announce that Sarah will have a son, and God asks, "Is anything too hard for the LORD?" Then God reveals to Abraham that he will judge Sodom, and Abraham intercedes with humility, asking that the city be spared if there are ten righteous people in it.
sum.24: Abraham died at the age of 175, and his sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him beside Sarah. God blessed Isaac. The twelve princes descended from Ishmael are also named. Rebekah gave birth to twins, Esau and Jacob. Esau, tired and hungry, sold his birthright to Jacob in exchange for a bowl of lentil stew, showing that he looked down on it.
sum.1: God finishes his work and blesses the seventh day as a day of rest. Then he forms the man from the dust, gives him life, and places him in the garden of Eden to take care of it, with the command not to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Seeing that the man was alone, God forms the woman, and the two are united as one flesh.
sum.39: In prison, Joseph serves two of Pharaoh's officials, the cupbearer and the baker, who are downcast because of their dreams. With God's help, Joseph announces that the cupbearer will be restored to his position and the baker will be hanged, and everything comes true within three days. However, the cupbearer forgets Joseph.
sum.23: Abraham, now an old man, made his servant swear that he would find a wife for Isaac from among Abraham's own relatives, not from the Canaanites. Trusting God to guide him through a prayer and through the kindness Rebekah showed him and his camels, the servant found her. Her family recognized that this was the work of God, and Rebekah agreed to go. Isaac received her as his wife and loved her.
sum.4: Genesis 5 traces the line of descendants from Adam to Noah, showing that each one lived many years, had children, and died. Only Enoch stands out: he walked with God, and God took him. The chapter ends with Noah, whose father hoped he would bring relief from the labor on the cursed ground, and with Noah's three sons: Shem, Ham, and Japheth.
sum.10: All of humanity spoke one language. In the land of Shinar, they decided to build a city and a tower so that they could make a name for themselves and avoid being scattered. God confused their languages and scattered them, and the place was called Babel. The chapter then follows the descendants of Shem down to Terah, whose son Abram, together with his barren wife Sarai, left Ur for Canaan, but stopped at Haran.
sum.19: Abraham told people in Gerar that Sarah was his sister, out of fear, and King Abimelech took her. God warned Abimelech in a dream, and Abimelech returned her with gifts. Abraham prayed, and God healed the king's household, showing that God cares for the innocent and protects his promises even when his servant fails.
sum.49: Joseph wept over his father Jacob and buried him with great honor in Canaan, in the cave of Machpelah. Afterward, his brothers feared that Joseph would take revenge on them, but Joseph forgave them and told them that God turned the evil into good in order to save many people. When Joseph was about to die, he asked his brothers to carry his bones to the promised land.
sum.38: Joseph was sold in Egypt to Potiphar, and God blessed him until he became the overseer of all of Potiphar's household. When Potiphar's wife pursued him, Joseph refused out of loyalty to God and to his master, but she falsely accused him, and he was sent to prison. There too God was with him and gave him favor.
sum.15: Sarai, who could not have children, gave her servant Hagar to Abram. But when Hagar became pregnant, she looked down on Sarai, and Sarai treated her harshly, so Hagar fled into the desert. There the angel of the LORD found her, told her to go back, promised her many descendants, and announced the son she would bear, Ishmael, meaning "God hears." Hagar realized that God sees her.
sum.34: God tells Jacob to go back to Bethel, and Jacob asks his household to put away their foreign gods and purify themselves so they can worship. There, God confirms his new name, Israel, and his promise. Afterward, Rachel dies in childbirth as she gives birth to Benjamin, and Isaac also dies. The twelve sons of Jacob are then listed.
sum.12: Abram returned from Egypt with Lot, and because the two of them had so much livestock, their herdsmen began to quarrel. Abram, showing generosity, let Lot choose first, and Lot picked the fertile plain near Sodom. Afterward God promised Abram all the land and descendants too many to count, and Abram worshiped God in Hebron.
sum.41: Jacob sends ten of his sons to Egypt to buy grain because of the famine. There, Joseph, who is now governor, recognizes them, tests them, and keeps Simeon imprisoned until they bring Benjamin. The brothers acknowledge their guilt over what they did to Joseph, and Jacob, deeply distressed, refuses to send Benjamin.
sum.28: Jacob arrives in Haran, meets his cousin Rachel at a well, and stays with his uncle Laban. He works seven years to earn Rachel as his wife, but Laban deceives him and gives him Leah first, so Jacob works another seven years for Rachel. God sees that Leah is not loved and gives her children: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah.
sum.11: God calls Abram to leave his country and promises to make him into a great nation and to bless all the families of the earth through him. Abram obeys and arrives in Canaan, where he worships God. Because of a famine, he goes down to Egypt, and there, out of fear, he says that Sarai is his sister; God intervenes, and Pharaoh lets them go.
sum.13: Four kings defeated the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah and carried off Lot, Abram's nephew, as a prisoner. Abram armed 318 of his trained servants, rescued Lot, and recovered everything that had been taken. Melchizedek, priest of God Most High, blessed him, and Abram gave him a tenth of everything. However, Abram refused to keep the riches offered by the king of Sodom.
sum.46: Joseph presents his family before Pharaoh, and Jacob blesses him. They settle in Goshen, the best land in Egypt. During the famine, Joseph buys money, livestock, and land from the people for Pharaoh, and the people come to depend on him for their survival. Before he dies, Jacob makes Joseph swear that he will bury him in the tomb of his ancestors.
sum.31: Jacob returns to his homeland and fears the meeting with his brother Esau, who is coming with four hundred men. He prays to God for protection, reminding God of his promises, and sends gifts ahead to calm Esau. That night he wrestles with a man until dawn. He is blessed, receives the name Israel, and is left limping.
sum.26: Isaac, now old and blind, wants to give his blessing to Esau, but Rebekah and Jacob deceive him, and Jacob receives the blessing. Esau weeps, is filled with hatred, and plans to kill Jacob, so Rebekah sends Jacob far away, to Haran. The chapter shows how deception and favoritism wound a family.
sum.37: Judah moved away from his brothers, and his sons Er and Onan died because of their wickedness, leaving Tamar a widow. Judah did not keep his promise to give her his son Shelah, so Tamar disguised herself and became pregnant by him. When Judah recognized his injustice, she gave birth to Perez and Zerah.
sum.48: Jacob gathers his twelve sons and, before he dies, speaks a blessing or prophetic word over each one. He rebukes Reuben, Simeon, and Levi, and gives special promises to Judah, from whom the ruler would come, and to Joseph. He then asks them to bury him in the cave of Machpelah, beside Abraham and Isaac, and he dies.
sum.40: Pharaoh dreams of seven fat cows being eaten by seven thin ones, and of seven full ears of grain being swallowed by seven scorched, withered ones. Joseph, giving God the credit, explains that seven years of plenty will come, followed by seven years of famine. Pharaoh appoints him governor over Egypt, and Joseph stores up grain to save the people.
sum.16: God appeared to Abram when he was ninety-nine years old. He changed his name to Abraham and promised him an everlasting covenant: many descendants, the land of Canaan, and that God would be his God. As a sign of this covenant, God commanded that every male be circumcised. God also announced that Sarah would have a son, Isaac, and Abraham obeyed that very same day.
sum.45: Jacob travels to Egypt with his whole family. At Beersheba, God promises him that he will go with him, that he will make his family into a great nation, and that he will bring him back. The chapter lists the seventy descendants who entered Egypt, and it tells of the tearful reunion with Joseph, who instructs them how to present themselves to Pharaoh so that they can settle in Goshen.
sum.25: Because of the famine, Isaac stays in Gerar, where God renews the promise he made to Abraham. Although Isaac lies out of fear, God blesses him, and even amid quarrels over the wells, God gives him room and peace. In the end, Abimelech acknowledges that God is with him.
sum.0: God creates the heavens, the earth, light, the seas, the plants, the stars, and the animals over six days, and he sees that everything is good. At the end, he creates man and woman in his own image, blesses them, and gives them the job of caring for creation. Everything God made was very good.
sum.21: God tests Abraham and asks him to offer Isaac, his only son, on the mountain. Abraham obeys and trusts that God will provide, but an angel stops him, and God provides a ram in place of the boy. God renews his promise to bless Abraham and, through his descendants, all the nations.
sum.47: Jacob, now old and ill, welcomes Joseph and formally adopts Joseph's sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, as his own. When he blesses them, he places his right hand on Ephraim, the younger, even though Joseph objects, and he says that God will make both of them great. He also reminds them that God will bring them back to the land of their fathers.
sum.5: When wickedness and violence filled the earth, God grieved and decided to bring a flood to destroy it. But Noah, a righteous man who walked with God, found favor, and God told him to build an ark to save his family and the animals. Noah obeyed everything God had commanded him.
sum.6: God tells Noah to enter the ark with his family and the animals, because He saw that Noah was righteous in his generation. After seven days, the flood covers the earth and every living thing dies, except those who were in the ark. In this way we see Noah's obedience and God's care in protecting him.
sum.35: Genesis 36 lists the descendants of Esau, who was also called Edom. Because both he and Jacob had become very wealthy, Esau moved to the hill country of Seir, where the Horites already lived. His sons became chiefs and kings in Edom, which shows that God also took care of Esau and his family.
sum.42: As the famine continued and the grain ran out, Jacob agreed to send Benjamin to Egypt, because Judah promised to take responsibility for him. The brothers took gifts and double the money with them. When Joseph saw Benjamin, he welcomed them into his house and held a feast for them. Moved with emotion, he wept in private, and then he served them all, giving Benjamin a much larger portion than the others.
sum.2: The serpent deceives the woman, and she and her husband eat the forbidden fruit. They feel shame and hide from God. God questions them, announces consequences of pain and hard labor, and promises a struggle between the woman's offspring and the serpent. He clothes them with animal skins and sends them out of the garden.
sum.33: Dinah went out to visit the women of the area, and Shechem took advantage of her and violated her. Afterward he wanted to marry her. Jacob's sons answered him with deceit: they demanded that every man in the town be circumcised. On the third day, while the men were still in pain, Simeon and Levi killed all the males and plundered the city. Jacob rebuked them for the danger they had put him in, but they showed no remorse.
sum.29: In Genesis 30, Rachel and Leah compete to have children, and several sons are born to Jacob through them and their servant women. Finally, God gives Rachel a son, Joseph. Afterward, Jacob makes an agreement with Laban about his wages in sheep, and by using peeled branches, his flock grows large. The text does not explain whether those branches had any real effect.
sum.22: Sarah died at the age of one hundred and twenty-seven in Hebron, and Abraham mourned for her and wept over her. Since he was a foreigner in that land, he negotiated with the Hittites and bought from Ephron the cave of Machpelah for four hundred shekels of silver. There he buried Sarah, and in this way he gained his first piece of property of his own in Canaan.
sum.18: Two angels arrive in Sodom, and Lot welcomes them into his home, but the men of the city want to harm them. The angels bring Lot and his family out before God destroys the cities with fire and sulfur; Lot's wife looks back and becomes a pillar of salt. God remembers Abraham and saves Lot.
sum.3: Cain and Abel each brought an offering to God. God looked with favor on Abel's offering but not on Cain's. God warned Cain that sin was crouching at his door and that he must master it, but Cain killed his brother. As punishment, Cain was made to live as a wanderer, yet even so God protected him. Seth was born, and people began to call on the name of the LORD.
sum.9: Genesis 10 lists the descendants of Noah's three sons (Shem, Ham, and Japheth) after the flood. It shows how their families spread out and formed nations, each with its own language and territory. It highlights Nimrod, a powerful hunter with cities such as Babel, and it reminds readers that all of humanity comes from Noah.
sum.30: God tells Jacob to return to his homeland, and he leaves secretly with his family and his possessions, while Rachel takes her father's household idols. Laban catches up with him, but God had already warned Laban in a dream, and the two of them make a covenant over a heap of stones. They part in peace, and God is witness between them.
